Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Saṃyuttanikāye

The Connected Collection

Sagāthāvaggaṭīkā

The Subcommentary on the Section with Verses

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

1. Saṃvaṇṇanārambhe [V 1.0001][M 1.0001] ratanattayavandanā saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa pabhavanissayavisuddhipaṭivedanatthaṃ, taṃ pana dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāsu viññūnaṃ bahumānuppādanatthaṃ, taṃ sammadeva tesaṃ uggahaṇadhāraṇādikkamaladdhabbāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbahitasukhanipphādanatthanti. Atha vā maṅgalabhāvato, sabbakiriyāsu pubbakiccabhāvato, paṇḍitehi samācaritabhāvato, āyatiṃ paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanato ca saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmakiriyāti. Atha vā ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇaṃ pūjanīyapūjāpuññavisesanibbattanatthaṃ, taṃ attano yathāladdhasampattinimittakassa kammassa balānuppadānatthaṃ, antarā ca tassa asaṃkocāpanatthaṃ, tadubhayaṃ anantarāyena aṭṭhakathāya parisamāpanatthanti idameva ca payojanaṃ ācariyena idhādhippetaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “iti me pasannamatino…pe… tassānubhāvenā”ti. Vatthuttayapūjā hi niratisayapuññakkhettasaṃbuddhiyā aparimeyyapabhāvo puññātisayoti bahuvidhantarāyepi lokasannivāse [V 1.0002] antarāyanibandhanasakalasaṃkilesaviddhaṃsanāya pahoti, bhayādiupaddavañca nivāreti. Yathāha “pūjārahe pūjayato”tiādi (dha. pa. 195; apa. thera 1.10.1), tathā “ye, bhikkhave, buddhe pasannā, agge te pasannā, agge kho pana pasannānaṃ aggo vipāko hotī”tiādi (itivu. 90).

1. At the beginning of the exposition, homage is paid to the Triple Gem in order to penetrate the origin, basis, and purity of the Dhamma to be explained. Further, this homage is intended to inspire great respect among the wise in regard to expositions of the Dhamma, ensuring that they properly learn, retain, and practice it correctly for the sake of the complete welfare and happiness of all. Alternatively, because of its auspicious nature, because it serves as a preliminary duty in all activities, because it is practiced by the wise, and because it sets an example for others to follow in the future, paying homage to the Triple Gem is performed in such expositions. Alternatively, paying homage to the Triple Gem generates the special merit of venerating what is worthy of veneration. This strengthens the kamma that is the cause of the fortune one has obtained, prevents its diminishment, and ensures the completion of the commentary without obstruction. This is precisely the purpose intended by the Teacher here, as will be stated: “Thus, with my mind full of faith… by its power.” Indeed, veneration of the Triple Gem is an excellence of merit of immeasurable power, arising from the realization of it as an unsurpassed field of merit. Even amidst the many obstacles in the world, it has the power to dispel all defilements connected with hindrances and to ward off dangers and calamities. As it is said: “For one who venerates those worthy of veneration…” (Dhp 195; Ap. Thera 1.10.1), and likewise: “Bhikkhus, those who have faith in the Buddha have faith in the supreme; for those with faith in the supreme, the result is supreme” (Iti 90).

“Buddhoti [M 1.0002] kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenapi jambudīpassa;

Dhammoti…pe…, saṅghoti…pe…, jambudīpassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.6);

“For one who proclaims ‘Buddha,’ the joy that arises in the body—truly, that joy is superior even to the whole of Jambudīpa. ‘Dhamma’… ‘Saṅgha’… truly, that joy is superior even to the whole of Jambudīpa.”

Tathā “yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11). “Araññe rukkhamūle vā…pe… bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso na hessatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.249) ca.

Likewise: “Mahānāma, on the occasion when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not assailed by lust, nor by hatred… nor by delusion…” (AN 6.10; 11.11). And: “In the forest, or at the foot of a tree… fear or terror or bristling of the hair will not arise” (SN 1.249).

Tattha yassa vatthuttayassa vandanaṃ kattukāmo, tassa guṇātisayayogasandassanatthaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādinā gāthattayamāha. Guṇātisayayogena hi vandanārahabhāvo, vandanārahe ca katā vandanā yathādhippetaṃ payojanaṃ sādhetīti. Tattha yassā desanāya saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, sā na vinayadesanā viya karuṇāppadhānā, nāpi abhidhammadesanā viya paññāppadhānā, atha kho karuṇāpaññāppadhānāti tadubhayappadhānameva tāva sammāsambuddhassa thomanaṃ kātuṃ tammūlakattā sesaratanānaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kiratīti karuṇā, paradukkhaṃ vikkhipati apanetīti attho. Atha vā kiṇātīti karuṇā, paradukkhe sati kāruṇikaṃ hiṃsati vibādhatīti attho. Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ kampanaṃ hadayakhedaṃ karotīti vā karuṇā. Atha vā kamiti sukhaṃ, taṃ rundhatīti karuṇā. Esā hi paradukkhāpanayanakāmatālakkhaṇā attasukhanirapekkhatāya kāruṇikānaṃ sukhaṃ rundhati vibandhatīti attho. Karuṇāya sītalaṃ karuṇāsītalaṃ, karuṇāsītalaṃ hadayaṃ assāti karuṇāsītalahadayo, taṃ karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.

Therein, wishing to pay homage to the Triple Gem, the author speaks three verses beginning with “with a heart cooled by compassion” to demonstrate its connection with surpassing qualities. For it is through connection with surpassing qualities that one becomes worthy of homage, and homage paid to one who is worthy fulfills the intended purpose. Now, the teaching that he wishes to expound is not, like the Vinaya teaching, chiefly concerned with compassion, nor, like the Abhidhamma teaching, chiefly concerned with wisdom; rather, it is chiefly concerned with both compassion and wisdom. Therefore, to praise the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is the root of the other jewels and thus the root of both, the phrase “with a heart cooled by compassion,” and so on, is used. Here, karuṇā (compassion) is so called because it scatters (kirati); that is, it dispels and removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, karuṇā is so called because it hurts (kiṇāti); that is, when others suffer, it afflicts or pains the compassionate one. Or, when others suffer, it causes the virtuous to tremble and makes their hearts ache; thus it is karuṇā. Alternatively, kaṃ means happiness, and karuṇā obstructs (rundhati) it. For this compassion, characterized by the desire to remove the suffering of others, obstructs the happiness of the compassionate one due to their indifference to their own happiness. ‘Cooled by compassion’ is karuṇāsītalaṃ. ‘One for whom the heart is cooled by compassion’ is karuṇāsītalahadayo. This is the sense of karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.

Tattha kiñcāpi paresaṃ hitopasaṃhārasukhādiaparihānicchanasabhāvatāya, byāpādāratīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya ca sattasantānagatasantāpavicchedanākārapavattiyā mettāmuditānampi cittasītalabhāvakāraṇatā upalabbhati, tathāpi paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattiyā parūpatāpāsahanarasā avihiṃsābhūtā [V 1.0003] karuṇāva visesena bhagavato cittassa cittapassaddhi viya sītibhāvanimittanti vuttaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Karuṇāmukhena vā mettāmuditānampi hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbā[M 1.0003].

Although loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are also found to be causes for the cooling of the mind—by their nature of wishing for others’ welfare and happiness not to decline, by their being the direct opposite of ill will and aversion, and by their functioning to cut off the torment in the mental continuums of beings—nevertheless, it is compassion in particular that is the cause of the cooling of the Blessed One’s mind, like tranquility of mind. This compassion functions by way of removing the suffering of others, its essence is being unable to endure the torment of others, and it is a state of non-harming. Thus it is said, “with a heart cooled by compassion.” Alternatively, it should be understood that loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are also implied as causes for the cooling of the heart, being mentioned by way of compassion.

Atha vā chaasādhāraṇañāṇavisesanibandhanabhūtā sātisayaṃ niravasesañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya savisayabyāpitāya mahākaruṇābhāvamupagatā karuṇāva bhagavato abhisayena hadayasītalabhāvahetūti āha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti.

Alternatively, it is compassion that is the cause of the Blessed One’s state of heart-coolness due to its abundance. This compassion has attained the state of great compassion by pervading its entire object-domain, just like the knowledge of omniscience, which is excellent, without remainder, and the basis for the six special unshared knowledges. Thus he said, “with a heart cooled by compassion.”

Atha vā satipi mettāmuditānaṃ sātisaye hadayasītibhāvanibandhanatte sakalabuddhaguṇavisesakāraṇatāya tāsampi kāraṇanti karuṇāva bhagavato “hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇa”nti vuttā. Karuṇānidānā hi sabbepi buddhaguṇā, karuṇānubhāvanibbāpiyamānasaṃsāradukkhasantāpassa hi bhagavato paradukkhāpanayanakāmatāya anekānipi asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ akilantarūpasseva niravasesabuddhakaradhammasambharaṇaniyatassa samadhigatadhammādhipateyyassa ca sannihitesupi sattasaṅghāṭasamupanītahadayūpatāpanimittesu na īsakampi cittasītibhāvassa aññathattamahosīti. Etasmiñca atthavikappe tīsupi avatthāsu bhagavato karuṇā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā.

Alternatively, even though loving-kindness and altruistic joy are excellent causes for the cooling of the heart, compassion is described as the ‘cause of the state of heart-coolness’ for the Blessed One because it is the cause of all the special qualities of a Buddha, and thus the cause of those states as well. For all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source. Indeed, for the Blessed One—whose torment of saṃsāric suffering was being extinguished by the power of compassion; who, out of a desire to remove the suffering of others, was intent on accumulating without remainder all the qualities that make a Buddha, untiringly for many incalculable aeons; and who had attained mastery over the Dhamma—there was not the slightest alteration in the coolness of his mind, even when confronted with causes of mental anguish brought on by the aggregation of beings. In this interpretation, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s compassion is included in all three periods.

Pajānātīti paññā, yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi paṭivijjhatīti attho. Paññāva ñeyyāvaraṇappahānato pakārehi dhammasabhāvajotanaṭṭhena pajjototi paññāpajjoto. Savāsanappahānato visesena hataṃ samugghāṭitaṃ vihataṃ. Paññāpajjotena vihataṃ paññāpajjotavihataṃ. Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, mohanamattameva vā tanti moho, avijjā. Sveva visayasabhāvapaṭicchādanakaraṇato andhakārasarikkhatāya tamo viyāti tamo. Paññāpajjotavihato mohatamo etassāti paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo, taṃ paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ. Sabbesampi hi khīṇāsavānaṃ satipi paññāpajjotena avijjandhakārassa vihatabhāve saddhādhimuttehi viya diṭṭhippattānaṃ sāvakehi paccekasambuddhehi ca savāsanappahānena sammāsambuddhānaṃ kilesappahānassa viseso vijjatīti sātisayena avijjāppahānena bhagavantaṃ thomento āha “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

One understands (pajānāti), thus it is wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that it penetrates things according to their own-nature in various ways. Wisdom itself is a lamp (pajjoto) because it illuminates the nature of phenomena in various ways, having abandoned the obstruction to the knowable; thus it is the ‘lamp of wisdom’ (paññāpajjoto). ‘Destroyed’ (vihataṃ) means especially struck, uprooted, because of the abandonment of the latent dispositions. ‘Destroyed by the lamp of wisdom’ is paññāpajjotavihataṃ. One is deluded (muyhati) by it, or it is deluded itself, or it is simply delusion; this is moho, ignorance (avijjā). It is like darkness (tamo) because it conceals the intrinsic nature of its object; thus it is called tamo. ‘He for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom’ is paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo. This is the sense of paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ. For although for all whose taints are destroyed the darkness of ignorance is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones’ abandonment of defilements is distinguished from that of the disciples liberated by faith, the attainers-of-view, and the Paccekabuddhas by the fact that it includes the abandonment of the latent dispositions. Therefore, praising the Blessed One for his excellent abandonment of ignorance, he says, “he for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.”

Atha vā antarena paropadesaṃ attano santāne accantaṃ avijjandhakāravigamassa nibbattitattā, tathā sabbaññutāya balesu ca vasībhāvassa samadhigatattā, parasantatiyañca dhammadesanātisayānubhāvena sammadeva tassa [M 1.0004] pavattitattā bhagavāva visesato mohatamavigamena thometabboti [V 1.0004] āha “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Imasmiñca atthavikappe “paññāpajjoto”ti padena bhagavato paṭivedhapaññā viya desanāpaññāpi sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is to be praised especially for the removal of the darkness of delusion because the complete removal of the darkness of ignorance was produced in his own continuum without another’s instruction; because he had attained mastery over omniscience and the powers; and because that same removal of ignorance occurred rightly in the continuums of others through the power of his excellent Dhamma teaching. Thus it is said, “he for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.” In this interpretation, it should be understood that the term ‘lamp of wisdom’ includes the Blessed One’s wisdom of teaching as well as his wisdom of penetration, either by way of a general designation or by the principle of single remainder.

Atha vā bhagavato ñāṇassa ñeyyapariyantikattā sakalañeyyadhammasabhāvāvabodhanasamatthena anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātena paññāpajjotena sabbañeyyadhammasabhāvacchādakassa mohandhakārassa vidhamitattā anaññasādhāraṇo bhagavato mohatamavināsoti katvā vuttaṃ “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Ettha ca mohatamavidhamanante adhigatattā anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ kāraṇūpacārena sasantāne mohatamavidhamananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhinīhārasampattiyā savāsanappahānameva hi kilesānaṃ ñeyyāvaraṇapahānanti, parasantāne pana mohatamavidhamanassa kāraṇabhāvato phalūpacārena anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “mohatamavidhamana”nti vuccatīti.

Alternatively, because the darkness of delusion, which conceals the nature of all knowable phenomena, is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom—which is called unobstructed knowledge because it is capable of awakening to the nature of all knowable phenomena and because the Blessed One’s knowledge has the knowable as its boundary—the destruction of the darkness of delusion is unique to the Blessed One. Therefore it is said, “he for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.” Here, since unobstructed knowledge is attained upon destroying the darkness of delusion, it should be understood that by a figurative expression based on the cause, unobstructed knowledge is said to destroy the darkness of delusion in one’s own continuum. For the abandonment of the obstruction to the knowable is precisely the abandonment of defilements together with their latent dispositions, accomplished through the great resolution. In the continuums of others, however, since it is the cause of the destruction of the darkness of delusion, unobstructed knowledge is called ‘the destroyer of the darkness of delusion’ by a figurative expression based on the effect.

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ avijjāsamugghātoyeveko pahānasampattivasena bhagavato thomanānimittaṃ gayhati, na pana sātisayaṃ niravasesakilesapahānanti? Tappahānavacaneneva tadekaṭṭhatāya sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghātassa jotitabhāvato. Na hi so tādiso kileso atthi, yo niravasesaavijjāppahānena na pahīyatīti.

But for what reason is the complete eradication of ignorance alone taken as a basis for praising the Blessed One in terms of the attainment of abandonment, and not the excellent and complete abandonment of all defilements? Because by the very statement of its abandonment, the complete eradication of the entire host of defilements is signified, due to their having a single foundation. For there is no defilement of such a kind that is not abandoned by the complete abandonment of ignorance.

Atha vā vijjā viya sakalakusaladhammasamuppattiyā niravasesākusaladhammanibbattiyā saṃsārappavattiyā ca avijjā padhānakāraṇanti tabbighātavacanena sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghāto vutto eva hotīti vuttaṃ “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

Alternatively, ignorance is the primary cause for the arising of all unwholesome qualities and for the continuation of saṃsāra, just as knowledge is for the arising of all wholesome qualities. Thus, by the statement of its destruction, the complete eradication of the entire host of defilements is indeed stated. Hence it was said: “he for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.”

Narā ca amarā ca narāmarā, saha narāmarehīti sanarāmaro, sanarāmaro ca so loko cāti sanarāmaraloko, tassa garūti sanarāmaralokagaru, taṃ sanarāmaralokagaruṃ. Etena devamanussānaṃ viya tadavasiṭṭhasattānampi yathārahaṃ guṇavisesāvahatāya bhagavato upakārataṃ dasseti. Na cettha padhānāppadhānabhāvo codetabbo. Añño hi saddakkamo, añño atthakkamo. Edisesu hi samāsapadesu padhānampi appadhānaṃ viya niddisīyati yathā “sarājikāya parisāyā”ti [M 1.0005] (apa. aṭṭha. 1.1.82). Kāmañcettha sattasaṅkhārokāsavasena tividho loko, garubhāvassa pana adhippetattā garukaraṇasamatthasseva sattalokassa vasena attho gahetabbo. So hi lokīyanti ettha puññapāpāni tabbipāko cāti “loko”ti vuccati. Amaraggahaṇena cettha upapattidevā adhippetā.

Humans and immortals are 'humans-and-immortals.' 'With humans and immortals' gives 'sanarāmaro.' 'The world with its humans and immortals' gives 'sanarāmaraloko.' 'A teacher to that' gives 'sanarāmaralokagaru.' To that 'teacher of the world with its humans and immortals.' By this it is shown that the Blessed One is helpful to the remaining beings according to their suitability, just as he is to devas and humans, by bringing them to attain special qualities. Here, the distinction between primary and secondary should not be raised as an issue. For the sequence of words is one thing, and the sequence of meaning is another. In such compound expressions, even a primary element may be indicated as if it were secondary, as in 'the assembly with its king.' Although the world is threefold—as the world of beings, the world of formations, and the world of space—since being a teacher is what is intended, the meaning should be taken here in terms of the world of beings, which is capable of showing reverence. For 'world' (loka) is so called because merit and demerit and their results are experienced therein. And here, by the term 'immortals,' deities by rebirth are intended.

Atha [V 1.0005] vā samūhattho loka-saddo samudāyavasena lokīyati paññāpīyatīti. Saha narehīti sanarā, sanarā ca te amarā cāti sanarāmarā, tesaṃ lokoti sanarāmaralokoti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Amara-saddena cettha visuddhidevāpi saṅgayhanti. Te hi maraṇābhāvato paramatthato amarā, narāmarānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.157). Tathā hi sabbānatthapariharaṇapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantamupakāritāya aparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya ca sabbasattuttamo bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhānaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “sanarāmaralokagaru”nti.

Alternatively, the word 'loka' has the sense of a collection, as it is regarded and designated as a multitude. 'With men' gives 'sanarā'; 'men and those immortals' gives 'sanarāmarā'; 'their world' gives 'sanarāmaraloko'—this should be connected in the same way as before. Here, the term 'immortals' also includes the devas of purity, for they are immortal in the ultimate sense due to the absence of death. The inclusion of 'men and immortals' is by way of an excellent designation, as in 'the Teacher of devas and humans.' Indeed, the Blessed One, the supreme among all beings, is the foremost object of reverence for countless beings in countless world-systems, due to his unsurpassed perfection of effort, which is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and is intent on providing complete welfare and happiness; due to his extreme helpfulness to the populace of devas and humans; and due to his being endowed with immeasurable, incomparable, powerful, and special qualities. Therefore he is called 'the teacher of the world with its humans and immortals.'

Sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato. Bhagavato hi veneyyajanupasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato sobhanaṃ, tathā lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya dutavilambitakhalitānukaḍḍhananippīḷanukkuṭikakuṭilākulatādi- dosarahitamavahasitarājahaṃsavasabhavāraṇamigarājagamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ ñāṇagamanañca vipulanimmalakaruṇāsativīriyādiguṇavisesasahitamabhinīhārato yāva mahābodhi niravajjatāya sobhanamevāti.

He is called Sugata because his going is beautiful. For the Blessed One's approach to those who are to be trained is entirely beautiful, as it brings about their welfare and happiness. So too, his bodily gait is beautiful. Because his physical body is adorned with the major and minor marks, his gait is free from such faults as being too fast, too slow, stumbling, dragging the feet, pressing down, being bent, crooked, or agitated; it surpasses the gait of a royal swan, a lordly bull, a noble elephant, or a lion. And the going of his knowledge, accompanied by special qualities such as vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, and energy, was flawless from his initial resolve all the way to his great enlightenment; thus it was truly beautiful.

Atha vā sayambhūñāṇena sakalamapi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanto ñāṇena sammā gato avagatoti sugato, tathā lokasamudayaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammataṃ āpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato, lokanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā gato adhigatoti sugato, lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā [M 1.0006] gato paṭipannoti sugato. “Sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato”tiādinā nayena (mahāni. 38) ayamattho vibhāvetabboti.

Alternatively, because with his self-originating knowledge he has correctly gone to and understood the entire world by way of the full understanding of comprehension, he is the Sugata. Likewise, because he has correctly gone beyond the origin of the world by abandoning it by way of the full understanding of abandonment, bringing it to a state of non-arising, he is the Sugata. Because he has correctly gone to and attained the cessation of the world, Nibbāna, by way of the full understanding of realization, he is the Sugata. Because he has correctly gone along and practiced the path leading to the cessation of the world by way of the full understanding of development, he is the Sugata. This meaning should be explained according to the method beginning: 'Because he does not go back to, does not return to, does not revert to those defilements that were abandoned by the path of stream-entry, he is Sugata' (Mahāni. 38).

Atha vā sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ, nibbānameva vā gato adhigatoti sugato. Yasmā vā bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ veneyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ kālayuttameva ca dhammaṃ bhāsati, tasmā sammā gadati vadatīti sugato da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Iti sobhanagamanatādīhi sugato, taṃ sugataṃ.

Alternatively, because he has gone to the beautiful place, perfect enlightenment, or has attained Nibbāna itself, he is the Sugata (Well-Gone). Or, because he speaks Dhamma that is true, factual, beneficial, and timely to those to be trained according to their suitability, he speaks rightly (sammā gadati); thus he is the Sugata (Well-Spoken), by changing the letter 'd' to 't'. Thus, because of his excellent going and so on, he is the Sugata. To that Sugata.

Puññapāpakehi upapajjanavasena gantabbato gatiyo, upapattibhavavisesā. Tā pana nirayādivasena pañcavidhā. Tā hi sakalassapi bhavagāmikammassa ariyamaggādhigamena avipākārahabhāvakaraṇena [V 1.0006] nivattitattā bhagavā pañcahipi gatīhi suṭṭhu mutto visaṃyuttoti āha “gativimutta”nti. Etena bhagavato katthacipi apariyāpannataṃ dasseti, yato bhagavā “devātidevo”ti vuccati. Tenāha –

Destinies (gati) are so called because they are destinations to be gone to by way of rebirth through merit and demerit; they are particular states of existence. These are of five kinds, such as the hells. Since all kamma leading to any state of existence has been averted by the attainment of the noble path, which renders it incapable of yielding a result, the Blessed One is well freed and dissociated from all five destinies. Thus the verse says 'liberated from destinies.' By this it is shown that the Blessed One is not included in any destiny, for which reason he is called 'the deva surpassing devas.' Therefore it is said:

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36);

“That kamma by which I might be reborn as a deva, or become a gandhabba or a bird; by which I might reach the state of a yakkha, or return to the human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, shattered, and eliminated.”

Taṃtaṃgatisaṃvattanakānañhi kammakilesānaṃ aggamaggena bodhimūleyeva suppahīnattā natthi bhagavato gatipariyāpannatāti accantameva bhagavā sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsasattanikāyehi suparimutto. Taṃ gativimuttaṃ. Vandeti namāmi, thomemīti vā attho.

For since the kamma and defilements that lead to this or that destiny were completely abandoned by the foremost path right at the root of awakening, the Blessed One is not included in any destiny. Thus the Blessed One is utterly liberated from all states of existence, wombs of rebirth, destinies, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings. To him, the one liberated from destinies. The meaning of 'I pay homage' is 'I bow down' or 'I praise'.

Atha vā gativimuttanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuppattiyā bhagavantaṃ thometi. Ettha hi dvīhi ākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā attahitasampattito parahitapaṭipattito ca. Tesu attahitasampatti anāvaraṇañāṇādhigamato, savāsanānaṃ sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ accantapahānato, anupādisesanibbānappattito ca veditabbā. Parahitapaṭipatti lābhasakkārādinirapekkhacittassa sabbadukkhaniyyānikadhammadesanato, viruddhesupi niccaṃ hitajjhāsayavasena ñāṇaparipākakālāgamanato ca. Sā panettha āsayato payogato ca duvidhā parahitapaṭipatti, tividhā [M 1.0007] ca attahitasampatti pakāsitā hoti, kathaṃ? “Karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena āsayato parahitapaṭipatti, sammāgadanatthena sugata-saddena payogato parahitapaṭipatti, “paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ gativimutta”nti etehi catusaccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugata-saddena tividhāpi attahitasampatti, avasiṭṭhatthena tena “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena ca sabbāpi attahitasampatti parahitapaṭipatti pakāsitā hotīti.

Alternatively, by 'liberated from destinies' the verse praises the Blessed One for his attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two ways: from the accomplishment of his own welfare and from his practice for the welfare of others. Of these, the accomplishment of his own welfare should be understood from his attainment of unobstructed knowledge, his utter abandonment of all defilements with their latent dispositions, and his attainment of Nibbāna without residue. The practice for the welfare of others should be understood from his teaching of the Dhamma that leads out from all suffering with a mind indifferent to gain and honor, and from the arrival of the time for the ripening of knowledge through a constant disposition for the welfare even of the hostile. Here, the practice for the welfare of others, which is twofold by way of disposition and effort, and the accomplishment of his own welfare, which is threefold, are revealed. How? By 'with a heart cooled by compassion,' the practice for the welfare of others out of disposition is revealed. By the word 'Sugata' in the sense of 'well-spoken,' the practice for the welfare of others out of effort is revealed. By 'who dispelled the mass of delusion with the lamp of wisdom' and 'liberated from destinies,' and by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of penetrating the Four Truths, the threefold accomplishment of his own welfare is revealed. And by the remaining meanings of that phrase 'who dispelled the mass of delusion with the lamp of wisdom,' all accomplishment of his own welfare and practice for the welfare of others are revealed.

Atha vā tīhi ākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā – hetuto phalato upakārato ca. Tattha hetu mahākaruṇā, sā paṭhamapadena dassitā. Phalaṃ catubbidhaṃ ñāṇasampadā pahānasampadā ānubhāvasampadā rūpakāyasampadā cāti. Tāsu ñāṇapahānasampadā dutiyapadena saccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugata-saddena pakāsitā honti, ānubhāvasampadā pana tatiyapadena, rūpakāyasampadā yathāvuttakāyagamanasobhanatthena sugata-saddena lakkhaṇānubyañjanapāripūriyā vinā tadabhāvato[V 1.0007]. Upakāro anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ karitvā tividhayānamukhena vimuttidhammadesanā. So sammāgadanatthena sugata-saddena pakāsito hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in three ways: from the cause, from the fruit, and from his helpfulness. Herein, the cause is great compassion, which is shown by the first phrase. The fruit is fourfold: the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of majesty, and the perfection of the form-body. Of these, the perfections of knowledge and abandonment are revealed by the second phrase and by the word 'Sugata' in its sense of penetrating the truths. The perfection of majesty is shown by the third phrase. The perfection of the form-body is shown by the word 'Sugata' in its sense of the beauty of his bodily gait, since this would not exist without the complete fulfillment of the major and minor marks. His helpfulness is the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation through the entrance of the three vehicles, including everyone without exception. This, it should be understood, is revealed by the word 'Sugata' in its sense of 'well-spoken'.

Tattha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ dasseti. Mahākaruṇāya sañcoditamānaso hi bhagavā saṃsārapaṅkato sattānaṃ samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhāro anupubbena pāramiyo pūretvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigatoti karuṇā sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ. “Paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena sammāsambodhiṃ dasseti. Anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ sammāsambodhīti vuccatīti. Sammāgamanatthena sugata-saddena sammāsambodhiyā paṭipattiṃ dasseti līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhallikattakilamathānuyoga-sassatucchedābhinivesādi-antadvayarahitāya karuṇāpaññāpariggahitāya majjhimāya paṭipattiyā pakāsanato sugata-saddassa. Itarehi sammāsambodhiyā padhānāppadhānabhedaṃ payojanaṃ dasseti. Saṃsāramahoghato sattasantāraṇañhettha padhānaṃ payojanaṃ, tadaññamappadhānaṃ. Tesu padhānena parahitapaṭipattiṃ dasseti, itarena attahitasampattiṃ, tadubhayena attahitāya paṭipannādīsu catūsu puggalesu bhagavato [M 1.0008] catutthapuggalabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena ca anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ, uttamavandanīyabhāvaṃ, attano ca vandanakiriyāya khettaṅgatabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Herein, by the phrase 'with a heart cooled by compassion,' the root of perfect self-enlightenment is shown. For the Blessed One, his mind impelled by great compassion, made the aspiration to rescue beings from the mire of saṃsāra and, by gradually fulfilling the perfections, attained unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. Thus compassion is the root of perfect self-enlightenment. By the phrase 'dispelling the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom,' perfect self-enlightenment is shown. For unobstructed knowledge is the proximate cause of the path knowledge, and the path knowledge, which has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, is called perfect self-enlightenment. By the word 'Sugata,' in the sense of having gone well, the practice for perfect self-enlightenment is shown, because the word 'Sugata' proclaims the middle practice, which is embraced by compassion and wisdom and is free from the two extremes, such as indulgence in sensual pleasures and devotion to self-mortification, sloth and restlessness, and clinging to views of eternalism and annihilationism. By the other terms, the distinction between the primary and secondary purpose of perfect self-enlightenment is shown. Herein, the primary purpose is the ferrying of beings across the great flood of saṃsāra; the other is secondary. Among these, by the primary, the practice for the welfare of others is shown; by the other, the attainment of one's own welfare. By both, the Blessed One's status as the fourth person among the four types of persons, such as one practicing for one's own welfare, is shown. And by that, his unsurpassed worthiness of offerings, his supreme venerability, and his being a field for one's act of veneration are shown.

Ettha ca karuṇāgahaṇena lokiyesu mahaggatabhāvappattāsādhāraṇaguṇadīpanato bhagavato sabbalokiyaguṇasampatti dassitā hoti, paññāgahaṇena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānamaggañāṇadīpanato sabbalokuttaraguṇasampatti. Tadubhayaggahaṇasiddho hi attho “sanarāmaralokagaru”ntiādinā vipañcīyatīti. Karuṇāgahaṇena ca upagamanaṃ nirupakkilesaṃ dasseti, paññāgahaṇena apagamanaṃ. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena lokasamaññānurūpaṃ bhagavato pavattiṃ dasseti lokavohāravisayattā karuṇāya, paññāgahaṇena samaññāya anatidhāvanaṃ. Sabhāvānavabodhena hi dhammānaṃ samaññaṃ atidhāvitvā sattādiparāmasanaṃ hotīti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattivihāraṃ dasseti, paññāgahaṇena tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ catusaccañāṇaṃ catupaṭisambhidāñāṇaṃ catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ, karuṇāgahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇassa gahitattā sesādhāraṇañāṇāni cha abhiññā aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇāni dasa balāni cuddasa buddhañāṇāni soḷasa ñāṇacariyā aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni sattasattati ñāṇavatthūnīti evamādīnaṃ anekesaṃ paññāpabhedānaṃ vasena ñāṇacāraṃ dasseti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena caraṇasampattiṃ, paññāgahaṇena vijjāsampattiṃ. Karuṇāgahaṇena [V 1.0008] attādhipatitā, paññāgahaṇena dhammādhipatitā. Karuṇāgahaṇena lokanāthabhāvo, paññāgahaṇena attanāthabhāvo. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena pubbakāribhāvo, paññāgahaṇena kataññutā. Karuṇāgahaṇena aparantapatā, paññāgahaṇena anattantapatā. Karuṇāgahaṇena vā buddhakaradhammasiddhi, paññāgahaṇena buddhabhāvasiddhi. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena paresaṃ tāraṇaṃ, paññāgahaṇena sayaṃ tāraṇaṃ. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena sabbasattesu anuggahacittatā, paññāgahaṇena sabbadhammesu virattacittatā dassitā hoti.

Herein, by the mention of compassion, the perfection of all the Blessed One's mundane qualities is shown by illuminating the uncommon virtues attained by those who have reached an exalted state in the world. By the mention of wisdom, the perfection of all his supramundane qualities is shown by illuminating the path knowledge that is the proximate cause of the knowledge of omniscience. The meaning established by mentioning both is elaborated in phrases such as 'honored by the world with its humans and devas.' By the mention of compassion, an undefiled approach is shown; by the mention of wisdom, the departure. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, the Blessed One’s conduct in accordance with worldly convention is shown, as compassion pertains to the sphere of worldly interaction; by the mention of wisdom, the non-transgression of convention is shown, for by not comprehending the true nature of things, one misapprehends convention, clinging to such concepts as 'a being.' Moreover, by the mention of compassion, the abiding in the attainment of great compassion is shown. By the mention of wisdom is shown the unimpeded knowledge of the three times, the knowledge of the four truths, the four analytical knowledges, and the four kinds of fearlessness. Since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included by the mention of compassion, by the mention of wisdom the range of knowledge is shown through its many divisions, such as the six higher knowledges, the unshaken knowledges in the eight assemblies, the ten powers, the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, the sixteen kinds of knowledge-conduct, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Similarly, by the mention of compassion, the perfection of conduct is shown; by the mention of wisdom, the perfection of knowledge. By the mention of compassion, sovereignty over oneself is shown; by the mention of wisdom, sovereignty of the Dhamma. By the mention of compassion, the state of being a protector of the world is shown; by the mention of wisdom, the state of being one's own protector. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, being a benefactor is shown; by the mention of wisdom, gratitude. By the mention of compassion, concern for others is shown; by the mention of wisdom, concern for oneself. Or, by the mention of compassion, the accomplishment of the qualities that make a Buddha is shown; by the mention of wisdom, the accomplishment of Buddhahood. Thus, by the mention of compassion, the ferrying of others across is shown; by the mention of wisdom, the ferrying of oneself across. Similarly, by the mention of compassion, a mind of helpfulness toward all beings is shown; by the mention of wisdom, a mind of dispassion toward all phenomena is shown.

Sabbesañca buddhaguṇānaṃ karuṇā ādi tannidānabhāvato, paññā pariyosānaṃ tato uttari karaṇīyābhāvato. Iti ādipariyosānadassanena sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena sīlakkhandhapubbaṅgamo [M 1.0009] samādhikkhandho dassito hoti. Karuṇānidānañhi sīlaṃ tato pāṇātipātādiviratippavattito, sā ca jhānattayasampayoginīti. Paññāvacanena paññākkhandho. Sīlañca sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhe, paññā pariyosānanti evampi ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇadassanena sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti nayato dassitattā. Eso eva hi niravasesato buddhaguṇānaṃ dassanupāyo, yadidaṃ nayaggahaṇaṃ, aññathā ko nāma samattho bhagavato guṇe anupadaṃ niravasesato dassetuṃ. Tenevāha –

Of all the Buddha's qualities, compassion is the beginning because it is their cause, and wisdom is the end because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all the Buddha's qualities are shown. Similarly, by the mention of compassion, the aggregate of concentration, which has the aggregate of virtue as its forerunner, is shown. For virtue has compassion as its cause, since it proceeds from abstinence from the destruction of life, etc., and that compassion is associated with the three jhānas. By the word 'wisdom,' the aggregate of wisdom is shown. And virtue is the beginning of all the Buddha's qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end. Thus, by showing them to be good in the beginning, the middle, and the end, all the Buddha's qualities are shown, as they are shown by way of method. Indeed, this alone is the way to show the Buddha's qualities completely, that is, this grasping of the method. Otherwise, who indeed would be able to point out the Blessed One's qualities completely, step by step? Therefore it is said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.425; udā. 53; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 4.5; cariyā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā, pakiṇṇakakathā; apa. 2.7.20) –

Even a Buddha might speak the praise of a Buddha for an entire eon without speaking of anything else; the eon would be exhausted in that long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Teneva ca āyasmatā sāriputtattherenapi buddaguṇaparicchedanaṃ pati anuyuttena “no hetaṃ, bhante”ti paṭikkhipitvā “api ca me, bhante, dhammanvayo vidito”ti (dī. ni. 2.146) vuttaṃ.

For this reason, when the Venerable Sāriputta was questioned about defining the limits of the Buddha's qualities, he rejected the idea, saying, 'No, venerable sir,' and then said, 'However, venerable sir, the causal sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.'

2. Evaṃ saṅkhepena sakalasabbaññuguṇehi bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni saddhammaṃ thometuṃ “buddhopī”tiādimāha. Tattha buddhoti kattuniddeso. Buddhabhāvanti kammaniddeso. Bhāvetvā sacchikatvāti [V 1.0009] ca pubbakālakiriyāniddeso. Yanti aniyamato kammaniddeso. Upagatoti aparakālakiriyāniddeso. Vandeti kiriyāniddeso. Tanti niyamanaṃ. Dhammanti vandanakiriyāya kammaniddeso. Gatamalaṃ anuttaranti ca tabbisesanaṃ.

2. Having thus briefly extolled the Blessed One with all the qualities of the Omniscient One, now, to praise the good Dhamma, he says 'buddhopī,' etc. Herein, 'buddho' is a designation of the agent. 'Buddhabhāvaṃ' is a designation of the object. 'Bhāvetvā sacchikatvā' is a designation of the prior action. 'Yaṃ' is an indefinite designation of the object. 'Upagato' is a designation of the subsequent action. 'Vandeti' is a designation of the action. 'Taṃ' is a specification. 'Dhammaṃ' is a designation of the object of the act of veneration. 'Gatamalaṃ' and 'anuttaraṃ' are its qualifiers.

Tattha buddhasaddassa tāva – “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā niddesanayena (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97) attho veditabbo. Atha vā savāsanāya aññāṇaniddāya accantavigamato, buddhiyā vā vikasitabhāvato buddhavāti buddho jāgaraṇavikasanatthavasena. Atha vā kassacipi ñeyyadhammassa anavabuddhassa abhāvena ñeyyavisesassa kammabhāvena [M 1.0010] aggahaṇato kammavacanicchāya abhāvena avagamanatthavaseneva kattuniddeso labbhatīti buddhavāti buddho yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti. Atthato pana pāramitāparibhāvito sayambhūñāṇena saha vāsanāya vihataviddhastaniravasesakileso mahākaruṇā sabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno buddho. Yathāha – “buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi. Tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192). Api-saddo sambhāvane. Tena “evaṃ guṇavisesayutto sopi nāma bhagavā”ti vakkhamānaguṇe dhamme sambhāvanaṃ dīpeti. Buddhabhāvanti sammāsambodhiṃ. Bhāvetvāti uppādetvā vaḍḍhetvā ca. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upagatoti patto, adhigatoti attho. Etassa “buddhabhāva”nti etena sambandho. Gatamalanti vigatamalaṃ, niddosanti attho. Vandeti paṇamāmi, thomemi vā. Anuttaranti uttararahitaṃ, lokuttaranti attho. Dhammanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyato saṃsārato ca apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo.

Herein, first, the meaning of the word 'Buddha' should be understood according to the explanation: 'Because he has understood the truths, he is a Buddha; because he awakens the people, he is a Buddha,' and so on. Or, because of the final departure from the sleep of ignorance together with its latent tendencies, or because his wisdom has blossomed, he is called 'Buddha,' in the sense of 'awakening' and 'blossoming.' Or, because there is no knowable phenomenon whatsoever that has not been understood, and thus no specific knowable is taken as an object, and because there is no need for a word in the objective case, the designation of agent is obtained purely in the sense of 'understanding.' Thus he is 'Buddha,' just as in the expression 'the initiated one does not give.' In essence, a Buddha is a continuum of aggregates whose defilements have been completely struck down and destroyed together with their latent tendencies by self-originated knowledge matured by the perfections, and who is the repository for the host of immeasurable qualities such as great compassion and the knowledge of omniscience. As it is said: 'The Blessed One is called 'Buddha' because he is self-originated, without a teacher, having by himself awakened to the truths among things unheard of before. Therein, he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.' The word 'api' is in the sense of esteem. Thus, regarding the Dhamma with the qualities to be stated, it shows high regard, as if to say: 'Even the Blessed One, who is endowed with such special qualities...' 'Buddhabhāvaṃ' means perfect self-enlightenment. 'Bhāvetvā' means having developed and cultivated it. 'Sacchikatvā' means having realized it directly. 'Upagato' means 'attained'; 'adhigato' has the same meaning. This is connected with 'buddhabhāvaṃ.' 'Gatamalaṃ' means 'stain-free,' that is, 'faultless.' 'Vandeti' means 'I pay homage' or 'I praise.' 'Anuttaraṃ' means 'without a superior,' that is, 'supramundane.' 'Dhamma' is so called because it upholds those who practice in accordance with what has been taught, preventing them from falling into the planes of misery and into saṃsāra.

Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – evaṃ vividhaguṇagaṇasamannāgato buddhopi bhagavā yaṃ ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā phalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ pana dhammaṃ sacchikatvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigato, tametaṃ buddhānampi buddhabhāvahetubhūtaṃ sabbadosamalarahitaṃ attano uttaritarābhāvena anuttaraṃ paṭivedhasaddhammaṃ namāmīti. Pariyattisaddhammassapi tappakāsanattā idha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā “abhidhammanayasamuddaṃ adhigacchi, tīṇi piṭakāni sammasī”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā pariyattidhammassapi sacchikiriyasammasanapariyāyo labbhatīti sopi idha vutto evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here is the brief meaning: Thus, endowed with such a collection of diverse virtues, the Blessed One, the Buddha, having developed the Dhamma designated as the Noble Path and having realized the Dhamma designated as the fruit and Nibbāna, attained unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. I pay homage to that very Dhamma of penetration, which is the cause of Buddhahood even for Buddhas, free from all faults and stains, and unsurpassed because there is nothing superior to it. The inclusion of the scriptural Dhamma should also be understood here, as it serves to illuminate it. Alternatively, since it is said in the commentary, “He reached the ocean of the Abhidhamma method and comprehended the three Piṭakas,” a method of realization and comprehension is obtained even for the scriptural Dhamma; thus it should be understood that this too is spoken of here.

Tathā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā sacchikatvā”ti ca vuttattā buddhakaradhammabhūtāhi pāramitāhi saha [V 1.0010] pubbabhāge adhisīlasikkhādayopi idha dhamma-saddena saṅgahitāti veditabbaṃ. Tāpi hi malapaṭipakkhatāya gatamalā anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttarā cāti. Tathā hi sattānaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthāya katamahābhinīhāro mahākaruṇādhivāsapesalajjhāsayo paññāvisesaparidhotanimmalānaṃ dānadamasaññamādīnaṃ uttamadhammānaṃ [M 1.0011] satasahassādhikāni kappānaṃ cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ niravasesānaṃ bhāvanāpaccakkhakaraṇehi kammādīsu adhigatavasibhāvo acchariyācinteyyamahānubhāvo adhisīlādhicittānaṃ paramukkaṃsapāramippatto bhagavā paccayākāre catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pesetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti.

Similarly, it should be understood that because it is said, “having developed and realized that Dhamma,” the trainings in the preliminary stage such as the training in higher virtue are also included here by the term “Dhamma,” along with the perfections, which are the Buddha-making qualities. These too, being the antidotes to stains, are “stainless,” and due to their unique nature, they are “unsurpassed.” For indeed, the Blessed One—who made the great resolve for the sake of the liberation of beings from all the suffering of the round of existence, and possessed an amiable disposition grounded in great compassion—for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand more, diligently, continuously, and completely developed and directly realized the supreme qualities such as giving, self-control, and restraint, which are stainless, being purified by special wisdom. Having thereby achieved mastery over actions and so on, endowed with marvelous and inconceivable great power, and having attained the supreme excellence of perfection in higher virtue and higher mind, the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment by directing the great diamond-like wisdom through the twenty-four hundred thousand koṭi openings of the conditional relations.

Ettha ca “bhāvetvā”ti etena vijjāsampadāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti etena vimuttisampadāya. Tathā paṭhamena jhānasampadāya, dutiyena vimokkhasampadāya. Paṭhamena vā samādhisampadāya, dutiyena samāpattisampadāya. Atha vā paṭhamena khayeñāṇabhāvena, dutiyena anuppādeñāṇabhāvena. Purimena vā vijjūpamatāya, dutiyena vajirupamatāya. Purimena vā virāgasampattiyā, dutiyena nirodhasampattiyā. Tathā paṭhamena niyyānabhāvena, dutiyena nissaraṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā hetubhāvena, dutiyena asaṅkhatabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā dassanabhāvena, dutiyena vivekabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā adhipatibhāvena, dutiyena amatabhāvena dhammaṃ thometi. Atha vā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā buddhabhāvaṃ upagato”ti etena svākkhātatāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti etena sandiṭṭhikatāya. Tathā purimena akālikatāya, pacchimena ehipassikatāya. Purimena vā opaneyyikatāya, pacchimena paccattaṃ veditabbatāya dhammaṃ thometi. “Gatamala”nti iminā saṃkilesābhāvadīpanena dhammassa parisuddhataṃ dasseti. “Anuttara”nti etena aññassa visiṭṭhassa abhāvadīpanena vipulaparipuṇṇataṃ. Paṭhamena vā pahānasampadaṃ dhammassa dasseti, dutiyena sabhāvasampadaṃ. Bhāvetabbatāya vā dhammassa gatamalabhāvo yojetabbo. Bhāvanābalena hi so dosānaṃ samugghātako hotīti. Sacchikātabbabhāvena anuttarabhāvo yojetabbo. Sacchikiriyānibbattito hi tatuttarikaraṇīyābhāvato anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttaroti. Tathā “bhāvetvā”ti etena saha pubbabhāgasīlādīhi sekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā honti. “Sacchikatvā”ti etena saha asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā asekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā hontīti.

Here, by “having developed” he praises the Dhamma for its accomplishment in knowledge; by “having realized,” for its accomplishment in liberation. Similarly, by the first for the accomplishment in jhāna, by the second for the accomplishment in deliverance. Or by the first for the accomplishment in concentration, by the second for the accomplishment in attainment. Or by the first for its nature as knowledge of destruction, by the second for its nature as knowledge of non-arising. Or by the first for its likeness to lightning, by the second for its likeness to a diamond. Or by the first for the attainment of dispassion, by the second for the attainment of cessation. Similarly, by the first for its nature as an escape, by the second for its nature as release. Or by the first for its nature as a cause, by the second for its nature as the unconditioned. Or by the first for its nature as vision, by the second for its nature as seclusion. Or by the first for its nature as a dominant condition, by the second for its nature as the deathless. Alternatively, by “having developed the Dhamma and attained Buddhahood,” he praises the Dhamma for being well-proclaimed; by “having realized,” for being directly visible. Similarly, by the first for being timeless, by the second for inviting one to come and see. Or by the first for leading inwards, by the second for being personally experienceable by the wise. By “stainless,” he shows the purity of the Dhamma by indicating the absence of defilements. By “unsurpassed,” he shows its vastness and completeness by indicating the absence of anything more excellent. Or, by the first he shows the Dhamma’s accomplishment in abandoning; by the second, its accomplishment in its intrinsic nature. The quality of being stainless should be connected with the Dhamma’s being something to be developed, for by the power of development it eradicates defilements. The quality of being unsurpassed should be connected with its being something to be realized, for having arisen from realization, it is unsurpassed because there is nothing further to be done and because it is unique. Similarly, by “having developed,” the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of one in training are shown, along with the preliminary practices such as virtue. By “having realized,” the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training are shown, along with the unconditioned element.

3. Evaṃ saṅkhepeneva sabbadhammaguṇehi saddhammaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni ariyasaṅghaṃ thometuṃ “sugatassā”tiādimāha. Tattha sugatassāti sambandhaniddeso[M 1.0012]. Tassa “puttāna”nti etena sambandho[V 1.0011]. Orasānanti puttavisesanaṃ. Mārasenamathanānanti orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaniddeso. Tena kilesapahānameva bhagavato orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaṃ anujānātīti dasseti. Aṭṭhannanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Tena ca satipi tesaṃ sattavisesabhāvena anekasahassasaṅkhābhāve imaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ nātivattantīti dasseti maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvānativattanato. Samūhanti samudāyaniddeso. Ariyasaṅghanti guṇavisiṭṭhasaṅghātabhāvaniddeso. Tena asatipi ariyapuggalānaṃ kāyasāmaggiyaṃ ariyasaṅghabhāvaṃ dasseti diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvato.

3. Having thus briefly praised the true Dhamma with all its qualities, now, to praise the noble Sangha, he states the words beginning “Of the Well-Gone One.” Herein, “of the Well-Gone One” is an indication of connection. Its connection is with “sons.” “True-born” is a qualifier of the sons. “Crushers of Māra’s army” is an indication of the reason for their being true-born sons. By this he shows that the very abandonment of the defilements is the reason one is authorized as a true-born son of the Blessed One. “Eight” is an indication of numerical delimitation. And by this he shows that although they may number many thousands because they are special beings, they do not go beyond this numerical delimitation, because they do not go beyond the states of being established in the path and established in the fruit. “Group” is an indication of a collection. “Noble Sangha” is an indication of their state as a community distinguished by its qualities. By this he shows that the state of being the noble Sangha exists even when there is no physical gathering of the noble individuals, because they are united by their commonality in view and virtue.

Tattha urasi bhavā jātā saṃbaddhā ca orasā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ orasaputtā attajātatāya pitu santakassa dāyajjassa visesena bhāgino honti, evametepi ariyapuggalā sammāsambuddhassa dhammassavanante ariyāya jātiyā jātatāya bhagavato santakassa vimuttisukhassa ariyadhammaratanassa ca ekantabhāginoti orasā viya orasā. Atha vā bhagavato dhammadesanānubhāveneva ariyabhūmiṃ okkamamānā okkantā ca ariyasāvakā bhagavato urena vāyāmajanitābhijātitāya nippariyāyena orasā puttāti vattabbataṃ arahanti. Sāvakehi pavattiyamānāpi hi dhammadesanā “bhagavato dhammadesanā”icceva vuccati tammūlikattā lakkhaṇādivisesābhāvato ca.

Herein, they are true-born (orasā) because they are born (bhavā), produced (jātā), and connected from the breast (urasi). For just as the true-born sons of beings, being born from their father’s own body, are special heirs to their father’s property, so too these noble individuals, having been born with the noble birth upon hearing the Dhamma from the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, are the sole heirs to the Blessed One’s property, the happiness of liberation and the jewel of the noble Dhamma. Thus they are true-born like true-born sons. Alternatively, the noble disciples who are entering and have entered the noble plane solely through the power of the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching deserve to be called, in the primary sense, true-born sons, since they are born from the Blessed One’s breast, as it were, generated by his utterance. For even a Dhamma teaching set in motion by the disciples is called “the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching” because it is rooted in him and because there is no difference in its essential characteristics.

Yadipi ariyasāvakānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamasamaye bhagavato viya tadantarāyakaraṇatthaṃ devaputtamāro, māravāhinī vā na ekantena apasādeti, tehi pana apasādetabbatāya kāraṇe vimathite tepi vimathitā eva nāma hontīti āha “mārasenamathanāna”nti. Imasmiṃ panatthe “māramārasenamathanāna”nti vattabbe mārasenamathanānanti ekadesasarūpekaseso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā khandhābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ viya devaputtamārassapi guṇamāraṇe sahāyabhāvūpagamanato kilesabalakāyo “senā”ti vuccati. Yathāha “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādi (su. ni. 438). Sā ca tehi diyaḍḍhasahassabhedā, anantabhedā vā kilesavāhinī satidhammavicayavīriyasamathādiguṇapaharaṇehi odhiso vimathitā [M 1.0013] vihatā viddhastā cāti mārasenamathanā, ariyasāvakā. Etena tesaṃ bhagavato anujātaputtataṃ dasseti.

Although at the time noble disciples attain the noble path, the devaputta Māra or Māra’s army does not necessarily assail them to create an obstacle, as they did for the Blessed One, still, when the cause that could be assailed by them is crushed, they too are indeed crushed. Hence it is said, “crushers of Māra’s army.” In this sense, it should be understood that while what should have been said is “crushers of Māra and Māra’s army,” the expression “crushers of Māra’s army” is used as a case of partial inclusion. Alternatively, just as with the aggregates-Māra and the formations-Māra, so too the devaputta-Māra becomes an ally in the killing of virtue, and thus the host of the force of defilements is called the “army.” As it is said: “Sensual pleasures are your first army,” etc. (Snp 438). And that army of defilements, with its one and a half thousand or infinite divisions, is crushed, struck down, and routed part by part by the noble disciples with the weapons of such qualities as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, and tranquility. Thus they are “crushers of Māra’s army.” By this is shown their status as the Blessed One’s faithful offspring.

Ārakattā kilesehi, anaye na iriyanato, aye ca iriyanato ariyā niruttinayena. Atha vā sadevakena lokena saraṇanti araṇīyato upagantabbato, upagatānañca tadatthasiddhito ariyā. Ariyānaṃ saṅghoti ariyasaṅgho. Ariyo ca so saṅgho cāti vā ariyasaṅgho. Bhagavato [V 1.0012] aparabhāge buddhadhammaratanānampi samadhigamo saṅgharatanādhīnoti assa ariyasaṅghassa bahūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ idheva “sirasā vande”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By way of etymology, they are noble (ariyā) because they are far (ārakā) from the defilements, because they do not fare (iriyanato) wrongly (anaye), and because they fare (iriyanato) rightly (aye). Alternatively, they are noble because they are to be gone to (araṇīya) as a refuge by the world with its gods, that is, they are to be approached, and because the goal of those who have approached them is accomplished. The noble Sangha is the Sangha of the noble ones; or, it is the noble Sangha because it is noble and it is a Sangha. It should be understood that the words “I revere with my head” are stated here in order to show the great helpfulness of this noble Sangha, for in the period after the Blessed One, the attainment of even the Buddha and Dhamma gems is dependent on the Sangha gem.

Ettha ca “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti, “mārasenamathanāna”nti etena pahānasampadaṃ sakalasaṃkilesapahānadīpanato, “aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena ñāṇasampadaṃ maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvadīpanato. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti etena pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti sabbasaṅghānaṃ aggabhāvadīpanato. Atha vā sugatassa orasānaṃ puttānanti ariyasaṅghassa visuddhanissayabhāvadīpanaṃ. Mārasenamathanānanti sammāujuñāyasāmīcippaṭipannabhāvadīpanaṃ. Aṭṭhannampi samūhanti āhuneyyādibhāvadīpanaṃ. Ariyasaṅghanti anuttarapuññakhettabhāvadīpanaṃ. Tathā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa lokuttarasaraṇagamanasabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanena hi te bhagavato orasaputtā jātā. “Mārasenamathanāna”nti etena abhinīhārasampadāya siddhaṃ pubbabhāge sammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Katābhinīhārā hi sammāpaṭipannā māraṃ māraparisaṃ vā abhivijinanti. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena paṭividdhastavipakkhe sekkhāsekkhadhamme dasseti puggalādhiṭṭhānena maggaphaladhammānaṃ pakāsitattā. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ dasseti. Saraṇagamanañca sāvakānaṃ sabbaguṇānaṃ ādi, sapubbabhāgapaṭipadā sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo majjhe, asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo pariyosānanti ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā saṅkhepato sabbe ariyasaṅghaguṇā pakāsitā honti.

Herein, by 'the legitimate sons of the Sugata,' it shows the Noble Sangha’s excellence of origin. By 'the crushers of Māra’s army,' it shows the excellence of abandonment, by indicating the abandonment of all defilements. By 'the community of the eight,' it shows the excellence of knowledge, by indicating the state of being established in the path and fruit. By 'the Noble Sangha,' it shows the excellence of origin, by indicating its preeminence among all Sanghas. Alternatively, 'the legitimate sons of the Sugata' indicates the Noble Sangha’s state of having a pure foundation. 'The crushers of Māra’s army' indicates the state of having practiced rightly, directly, methodically, and properly. 'The community of the eight' indicates their state of being worthy of gifts and so on. 'The Noble Sangha' indicates their state as an unsurpassed field of merit. Thus, by 'the legitimate sons of the Sugata,' it clarifies the Noble Sangha’s nature of having gone to the supramundane refuge. For it is by going to the supramundane refuge that they are born as the Blessed One’s legitimate sons. By 'the crushers of Māra’s army,' it shows the right practice in the preliminary stage, accomplished through the perfection of their aspiration. For those who have made the aspiration and practice rightly conquer Māra and his host. By 'the community of the eight,' it shows the qualities of trainees and adepts who have penetrated the truth and abandoned its opposites, since the qualities of the path and fruit are declared with individuals as their basis. By 'the Noble Sangha,' it shows their state as the foremost recipients of offerings. The going for refuge is the beginning of all the disciples’ virtues; the practice of the trainees with its preliminary part—the aggregates of virtue and so on—is the middle; the aggregates of virtue and so on of the adepts are the conclusion. Thus, in brief, all the qualities of the Noble Sangha are declared as good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.

4. Evaṃ gāthāttayena saṅkhepato sakalaguṇasaṃkittanamukhena ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni taṃ nipaccakāraṃ yathādhippete payojane pariṇāmento [M 1.0014] “iti me”tiādimāha. Tattha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, buddhadhammasaṅghā. Tesañhi “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā yathābhūtaguṇe āvajjentassa amatādhigamahetubhūtaṃ anappakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjati. Yathāha –

4. Thus, having with these three stanzas briefly paid homage to the Triple Gem by way of proclaiming all its qualities, now directing that reverence toward its intended purpose, he says, 'Thus by me,' etc. Herein, 'gem' (ratana) has the meaning of generating delight—namely, the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For when one adverts to their qualities as they really are, beginning with 'The Blessed One is such…,' abundant joy and gladness arise, which become a cause for the attainment of the Deathless. As it is said:

“Yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgataṃ ārabbha. Ujugatacitto kho pana, mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

“Mahānāma, on an occasion when a noble disciple is recollecting the Tathāgata, his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, not obsessed by delusion. On that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Tathāgata. A noble disciple whose mind is straight, Mahānāma, gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is gladdened, rapture is born in him,” and so on.

Cittīkatādibhāvo [V 1.0013] vā ratanaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Alternatively, the meaning of 'gem' is the state of being prized, and so on. For it has been said:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; su. ni. aṭṭha. 226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50) –

“Prized and of great value, incomparable, difficult to see, for the use of superior beings—for that reason it is called a gem.”

Cittīkatabhāvādayo ca anaññasādhāraṇā buddhādīsu eva labbhantīti.

And the state of being prized and so on are qualities not shared by others, found only in the Buddha and so on.

Vandanāva vandanāmayaṃ yathā “dānamayaṃ sīlamaya”nti. Vandanā cettha kāyavācācittehi tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaninnatā, thomanā vā. Pujjabhavaphalanibbattanato puññaṃ, attano santānaṃ punātīti vā. Suvihatantarāyoti. Suṭṭhu vihatantarāyo. Etena attano pasādasampattiyā, ratanattayassa ca khettabhāvasampattiyā taṃ puññaṃ atthappakāsanassa upaghātakaupaddavānaṃ vihanane samatthanti dasseti. Hutvāti pubbakālakiriyā. Tassa “atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena sambandho. Tassāti yaṃ ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ, tassa. Ānubhāvenāti balena.

'Consisting of veneration' (vandanāmayaṃ) is veneration itself, just as in 'consisting of giving' and 'consisting of virtue.' Here, veneration is the inclination of body, speech, and mind toward the qualities of the Three Gems, or it is praise. It is 'merit' (puñña) because it generates the fruit of a worshipful state, or because it purifies (punāti) one’s own continuity. 'Having well-removed obstacles': the obstacles are well removed. By this it is shown that this merit—through the accomplishment of one’s own confidence and the accomplishment of the Triple Gem’s state as a field—is capable of removing the destructive dangers that obstruct the explanation of the meaning. 'Having done so' (hutvā) is a past participle. It is connected with 'I will explain the meaning.' 'Of that' means of that merit consisting of veneration for the Triple Gem. 'By the power of' means by the strength.

5. Evaṃ ratanattayassa nipaccakāre payojanaṃ dassetvā idāni yassā dhammadesanāya atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmo, tassā tāva guṇābhitthavanavasena upaññāpanatthaṃ “saṃyuttavaggapaṭimaṇḍitassā”tiādi vuttaṃ, devatāsaṃyuttādisaṃyuttehi ceva naḷavaggādivaggehi ca vibhūsitassāti attho. Tattha [M 1.0015] “saṃyutta”nti “saṃyogo”ti ca atthato ekaṃ. Kesaṃ saṃyuttaṃ? Suttavaggānaṃ. Yathā hi byañjanasamudāyo padaṃ, evaṃ atthesu ca katāvadhiko padasamudāyo vākyaṃ, vākyasamudāyo suttaṃ, suttasamudāye vaggoti samaññā, tathā suttavaggasamudāye saṃyuttasamaññā. Saṃyujjantīti ettha suttavaggāti saṃyuttaṃ. Yadipi avayavavinimutto samudāyo nāma paramatthato natthi, avayave eva taṃtaṃsannivesavisiṭṭhe upādāya padādisamaññā viya suttavaggasamaññā saṃyuttasamaññā āgamasamaññā ca, tathāpi paramatthato avijjamānopi samudāyo buddhiparikappitarūpena vijjamāno viya gayhamāno avayavānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvena voharīyati yathā “rukkhe sākhā”ti, tasmā vuttaṃ “saṃyuttavaggapaṭimaṇḍitassā”ti.

5. Having thus shown the purpose of reverence for the Triple Gem, now, wishing to comment on the meaning of that Dhamma teaching, first, to introduce it by way of extolling its qualities, it is said, 'adorned with connected divisions,' etc., meaning that it is embellished with the Devatāsaṃyutta and other connected collections, as well as the Naḷavagga and other divisions. Herein, 'connected' (saṃyutta) and 'connection' (saṃyoga) are one in meaning. Connected to what? To the divisions of suttas. Just as a collection of syllables is a word, a collection of words with a defined meaning is a sentence, a collection of sentences is a sutta, and a collection of suttas is designated a 'division' (vagga), so a collection of sutta divisions is designated a 'connected collection' (saṃyutta). Here, the sutta divisions are connected (saṃyujjanti); thus it is a 'connected collection' (saṃyutta). Although, in an ultimate sense, a collection separate from its parts does not exist—just as designations like 'word,' etc., exist dependent on the specific arrangement of constituents, so too do the designations 'sutta division,' 'connected collection,' and 'scriptural collection' (āgama)—nevertheless, a collection, though not ultimately existent, is treated as if it exists, being grasped as a mental construct, and serves as a basis for its parts, just as one says, 'branches on a tree.' Therefore, it is said, 'adorned with connected divisions.'

Nanu saṃyuttavaggo eva āgamo, tassa pana kehi maṇḍananti? Na codetabbametaṃ. Bhavati hi abhinnepi vatthusmiṃ yathādhippetavisesāvabodhanato bhedakasamudācāro yathā “silāputtakassa [V 1.0014] sarīra”nti. Āgamissanti ettha, etena, etasmā vā attatthaparatthādayoti āgamo, ādikalyāṇādiguṇasampattiyā uttamaṭṭhena taṃtaṃabhipatthitasamiddhihetutāya paṇḍitehi varitabbato varo, āgamo ca so varo cāti āgamavaro. Āgamasammatehi vā varoti āgamavaro, saṃyutto ca so āgamavaro cāti saṃyuttāgamavaro, tassa. Buddhānaṃ anubuddhā buddhānubuddhā, buddhānaṃ saccapaṭivedhaṃ anugamma paṭividdhasaccā aggasāvakādayo ariyā. Tehi atthasaṃvaṇṇanāguṇasaṃvaṇṇanānaṃ vasena saṃvaṇṇitassa.

But is not the division of the Saṃyutta itself the scriptural collection? By what, then, is it adorned? This objection should not be raised. For even with an undivided object, a distinguishing expression is used to convey a specific intended meaning, as in 'the body of a stone doll.' 'Scriptural collection' (āgama) is so called because one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, etc., 'come' (āgacchanti) to it, by it, or from it. It is 'excellent' (vara) because it possesses the accomplishment of qualities such as being good in the beginning, and because, in the highest sense, it is the cause for the fulfillment of various aspirations, it should be 'chosen' (varitabba) by the wise. It is a scriptural collection and it is excellent, thus it is an 'excellent scriptural collection' (āgamavaro). Or, it is excellent as agreed upon by the scriptural collections, thus it is an 'excellent scriptural collection.' It is connected and it is an excellent scriptural collection, thus it is the 'Connected and Excellent Scriptural Collection' (saṃyuttāgamavaro), of which... 'By those awakened after the Buddha' (buddhānubuddha): this refers to the noble ones, such as the chief disciples, who penetrated the truths by following the Buddha’s penetration of the truths. 'Explained by them' means explained by way of commenting on its meaning and commenting on its qualities.

Atha vā buddhā ca anubuddhā ca buddhānubuddhāti yojetabbaṃ. Sammāsambuddheneva hi vinayasuttaabhidhammānaṃ pakiṇṇakadesanādivasena yo paṭhamaṃ attho vibhatto, so eva pacchā tesaṃ atthavaṇṇanāvasena saṅgītikārehi saṅgahaṃ āropitoti. Ettha ca saṃyuttānaṃ vaggā samūhāti saṃyuttavaggā, sagāthāvaggādayo. Tappariyāpannatāya saṃyuttesu vaggā saṃyuttavaggā, naḷavaggādayo. Saṃyuttāva vaggā saṃyuttavaggā. Tividhepi te ekasesanayena gahetvā vuttaṃ “saṃyuttavaggapaṭimaṇḍitassā”ti.

Alternatively, 'the Buddha and those awakened after' should be construed as buddhānubuddhā. For the meaning that was first analyzed by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One himself by way of miscellaneous discourses on the Vinaya, Suttas, and Abhidhamma, was later compiled by the Reciters by way of a commentary on their meaning. Here, 'divisions of the Saṃyutta' (saṃyuttavagga) can mean: (1) the divisions that are collections of Saṃyuttas, such as the Sagāthāvagga; (2) the divisions within the Saṃyuttas, such as the Naḷavagga, because they are included in them; and (3) the Saṃyuttas themselves as divisions. Taking all three by the principle of ellipsis, it is said, 'adorned with the divisions of the Saṃyutta.'

Tattha sagāthāvagge tāva ekādasa saṃyuttāni aṭṭhatiṃsa vaggā. Nidānavagge nava saṃyuttāni ekūnacattālīsa vaggā. Khandhavagge ekādasa saṃyuttāni [M 1.0016] ekūnasaṭṭhi vaggā. Saḷāyatanavagge nava saṃyuttāni aṭṭhatiṃsa vaggā. Mahāvagge dvādasa saṃyuttāni aṭṭhacattālīsa vaggā. Idamettha saṃyuttantaravaggānaṃ parimāṇaṃ.

id

Ñāṇappabhedajananassāti paṭiccasamuppādakhandhāyatanādikathābahulatāya gambhīrañāṇacariyāvibhāvanato paññāvibhāgasamuppādakassa. Idha pana “paññāppabhedajananassā”ti svāyamāgamo thomito, saṃvaṇṇanāsu cāyaṃ ācariyassa pakati, yadidaṃ taṃtaṃsaṃvaṇṇanānaṃ ādito tassa tassa saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa visesaguṇakittanena thomanā. Tathā hi sumaṅgalavilāsinīpapañcasūdanīmanorathapūraṇīaṭṭhasālinīādīsu ca yathākkamaṃ “saddhāvahaguṇassa, paravādamathanassa, dhammakathikapuṅgavānaṃ vicittapaṭibhānajananassa, tassa gambhīrañāṇehi ogāḷhassa abhiṇhaso nānānayavicittassa abhidhammassā”tiādinā thomanā katā.

id

6. Attho kathīyati etāyāti atthakathā, atthakathāva aṭṭhakathā ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā yathā “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho”ti. Āditoti ādimhi paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ. Chaḷabhiññatāya paramena cittavasibhāvena samannāgatattā jhānādīsu pañcavidhavasitāsambhāvato ca vasino, therā mahākassapādayo[V 1.0015]. Tesaṃ satehi pañcahi. Yāti yā aṭṭhakathā. Saṅgītāti atthaṃ kathetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne “ayaṃ etassa attho, ayaṃ etassa attho”ti saṅgahetvā vuttā. Anusaṅgītā ca yasattherādīhi pacchāpi dutiyatatiyasaṅgītīsu. Iminā attano saṃvaṇṇanāya āgamanavisuddhiṃ dasseti.

6. id

7. Sīhassa lānato gahaṇato sīhaḷo, sīhakumāro, tabbaṃsajātatāya tambapaṇṇidīpe khattiyā, tesaṃ nivāsatāya tambapaṇṇidīpassa ca sīhaḷabhāvo veditabbo. Ābhatāti jambudīpato ānītā. Athāti pacchā. Aparabhāge hi nikāyantaraladdhīhi asaṅkaratthaṃ sīhaḷabhāsāya aṭṭhakathā ṭhapitāti. Tena mūlaṭṭhakathā sabbasādhāraṇā na hotīti idaṃ atthappakāsanaṃ ekantena karaṇīyanti dasseti. Tenevāha “dīpavāsīnamatthāyā”ti. Ettha dīpavāsīnanti jambudīpavāsīnaṃ, sīhaḷadīpavāsīnaṃ vā atthāya sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapitāti yojanā.

7. id

8. Apanetvāti [M 1.0017] kañcukasadisaṃ sīhaḷabhāsaṃ apanetvā. Tatoti aṭṭhakathāto. Ahanti attānaṃ niddisati. Manoramaṃ bhāsanti māgadhabhāsaṃ. Sā hi sabhāvaniruttibhūtā paṇḍitamanaṃ ramayati. Tenevāha “tantinayānucchavika”nti, pāḷigatiyā anulomikaṃ pāḷichāyānuvidhāyininti attho. Vigatadosanti asabhāvaniruttibhāsantararahitaṃ.

8. id

9. Samayaṃ avilomentoti siddhantaṃ avirodhento. Etena atthadosābhāvamāha. Aviruddhattā eva hi theravādāpi idha pakāsīyissanti. Theravaṃsadīpānanti thirehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā therā, mahākassapādayo. Tehi āgatā ācariyaparamparā theravaṃso, tappariyāpannā hutvā āgamādhigamasampannattā paññāpajjotena tassa samujjalanato theravaṃsadīpā, mahāvihāravāsino, tesaṃ. Vividhehi ākārehi nicchīyatīti vinicchayo, gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu khilamaddanākārena pavattā vimaticchedanī kathā. Suṭṭhunipuṇo saṇho vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Atha vā vinicchinotīti vinicchayo vuttappakāravisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo cheko vinicchayo etesanti yojetabbaṃ. Etena mahākassapāditheraparamparāgato, tato eva ca aviparīto saṇho sukhumo mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vinicchayo, tassa pamāṇabhūtataṃ dasseti.

9. id

10. Sujanassa cāti ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena “na kevalaṃ jambudīpavāsīnameva atthāya[V 1.0016], atha kho sādhujanatosanatthañcā”ti dasseti. Tena ca “tambapaṇṇidīpavāsīnampi atthāyā”ti ayamattho siddho hoti uggahaṇādisukaratāya tesampi bahukārattā. Ciraṭṭhitatthanti ciraṭṭhitiatthaṃ, cirakālappavattanāyāti attho. Idañhi atthappakāsanaṃ aviparītapadabyañjanasunikkhepassa atthasunayassa ca upāyabhāvato saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiyā pavattati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “dveme, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhammassa ṭhitiyā asammosāya anantaradhānāya saṃvattanti. Katame dve? Sunikkhittañca padabyañjanaṃ attho ca sunīto”ti (a. ni. 2.20).

10. id

11-12. Yaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, tassā mahattaṃ pariharituṃ “sāvatthipabhūtīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “na idha bhiyyo vitthārakathaṃ [M 1.0018] karissāmi, na taṃ idha vicārayissāmī”ti ca. Saṅgītīnaṃ dvinnanti dīghamajjhimanikāyānaṃ.

id

13. “Na idha bhiyyo vitthārakathaṃ karissāmī”ti sāmaññato vuttassa atthassa avassayaṃ dassetuṃ “suttānaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

13. id

14. Yaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ kattukāmo, tadekadesabhāvena visuddhimaggo gahetabboti kathikānaṃ upadesaṃ karonto tatta vicāritadhamme uddesavasena dasseti “sīlakathā”tiādinā. Tattha sīlakathāti cārittavārittādivasena sīlassa vitthārakathā. Dhutadhammāti piṇḍapātikaṅgādayo terasa kilesadhunanakadhammā. Kammaṭṭhānāni sabbānīti pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhattiṃsa, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dveti niravasesāni yogakammassa bhāvanāya pavattiṭṭhānāni. Cariyāvidhānasahitoti rāgacariyādīnaṃ sabhāgādividhānena sahito. Jhānāni cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo catasso arūpasamāpattiyo. Aṭṭhapi vā paṭiladdhamattāni jhānāni, samāpajjanavasibhāvappattiyā samāpattiyo. Jhānāni vā rūpārūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo phalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattiyo.

14. id

15. Lokiyalokuttarabhedā cha abhiññāyo sabbā abhiññāyo. Ñāṇavibhaṅgādīsu āgatanayena ekavidhādinā paññāya saṅkaletvā sampiṇḍetvā nicchayo paññāsaṅkalananicchayo.

15. id

16. Paccayadhammānaṃ hetuādīnaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ hetupaccayādibhāvo paccayākāro, tassa desanā paccayākāradesanā, paṭiccasamuppādakathāti attho. Sā pana nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkararahitatāya suṭṭhuparisuddhā, ghanavinibbhogassa ca sudukkaratāya nipuṇā saṇhasukhumā, ekattanayādisahitā [V 1.0017] ca tattha vicāritāti āha “suparisuddhanipuṇanayā”ti. Paṭisambhidādīsu āgatanayaṃ avisajjetvāva vicāritattā avimuttatantimaggā.

16. The mode of conditionality is the state of conditioning phenomena, such as the root-condition, being a condition for conditionally arisen phenomena. The teaching of this is the “teaching of the mode of conditionality,” which means the discourse on dependent origination. Moreover, that teaching is thoroughly pure because it is free from mixture with the doctrines of other schools; and it is skillful, subtle, and refined because the analysis of what is dense is very difficult. It is also investigated there together with the method of unity, etc.; therefore, he says it is “of a very pure and skillful method.” Because the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, etc., is investigated without being abandoned, it is a path that has not abandoned the canonical tradition.

17. Iti pana sabbanti iti-saddo parisamāpane, pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāre, etaṃ sabbanti attho. Idhāti imissā aṭṭhakathāya. Na taṃ vicārayissāmi punaruttibhāvatoti adhippāyo.

17. In “iti pana sabbaṃ,” the word “iti” signifies conclusion, and the word “pana” is a verbal embellishment; the meaning is “all this.” “Here” means in this commentary. The intention is, “I will not investigate it, as it would be a repetition.”

18. Idāni [M 1.0019] tasseva avicāraṇassa ekantakāraṇaṃ niddhārento “majjhe visuddhimaggo”tiādimāha. Tattha “majjhe ṭhatvā”ti etena majjhaṭṭhabhāvadīpanena visesato catunnaṃ āgamānaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā visuddhimaggo, na sumaṅgalavilāsiniādayo viya asādhāraṇaṭṭhakathāti dasseti. “Visesato”ti ca idaṃ vinayābhidhammānampi visuddhimaggo yathārahaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti evāti katvā vuttaṃ.

18. Now, determining the decisive reason for that very non-investigation, he says, “the Visuddhimagga in the middle,” etc. Here, with “standing in the middle,” by this indication of its central position, he shows that the Visuddhimagga is a commentary common especially to the four Nikāyas, not an uncommon commentary like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. And “especially” is said because the Visuddhimagga is indeed an explanation of the meaning of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma as well, as is appropriate.

19. Iccevāti iti eva. Tampīti visuddhimaggampi. Etāyāti sāratthappakāsiniyā.

19. “Icceva” is “iti eva” (thus). “That too” means the Visuddhimagga too. “By this” means by the Sāratthappakāsinī.

Ettha ca “sīhaḷadīpaṃ ābhatā”tiādinā aṭṭhakathākaraṇassa nimittaṃ dasseti, “dīpavāsīnamatthāya sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā”ti etehi payojanaṃ, “saṃyuttāgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena piṇḍatthaṃ, “apanetvāna tatohaṃ sīhaḷabhāsa”ntiādinā “sāvatthipabhūtīna”ntiādinā “sīlakathā”tiādinā ca karaṇappakāraṃ. Heṭṭhimanikāyesu visuddhimagge ca vicāritānaṃ atthānaṃ avicāraṇampi hi idha karaṇappakāro evāti.
