Here, with “brought to the island of Sīhaḷa,” etc., he shows the reason for composing the commentary. With “for the benefit of the island-dwellers, for the satisfaction of good people, and for the long duration of the Dhamma,” he shows the purpose. With “I will explain the meaning of the excellent Saṃyutta Āgama,” he shows the concise meaning. With “Having removed the Sīhaḷa language from that,” etc., “of Sāvatthī and so on,” etc., and “discourse on virtue,” etc., he shows the method of composition. Indeed, the non-investigation here of meanings already examined in the earlier Nikāyas and in the Visuddhimagga is also a method of composition.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Introductory Discourse is concluded.

1. Devatāsaṃyuttaṃ

1. The Connected Discourses with Devatās

1. Naḷavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Reed

1. Oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on Crossing the Flood

Vibhāgavantānaṃ [V 1.0018][M 1.0020] sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanavaseneva hotīti paṭhamaṃ tāva saṃyuttavaggasuttādivasena saṃyuttāgamassa vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha saṃyuttāgamo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti yaṃ vuttaṃ – “saṃyuttāgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti, tasmiṃ vacane. Tatthāti vā “etāya aṭṭhakathāya vijānātha saṃyuttanissitaṃ attha”nti ettha yaṃ saṃyuttaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, tattha. Pañca vaggā etassāti pañcavaggo. Avayavena viggaho, samudāyo samāsattho.

Since the elucidation of the intrinsic nature of things that have divisions occurs only by way of seeing the divisions, first, in order to show the division of the Saṃyutta Āgama by way of its chapters, suttas, and so on, he says: ‘Herein, what is called the Saṃyutta Āgama…,’ and so on. Herein, the word ‘herein’ refers to what was said in the statement: ‘I will explain the meaning of the excellent Saṃyutta Āgama.’ Or, ‘herein’ refers to where the term ‘Saṃyutta’ has been used in the phrase: ‘by means of this commentary, understand the meaning connected with the Saṃyutta.’ It has five chapters, thus it is the Pañcavagga. The analysis is by way of its parts; the collection is the meaning of the compound.

Idāni taṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṃvaṇṇetukāmo attano saṃvaṇṇanāya tassa paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkameneva pavattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ, “tassa vaggesu sagāthāvaggo ādī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathāpaccayaṃ tattha tattha desitattā paññattattā ca vippakiṇṇānaṃ dhammavinayānaṃ saṅgahetvā gāyanaṃ kathanaṃ saṅgīti, mahāvisayattā pūjaniyattā ca mahatī saṅgīti mahāsaṅgīti. Paṭhamā mahāsaṅgīti paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti, tassā pavattitakālo paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikālo, tasmiṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle.

Now, wishing to comment on it from the beginning, in order to show that his commentary proceeds in the very same sequence in which the text was laid down at the First Great Council, it is said: ‘Among its chapters, the Sagāthāvagga is the first,’ and so on. Therein, because the scattered Dhamma and Vinaya, which had been taught and laid down here and there according to the occasion, were collected and chanted together, this is a ‘council’ (saṅgīti). Because it was great in scope and worthy of reverence, a great council is a ‘Great Council’ (mahāsaṅgīti). The first great council is the ‘First Great Council’ (paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti). The time when it occurred is the time of the First Great Council; at that time of the First Great Council.

Nidadāti desanaṃ desakālādivasena aviditaṃ viditaṃ katvā nidassetīti nidānaṃ. Yo loke ganthassa upogghātoti vuccati, svāyamettha “evaṃ me suta”nti-ādiko gantho veditabbo, na pana “sanidānāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.126) viya attajjhāsayādidesanuppattihetu. Tenevāha – “evaṃ me sutanti-ādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādī”ti. Kāmañcettha yassaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkamena saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, sā vitthārato vattabbā, sumaṅgalavilāsiniyaṃ [V 1.0019] pana attanā vitthāritattā tattheva gahetabbāti imissā saṃvaṇṇanāya mahattaṃ pariharanto “sā panesā”tiādimāha.

It lays down the teaching, making the unknown known by indicating the speaker, time, and so on; thus it is an ‘introduction’ (nidāna). What in the world is called the prologue of a book, that here should be understood as the text beginning ‘Thus have I heard,’ and not, as in passages such as ‘Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma with its cause’ (AN 3:126), the cause for the arising of the teaching, such as one’s own intention. For that reason he said: ‘The introduction, beginning with “Thus have I heard,” was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council,’ and so on. Although, if one wishes to compose a commentary on the sequence in which it was laid down at the First Great Council, that should be stated in detail, since it has been explained in detail by himself in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, it should be taken from there. Thus, avoiding the great length of this commentary, he says, ‘But this…,’ and so on.

1. Evaṃ bāhiranidāne vattabbaṃ atidisitvā idāni abbhantaranidānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṃvaṇṇetuṃ “yaṃ paneta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karontena saṃvaṇṇetabbe dhamme padavibhāgaṃ padatthañca dassetvā tato paraṃ piṇḍatthādidassanavasena saṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā, tasmā padāni tāva dassento [M 1.0021] “evanti nipātapada”nti-ādimāha. Tattha padavibhāgoti padānaṃ viseso, na padaviggaho. Atha vā padāni ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgo. Padaviggaho ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgoti vā ekasesavasena padapadaviggahā padavibhāgasaddena vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha padaviggaho “jetassa vanaṃ jetavana”ntiādinā samāsapadesu daṭṭhabbo.

1. Having thus dealt with what should be said on the external introduction by way of transference, now, in order to comment on the internal introduction from the beginning, it is said: ‘Now, as to this…,’ and so on. Herein, since one who is commenting must, in regard to the teaching to be commented upon, first show the division of words and the meaning of the words, and thereafter the commentary should be made by way of showing the collected meaning, etc., therefore, first showing the words, he says: ‘The word evaṃ is a particle,’ and so on. Herein, ‘division of words’ means the distinction of words, not the analysis of words. Or, ‘words and division of words’ is ‘division of words.’ Or, it should be understood that by way of ellipsis, ‘words and analysis of words’ are expressed by the term ‘division of words.’ Herein, analysis of words should be seen in compound words, as in ‘Jeta’s grove is Jetavana.’

Atthatoti padatthato. Taṃ pana padatthaṃ atthuddhārakkamena paṭhamaṃ evaṃsaddassa dassento “evaṃsaddo tāvā”tiādimāha. Avadhāraṇādīti ettha ādi-saddena idamatthapucchāparimāṇādiatthānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni (dī. ni. 1.163, 165), evaṃvidho evamākāro”ti ca ādīsu idaṃ-saddassa atthe evaṃ-saddo. Gata-saddo hi pakārapariyāyo, tathā vidhākāra-saddo ca. Tathā hi gatavidhaākārasadde lokiyā pakāratthe vadanti. “Evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū āmuttamālābharaṇā odātavatthavasanā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārenti, seyyathāpi tvaṃ etarahi sācariyakoti. No hidaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.286) pucchāyaṃ, “evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ (a. ni. 1.48), evamāyupariyanto”ti (pārā. 12) ca ādīsu parimāṇe.

‘Atthato’ means ‘in terms of meaning,’ that is, in terms of the meaning of the words. Showing that meaning of the words in the order of extracting the sense, he first shows the meaning of the word evaṃ, saying: ‘First, the word evaṃ…,’ and so on. In the phrase ‘ascertainment, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ should be understood as including the meanings of pointing, questioning, measure, and so on. For example, in phrases like ‘evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni’ (DN 1, §1.27), ‘of such a kind, of such a form,’ and so on, the word evaṃ has the meaning of the word idaṃ (this). For the word gata is a synonym for ‘manner,’ and so too are the words vidha and ākāra. Indeed, worldly people use the words gata, vidha, and ākāra in the sense of ‘manner.’ In instances like, ‘Evaṃ su te sunhātā… paricārenti… No hidaṃ, bho gotamā’ (DN 3, §1.15), it is used in questioning. And in phrases like ‘so quick to change’ (AN 1:48) and ‘such is the end of life’ (Vin Pārā 12), it denotes measure.

Nanu ca “evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā, evamāyupariyanto”ti ettha evaṃ-saddena pucchanākāraparimāṇākārānaṃ vuttattā ākārattho eva evaṃ-saddoti? Na, visesasabbhāvato. Ākāramattavācako hi evaṃ-saddo, ākāratthoti adhippeto yathā “evaṃ byākho”tiādīsu, na pana ākāravisesavācako. Evañca katvā, “evaṃ jātena maccenā”tiādīni (dha. pa. 53) upamādīsu udāharaṇāni upapannāni honti. Tathā hi “yathāpi…pe… bahu”nti (dha. pa. 53)? Ettha puppharāsiṭṭhāniyato manussūpapattisappurisūpanissaya-saddhammassavana- yonisomanasikāra-bhogasampattiādidānādipuññakiriyahetusamudāyato sobhāsugandhatādiguṇayogato mālāguḷasadisiyo pahūtā puññakiriyā maritabbasabhāvatāya maccena sattena kattabbāti jotitattā [V 1.0020] puppharāsimālāguḷāva upamā, tesaṃ upamākāro yathā-saddena aniyamato vuttoti “evaṃ-saddo upamākāranigamanattho”ti [M 1.0022] vatthuṃ yuttaṃ, so pana upamākāro niyamiyamāno atthato upamāva hotīti āha “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti. Tathā “evaṃ iminā ākārena abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā upadisiyamānāya samaṇasāruppāya ākappasampattiyā yo tattha upadisanākāro, so atthato upadeso evāti vuttaṃ, “evaṃ te…pe… upadese”ti. Tathā “evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”ti ettha ca bhagavatā yathāvuttamatthaṃ aviparītato jānantehi kataṃ tattha saṃvijjamānaguṇānaṃ pakārehi haṃsanaṃ udaggatākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ. Yo tattha sampahaṃsanākāroti yojetabbaṃ.

Is it not the case that in ‘evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā’ and ‘evamāyupariyanto,’ since the manner of questioning and the manner of measure are stated by the word evaṃ, the word evaṃ just has the meaning of ‘manner’? No, because of the existence of a specific meaning. For the word evaṃ expresses only manner in general, as intended in the sense of ‘manner’ in such phrases as ‘thus a tiger,’ but it does not express a specific manner. This being so, examples in similes and so on, such as ‘evaṃ jātena maccenā’ (Dhp 53), become appropriate. For in the passage beginning ‘yathāpi… bahu’ (Dhp 53), the simile is a heap of flowers or a garland. This is because it is illuminated that many meritorious actions—which are similar to garlands and bouquets due to their connection with qualities such as beauty and fragrance, and which arise from the collection of causes for meritorious actions such as giving, etc., namely, human rebirth, reliance on good people, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and attainment of wealth—should be performed by a mortal being who is by nature subject to death. The manner of that simile is expressed indefinitely by the word yathā, so it is proper to say that the word evaṃ has the meaning of concluding the manner of the simile. But when that manner of the simile is specified, in meaning it becomes the simile itself; thus he says, ‘it has come in the sense of a simile.’ Similarly, with regard to the accomplishment in deportment proper for an ascetic, which is being taught in the phrase ‘evaṃ iminā ākārena abhikkamitabba,’ the manner of instruction there is, in meaning, the instruction itself; thus it is said, ‘evaṃ te… in the sense of instruction.’ Likewise, in the phrase ‘evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā,’ there is acclamation—making exultant—by those who know without distortion the meaning stated by the Blessed One, by means of the qualities present there. It should be connected as: ‘the manner of acclamation there.’

Evamevaṃ panāyanti ettha garahaṇākāroti yojetabbaṃ, so ca garahaṇākāro vasalīti-ādikhuṃsanasaddasannidhānato idha evaṃ-saddena pakāsitoti viññāyati. Yathā cettha, evaṃ upamākārādayopi upamādivasena vuttānaṃ puppharāsiādisaddānaṃ sannidhānatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ, bhanteti pana dhammassa sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāre sanniyojitehi bhikkhūhi attano tattha ṭhitabhāvassa paṭijānanavasena vuttattā ettha evaṃ-saddo “vacanasampaṭicchanattho”ti vutto. Tena evaṃ, bhanteti sādhu, bhante, suṭṭhu, bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti. Evañca vadehīti yathāhaṃ vadāmi, evaṃ samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ vadehīti yo evaṃ vadanākāro idāni vattabbo, so evaṃ-saddena nidassīyatīti “nidassanattho”ti vuttoti. Evaṃ noti etthāpi nesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ ahitadukkhāvahabhāve sanniṭṭhānajananatthaṃ anumatigahaṇavasena “saṃvattanti vā no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotī”ti pucchāya katāya “evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti vuttattā tadākārasanniṭṭhānaṃ evaṃ-saddena vibhāvitanti viññāyati. So pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanākāro niyamiyamāno avadhāraṇattho hotīti āha – “evaṃ no ettha hotītiādīsu avadhāraṇe”ti.

In ‘Evamevaṃ panāyanti,’ it should be connected as ‘the manner of censure.’ That manner of censure is understood to be expressed here by the word evaṃ because of its proximity to words of abuse such as ‘outcaste.’ And just as here, so too the manner of simile and so on should be understood from the proximity of words such as ‘heap of flowers,’ which are stated by way of simile, etc. But ‘Evaṃ, bhante’ is spoken by bhikkhus who have been enjoined to listen and attend carefully to the Dhamma, as a way of professing their own stance in that matter; hence here the word evaṃ is said to have ‘the meaning of assenting to a statement.’ Therefore, ‘Evaṃ, bhante’ means ‘Good, venerable sir; well said, venerable sir.’ In ‘And speak thus,’ the manner of speaking that is now to be expressed—‘Just as I speak, so you should speak to the ascetic Ānanda’—is indicated by the word evaṃ; hence it is said to have ‘the meaning of demonstration.’ In ‘Thus it is for us,’ here too, in order to generate a firm conclusion about the fact that the aforementioned things are unbeneficial and bring suffering, when the question is asked by way of seeking agreement—‘Do they conduce to our welfare or not? What is your opinion on this?’—it is replied, ‘Thus it is for us here.’ Thus it is understood that the firm conclusion about that manner is made clear by the word evaṃ. But that manner in which those things conduce to what is unbeneficial and to suffering, being specified, has the meaning of ascertainment. Thus he says: ‘In such phrases as “Thus it is for us here,” it is in the sense of ascertainment.’

Nānānayanipuṇanti ekattanānattaabyāpāraevaṃdhammatāsaṅkhātā, nandiyāvaṭṭatipukkhalasīhavikkīḷitaaṅkusadisālocanasaṅkhātā vā ādhārādibhedavasena nānāvidhā nayā nānānayā. Nayā vā pāḷigatiyo tā ca paññattianupaññattiādivasena saṃkilesabhāgiyādilokiyāditadubhayavomissakādivasena kusalādivasena khandhādivasena saṅgahādivasena samayavimuttādivasena ṭhapanādivasena kusalamūlādivasena tikappaṭṭhānādivasena [M 1.0023] ca nānappakārāti nānānayā, tehi nipuṇaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumanti nānānayanipuṇaṃ. Āsayova ajjhāsayo, te ca sassatādibhedena tattha ca apparajakkhatādibhedena aneke, attajjhāsayādayo eva vā samuṭṭhānaṃ uppattihetu etassāti anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ[V 1.0021]. Atthabyañjanasampannanti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇaṃ upanetabbābhāvato, saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatanti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Skilled in various methods' means skilled in what is designated as the non-operation concerning unity and diversity and the nature of phenomena. Or, it refers to the examination known as the right-turning spiral, the three-peaked, the lion’s play, and the goad-like scrutiny, which are of various kinds based on differences of support and so on. The methods, or the ways of the Pāli texts, are diverse in many ways: through designation and additional designation, through being connected with defilement or the mundane, through both or mixed, through the wholesome and so on, through aggregates and so on, through inclusion and so on, through the temporally liberated and so on, through establishing and so on, through wholesome roots and so on, through the threefold framework and so on. To be skilled in these in a subtle and refined way is to be 'skilled in various methods.' 'Disposition' means inclination, and these are of many kinds, such as eternalism and so on, and within that, the inclinations of those with little dust and others. Alternatively, one’s own inclinations and so on are the cause of its origin—thus, 'arising from many dispositions.' 'Complete in meaning and expression' means fully endowed with meaning and expression, as there is nothing further to be added. Or, the meaning should be understood as being endowed with six aspects of meaning—presentation, revelation, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with six aspects of expression—letters, words, syllables, phrases, language, and definition.

Vividhapāṭihāriyanti ettha pāṭihāriyapadassa vacanatthaṃ (udā. aṭṭha. 1; itivu. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā; dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 2) “paṭipakkhaharaṇato rāgādikilesāpanayanato pāṭihāriya”nti vadanti. Bhagavato pana paṭipakkhā rāgādayo na santi ye haritabbā, puthujjanānampi vigatūpakkilese aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe iddhividhaṃ pavattati, tasmā tattha pavattavohārena ca na sakkā idha “pāṭihāriya”nti vattuṃ. Sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato veneyyagatā ca kilesā paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ haraṇato “pāṭihāriya”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ. Atha vā bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā hontīti. Paṭīti vā ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 985; cūḷani. vatthugāthā 4) viya, tasmā samāhite citte vigatūpakkilese katakiccena pacchāharitabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā haraṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ, iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo ca vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena ca sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upattilesesu parasattānaṃ upakkilesaharaṇāni hontīti paṭihāriyāni bhavanti, paṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ. Paṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanisamudāye bhavaṃ ekekaṃ pāṭihāriyanti vuccati. Paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ, tasmiṃ vā nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Tassa pana iddhiādibhedena visayabhedena ca bahuvidhassa [M 1.0024] bhagavato desanāyaṃ labbhamānattā āha “vividhapāṭihāriya”nti.

Regarding 'various miracles,' here the etymological meaning of the word 'pāṭihāriya' is given: they say it is 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes adversaries, because it dispels defilements such as lust. However, the Blessed One has no adversaries—no lust or other defilements to be removed. Even for ordinary people, psychic power operates in a mind that is free from imperfections, endowed with the eight qualities, and has its adversaries destroyed. Therefore, based on the conventional usage there, it cannot be said that 'pāṭihāriya' applies here. But if the defilements pertaining to those to be trained are the adversaries for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, then their removal can be called 'pāṭihāriya.' In this case, it is appropriate. Alternatively, the adversaries for the Blessed One and his dispensation are the sectarians. Their removal is 'pāṭihāriya,' for they are removed and dispelled by psychic power, instruction, and admonition, by means of removing their views and through their inability to proclaim their views. Or, the word 'paṭi' suggests the meaning of 'afterward,' as in phrases like 'after he had entered, another brahmin arrived.' Therefore, what is to be brought forth afterward by one with a concentrated mind, free from imperfections and having fulfilled his purpose, is called 'pāṭihāriya.' Or, after one’s own imperfections have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the path, the subsequent removal is 'pāṭihāriya.' Psychic power, instruction, and admonishment are to be set in motion again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from imperfections and has done what had to be done. Moreover, when one’s own imperfections have been removed, the removal of the imperfections of other beings also occurs—these are called 'paṭihāriyāni.' 'Paṭihāriya' itself is 'pāṭihāriya.' Alternatively, each individual component occurring within the collection of psychic power, instruction, and admonishment is called a 'pāṭihāriya.' Or, the fourth jhāna and the path are 'pāṭihāriya' because they remove adversaries; or what is born from that, or has that as its sign, or comes from that is 'pāṭihāriya.' Since this is found in the Blessed One’s teaching in many varieties—distinguished by psychic power, etc., and by different objects—it is said, 'various miracles.'

Na aññathāti bhagavato sammukhā sutākārato na aññathāti attho, na pana bhagavato desitākārato. Acinteyyānubhāvā hi bhagavato desanā. Evañca katvā “sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātu”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ bhavati, dhāraṇabaladassanañca na virujjhati sutākāraavirajjhanassa adhippetattā. Na hettha atthantaratāparihāro dvinnampi atthānaṃ ekavisayattā. Itarathā thero bhagavato desanāya sabbathā paṭiggahaṇe samattho asamattho cāti āpajjeyyāti.

'Not otherwise' means not otherwise than the way it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One, but this does not apply to the manner in which it was taught by the Blessed One. For the teaching of the Blessed One has inconceivable power. This being so, the statement, 'Who is capable of understanding in every way?' is justified, and the demonstration of the power of retention is not contradicted, since what is intended is non-deviation from the way it was heard. Here, there is no abandonment of a different meaning, because both meanings pertain to the same subject. Otherwise, the elder would fall into the position of being both entirely capable and incapable of grasping the Blessed One's teaching.

“Yo [V 1.0022] paro na hoti, so attā”ti evaṃ vuttāya niyakajjhattasaṅkhātāya sasantatiyā vattanato tividhopi me-saddo kiñcāpi ekasmiṃ eva atthe dissati, karaṇasampadānasāminiddesavasena pana vijjamānaṃ bhedaṃ sandhāyāha, “me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissatī”ti.

Although the word 'me' appears in a single meaning—referring to one's own continuity, which is designated as one's own internal self and spoken of as, 'He who is not another, that is the self'—it is nevertheless threefold. Referring to the existing distinction by way of its indication as instrument, recipient, and owner, he said: 'The word 'me' is seen in three meanings.'

Kiñcāpi upasaggo kiriyaṃ viseseti, jotakabhāvato pana satipi tasmiṃ suta-saddo eva taṃ taṃ attaṃ vadatīti anupasaggassa suta-saddassa atthuddhāre saupasaggassa gahaṇaṃ na virujjhatīti dassento “saupasaggo anupasaggo cā”tiādimāha. Assāti suta-saddassa. Kammabhāvasādhanāni idha sutasadde sambhavantīti vuttaṃ “upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vā attho”ti. Mayāti atthe satīti yadā me-saddassa kattuvasena karaṇaniddeso, tadāti attho. Mamāti atthe satīti yadā sambandhavasena sāminiddeso, tadā.

Although a prefix qualifies a verb, nevertheless, because of its indicative nature, even when a prefix is present the word 'suta' itself expresses that meaning. Showing that taking the prefixed form does not contradict extracting the meaning of the unprefixed 'suta,' he said, 'both with and without a prefix,' etc. 'Of this' (`assa`) means of the word 'suta.' Here, it is stated that derivations in the sense of object and state are possible for the word 'suta,' hence it is said, 'the meaning is either "what has been ascertained" or "the act of ascertaining".' When the meaning is 'by me' (`mayā`), that is, when there is an instrumental indication for the word 'me' in the place of the agent, that is the meaning. When the meaning is 'of me' (`mama`), that is, when there is an indication of ownership by way of relation, that is the meaning.

Suta-saddasannidhāne payuttena evaṃ-saddena savanakiriyājotakena bhavitabbanti vuttaṃ “evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassana”nti. Ādi-saddena sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ pañcadvārikaviññāṇānaṃ tadabhinīhaṭānañca manodvārikaviññāṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sabbesampi vākyānaṃ evakāratthasahitattā “suta”nti etassa sutamevāti ayamattho labbhatīti āha “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti. Etena avadhāraṇena nirāsaṅkataṃ dasseti. Yathā ca sutaṃ sutamevāti niyametabbaṃ, taṃ sammā sutaṃ hotīti āha “anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Atha vā saddantaratthāpohanavasena [M 1.0025] saddo atthaṃ vadatīti sutanti asutaṃ na hotīti ayametassa atthoti vuttaṃ “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti. Iminā diṭṭhādivinivattanaṃ karoti.

It is said that the word 'evaṃ', when used in proximity to the word 'suta', must be an indicator of the action of hearing; thus it is stated: ''Evaṃ' is an indication of the function of ear-consciousness and other consciousnesses.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of the five-door consciousnesses such as receiving-consciousness, and the mind-door consciousnesses brought forth from them, should be understood. Since all sentences contain the meaning of the particle 'eva' (only), for 'suta' the meaning 'heard only' is obtained; thus he says, 'by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing.' By this determination, freedom from doubt is shown. And just as what is heard must be determined as 'heard only,' so that it is properly heard, he says this is 'an indication of grasping that is neither deficient, excessive, nor distorted.' Or alternatively, a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meaning of other words, so 'heard' means 'it is not unheard'; this is its meaning, as stated: 'by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing.' By this, he brings about the turning away from what is seen, etc.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – na idaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, na sayambhūñāṇena sacchikataṃ, atha kho sutaṃ, tañca kho sammadevāti. Tenevāha “anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Avadhāraṇatthe vā evaṃ-sadde ayamatthayojanā karīyatīti tadapekkhassa suta-saddassa ayamattho vutto “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti. Tenevāha “anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Savanasaddo cettha kammattho veditabbo “suyyatī”ti.

This is what is said: 'This was not seen by me, nor realized by self-originated knowledge, but rather it was heard, and that too, rightly.' Therefore he said it is 'an indication of grasping that is neither deficient, excessive, nor distorted.' Or, when the word 'evaṃ' has the sense of determination, this construction of meaning is made, and in dependence on that, this meaning of the word 'suta' is stated: 'by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing.' Therefore he said it is 'an indication of grasping that is neither deficient, excessive, nor distorted.' Here, the word 'savana' should be understood in the objective sense, as in 'it is heard.'

Evaṃ savanahetusavanavisesavasena padattayassa ekena pakārena atthayojanaṃ dassetvā idāni pakārantarehi taṃ dassetuṃ “tathā eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassāti yā sā bhagavato sammukhā [V 1.0023] dhammassavanākārena pavattā manodvāraviññāṇavīthi, tassā. Sā hi nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattetuṃ samatthā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “sotadvārānusārenā”ti. Nānappakārenāti vakkhamānānaṃ anekavihitānaṃ byañjanatthaggahaṇānaṃ nānākārena. Etena imissā yojanāya ākārattho evaṃ-saddo gahitoti dīpeti. Pavattibhāvappakāsananti pavattiyā atthitāpakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsananti yasmiṃ ārammaṇe vuttappakārā viññāṇavīthi nānappakārena pavattā, tassa dhammattā vuttaṃ, na suta-saddassa dhammatthattā. Vuttassevatthassa pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ “ayaṃ hetthā”tiādi. Tattha viññāṇavīthiyāti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, mayāti kattuatthe.

Thus, having shown the construction of meaning for the three words in one way—by way of the cause of hearing and the distinction of hearing—now, to show it in other ways, 'just so,' etc., is said. Herein, 'of that' refers to that stream of mind-door consciousness which occurs in the presence of the Blessed One in the form of hearing the Dhamma. For it is capable of occurring in various ways with regard to the object. And so it is said, 'following the ear-door.' 'In various ways' means in the diverse ways of grasping the many kinds of meanings and expressions that will be spoken of. By this, it is indicated that in this construction, the word 'evaṃ' is taken in the sense of manner. 'Showing the state of occurrence' means revealing the existence of the occurrence. 'Heard' means an exposition of the Dhamma; this is said because that object in which the stream of consciousness occurred in the manner described has the nature of Dhamma, not because the word 'suta' has the meaning 'Dhamma.' The clarification of the meaning just stated is 'this here,' etc. Herein, 'by the stream of consciousness' is an instrumental word in the sense of instrument; 'by me' is in the sense of agent.

Evanti niddisitabbappakāsananti nidassanatthamevaṃ saddaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ nidassetabbassa niddisitabbattābhāvābhāvato. Tena evaṃ-saddena sakalampi suttaṃ paccāmaṭṭhanti dasseti. Suta-saddassa kiriyāsaddattā savanakiriyāya ca sādhāraṇaviññāṇappabandhapaṭibaddhattā tattha ca puggalavohāroti vuttaṃ “sutanti puggalakiccappakāsana”nti. Na hi puggalavohārarahite dhammappabandhe savanakiriyā labbhatīti.

'Evaṃ' is for indicating what should be pointed out. This is said taking the word 'evaṃ' for the purpose of illustration, because what is to be illustrated is indeed something to be indicated. Thereby it shows that the entire sutta is reviewed by this word 'evaṃ'. Because the word 'suta' is a verbal noun, and because the act of hearing is connected with the stream of ordinary consciousness, wherein the conventional designation of a person is found, it is said: '“Suta” is the disclosure of a person’s function.' For the act of hearing is not found in a stream of dhammas devoid of the conventional designation of a person.

Yassa cittasantānassātiādipi ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā purimayojanāya aññathā atthayojanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha ākārapaññattīti upādāpaññatti eva dhammānaṃ pavattiākārupādānavasena tathā [M 1.0026] vuttā. Sutanti visayaniddesoti sotabbabhūto dhammo savanakiriyākattupuggalassa savanakiriyāvasena pavattiṭṭhānanti katvā vuttaṃ. Cittasantānavinimuttassa paramatthato kassaci kattu abhāvepi saddavohārena buddhiparikappitabhedavacanicchāya cittasantānato aññaṃ viya taṃsamaṅgiṃ katvā vuttaṃ “cittasantānena taṃsamaṅgīno”ti. Savanakiriyāvisayopi sotabbadhammo savanakiriyāvasena pavattacittasantānassa idha paramatthato kattubhāvato, savanavasena cittappavattiyā eva vā savanakiriyābhāvato taṃkiriyākattu ca visayo hotīti vuttaṃ “taṃsamaṅgīno kattuvisaye”ti. Sutākārassa ca therassa sammānicchitabhāvato āha “gahaṇasanniṭṭhāna”nti. Etena vā avadhāraṇatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā ayamatthayojanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase 'of which mental continuum,' etc., is also stated to show a different explanation of the meaning from the previous construction, by taking the word 'evaṃ' as signifying mode. Here, 'designation of mode' is derivative designation, so called because it is derived from the mode of occurrence of dhammas. '“Suta” is the indication of the object': this is said because the Dhamma to be heard is the basis for the occurrence of the act of hearing for the person performing that act. Although in the ultimate sense there is no agent apart from the mental continuum, through conventional speech, due to the desire to express a distinction conceived by the intellect, it is spoken of as if there were another endowed with it, separate from the mental continuum; hence it is said, 'of one endowed with that mental continuum.' The object of the act of hearing, the Dhamma to be heard, is also the object of the agent endowed with that act; this is said because here, in the ultimate sense, the mental continuum that has occurred by way of hearing is the agent, or because the act of hearing is simply the occurrence of the mind by way of hearing. And because the mode of what was heard was rightly ascertained by the Elder, he says, 'the ascertainment of the grasping.' Or, it should be understood that this explanation of meaning is made by taking the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of determination.

Pubbe sutānaṃ nānāvihitānaṃ suttasaṅkhātānaṃ atthabyañjanānaṃ upadhāritarūpassa ākārassa nidassanassa, avadhāraṇassa vā pakāsanasabhāvo evaṃ-saddoti tadākārādiupadhāraṇassa puggalapaññattiyā upādānabhūtadhammappabandhabyāpāratāya vuttaṃ “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso”ti. Savanakiriyā pana puggalavādinopi viññāṇanirapekkhā natthīti visesato viññāṇabyāpāroti āha [V 1.0024] “sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Meti saddappavattiyā ekanteneva sattavisayattā viññāṇakiccassa ca tattheva samodahitabbato “meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso”ti vuttaṃ. Avijjamānapaññattivijjamānapaññattisabhāvā yathākkamaṃ evaṃ-saddasuta-saddānaṃ atthāti te tathārūpa-paññatti-upādānabhūta-dhammappabandhabyāpārabhāvena dassento āha – “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso, sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Ettha ca karaṇakiriyākattukamma-visesappakāsanavasena puggalabyāpāravisaya-puggalabyāpāranidassanavasena gahaṇākāragāhakatabbisayavisesaniddesavasena kattukaraṇabyāpāra-kattuniddesavasena ca dutiyādayo catasso atthayojanā dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The word 'evaṃ' has the nature of disclosing the indication, or the determination, of the mode, which is the ascertained form of the meaning and phrasing of the various previously heard teachings designated as suttas. Because the ascertainment of that mode, etc., is an operation of the stream of dhammas that is the basis for personal designation, it is said: '“Evaṃ” is the indication of a person's function.' However, since even for personalists the act of hearing is not independent of consciousness, it is specifically an operation of consciousness; thus he says: '“Suta” is the indication of consciousness's function.' Since the word 'me' in its occurrence refers exclusively to a being, and since the function of consciousness must be included right there, it is said: '“Me” is the indication of the person connected with both functions.' The meanings of the words 'evaṃ' and 'suta' have the nature of non-existent designation and existent designation respectively. Showing them as being the operation of the stream of dhammas that is the basis for such designations, he says: '“Evaṃ” is the indication of a person's function; “suta” is the indication of consciousness's function.' And here it should be understood that the second and the following three explanations of the meaning are shown in four ways: (1) by way of explaining the distinction between instrument, action, agent, and object; (2) by way of indicating the sphere of a person's operation and the indication of a person's operation; (3) by way of indicating the distinction between the mode of grasping, the grasper, and its object; and (4) by way of indicating the agent through the operation of the agent and the instrument.

Sabbassapi saddādhigamanīyassa atthassa paññattimukheneva paṭipajjitabbattā sabbapaññattīnañca vijjamānādivasena chasu paññattibhedesu antogadhattā tesu “eva”ntiādīnaṃ paññattīnaṃ sarūpaṃ niddhārento āha “evanti ca meti cā”tiādi. Tattha evanti ca meti ca vuccamānassa atthassa ākārādino [M 1.0027] dhammānaṃ asalakkhaṇabhāvato avijjamānapaññattibhāvoti āha “saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññattī”ti. Tattha saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasenāti bhūtatthauttamatthavasena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtattho, anussavādīhi gahetabbo viya anuttamattho ca na hoti, so rūpasaddādisabhāvo, ruppanānubhavanādisabhāvo vā attho saccikaṭṭho paramattho cāti vuccati, na tathā evaṃ meti padānaṃ atthoti. Etamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “kiñhetthata”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sutanti pana saddāyatanaṃ sandhāyāha “vijjamānapaññattī”ti. Teneva hi “yañhi taṃ ettha sotena upaladdha”nti vuttaṃ. Sotadvārānusārena upaladdhanti pana vutte atthabyañjanādi sabbaṃ labbhatīti. Taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbatoti sotapathamāgate dhamme upādāya tesaṃ upadhāritākārādino paccāmasanavasena evanti, sasantatipariyāpanne khandhe upādāya meti vattabbattāti attho. Diṭṭhādisabhāvarahite saddāyatane pavattamānopi sutavohāro “dutiyaṃ tatiya”ntiādiko viya paṭhamādīni diṭṭhamutaviññāte apekkhitvā pavattoti āha “diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato”ti. Asutaṃ na hotīti hi sutanti pakāsitoyamatthoti.

Since every meaning attainable through words must be accessed through the medium of designation, and since all designations are included in the six kinds of designation based on existence, etc., determining the nature of designations such as 'evaṃ,' he says, '“Evaṃ” and “me,”' etc. Therein, because the meaning expressed by 'evaṃ' and 'me'—the mode, etc.—is not the intrinsic characteristic of dhammas, it is a non-existent designation. Thus he says: 'a non-existent designation in the sense of the real and the ultimate meaning.' Here, 'in the sense of the real and the ultimate meaning' means in the sense of the true meaning and the supreme meaning. This is what is said: A meaning that is not unreal like a magical illusion or a mirage, and not a non-supreme meaning to be grasped through hearsay, etc., but is the intrinsic nature of form, sound, etc., or the nature of being afflicted, experienced, etc., is called 'real' and 'ultimate meaning.' The meaning of the words 'evaṃ' and 'me' is not like that. To make this very meaning clearer, 'What is here?' etc., is said. But with reference to the sound base, he says 'suta' is an 'existent designation.' For that reason it is said: 'For whatever is apprehended here by the ear.' But when it is said 'apprehended in accordance with the ear-door,' all meaning and phrasing are obtained. The meaning is: 'It should be spoken of by taking up this or that.' 'Evaṃ' is said by way of reviewing their ascertained mode, etc., having taken up the dhammas that have come into the range of the ear; 'me' is to be said having taken up the aggregates included in one's own continuity. Although the conventional usage 'suta' occurs in relation to the sound base, which is devoid of the nature of the seen, etc., it proceeds in dependence on the seen, sensed, and cognized, just as 'second,' 'third,' etc., proceed in dependence on a first. Thus he says: 'because it is to be spoken of in dependence on the seen, etc.' For the meaning disclosed by 'suta' is: 'It is not what is unheard.'

Attanā paṭividdhā suttassa pakāravisesā evanti therena paccāmaṭṭhāti āha “asammohaṃ dīpetī”ti. Nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hotīti etena vakkhamānassa suttassa nānappakārataṃ duppaṭivijjhatañca dasseti. Sutassa asammosaṃ dīpetīti sutākārassa yāthāvato dassiyamānattā vuttaṃ. Asammohenāti sammohābhāvena, paññāya eva vā savanakālasambhūtāya taduttarakālapaññāsiddhi[V 1.0025]. Evaṃ asammosenāti etthāpi vattabbaṃ. Byañjanānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo ākāro nātigambhīro yathāsutadhāraṇameva tattha karaṇīyanti satiyā byāpāro adhiko, paññā tattha guṇībhūtāti vuttaṃ “paññāpubbaṅgamāyā”tiādi paññāya pubbaṅgamāti katvā. Pubbaṅgamatā cettha padhānatā “manopubbaṅgamā”tiādīsu viya. Pubbaṅgamatāya vā cakkhuviññāṇādīsu āvajjanādīnaṃ viya appadhānatte paññā pubbaṅgamā etissāti ayampi attho yujjati, evaṃ sati pubbaṅgamāyāti etthāpi vuttavipariyāyena yathāsambhavaṃ attho veditabbo. Atthabyañjanasampannassāti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇassa[M 1.0028], saṅkāsana-pakāsana-vivaraṇa-vibhajana-uttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi, akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatassāti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Thus' the special modes of the sutta penetrated by himself were reviewed by the Elder; thus he says, 'He shows non-confusion.' By this, 'he is capable of penetration in various ways,' he shows the multifariousness and difficulty of penetration of the sutta about to be spoken. 'He shows the non-forgetfulness of what was heard': this is said because the mode of what was heard is shown as it really is. 'Without confusion' means by the absence of confusion, or by the wisdom that arose at the time of hearing, the attainment of wisdom at a later time is accomplished. This should also be said here for 'Thus, without forgetfulness.' The mode in which the phrasing is to be penetrated is not very profound; what is to be done there is just to retain it as heard. Thus the operation of mindfulness is predominant, and wisdom is secondary. Hence it is said, 'by mindfulness preceded by wisdom,' taking it as 'wisdom is its forerunner.' And here, 'being the forerunner' means being primary, as in 'mind is the forerunner,' etc. Or, if 'being the forerunner' implies a non-primary role, as attention, etc., have in relation to eye-consciousness, etc., then this meaning also fits: 'wisdom is its forerunner.' In this case, for the phrase 'preceded by mindfulness,' the meaning should be understood, as may be possible, in the reverse way of what has been said. 'Endowed with meaning and phrasing' means complete in meaning and phrasing. Or the meaning should be seen as: endowed with the six terms of meaning—elucidation, exposition, disclosure, analysis, making plain, and designation; and with the six terms of phrasing—letters, words, phrasing, mode, etymology, and indication.

Yoniso manasikāraṃ dīpeti evaṃ-saddena vuccamānānaṃ ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthānaṃ aviparītasaddhammavisayattāti adhippāyo. Avikkhepaṃ dīpetīti “oghataraṇasuttaṃ kattha bhāsita”ntiādipucchāvasena pakaraṇappavattassa vakkhamānassa suttassa savanaṃ samādhānamantarena na sambhavatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vikkhittacittassātiādi tassevatthassa samatthanavasena vuttaṃ. Sabbasampattiyāti atthabyañjanadesaka-payojanādisampattiyā. Aviparītasaddhammavisayehi viya ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthehi yonisomanasikārassa, saddhammassavanena viya ca avikkhepassa yathā yonisomanasikārena phalabhūtena attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatānaṃ siddhi vuttā tadavinābhāvato, evaṃ avikkhepeneva phalabhūtena kāraṇabhūtānaṃ saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayānaṃ siddhi dassetabbā siyā assutavato sappurisūpanissayarahitassa ca tadabhāvato. “Na hi vikkhittacitto”tiādinā samatthanavacanena pana avikkhepena kāraṇabhūtena sappurisūpanissayena ca phalabhūtassa saddhammassavanassa siddhi dassitā. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo yutto siyā, saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayā na ekantena avikkhepassa kāraṇaṃ bāhiraṅgattā. Avikkhepo pana sappurisūpanissayo viya saddhammassavanassa ekantakāraṇanti, evampi avikkhepena sappurisūpanissayasiddhijotanā na samatthitāva, no na samatthitā vikkhittacittānaṃ sappurisapayirūpāsanābhāvassa atthasiddhito. Ettha ca purimaṃ phalena kāraṇassa siddhidassanaṃ nadīpūrena viya upari vuṭṭhisabbhāvassa. Dutiyaṃ kāraṇena phalassa siddhidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ ekantavassinā viya meghavuṭṭhānena vuṭṭhippavattiyā.

It indicates wise attention by the word 'thus,' the intention being that what is expressed by it has the meanings of mode, illustration, and determination, which pertain to the undistorted good Dhamma. It indicates non-distraction because listening to the sutta about to be taught—which proceeds by way of questions such as, 'Where was the Oghataraṇa Sutta spoken?'—is not possible without concentration. The words 'for one with a scattered mind,' etc., are stated to support this same point. 'All accomplishments' refers to the accomplishment of meaning, phrasing, teaching, purpose, and so on. Just as the accomplishment of right resolve of self and previously done merit (the causes) is stated through wise attention (the fruit), so too the accomplishment of listening to the good Dhamma and associating with superior persons (the causes) should be shown by non-distraction (the fruit), for this is absent in one who has not heard and lacks association with superior persons. However, with the supporting statement beginning 'For a distracted mind does not...,' the accomplishment of listening to the good Dhamma (the fruit) is shown by non-distraction and association with superior persons (the causes). Herein, this intention would be fitting: listening to the good Dhamma and associating with superior persons are not the exclusive cause of non-distraction, as they are external factors. But non-distraction, like association with superior persons, is an exclusive cause for listening to the good Dhamma. Even so, the indication of the accomplishment of association with superior persons by means of non-distraction is not established. Yet it is not that it is not established, since it is factually established that those with distracted minds lack attendance on superior persons. Herein, the former case—showing the accomplishment of the cause by the fruit—is like inferring the existence of rain upstream from a river's flooding. The latter—showing the accomplishment of the fruit by the cause—should be seen as like inferring the occurrence of rain from the gathering of clouds that invariably bring it.

Bhagavato vacanassa atthabyañjanapabheda-paricchedavasena sakalasāsanasampatti-ogāhanākāro niravasesaparahita-pāripūrikāraṇanti vuttaṃ “evaṃ bhaddako ākāro”ti. Yasmā na hotīti sambandho[V 1.0026]. Pacchimacakkadvayasampattinti attasammāpaṇidhi-pubbekatapuññatā-saṅkhātaṃ guṇadvayaṃ. Aparāparavuttiyā cettha cakkabhāvo, caranti etehi sattā, sampattibhavesūti vā[M 1.0029]. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.31). Purimapacchimabhāvo cettha desanakkamavasena daṭṭhabbo. Pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyāti pacchimacakkadvayassa ca atthitāya. Sammāpaṇihitatto pubbe ca katapuñño suddhāsayo hoti tadasuddhihetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ dūrībhāvatoti āha “āsayasuddhi siddhā hotī”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti (dha. pa. 43) “katapuññosi, tvaṃ ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo”ti (dī. ni. 2.207) ca. Tenevāha “āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhī”ti. Payogasuddhiyāti yonisomanasikārapubbaṅgamassa dhammassavanapayogassa visadabhāvena. Tathā cāha “āgamabyattisiddhī”ti, sabbassa vā kāyavacīpayogassa niddosabhāvena. Parisuddhakāyavacīpayogo hi vippaṭisārābhāvato avikkhittacitto pariyattiyaṃ visārado hotīti.

The mode of comprehending all the accomplishments of the teaching—by way of classifying the meaning and phrasing of the Blessed One's speech—is called 'an excellent mode' because it is the cause for the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others without remainder. The connection is 'because it is not otherwise.' 'The accomplishment of the latter two wheels' refers to the pair of qualities called right self-application and previously done merit. Here, they are wheels because of their successive operation, or because beings fare on by means of them in states of accomplishment. It is with reference to these that it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels; when gods and human beings are endowed with them, the four-wheeled vehicle turns for them,' and so on (AN 4.31). The distinction between earlier and later here should be understood according to the sequence of the teaching. 'By the accomplishment of the latter two wheels' means by the existence of the latter two wheels. One with a rightly directed mind and who has previously done merit has a pure disposition, because the defilements that cause its impurity have been removed. Thus he says: 'purity of disposition is accomplished.' For it is said: 'A rightly directed mind can do one better than that' (Dhp 43), and 'You have made merit, Ānanda. Apply yourself to the striving. You will soon be without taints' (DN 2.207). Therefore he says: 'Through purity of disposition, the accomplishment of proficiency in attainment.' 'Through purity of practice' means through the clarity of the practice of listening to the Dhamma, which is preceded by wise attention. And so he says: 'the accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures,' or by the faultlessness of all bodily and verbal practice. For one whose bodily and verbal practice is pure, being without remorse and with an undistracted mind, becomes skilled in the scriptural learning.

Nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakenātiādinā atthabyañjanesu therassa evaṃ-saddasuta-saddānaṃ asammohāsammosadīpanato catupaṭisambhidāvasena atthayojanaṃ dasseti. Tattha sotabbabhedapaṭivedhadīpakenāti etena ayaṃ suta-saddo evaṃ-saddasannidhānato, vakkhamānāpekkhāya vā sāmaññeneva sotabbadhammavisesaṃ āmasatīti dīpeti. Manodiṭṭhīhi pariyattidhammānaṃ anupekkhanasuppaṭivedhā visesato manasikārapaṭibaddhāti te vuttanayena yonisomanasikāradīpakena evaṃ saddena yojetvā, savanadhāraṇavacīparicayā pariyattidhammānaṃ visesena sotāvadhānapaṭibaddhāti te vuttanayena avikkhepadīpakena suta-saddena yojetvā dassento sāsanasampattiyā dhammassavane ussāhaṃ janeti. Tattha dhammāti pariyattidhammā. Manasā anupekkhitāti “idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā, ettakā ettha anusandhiyo”tiādinā nayena manasā anupekkhitā. Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhāti nijjhānakkhanti bhūtāya, ñātapariññāsaṅkhātāya vā diṭṭhiyā tattha tattha vuttarūpārūpadhamme “iti rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā paṭividdhā.

By the words 'by illuminating the various kinds of penetration,' etc., he shows the Elder's application of the meaning by way of the four analytical knowledges, as this illuminates the absence of confusion and delusion regarding the words 'thus' and 'heard' in relation to the meaning and the phrasing. Herein, by the phrase 'by illuminating the penetration of the different kinds of things to be heard,' he indicates that this word 'heard' (suta), either due to its proximity to the word 'thus' or in anticipation of what is to be said, generally touches upon the specific qualities of the Dhamma to be heard. Since the reflection upon and good penetration of the scriptural teachings by mind and view are especially connected with mental application, he connects them in the way stated with the word 'thus,' which illuminates wise attention. And since hearing, retaining, and verbal familiarity with the scriptural teachings are especially connected with attention of the ear, he connects them in the way stated with the word 'heard,' which illuminates non-distraction. In showing this, he generates enthusiasm for listening to the Dhamma for the accomplishment of the teaching. Herein, 'Dhamma' refers to the scriptural teachings. 'Reflected upon with the mind' means reflected upon with the mind in such ways as: 'Here virtue is spoken of, here concentration, here wisdom; there are this many connections here,' etc. 'Well penetrated by view' means penetrated by the view that has become reflective acceptance, or by the view called 'full understanding by comprehension,' having thoroughly determined the material and immaterial phenomena spoken of in various places, such as: 'This is material form, this much is material form,' etc.

Sakalena vacanenāti pubbe tīhi padehi visuṃ visuṃ yojitattā vuttaṃ. Attano adahantoti “mameda”nti attani aṭṭhapento. Bhummatthe cetaṃ [M 1.0030] sāmivacanaṃ. Asappurisabhūminti akataññutaṃ. “Idhekacco pāpabhikkhu tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahatī”ti (pārā. 195) evaṃ vuttaṃ anariyavohārāvatthaṃ, sā eva anariyavohārāvatthā asaddhammo[V 1.0027]. Nanu ca ānandattherassa “mamedaṃ vacana”nti adhimānassa, mahākassapattherādīnañca tadāsaṅkāya abhāvato asappurisabhūmi-samatikkamādivacanaṃ niratthakanti? Nayidamevaṃ. “Evaṃ me suta”nti vadantena ayampi attho vibhāvitoti dassanato. Keci pana “devatānaṃ parivitakkāpekkhaṃ tathāvacananti edisī codanā anavakāsā”ti vadanti. Tasmiṃ kira khaṇe ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “bhagavā ca parinibbuto, ayañca āyasmā desanākusalo idāni dhammaṃ deseti, sakyakulappasuto tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto. Kiṃ nu kho sayaṃ sacchikataṃ dhammaṃ deseti? Udāhu bhagavato eva vacanaṃ yathāsuta”nti, evaṃ tadāsaṅkitappakārato asappurisabhūmisamokkamādito atikkamādi vibhāvitanti. Appetīti nidasseti. Diṭṭhadhammika-samparāyika-paramatthesu yathārahaṃ satte netīti netti, dhammo eva netti dhammanetti.

'With the entire utterance' is said because it was previously connected separately with the three phrases. 'Not placing it on oneself' means not establishing it in oneself as 'this is mine.' This genitive has the sense of the locative. 'The plane of the ignoble' means ingratitude. The state of ignoble conduct spoken of thus, 'Here, some bad bhikkhu, having learned the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, claims it for himself' (Pārā 195), that very state of ignoble conduct is the bad Dhamma. Now, is not the statement about transcending the plane of the ignoble, etc., meaningless, since there was no conceit in the Elder Ānanda of thinking 'This is my utterance,' nor any such suspicion on the part of the great elders like Mahākassapa? This is not so. For by saying 'Thus have I heard,' this meaning is also made clear for the purpose of explanation. Some, however, say: 'Such a charge is baseless, for that statement was made in consideration of the thoughts of the devas.' At that moment, it is said, a thought arose in the minds of some devas: 'The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, and this venerable one, skilled in teaching, now teaches the Dhamma. He is born of the Sakyan clan, the son of the Tathāgata's paternal uncle. Now, is he teaching a Dhamma he has realized himself? Or is it the Blessed One's own utterance as he heard it?' Thus, the transcending, etc., of the plane of the ignoble is clarified by dispelling the suspicion that arose in this way. 'He applies' means he shows. Because it leads beings to the goals of this life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, as is fitting, it is a guide (netti); the Dhamma itself is the guide, the Dhamma-guide.

Daḷhataraniviṭṭhā vicikicchā kaṅkhā, nātisaṃsappanā matibhedamattā vimati. Assaddhiyaṃ vināsetīti bhagavatā bhāsitattā sammukhāvassa paṭiggahitattā khalitaduruttādigahaṇadosābhāvato ca. Ettha ca paṭhamādayo tisso atthayojanā ākārādiatthesu aggahitavisesameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā dassitā, tato parā catasso ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vibhāvitā. Pacchimā pana tisso yathākkamaṃ ākāratthaṃ nidassanatthaṃ avadhāraṇatthañca evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā yojitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Kaṅkhā is doubt (vicikicchā) that is more firmly settled; vimati is a mere difference of opinion that does not spread very far. It destroys faithlessness because it was spoken by the Blessed One, because it was accepted in his presence, and because there is no fault of taking up what is mistaken, badly spoken, etc. Herein, the first three applications of the meaning are shown by taking the word 'thus' without grasping a specific sense among its meanings of mode, etc. The next four are explained by taking the word 'thus' only in the sense of mode. The final three, however, should be understood as being applied by taking the word 'thus' in the sense of mode, illustration, and determination, respectively.

Eka-saddo aññaseṭṭhaasahāyasaṅkhayādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.27) aññatthe dissati. “Cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.228; pārā. 11) seṭṭhe, “eko vūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.405) asahāye, “ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) saṅkhayāyaṃ. Idhāpi saṅkhayāyanti dassento āha “ekanti [M 1.0031] gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso”ti. Kālañca samayañcāti yuttakālañca paccayasāmaggiñca. Khaṇoti okāso. Tathāgatuppādādiko hi maggabrahmacariyassa okāso tappaccayassa paṭilābhahetuttā. Khaṇo eva ca samayo, yo khaṇoti ca samayoti ca vuccati, so eko evāti hi attho. Mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Samayopi khoti sikkhāpadapūraṇassa hetupi. Samayappavādaketi diṭṭhippavādake. Tattha hi nisinnā titthiyā attano attano samayaṃ pavadanti. Atthābhisamayāti hitapaṭilābhā. Abhisametabboti abhisamayo, abhisamayo attho abhisamayatthoti pīḷanādīni abhisametabbabhāvena ekībhāvaṃ upanetvā [V 1.0028] vuttāni. Abhisamayassa vā paṭivedhassa visayabhūto attho abhisamayatthoti tāneva tathā ekattena vuttāni. Tattha pīḷanaṃ dukkhasaccassa taṃsamaṅgino hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ, santāpo dukkhadukkhatādivasena santāpanaṃ paridahanaṃ.

The word 'eka' is seen in such meanings as 'other,' 'chief,' 'without a companion,' 'enumeration,' and so on. Thus it is seen in the sense of 'other' in such passages as: 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, anything else is foolish,' as some assert (MN 3.27). In 'unification of mind' (DN 1.228; Pārā. 11), it is used in the sense of 'chief.' In 'alone, withdrawn' (DN 1.405), it is used in the sense of 'without a companion.' In 'There is, bhikkhus, only one moment and occasion for living the holy life' (AN 8.29), it is used in the sense of 'enumeration.' Here too, indicating that it is used in the sense of enumeration, it is said: '“One” is a designation indicating a count and limitation.' 'Time and occasion' means the suitable time and the convergence of conditions. 'Moment' means opportunity. For the arising of a Tathāgata and so on is an opportunity for the path of the holy life, since it is a cause for obtaining the conditions for it. The moment is the same as the occasion. The meaning is that what is called 'moment' and 'occasion' is just one. 'The Great Occasion' means a great assembly. 'Occasion' is also a cause for the fulfillment of the training rules. 'Proponents of occasions' means proponents of views. For there, the sectarians, having sat down, each proclaim their own 'occasion' (i.e., doctrine). 'Breakthrough to the meaning' means the attainment of what is beneficial. 'What is to be fully understood' is a breakthrough. The meaning that is a breakthrough is the 'meaning of the breakthrough.' Thus 'oppression,' etc., are spoken of by bringing them to a state of unity through their quality of being what is to be fully understood. Or, the meaning that is the object of breakthrough or penetration is the 'meaning of the breakthrough'; thus those same things are spoken of in that way as a unity. Therein, 'oppression' refers to the truth of suffering, the affliction of one who possesses it, the causing of injury, the state of not being dispersed. 'Torment' is the scorching, the burning, by way of the suffering due to suffering, etc.

Tattha sahakārikāraṇaṃ sannijjhaṃ sameti samavetīti samayo, samavāyo. Sameti samāgacchati ettha maggabrahmacariyaṃ tadādhārapuggalehīti samayo, khaṇo. Sameti ettha, etena vā saṃgacchati satto, sabhāvadhammo vā sahajātādīhi, uppādādīhi vāti samayo, kālo. Dhammappavattimattatāya atthato abhūtopi hi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ karaṇaṃ viya ca parikappanāmattasiddhena rūpena voharīyatīti. Samaṃ, saha vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samayo, samūho yathā “samudāyo”ti. Avayavasahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūhoti. Avasesapaccayānaṃ samāgame eti phalaṃ etasmā uppajjati pavattati cāti samayo, hetu yathā “samudayo”ti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambandho eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayo, diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhantīti. Samiti saṃgati samodhānanti samayo, paṭilābho. Samassa nirodhassa yānaṃ, sammā vā yānaṃ apagamo apavatti samayo, pahānaṃ. Abhimukhaṃ ñāṇena sammā etabbo adhigantabboti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparīto sabhāvo. Abhimukhabhāvena sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvāvabodho[M 1.0032]. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe samayasaddappavatti veditabbā. Samayasaddassa atthuddhāre abhisamayasaddassa udāharaṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Assāti samayasaddassa. Kālo attho samavāyādīnaṃ atthānaṃ idha asambhavato desadesakaparisānaṃ viya suttassa nidānabhāvena kālassa apadisitabbato ca.

Therein, because the cooperating causes, being present, come together (sameti, samaveti), it is a 'concurrence' (samayo, samavāyo). Because the path and the holy life come together (sameti, samāgacchati) here in the persons who are their support, it is an 'occasion' (samayo), a moment (khaṇo). Because a being or a natural phenomenon comes together (sameti) or coincides (saṅgacchati) here or with this, with its conascent conditions, etc., or with arising, etc., it is 'time' (samayo, kālo). For although time is in reality non-existent, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is spoken of in a form established by mere conceptualization as if it were a basis or instrument for the occurrence of phenomena. Because there is a going (ayanaṃ), occurrence (pavatti), or standing together (avaṭṭhānaṃ) of the parts equally (samaṃ) or together (saha), it is an 'assembly' (samayo, samūho), as in 'collection' (samudāyo). For an assembly is just the standing together of the parts. Because when the remaining conditions come together (samāgame), the fruit comes (eti), arises, and proceeds from it, it is a 'cause' (samayo, hetu), as in 'origin' (samudayo). Because a connection comes together (sameti) in the sense of a fetter, and it proceeds (eti) in its own domain; or because, due to firm grasping, beings yoked by it proceed (ayanti) according to their adherence, it is a 'view' (samayo, diṭṭhi). For beings are very strongly bound by the fetter of views. Because there is a coming together (samiti), a meeting (saṅgati), a convergence (samodhānaṃ), it is an 'attainment' (samayo, paṭilābho). Because it is the going (yānaṃ) to calm and cessation; or the right (sammā) going (yānaṃ), removal, non-occurrence, it is 'abandoning' (samayo, pahānaṃ). Because it is to be rightly gone to (etabbo) and attained (adhigantabbo) directly with knowledge, it is a 'breakthrough' (abhisamayo), the unperverted nature of phenomena. Because one rightly goes (eti, gacchati) and awakens (bujjhati) by facing it directly, it is a 'breakthrough' (abhisamayo), the understanding of the unperverted nature of phenomena. Thus the use of the word 'samaya' in each of these meanings should be understood. In the explanation of the meaning of the word 'samaya,' the example of the word 'abhisamaya' should be understood in the way already stated. 'Of this' means of the word 'samaya.' The meaning is 'time,' because here the meanings 'concurrence,' etc., are not possible, and because time is to be indicated as the basis of the sutta, just as the assemblies of teachers of the different regions are.

Kasmā panettha aniyamitavaseneva kālo niddiṭṭho? Na utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyamitoti āha “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyamaṃ akatvā samayasaddassa vacane ayampi guṇo laddho hotīti dassento “ye vā ime”tiādimāha. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti. Tattha diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo devasikaṃ jhānaphalasamāpattīhi vītināmanakālo, visesato sattasattāhāni. Suppakāsāti dasasahassilokadhātupakampana-obhāsapātubhāvādīhi pākaṭā. Yathāvuttappabhedesu eva samayesu ekadesaṃ pakārantarehi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “yo cāya”ntiādimāha. Tathā hi ñāṇakiccasamayo, attahitapaṭipattisamayo [V 1.0029] ca abhisambodhisamayo, ariyatuṇhībhāvasamayo, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo, karuṇākiccaparahitapaṭipattidhammīkathāsamayā, desanāsamayo eva.

Why is time indicated here in an unfixed way? To show that it is not fixed by way of seasons, years, etc., it is said: 'For although in this case,' etc. To show that by not making a determination by way of seasons, years, etc., this advantage is also gained in the use of the word 'samaya,' it is said: 'or whatever these may be,' etc. For a general indication establishes itself in the particular. Therein, the 'occasion for dwelling happily in this very life' is the time of passing the days with the attainments of jhāna and fruition, especially the seven weeks. 'Well-proclaimed' means made manifest by the quaking of the ten-thousand-world-system, the appearance of a radiance, and so on. To show a portion of the aforesaid kinds of occasions by collecting them in other ways, it is said: 'And this,' etc. For thus there are: the occasion for the task of knowledge and the occasion for the practice for one's own welfare, which is the occasion of perfect enlightenment; the occasion of noble silence; the occasion of dwelling happily in this very life; and the occasions for the task of compassion, the practice for the welfare of others, and talk on the Dhamma, which are indeed the occasion of giving a discourse.

Karaṇavacanena niddeso katoti sambandho. Tatthāti abhidhammatadaññasuttapadavinayesu. Tathāti bhummakaraṇehi. Adhikaraṇattho ādhārattho. Bhāvo nāma kiriyā, tāya kiriyantaralakkhaṇaṃ bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha yathā kālo sabhāvadhammaparicchinno sayaṃ paramatthato avijjamānopi ādhārabhāvena paññāto taṅkhaṇappavattānaṃ tato pubbe parato ca abhāvato “pubbaṇhe jāto, sāyanhe gacchatī”ti ca ādīsu, samūho ca avayavavinimutto visuṃ avijjamānopi kappanāmattasiddho avayavānaṃ ādhārabhāvena paññāpīyati yathā “rukkhe sākhā, yavarāsiyaṃ sambhūto”tiādīsu, evaṃ idhāpīti dassento āha “adhikaraṇañhi…pe… dhammāna”nti. Yasmiṃ kāle, dhammapuñje vā kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ eva kāle dhammapuñje ca phassādayopi hontīti ayaṃ hi tattha attho. Yathā ca “gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato”ti dohanakiriyāya gamanakiriyā lakkhīyati, evaṃ idhāpi yasmiṃ samaye, tasmiṃ samayeti ca vutte [M 1.0033] “satī”ti ayamattho viññāyamāno eva hoti padatthassa sattāvirahābhāvatoti samayassa sattākiriyāya cittassa uppādakiriyā phassādibhavanakiriyā ca lakkhīyati. Yasmiṃ samayeti yasmiṃ navame khaṇe, yasmiṃ yonisomanasikārādihetumhi, paccayasamavāye vā sati kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe, hetumhi, paccayasamavāye vā phassādayopi hontīti ubhayattha samayasadde bhummaniddeso kato lakkhaṇabhūtabhāvayuttoti dassento āha “khaṇa…pe… lakkhīyatī”ti.

The connection is that the indication is made with the instrumental case. 'Therein' means in the Abhidhamma, the other Sutta passages, and the Vinaya. 'Thus' means with the locative and instrumental cases. The meaning of 'basis' (adhikaraṇa) is the meaning of 'receptacle' (ādhāra). 'State' (bhāva) means action (kiriyā); the marking of one action by another action is the 'locative absolute construction' (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇaṃ). Therein, just as time—which is delimited by natural phenomena and is itself ultimately non-existent—is designated as a basis because of the non-existence of what precedes and follows the things occurring at that moment, as in 'born in the morning, he goes in the evening'; and just as a collection—which is separate from its parts and individually non-existent, being established by mere conceptualization—is designated as a basis for its parts, as in 'a branch on the tree,' 'produced in a heap of barley'; so too here. To show this, it is said: 'For the basis ... of phenomena.' The meaning here is this: 'At what time, or in what collection of phenomena, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises, at that very time, and in that very collection of phenomena, contact and so on also exist.' And just as in 'he went while the cows were being milked; he came when they had been milked,' the action of going is marked by the action of milking, so too here, when it is said 'at what time ... at that time,' the meaning 'being' (sati) is understood because the meaning of the word is not devoid of existence. Thus, by the action of the existence of the time, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the occurrence of contact, etc., are marked. 'At what time' means: when there is the ninth moment, or when there is a cause such as wise attention, or when there is a convergence of conditions, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises; at that very moment, or when there is that cause, or that convergence of conditions, contact and so on also exist. To show that in both places the word 'samaya' is given a locative indication because it is connected with a state that serves as a mark, it is said: 'the moment ... is marked.'

Hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati “annena vasati, vijjāya vasati, pharasunā chindati, kudālena khaṇatī”tiādīsu viya. Vītikkamañhi sutvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā otiṇṇavatthukaṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā vigarahitvā ca taṃ taṃ vatthuotiṇṇakālaṃ anatikkamitvā teneva kālena sikkhāpadāni paññapento bhagavā viharati sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno tatiyapārājikādīsu viya.

The meaning of 'cause' and 'instrument' are both possible, as in such examples as: 'He lives by means of food,' 'he lives by means of knowledge,' 'he cuts with an axe,' 'he digs with a spade.' For, having heard of a transgression, the Blessed One has the Sangha of bhikkhus assembled, questions the person who committed the offense, and after reproving him, without letting the time when that offense was committed pass by, he dwells laying down the training rules at that very time, having regard for the reason for laying down the training rule, as in the case of the third pārājika offense and so on.

Accantameva ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva desanāniṭṭhānaṃ. Parahitapaṭipattisaṅkhātena karuṇāvihārena. Tadatthajotanatthanti accantasaṃyogatthajotanatthaṃ. Upayoganiddeso kato yathā “māsaṃ sajjhāyatī”ti[V 1.0030]. Porāṇāti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Abhilāpamattabhedoti vacanamattena viseso. Tena suttavinayesu vibhattibyattayo katoti dasseti.

Continuously, from the beginning right up to the conclusion of the discourse. With the abiding in compassion, which is reckoned as the practice for the welfare of others. 'To illuminate that meaning' means to illuminate the meaning of continuous connection. An indication of extent is made, as in 'he recites for a month.' 'The ancients' means the commentary teachers. 'A difference in mere designation' means a distinction in wording only. He shows that thereby an interchange of case endings is made in the Suttas and the Vinaya.

Seṭṭhanti seṭṭhavācakaṃ vacanaṃ “seṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato, tathā “uttama”nti etthāpi. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogato, garukaraṇārahatāya vā gāravayutto. Vuttoyeva, na pana idha vattabbo visuddhimaggassa imissā aṭṭhakathāya ekadesabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

'Chief' (seṭṭha): the word expressive of what is chief is called 'chief' because it accompanies the quality of being chief; similarly also in the case of 'supreme' (uttama). 'Connected with gravity' (gāravayutto) means endowed with the state of gravity because of its connection with the quality of gravity, or it is 'connected with gravity' because it is worthy of being made grave (i.e., respected). It has already been stated. The intention is that it should not be stated here again, because the Visuddhimagga is a part of this commentary.

Aparo nayo (itivu. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā; sārattha. ṭī. 1.1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.144) – bhāgavāti bhagavā, bhatavāti bhagavā, bhāge vanīti bhagavā, bhage vanīti bhagavā, bhattavāti bhagavā, bhage vamīti bhagavā, bhāge vamīti bhagavā.

Another method (Itivuttaka Aṭṭhakathā, Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā; Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 1.1, Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā 1.144): He is Bhagavā as one who possesses portions (bhāgavā), as one who has cultivated (bhatavā), as one who frequented portions (bhāge vanī), as one who desired portions (bhage vanī), as one who has partaken (bhattavā), as one who emitted portions (bhage vamī), and as one who emitted portions (bhāge vamī).

“Bhāgavā [M 1.0034] bhatavā bhāge, bhage ca vani bhattavā;

Bhage vami tathā bhāge, vamīti bhagavā jino”.

“Because he possessed portions, cultivated, frequented portions,

Partook, emitted portions, and again emitted them,

The Victor is for these reasons called the Bhagavā.”

Tattha kathaṃ bhāgavāti bhagavā? Ye te sīlādayo dhammakkhandhā guṇabhāgā guṇakoṭṭhāsā, te anaññasādhāraṇā niratisayā tathāgate atthi upalabbhanti. Tathā hissa sīlaṃ samādhi paññā vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ, hirī ottappaṃ, saddhā vīriyaṃ, sati sampajaññaṃ, sīlavisuddhi diṭṭhivisuddhi, samatho vipassanā, tīṇi kusalamūlāni, tīṇi sucaritāni, tayo sammāvitakkā, tisso anavajjasaññā, tisso dhātuyo, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, cattāro ariyamaggā, cattāri ariyaphalāni, catasso paṭisambhidā, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇāni, cattāro ariyavaṃsā, cattāri vesārajjañāṇāni, pañca padhāniyaṅgāni, pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi, pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhi, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, pañca nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, pañca vimuttāyatanañāṇāni, pañca vimuttiparipācanīyā saññā, cha anussatiṭṭhānāni, cha gāravā, cha nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, cha satatavihārā, cha anuttariyāni, cha nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā, cha abhiññā, cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni, satta aparihāniyā dhammā, satta ariyadhammā, satta ariyadhanāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, satta sappurisadhammā, satta nijjaravatthūni, satta saññā, sattadakkhiṇeyyapuggaladesanā, sattakhīṇāsavabaladesanā, aṭṭhapaññāpaṭilābhahetudesanā aṭṭha sammattāni, aṭṭhalokadhammātikkamo, aṭṭha [V 1.0031] ārambhavatthūni, aṭṭhaakkhaṇadesanā, aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā, aṭṭhaabhibhāyatanadesanā, aṭṭha vimokkhā, nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni, navasattāvāsadesanā, nava āghātapaṭivinayā, nava saññā, navanānattā, nava anupubbavihārā, dasa nāthakaraṇā dhammā, dasa kasiṇāyatanāni, dasa kusalakammapathā, dasa sammattāni, dasa ariyavāsā, dasa asekkhadhammā, dasa tathāgatabalāni, ekādasa mettānisaṃsā, dvādasa dhammācakkākārā, terasa dhutaguṇā, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, pañcadasa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā, soḷasavidhā ānāpānassati, soḷasa aparantapanīyā dhammā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni, paññāsa udayabbayañāṇāni, paropaññāsa kusalā dhammā, sattasattati ñāṇavatthūni, catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhasamāpattisañcārimahāvajirañāṇaṃ[M 1.0035], anantanayasamantapaṭṭhāna-pavicaya-paccavekkhaṇadesanāñāṇāni, tathā anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantānaṃ sattānaṃ āsayādivibhāvanañāṇāni cāti evamādayo anantāparimāṇabhedā anaññasādhāraṇā niratisayā guṇabhāgā guṇakoṭṭhāsā saṃvijjanti upalabbhanti, tasmā yathāvuttavibhāgā guṇabhāgā assa atthīti “bhāgavā”ti vattabbe ākārassa rassattaṃ katvā “bhagavā”ti vutto. Evaṃ tāva bhāgavāti bhagavā.

Herein, how is he Bhagavā in the sense of 'one who possesses portions' (bhāgavā)? Those aggregates of qualities beginning with virtue, which are portions of excellence and divisions of virtue, exist and are found in the Tathāgata as unique and unsurpassed. For indeed, his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation; his moral shame and moral dread; his faith, energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension; purity of virtue and purity of view; serenity and insight; the three wholesome roots; the three kinds of good conduct; the three right thoughts; the three blameless perceptions; the three elements; the four foundations of mindfulness; the four right efforts; the four bases of spiritual power; the four noble paths; the four noble fruits; the four analytical knowledges; the knowledges that comprehend the four modes of generation; the four noble lineages; the four kinds of intrepidity; the five factors of striving; the five-factored right concentration; the five-knowledged right concentration; the five faculties; the five powers; the five elements of escape; the five knowledges of the bases of liberation; the five perceptions that mature liberation; the six stations of recollection; the six grounds for respect; the six elements of escape; the six constant abidings; the six unsurpassed things; the six perceptions leading to penetration; the six direct knowledges; the six uncommon knowledges; the seven principles of non-decline; the seven noble qualities; the seven noble treasures; the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven qualities of a superior person; the seven grounds for dispelling; the seven perceptions; the seven designations of persons worthy of offerings; the seven designations of the powers of one whose taints are destroyed; the eight designations of the causes for obtaining wisdom; the eight rightnesses; the eight transcendences of worldly conditions; the eight grounds for initiative; the eight designations of inopportune moments; the eight thoughts of a great man; the eight designations of the spheres of mastery; the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention; the nine factors of striving for purity; the nine designations of the abodes of beings; the nine ways of removing resentment; the nine perceptions; the nine kinds of diversity; the nine successive abidings; the ten qualities that make a protector; the ten kasiṇa bases; the ten wholesome courses of action; the ten rightnesses; the ten noble abodes; the ten qualities of one beyond training; the ten powers of the Tathāgata; the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma; the thirteen ascetic qualities; the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha; the fifteen qualities that mature liberation; the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing; the sixteen qualities that prevent future anxiety; the eighteen qualities of a Buddha; the nineteen reflective knowledges; the forty-four bases of knowledge; the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away; the more than fifty wholesome states; the seventy-seven bases of knowledge; the great diamond-like knowledge that ranges through meditative attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand crores; the knowledges for teaching that involve investigation and reflection upon the Conditional Relations with its infinite methods; and the knowledges for discerning the inclinations and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—such and other countless, immeasurable, unique, unsurpassed portions of excellence and divisions of virtue are found and exist in him. Therefore, because he possesses these portions of excellence with their described divisions, while the term should be 'Bhāgavā' (possessor of portions), the long vowel is shortened and he is called 'Bhagavā'. Thus, in this way, he is Bhagavā in the sense of 'one who possesses portions'.

“Yasmā sīlādayo sabbe, guṇabhāgā asesato;

Vijjanti sugate tasmā, bhagavāti pavuccati”.

“Because all portions of qualities, beginning with virtue,

Are found completely in the Sugata,

Therefore he is called the Bhagavā.”

Kathaṃ bhatavāti bhagavā? Ye te sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpannehi manussattādike aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā sammāsambodhiyā katamahābhinīhārehi mahābodhisattehi paripūritabbā dānapāramī, sīla, nekkhamma, paññā, vīriya, khanti, sacca, adhiṭṭhāna, mettā, upekkhāpāramīti dasa pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsa pāramiyo, dānādīni cattāri saṅgahavatthūni, saccādīni cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni, aṅgapariccāgo, jīvita, rajja, putta, dārapariccāgoti pañca mahāpariccāgā, pubbayogo, pubbacariyā, dhammakkhānaṃ, ñātatthacariyā, lokatthacariyā, buddhicariyāti evamādayo, saṅkhepato vā sabbe puññañāṇasambhārā buddhakaradhammā, te mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya kappānaṃ satasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni yathā hānabhāgiyā saṃkilesabhāgiyā ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na honti, atha kho uttaruttari visesabhāgiyāva honti, evaṃ sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ anavasesato bhatā sambhatā assa atthīti “bhatavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vutto niruttinayena ta-kārassa ga-kāraṃ katvā[V 1.0032]. Atha vā bhatavāti teyeva yathāvutte buddhakaradhamme vuttanayeneva bhari, sambhari, paripūresīti attho. Evampi bhatavāti bhagavā.

How is he Bhagavā in the sense of 'one who has cultivated' (bhatavā)? Those Buddha-making qualities that must be fulfilled by great bodhisattvas who have made the great resolve for perfect self-enlightenment—having brought together the eight factors beginning with human existence for the welfare of the entire world—namely: the ten perfections, the ten sub-perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections, thus thirty perfections in total; the four bases of sympathy; the four determinations of wisdom, truth, relinquishment, and peace; the five great sacrifices of limbs, life, kingdom, children, and wife; former application, former conduct, proclaiming the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of relatives, conduct for the welfare of the world, and conduct of a Buddha; and in brief, all the accumulations of merit and knowledge that are the Buddha-making qualities. From the time of his great resolve, for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more, he cultivated and accumulated these qualities so that they were not connected with decline, defilement, or stagnation, but were instead connected with ever-higher distinction. Because he carefully, continuously, and completely cultivated and accumulated them, while he should be called 'Bhatavā', he is called 'Bhagavā' by changing the letter 't' to 'g' according to the rules of etymology.
