Alternatively, 'bhatavā' means that he bore, accumulated, and fulfilled those same Buddha-making qualities in the way described. In this way too, he is Bhagavā in the sense of 'one who has cultivated'.

“Sammāsambodhiyā sabbe, dānapāramiādike;

Sambhāre bhatavā nātho, tasmāpi bhagavā mato”.

“The Protector cultivated all the provisions for perfect self-enlightenment, such as the perfection of giving; therefore, he is considered the Bhagavā.”

Kathaṃ bhāge vanīti bhagavā? Ye te catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā devasikaṃ vaḷañjanakasamāpattibhāgā, te anavasesato lokahitatthaṃ [M 1.0036] attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ niccakappaṃ vani, bhaji, sevi, bahulamakāsīti bhāge vanīti bhagavā. Atha vā abhiññeyyadhammesu kusalādīsu khandhādīsu ca ye te pariññeyyādivasena saṅkhepato vā catubbidhā abhisamayabhāgā, vitthārato pana “cakkhu pariññeyyaṃ sotaṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ pariññeyya”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.21) aneke pariññeyyabhāgā, “cakkhussa samudayo pahātabbo…pe… jarāmaraṇassa samudayo pahātabbo”tiādinā pahātabbabhāgā, “cakkhussa nirodho…pe… jarāmaraṇassa nirodho sacchikātabbo”tiādinā sacchikātabbabhāgā, “cakkhunirodhagāminīpaṭipadā”tiādinā, “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā ca anekabhedā bhāvetabbabhāgā ca dhammā, te sabbe vani, bhaji, yathārahaṃ gocarabhāvanāsevanānaṃ vasena sevi. Evampi bhāge vanīti bhagavā. Atha vā “ye ime sīlādayo dhammakkhandhā sāvakehi sādhāraṇā guṇakoṭṭhāsā guṇabhāgā, kinti nu kho te vineyyasantānesu patiṭṭhapeyya”nti mahākaruṇāya vani abhipatthayi, sā cassa abhipatthanā yathādhippetaphalāvahā ahosi. Evampi bhāge vanīti bhagavā.

How is he Bhagavā in the sense of ‘one who frequented portions’ (bhāge vanī)? Those portions of meditative attainment for daily use, numbering twenty-four hundred thousand crores—he desired, frequented, cultivated, and made much of them completely and constantly, for the welfare of the world and for his own pleasant abiding in this very life. Thus, he is Bhagavā because he frequented portions. Or again: in the phenomena to be directly known, such as the wholesome, and in the aggregates, etc., there are the fourfold portions of realization. In detail, there are the many portions to be fully understood, as in: “The eye is to be fully understood, the ear… aging-and-death is to be fully understood”; the portions to be abandoned, as in: “The origin of the eye is to be abandoned… the origin of aging-and-death is to be abandoned”; the portions to be realized, as in: “The cessation of the eye… the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized”; and the many kinds of portions to be developed, as in: “The path leading to the cessation of the eye,” and “The four establishments of mindfulness.” All these he sought, frequented, and cultivated appropriately by way of engagement, development, and practice. In this way too, he is Bhagavā because he frequented portions. Or again, how is he Bhagavā in the sense of ‘one who desired portions’ (bhāge vanī)? With great compassion he desired and wished, “How can I establish in the minds of trainable beings these aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue, these common portions of excellence, these divisions of virtue?” And that aspiration of his bore the intended fruit. In this way too, he is Bhagavā because he desired portions.

“Yasmā ñeyyasamāpatti-guṇabhāge tathāgato;

Bhaji patthayi sattānaṃ, hitāya bhagavā tato”.

“Because the Tathāgata frequented and desired the portions of qualities, the knowable, and attainments, for the welfare of beings, he is therefore Bhagavā.”

Kathaṃ bhage vanīti bhagavā? Samāsato tāva katapuññehi payogasampannehi yathāvibhavaṃ bhajīyantīti bhagā, lokiyalokuttarasampattiyo. Tattha lokiye tāva tathāgato sammāsambodhito pubbe bodhisattabhūto paramukkaṃsagate, vani, bhaji, sevi, yattha patiṭṭhāya niravasesato buddhakaradhamme samannānento buddhadhamme paripācesi, buddhabhūto pana te niravajjesu upasaṃhite anaññasādhāraṇe lokuttarepi, vani, bhaji, sevi, vitthārato pana padesarajja-issariyacakkavattisampatti-devarajjasampattiādivasena jhāna-vimokkha-samādhisamāpatti-ñāṇadassana-maggabhāvanā-phalasacchi-kiriyādi-uttarimanussadhammavasena [V 1.0033] ca anekavihite anaññasādhāraṇe, bhage, vani, bhaji, sevi. Evampi bhage vanīti bhagavā.

How is he Bhagavā in the sense of ‘one who frequented portions’ (bhage vanī)? In brief, worldly and supramundane accomplishments are called ‘fortunes’ or ‘portions’ (bhagā) because they are partaken of according to one’s ability by those who have performed meritorious deeds and are endowed with application. Among these, in the worldly sphere, the Tathāgata, before his perfect self-enlightenment while he was a bodhisatta, sought, frequented, and cultivated the supreme state. Established in that state, he brought the Buddha-making qualities to maturity and perfected the qualities of a Buddha. Then, having become a Buddha, he also sought, frequented, and cultivated those blameless, unique supramundane fortunes. In detail, he sought, frequented, and cultivated the many kinds of unique fortunes, such as the accomplishment of regional kingship, sovereignty, and universal rulership, the accomplishment of divine kingship, and also the superior human states such as the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, meditative attainments, knowledge and vision, the development of the path, and the realization of the fruit. Thus, he is Bhagavā because he frequented portions.

“Yā [M 1.0037] tā sampattiyo loke, yā ca lokuttarā puthu;

Sabbā tā bhaji sambuddho, tasmāpi bhagavā mato”.

“Whatever worldly accomplishments there are, and the various supramundane ones; the Perfectly Enlightened One has partaken of them all, therefore he is considered the Bhagavā.”

Kathaṃ sattavāti bhagavā? Bhattā daḷhabhattikā assa bahū atthīti bhattavā. Tathāgato hi mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādi-aparimitanirupamappabhāva-guṇavisesasamaṅgibhāvato sabbasattuttamo, sabbānatthaparihārapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantupakāritāya dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasīti anubyañjanabyāmappabhādi anaññasādhāraṇavisesapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya yathābhuccaguṇādhigatena “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinayappavattena lokattayabyāpinā suvipulena suvisuddhena ca thutighosena samannāgatattā ukkaṃsapāramippattāsu appicchatāsantuṭṭhiādīsu suppatiṭṭhitabhāvato dasabalacatuvesārajjādi-niratisayaguṇavisesa-samaṅgībhāvato ca rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno, ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno, lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno, dhammappamāṇo dhammappasannoti evaṃ catuppamāṇike lokasannivāse sabbathāpi pasādāvahabhāvena samantapāsādikattā aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ sadevamanussānaṃ ādarabahumānagāravāyatanatāya paramapemasambhattiṭṭhānaṃ. Ye tassa ovāde patiṭṭhitā aveccappasādena samannāgatā honti, kenaci asaṃhāriyā tesaṃ pasādabhatti samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā. Tathā hi te attano jīvitapariccāgepi tattha pasādaṃ na pariccajanti, tassa vā āṇaṃ daḷhabhattibhāvato.

How is the Bhagavā one who has devotees (bhattavā)? Because he has many devotees with steadfast devotion, he is called bhattavā. Indeed, the Tathāgata is the supreme among all beings, for he possesses an immeasurable, incomparable, and powerful array of special qualities, such as great compassion and the knowledge of omniscience. He is the supreme object of reverence, respect, and honor for countless beings, gods and humans alike, and the basis for their utmost love and devotion. This is due to his unsurpassed accomplishment in striving, which is dedicated to providing for their complete welfare and happiness, preceded by the removal of all that is unbeneficial; due to his being extremely helpful to the populace of gods and humans; due to his physical body being adorned with unique special features not shared by others, such as the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura; due to his being endowed with a vast and utterly pure renown that pervades the three worlds, a renown that has arisen from the realization of his qualities as they truly are, expressed in such ways as, ‘Indeed, the Bhagavā is so...’; due to his being perfectly established in such qualities as fewness of wishes and contentment, which have reached the pinnacle of perfection; and due to his possessing such unsurpassed special qualities as the ten powers and the four kinds of fearlessness. Thus, in this world with its four standards of measure—those who measure by form and are pleased by form, those who measure by voice and are pleased by voice, those who measure by austerity and are pleased by austerity, and those who measure by the Dhamma and are pleased by the Dhamma—he is universally inspiring, arousing confidence in every way. Those who are established in his instruction become endowed with unwavering confidence, and their faith and devotion cannot be shaken by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, by Māra, or by Brahmā. Indeed, even at the cost of their own lives they would not abandon their faith in him, so firm is their devotion to his command.

Tenevāha –

Therefore it is said:

“Yo ve kataññū katavedi dhīro;

Kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hotī”ti. (jā. 2.17.78);

“One who is grateful, who knows what has been done, a wise one; a good friend, and steadfast in devotion.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāsamuddo ṭhitadhammo velaṃ nātivattati, evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (udā. 45; cūḷava. 385) ca. –

“Just as, bhikkhus, the great ocean is of a stable nature and does not transgress its shoreline, even so, bhikkhus, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.”

Evaṃ [V 1.0034][M 1.0038] bhattavāti bhagavā niruttinayena ekassa ta-kārassa lopaṃ katvā itarassa ga-kāraṃ katvā.

Thus, bhattavā becomes bhagavā by the method of etymology: by eliding one letter ‘t’ and changing the other to a ‘g’.

“Guṇātisayayuttassa, yasmā lokahitesino;

Sambhattā bahavo satthu, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“Because many are devoted to the Teacher, who is endowed with surpassing qualities and seeks the world’s welfare, for that reason he is called Bhagavā.”

Kathaṃ bhage vamīti bhagavā? Yasmā tathāgato bodhisattabhūtopi aparimāṇāsu jātīsu pāramiyo paripūrento bhagasaṅkhātaṃ siriṃ issariyaṃ yasañca vami uggiri, kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍayi, carimattabhāvepi hatthagataṃ cakkavattisiriṃ devalokādhipaccasadisaṃ catudīpissariyaṃ cakkavattisampattisannissayaṃ sattaratanasamujjalaṃ yasañca tiṇāyapi amaññamāno nirapekkho pahāya abhinikkhamitvā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tasmā ime sirīādike bhage vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā, sineruyugandharauttarakuruhimavantādibhājanalokavisesasannissayā sobhā kappaṭṭhiyabhāvato, tepi bhagavā vami tannivāsisattāvāsasamatikkamato tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahīti. Evampi bhage vamīti bhagavā.

How is he Bhagavā in the sense that he has emitted fortunes (bhage vamī)? Because the Tathāgata, even when he was a bodhisatta fulfilling the perfections through countless births, emitted—discharged without concern like a lump of spittle—the fortune (bhaga) comprising glory, sovereignty, and fame. And in his final existence, regarding as no more than a blade of grass the glory of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands—a sovereignty over the four continents equal to lordship in the world of the devas, the splendor of the seven treasures, and fame—he renounced it all without attachment, went forth, and awakened to perfect self-enlightenment. Therefore, because he emitted these fortunes such as glory, he is Bhagavā. Or alternatively, bhāni is a name for the constellations. Things that go along with them are bhagā. The splendors of the receptacle world, which are dependent on special regions such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavanta, are called bhagā because they last for an eon. The Bhagavā emitted even these by transcending the abodes of the beings dwelling there, by having abandoned the desire and lust connected with them. In this way too, he is Bhagavā because he has emitted fortunes.

“Cakkavattisiriṃ yasmā, yasaṃ issariyaṃ sukhaṃ;

Pahāsi lokacittañca, sugato bhagavā tato”.

“Because the Sugata abandoned the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, fame, sovereignty, and happiness, and the worldly mind as well, therefore he is the Bhagavā.”

Kathaṃ bhāge vamīti bhagavā? Bhāgā nāma sabhāgadhammakoṭṭhāsā, te khandhāyatanadhātādivasena, tatthāpi rūpavedanādivasena pathaviyādivasena atītādivasena ca anekavidhā, te ca bhagavā sabbaṃ papañcaṃ sabbaṃ yogaṃ sabbaṃ ganthaṃ sabbaṃ saṃyojanaṃ samucchinditvā amatadhātuṃ samadhigacchanto vami uggiri, anapekkho chaḍḍayi na paccāvami. Tathā hesa “sabbatthakameva pathaviṃ āpaṃ tejaṃ vāyaṃ, cakkhuṃ sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhaṃ kāyaṃ manaṃ, rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe dhamme, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ, cakkhusamphassaṃ…pe… manosamphassaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ saññaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ saññaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ cetanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ cetanaṃ, rūpataṇhaṃ…pe… dhammataṇhaṃ, rūpavitakkaṃ…pe… dhammavitakkaṃ, rūpavicāraṃ…pe… dhammavicāra”ntiādinā anupadadhammavibhāgavasenapi sabbeva dhammakoṭṭhāse anavasesato vami uggiri, anapekkhapariccāgena chaḍḍayi. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃ [M 1.0039] taṃ, ānanda, cattaṃ vantaṃ muttaṃ pahīnaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ tathāgato puna paccāvamissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.183). Evampi [V 1.0035] bhāge vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāge vamīti sabbepi kusalākusale sāvajjānavajje hīnapaṇīte kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme ariyamaggañāṇamukhena vami uggiri, anapekkho pariccaji pajahi, paresañca tathattāya dhammaṃ desesi. Vuttampi cetaṃ “dhammāpi vo, bhikkhave, pahātabbā, pageva adhammā (ma. ni. 1.240). Kullūpamaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāyā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.240). Evampi bhāge vamīti bhagavā.

How is he Bhagavā in the sense that he emitted portions (`bhāge vamī`)? `Bhāgas` are divisions of phenomena having a common nature, namely, the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so on. These are of many kinds: in terms of form, feeling, etc.; in terms of earth, etc.; and in terms of past, etc. The Blessed One, while attaining the deathless element, emitted and discharged all these, having cut off all proliferation, all yokes, all bonds, and all fetters; he discarded them without concern and did not take them up again. Thus, by way of a detailed analysis of phenomena term by term, he emitted and discharged without remainder all these divisions of phenomena: earth, water, fire, air; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, mental phenomena; eye-consciousness… mind-consciousness; eye-contact… mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact… feeling born of mind-contact; perception born of eye-contact… perception born of mind-contact; volition born of eye-contact… volition born of mind-contact; craving for forms… craving for mental phenomena; thought on forms… thought on mental phenomena; examination of forms… examination of mental phenomena. He cast them away by relinquishing them without concern. For it has been said: “Ānanda, it is impossible that the Tathāgata would take back that which has been given up, emitted, released, abandoned, and relinquished” (DN 16). In this way, too, he is Bhagavā because he emitted portions. Or alternatively, in the sense that he emitted portions: by means of the knowledge of the noble path, he emitted, discharged, relinquished, and abandoned all things—wholesome and unwholesome, blameable and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and bright with their counterparts. And he taught the Dhamma to others so that they too could become thus. For it has been said: “Bhikkhus, even teachings are to be abandoned, how much more so wrong teachings” (MN 22). And: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping” (MN 22). In this way, too, he is Bhagavā because he emitted portions.

“Khandhāyatanadhātādi-dhammabhāgā-mahesinā;

Kaṇhasukkā yato vantā, tatopi bhagavā mato”.

“Since the divisions of phenomena—the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so on, both dark and bright—have been emitted by the Great Sage, therefore he is considered the Bhagavā.”

Tena vuttaṃ –

Therefore it was said:

“Bhāgavā bhatavā bhāge, bhage ca vani bhattavā;

Bhage vami tathā bhāge, vamīti bhagavā jino”ti.

“He was fortunate (`bhāgavā`), was honored (`bhattavā`), and analyzed the portions (`bhāge`); being honored, he conquered craving for the portions; he emitted the portions (`bhage vami`); thus, because he emitted the portions (`bhāge vamī`), the Victor is the Bhagavā.”

Dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karotīti “yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti vacanato dhammassa satthubhāvapariyāyo vijjatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo parehi abhejjasarīrattā. Na hi bhagavato rūpakāye kenaci sakkā antarāyaṃ kātunti. Desanāsampattiṃ niddisati vakkhamānassa sakalassa suttassa “eva”nti nidassanato. Sāvakasampattiṃ niddisati paṭisambhidāppattena pañcasu ṭhānesu bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitena mayā mahāsāvakena sutaṃ, tañca kho mayāva sutaṃ, na anussutaṃ na paraṃparābhatanti imassatthassa dīpanato. Kālasampattiṃ niddisati bhagavāsaddasannidhāne payuttassa samayasaddassa buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitabhāvadīpanato. Buddhuppādaparamā hi kālasampadā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

He makes the Dhamma-body directly perceptible. For it is said: “Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you will be your teacher after I am gone.” This shows that the Dhamma takes the role of the teacher. His physical body is like a mass of diamond, unbreakable by others. Indeed, no one can bring about injury to the Blessed One’s form-body. The perfection of the teaching is indicated by the word “Thus,” which introduces the entire sutta to be spoken. The perfection of the disciples is indicated by the fact that it was heard by “me,” that is, by the great disciple who had attained the analytical knowledges, who was placed by the Blessed One at the head in five respects; and it was heard by me directly, not from hearsay or from tradition. The perfection of time is indicated by the word “time,” used in conjunction with the word “Blessed One,” which shows that the time was adorned by the Buddha’s appearance. For the supreme perfection of time is the appearance of a Buddha. Therefore it is said:

“Kappakasāye kaliyuge, buddhuppādo aho mahacchariyaṃ;

Hutāvahamajjhe jātaṃ, samuditamakarandamaravinda”nti.

“In the age of strife, the dregs of the eon, ah, the appearance of a Buddha is a great wonder! It is like a lotus with abundant nectar born in the midst of a sacrificial fire.”

Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ niddisati guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamabhāvadīpanato garugāravādhivacanabhāvato.

The word “Bhagavā” indicates the perfection of the Teacher, because it reveals his state as the supreme being distinguished by his virtues and because it is an expression of deep respect and reverence.

Avisesenāti [V 1.0036][M 1.0040] na visesena, vihārabhāvasāmaññenāti attho. Iriyāpatha…pe… vihāresūti iriyāpathavihāro, dibbavihāro, brahmavihāro, ariyavihāroti etesu catūsu vihāresu. Samaṅgīparidīpananti samaṅgībhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Etanti “viharatī”ti etaṃ padaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ “idhekacco gihīhi saṃsaṭṭho viharati sahanandī sahasokī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.241) iriyāpathavihāre āgataṃ. “Yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, samaye bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (dha. sa. 160; vibha. 624) ettha dibbavihāre. “So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77; 2.309; 3.230) brahmavihāre. “So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tassāyeva kathāya pariyosāne tasmiṃ eva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi, yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) ariyavihāre.

Not in a particular way, but in the general sense of 'dwelling'—this is the meaning. The 'modes of deportment' (iriyāpatha)... in the 'dwellings' (vihāresu) refers to the dwelling of deportment, the divine dwelling, the brahma dwelling, and the noble dwelling—these four dwellings. The explanation of 'being well-equipped' (samaṅgīparidīpanaṃ) is the explanation of the state of being well-equipped. 'This' refers to the word 'dwells' (viharatī). For thus, it is found in the dwelling of deportment, as in: 'Here, a certain person dwells associating with householders, sharing their joys and sharing their sorrows,' etc. (SN 35.241). In the divine dwelling, as in: 'At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna' (Dhs 160; Vibh 262). In the brahma dwelling, as in: 'He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,' etc. (DN 13, etc.). In the noble dwelling, as in: 'So I, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very talk, steadied my mind internally, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it on that same preliminary sign of concentration, by which I always dwell,' etc. (MN 36).

Tattha iriyanaṃ vattanaṃ iriyā, kāyappayogo. Tassā pavattanupāyabhāvato ṭhānādi iriyāpatho. Ṭhānasamaṅgī vā hi kāyena kiñci kareyya gamanādīsu aññatarasamaṅgī vā. Atha vā iriyati pavattati etena attabhāvo kāyakiccaṃ vāti iriyā, tassā pavattiupāyabhāvato iriyā ca so patho cāti iriyāpatho, ṭhānādi eva. So ca atthato gatinivattiādiākārena pavatto catusantatirūpapabandho eva. Viharaṇaṃ, viharati etenāti vā vihāro, iriyāpatho eva vihāro iriyāpathavihāro. Divi bhavo dibbo, tattha bahulappavattiyā brahmapārisajjādidevaloke bhavoti attho. Tattha yo dibbānubhāvo, tadatthāya saṃvattatīti vā dibbo, abhiññābhinīhāravasena mahāgatikattā vā dibbo, dibbo ca so vihāro cāti dibbavihāro, catasso rūpāvacarasamāpattiyo. Āruppasamāpattiyopi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Brahmūnaṃ, brahmāno vā vihārā brahmavihārā, catasso appamaññāyo. Ariyānaṃ, ariyā vā vihārā ariyavihārā, cattāri sāmaññaphalāni. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanantiādi yadipi bhagavā ekenapi iriyāpathena cirataraṃ kālaṃ attabhāvaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkoti, tathāpi upādinnakasarīrassa nāma ayaṃ sabhāvoti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ[M 1.0041]. Yasmā vā bhagavā yattha katthaci vasanto vineyyānaṃ dhammaṃ desento, nānāsamāpattīhi ca kālaṃ vītināmento vasatīti sattānaṃ attano ca vividhaṃ hitasukhaṃ harati upaneti uppādeti, tasmā vividhaṃ haratīti evamettha attho veditabbo.

Here, 'iriyā' is the act of moving about, the application of the body. Because it is a means of sustaining activity, standing and so forth are called 'iriyāpatha' (modes of deportment). For one endowed with standing, the body performs some action, or one endowed with any of the modes of walking and so forth. Alternatively, 'iriyā' is that by which one's existence or bodily function moves or proceeds; and because it serves as a means of such proceeding, it is called 'iriyāpatha'—a mode of deportment—namely, standing and so forth. In essence, this is simply the continuous flow of the fourfold series of material phenomena, manifesting as movement, cessation, and other forms. 'Viharaṇa' is dwelling, or 'vihāra' is that by which one dwells; thus, 'iriyāpatha' itself is a 'vihāra,' hence 'iriyāpathavihāra' (dwelling in deportment). 'Divine' (dibba) means existing in the divine plane, meaning existing in the celestial realms such as those of the Brahmā's retinue, due to frequent occurrence there. Alternatively, 'dibba' means that which conduces to divine power, or that which is great due to the attainment of supernormal knowledge. Thus, 'dibbavihāra' (divine dwelling) refers to the four meditative attainments of the form realm. The formless attainments are also included here. The dwellings of the Brahmās, or the Brahmā dwellings, are the four illimitables (brahmavihārā). The dwellings of the Noble Ones, or the Noble Ones' dwellings, are the four fruits of recluseship (ariyavihārā). Even if the Blessed One could sustain his bodily existence for a long time using just one posture, it is stated to show that this is the natural condition of a body sustained by clinging. Alternatively, because the Blessed One, dwelling wherever he resides, teaching the Dhamma to those who are trainable and spending time in various meditative attainments, brings, produces, and fosters diverse welfare and happiness for beings and himself, therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'he brings variety' (vividhaṃ harati).

Paccatthike jinātīti jeto. Jeta-saddo hi sota-saddo viya kattusādhanopi atthīti. Rañño [V 1.0037] vā paccatthikānaṃ jitakāle jātattā jeto. Rañño hi attano jayaṃ tattha āropetvā jitavāti jetoti kumāro vutto. Maṅgalakāmatāya vā jetotissa nāmaṃ kataṃ, tasmā “jeyyo”ti etasmiṃ atthe “jeto”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tassa jetassa rājakumārassa. Vanetiādito paṭṭhāyeva taṃ tassa santakanti dassetuṃ “taṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbakāmasamiddhitāya vigatamalamaccheratāya karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca niccakālaṃ upaṭṭhapito anāthānaṃ piṇḍo etassa atthīti anāthapiṇḍiko, tassa anāthapiṇḍikassa. Yadi jetavanaṃ, kathaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmoti āha “anāthapiṇḍikenā”tiādi. Pañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyā āramanti ettha pabbajitāti ārāmo, tasmiṃ ārāme. Yadipi so bhūmibhāgo koṭisantharena mahāseṭṭhinā kīto, rukkhā pana jetena na vikkītāti taṃ “jetavana”nti vattabbataṃ labhatīti vadanti. Ubhinnampi vā tattha pariccāgavisesakittanatthaṃ ubhayavacanaṃ, jetenapi hi bhūmibhāgavikkayena laddhadhanaṃ tattha dvārakoṭṭhakakaraṇavasena viniyuttaṃ. Sāvatthijetavanānaṃ bhūmibhāgavasena bhinnattā vuttaṃ “na hi sakkā ubhayattha ekaṃ samayaṃ viharitu”nti.

'He conquers enemies,' thus he is Jeta. For the word 'Jeta,' like the word 'sota' (stream), can also denote the agent. Or, he is called Jeta because he was born at the time the king had conquered his enemies. For the king, having ascribed his own victory thereto, called the prince 'Jeta,' saying, 'he has conquered.' Or, out of a desire for auspiciousness, the name 'Jeta' was given to him; therefore, it should be understood that in this sense 'Jeta' is said with the meaning of 'Jeyya' (victorious). Of that Prince Jeta. To show that it was his possession from the very beginning, it is said, 'that indeed,' etc. Because a constant supply of alms for the destitute was established by him, due to his fulfillment of all desires, his freedom from the stain of miserliness, and his endowment with qualities like compassion, he was called Anāthapiṇḍika (Feeder of the Destitute). Of that Anāthapiṇḍika. If it is Jeta's Grove, how is it Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery? He answers, 'by Anāthapiṇḍika,' etc. Because the ordained delight in it due to its endowment with the five requisites for a dwelling, it is called a monastery (ārāma). In that monastery. Although that piece of land was bought by the great merchant by paving it with a crore of coins, the trees were not sold by Jeta; therefore, they say it comes to be called 'Jeta’s Grove.' Or, the dual reference is for the sake of extolling the particular act of relinquishment by both, for Jeta, too, used the wealth gained from the sale of the land to construct the gatehouse there. Because Sāvatthī and Jeta's Grove were separate portions of land, it is said: 'For it is not possible to dwell in both places at the same time.'

Apākaṭāti sakko suyāmotiādinā anabhiññātā. Abhiññātānampi aññatarasaddo dissateva ekasadisāyattattāti dassetuṃ “abhijānāti no”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ahunā idāneva. Sādhāraṇavacanaṃ dibbataṃ antonītaṃ katvā. Devo eva devatā purisepi vattanato. Tenevāha “imasmiṃ panatthe”tiādi. Nanu ca rūpāvacarasattānaṃ purisindriyaṃ natthi, yena te purisāti vucceyyuṃ? Yadipi purisindriyaṃ natthi, purisasaṇṭhānassa pana purisavesassa ca vasena purisapuggalātveva vuccanti purisapakatibhāvato.

'Apākaṭā' means 'not well-known,' as in 'Sakko, Suyāmo,' etc., thus not being widely recognized. To show that even among the well-known the word 'aññatara' (a certain one) appears, due to their being of a single likeness, it is said, 'he does not recognize,' etc. 'Ahunā' means 'just now.' The common term 'devatā' is used with the meaning of 'divinity' included within it. 'A deva is indeed a devatā,' since it also applies to males. Therefore, he said, 'but in this sense,' etc. Is it not the case that beings of the form realm lack the male faculty, by which they could be called males? Although the male faculty is absent, they are still called male individuals on account of their male form and male appearance, because of their male nature.

Abhikkantāti [M 1.0042] atikkantā, vigatāti atthoti āha “khaye dissatī”ti. Teneva hi “nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo”ti upari vuttaṃ. Abhikkantataroti ativiya kantataro. Tādiso ca sundaro bhaddako nāma hotīti āha “sundare dissatī”ti. Koti devanāgayakkhagandhabbādīsu ko katamo? Meti mama. Pādānīti pāde. Iddhiyāti imāya evarūpāya deviddhiyā. Yasasāti iminā edisena parivārena paricchadena ca. Jalanti vijjotamāno. Abhikkantenāti ativiya kantena kamaniyena abhirūpena. Vaṇṇenāti chavivaṇṇena sarīravaṇṇanibhāya. Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disāti sabbāpi disā pabhāsento cando viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekālokaṃ karontoti gāthāya attho. Abhirūpeti uḷārarūpe sampannarūpe.

'Abhikkantā' means 'surpassed,' 'gone beyond'; the meaning is 'departed,' thus it is said, 'it is seen in the sense of destruction.' Therefore, 'the first watch has passed' was stated above. 'Abhikkantataro' means 'exceedingly more lovely.' Such a one is called beautiful and excellent; thus it is said, 'it is seen in the sense of beauty.' 'Ko' means 'which one' among gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and others? 'Me' means 'my.' 'Pādāni' means 'the feet.' 'Iddhiyā' means 'by this kind of divine power.' 'Yasasā' means 'by such a retinue and retinue.' 'Jalanti' means 'shining.' 'Abhikkantena' means 'by that which is exceedingly lovely, desirable, and beautiful.' 'Vaṇṇena' means 'by the complexion,' by the lustre of the body's color. 'Illuminating all directions' means illuminating all the directions, like the moon or the sun, making a single radiance, a single light—this is the meaning of the verse. 'Abhirūpe' means 'in a magnificent form, in a perfect form.'

Kañcanasannibhattacatā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaggahaṇena gahitāti adhippāyenāha “chaviya”nti. Chavigatā [V 1.0038] pana vaṇṇadhātu eva “suvaṇṇavaṇṇo”ti ettha vaṇṇaggahaṇena gahitāti apare. Vaṇṇanaṃ kittiyā ugghosananti vaṇṇo, thuti. Vaṇṇīyati asaṅkarato vavatthapīyatīti vaṇṇo, kulavaggo. Vaṇṇīyati phalaṃ etena yathāsabhāvato vibhāvīyatīti vaṇṇo, kāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇanaṃ dīgharassādivasena saṇṭhahananti vaṇṇo, saṇṭhānaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati aṇumahantādivasena pamīyatīti vaṇṇo, pamāṇaṃ. Vaṇṇeti vikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti vaṇṇo, rūpāyatanaṃ. Evaṃ tena tena pavattinimittena vaṇṇasaddassa tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe pavatti veditabbā. Iddhiṃ māpetvāti vatthālaṅkārakāyādīhi obhāsamuñcanādivasena dibbaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ nimminitvā. Kāmāvacarā anabhisaṅkhatenapi āgantuṃ sakkonti oḷārikarūpattā. Tathā hi te kabaḷīkārabhakkhā. Rūpāvacarā na sakkonti tato sukhumatararūpattā. Tenāha “tesaṃ hī”tiādi. Tattha “atisukhumo”ti mūlapaṭisandhirūpaṃ sandhāya vadati. Na tena iriyāpathakappanaṃ hotīti etena brahmalokepi brahmāno yebhuyyena nimmitarūpeneva pavattantīti dasseti. Itarañhi ativiya sukhumaṃ rūpaṃ kevalaṃ cittuppādassa nissayādhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ saṇṭhānavantaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati.

With the intention that 'skin like gold' is grasped by the grasping of a golden color, he says 'by the skin.' Others say that the color element in the skin is itself grasped here by the grasping of color as 'golden-colored.' 'Vaṇṇa' is praise, a proclamation of fame. 'Vaṇṇa' is a class, a caste, as it is distinguished without confusion. 'Vaṇṇa' is a cause, as the fruit is revealed by it according to its nature. 'Vaṇṇa' is form, as it is the establishing of distinctions such as long and short. 'Vaṇṇa' is measure, as it is measured by distinctions such as small and large. 'Vaṇṇa' is the visible-form base, as it reveals the state of having reached the heart which is undergoing change. Thus, the application of the word 'vaṇṇa' in its various meanings should be known according to its respective reasons for application. 'Having created a psychic power' means having created a divine manifestation of psychic power by way of emitting radiance from robes, ornaments, the body, and so on. Beings of the sense-sphere can come even without special preparation because their form is coarse. For they consume physical food. Beings of the form-sphere cannot, because their form is more subtle than that. Therefore, he says 'for them,' etc. Therein, when he says 'extremely subtle,' he speaks in reference to the root rebirth-linking form. By this—'the assumption of postures does not occur by means of it'—he shows that even in the Brahma-world, brahmās for the most part exist by means of a created form. For the other form is exceedingly subtle; it exists merely as a basis and foundation for the arising of consciousness, having a stable nature.

Anavasesattaṃ sakalatā. Yebhuyyatā bahulabhāvo. Abyāmissatā vijātiyena asaṅkaro. Sukhena hi avokiṇṇatā tattha adhippetā[M 1.0043]. Anatirekatā taṃparamatā visesābhāvo. Kevalakappanti kevalaṃ daḷhaṃ katvāti attho. Saṅghabhedāyāti saṅghe vivādāya, vivāduppādāyāti attho. Kevalaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ sabbasaṅkhatavivittattā, etassa taṃ atthīti kevalī, sacchikatanirodho khīṇāsavo. Tenāha “visaṃyogo attho”ti.

'The state of having no remainder' is entirety. 'Preponderance' is abundance. 'Non-mixture' is not being mixed with what is of a different kind. For what is intended there is not being interspersed with suffering. 'Non-excess' is that being the ultimate, the absence of anything special. 'Kevalakappaṃ' means making it entirely firm. 'For schism in the Saṅgha' means for dispute in the Saṅgha, for the arising of dispute. 'Kevala' is said of Nibbāna because it is secluded from all that is conditioned; one who has this is a 'kevalī,' one who has realized cessation, a destroyer of the taints. Therefore, he says, 'the meaning is disassociation.'

Kappasaddo panāyaṃ saupasaggo anupasaggo cāti adhippāyena okappaniyapade labbhamānaṃ kappasaddamattaṃ dasseti, aññathā kappapadaṃ anidassanameva siyā. Samaṇakappehīti vinayasiddhehi samaṇavohārehi. Niccakappanti niccakālaṃ. Paññattīti nāmaṃ. Nāmañhetaṃ tassa āyasmato, yadidaṃ kappoti. Kappitakesamassūti kattarikāya cheditakesamassu. Dvaṅgulakappoti majjhanhikavelāya vītikkantāya dvaṅgulatāvikappo. Lesoti apadeso. Anavasesaṃ pharituṃ samatthassapi obhāsassa kenacipi kāraṇena ekadesapharaṇampi siyā, ayaṃ pana sabbasova pharatīti dassetuṃ samantattho kappa-saddo gahitoti āha “anavasesaṃ samantato”ti. Īsaṃ asamattaṃ, kevalaṃ vā kevalakappaṃ. Bhagavato ābhāya anobhāsitameva hi padesaṃ devatā attano pabhāya obhāsenti. Na hi bhagavato pabhā kāyaci pabhāya abhibhuyyati, sūriyādīnampi pabhaṃ sā abhibhuyya tiṭṭhatīti.

With the intention that this term 'kappa' is found both with and without a prefix, he shows merely the word 'kappa' as it is found in the word 'okappaniya'; otherwise, the word 'kappa' would be without an example. 'By the practices of ascetics' means by the conventions of ascetics established in the Vinaya. 'Niccakappaṃ' means always. 'A designation' means a name. This, namely Kappa, is the name of that venerable one. 'With hair and beard trimmed' means with hair and beard cut with scissors. 'Dvaṅgulakappo' is the allowance of two finger-breadths after the time of midday has passed. 'A pretext' means an excuse. Although a radiance may be capable of pervading without remainder, for some reason it might pervade only a part. But to show that this one pervades entirely, the word 'kappa' is taken in the sense of 'all-encompassing'; thus it is said, 'without remainder, all around.' It can mean 'slightly,' 'incomplete,' or 'entirely,' as in 'kevalakappaṃ' (wholly complete). For deities illuminate with their own radiance only a place not illuminated by the radiance of the Blessed One. Indeed, the radiance of the Blessed One is not overcome by any other radiance; it stands having surpassed even the radiance of the sun and other luminaries.

Yena [V 1.0039] vā kāraṇenāti hetumhi idaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Hetuattho hi kiriyāya kāraṇaṃ, na karaṇaṃ viya kiriyattho, tasmā nānappakāra-guṇavisesādhigamanatthā idha upasaṅkamanakiriyāti “annena vasati, vijjāya vasatī”tiādīsu viya hetuatthameva taṃ karaṇavacanaṃ yuttaṃ na karaṇatthaṃ tassa ayujjamānattāti vuttaṃ “yena vā kāraṇenā”tiādi. Bhagavato satatappavattaniratisaya-sāduvipulamatarasa-saddhammaphalatāya sāduphalaniccaphalitamahārukkhena bhagavā upamito. Sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyaggahaṇeneva hi mahākāruṇikassa sāduphalatā gahitāti. Upasaṅkamīti upasaṅkantā. Sampattakāmatāya hi kiñci ṭhānaṃ gacchanto [M 1.0044] taṃtaṃpadesātikkamanena upasaṅkami, upasaṅkantoti vattabbataṃ labhati. Tenāha “gatāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti, upagatāti attho. Upasaṅkamitvāti pubbakālakiriyāniddesoti āha “upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpana”nti. Tatoti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ pattā “upasaṅkamī”ti vuttā, tato upagataṭṭhānato.

By whatever reason: this is an instrumental expression in the sense of cause. For the meaning of 'cause' is the reason for an action, not, like an 'instrument,' the means of an action. Therefore, since the action of approaching here is for the purpose of attaining various special qualities, this instrumental expression is properly used in the sense of cause—as in such phrases as 'he lives by means of food' and 'he lives by means of knowledge'—and not in the sense of instrument, as that would be unsuitable. Thus it is said, 'by whatever reason,' etc. The Blessed One is compared to a great tree that is always fruitful with sweet fruits, on account of his True Dhamma which is a fruit that is constantly available, unsurpassed, sweet, abundant, and of choice flavor. For the sweet-fruit-like nature of the Greatly Compassionate One is understood simply by grasping the intention to enjoy the sweet fruit. They approached means those who were approaching. For when one goes to some place out of a desire to reach it, by traversing various regions one is said to 'approach,' one obtains the designation 'one who is approaching.' Hence he says, 'it is said "gone,"' the meaning being 'arrived.' Having approached is an indication of a prior action; thus he says, 'it is an illustration of the conclusion of the act of approaching.' From there means from the place they arrived at, which is the place they are said to have 'approached'; from that place they had come to.

Gatinivattiatthato sāmaññato āsanampi ṭhānaggahaṇena gayhatīti vuttaṃ “āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ tiṭṭhantī”ti. Nisinnāpi hi gamanato nivattā nāma honti ṭhatvā nisīditabbattā, yathāvuttaṭṭhānādayopi āsaneneva saṅgahitāti. Atidūraaccāsannapaṭikkhepena nātidūranaccāsannaṃ nāma gahitaṃ. Taṃ pana avakaṃsato ubhinnaṃ pasāritahatthasaṅghaṭṭanena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gīvaṃ pasāretvāti gīvaṃ parivattanavasena pasāretvā.

In the general sense of ceasing movement, standing is also included by the term for posture (āsana); thus it is said: 'being skilled in seating, they stood to one side.' For even those who are seated are said to have ceased from going, because one sits down after having stood. Likewise, the aforesaid positions and so on are included under 'seating.' By the exclusion of what is too far and too close, the phrase 'not too far and not too close' is to be understood. This, in turn, should be seen as the space where the outstretched hands of both would meet. Having stretched their necks means having stretched their necks by way of turning them.

Kāmaṃ “katha”nti ayamākārapucchā, taraṇākāro idha pucchito. So pana taraṇākāro atthato kāraṇamevāti āha “kathaṃ nūti kāraṇapucchā”ti? Pākaṭo abhisambodhiyaṃ mahāpathavīkampanādianekacchariyapātubhāvādinā.

Granted, 'How?' is a question about the mode; here the mode of crossing is being asked. But that mode of crossing is, in meaning, simply the cause; therefore he said: 'How now?' is a question about the cause. He became manifest at his full enlightenment through the appearance of many wonders such as the great earthquake and so on.

Marisanaṭṭhena pāpānaṃ rogādianatthānaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena māriso, dukkharahito. Tenāha “niddukkhāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Nirayapakkhe piyālapanavacanavasena upacāravacanañcetaṃ yathā “devānaṃ piyā”ti. Tenevāha “yadi eva”ntiādi. Saṅkunā saṅkūti matthakato samakoṭṭitena yāva hadayapadesā nibbijjhitvā otiṇṇena saṅkunā pādatalato samakoṭṭito saṅku nibbijjhitvā ārohanto hadaye hadayassa padese samāgaccheyya, atha nesaṃ saṅkūnaṃ samāgamasamakāle naṃ yathātikkantasaṅkukaraṇakālaṃ jāneyyāsi. Kiñci nimittaṃ upādāya kismiñci atthe pavattassa saddassa tannimittarahite pavatti ruḷhī nāma gamanakiriyārahite sāsanādimati paṭipiṇḍe yathā gosaddassa.

Because he crushes evils and overcomes diseases and other misfortunes, he is a mārisa, one devoid of suffering. Therefore it is said: 'This means "without suffering."' In the case of hell, this is a metaphorical expression, a term of endearment, like 'beloved of the devas.' Hence it is said, 'if so,' etc. A stake with a stake: a stake hammered down evenly from the top of the head, having pierced as far as the heart region, would meet at the heart, in the heart region, with a stake hammered up evenly from the sole of the foot, piercing upwards. Then, at the very moment of the meeting of these stakes, you should know that time to be the time of the stake's utmost penetration. The usage of a word—which operates in a certain meaning based on some feature—in the absence of that feature is called ruḷhī, 'conventional usage'; just as the word 'cow' is used for a clay model of a cow that has a dewlap and so on but is devoid of the action of going.

Oghamatarīti [V 1.0040] yesaṃ oghānaṃ taraṇaṃ pucchitaṃ, te gaṇanaparicchedato sarūpato ca dassetuṃ “cattāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kasmā panettha cattāro [M 1.0045] eva oghā vuttā, te ca kāmādayo evāti? Na codetabbametaṃ, yasmā dhammānaṃ sabhāvakiccavisesaññunā bhagavatā sabbaṃ ñeyyaṃ yāthāvato abhisambujjhitvā ettakāva oghā desitā, ime eva ca desitāti. Vaṭṭasmiṃ ohananti osīdāpentīti oghā, ohananti heṭṭhā katvā hananti gāmenti, tathābhūtā satte adho gāmenti nāma. Ayañca attho “sabbopi cesā”tiādinā parato aṭṭhakathāyameva āgamissati. Kāmanaṭṭhena kāmo, kāmo ca so yathāvuttenatthena ogho cāti, kāmesu oghoti vā kāmogho. Bhavogho nāma bhavarāgoti dassetuṃ “rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo jhānanikanti cā”ti vuttaṃ. Sumaṅgalavilāsinīādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.312) pana “sassatadiṭṭhisahagatarāgo cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭhamo upapattibhavesu rāgo, dutiyo kammabhave. Bhavadiṭṭhivinimuttassa diṭṭhigatassa abhāvato. “Dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo diṭṭhogho”ti vuttaṃ, catusaccantogadhattā sabbassa ñeyyassa “catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ avijjogho”ti āha.

He crossed the flood: To show the floods—the crossing of which was asked about—both by numerical definition and by their nature, it is said, 'four,' etc. Why are only four floods mentioned here, and are they only sensuality and so on? This should not be questioned, for the Blessed One, the knower of the specific nature and function of phenomena, having fully awakened to all that is to be known as it really is, taught just this many floods, and taught only these. They are called 'floods' (oghā) because they cause beings to sink down into the round of existence. Ohananti means they strike down, they submerge; thus they are said to submerge beings downwards. This meaning will also be found later in the commentary with the words 'and all of this,' etc. Kāma (sensuality) is so called from its nature of desiring. That desire, in the aforesaid sense, is a flood; or, it is the flood in regard to sensual pleasures, thus kāmogha, the flood of sensuality. To show that the flood of existence (bhavogha) is lust for existence, it is said: 'desire and lust for form and formless existences, and delight in the jhānas.' But in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and other works it is said: 'and lust associated with the view of eternalism.' Therein, the first is lust in regard to rebirth-existences, the second in regard to kamma-existence. This is because for one liberated from the view of existence, there is an absence of wrong view. 'The sixty-two views are the flood of views,' it is said. Because all that is knowable is included within the Four Truths, he said: 'Ignorance concerning the four truths is the flood of ignorance.'

Idāni tesaṃ oghasaṅkhātānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ, pavattiṭṭhānaṃ pana kāmaguṇādayo dassitā eva. “Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu chandarāgo kāmogho”ti ettha bhavoghaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbo lobho kāmoghoti yuttaṃ siyā. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo bhavadiṭṭhisampayuttattā bhavoghoti aṭṭhakathāsu vutto, bhavogho pana diṭṭhigatavippayuttesu eva uppajjatīti pāḷiyaṃ vutto. Tenevāha – “bhavogho catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttalobhasahagatacittuppādesu uppajjatī”ti. Tasmā diṭṭhisahagatalobhopi kāmoghoti yuttaṃ siyā. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikadukkhānañhi kāraṇabhūtā kāmāsavādayopi dvidhā vuttā, āsavā eva ca oghā. Kāmāsavaniddese ca kāmesūti kāmarāgadiṭṭhirāgādīnaṃ ārammaṇabhūtesu tebhūmakesu vatthukāmesūti attho sambhavati. Tattha hi uppajjamānā sāyaṃ taṇhā sabbāpi na kāmacchandādināmaṃ na labhatīti.

Now, to show the place of arising for those evil states called floods, it is said, 'Therein,' etc.; for their sphere of occurrence has already been shown to be the cords of sensual pleasure and so on. In regard to the statement, 'Desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is the flood of sensuality,' it would be reasonable to say that, setting aside the flood of existence, all greed is the flood of sensuality. Lust accompanied by the view of eternalism is called the flood of existence in the commentaries because it is associated with the view of existence; but in the Pāli canon it is said that the flood of existence arises only in states dissociated from views. Hence he says: 'The flood of existence arises in four types of consciousness accompanied by greed that are dissociated from views.' Therefore, it would be reasonable to say that greed accompanied by views is also the flood of sensuality. For the taints of sensuality and so on, which are the cause of suffering in this present life and in future lives, are also spoken of in two ways, and the taints are indeed the floods. And in the exposition of the taint of sensuality, the meaning of 'in sensual pleasures' can be taken as 'in the objects of sensual pleasure in the three planes of existence, which are the objects for sensual lust, lust connected with views, and so on.' For not all craving that arises there obtains the name 'sensual desire,' etc.

Yadi pana pañcakāmaguṇiko ca rāgo kāmoghoti vuttoti katvā brahmānaṃ vimānādīsu rāgassa diṭṭhirāgassa ca kāmoghabhāvo paṭisedhitabbo siyā, evaṃ sati kāmoghabhavoghavinimuttena nāma lobhena bhavitabbaṃ[M 1.0046]. So yadā diṭṭhigatavippayuttesu uppajjati, tadā tena sampayutto avijjogho oghavippayuttoti domanassavicikicchuddhaccasampayuttassa viya tassapi oghavippayuttatā vattabbā siyā “catūsupi diṭṭhigatavippayuttalobhasahagatesu cittuppādesu uppanno moho siyā oghasampayutto siyā oghavippayutto”ti. “Kāmogho aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatesu [V 1.0041] cittuppādesu uppajjatī”ti, “kāmoghaṃ paṭicca diṭṭhogho avijjogho”ti ca vacanato diṭṭhisahagato kāmogho na hotīti na sakkā vattuṃ. Tathā hettha “rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo jhānanikanti ca bhavogho nāmāti ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ sassatadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo”ti.

But if, on the grounds that it is said that lust related to the five cords of sensual pleasure is the flood of sensuality, one were to deny the flood-nature of lust and lust connected with views in regard to the mansions of the Brahmās and so on, then there would have to be a type of greed that is free from the flood of sensuality and the flood of existence. When that greed arises in states dissociated from views, then the flood of ignorance associated with it would have to be called 'dissociated from the floods,' just as one would have to say that delusion associated with displeasure, doubt, and restlessness is dissociated from the floods, as in the statement: 'Delusion that has arisen in the four types of consciousness accompanied by greed dissociated from views may be either associated with the floods or dissociated from the floods.' Because of the statements, 'The flood of sensuality arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed' and 'Conditioned by the flood of sensuality, the flood of views and the flood of ignorance arise,' it cannot be said that greed accompanied by views is not the flood of sensuality. Similarly, here it is said only this much: 'Desire and lust for form and formless existences, and delight in the jhānas, are called the flood of existence'; it is not said, 'lust accompanied by the view of eternalism.'

Adhogamanaṭṭhenāti heṭṭhāpavattanaṭṭhena. Heṭṭhāpavattanañcettha na kevalaṃ apāyagamaniyabhāvena, atha kho saṃsāratarakāvarodhanenapīti dassetuṃ “uparibhavañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ nibbānaṃ arūpibhāvā adesaṃ, na tassa ṭhānavasena uparigahaṇaṃ, sabbasaṅkhatavinissaṭattā pana sabbassapi bhavassa uparīti vattabbataṃ arahatīti katvā vuttaṃ “uparibhavaṃ nibbāna”nti. “Mahāudakogho”tiādīsu rāsaṭṭho ogha-saddoti “mahā heso kilesarāsī”ti vuttaṃ sesesupīti bhavoghādīsupi.

By 'descending' is meant the state of falling downwards. Here, falling downwards is not only in the sense of leading to the lower realms, but also to show the obstruction to crossing saṃsāra, and thus it is said, 'and the higher existence,' and so on. Although Nibbāna is formless and without a place, it is not taken as 'higher' in the sense of a location. However, because it is free from all conditioned things, it deserves to be called 'above all existence,' and thus it is said, 'Nibbāna is the higher existence.' In phrases like 'the great flood of water,' the word 'flood' has the meaning of 'mass,' and thus it is said, 'this is the great mass of defilements.' The same applies to the rest, such as the flood of existence, and so on.

Appatiṭṭhahantoti kilesādīnaṃ vasena asantiṭṭhanto, asaṃsīdantoti attho. Anāyūhantoti abhisaṅkhārādivasena na āyūhanto majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ vilaṅghitvā nibbuyhanto. Tenāha – “avāyamanto”ti, micchāvāyāmavasena avāyamantoti adhippāyo. Gūḷhanti saṃvutaṃ. Paṭicchannanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Atthavasena vā saṃvuttaṃ gūḷhaṃ, saddavasenapi apākaṭaṃ paṭicchannaṃ antaradīpādike ṭhātabbaṭṭhāne. Āyūhantāti hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamantā. Etaṃ atthajātaṃ, etaṃ vā vissajjanaṃ.

'Not standing firm' means not being established by way of defilements and so on; that is, not sinking down. 'Not striving' means not accumulating by way of volitional formations and so on, being swept away by transgressing the middle path. Therefore, it is said, 'not attempting,' the implied meaning being not attempting by way of wrong effort. 'Concealed' means covered. 'Hidden' is a synonym for that. Or, in terms of meaning, 'concealed' is covered; and in terms of the word, 'hidden' is unmanifest, in a place where it should be kept, such as an inner lamp. 'Striving' means endeavoring with hands and feet. This is the collection of meanings, or this is the explanation.

Idāni yenādhippāyena bhagavatā tathāgūḷhaṃ katvā pañho kathito, taṃ dassetuṃ “kiṃ panātiādi vuttaṃ. Niggahamukhenāti veneyyānaṃ vinayaupāyabhūtaniggahavasena. Tenāha ye paṇḍitamānino”tiādi. Pavayha pavayhāti ophuṇitvā ophuṇitvā.

Now, to show the intention with which the Blessed One posed the question in such a concealed way, it is said, 'What then,' and so on. By way of reproof: that is, by way of reproof which is a means of discipline for those to be trained. Therefore, it is said, 'those who are conceited about their learning,' and so on. 'Pavayha pavayha' means having plunged in, having plunged in.

Soti [M 1.0047] devaputto nihatamāno ahosi yathāvissajjitassa atthassa ajānanto. Yathāti aniyamavacanaṃ niyamaniddiṭṭhaṃ hoti, taṃsambandhañca kathanti pucchāvacananti tadubhayassa atthaṃ dassento “yathāhaṃ jānāmi, evaṃ me kathehī”ti āha.

That devaputta Soti was disheartened, not understanding the meaning of what had been explained. The word 'yathā' is an indefinite term that becomes definite when specified. Showing the meaning of both the discourse connected with it and the question, he said, 'Explain to me in such a way that I may know.'

Yadāsvāhanti yadā su ahaṃ, su-kāro nipātamattaṃ “yadidaṃ kathaṃ sū”tiādīsu viya. Sabbapadesūti “tadāssu saṃsīdāmī”tiādīsu tīsupi padesu. Atarantoti oghānaṃ atikkamanatthaṃ taraṇappayogaṃ akaronto. Tatthevāti oghaniyaoghesu eva. Osīdāmīti nimujjāmi [V 1.0042] oghehi ajjhotthaṭo homi. Nibbuyhāmīti oghehi nibbūḷho homi. Ṭhātuṃ asakkonto asaṃsīdanto. Ativattāmīti anupayogaṃ atikkamāmi, apanidhānavasena sammāpaṭipattiṃ virādhemīti attho. Ṭhāne ca vāyāme cāti vakkhamānavibhāge patiṭṭhahane vāyāme ca dosaṃ disvāti patiṭṭhānāyūhanesu saṃsīdananibbuyhanasaṅkhātaṃ taraṇassa vibandhanabhūtaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvāna. Idaṃ bhagavatā bodhimūle attanā pavattita-pubbabhāga-manasikāravasena vuttaṃ. Atiṭṭhanto avāyamantoti patiṭṭhānāyūhanakaraṇakilesādīnaṃ parivajjanena asaṃsīdanto anibbuyhanto. Devatāyapi paṭividdho tadattho upanissayasampannatāya vimuttiparipācanīyadhammānaṃ paripakkattā. Na pana pākaṭo vipañcitaññūādīnaṃ, ugghaṭitaññūnaṃ pana yathā tassā devatāya, tathā pākaṭo evāti. Satta dukā idāni vuccamānarūpā dassitā porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Kilesavasena santiṭṭhantoti lobhādīhi abhibhūtatāya saṃsāre patiṭṭhahanto sammā appaṭipajjanena tattheva saṃsīdati nāma. Abhisaṅkhāravasenāti tatthevābhisaṅkhāracetanāya cetento sammāpaṭipattiyogyassa khaṇassa ativattanena nibbuyhati nāma. Iminā nayena sesadukesupi attho veditabbo.

'Yadāsvāhaṃ' means 'yadā su ahaṃ'; the particle 'su' is merely an expletive, as in 'yadidaṃ kathaṃ sū,' and so on. 'In all instances' refers to all three instances, such as 'tadāssu saṃsīdāmi,' and so on. 'Not crossing' means not making the effort to cross over the floods. 'Right there' means right there in the floods. 'I sink' means I immerse myself, I am overwhelmed by the floods. 'I am swept away' means I am carried away by the floods. 'I pass beyond' means I transgress the non-application; I miss the right practice by abandoning it—this is the meaning. 'In standing and striving' refers to seeing the fault in standing firm and striving, as will be explained in the division; that is, seeing the danger that is an impediment to crossing, which is called sinking and being swept away in establishing and exerting. This was spoken by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree, based on his own prior reflection and attention. 'Not standing, not striving' means not sinking and not being swept away by avoiding the defilements and so on that cause standing and striving. Even the deity penetrated that meaning due to the perfection of supporting conditions, the maturity of the qualities conducive to liberation. However, it was not evident to those of slow understanding, but it was clear to those of quick understanding, just as it was to that deity. Now, the seven pairs are explained as shown in the ancient commentary. 'Standing firm by way of defilements' means one who stands firm in saṃsāra, overcome by greed and so on, sinks right there by not practicing rightly. 'By way of volitional formations' means one who intends with volitional formations right there, by passing beyond the moment suitable for right practice, is swept away. In this way, the meaning of the remaining pairs should also be understood.

Ettha ca vaṭṭamūlakā kilesāti tesaṃ vasena saṃsāre avaṭṭhānaṃ taṃtaṃkammunā tattha tattha bhave abhinibbatti, kilesā pana tesaṃ paccayamattaṃ. Tattha tattha bhave aparāparaṃ nibbattento saṃsāre nibbuyhati nāmāti imassa atthassa dassanavasena paṭhamaduko vutto. Ime sattā saṃsāre paribbhamantā duvidhā taṇhācaritā diṭṭhicaritā cāti tesaṃ saṃsāranāyikabhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ vasena santiṭṭhanaṃ, tadaññesaṃ pavattipaccayānaṃ vasena [M 1.0048] āyūhananti imassa atthassa dassanavasena dutiyaduko vutto. Saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādadassanasabhāvāya taṇhāya vasena visesato patiṭṭhānaṃ, amuttimagge muttimaggaparāmāsato tathā āyūhanampi diṭṭhiyā vasena hotīti dassetuṃ tatiyaduko vutto. Catutthaduke pana adhippāyo aṭṭhakathāya eva vibhāvito. Yasmā “sassato attā”ti abhinivisanto arūparāgaṃ, asaññūpagaṃ vā avimokkhaṃyeva vimokkhoti gahetvā saṃsāre eva olīyati. Tenāha “olīyanābhinivesā hi bhavadiṭṭhī”ti. Yasmā pana kāmabhavādīsu yaṃ vā taṃ vā bhavaṃ patvā attā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇāti abhinivisanto bhavavippamokkhāvahāya sammāpaṭipattiyā appaṭipajjanena taṃ ativattati. Tena vuttaṃ “atidhāvanābhinivesā vibhavadiṭṭhī”ti.

Here, the defilements are the root of the cycle of existence. Due to them, there is standing firm in saṃsāra, and rebirth here and there by means of various kamma. The defilements, however, are merely a condition for them. Being reborn again and again in various existences, one is indeed swept away in saṃsāra—this is the meaning shown by the first pair. These beings, wandering in saṃsāra, are of two kinds: those whose conduct is dominated by craving and those whose conduct is dominated by views. The standing firm is by way of those phenomena that are the leaders in saṃsāra, while the striving is by way of other conditions for continuation—this is the meaning shown by the second pair. The standing firm is especially by way of craving, which is by nature seeing gratification in the things that bind. Likewise, the striving is by way of views, due to mistaking a path that does not lead to liberation for the path to liberation—this is to show the meaning of the third pair. In the fourth pair, however, the meaning is clarified in the commentary itself. Because one who adheres to the belief 'the self is eternal' becomes entangled in craving for formless realms or the realm of non-perception, taking an unliberated state itself as liberation, he remains stuck in saṃsāra. Hence it is said: 'The view of eternalism is indeed an adherence due to lingering.' But one who believes that upon reaching any state of existence—whether in the realm of sensual desire or another—the self is annihilated and destroyed, that it does not exist after death, such a person, by not practicing the right path leading to liberation from existence, passes beyond it. Therefore, it is said: 'The view of annihilationism is an adherence due to rushing past.'

Līnavasena santiṭṭhantoti kosajjādivasena saṃkocāpajjanena sammā appaṭipajjanto. Uddhaccavasena āyūhantoti sammāsamādhino abhāvena vikkhepavasena pañcamo duko vutto. Yathā kāmasukhaṃ paviṭṭhassa samādhānaṃ natthi cittassa upakkiliṭṭhattā, evaṃ attaparitāpanamanuyuttassa kāyassa [V 1.0043] upakkiliṭṭhattā. Iti cittakāyaparikkilesakarā dve antā taṇhādiṭṭhinissayatāya saṃsīdananibbuyhananimittā vuttā chaṭṭhaduke. Pubbe sappadesatova saṃkilesadhammā “saṃsīdananimitta”nti dassitāti idāni nippadesato dassanavasena, pubbe ca sādhāraṇato abhisaṅkhāradhammā “nibbuyhananimitta”nti dassitāti idāni puññāneñjābhisaṅkhāre eva “āyūhananimitta”nti dassanavasena sattamaduko vutto. Evañhi duggatisugatūpapattivasena saṃsīdananibbuyhanāni vibhajja dassitāni hontīti. Tenevāha “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi. Adhobhāgaṃ duggatiṃ gamentīti adhobhāgaṅgamanīyā anunāsikalopaṃ akatvā. Tathā uparibhāgaṃ gamentīti uparibhāgaṅgamanīyā.

'Standing firm by way of sluggishness' means failing to practice rightly due to shrinking back by way of laziness and so on. 'Striving by way of restlessness' means the fifth pair is stated as distraction due to the absence of right concentration. Just as one immersed in sensual pleasure lacks composure because the mind is defiled, so too one devoted to self-mortification lacks composure because the body is defiled. Thus, the two extremes that defile mind and body, being rooted in craving and wrong view, are described as the causes of sinking and being swept away in the sixth pair. Previously, defilements were shown as 'causes of sinking' with specific application; now, they are shown without specific application. And previously, volitional formations were shown as 'causes of being swept away' in general; now, meritorious and imperturbable formations specifically are shown as 'causes of striving' in the seventh pair. For in this way, sinking and being swept away are shown distinguished according to rebirth in unhappy and happy destinations. Hence it is said, 'And it was also stated,' and so on. 'Leading to the lower realm' means 'adhobhāgaṅgamanīyā' without eliding the nasal. Similarly, 'leading to the higher realm' means 'uparibhāgaṅgamanīyā'.

Ettha ca oghataraṇaṃ pucchitena bhagavatā “appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūha”nti tassa pahānaṅgameva dassitaṃ, na sampayogaṅganti? Na evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, yāvatā yena patiṭṭhānaṃ hoti, yena ca āyūhanaṃ, tadubhayapaṭikkhepamukhena tappaṭipakkhadhammadassanametanti. Na hesa a-kāro kevalaṃ paṭisedhe, atha [M 1.0049] kho paṭipakkhe “akusalā dhammā, ahito, adhammo”tiādīsu viya, tasmā appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti patiṭṭhānāyūhanānaṃ paṭipakkhavasena pavattamāno tathāpavattihetūvāti ayamettha attho. Khoti ca avadhāraṇatthe nipāto “assosi kho”tiādīsu (pārā. 1) viya. Tena appatiṭṭhānassa ekaṃsikataṃ dasseti. Soyaṃ kho-saddo “anāyūha”nti etthāpi ānetvā vattabbo. Anāyūhanampi hi ekaṃsikamevāti tassa paṭipakkho saha vipassanāya ariyamaggo. Tena hi oghataraṇaṃ hoti, na aññathā. Evamayaṃ yathānusandhidesanā katā, devatā ca sahavipassanaṃ maggaṃ paṭivijjhīti paṭhamaphale patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “imaṃ pañhavissajjana”ntiādi.

Here, when asked about crossing the flood, did the Blessed One, by saying, 'without standing, without striving,' show only the aspect of abandoning it, and not the aspect of application? It should not be seen thus. Rather, it is the teaching of the opposing principle by rejecting both that by which there is standing and that by which there is striving. For this 'a-' prefix is not merely for negation, but indeed for the opposite, as in 'unwholesome states,' 'unbeneficial,' 'unrighteous,' and so on. Therefore, 'without standing, without striving' means that it proceeds by way of the opposite of standing and striving, and that is the cause for such a proceeding—this is the meaning here. And 'kho' is a particle in the sense of emphasis, as in 'he heard indeed,' and so on (Pārā. 1). By this, it shows the decisiveness of being without standing. This particle 'kho' should also be brought to 'without striving.' For not striving is likewise decisive, and its opposite, together with insight, is the Noble Path. For by that, there is crossing of the flood, and not otherwise. Thus, this teaching was given in accordance with the connection, and the deity penetrated the path together with insight and became established in the first fruition. Therefore, it is said, 'this answer to the question,' and so on.

“Cirassā”ti iminā samānatthaṃ padantarametanti āha “cirassa kālassā”ti yathā “mamaṃ vā, bhikkhave”ti (dī. ni. 1.5-6) ettha “mamā”ti iminā samānatthaṃ padantaraṃ mamanti. Na diṭṭhapubbāti adassāvī. Adassāvitā ca disvā kattabbakiccassa asiddhatāya veditabbā. Aññathā kā nāma sā devatā, yā bhagavantaṃ na diṭṭhavatī? Tenāha “kiṃ panimāyā”tiādi. Dassanaṃ upādāya evaṃ vattuṃ vattatīti yadā kadāci kañci piyajātikaṃ disvā taṃ dassanaṃ upādāya “cirena vata mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ passāmā”ti adiṭṭhapubbaṃ diṭṭhapubbaṃ vā evaṃ vattuṃ yujjati, ayaṃ loke niruḷhe samudācāroti dasseti. Brahmaṃ vā vuccati ariyamaggo, tassa aṇanato jānanato paṭivijjhanato brāhmaṇo. Kilesanibbānenāti kilesānaṃ [V 1.0044] accantasamucchedasaṅkhātena nibbānena nibbutaṃ sammadeva vūpasanta-sabbakilesadaratha-pariḷāhaṃ. Āsattavisattādīhīti ādi-saddena visatādiākāre saṅgaṇhāti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

By cirassā is meant another word with the same meaning, namely, cirassa kālassā (after a long time), just as in the passage 'me, bhikkhus' (DN 1.5-6), mamaṃ is another word with the same meaning as mamā. Not seen before means one who has not seen. And this state of not having seen should be understood in terms of the non-accomplishment of the duty that should be done upon seeing. Otherwise, what kind of deity could there be who had not seen the Blessed One? Hence it is said: 'But what about this one?' and so on. It is proper to speak thus based on the seeing: whenever one sees some dear person, based on that seeing one may say, 'Indeed, it has been a long time since we have seen the venerable one,' whether one has seen them before or not. This, he shows, is the established convention in the world. Brahma is said to be the noble path; because one knows, understands, and penetrates it, one is a brāhmaṇa. By the quenching of defilements: quenched by Nibbāna, which is defined as the utter extirpation of defilements, with all distress and fever arising from defilements perfectly pacified. By āsattavisattādīhi (by attachment, entanglement, etc.): with the word 'etc.' he includes the forms starting with visata. For it has been said:

“Visatāti visattikā, visaṭāti visattikā, visālāti visattikā, visakkatīti visattikā, visaṃvādikāti visattikā, visaṃ haratīti visattikā, visamūlāti visattikā, visaphalāti visattikā, visaparibhogoti visattikā, visālā vā pana sā taṇhā rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe dhamme kule gaṇe visatā vitthatāti visattikā”ti (mahāni. 3).

Because it spreads (visatā), it is called visattikā (craving). Because it is scattered (visaṭā), it is called visattikā. Because it is vast (visālā), it is called visattikā. Because it adheres (visakkati), it is called visattikā. Because it is deceptive (visaṃvādikā), it is called visattikā. Because it carries poison (visaṃ harati), it is called visattikā. Because its root is poison (visamūlā), it is called visattikā. Because its fruit is poison (visaphalā), it is called visattikā. Because its enjoyment is poison (visaparibhogo), it is called visattikā. Or else, that craving (taṇhā) is vast (visālā); because it spreads (visatā) and is extensive (vitthatā) in regard to forms, sounds, odours, tastes, tangibles, mental phenomena, families, and groups, it is called visattikā.

Tattha [M 1.0050] visatāti vitthatā rūpādīsu tebhūmakadhammesu abhibyāpanavasena visaṭāti purimavacanameva ta-kārassa ṭa-kāraṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Visālāti vipulā. Visakkatīti parisakkati, sahati vā. Ratto hi rāgavatthunā pādena tāḷiyamānopi sahatīti. Osakkanaṃ vipphandanaṃ vā “visakkana”ntipi vadanti. Aniccādiṃ niccādito. Gaṇhātīti visaṃvādikā hoti. Visaṃ haratīti tathā tathā kāmesu ānisaṃsaṃ passantī vividhehi ākārehi nekkhammābhimukhappavattito cittaṃ saṃharati saṃkhipati, visaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, taṃ harati, vahatīti attho. Dukkhanibbattakakammassa hetubhāvato visamūlā. Visaṃ vā dukkhābhibhūtā vedanā mūlaṃ etissāti visamūlā. Dukkhasamudayattā visaṃ phalaṃ etissāti visaphalā. Taṇhāya rūpādikassa dukkhasseva paribhogo hoti, na amatassāti visaparibhogoti vuttā, sabbattha niruttivasena padasiddhi veditabbā. Yo panettha padhāno attho, taṃ dassetuṃ puna “visālā vā panā”tiādi vuttanti evamettha visattikāpadassa attho veditabbo. Tiṇṇaṃ paṭhamadutiyamaggehi. Nittiṇṇaṃ tatiyamaggena. Uttiṇṇaṃ catutthamaggena.

Herein, visatā means extensive, in the sense of pervading the phenomena of the three planes, such as forms, etc. Visaṭā is just the preceding word spoken with a ṭa made from the ta. Visālā means vast. Visakkati means it crawls about, or it endures; for one who is impassioned endures even when struck by the foot of an object of passion. Some also call retreating or struggling visakkana. Because it grasps what is impermanent, etc., as permanent, etc., it is deceptive (visaṃvādikā). It carries poison (visaṃ harati): seeing gratification in sensual pleasures in such and such a way, it draws back and contracts the mind in various ways from its orientation towards renunciation. Or, poison (visa) is suffering (dukkha); it carries (harati) or bears (vahati) it; that is the meaning. It is rooted in poison (visamūlā) because it is the cause of kamma that produces suffering. Or, its root is feeling that is overwhelmed by suffering, which is poison; hence it is rooted in poison. Its fruit is poison (visaphala) because it is an origin of suffering. Because of craving, the enjoyment of forms, etc., is only an enjoyment of suffering, not of the deathless; thus it is said to be enjoyment of poison (visaparibhogo). In all cases, the derivation of the word should be understood by way of etymology. To show the principal meaning here, it is again stated, 'Or else, it is vast...' etc. In this way the meaning of the word visattikā should be understood. Crossed over by means of the first and second paths. Thoroughly crossed over by means of the third path. Gone beyond by means of the fourth path.

Samanuññoti sammadeva katānuñño. Tenāha “ekajjhāsayo ahosī”ti. Antaradhāyīti adassanaṃ agamāsi. Yathā pana antaradhāyi, taṃ dassetuṃ “abhisaṅkhatakāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Mālehīti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ, “mālāhī”ti keci paṭhanti, “malyehī”ti vattabbe ya-kāralopaṃ katvā niddeso. Ayaṃ tāva aṭṭhakathāya līnatthavaṇṇanā.

Samanuñño means one who has been rightly permitted. Therefore he said, 'he became of a single intention.' Antaradhāyī means he went out of sight. To show how he disappeared, it is said, 'with a constructed body,' etc. Mālehī is stated with an inversion of gender. Some read it as mālāhī; when it should be malyehī, the explanation is given with the elision of the ya. This, for now, is the explanation of the hidden meaning from the commentary.

Nettinayavaṇṇanā

Explanation by the Netti Method

Idāni pakaraṇanayena pāḷiyā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Sā pana atthavaṇṇanā yasmā desanāya [V 1.0045] samuṭṭhānappayojanabhājanesu piṇḍatthesu ca niddhāritesu sukarā hoti suviññeyyā ca, tasmā suttadesanāya samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamaṃ niddhārayissāma. Tattha samuṭṭhānaṃ tāva desanānidānaṃ, taṃ sādhāraṇaṃ asādhāraṇanti duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇampi abbhantarabāhirabhedato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ abbhantarasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma lokanāthassa mahākaruṇā. Tāya hi samussāhitassa bhagavato veneyyānaṃ dhammadesanāya cittaṃ udapādi, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “sattesu ca [M 1.0051] kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.283; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 9). Ettha ca hetuavatthāyapi mahākaruṇāya saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo yāvadeva saṃsāramahoghato saddhammadesanāhatthadānehi sattasantāraṇatthaṃ taduppattito. Yathā ca mahākaruṇā, evaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dasabalañāṇādīni ca desanāya abbhantarasamuṭṭhānabhāvena vattabbāni. Sabbañhi ñeyyadhammaṃ tesaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ sattānañca āsayānusayādiṃ yāthāvato jānanto bhagavā ṭhānāṭṭhānādīsu kosallena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vicittanayadesanaṃ pavattesīti. Bāhiraṃ pana sādhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ dasasahassamahābrahmaparivāra-sahampatimahābrahmuno ajjhesanaṃ. Tadajjhesanuttarakālañhi dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇājanitaṃ appossukkataṃ paṭippassambhetvā dhammassāmī dhammadesanāya ussāhajāto ahosi. Asādhāraṇampi abbhantarabāhirabhedato duvidhameva. Tattha abbhantaraṃ yāya mahākaruṇāya yena ca desanāñāṇena idaṃ suttaṃ pavattitaṃ, tadubhayaṃ veditabbaṃ bāhiraṃ pana tassā devatāya pucchā, pucchāvasiko hesa suttanikkhepo. Tayidaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva.

Now we will give an explanation of the meaning of the Pāli text according to the method of the treatises. Since that explanation becomes easy to do and easy to understand when the origins, purposes, recipients, and summary meanings of the teaching have been determined, we will therefore first determine the origins and so on of the sutta's teaching. Therein, the origin of the teaching is twofold: common and uncommon. The common is again twofold, by way of internal and external. Here, the common internal origin is the great compassion of the Lord of the World. For, spurred on by it, the thought arose in the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma to those who could be trained. This is what is meant when it is said: 'And out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,' etc. (MN 26; SN 6:1; Mv I 5,4). Here, great compassion should be understood as included even in the causal stage, inasmuch as it arises for the purpose of ferrying beings across the great flood of saṃsāra by giving the hand of the teaching of the true Dhamma. And just as great compassion, so too the knowledge of omniscience, the ten powers, etc., should be spoken of as internal origins of the teaching. For the Blessed One, knowing as they really are all knowable phenomena, the way they should be taught, and the dispositions, latent tendencies, etc., of beings, set in motion a teaching with diverse methods suited to the temperament of those to be trained, with his skill in the possible and impossible, etc. The common external origin, however, is the request of the great brahmā Sahampati, attended by his retinue of ten thousand great brahmās. For it was after his request that the Master of the Dhamma, having pacified the reluctance born from reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, became eager to teach the Dhamma. The uncommon origin is also twofold: internal and external. Herein, the internal should be understood as that great compassion and that knowledge of teaching by which this sutta was set in motion. The external, however, is the question of that deity, for this exposition of a sutta is based on a question. This is indeed what has come down in the Pāli.

Payojanampi sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ anukkamena yāva anupādāparinibbānaṃ vimuttirasattā bhagavato desanāya. Tenevāha “etadatthā kathā, etadatthā mantanā”tiādi (pari. 366). Asādhāraṇaṃ pana tassā devatāya dassanamaggasamadhigamo, ubhayampetaṃ bāhirameva. Sace pana veneyyasantānagatampi desanābalasiddhisaṅkhātaṃ payojanaṃ adhippāyasamijjhanabhāvato yathādhippetatthasiddhiyā mahākāruṇikassa bhagavatopi payojanamevāti gaṇheyya, iminā pariyāyenassa abbhantaratāpi siyā.

The purpose, too, is twofold: common and uncommon. Here, the common purpose of the Blessed One's teaching is its having the taste of liberation, progressively up to final Nibbāna without residue of clinging. Hence he said: 'For this purpose is the talk, for this purpose is the discussion,' etc. (Pari. 366). The uncommon purpose, however, is that deity’s attainment of the path of vision; but both of these are external. If, however, one were to take the purpose consisting of the accomplishment of the teaching's power in the mental continuum of those to be trained as being a purpose for the greatly compassionate Blessed One himself—on account of the fulfillment of his intention, leading to the achievement of the intended goal—then in this way it could also be internal.

Apica tassā devatāya oghataraṇākārassa yāthāvato anavabodho imissā desanāya samuṭṭhānaṃ, tadavabodho payojanaṃ. So hi imāya desanāya bhagavantaṃ payojeti tannipphādanaparāyaṃ desanāti katvā. Yañhi desanāya sādhetabbaṃ phalaṃ, taṃ ākaṅkhitabbattā desakaṃ desanāya payojetīti payojananti vuccati. Tathā devatāya tadaññesañca vineyyānaṃ patiṭṭhānāyūhanavissajjanañcettha payojanaṃ[M 1.0052]. Tathā saṃsāracakkanivatti-saddhammacakkappavattisassatādimicchācāra-nirākaraṇaṃ [V 1.0046] sammāvādapurekkhāro akusalamūlasamūhananaṃ kusalamūlasamāropanaṃ apāyadvārapidahanaṃ saggamokkhadvāravivaraṇaṃ pariyuṭṭhānavūpasamanaṃ anusayasamugghātanaṃ “mutto mocessāmī”ti purimapaṭiññāavisaṃvādanaṃ tappaṭipakkhamāramanorathavisaṃvādanaṃ titthiyasamayanimmathanaṃ buddhadhammapatiṭṭhāpananti evamādīnipi payojanāni idha veditabbāni.

Further, that deity's lack of proper understanding of the way to cross the flood is the origin of this teaching, and the understanding of it is the purpose. For that understanding motivates the Blessed One to this teaching, since the teaching is intent on its accomplishment. Indeed, the fruit to be achieved by the teaching, because it is desirable, motivates the teacher to the teaching; thus it is called 'purpose.' Likewise, a purpose here is the relinquishment of standing and striving for that deity and other trainees. Furthermore, the following should also be understood here as purposes: the stopping of the wheel of saṃsāra and the setting in motion of the wheel of the true Dhamma; the rejection of wrong conduct such as eternalism; the promotion of right view; the eradication of unwholesome roots and the implanting of wholesome roots; the closing of the doors to the planes of misery and the opening of the doors to heaven and liberation; the pacification of obsessions and the uprooting of latent tendencies; the non-falsification of the previous promise, 'Freed, I shall free others'; the thwarting of the desires of Māra, its opponent; the crushing of the theories of the sectarians; and the establishment of the Buddha's Dhamma.

Yathā devatā oghataraṇe saṃsayapakkhandā, tādisā aññe ca saṅkhātadhammānaṃ sammāsambuddhassa ca paṭipattiṃ ajānantā asaddhammassavana-dhāraṇa-paricaya-manasikāravipallatthabuddhikā saddhammassavana-dhāraṇa-paricayavimukhā ca bhavavimokkhesino vineyyā imissā desanāya bhājanaṃ.

Just as that deity was plunged in doubt about crossing the flood, so too other trainees who seek liberation from existence are the recipients of this teaching: namely, those who do not know the practice of those who have understood the Dhamma and of the Perfectly Enlightened One; those whose intelligence is perverted by listening to, retaining, becoming familiar with, and attending to the false Dhamma; and who are averse to listening to, retaining, and becoming familiar with the true Dhamma.

Piṇḍatthā pana “appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūha”nti padadvaye catusaccakammaṭṭhānānuyogavasena yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro kusalamūlasamāyogo olīyanātidhāvanāvissajjanaṃ upāyavinibandhavidhamanaṃ micchābhinivesadūrībhāvo taṇhāvijjāvisodhanaṃ vaṭṭattayavicchedanupāyo āsavogha-yoga-ganthāgati-taṇhuppādupādānaviyogo cetokhilavivecanaṃ abhinandananivāraṇaṃ saṃsaggātikkamo vivādamūlapariccāgo akusalakammapathaviddhaṃsanaṃ micchattātivattanaṃ anusayamūlacchedo. Sabbakilesa-darathapariḷāha-sārambhapaṭippassambhanaṃ dassanasavananiddeso vijjūpamavajirūpamadhammāpadeso apacayagāmidhammavibhāvanā pahānattayadīpanā sikkhattayānuyogo samathavipassanānuṭṭhānaṃ bhāvanāsacchikiriyāsiddhi sīlakkhandhādipārisuddhīti evamādayo veditabbā.

But as to the summary meaning of the two terms 'not standing' and 'not striving,' the following should be understood: the frequent practice of wise attention by way of devotion to the meditation subject of the four truths; association with wholesome roots; the abandonment of sluggishness and restlessness; the destruction of the bonds of attachment; removal from wrong adherence; the purification from craving and ignorance; the means for cutting off the three rounds; disengagement from the taints, floods, yokes, knots, wrong courses, the arising of craving, and clinging; the discernment of mental barrenness; the prevention of delight; the overcoming of association; the abandoning of the root of disputes; the demolition of the unwholesome courses of action; the overcoming of wrongness; the cutting off of the root of the underlying tendencies; the calming of all defilements, distress, fever, and impetuosity; the instruction on seeing and hearing; the teaching of the Dhamma like lightning and like a diamond; the explanation of the Dhamma that leads to non-accumulation; the illumination of the threefold abandonment; devotion to the threefold training; the undertaking of serenity and insight; the success of realization through development; and the purity of the aggregates of virtue, and so on.

Tattha yesaṃ kilesādīnaṃ vasena patiṭṭhāti saṃsīdati, yesañca abhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ vasena āyūhati nibbuyhati, ubhayametaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, tappabhāvitā tadubhayanissitā ca khandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, tadubhayamattho, “appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūha”nti adhippetassa atthassa paṭicchannaṃ katvā desanā upāyo mānaniggaṇhanavasena tassā devatāya saccābhisamayakāraṇabhāvato patiṭṭhānāyūhanapaṭikkhepopadesena caturoghanirattharaṇatthikehi antadvayarahitā majjhimā paṭipatti paṭipajjitabbāti ayamettha bhagavato āṇattīti ayaṃ desanāhāro.

Herein, that by which one stands and sinks—namely, the defilements and so on—and that by which one strives and is swept away—namely, the formations and so on—both of these are the truth of the origin.
