The aggregates produced by them and dependent on both are the truth of suffering. The teaching is a method that conceals the meaning of both these truths, the meaning intended by 'not standing' and 'not striving.' Because it is a cause for that deity's realization of the truths by way of subduing his pride, this is the Blessed One's command here: by the instruction on the rejection of standing and striving, the middle path, devoid of the two extremes, should be practiced by those who wish to cross over the four floods. This is the method of exposition.

Parasaṃsayapakkhandanatāya [M 1.0053] ñātukāmatāya ca kathaṃ nūti pucchāvasena vuttaṃ? Abhimukhabhāvato ekapuggalabhāvato ca “tva”nti vuttaṃ. Paramukkaṃsagatassa garubhāvassa anaññayogyassa saddhammadhurassa paridīpanato sādhūti marisasīlādiguṇatāya “mārisā”ti vuttaṃ[V 1.0047]. Avahananato rāsibhāvato ca “ogha”nti vuttaṃ. Ñātuṃ icchitassa atthassa katattā pariyosāpitattā “itī”ti vuttaṃ. Saṃsīdanalakkhaṇassa patiṭṭhānassa akātabbato sabbaso ca akatattā. “Appatiṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ. Tayidaṃ akaraṇaṃ ekaṃsikanti khoti avadhāraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Tassa ca appatiṭṭhānassa sasantatigatattā “tva”nti ca pucchitattā “aha”nti vuttaṃ. Devatāya sambodhanato piyālapanato ca, “āvuso”ti vuttaṃ. Nibbuyhanalakkhaṇassa āyūhanassa akātabbato sabbaso ca akatattā anāyūhanti vuttaṃ. Tiṇṇākārassa oghānaṃ anicchitabhāvato eva tattha saṃsayassa anapagatattā oghataraṇassa ca avisesattā “yathā kathaṃ panā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā saṃsīdanalakkhaṇaṃ patiṭṭhānaṃ saṃsāre ca saṇṭhānanti anatthantarattā abhinnakālikaṃ. Tathā nibbuyhanalakkhaṇaṃ āyūhanaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā ativattananti anatthantarattā abhinnakālikanti vuttaṃ “yadā svāhaṃ…pe… tadāssu nibbuyhāmī”ti. Tadubhayassa paṭipakkhabhāvato paṭibāhanato ca oghātiṇṇāti vuttaṃ “evaṃ khvāhaṃ…pe… oghamatari”nti.

Why was it said by way of a question, 'How, indeed?' Because of the desire to know and to dispel the doubts of others. Because of being face-to-face and being a single person, 'you' was said. Because it illuminates the supreme, venerable, and unequalled sweetness of the good Dhamma, 'good' (sādhu) was said; and due to qualities such as being worthy of respect, 'sir' (mārisa) was said. Because it carries one down and because it is a mass, 'flood' was said. Because the meaning that was wished to be known has been dealt with and concluded, 'thus' (iti) was said. Because standing, which has the characteristic of sinking, is not to be done and is entirely undone, 'not standing' was said. The word 'indeed' (kho) was said for the sake of emphasis, meaning 'this non-doing is certain.' And because that 'not standing' pertains to one's own continuity, and because 'you' was asked, 'I' was said. Because it is an address to the deity and an affectionate utterance, 'friend' (āvuso) was said. Because striving, which has the characteristic of being swept away, is not to be done and is entirely undone, 'not striving' was said. Because the three kinds of floods are not desired, because doubt about them has not been removed, and because the crossing of the flood is not specific, 'But how then?' was said. Similarly, standing, which has the characteristic of sinking, and remaining in saṃsāra are not different in meaning and are simultaneous. Likewise, striving, which has the characteristic of being swept away, and transgressing the right practice are not different in meaning and are simultaneous. Thus it is said: 'When I...pe... then I am swept away.' Because both are opposed and warded off, 'one who has crossed the flood' was said: 'Thus indeed I...pe... crossed the flood.'

Ekabuddhantarantarikattā sudūrakālikatāya “cirassa”nti vuttaṃ. Antarā adiṭṭhapubbatāya vimhayanīyatāya ca “vatā”ti vuttaṃ. Tadā upalabbhamānatāya attapaccakkhatāya ca “passāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Bāhitapāpato brahmassa ca ariyamaggassa aṇanato paṭivijjhanato “brāhmaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Kilesasantāpavūpasamanato dukkhasantāpavūpasamanato ca sabbaso nibbutattā “parinibbuta”nti vuttaṃ. Taraṇapayogassa nibbattitattā upari taritabbābhāvato ca “tiṇṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Ñāṇacakkhunā oloketabbato lujjanato palujjanato ca “loke”ti vuttaṃ. Visayesu sañjanato jātabhāvato “visattika”nti vuttaṃ. Ñāṇassa paccakkhabhāvato nigamanato ca “ida”nti vuttaṃ. Bhāsitattā parisamattattā ca “avocā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ gahitattā paccāmasanato ca “sā devatā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭikkhepassa abhāvato atthassa anumoditabbato “samanuñño”ti vuttaṃ. Vineyyānaṃ [M 1.0054] sāsanato paramatthasampattito ca “satthā”ti vuttaṃ. Cakkhupathātikkamena tirobhāvūpagamanato “antaradhāyī”ti vuttanti ayaṃ anupadavicayato vicayahāro.

Because it is separated by the interval of one Buddha and because it is after a very long time, 'after a long time' was said. Because it had not been seen before in the interim and because it is wonderful, 'indeed!' (vatā) was said. Because he was found then and because it was directly perceived by himself, 'I see' was said. Because he has banished evil and because he has gone to and penetrated the sublime noble path, 'brahmin' was said. Because he has calmed the fever of defilements and the fever of suffering, and because he is completely extinguished, 'fully extinguished' was said. Because the endeavor of crossing has been accomplished and because there is nothing further to be crossed, 'crossed over' was said. Because it is to be looked upon with the eye of wisdom and because it crumbles and disintegrates, 'the world' was said. Because of attachment to objects and because of its born nature, 'attachment' was said. Because it is directly perceived by knowledge and because it is a conclusion, 'this' was said. Because it was spoken and because it was completed, 'he said' was said. Because it was first grasped and then reflected upon, 'that deity' was said. Because there was no rejection and because the meaning was to be approved, 'consenting' was said. Because he instructs those who can be trained and because he has attained the ultimate goal, 'the Teacher' was said. Because of passing beyond the range of vision and undergoing disappearance, 'vanished' was said. This is the method of analysis by way of word-by-word investigation.

Appatiṭṭhānānāyūhanehi oghataraṇaṃ yujjati kilesābhisaṅkhāravijahanena pārasampattisamijjhanato. Sabbakilesa-taṇhādiṭṭhi-taṇhāyatana-sassatādivasena santiṭṭhato saṃsāre saṃsīdanaṃ hotīti yujjati kāraṇassa suppatiṭṭhitabhāvato. Abhisaṅkharaṇakicce kilesābhisaṅkhāre vijjamāne sabbadiṭṭhābhinivesa-atidhāvanābhinivesādīnaṃ vasena āyūhantassa saṃsāramahoghena nibbuyhanaṃ [V 1.0048] hotīti yujjati sammāpaṭipattiyā ativattanato. Brahmassa ariyamaggassa aṇanato paṭivijjhanato brāhmaṇabhāvo yujjjati bāhitapāpattā. Sammadeva santadhammasamadhigamato parinibbutabhāvo yujjati sabbaso savāsanapahīnakilesattā. Tathā ca visattikāya tiṇṇabhāvo yujjati yathā yāya lesopi na dissati, evaṃ aggamaggena tassā samucchinnattāti ayaṃ yuttihāro.

Crossing the flood by not standing and not striving is fitting, because by abandoning the defilements and formations, one succeeds in reaching the further shore. Sinking in saṃsāra is fitting for one who stands still by way of all defilements—craving, views, craving for the sense bases, eternalism, etc.—because the cause is well established. When the function of forming exists and defiled formations are present, for one who strives by way of adherence to all views, adherence to excessive pursuit, and so on, being swept away by the great flood of saṃsāra is fitting, because of transgressing the right practice. Brahminhood is fitting because of going to and penetrating the sublime noble path, and because of having banished evil. The state of being fully extinguished is fitting because of having rightly realized the peaceful Dhamma, since the defilements have been abandoned in all ways, together with their latent dispositions. And likewise, the state of having crossed over attachment is fitting, for not even a trace of it is seen, as it has been utterly cut off by the supreme path. This is the method of logical consistency.

Kilesavaṭṭavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ visesato kammavaṭṭassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Abhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanañca vipākavaṭṭassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Appatiṭṭhānānāyūhanāni oghataraṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, oghataraṇaṃ anupādisesanibbānassa. Taṇhāvasena patiṭṭhānassa assādānupassitā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā – “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.52, 56).

Standing, by way of the round of defilements, is the proximate cause especially for the round of kamma. And striving, by way of formations, is the proximate cause for the round of results. Not standing and not striving are the proximate cause for crossing the flood; crossing the flood is the proximate cause for Nibbāna without residue remaining. Contemplating gratification is the proximate cause for standing, by way of craving. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are fetters, craving increases.' (SN 2.52, 56).

Khandhāvijjā-phassa-saññā-vitakkāyonisomanasikāra-pāpamittaparatoghosā diṭṭhivasena patiṭṭhānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathāha – paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.124) “khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanaavasesakilesābhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Iminā nayena yathārahaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhādivasena patiṭṭhānāyūhanānaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvo vattabbo. Sesamettha pāḷito eva suniddhāriyaṃ. Ayaṃ padaṭṭhānahāro.

The aggregates, ignorance, contact, perception, thought, unwise attention, bad friends, and the voice of another are the proximate cause for standing, by way of views. As it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.124): 'The aggregates are a basis for views, ignorance too is a basis for views,' and so on. Craving, views, delight, the remaining defilements, and formations are the proximate cause for striving. In this way, how these are the proximate causes for standing and striving by way of craving, views, and so on, should be explained as is appropriate. The rest here should be clearly determined from the Pāli text itself. This is the method of proximate causes.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti patiṭṭhānāyūhanapaṭikkhepena vissajjentena niyyānāvahā sammāpaṭipatti gahitā ekantato oghanittharaṇūpāyabhāvato. Taggahaṇena ca sabbepi sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā gahitā honti niyyānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattāti ayaṃ lakkhaṇahāro.

By the answer 'not standing, not striving,' which rejects standing and striving, the right practice that brings release is grasped, because it is exclusively the means for crossing the flood. And by grasping that, all thirty-seven aids to enlightenment are also grasped, because they have the single characteristic of release. This is the method of characteristics.

Nidānamassā [M 1.0055] devatāya oghataraṇākārassa yāthāvato anavabodhoti vuttovāyamattho. Aññepi ye imaṃ desanaṃ nissāya oghataraṇūpāyaṃ paṭivijjhanti, tepi imissā desanāya nidānanti daṭṭhabbā. “Kathaṃ nu kho imaṃ desanaṃ nissāya sammadeva paṭivijjhantā catubbidhampi oghaṃ tarantā sakalasaṃsāramahoghato nitthareyyuṃ, pare ca tattha patiṭṭhapeyyu”nti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Padanibbacanaṃ niruttaṃ, taṃ “eva”ntiādinidānapadānaṃ “katha”ntiādipāḷipadānañca aṭṭhakathāya tassā līnatthavaṇṇanāya ca vuttanayānusārena sukarattā ativitthārabhayena na vitthārayimha.

The source of this discourse is that deity's lack of true understanding of the mode of crossing the flood. This meaning has already been stated. Others too, who, relying on this discourse, penetrate the means for crossing the flood, should be seen as a source for this discourse. 'How indeed, by relying on this discourse, might those who rightly penetrate it cross the fourfold flood, be delivered from the great flood of all saṃsāra, and establish others in that?' This was the Blessed One's intention here. Etymology is the explanation of words. Since this—for the words of the introduction beginning with 'evaṃ' and for the Pāli words beginning with 'kathaṃ'—is easy to understand according to the method stated in the commentary and its explanation of the hidden meaning, we have not elaborated on it for fear of excessive prolixity.

Pada-padattha-desanā-nikkhepa-suttasandhi-vasena pañcavidhā sandhi. Tattha padassa padantarena sambandho [V 1.0049] padasandhi. Tathā padatthassa padatthantarena sambandho padatthasandhi, yo “kiriyākārakasambandho”ti vutto. Nānānusandhikassa taṃtaṃanusandhīti sambandho, ekānusandhikassa pana pubbāparasambandho desanāsandhi, yā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pucchānusandhi ajjhāsayānusandhi yathānusandhī”ti tidhā vibhattā. Ajjhāsayo cettha attajjhāsayo parajjhāsayoti dvidhā veditabbo. Nikkhepasandhi catunnaṃ suttanikkhepānaṃ vasena veditabbā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ papañcasūdanīṭīkāyaṃ vuttanayena gahetabbaṃ. Suttasandhi idha paṭhamanikkhepavasena veditabbā.

Connection is fivefold by way of word-connection, meaning-connection, exposition-connection, summary-connection, and sutta-connection. Herein, the connection of a word with another word is word-connection. Similarly, the connection of a word's meaning with another word's meaning is meaning-connection, which is called 'the connection of action and agent'. For one with various continuities, the connection is 'that-that continuity'; but for one with a single continuity, the prior-and-posterior connection is exposition-connection, which is divided threefold in the commentaries as 'question-continuity, inclination-continuity, and natural-continuity'. Herein, inclination should be understood as twofold: one's own inclination and another's inclination. Summary-connection should be understood by way of the four summaries of the suttas. Whatever needs to be said here should be taken according to the method stated in the Papañcasūdanī-ṭīkā. Sutta-connection here should be understood by way of the first summary.

“Kasmā panettha oghataraṇasuttameva paṭhamaṃ nikkhitta”nti nāyamanuyogo katthaci na pavattati? Apica “appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhaṃ oghamatari”nti patiṭṭhānāyūhanapaṭikkhepavasena antadvayavivajjanamukhena vā majjhimāya paṭipadāya vibhāvanato sabbapaṭhamamidaṃ suttaṃ idha nikkhittaṃ. Antadvayaṃ anupagamma majjhimāya paṭipattiyā saṅkāsanaparañhi buddhānaṃ sāsananti. Yaṃ pana ekissā desanāya desanantarena saddhiṃ saṃsandanaṃ, ayampi desanāsandhi. Sā idha evaṃ veditabbā –

Does the question, 'Why is the Oghataraṇa Sutta placed first here?' not arise? Moreover, because it reveals the Middle Way by rejecting standing and striving, and by avoiding the two extremes, through the statement 'not standing, not striving, one crossed the flood,' this sutta is placed first here. For the teaching of the Buddhas aims to illuminate the Middle Way without approaching the two extremes. Furthermore, that which connects one exposition with another exposition is also exposition-connection. This should be understood here thus:

“Appatiṭṭhaṃ…pe… anāyūhaṃ oghamatari”nti ayaṃ desanā –

This exposition is: 'Not standing [...] not striving, one crossed the flood'.

“Sabbadā sīlasampanno, paññavā susamāhito;

Āraddhavīriyo pahitatto, oghaṃ tarati duttaraṃ.

Always endowed with virtue, wise, well-composed, with aroused energy and resolute mind, one crosses the flood, so difficult to cross.

“Virato kāmasaññāya, rūpasaṃyojanātigo;

Nandīrāgaparikkhīṇo, so gambhīre na sīdati; (Saṃ. ni. 1.96);

Saddhāya [M 1.0056] tarati oghaṃ, appamādena aṇṇavaṃ. (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 186);

Abstaining from sensual perception, transcending the fetter of form; with delight and lust destroyed, one does not sink in the deep. By faith one crosses the flood, by diligence the ocean.

“Pañca chinde pañca jahe, pañca cuttari bhāvaye;

Pañcasaṅgātigo bhikkhu, oghatiṇṇoti vuccati. (saṃ. ni. 1.5; dha. pa. 370);

Cut off five, abandon five, further cultivate five; a bhikkhu who has transcended the five attachments is called one who has crossed the flood.

“Tasmā [V 1.0050] jantu sadā sato, kāmāni parivajjaye;

Te pahāya tare oghaṃ, nāvaṃ sitvāva pāragū. (su. ni. 777; mahāni. 6; netti. 5);

Therefore, a being, always mindful, should avoid sensual pleasures. Having abandoned them, one crosses the flood, as one who has bailed out a ship reaches the far shore.

“Ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī, maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe, tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 5.384, 409; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 107; paṭhamavagga 121; netti. 170) –

The compassionate one, seeing the end of birth, knows the direct path. By this path, those in the past have crossed, and those who will cross and those who are crossing, cross the flood.

Evamādīhi desanāhi saṃsandatīti ayaṃ catubyūho hāro.

By such expositions it is connected; thus this is the fourfold mode.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti ettha saṃkilesavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ āyūhanañca. Tena ayonisomanasikāro dīpito, santakilesavasena anāyūhanena yonisomanasikāro. Tattha ayonisomanasikaroto taṇhāvijjā pavaḍḍhati. Tesu taṇhāgahaṇena ca taṇhāmūlakā dhammā āvattanti. Avijjāgahaṇena avijjāmūlakaṃ sabbaṃ bhavacakkaṃ āvattati. Yonisomanasikāraggahaṇena ca yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā āvattanti catubbidhañca sampatticakkaṃ. Patiṭṭhānāyūhanapaṭikkhepena pana sammāpaṭipatti dīpitā, sā ca saṅkhepato sīlādisaṅgahā. Tattha sīlaggahaṇena ekādasa sīlānisaṃsā āvattanti, samādhiggahaṇena pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi pañcaññāṇiko sammāsamādhi samādhiparikkhārā ca āvattanti. Paññāgahaṇena paññā ca sammādiṭṭhīti sammādiṭṭhisudassanā sabbepi ariyamaggadhammā āvattantīti ayaṃ āvatto hāro.

Here, in the phrase 'without a foothold, without exertion,' establishment and exertion are by way of defilements. By them, unwise attention is indicated; and by the absence of exertion due to the calming of defilements, wise attention is indicated. Herein, for one who attends unwisely, craving and ignorance increase. Among these, by grasping craving, phenomena rooted in craving recur. By grasping ignorance, the entire wheel of existence rooted in ignorance recurs. And by grasping wise attention, phenomena rooted in wise attention recur, as well as the fourfold wheel of accomplishment. However, by the rejection of establishment and exertion, right practice is indicated, which is briefly comprised of virtue and so on. Herein, by grasping virtue, the eleven benefits of virtue recur; by grasping concentration, the five-factored right concentration, the five-knowledge right concentration, and the requisites of concentration recur; by grasping wisdom, wisdom and right view—thus, through the clear vision of right view—all the noble path factors recur. This is the recurrent mode.

Patiṭṭhānaṃ kilesādivasena sattavidhaṃ. Āyūhanaṃ abhisaṅkhārādivasena sattavidhaṃ. Tathā tappaṭipakkhato appatiṭṭhānaṃ anāyūhanañca. Ayamettha dhammavibhatti. Padaṭṭhānabhūmivibhattiyo pana heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbā. Ayaṃ vibhattihāro.

Establishment is sevenfold by way of defilements and so on. Exertion is sevenfold by way of formations and so on. Similarly, from their opposites arise non-establishment and non-exertion. This is the division of phenomena here. However, the divisions of proximate causes and grounds should be understood according to the method stated below. This is the mode of division.

Pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ sammadeva sampādetvā samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ katvā bhāvanaṃ ussakkento kilesādīnaṃ dūrīkaraṇato tesaṃ vasena asaṃsīdanto [M 1.0057] anibbuyhanto appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhaṃ oghaṃ tarati. Kilesādīnaṃ vasena pana saṃsīdanto nibbuyhanto saṃsāre patiṭṭhānato āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiyā āyūhanato oghaṃ na taratīti ayaṃ parivatto hāro.

Having rightly fulfilled the preliminary practice, having made serenity and insight yoked together, and striving in development, one crosses the flood without a foothold and without exertion by distancing oneself from defilements and so on, not sinking due to their influence, and not being submerged. However, one who sinks due to the influence of defilements and so on, is submerged, establishes oneself in saṃsāra, and exerts oneself for the arising of future rebirth, does not cross the flood. This is the mode of transformation.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ [V 1.0051] asantiṭṭhanto asaṃsīdanto anibbisaṃ anavinibbisanti pariyāyavacanaṃ, anāyūhaṃ anibbuyhanto acetento apakappentoti pariyāyavacanaṃ, oghaṃ kilesasamuddanti pariyāyavacanaṃ, atari atikkami accavāyīti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi pariyāyavacanaṃ veditabbanti ayaṃ vevacano hāro.

'Without a foothold' is a synonym for 'not settling down, not sinking, not plunging, not being completely immersed.' 'Without exertion' is a synonym for 'not being submerged, not intending, not planning.' 'The flood' is a synonym for 'the ocean of defilements.' 'Crossed' is a synonym for 'transcended, passed beyond.' In this way, synonyms should be understood in the remaining terms as well. This is the mode of synonyms.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti ettha patiṭṭhaṃ āyūhanti kilesānaṃ kiccakaraṇapaññatti. Pariyuṭṭhānānaṃ vibhāvanapaññatti. Abhisaṅkhārānaṃ viruhanapaññatti. Taṇhāya assādapaññatti. Diṭṭhiyā parinipphandanapaññatti. Bhavadiṭṭhiyā bhavābhinivesapaññatti. Vibhavadiṭṭhiyā vipallāsapaññatti. Kāmasukhānuyogassa kāmesu anugijjhanapaññatti. Attakilamathānuyogassa attaparitāpanapaññatti. Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti pana abhiññeyyadhammānaṃ abhiññāpaññatti. Pariññeyyadhammānaṃ pariññāpaññatti. Oghamatarinti pahātabbadhammānaṃ pahānapaññatti. Maggassa bhāvanāpaññatti. Nirodhassa sacchikiriyāpaññattīti ayaṃ paññattihāro.

Here, in the phrase 'without a foothold, without exertion,' the terms 'foothold' and 'exertion' are a designation for: the performance of the function of defilements; the manifestation of obsessions; the growth of formations; the enjoyment of craving; the agitation of views; the adherence to existence through the view of existence; the perversion through the view of annihilation; the clinging to sensual pleasures through indulgence in sensual pleasures; and self-torment through the practice of self-mortification. However, 'without a foothold, without exertion' is a designation for: the direct knowledge of things to be directly known; the full understanding of things to be fully understood. 'Crossed the flood' is a designation for: the abandoning of things to be abandoned; the development of the path; and the realization of cessation. This is the mode of designations.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti ettha patiṭṭhānāyūhanaggahaṇena oghaggahaṇena ca samudayasaccaṃ gahitaṃ. Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhaṃ atarinti pana padattayena maggasaccaṃ gahitaṃ, hetugahaṇena ca hetumato gahaṇaṃ siddhamevāti dukkhanirodhasaccāni atthato gahitānevāti ayaṃ saccehi otaraṇā. Tattha ye lokiyā pañcakkhandhā, yesaṃ vasena patiṭṭhānāyūhanasiddhi. Ye lokuttarā cattāro khandhā, yesaṃ vasena oghataraṇasiddhi. Ayaṃ khandhamukhena otaraṇā. Ye eva pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, te cattāro khandhā dvāyatanāni dve dhātuyoti ayaṃ āyatanamukhena dhātumukhena ca otaraṇā. Tathā appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti ettha patiṭṭhānāyūhanaggahaṇena kilesābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Kilesābhisaṅkhārādayo oghā ca saṅkhārakkhandhā dhammāyatanaṃ dhammadhātu ca, appatiṭṭhānānāyūhanaggahaṇena oghataraṇavacanena ca saha vipassanāya maggo kathito. Evañca saṅkhārakkhandho dhammāyatanaṃ dhammadhātu ca [M 1.0058] gahitāti evampi khandhamukhena āyatanamukhena dhātumukhena otaraṇā. Vipassanā ce aniccānupassanā, animittamukhena vimokkhamukhaṃ, dukkhānupassanā ce, appaṇihitavimokkhamukhaṃ, anattānupassanā ce, suññatavimokkhamukhanti evaṃ vimokkhamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Magge sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo dhammāyatanadhammadhātū anāsavā ca evampi kho khandhādimukhena otaraṇāti ayaṃ otaraṇo hāro.

Here, by grasping establishment and exertion and by grasping the floods, the truth of origination is grasped. However, by the triad of terms 'without a foothold, without exertion, one crossed,' the truth of the path is grasped; and since the grasping of the effect is accomplished by grasping the cause, the truths of suffering and its cessation are thereby grasped in meaning. This is the descent by means of the truths. Herein, the five mundane aggregates are those by means of which the accomplishment of establishment and exertion occurs. The four supramundane aggregates are those by means of which the accomplishment of crossing the flood occurs. This is the descent by way of the aggregates. Those same five aggregates, twelve sense bases, and eighteen elements correspond to these four aggregates, two sense bases, and two elements. This is the descent by way of the sense bases and by way of the elements. Likewise, here, by grasping establishment and exertion, defilements, formations, and so on are grasped. Defilements, formations, and so on, as well as the floods, are the aggregate of formations, the base of phenomena, and the element of phenomena. By grasping non-establishment and non-exertion, and by the statement 'crossing the flood,' the path is taught along with insight. And thus, the aggregate of formations, the base of phenomena, and the element of phenomena are grasped. In this way, too, there is a descent by way of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements. If insight is the contemplation of impermanence, the door to liberation is the signless; if it is the contemplation of suffering, the door to liberation is the desireless; if it is the contemplation of non-self, the door to liberation is emptiness. Thus, there is a descent by way of the doors to liberation. On the path are the trainee's aggregates of virtue and so on, the base of phenomena, the element of phenomena, and the taintless qualities. In this way, too, there is a descent by way of the aggregates and so on. This is the mode of descent.

Appatiṭṭhanti ārambho. Anāyūhanti padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi, tathā oghanti. Atarinti pana padasuddhi ceva ārambhasuddhi cāti ayaṃ sodhano hāro.

'Without a foothold' is the beginning. 'Without exertion' is purity of the word, but not purity of the beginning; likewise 'the flood.' However, 'crossed' is both purity of the word and purity of the beginning. This is the mode of purification.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ [V 1.0052] anāyūhanti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiādivasena patiṭṭhānāyūhanānaṃ sādhāraṇato paṭikkhepacodanāti katvā oghamatarinti taṃ vikappetvā visesavacanaṃ. Oghataraṇañhi cattāro ariyamaggā. Tattha paṭhamadutiyamaggā avisesena diṭṭhoghataraṇaṃ, tatiyamaggo kāmoghataraṇaṃ, aggamaggo sesoghataraṇanti ayaṃ adhiṭṭhāno hāro.

Generally, 'without a foothold, without exertion' is a determination and an exhortation to reject establishment and exertion, which are common by way of craving, views, and so on. Having analyzed this, 'one crossed the flood' is a specific statement. For crossing the flood means the four noble paths. Herein, the first and second paths, without distinction, cross the flood of views; the third path crosses the flood of sensual desire; and the highest path crosses the remaining floods. This is the mode of determination.

Kilesavasena patiṭṭhānassa ayonisomanasikāro hetu. Abhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanassa kilesā hetū. Appatiṭṭhānānāyūhanānaṃ pana yathākkamaṃ yonisomanasikārapahānāni hetū. Saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassanā taṇhāvasena yathārahaṃ tassa hetū. Tenāha bhagavā – “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti. Khandhāvijjāphassasaññāvitakkāyonisomanasikārapāpamittaparatoghosā diṭṭhivasena patiṭṭhānassa hetū. Tenāha – paṭisambhidāmagge “khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Taṇhābhinandanā avasesakilesābhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanassa hetū. Iminā nayena yathārahaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhivasena patiṭṭhānāyūhanānaṃ hetuvibhāgo niddhāretabbo, tabbipariyāyena appatiṭṭhānānāyūhanānaṃ. Kilesuppādane hi sammadeva ādīnavadassanaṃ appatiṭṭhānassa hetū, abhisaṅkharaṇe ādīnavadassanaṃ anāyūhanassa hetū, vipassanāya ussukkāpanaṃ oghataraṇassa hetūti ayaṃ parikkhāro hāro.

Unwise attention is the cause of foundation by way of defilements. Defilements are the cause of accumulation by way of volitional formations. However, the causes of non-foundation and non-accumulation are, respectively, wise attention and abandonment. The contemplation of gratification in things conducive to fetters is, by way of craving, the appropriate cause of it. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Monks, for one who contemplates gratification in things conducive to fetters, craving increases." The aggregates, ignorance, contact, perception, thought, unwise attention, bad friends, and external influences are causes of foundation by way of views. Therefore it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "The aggregates are also a basis for views, ignorance is also a basis for views," and so on. Rejoicing in craving and the remaining defilements are causes of accumulation by way of volitional formations. In this way, the distinction of the causes of foundation and accumulation by way of craving and views should be determined as appropriate, and conversely, the causes of non-foundation and non-accumulation. For in the arising of defilements, seeing danger rightly is the cause of non-foundation; in the accumulation of volitional formations, seeing danger is the cause of non-accumulation; and arousing zeal for insight is the cause of crossing the flood – this is the arrangement of requisites.

Yathāvuttavibhāgehi [M 1.0059] patiṭṭhānāyūhanehi catubbidhassapi oghassa parisuddhi. Appatiṭṭhānānāyūhanehi pana sotānaṃ saṃvaro sabbaso pidhānañcāti catubbidhassapi oghassa visesato pidhānaṃ appavattikaraṇaṃ. Ariyamaggassa bhāvanāya hi kilesavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ abhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanaṃ upacchinnaṃ, tassa sabbepi oghā tiṇṇā sammatiṇṇā pahīnā hontīti ayaṃ samāropano hāro.

Through the distinctions stated above, the fourfold flood is clarified by means of foundation and accumulation. But through non-foundation and non-accumulation, restraint of the streams and complete closing off are specifically the suppression and prevention of the fourfold flood. For by the development of the Noble Path, foundation by way of defilements and accumulation by way of volitional formations are cut off. For such a one, all the floods are crossed, fully crossed, and abandoned – this is the method of application.

Appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhanti ettha patiṭṭhāgahaṇena taṇhāvijjā gahitā. Tāsaṃ hi vasena satto tattha tattha bhave patiṭṭhāti. Āyūhanaggahaṇena tappaccayā abhisaṅkhāradhammā gahitā. Tattha taṇhāya visesato rūpadhammā adhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāya arūpadhammā. Tesaṃ yathākkamaṃ samatho ca vipassanā ca paṭipakkhā, te “appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhaṃ oghamatari”nti padehi pakāsitā honti, tesu samathassa cetovimutti phalaṃ, vipassanāya paññāvimutti. Tathā hi sā “rāgavirāgā avijjāvirāgā”ti visesetvā vuccati. Tattha taṇhāvijjā abhisaṅkhāro ca samudayasaccaṃ, tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhūtā rūpārūpadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā oghataraṇapariyāyena vuttā maggasaccaṃ. Taṇhāgahaṇena cettha māyā-sāṭheyyamānātimāna-madappamāda-pāpicchatā-pāpamittatā-ahirikānottappādivasena [V 1.0053] akusalapakkho netabbo. Avijjāgahaṇena viparītamanasikāra-kodhūpanāha-makkhapaḷāsa-issāmacchariya-sārambha- dovacassatā-bhavadiṭṭhiādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo. Vuttavipariyāyena amāyāasāṭheyyādiaviparītamanasikārādivasena. Tathā samathapakkhiyānaṃ saddhindriyānaṃ vipassanāpakkhiyānaṃ aniccasaññādīnañca vasena vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ nandiyāvattassa nayassa bhūmi.

When it is said 'unestablished, not accumulating,' here, by the grasping of 'establishment' (patiṭṭhā), craving and ignorance are understood. Indeed, by way of these, a being becomes established here and there in existence. By the grasping of 'accumulation' (āyūhana), the volitional formations dependent on them are understood. Therein, material phenomena are specifically the basis for craving, and immaterial phenomena for ignorance. Serenity and insight are, respectively, their opposites. They are revealed by the words 'unestablished, not accumulating, he crossed the flood.' Among these, the fruit of serenity is liberation of mind, and of insight, liberation by wisdom. Thus, it is specifically stated as 'dispassion from lust, dispassion from ignorance.' Here, craving, ignorance, and volitional formations are the truth of origin. The material and immaterial phenomena that serve as their basis are the truth of suffering. Their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation. The path of fully understanding cessation, spoken of by way of crossing the flood, is the truth of the Path. In this context, by the grasping of craving, the unwholesome side—consisting of deceit, dishonesty, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, heedlessness, evil desires, bad companionship, lack of shame, and lack of dread—should be understood. By the grasping of ignorance, the unwholesome side—consisting of perverted attention, anger, hostility, hypocrisy, malice, envy, stinginess, contentiousness, intractability, views of existence, and so on—should be understood. Conversely, the wholesome side should be understood by way of non-deceit, non-dishonesty, non-perverted attention, and so on. Similarly, the pure side should be understood by way of the faculties of faith pertaining to serenity, and by way of the perceptions of impermanence and so on pertaining to insight. This is the foundation of Nandiyāvatta’s method.

Tathā vuttanayena gahitesu taṇhāvijjātappakkhiyadhammesu taṇhā lobho, avijjā moho, avijjāya sampayutto lohite sati pubbo viya taṇhāya sati sijjhamāno āghāto doso iti tīhi akusalamūlehi gahitehi, tappaṭipakkhato “appatiṭṭha”ntiādivacanehi ca tīṇi akusalamūlāni tīṇi kusalamūlāni ca siddhāni eva honti. Idhāpi lobho sabbāni sāsavakusalamūlāni āyūhanadhammā ca samudayasaccaṃ, tannibbattā tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānagocarabhūtā ca upādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā saccayojanā yojetabbā. Phalaṃ panettha vimokkhattayavasena [M 1.0060] niddhāretabbaṃ, tīhi akusalamūlehi tividhaduccarita-saṃkilesamalavisamaakusalasaññā-vitakkādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo, tathā tīhi kusalamūlehi tividhasucarita-samakusalasaññā-vitakka-samādhi-vimokkhamukhādivasena vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ tipukkhalassa nayassa bhūmi.

In the manner thus stated, among the states taken by way of craving, ignorance, and their respective sides: craving is greed, ignorance is delusion, and aversion, which is hatred, associated with ignorance, arises in the presence of craving, just as pus forms in the presence of blood. Thus, by these three unwholesome roots being taken, and from their opposites, by the words 'unestablished' and so on, the three unwholesome roots and the three wholesome roots are indeed established. Here too, greed, all tainted wholesome roots, and accumulative phenomena are the truth of origin. The aggregates of clinging, which arise from that and serve as their basis and sphere, should be connected with the truth of suffering, and so on, by way of the connection of the Truths. The fruit here should be determined by way of the three liberations. The unwholesome side should be understood by way of the three unwholesome roots, by way of threefold misconduct, defilements, taints, uneven unwholesome perceptions, thoughts, and so on. Similarly, the pure side should be understood by way of the three wholesome roots, by way of threefold good conduct, even wholesome perceptions, thoughts, concentration, gateways to liberation, and so on. This is the foundation of the method of the three individuals.

Tathā vuttanayena gahitesu taṇhāvijjātappakkhiyadhammesu visesato taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena asubhe “subha”nti, dukkhe “sukha”nti ca vipallāsā, avijjādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena “anicce nicca”nti anattani “attā”ti vipallāsā veditabbā. Tesaṃ paṭipakkhato “appatiṭṭha”ntiādivacanehi ca laddhehi sativīriyasamādhipaññindriyehi cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni siddhāneva honti.

In the manner thus stated, among the states taken by way of craving, ignorance, and their respective sides: especially, the distortions—regarding the unattractive as 'attractive' and the painful as 'pleasure'—are to be understood by way of craving and views. And the distortions—regarding the impermanent as 'permanent' and the non-self as 'self'—are to be understood by way of ignorance and views. And from their opposites, through the words 'unestablished' and so on, and through the obtained faculties of mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom, the four foundations of mindfulness are indeed established.

Tattha catūhi indriyehi cattāro puggalā niddisitabbā. Kathaṃ? Duvidho hi taṇhācarito mudindriyo tikkhindriyoti, tathā diṭṭhicarito. Tesu paṭhamo asubhe “subha”nti vipariyesaggāhī satibalena yathābhūtaṃ kāyasabhāvaṃ sallakkhento bhāvanābalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ samugghātetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Dutiyo asukhe “sukha”nti vipariyesaggāhī “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā vuttena vīriyasaṃvarabhūtena vīriyabalena paṭipakkhaṃ vinodento bhāvanābalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ viddhaṃsetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Tatiyo [V 1.0054] anicce “nicca”nti ayāthāvaggāhī samathabalena samāhitacitto saṅkhārānaṃ taṅkhaṇikabhāvaṃ sallakkhento bhāvanābalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ samugghātetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Catuttho santati-samūha-kiccārammaṇa-ghanavañcitatāya phassādidhammapuñjamatte anattani “attā”ti micchābhinivesī catukoṭikasuññatāmanasikārena taṃ micchābhinivesaṃ viddhaṃsetvā sāmaññaphalaṃ sacchikaroti. Subhasaññāsukhasaññādīhi catūhi vā vipallāsehi samudayasaccaṃ, tesamadhiṭṭhānārammaṇabhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā saccayojanā veditabbā. Phalaṃ panettha cattāri sāmaññaphalāni, catūhi cettha vipallāsehi caturāsavoghayoga-kāyagantha-agati-taṇhuppādupādāna-sattaviññāṇaṭṭhiti-apariññādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo, tathā catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi catubbidhajhāna-vihārādhiṭṭhāna-sukhabhāgiyadhamma-appamaññāsammappadhāniddhipādādivasena vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ sīhavikkīḷitassa nayassa bhūmi.

Here, four types of individuals should be indicated by means of the four faculties. How? Indeed, the craving-prone individual is twofold: one with dull faculties and one with sharp faculties; similarly, the view-prone individual. Among these, the first, who grasps the inversion 'beautiful' in what is unattractive, discerning the true nature of the body with the power of mindfulness, uproots that distortion with the power of development and enters the fixed course of rightness. The second, who grasps the inversion 'pleasant' in what is suffering, 'does not tolerate the arising of sensual thoughts,' as stated. Dispelling the opposing factors with the power of energy, which is restraint, he shatters that distortion by the power of development and enters the fixed course of rightness. The third, who grasps the inversion 'permanent' in what is impermanent, with his mind composed through the power of tranquility, discerning the momentary nature of formations, uproots that distortion by the power of development and enters the fixed course of rightness. The fourth, who is deceived by the compactness of continuity, group, function, and object, clinging wrongly to what is merely a heap of contact and other phenomena as 'self,' shatters that wrong adherence through the contemplation of emptiness in four ways and realizes the fruit of recluseship. Or, by way of the four distortions such as the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure, the truth of origin is understood. The five aggregates of clinging, which serve as the basis and object of these distortions, are the truth of suffering, and so on; the connection of the Truths should be understood. Here, the four fruits of recluseship are the result. The unwholesome side should be understood by way of the four distortions, by way of the four taints, floods, yokes, bodily knots, wrong destinations, the arising of craving, clinging, the seven stations of consciousness, non-full understanding, and so on. Likewise, the pure side should be understood by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, by way of the four kinds of jhānas, abidings, resolutions, factors pertaining to happiness, immeasurables, right efforts, bases of psychic power, and so on. This is the foundation of the lion's play method.

Imesaṃ [M 1.0061] pana tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ siddhiyā vohāranayadvayaṃ siddhameva hoti. Tathā hi atthanayānaṃ disābhūtadhammālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ, tesaṃ samānayanaṃ aṅkusoti pañcapi nayā idha niyuttāti veditabbā. Idañca suttaṃ soḷasavidhe suttantapaṭṭhāne nibbedhasekkhabhāgiyaṃ byatirekamukhena patiṭṭhānāyūhanāni gahitānīti saṃkilesanibbedhasekkhabhāgiyaṃ cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhavīsatividhe pana suttantapaṭṭhāne lokiyalokuttaraṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇañeyyaṃ dassanabhāvanaṃ sakavacanaṃ vissajjanīyaṃ kusalaṃ anuññātanti veditabbaṃ.

However, for the accomplishment of these three modes of meaning, the two modes of conventional expression are indeed established. Thus, the examination of phenomena that are directions is the 'direction-examination' among the modes of meaning, and their unification is the 'goad'; thus, all five modes are to be understood as applied here. And this sutta, in the sixteenfold classification of Sutta foundations, is to be seen as belonging to the category of penetration and the learner’s portion, and also as belonging to the category of defilement, penetration, and the learner’s portion, since foundation and accumulation are taken by way of the method of difference. However, in the twenty-eightfold classification of Sutta foundations, it is to be understood as worldly and supramundane, having seven bases, knowledge and the knowable, vision and cultivation, one’s own statement, the reply, the wholesome, and the permitted.

Oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Oghataraṇa Sutta is concluded.

2. Nimokkhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Nimokkha Sutta

2. Paṭhamamāgatanti saṃvaṇṇanāvasena paṭhamasuttādīsu paṭhamaṃ āgatapadaṃ. Uttānatthanti pākaṭatthaṃ. Apubbaṃyeva hi duviññeyyatthañca padaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbaṃ. Noti pucchāyaṃ nu-saddena samānattho nipātoti āha “jānāsi noti jānāsi nū”ti. Vaṭṭato nimuccanti tena sattāti nimokkho, maggo. So ca pamuccanti tenāti pamokkho, pamuccanante pana adhigantabbattāphalaṃ “pamokkho”ti vuttaṃ, yathā arahattaṃ “rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo”ti vuttaṃ. Teti sattā. Viviccatīti visuṃ asammisso hoti, vigacchatīti attho. Viviccati dukkhaṃ etasmāti viveko. Dutiyavikappe pana sakalavaṭṭadukkhato sattā nimuccanti ettha pamuccanti viviccanti cāti nimokkho pamokkho viveko, nibbānanti attho [V 1.0055] veditabbo. Etthāti ca nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avadhāraṇattho kho-kāro “assosi kho”tiādīsu viya.

2. “First arrived” (paṭhamamāgataṃ) means the word that appears first in the first sutta and so on, by way of explanation. “Clear in meaning” (uttānatthaṃ) means evident in meaning. For a word whose meaning is both unprecedented and difficult to understand must be explained. The particle “no” (no) has the same meaning as the interrogative particle “nu”; thus he says: “‘jānāsi no’ means ‘jānāsi nu’ (do you know?).” Beings are freed (nimuccanti) from the round by that—thus, “nimokkho” (liberation) is the path. And beings are completely freed (pamuccanti) by that—thus, “pamokkho” (complete liberation). But because the fruit is to be attained at the end of complete liberation, it is called “pamokkha,” just as arahantship is described as “the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion.” “They” (te) refers to beings. “Is secluded” (viviccati) means is separate, not mixed; the meaning is “goes away.” Suffering is secluded from this (viviccati dukkhaṃ etasmā)—thus, “viveko” (seclusion). In the second alternative, however, beings are freed, completely freed, and secluded from all the suffering of the round in this—thus, “nimokkho,” “pamokkho,” and “viveko” are to be understood as meaning Nibbāna. And here, the locative word (ettha) should be understood in the sense of a cause. The particle “kho” has the meaning of emphasis, as in “he heard, indeed,” and so on.

Nandīmūlako bhavo nandībhavo purimapade uttarapadalopena “sākabhakkho patthavo sākapatthavo”ti yathā. Paṭhamaṃ kammavaṭṭapadhānaṃ atthaṃ vatvā puna kilesakammānaṃ vasena ubhayappadhānaṃ atthaṃ vadanto “nandiyā cā”tiādimāha. Purimanayeti nandīmūlako kammabhavo nandībhavoti etasmiṃ pakkhe. Nandībhavenāti nandībhavapadena. Tividhakammābhisaṅkhāravasenāti puññābhisaṅkhārādivasena kāyasaṅkhārādivasena ca tippakārassa kammābhisaṅkhārassa [M 1.0062] vasena. Saṅkhārakkhandho gahito cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhassa. Saññāviññāṇehīti “saññāviññāṇasaṅkhayā”ti evaṃ vuttasaññāviññāṇapadehi. Taṃsampayuttā cāti tena yathāvuttasaṅkhārakkhandhena samaṃ yuttā eva. Dve khandhāti saññāviññāṇakkhandhā.

“Existence rooted in delight” (nandīmūlako bhavo) is “delight-existence” (nandībhavo), by elision of the latter part of the first word, just as in “sākabhakkho patthavo” becoming “sākapatthavo.” First, having stated the meaning with the round of kamma as primary, then stating the meaning with both defilements and kamma as primary by way of “and of delight” (nandiyā ca), and so on. According to the previous method: in this case, `nandībhavo` is kamma-existence rooted in delight. “By delight-existence” (nandībhavena) means by the term “delight-existence.” “By means of the threefold kamma-formation” (tividhakammābhisaṅkhāravasena) means by way of the three kinds of kamma-formations, that is, by way of meritorious formations, etc., and by way of bodily formations, etc. The formation aggregate is taken because intention is predominant in the formation aggregate. “By perception and consciousness” (saññāviññāṇehi) means by the terms “perception” and “consciousness” as stated thus: “by the count of perception and consciousness” (saññāviññāṇasaṅkhayā). “And associated with that” (taṃsampayuttā ca) means indeed associated together with that aforementioned formation aggregate. “The two aggregates” (dve khandhā) refers to the perception and consciousness aggregates.

Nanu ettha vedanākkhandho na gahitoti? No na gahitoti dassento “tehi panā”tiādimāha. Tīhi khandhehīti saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhehi. Gahitāva avinābhāvato. Na hi vedanārahito koci cittuppādo atthi. Anupādiṇṇakānanti kusalākusalānaṃ. Na hettha kiriyākhandhānaṃ appavatti adhippetā. Appavattivasenāti anuppattidhammatāpattivasena. Nibbattanavasena kammakilesehi upādīyatīti upādi, pañcakkhandhā. Upādino seso upādiseso, saha upādisesenāti saupādisesaṃ. Nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ sakalakammakilesavūpasamatthassa jotitattā. Heṭṭhā dvīhi padehi anupādiṇṇakakkhandhā gahitāti “vedanāna”nti ettha upādiṇṇakaggahaṇaṃ yuttanti āha “upādiṇṇakavedanāna”nti. Nirodhenāti tappaṭibaddhachandarāganirodhavasena nirujjhanena. Upasamenāti accantūpasamena appavattanena. Evañca katvā ca-saddaggahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Tesanti tassā vedanāya taṃsampayuttānañca tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ. Vatthārammaṇavasenāti vatthubhūtānaṃ channaṃ ārammaṇabhūtānañca sabbesampi upādiṇṇakarūpadhammānaṃ vasena.

“But is not the aggregate of feeling not taken here?” To show that it is not not taken, he says “But by those” (tehi pana) and so on. “By the three aggregates” (tīhi khandhehi) refers to the aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness. It is certainly taken because they are inseparable. For there is no arising of consciousness without feeling. “Of the non-grasped” (anupādiṇṇakānaṃ) means of the wholesome and unwholesome. Here, the non-occurrence of the functional aggregates is not intended. “By way of non-occurrence” (appavattivasena) means by way of attaining the state of non-arising. That which is grasped by kamma and defilements by way of generation is “grasping” (upādi), that is, the five aggregates. The remainder of what is grasped is the “residue of grasping” (upādisesa). “With a residue of grasping” (saupādisesaṃ) means together with the residue of grasping. Nibbāna is spoken of, since the meaning of the pacification of all kamma and defilements has been illuminated. Below, by two terms, the non-grasped aggregates are taken. Therefore, it is appropriate to take “of feelings” (vedanānaṃ) here as referring to the grasped; hence he says, “of the grasped feelings” (upādiṇṇakavedanānaṃ). “By cessation” (nirodhena) means by its ceasing, by way of the cessation of the desire and lust connected with it. “By pacification” (upasamena) means by complete pacification, by non-occurrence. And thus, the inclusion of the word “and” (ca) is justified. “Of these” (tesaṃ) refers to that feeling and the three aggregates associated with it. “By way of basis and object” (vatthārammaṇavasena) means by way of all the grasped material phenomena that are the sixfold basis and objects.

Kasmā pana heṭṭhā cattāro arūpakkhandhāyeva vuttā, rūpakkhandho na gahitoti? Visesabhāvato. Saupādisesanibbānappattiyañhi upādiṇṇakarūpadhammānaṃ viya anupādiṇṇakarūpadhammānaṃ appavattiyeva natthi. Dutiyanayeti nandiyā ca bhavassa cāti etamhi pakkhe. Nandiggahaṇena saṅkhārakkhandho gahito taṃsahacaraṇato. Upapattibhavasaṅkhāto rūpakkhandhoti upādiṇṇakarūpadhammameva vadati. Taggahaṇeneva ca tannimittakāni utuāhārajāni, viññāṇaggahaṇena [V 1.0056] cittajānīti catusantatirūpassapettha gahitatā veditabbā. Saññādīhīti saññāviññāṇavedanāgahaṇehi tayo khandhā gahitā, tañca kho upādiṇṇā anupādiṇṇāti vibhāgaṃ akatvā avisesato. Avisesena hi pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ appavatti nibbānaṃ. Tenāha “evaṃ…pe… nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ hotī”ti. “Nibbāna”nti hi idha amatamahānibbānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Imameva ca nayanti idaṃ yathāvuttaṃ dutiyameva. Cattāro [M 1.0063] mahānikāye dhāretīti catunikāyiko. Bhaṇḍikanāmako thero bhaṇḍikatthero. Itīti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Nibbānavasenevāti paṭhamanaye saupādisesanibbānassa anupādisesanibbānassa ca, dutiye pana “amatamahānibbānassā”ti sabbathāpi nibbānasseva vasena bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi samāpesīti.

“But why below were only the four formless aggregates spoken of, and the form aggregate not taken?” Because of its special nature. For in the attainment of Nibbāna with residue, non-grasped material phenomena do not cease to occur, just as grasped material phenomena do not. In the second method: in the case of “and of delight and of existence” (nandiyā ca bhavassa ca). By taking “delight” (nandi), the formation aggregate is taken, because it accompanies it. The form aggregate, designated as rebirth-existence, refers only to grasped material phenomena. And by taking that, those phenomena born of temperature and nutriment which are its condition are implied; by taking consciousness, those born of mind are implied. Thus, the inclusion here of form of fourfold continuity should be understood. “By perception and so on” (saññādīhi) means that by the taking of perception, consciousness, and feeling, three aggregates are taken, and that without making a distinction between grasped and non-grasped, that is, without distinction. For Nibbāna is the non-occurrence of the five aggregates without distinction. Therefore, he said: “Thus… Nibbāna has been explained.” For here, “Nibbāna” (nibbānaṃ) is intended as the Deathless, the Great Nibbāna. And “this very method” (imameva ca nayaṃ) means this very second method as stated. “He bears in mind the four great Nikāyas” (cattāro mahānikāye dhāreti) means he is a master of the four Nikāyas. The elder named Bhaṇḍika is Elder Bhaṇḍika. “Thus” (iti) is a reference to the manner stated. “By way of Nibbāna alone” (nibbānavaseneva) means that in the first method, it is by way of Nibbāna with residue and Nibbāna without residue; in the second, however, it is by way of “the Deathless, the Great Nibbāna.” Thus in every way, the Blessed One concluded and completed his teaching by way of Nibbāna alone.

Nimokkhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nimokkha Sutta is completed.

3. Upanīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Upanīya Sutta.

3. Anekatthattā dhātusaddānaṃ upasaggavasena atthavisesavācako hotīti āha “upanīyatīti parikkhīyati nirujjhatī”ti. Vinassatīti attho. Upanīyatīti vā saraseneva jīvitassa maraṇūpagamanaṃ vuttanti āha – “upagacchati vā, anupubbena maraṇaṃ upetīti attho”ti. Kāmañcettha “upanīyatī”ti padaṃ apākaṭakammavisesaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā pana “sabbaṃ ārogyaṃ byādhipariyosānaṃ, sabbaṃ yobbanaṃ jarāpariyosānaṃ, sabbaṃ jīvitaṃ maraṇapariyosāna”nti, “upanīyati jīvita”nti vuttattā “maraṇaṃ upetī”ti vuttaṃ. Kammakattuvasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ.

3. Because verbal root words have many meanings, a prefix serves to express a specific meaning. Thus, he says: '“Is led on” (upanīyati) means “it is exhausted, it ceases.”' The meaning is 'it perishes.' Or, he says that “is led on” (upanīyati) is said to mean the approaching of death by life by its very nature. Thus, he says: 'Or it approaches; the meaning is it gradually approaches death.' And although here the word 'upanīyati' is stated as a verb with an unspecified object, just as it is said: 'All health ends in sickness, all youth ends in old age, all life ends in death,' so too, because it is said 'life is led on,' it is therefore said 'it approaches death.' This is stated in the sense of the grammatical object.

Idāni kammasādhanavasena atthaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gopālena gogaṇo nīyati yathicchitaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Jīvanti tena sattā, sahajātadhammā vāti jīvitaṃ, tadeva tesaṃ anupālane ādhipaccasabbhāvato indriyanti āha “jīvitanti jīvitindriya”nti parittanti ittaraṃ. Tenāha “thoka”nti. Pabandhānupacchedassa paccayabhāvo idha jīvitassa maraṇakiccanti adhippetanti āha “sarasaparittatāya cā”tiādi. Āyūti ca paramāyu idhādhippetaṃ, tañca ajjakālavasena veditabbaṃ.

Now, to explain the meaning by way of its instrumental function, 'just as' and so forth is stated. Just as a cowherd leads a herd of cattle to a desired place, so by this do beings live. 'Life' means either co-nascent phenomena or that very thing which, in sustaining them, is called a faculty due to its nature of dominance; thus, it is said: 'Life means the life faculty.' 'Limited' means momentary. Therefore, it is said: 'brief.' Here, the state of being a condition for the non-interruption of the continuum is intended as the function of life, which is the task of death. Thus, it is said: 'due to its being a stream and momentary,' and so on. 'Lifespan' here refers to the maximum lifespan, and that should be understood according to the present time.

Imasmiñhi buddhuppāde ayaṃ kathāti jīvitassa atiittarabhāvadīpanaparā ayaṃ desanā. Jīvitindriyavasena jīvitakkhayaṃ niyamento “ekacittappavattimattoyevā”ti āha, ekassa cittuppādassa [V 1.0057] pavattikkhaṇamatto evāti attho. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pavattamānanti nemirathīsā vattantī ekeneva nemippadesena [M 1.0064] pavattati ekasmiṃ khaṇeti adhippāyo. “Ekeneva tiṭṭhatī”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ekacittakkhaṇikanti ekacittakkhaṇamattavantaṃ. Tasmiṃ citteti tasmiṃ yasmiṃ kismiñci ekasmiṃ citte. Niruddhamatteti niruddhabhāvappattamatte. Niruddhoti vuccatīti matoti vuccati taṃsamaṅgī satto paramatthato. Avisesaviduno pana aviññāyamānantarena anusandhānassa niruddhanaṃ nirodhaṃ sallakkhenti. Yathāvuttamatthaṃ suttena vibhāvetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena tīsupi kālesu sattānaṃ paramatthato jīvanaṃ maraṇaṃ cittakkhaṇavasenevāti dasseti.

For at the arising of the Buddha, this discourse was taught to illuminate the extremely momentary nature of life. When determining the cessation of life by way of the life faculty, it is said: 'merely the duration of a single thought-moment'—meaning just the moment of a single thought's arising. Now, to clarify that meaning through a simile, 'just as' and so forth is stated. There, 'while moving' means that the rim of a chariot wheel, while turning, moves by just a single point of the rim at any one moment—that is the intention. The same applies to 'stands by just one.' 'Momentary as a single thought' means possessing only a single thought-moment. 'In that thought' refers to that, any single thought whatsoever. 'Just ceased' means having reached the state of cessation. 'Ceased' is called 'dead'—that being, in the ultimate sense, is endowed with that. But the unwise, lacking discernment, perceive cessation as annihilation without understanding the connection. To elucidate the aforesaid meaning with a sutta, 'as he said' and so forth is stated. Thereby, it shows that in all three times, the living and dying of beings, in the ultimate sense, depend on the moment of thought.

Jīvitanti jīvitindriyaṃ. Attabhāvoti jīvitavedanāviññāṇāni ṭhapetvā avasiṭṭhadhammā adhippetā. Sukhadukkhāti sukhadukkhā vedanā, upekkhāpi idha sukhadukkhāsveva antogadhā iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvato. Kevalāti attanā, niccabhāvena vā avomissā. Ekacittasamāyuttāti ekakena cittena sahitā. Lahuso vattate khaṇoti vuttanayena ekacittakkhaṇikatāya lahuko atiittaro jīvitādīnaṃ khaṇo vattati.

'Life' means the life faculty. 'Individual existence' refers to the remaining phenomena, excluding life, feeling, and consciousness. 'Pleasure and pain' means pleasant and painful feelings; even equanimity is included here under pleasure and pain because of its desirable or undesirable nature. 'Mere' means by itself, or unmixed with permanence. 'Associated with a single thought' means accompanied by a single thought. 'Swiftly passes in a moment'—as explained, due to its existence for a single moment of thought, the moment of life and so on passes swiftly, being extremely momentary.

Ye niruddhā marantassāti cavantassa sattassa cutito uddhaṃ niruddhāti vattabbā ye khandhā. Tiṭṭhamānassa vā idhāti ye vā idha pavattiyaṃ tiṭṭhamānassa dharantassa bhaṅgappattiyā niruddhā khandhā, sabbepi sadisā te sabbepi ekasadisā gatā atthaṅgatā appaṭisandhiyā puna āgantvā paṭisandhānābhāvena vigatā. Yathā hi cutikhandhā na nibbattanti, evaṃ tato pubbepi khandhā. Tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitanti adhippāyo.

Those aggregates that cease for one who is dying—that is, those aggregates that should be said to have ceased subsequent to the passing of a being who is passing away. Or, for one who remains here—that is, those aggregates that cease for one persisting and continuing in this course of existence, having reached dissolution—all of them are similar. All have gone to the same state, have vanished, gone to their end, without renewed rebirth, having disappeared due to the absence of renewed linking. Just as the aggregates at death do not arise again, so too the aggregates before that. Therefore, the meaning is that the life of beings lasts only a single mind-moment.

Anibbattena na jātoti anuppannena cittena jāto na hoti “anāgate cittakkhaṇe na jīvittha na jīvati jīvissatī”ti vattabbato. Paccuppannena vattamānena cittena jīvati jīvamāno nāma hoti, na jīvittha na jīvissati. Cittabhaṅgā mato lokoti cuticittassa viya sabbassapi tassa tassa cittassa bhaṅgappattiyā ayaṃ loko paramatthato mato nāma hoti “atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvittha na jīvati na jīvissatī”ti vattabbato, niruddhassa appaṭisandhikattā. Evaṃ santepi paññatti paramatthiyā, yāyaṃ taṃ taṃ pavattaṃ cittaṃ upādāya “tisso jīvati, phusso jīvatī”ti vacanappavattiyā [M 1.0065] visayabhūtā santānapaññatti, sā ettha paramatthiyā paramatthabhūtā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.76).

'Not born by what is unborn' means one is not born by a consciousness that has not arisen, because it can be said: 'In a future moment of consciousness, one has not lived, does not live, nor will live.' One is called 'living' by the presently occurring, current consciousness—one who is living now—but not 'has lived' or 'will live.' 'The world dies with the dissolution of consciousness' means that just as with the death-consciousness, so too, upon the dissolution of each and every consciousness, this world is, in the ultimate sense, called 'dead,' because it can be said: 'In a past moment of consciousness, one has lived, does not live, nor will live,' since what has ceased does not relink. Even so, a convention exists in relation to the ultimate. That continuous convention, which is the basis for the usage of speech such as 'Tissa lives, Phussa lives,' arises by taking that particular occurring consciousness as its basis. Here, that convention, which pertains to the ultimate, is itself an ultimate reality. As it has been said: 'Lineage and name do not decay' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.76).

Na [V 1.0058] santi tāṇāti jaraṃ upagatassa tato taṃnimittaṃ yaṃ vā pāpakārino pāpakammānaṃ upaṭṭhānavasena puññakārino piyavippayogavasena cittadukkhaṃ ubhayesampi bandhanacchedanādivasena vitujjamānaṃ anappakaṃ sarīradukkhaṃ sammohappatti ca hoti, tato tāyantā na santi. Tenāha – “tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ saraṇaṃ bhavituṃ samatthā nāma keci natthī”ti. Bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, bhayanimittanti āha “bhayavatthū”ti. Taggahaṇena ca cittutrāsalakkhaṇaṃ bhayaṃ gahitameva, sati nimitte nemittaṃ santamevāti. Pubbacetananti ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ nānāvajjanavīthiyaṃ sampavattaṃ upacārajjhānacetanaṃ. Aparacetananti vasībhāvāpādanavasena parato samāpajjanavasena ca pavattaṃ samāpatticetanaṃ. Muñcacetananti vikkhambhanavasena pavattaṃ paṭhamappanācetanaṃ. Kusalajjhānassa vipākajjhāneva labbhamānaṃ sukhaṃ jhānasukhaṃ. Iṭṭhapariyāyo cettha sukha-saddo. Jhāne apekkhā jhānanikanti. Jhānassa assādavasena pavatto lobho jhānassādo. Yena te te brahmāno jhānato vuṭṭhāya “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”nti vācaṃ nicchāresunti. Yathā devā sukhabahulā tihetupaṭisandhikāvāti paṭipajjantā jhānaṃ adhigantuṃ bhabbā, na itareti “kāmāvacaradevesū”ti vuttaṃ. Kāmāvacarā ca uparidevā ca kāmāvacaradevāti ekadesasarūpekaseso daṭṭhabbo. Tena manussānampi ekaccānaṃ sabbesampi vā saṅgaho siddho hoti patthanāparikappanāya visayabhāvato. Tenāha “aho vatime ca…pe… tiṭṭheyyu”nti. Thullāni phusitāni vipphurāni etthāti thullaphusitako, kālo, deso vā. Tasmiṃ thullaphusitake.

There is no protection. For one who has reached old age, due to that sign—whether for evildoers due to the arising of their bad deeds, or for the virtuous due to separation from loved ones—there is mental suffering. For both, there is also considerable bodily suffering due to being afflicted by bonds, cutting, and so forth, and the onset of delusion. Therefore, there are no protectors. Hence it is said: 'There is no one capable of being a refuge, shelter, or sanctuary.' That from which one fears is fear, and the basis of fear is termed 'the grounds of fear.' By taking this, the characteristic of fear—trembling of mind—is understood. When there is a cause, the effect is present. 'Prior volition' refers to the access concentration volition that has arisen in a single attention-directing cognitive process or in multiple attention-directing cognitive processes. 'Subsequent volition' refers to the absorption volition that has arisen by way of producing mastery and by way of subsequent attainment. 'Releasing volition' refers to the initial attainment volition that has arisen by way of suppression. The happiness attainable in the resultant absorption of a wholesome absorption is absorption-bliss. Here, the word 'happiness' denotes what is agreeable. The expectation in absorption is 'absorption-desire.' The greed that arises due to the savoring of absorption is 'absorption-savoring,' by which those brahmās, emerging from absorption, exclaim, 'Ah, bliss! Ah, bliss!' Just as the devas, who are abundant in happiness and have three-rooted rebirth-linking, are capable of attaining absorption, but not others—thus, it is said: 'among the sense-sphere devas.' The sense-sphere devas and the higher devas are to be understood as 'sense-sphere devas' by the grammatical rule of elision of one member of a similar class. Thus, even among humans, some—or all—are included by way of aspiration and conceptualization due to the nature of their objects. Hence it is said: 'Ah, if only these beings... were to remain...' 'Where gross contacts have spread and expanded'—this is the 'place of gross contacts,' whether referring to time or location. In that place of gross contacts...

“Puññāni kayirātha sukhāvahānī”ti vuttattā “aniyyānikaṃ vaṭṭakathaṃ kathetī”ti vuttaṃ. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko, kilesehi āmasitabbato āmisañcāti lokāmisaṃ. Nippariyāyāmisaṃ pana loke āmisantipi lokāmisaṃ. Pariyāyeti sabhāvato parivattetvā ñāpeti etenāti pariyāyo, leso, kāraṇaṃ vāti āha “nippariyāyena cattāro paccayā”ti, vaṭṭassa ekantato bālalokeheva [M 1.0066] āmasitabbabhāvato pariyāyāmisatā vuttā. Idha pari..pe… adhippetaṃ vivaṭṭapaṭiyogino icchitattā. Catupaccayāpekkhañhi pahānaṃ. Ekaccassa sakalavaṭṭāpekkhappahānassapi paccayo hotīti “vaṭṭatiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Vūpasamati ettha sakalavaṭṭadukkhanti santi, asaṅkhatadhātūti āha “nibbānasaṅkhāta”nti.

'Perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness,' it is said, and thus, 'engaging in talk of the cycle that is not conducive to liberation' is mentioned. The world, in the sense of breaking up and dissolving, is called 'worldly bait' because it is to be grasped by defilements. However, bait in the direct sense, being bait in the world, is also 'worldly bait'. 'Circumlocution' means that which, by turning away from its own nature, makes something known—thus, it is called 'circumlocution,' a pretext, or a reason. Hence, it is said, 'the four requisites without circumlocution.' The bait of the cycle is described as circumlocutory bait because it is to be grasped entirely by the foolish world. Here... is intended, because the opposite of the cycle is desired. For abandonment is dependent on the four requisites. For some, even the complete abandonment dependent on the entire cycle is a condition—thus, it is said, 'just the cycle,' with some reservation. 'It subsides'—here, the suffering of the entire cycle ceases, and it is called 'the unconditioned element,' hence it is said, 'designated as Nibbāna.'

Upanīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Upanīya Sutta is concluded.

4. Accentisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Accentisutta

4. Kālayanti [V 1.0059] khepentīti kālā. Purebhattādayo hi kālā dhammappavattimattatāya paramatthato avijjamānāpi lokasaṅketamattasiddhā tassāyeva dhammappavattiyā gatagatāya anivattanato taṃ taṃ dhammappavattiṃ khepentā vināsayantā viya sayañca tāhi saddhiṃ accentā viya honti. Tenāha – “kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā”ti (jā. 1.2.190). “Tarayanti rattiyo”ti etthāpi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. “Etaṃ bhayaṃ maraṇe pekkhamāno”ti vuccamānattā puggalaṃ maraṇūpagamanāya tarayantīti attho vutto. Vayoguṇāti ettha koṭṭhāsā guṇā. Titthiyānaṃ hi carimacittena sakalacitte vayasamūhe vayasamaññāti āha – “paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavayānaṃ guṇā, rāsayoti attho”ti. Ānisaṃsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho “vākaciraṃ nivāsesiṃ, dvādasaguṇamupāgata”ntiādīsu (bu. vaṃ. 2.30) viya. “Tandiguṇāhaṃ karissāmi, diguṇaṃ diguṇaṃ vaddheyyā”ti ca evamādīsu pana tabbhāvavuttiattho guṇaṭṭho.

4. 'They measure and spend'—thus, they are 'times' (kālā). For times such as the forenoon, though ultimately non-existent due to being merely the occurrence of phenomena, are established merely by worldly convention. Because they do not turn back from the flow of those very phenomena once they have occurred, they seem to consume and destroy those very occurrences of phenomena, and they themselves seem to pass away along with them. Therefore it is said: 'Time devours all beings, along with itself' (Jā. 1.2.190). Here too, in 'the nights hasten on,' the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated. Since it is said, 'seeing this fear in death,' the meaning is that it causes a person to hasten towards approaching death. In 'the stages of life' (vayoguṇā), the 'guṇā' are portions. For the sectarians hold that with the final thought, the entire collection of ages in the whole mind is the concept of age—thus, it is said: 'The "guṇā" are the first, middle, and last stages of life, meaning the collection.' The meaning of 'guṇa' as benefit is seen in phrases like 'I wore bark-cloth, endowed with twelve qualities' (Bv. 2.30) and so on. But in phrases like 'I will make it threefold, may it increase twofold, twofold,' and so on, the meaning of 'guṇa' refers to the sense of being in that state.

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāma sahassato”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1313; udā. 53; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.76) –

'Countless are the names of the great sage, along with his qualities; By a single quality, a name might be derived, even a thousandfold.' (Dhs.A. 1313; Ud. 53; Paṭis.A. 1.1.76)

Ādīsu pasaṃsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho daṭṭhabbo. “Vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahantī”ti ettha attho “accenti kālā”ti ettha vuttanayo eva. Paṭhamamajjhimavayāti paṭhamaggahaṇañcettha vayassa gatassa apunarāvattidassanatthaṃ kataṃ. Tenevāha – “maraṇakkhaṇe pana tayopi vayā jahantevā”ti.

In these and similar instances, the meaning of 'guṇa' as praise should be understood. Here, the meaning of 'the stages of life gradually abandon' is the same as the method stated in 'times pass away.' Here, the mention of 'first and middle ages' is made to show that age, once gone, does not return. Therefore it is said: 'At the moment of death, however, all three ages are indeed abandoned.'

Ettha [M 1.0067] ca pāḷiyaṃ “accenti kālā”ti sāmaññato kālassa apagamanaṃ dassitaṃ, puna taṃ visesatopi dassetuṃ itaradvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mudindriyassa vasena “vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahantī”ti vuttaṃ, majjhimindriyassa vasena “tarayanti rattiyo”ti vuttanti adhippāyena “kālāti purebhattādayo kālā”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā tattha ādi-saddena pacchābhattapaṭhamayāma-muhuttakālādi-kālakoṭṭhāso eva aṇupabhedo kālavibhāgo gahitoti veditabbo. Sesanti idha dvīsu gāthāsu pacchimaddho. So hi idha atthato adhigatattā anantarasutte ca vuttattā atidisito.

Here, in the Pāli text, 'times pass away' generally shows the passing of time, and the other two phrases are stated to show this specifically. In the commentary, however, 'the stages of life gradually abandon' is stated with reference to those of dull faculties, and 'the nights hasten on' is stated with reference to those of middling faculties. With this intention, it is said: 'times are times such as the forenoon.' Therefore, it should be understood that by the word 'etc.' there, only the minute subdivisions of time, such as the afternoon, the first watch of the night, moments, and other portions of time, are included as divisions of time. The 'rest' here refers to the latter half of the two verses. For its meaning is understood here, and it is also stated in the immediately subsequent sutta, thus it is referred to by extension.

Accentisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Accentisutta is concluded.

5. Katichindasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Katichinda Sutta

5. Chindantoti [V 1.0060] samucchindanto. Kati chindeyyāti kittake pāpadhamme samucchindeyya, anuppattidhammataṃ pāpeyya. Sesapadesupīti sesesupi dvīsu padesu. Jahanto kati jaheyya, bhāvento kati uttari bhāveyyāti imamatthaṃ “eseva nayo”ti iminā atidisati. Catutthapadassa pana attho sarūpeneva dassito. Atthato ekanti bhāvatthato ekaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kimatthaṃ pariyāyantaraṃ gahitanti āha “gāthābandhassa panā”tiādi. Atthato ettha punarutti atthevāti āha “saddapunaruttiṃ vajjayantī”ti. Saṅgaṃ atikkamayatīti saṅgātigoti āha “ayamevattho”ti.

5. 'Chindanto' means completely cutting off. 'Kati chindeyya' means how many evil qualities one should completely cut off, so as to make them states of non-arising. 'Sesapadesupi' means in the remaining two phrases as well. The meaning of 'how many should one abandon by abandoning, how many should one further develop by developing' is referred to by extension with 'this is the method.' The meaning of the fourth phrase, however, is shown in its own form. In meaning, it is one; in the sense of its nature, it is one. If so, for what purpose is a different mode of expression adopted? He says: 'But for the sake of the verse composition,' and so on. He says that there is indeed repetition in meaning here, while avoiding verbal repetition. 'Saṅgaṃ atikkamayatīti' means he transcends attachment; thus, he is 'saṅgātigo' (one who has transcended attachment)—thus he says: 'this is the meaning.'

Oraṃ vuccati kāmadhātu, paṭisandhiyā paccayabhāvena tañca bhajantīti orambhāgiyāni. Tattha ca kammaṃ tabbipākaṃ satte dukkhaṃ, kammunā vipākaṃ, sattena dukkhaṃ saṃyojentīti saṃyojanāni, sakkāyadiṭṭhi-vicikicchā-sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāmarāga-paṭighā. Uddhaṃ vuccati catasso arūpadhātuyo, vuttanayena taṃ bhajantīti uddhambhāgiyāni, saṃyojanāni rūpārūparāgamānuddhaccāvijjā. Āropitavacanānurūpeneva evamāhāti “pañca chinde pañca jahe”ti evaṃ kathesi tassā devatāya sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ. Na kevalaṃ tāya devatāya vuttavacanānurūpato eva, atha kho tesu saṃyojanesu [M 1.0068] vattabbākāratopīti dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena orambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma garūni ducchedāni gāḷhabandhanabhāvato, tasmā tāni sandhāya “pañca chinde”ti vuttaṃ.

The lower part is called the sense-sphere, and because they pertain to it by being a condition for rebirth-linking, they are called the lower fetters. And therein, those that fetter—binding result to action, and suffering to beings—are the fetters: identity view, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will. The upper part is called the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and because they pertain to it in the way stated, they are called the higher fetters: the fetters are desire for form, desire for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. In accordance with the conventional expression, he spoke thus: 'Cut off five, abandon five,' for the sake of that deity's easy comprehension. Not only was this spoken in accordance with the words spoken by that deity, but also to show the manner in which these fetters should be discussed, hence the phrase 'or alternatively,' and so on, is stated. Therefore, the lower fetters are indeed heavy and hard to sever due to their deeply binding nature; thus, referring to them, it is said, 'Cut off five.'

Uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni pana lahūni succhedāni heṭṭhā pavattitānukkamena bhāvanānayena pahātabbato, tasmā tāni sandhāya “pañca jahe”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “pādesu baddhapāsasakuṇo viyā”tiādi. Visesanti bhāvanānaṃ visesaṃ vipassanābhāvanaṃ bhāvento uppādento vipaccento vaḍḍhento ca. Saṃsārapaṅke sañjanaṭṭhena rāgo eva saṅgo “rāgasaṅgo”. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yasmā ettha rāga-moha-diṭṭhi-tabbhāgiyasakkāyadiṭṭhi-sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāmarāgāvijjā atthato oghā eva, itare tadekaṭṭhā, tasmā bhagavā saṃyojanappahānasaṅgātikkamehi oghataraṇaṃ kathesi. Lokiyalokuttarāni kathitāni “bhāvaye”ti pubbabhāgāya maggabhāvanāya adhippetattā.

The higher fetters, however, are light and easy to sever, as they are to be abandoned by the method of development in sequence, following what has proceeded below. Therefore, with reference to them, it is said, 'Abandon five.' Thus it is said: 'Like a bird with a snare bound to its feet,' and so on. Developing 'further' means developing, generating, maturing, and increasing the special meditation, namely insight meditation. Lust itself is an attachment, 'the attachment of lust,' because of its clinging nature in the mire of saṃsāra. This method applies to the rest as well. Since here lust, delusion, views, and the fetters pertaining to them—identity view, clinging to rites and rituals, sensual desire, and ignorance—are, in essence, indeed the floods, while the others share the same meaning, therefore the Blessed One taught crossing the flood through the abandonment of fetters and the transcending of attachments. The mundane and supramundane are spoken of by 'one should develop' because the development of the path in its preliminary stage is intended.

Katichindasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Katichinda Sutta is concluded.

6. Jāgarasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Jāgara Sutta

6. Jāgaratanti [V 1.0061] anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Tenāha “indriyesu jāgarantesū”ti. “Vissajjanagāthāyaṃ panā”ti imassa padassa “ayamattho veditabbo”ti iminā sambandho. Pucchāgāthāya pana attho imināva nayena viññāyatīti adhippāyo. Pañca jāgarataṃ suttāti ettha “suttā”ti padaṃ apekkhitvā pañcāti paccattavacanaṃ “jāgarata”nti padaṃ apekkhitvā sāmivasena pariṇāmetabbaṃ “pañcannaṃ jāgarata”nti. Tenāha – “pañcasu indriyesu jāgarantesū”ti, jāgarantesu baddhābhāvena sakiccappasutatāya sakiccasamatthatāya cāti attho. Sottaṃva suttā pamādaniddābhāvato. Tameva suttabhāvaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya dassetuṃ “kasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pamajjati, pamādo vā etassa atthīti pamādo, tassa bhāvo pamādatā, tāya, pamattabhāvenāti attho.

6. 'Jāgarataṃ' is a genitive absolute construction. Therefore it is said, 'while the faculties are vigilant.' The phrase 'But in the reply verse' is connected with 'this meaning is to be understood.' The intention is that the meaning of the question verse is understood by this same method. In the phrase 'pañca jāgarataṃ suttā' (five are asleep among the waking), with respect to the word 'suttā', 'pañca' is in the nominative. With respect to the word 'jāgarataṃ', it should be construed in the genitive as 'pañcannaṃ jāgarataṃ' (of the five who are waking). Therefore it is said, 'while the five faculties are vigilant,' meaning, while they are vigilant, they are not bound, being intent on their duties and capable of their duties. They are asleep like a stream, due to the absence of the sleep of negligence. To show that very state of being asleep through a discussion based on an individual, 'why?' and so forth was stated. One is negligent, or negligence exists for them, thus they are 'negligent' (pamādo); the state of that is 'negligence' (pamādatā); by that, meaning by the state of being negligent.

Evaṃ [M 1.0069] gāthāya paṭhamassa pādassa atthaṃ vatvā dutiyassa vattuṃ “evaṃ suttesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho vuttanayena veditabbo. Yasmā appahīnasupanakiriyāvasena sanīvaraṇassa puggalassa anuppannarāgarajādayo uppajjanti, uppannā pavaḍḍhanti, tasmā vuttaṃ “nīvaraṇeheva kilesarajaṃ ādiyatī”ti. Tenevāha “purimā”tiādi. Purimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ aparāparuppattiyā paccayabhāvo hettha ādiyanaṃ. Pañcahi indriyehi parisujjhatīti maggapariyāpannehi saddhādīhi pañcahi indriyehi sakalasaṃkilesato visujjhati. Paññindriyameva hi anaññātaññassāmītindriyādīni, itarāni ca anvayānīti.

Having thus explained the meaning of the first line of the verse, to explain the second, ‘thus in the suttas’ and so forth was stated. Its meaning should be understood in the way explained. Because for a person with hindrances, due to the unabandoned state of drowsiness, the unarisen dust of lust and so forth arises, and that which has arisen increases, therefore it is said, ‘through the hindrances one accumulates the dust of defilements.’ Therefore he said, ‘the former’ and so forth. Here, ‘accumulating’ means being the condition for the successive arising of the latter from the former. ‘He is purified by the five faculties’ means he is completely purified of all defilements by the five faculties of faith and so forth included within the path. For the wisdom faculty alone is the faculty of ‘I shall know the unknown’ and so forth, while the others are its consequents.

Jāgarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Jāgarasutta is concluded.

7. Appaṭividitasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Appaṭividita Sutta

7. Pavattinivattitadubhayahetuvibhāgassa dhammassapi catusaccantogadhattā āha “dhammāti catusaccadhammā”ti. Cattāripi hi ariyasaccāni catusaccantogadhāni. Appaṭividdhāti pariññābhisamayādivasena anabhisamitā. Diṭṭhigatavādesūti diṭṭhigatasaññitesu vādesu. Diṭṭhigatehi te pavattitā. Ito paresanti ito sāsanikehi paresaṃ aññesaṃ. Dhammatāyāti sabhāvena, sayamevāti attho. Gacchantīti pavattanti diṭṭhivādaṃ paggayha tiṭṭhanti. Parenāti diṭṭhigatikena. Nīyantīti diṭṭhivādasaṅgaṇhane uyyojīyanti. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi. Pabujjhitunti [V 1.0062] pamādaniddāya paṭibujjhituṃ. Paṭipadā yathādesitassa dhammassa kathitatāya, paṭibujjhituṃ yoniso pavattiyamānattā bhaddikā.

7. Because the Dhamma, which has the distinction of causes for both continuance and cessation, is also encompassed by the Four Truths, it is said: 'Dhamma refers to the Four Truths.' Indeed, all four Noble Truths are encompassed within the Four Truths. 'Not penetrated' means not fully realized by way of full comprehension, realization, and so forth. 'In statements of views' refers to discussions designated as speculative views. These views are propagated by those holding them. 'Others beyond this' means others apart from those within this Dispensation. 'By the nature of things' signifies by its intrinsic nature, by itself—this is the meaning.
