'They proceed' means they persist, taking up their views and standing upon them. 'By another' refers to one holding a speculative view. 'They are led' means they are incited into the adherence to speculative views. Therefore it is said: 'Herein...' and so forth. 'To awaken' means to awaken from the sleep of negligence. The path is auspicious because the Dhamma as taught has been spoken, and because it proceeds with wise attention for the purpose of awakening.

Hetunāti ñāyena. Kāraṇenāti catusaccānaṃ sambodhayuttiyā. Hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya sabbaṃ ñeyyaṃ jānātīti sabbaññū, teneva sabbaññutābhisambodhena buddhoti sabbaññubuddho. Paccekaṃ parehi asādhāraṇatāya visuṃ sayambhuñāṇena saccāni buddhavāti paccekabuddho. Paropadesena catusaccaṃ bujjhatīti catusaccabuddho. Tathā hi so sayambhutāya abhāvato kevalaṃ catusaccabuddhoti vuccati. Sutena sutamayañāṇena khandhādibhedaṃ ñeyyaṃ buddhavāti sutabuddho. Sabbaññubuddhapaccekabuddhe [M 1.0070] ṭhapetvā avasesā aggasāvakamahāsāvakāpi pakatisāvakāpi vītarāgā avasesā khīṇāsavā. Tayopi purimā vaṭṭanti sambuddhātiādivacanato. Sannivasati etenāti sannivāso, caritaṃ. Lokassa sannivāso lokasannivāso, tasmiṃ. Kāyaduccaritādibhede visame. Satisammosena visame vā sattanikāye. So hi visamayogato visamo. Rāgavisamādike visame vā kilesajāte. Taṃ visamaṃ pahāya taṃ visamaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā samaṃ sadisaṃ yuttarūpaṃ, purimakehi vā sambuddhehi samaṃ sadisaṃ caranti vattanti.

'By reason' means by logical method. 'By cause' means by the fitness for awakening to the Four Truths. Because he knows all that is to be known, like an āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand, he is the All-Knowing One; by that very all-knowing enlightenment, he is the Buddha, the All-Knowing Buddha. Because he awakens to the truths for himself, by self-arisen knowledge that is unique and not shared with others, he is a Paccekabuddha. Because he awakens to the Four Truths through the instruction of others, he is a Catusaccabuddha. Indeed, because of the absence of self-arisen knowledge, he is called merely a Catusaccabuddha. Because he awakens to what is to be known, such as the divisions of the aggregates, through knowledge derived from learning, he is a Sutabuddha. Excluding the All-Knowing Buddha and the Paccekabuddha, the remaining ones—chief disciples, great disciples, and ordinary disciples—are free from lust, the remaining ones are those whose taints are destroyed. Even these three former types are suitable, because of the statement beginning with 'Sambuddha' and so forth. That by which one dwells together is a dwelling, a mode of conduct. The dwelling of the world is the world-dwelling; in that. In the uneven, such as the divisions of bodily misconduct. Or, in the multitude of beings that is uneven due to the confusion of mindfulness. For it is uneven due to uneven association. Or, in the uneven arising of defilements, such as the unevenness of lust. Having abandoned that unevenness, having disregarded that unevenness, they live and act evenly, similarly, and suitably, or evenly and similarly to the former Buddhas.

Appaṭividitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Appaṭividita Sutta is concluded.

8. Susammuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Susammuṭṭha Sutta

8. Susammuṭṭhāti suṭṭhu ativiya sammuṭṭhā. Satta sekkhā hi susammusitā vinaṭṭhā. Kathaṃ pana te anadhigatā naṭṭhā nāma hontīti āha “yathā hī”tiādi. Adhigatassāti adhigato assa. So vadantoti sambandho. Sesanti “dhammā”tiādi. Purimasadisamevāti anantaragāthāya vuttasadisameva.

8. ‘Susammuṭṭhā’ means utterly and exceedingly confused. Indeed, the seven trainees are well confused and thus ruined. But how are those who have not attained said to be ruined? He says, ‘Just as…’ and so on. ‘Adhigatassā’ means ‘for him who has attained.’ ‘So vadanto’ indicates the connection. The rest is ‘dhammā’ and so forth. ‘Purimasadisamevā’ means ‘it is just similar to what was said in the immediately preceding verse’.

Susammuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Susammuṭṭha Sutta is concluded.

9. Mānakāmasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Mānakāma Sutta

9. Seyyādibhedaṃ mānaṃ appahāya taṃ paggayha vicaranto kāmento nāma hotīti āha “mānaṃ kāmentassa icchantassā”ti. Damati cittaṃ etenāti damo, satisambojjhaṅgādiko samādhipakkhiko damo. Manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni dametīti damo, indriyasaṃvaro. Kilese dameti pajahatīti damo, paññā. Upavasanavasena kāyakammādiṃ dametīti damo, uposathakammaṃ. Kodhūpanāhamakkhamānādike [V 1.0063] dameti vinetīti damo, adhivāsanakhanti. Tenevāti “damo”ti samādhipakkhikadhammānaṃ eva adhippetattā[M 1.0071]. “Na monaṃ atthī”ti ca pāṭho. Asamāhitassāti samādhipaṭikkhepo jotito.

9. One who wanders without abandoning conceit in its divisions of superiority and so forth, holding on to it, is called one who desires it; thus it is said, ‘for one who desires, who wishes for, conceit.’ That by which one tames the mind is taming (dama); this is the taming associated with concentration, such as the awakening-factor of mindfulness. One tames the sense faculties with the mind as the sixth—this is taming; it is sense restraint. One tames, one abandons, defilements—this is taming; it is wisdom. By way of observance, one tames bodily actions and so forth—this is taming; it is the Uposatha observance. One tames, one disciplines, anger, resentment, contempt, conceit, and so forth—this is taming; it is the patience of endurance. For that reason, by ‘taming’ (dama), it is the qualities associated with concentration that are intended. There is also the reading ‘na monaṃ atthi’ (there is no sagacity). ‘For one unconcentrated’—this illuminates the rejection of concentration.

Maccudheyyassa pārataraṇassa vuccamānattā “monanti catumaggañāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Na hi tato aññena taṃ sambhavati. Jānāti asammohapaṭivedhavasena paṭivijjhatīti attho. Maccu dhīyati etthāti maccudheyyaṃ, khandhapañcakaṃ maraṇadhammattā. Tassevāti maccudheyyasseva. Pāraṃ paratīrabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ. Tareyyāti ettha taraṇaṃ nāma ariyamaggabyāpāroti āha “paṭivijjheyya pāpuṇeyyā”ti. Tathā hi vakkhati “paṭivedhataraṇaṃ nāma vutta”nti. “Na tareyya na paṭivijjheyya na pāpuṇeyya vā”ti ayamettha pāṭho yutto. Aññathā “idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādivacanaṃ virujjheyya. Eko araññe viharantoti ekākī hutvā araññe viharantoti attho.

Because the crossing over of death's realm is spoken of, it is said, ‘“mona” means the knowledge of the four paths.’ For this is not possible by anything other than that. The meaning is that one knows, one penetrates by way of the penetration of non-delusion. Death is placed here, thus it is ‘death's realm’ (maccudheyyaṃ); this is the five aggregates, because they are subject to death. ‘Tassevā’ means ‘of that very death's realm.’ The far shore, which has become the other bank, is Nibbāna. Regarding ‘tareyya’ (he would cross), here ‘crossing’ is the activity of the noble path; thus he says, ‘he would penetrate, he would attain.’ For thus it will be said, ‘penetration is called crossing.’ ‘Na tareyya na paṭivijjheyya na pāpuṇeyya vā’ (He would not cross, he would not penetrate, or he would not attain)—this is the proper reading here. Otherwise, the statement beginning ‘idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti’ (this is what is said) would be contradicted. ‘Dwelling alone in the forest’ means dwelling in the forest having become solitary.

Kāmaṃ heṭṭhimamaggehipi ekaccassa mānassa pahānaṃ labbhati. Aggamaggeneva pana tassa anavasesato pahānanti āha – “arahattamaggena navavidhamānaṃ pajahitvā”ti. Upacārasamādhipubbako appanāsamādhīti vuttaṃ “upacārappanāsamādhīhī”ti, na upacārasamādhimattena samādhimattaṃ sandhāya paccekaṃ vākyaparisamāpanassa ayujjanato. Na hi appanaṃ appattaṃ lokuttarajjhānaṃ atthi. “Sucetaso”ti cittassa ñāṇasahitatāya lakkhaṇavacananti āha “ñāṇasampayuttatāyā”tiādi. Tathā hi vakkhati “sucetasoti ettha cittena paññā dassitā”ti. “Sabbadhi vippamutto”ti sabbesu bhavādīsu visaṃsaṭṭhacitto sabbaso khandhādīhi visaṃyutto hotīti vuttaṃ “sabbesu khandhāyatanādīsu vippamutto hutvā”ti. Pariññāpaṭivedho sacchikiriyapaṭivedhena vinā natthīti āha “tebhūmaka…pe… vutta”nti.

Indeed, the abandonment of some kinds of conceit is obtained even through the lower paths. However, its abandonment without remainder is only through the highest path, as stated: ‘having abandoned the ninefold conceit by the path of arahantship.’ It is said ‘through access and absorption concentration’ because absorption concentration is preceded by access concentration. This is not said with reference to mere access concentration, because it would be unsuitable to complete the sentence referring to concentration in that sense alone. For there is no supramundane jhāna that has not attained absorption. ‘Sucetaso’ is a term indicating the characteristic of the mind being accompanied by knowledge, as stated: ‘due to being associated with knowledge,’ etc. For it will be said: ‘Here in “sucetaso,” wisdom is shown by the word “citta” (mind).’ ‘Liberated everywhere’ means that the mind is detached from all states of existence, etc., and is completely disjoined from the aggregates, etc., as stated: ‘being liberated in all respects from the aggregates, sense bases, etc.’ The penetration of full understanding does not exist without the penetration of realization, as stated: ‘the three-planed… etc. … was said.’

Mānaṃ nissāya duccaritacaraṇato māno nāmāyaṃ sīlabhedano. Tasmāti mānassa sīlapaṭipakkhabhāvato. Iminā paṭipakkhappahānakittanena. Adhicittasikkhā kathitā sarūpato evāti adhippāyo. Ettha cittenāti su-saddena visesitacittena. Tasmāti paññāya dassitattā. Imināti “sucetaso”ti iminā padena. Adhisīlasikkhā adhicittasikkhā adhipaññāsikkhāti sīlādīnipi visesetvā vuttāni. Sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanavisesitabbatāti taṃ dassento “adhisīlañca nāma sīle sati hotī”tiādiṃ vatvā tadubhayaṃ [M 1.0072] vibhāgena dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭhamanayo saṅkaravasena pavattoti asaṅkaravasena dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādinā [V 1.0064] dutiyanayo vutto. “Samāpannā”ti etthāpi “nibbānaṃ patthayantenā”ti ānetvā sambandho. Vipassanāya pādakabhāvaṃ anupagatāpi tadatthaṃ nibbattanādivasena samāpannāti ayamattho purimanayato viseso. Adhipaññāya panettha purimanayato viseso natthīti sā anuddhaṭā. Samodhānetvāti pariyāyato sarūpato ca saṅgahetvā. Sakalasāsananti tissannaṃ kathitattā eva sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sakalasāsanaṃ kathitaṃ hotīti.

Relying on conceit leads to misconduct; thus, this conceit is a breaker of virtue. Therefore means: because conceit is the opponent of virtue. By this mention of abandoning the opponent, the higher training in mind is explained in its own nature—this is the intention. Here, 'cittena' (by mind) means by a mind specified by the prefix 'su-'. Therefore means: because it is shown by wisdom. By this means: by the word 'sucetaso'. The higher trainings in virtue, mind, and wisdom are thus stated as distinguished. To show the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, both when they co-exist and when they diverge, it is said, 'Higher virtue, indeed, exists when virtue is present,' etc., and to show both separately, 'therefore,' etc., is stated. The first method proceeds by way of mixture; to show it without mixture, the second method is stated with 'moreover,' etc. In 'samāpannā' here too, the connection is to be brought in as 'by one aspiring for Nibbāna'. Even if it has not become a basis for insight, it is 'attained' in the sense of producing that purpose; this meaning is the distinction from the previous method. Here, regarding higher wisdom, there is no distinction from the previous method, so it is not extracted. 'Having summarized' means having gathered both by way of expression and by way of essence. 'The entire teaching' means: because these three have been stated, the collection of the threefold training, the entire teaching, is thereby stated.

Mānakāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mānakāma Sutta is completed.

10. Araññasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Arañña Sutta

10. Santakilesānanti vūpasantakilesapariḷāhānaṃ. Yasmā sīlādiguṇasambhavaṃ tato eva bhayasantañca upādāya paṇḍitā “santo”ti vuccanti, tasmā vuttaṃ “paṇḍitānaṃ vā”ti. Tenāha “santo have”tiādi. Seṭṭhacārīnanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ carantānaṃ. Yasmā puthujjanakalyāṇato paṭṭhāya bhikkhu maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ vasati nāma, tasmā āha “maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ vasantāna”nti. Ariyānaṃ pana mukhavaṇṇassa pasīdane vattabbameva natthi. Mūlakammaṭṭhānanti pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Visabhāgasantatīti nānārammaṇesu pavattacittasantati. Sā hi vikkhepabyākulatāya appasannā samāhitacittasantatiyā visabhāgasantati. Okkamatīti samādhisabhāgā cittasantati samathavīthiṃ anupavisati. Cittaṃ pasīdatīti kammaṭṭhānanirataṃ bhāvanācittaṃ sandhāyāha, taṃ pasannaṃ hutvā pavattati. Lohitaṃ pasīdatīti cittakālussiyassābhāvato lohitaṃ anāvilaṃ hoti. Parisuddhāni honti kāraṇassa parisuddhabhāvato. Tālaphalamukhassa viya mukhassa vaṇṇo hotīti mukha-saddassa ādimhi pamuttapadena yojetabbo. Evañhi cassa pamuttaggahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti tālaphalamukhassa vaṇṇasampadāsadisattā. Tibhūmako eva tebhūmako.

10. "Santakilesānaṃ" means of those whose defilements and distress have been pacified. Because the wise are called "santo" on account of the arising of virtues such as morality and the pacification of fear from that very source, it is said, "paṇḍitānaṃ vā" (or of the wise). Therefore, he said, "santo have" (indeed, the peaceful), etc. "Seṭṭhacārīnaṃ" means of those who practice the highest conduct. Because, starting from a virtuous worldling, a bhikkhu indeed dwells the life of the path and the holy life, he said, "maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ vasantānaṃ" (of those dwelling the life of the path and the holy life). For the noble ones, however, there is nothing at all to be said regarding the serenity of their facial complexion. "Mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ" means the preparatory meditation subject. "Visabhāgasantati" means the continuity of mind occurring with diverse objects. For that, being uncalm due to distraction and agitation, is a continuity dissimilar to the continuity of a concentrated mind. "Okkamati" means the continuity of mind, similar in nature to concentration, enters the path of tranquility. "Cittaṃ pasīdati"—he says this referring to the meditation mind devoted to the meditation subject; it becomes serene and continues. "Lohitaṃ pasīdati" means the blood becomes clear due to the absence of mental turbidity. They become purified due to the purity of the cause. "Tālaphalamukhassa viya mukhassa vaṇṇo hoti"—this should be connected with the word "pamutta" at the beginning of the word "mukha". For in this way, the inclusion of "pamutta" is justified, because of the similarity to the excellence of the complexion of a palmyra fruit's face. "Tebhūmako" is the same as "tibhūmako" (of the three planes).

Atītaṃ nānusocanti atītaṃ paccayalābhaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ katvā na socanti na anutthunanti. Jappanataṇhāya vasena na parikappantīti āha “na patthentī”ti[M 1.0073]. Yena kenacīti itarītarena. Taṅkhaṇe laddhenāti sannidhikāraparibhogābhāvamāha. Tividhenapi kāraṇenāti tippakārena hetunā, tilakkhaṇasantosanimittanti attho.

'They do not grieve over the past' means, having made the past gain of requisites a mark, they do not sorrow, they do not lament. Because they do not form intentions by way of chattering craving, he said, 'they do not long for'. 'Yena kenaci' (by whatever) means by one or the other. 'Taṅkhaṇe laddhena' (with what is obtained at that moment) indicates the absence of enjoying stored-up things. 'Tividhenapi kāraṇena' (for a threefold reason) means for a cause of three kinds; the meaning is the sign of contentment with the three characteristics.

Vināsanti vināsanahetuṃ. Vinassanti etehīti vināso, lobhadosā tadekaṭṭhā ca pāpadhammā[V 1.0065]. Arūpakāyassa viya rūpakāyassapi visesato sukkhabhāvakāraṇanti āha “etena kāraṇadvayenā”ti. Lutoti lūno.

'Vināsanti' (they perish) means the cause of perishing. 'Vināso' (destruction) is that by which they perish: greed, hatred, and evil states that are of one substance with them. Just as for a formless body, so also for a form-body, it is the cause of its withering away in particular; thus he said, 'etena kāraṇadvayena' (for this twofold reason). 'Luto' means cut off.

Araññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Arañña Sutta is concluded.

Naḷavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Naḷavagga is concluded.

2. Nandanavaggo

2. The Nandana Chapter

1. Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Nandana Sutta

11. “Tatra bhagavā”ti vutte na tathā byañjanānaṃ siliṭṭhatā, yathā “tatra kho bhagavā”ti vutteti āha “byañjanasiliṭṭhatāvasenā”ti. Parisajeṭṭhaketi parisāya jeṭṭhake, ye tassā desanāya visesato bhājanabhūtā. Parisajeṭṭhake bhikkhūti catuparisajeṭṭhake bhikkhū. Catunnaṃ hi parisānaṃ jeṭṭhā bhikkhuparisā paṭhamuppannattā. Āmantesīti sambodhesi, sambodhanañca jānāpananti āha “jānāpesī”ti. Bhadanteti garugāravasappatissavavacanametaṃ, atthato pana bhadanteti bhaddaṃ tava hotu attano niṭṭhānapariyosānattā paresañca santatāvahattā. Bhagavato paccassosunti ettha bhagavatoti sāmivacanaṃ āmantanameva sambandhiatthapadaṃ apekkhatīti adhippāyenāha “bhagavato vacanaṃ patiassosu”nti. Bhagavatoti pana idaṃ patissavanasambandhena sampadānavacanaṃ yathā “devadattassa paṭissuṇātī”ti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ nidānavaggassa ādisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ āgamissati.

11. When 'Tatra bhagavā' (There, the Blessed One) is said, the phrasing is not as smooth as when 'Tatra kho bhagavā' (There indeed, the Blessed One) is said; thus it is stated, 'due to the smoothness of phrasing'. 'Parisajeṭṭhake' means the elders in the assembly, those who were especially worthy vessels for that teaching. 'Parisajeṭṭhake bhikkhū' means the elder bhikkhus of the fourfold assembly. For among the four assemblies, the assembly of bhikkhus is the eldest because it arose first. 'Āmantesī' (he addressed) means he roused; and rousing is a way of making known, thus it is said, 'jānāpesī' (he informed). 'Bhadante' (Venerable sir) is a term expressing deep respect, reverence, and deference. In meaning, however, 'bhadante' implies, 'May it be well with you,' because of the fulfillment and conclusion for oneself and the bringing of continuous welfare for others. In 'Bhagavato paccassosuṃ' (they responded to the Blessed One), 'Bhagavato' is a genitive which expects a related word, namely the address; with this intention, it is said, 'bhagavato vacanaṃ patiassosuṃ' (they responded to the Blessed One's word). Moreover, this 'Bhagavato' is a dative in connection with the response, as in 'he responds to Devadatta'. Whatever should be said here will come in the commentary on the first sutta of the Nidānavagga.

Tāvatiṃsakāyoti tāvatiṃsasaññito devanikāyo. Dutiyadevalokoti chasu kāmalokesu dutiyo devaloko. Tettiṃsa janā sahapuññakārino tattha uppannā, taṃsahacaritaṭṭhānaṃ tāvatiṃsaṃ[M 1.0074], tannivāsinopi tāvatiṃsanāmakā sahacaraṇañāyenāti āha “maghena māṇavenā”tiādi. Ayaṃ pana kecivādo byāpanno hotīti taṃ arocentena “vadantī”ti vuttaṃ. Byāpannataṃ dassento “yasmā panā”tiādimāha. Tathā hi vakkhati “evaṃ hi niddosaṃ padaṃ hotī”ti. Nāmapaṇṇattiyevāti atthanirapekkhattā niruḷhasamaññā eva.

'Tāvatiṃsakāyo' means the host of devas known as Tāvatiṃsa. 'Dutiyadevaloko' means the second deva world among the six desire-sphere worlds. Thirty-three people who performed merit together were reborn there; that place of their co-faring is Tāvatiṃsa, and its inhabitants are also named Tāvatiṃsa by the principle of association; thus he said, 'by Magha the young man,' etc. But since this view of some is corrupt, one who disapproves of it says 'vadanti' (they say). Showing the corruption, he said, 'yasmā panā' (but because), etc. For he will say, 'evaṃ hi niddosaṃ padaṃ hoti' (for thus the word becomes faultless). 'Nāmapaṇṇattiyeva' means: because it is independent of meaning, it is purely a conventional term.

Taṃ vananti taṃ upavanaṃ. Paviṭṭhe paviṭṭhe dukkhappattepi attano sampattiyā nandayati, pageva [V 1.0066] adukkhappatteti dassetuṃ “pañcasu hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pavesitānanti pakoṭṭhavārena pavesitānampīti adhippāyo. Cavanakāleyeva thokaṃ dissamānavikārā hutvā cavanti, te sandhāya “himapiṇḍo viya vilīyantī”ti vuttaṃ. Ye pana adissamānavikārā sahasā antaradhāyanti, te sandhāya “dīpasikhā viya vijjhāyantī”ti vuttanti vadanti. Nandayati pakatiyā somanassitaṃ domanassitañca. Nandaneti evaṃanvatthanāmake uyyāne. Parivutāti “devatā”ti vacanaṃ upādāya itthiliṅgavasena vuttaṃ. Devaputto hi so.

'Taṃ vanaṃ' (that wood) means that park. To show that it delights with its own prosperity each and every one who has entered, even one afflicted by suffering—how much more so one not afflicted by suffering—it is said, 'pañcasu hi' (for in five ways), etc. 'Pavesitānaṃ' (of those made to enter) means even those who have been brought in through the gateway—this is the intention. At the very time of passing away, having slight visible changes, they pass away; referring to them, it is said, 'they dissolve like a lump of snow'. But referring to those who vanish suddenly without visible changes, it is said, 'they are extinguished like a lamp flame,' they say. It delights both the naturally joyful and the sorrowful. 'Nandane'—in the park with a name that fits its meaning. 'Parivutā' (surrounded) is said in the feminine gender on account of the word 'devatā'. For he was a devaputta.

Divi bhavattā dibbāti āha “devaloke nibbattehī”ti. Kāmetabbatāya kāmabandhanehi, tathā aññamaññaṃ asaṃkiṇṇasabhāvatāya kāmakoṭṭhāsehi. Upetāti upagatā samannāgatā. Paricārayamānāti pariramamānā. Idañhi padaṃ apekkhitvā “kāmaguṇehī”ti kattari karaṇavacanaṃ, purimāni apekkhitvā sahayoge. Ramamānā carantīti katvā vuttaṃ “ramamānā”ti. Paricārayamānāti vā parito samantato cārayamānāti atthoti āha “indriyāni sañcārayamānā”ti. Paṭhamanaye hi anubhavanattho paricaraṇasaddo, dutiyanaye parivattanattho. So panāti “tāyaṃ velāya”nti vuttakālo. Adhunāti sampati. So vicarīti sambandho. Kāmaguṇehīti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Ovutoti yathā taṃ na ñāyati, evaṃ pihitacitto. Nivuto pariyonaddhoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Tenāha “lokābhibhūto”ti. Āsabhinti seṭṭhaṃ “aggohamasmi lokassā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.31; ma. ni. 3.207) bhāsanto bodhisatto viya.

"Dibbā" (divine) means "born in the heavenly realm," because of being in the divine realm. Due to being desirable, by sensual ties, and likewise, by sensual divisions on account of their distinct and unmixed nature. "Upeta" means "approached" or "endowed," possessing. "Paricārayamānā" means "enjoying themselves." Here the phrase "with sensual pleasures" takes the instrumental as the agent, and the preceding words are in conjunction with it. Considering "Ramamānā caranti" as "they move about enjoying," hence the term "ramamānā." Or "paricārayamānā" means "moving all around," hence the explanation "indriyāni sañcārayamānā" (activating the senses). In the first sense, the term "paricaraṇa" conveys the sense of enjoyment, while in the second, it conveys the sense of movement. "So pana" refers to the time mentioned earlier, "at that time." "Adhunā" means "now" or "at present." The connection is 'so vicarī'. "Kāmaguṇehi" is the instrumental case indicating the cause. "Ovuto" means "covered," such that it is not known, thus having a mind concealed. "Nivuto pariyonaddho" is a synonym for the same; therefore, the explanation "overcome by the world." "Āsabhi" means "the best," like the Bodhisatta saying "I am the foremost in the world," etc. (Dī. Ni. 2.31; Ma. Ni. 3.207).

Kevalaṃ [M 1.0075] dassanaṃ kimatthiyanti āha – “ye…pe… vasenā”ti, tasmiṃ nandanavane avaṭṭhitakāmabhāgānubhavanavasenāti attho. Naradevānanti purisabhūtadevatānaṃ. Tenāha “devapurisāna”nti. Appakaṃ adhikaṃ ūnaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ nāma na hotīti “tikkhattuṃ dasanna”nti vuttaṃ. “Tettiṃsāna”nti hi vattabbe ayaṃ ruḷhī. Parivārasaṅkhātena, na kittisaṅkhātenāti adhippāyo. Sīlācārādiguṇanemittikā hi kitti. “Tāvatiṃsā devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā”ti evamādivacanena yase icchite avisesetvāva “yasena sampannāna”nti sakkā vattuṃ.

"The mere sight, what is its purpose?" He says, "Those... by means of..." The meaning is: by means of the enjoyment of the portions of desire established in that Nandana Grove. "Naradevānaṃ" (of the divine men) means of the gods who are in the form of men. Therefore, he says "devapurisānaṃ" (divine men). There is nothing that can be called a little more or a little less that is suitable for counting, hence it is said: "tikkhattuṃ dasannaṃ" (three times ten). Though "tettiṃsānaṃ" (of the thirty-three) should be said, this is the conventional usage. It is meant by the number of the retinue, not by the number of fame. For fame is caused by qualities such as virtue and conduct. With statements like "The Tāvatiṃsa gods are long-lived, beautiful, and abundant in happiness," it is possible to say "yasena sampannānaṃ" (endowed with glory) without specifying, even if glory is intended.

Ariyasāvikāti sotāpannā. “Sakadāgāminī”ti keci. Adhippāyaṃ vivaṭṭetvāti yathā tvaṃ andhabāle maññasi, dhammasabhāvo evaṃ na hotīti tassā devatāya adhippāyaṃ viparivattetvā. Ekantato sukhaṃ nāma nibbānameva. Kāmā hi dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammāti iminā [V 1.0067] adhippāyena tassā adhippāyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā. Kāmaṃ catutthabhūmakāpi saṅkhārā aniccā eva, te pana sammasanūpagā na hontīti tebhūmakaggahaṇaṃ sammasanayoggena. Hutvāti pubbe avijjamānā paccayasamavāyena bhavitvā uppajjitvā. Etena nesaṃ bhāvabhāgo dassito. Abhāvatthenāti sarasanirodhabhūtena viddhaṃsanabhāvena.

"Ariyasāvikā" (the noble female disciple) means a stream-enterer. Some say, "a once-returner." 'Having turned back the intention' means having reversed the intention of that deity, thinking: 'The true nature of things is not as you, blind fool, imagine.' Unalloyed happiness is indeed Nibbāna. For sensual pleasures are suffering and subject to change—with this intention, having refuted her intention. Indeed, even the formations of the fourth plane are impermanent, but they are not subject to thorough comprehension—thus, the taking of the three planes is in connection with the practice of thorough comprehension. "Hutvā" (having been) means previously non-existent, having come into being and arisen through the convergence of conditions. By this, their aspect of becoming is shown. "Abhāvatthena" (in the sense of non-being) means by the nature of destruction, which is the cessation of its own essence.

Aniccā addhuvā, tato eva “mayhaṃ ime sukhā”ti vā na iccāti aniccā. Uppādavayasabhāvāti khaṇe khaṇe uppajjananirujjhanasabhāvā. Tenāha “uppa…pe… vevacana”nti. Purimassa vā pacchimaṃ kāraṇavevacananti āha “yasmā vā”tiādi. Tadanantarāti tesaṃ uppādavayānaṃ antare. Vemajjhaṭṭhānanti ṭhitikkhaṇaṃ vadati. Ye pana “saṅkhārānaṃ ṭhiti natthī”ti vadanti, tesaṃ taṃ micchā. Yathā hi tasseva dhammassa uppādāvatthāya bhinnā bhaṅgāvatthā icchitā, aññathā aññaṃ uppajjati, aññaṃ nirujjhatīti āpajjati, evaṃ uppannassa bhaṅgābhimukhāvatthā icchitabbā, sāva ṭhitikkhaṇo. Na hi uppajjamāno bhijjatīti sakkā viññātunti. Vūpasamasaṅkhātanti accantaṃ vūpasamasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānameva sukhaṃ, na tayā adhippetā kāmāti adhippāyo.

Impermanent, unstable—hence, they are called "impermanent" because one does not desire, "These pleasures are mine." Their nature is arising and ceasing—their nature is to arise and vanish moment by moment. Therefore, it is said, "arising... and so on... a synonym." Regarding the former or the latter as a causal synonym—thus it is stated, "because of which" and so on. In the interval—that is, between their arising and vanishing. The state in between—this refers to the moment of duration. But those who say, "There is no duration for conditioned things," their view is wrong. For just as, for the same phenomenon, a distinct state of dissolution is posited from the state of arising—otherwise, it would follow that one thing arises and another ceases—so too, for what has arisen, a state tending toward dissolution must be posited, and that is the moment of duration. For it is impossible to understand that what is arising is simultaneously disintegrating. Designated as cessation—absolute cessation, Nibbāna itself, is happiness, not the sense pleasures you intended—this is the meaning.

Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nandana Sutta is concluded.

2. Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Nandati Sutta

12. Nandatīti [M 1.0076] ettha nandanaṃ sappītikakāmataṇhākiccanti āha – “tussatī”ti, tasmā kāmaparitosena haṭṭhatuṭṭho hotīti attho. Puttimāti puttavā. Pahūte cāyaṃ mā-saddoti āha “bahuputto”ti. Bahuputtatāgahaṇena idaṃ payojananti dassento “tassa hī”tiādimāha. Pūrentīti padaṃ apekkhitvā dhaññassāti sāmivacanaṃ. Iti āhāti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha, evaṃadhippāyo hutvāti attho. Gosāmikoti gomā. Idhāpi pahūte mā-saddo. Gorasasampattinti gorasehi nipphajjanasampattiṃ. Upadhīti paccattabahuvacanaṃ. Hīti hetuatthe nipāto. Nandayanti pītisomanassaṃ janayantīti nandanā. Kāmaṃ dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato nippariyāyato kāmā “upadhī”ti vattabbataṃ arahanti, tassā pana devatāya adhippāyavasenāha “sukhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato”ti. Kilesavatthuhetukattā sesapadadvayassa kiñcāpi sabbaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ kilesahetukaṃ, visesato pana pāpadhammā apāyūpapattiṃ nibbattentīti āha – “kilesāpi apāyadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato”ti. Upasaṃharamānāti upanentā uppādentā. Manussajātikopi dullabhaghāsacchādanatāya [V 1.0068] dukkhabahulo peto viyāti manussapeto. Manussajātikopi vuttarūpo anatthapātito parehi hiṃsito samāno nerayiko viyāti manussanerayiko.

12. "He delights" – here, 'delight' refers to the function of sensual craving that is pleasurable, as it is said: "he is satisfied." Therefore, the meaning is that he becomes joyful and elated through the gratification of sensual pleasures. "Puttimā" means one who has sons. And here, the suffix '-mā' is used to indicate abundance, as it is said: "having many sons." To show the purpose of mentioning having many sons, he says: "for him indeed," and so on. With reference to the word "they fulfill," "of grain" is in the genitive case. "Thus he says" – means he speaks with this meaning in mind, having this intention. "Gosāmiko" means owner of cattle; "gomā" means one who possesses cattle. Here too, the suffix '-mā' denotes abundance. "Abundance of dairy products" refers to the prosperity produced by dairy products. "Upadhi" is in the nominative plural. "Hī" is a particle indicating cause. "Nandanā" (delights) are so called because they generate joy and happiness. Because sensual pleasures, directly, are the basis of suffering, they deserve to be called "upadhi." However, from the perspective of that deity's intention, it is said: "because they are the basis of happiness." Because the remaining two terms have defilements as their fundamental cause, although all suffering in saṃsāra has defilements as its cause, yet especially because unwholesome states produce rebirth in the lower realms, it is said: "defilements too are the basis of suffering in the lower realms." "Bringing near" means drawing close or producing. Even one of human birth, due to the difficulty of obtaining food and clothing, is as miserable as a hungry ghost – thus, a 'human ghost.' Even one of human birth, who is thrown into misfortune and harmed by others, as described, is like a hell-being – thus, a 'human hell-being.'

Phalena rukkhato phalaṃ pātento viya. Tatheva navahākārehīti yathā tīsu kālesu nāsamaraṇabhedanavasena puttimā puttanimittaṃ, tatheva gomā gonimittaṃ socati navappakārehi. Pañca kāmaguṇopadhīpi naraṃ socentīti yojanā. Tassāti yo uttari anugijjhati tassa. Kāmayānassāti jātakāmacchandassa. Jantunoti sattassa. Parihāyanti ce vinassanti ce. Sallaviddhovāti sallena viddho viya. Ruppatīti vikāraṃ āpajjati, socatīti attho. Narassa socanā sokaghaṭṭanapaccayo. Upadhayo natthīti kāmaṃ kilesābhisaṅkhārūpadhayo tāva khīṇāsavassa nattheva maggādhigamena nirodhitattā, khandhūpadhayo pana kathanti? Tepi tassa saupādisesakālepi aṭṭhuppattihetubhūtā na santeva, ayañca anupādisesakāle. Tenāha “so nirupadhi mahākhīṇāsavo”ti.

Like one knocking down a fruit from a tree with another fruit. So too in nine ways: just as one with sons grieves on account of his sons, and one with cattle grieves on account of his cattle, by way of destruction, death, and dissolution in the three periods of time, so one grieves in nine ways. The five strands of sensual pleasure as attachments also cause a person to grieve—this is the connection. "For him" means for one who clings further. "Of one desiring" means of one for whom sensual desire has arisen. "For a being" means for a creature. "They decline and perish." "Like one struck by an arrow" means like one pierced by an arrow. "Ruppati" means 'undergoes change,' that is, 'grieves.' For a person, grieving is the cause of sorrow’s affliction. "There are no attachments"—indeed, for one whose taints are destroyed, the attachments of defilements and formations are no more, having been eradicated by the attainment of the path. But what of the aggregates as attachments? Even during the time when residue remains, they do not exist as causes for future arising, and this is in the state of no residue remaining. Therefore, it is said: "He is free from attachments, the great one whose taints are destroyed."

Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nandati Sutta is concluded.

3. Natthiputtasamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Natthiputtasama Sutta

13. Puttapemaṃ [M 1.0077] puttaggahaṇena gahitaṃ uttarapadalopenāti āha “puttapemasama”nti. Gosamitanti gohi samaṃ kataṃ. Tenāha “gohi sama”nti. Sūriyassa samāti sūriyasamā. Avayavasambandhe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Avayavo cettha ābhā evāti viññāyati “anantaraṃ ābhā”ti vuccamānattāti āha “sūriyābhāya samā”tiādi. Mahoghabhāvena saranti savantīti sarā, mahantā jalāsayā. Sabbe te samuddaparamā orimajanehi adiṭṭhaparatīrattā tassa.

13. The expression 'love for a son' is formed by taking the word 'son' with the omission of the latter word; hence it is said 'equal to the love for a son.' 'Equal to cows' means made equal with cows. Therefore, it is said 'equal with cows.' 'Equal to the sun' means sun-equal. This is a genitive case in the sense of a part-whole relationship. Here, the part is radiance itself; this is understood because it is said 'radiance immediately after.' Thus it is said 'equal to the sun's radiance,' and so on. Because they flow, streaming with the nature of a great flood, they are called 'rivers'; they are large reservoirs of water. All of them have the ocean as their ultimate destination, its further shore being unseen by people on this side.

Natthi attasamaṃ pemanti gāthāya paṭhamagāthāyaṃ vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Attapemena samaṃ pemaṃ nāma natthīti ayamattho. Anudakakantāre ghammasantāpaṃ asahantiyā aṅke ṭhapitaputtakaṃ kandantaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā tassa upari ṭhatvā mataitthivatthunā dīpetabbaṃ. Tenāha – “mātāpitādayo hi chaḍḍetvāpi puttadhītādayo”ti. Tathā cāha –

Regarding the verse 'There is no love equal to self-love,' the meaning should be understood in the way stated in the first verse. This is the meaning: there is no love equal to self-love. It should be illustrated by the story of the dead woman who, in a waterless desert, unable to bear the scorching heat, laid her crying child, who had been on her lap, down on the ground and stood over him. Therefore it was said: 'Parents and others, indeed, abandon even their sons and daughters.' And so it was said:

“Sabbā disā anuparigamma cetasā,

Nevajjhagā piyataramattanā kvaci;

Evaṃ [V 1.0069] piyo puthu attā paresaṃ,

Tasmā na hiṃse paramattakāmo”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.119; udā. 41; netti. 113);

"Having traversed all quarters with the mind, one nowhere found anything dearer than oneself. In the same way, others hold themselves dear; therefore one who loves oneself should not harm another."

Dhaññena samaṃ dhanaṃ nāma natthi, yasmā tappaṭibaddhā āhārūpajīvīnaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitavutti. Tathārūpe kāleti dubbhikkhakāle. Ekadesaṃyeva obhāsantīti ekasmiṃ khaṇe catūsu mahādīpesu obhāsaṃ pharituṃ asamatthattā sūriyassapi, pageva itaresaṃ. Bodhisattassa udayabbayassa ñāṇānubhāvena sakalajātikhettaṃ ekālokaṃ ahosīti āha “paññā…pe… sakkotī”ti. Tamaṃ vidhamatīti pubbenivāsañāṇādayo paññā yattha pavattanti, tamanavasesaṃ byāpetvā ekappahārena pavattanato. “Vuṭṭhiyā pana pavattamānāya yāva ābhassarabhavanā”ti pacuravasena vuttaṃ.

There is no wealth equal to grain, for the livelihood of beings who subsist on food is tied to it. 'At such a time' means at a time of famine. 'It illuminates only one part' means that even the sun is unable to spread light across the four great continents in a single moment, let alone others. By the power of the Bodhisatta’s knowledge of arising and passing away, the entire field of birth became a single light; thus it is said, 'wisdom... is able.' 'It dispels darkness': where wisdom, such as the knowledge of past lives and so on, operates, it does so by pervading all darkness without remainder in a single strike. 'But when rain is falling, up to the Ābhassara realm'—this is said in an abundant sense.

Natthiputtasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Natthiputtasama Sutta is concluded.

4. Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta

14. Khettato [M 1.0078] vivādā satte tāyatīti khattiyo. Vadati devatā attano ajjhāsayavasena. Dvipadādīnanti ādi-saddena catuppadabhariyaputtā gahitā. Buddhādayoti ādi-saddena ājānīyasussūsabhariyassavaputtā. Dvipadānaṃ seṭṭhoti ettha dvipadānaṃ eva seṭṭhoti nāyaṃ niyamo icchito, seṭṭho evāti pana icchito, tasmā sambuddho dvipadesu aññesu tattha ca uppajjanato seṭṭho eva sabbesampi uttaritarassa abhāvatoti ayamettha attho. Tenāha “uppajjamāno panesā”tiādi. Kāraṇākāraṇaṃ ājānātīti ājānīyo. Gaṇhāpethāti yathā udako na temissati, evaṃ vāḷaṃ gaṇhāpetha. “Asussūsā”ti keci paṭhanti. Āsuṇamānoti sappaṭissavo hutvā vacanasampaṭicchako.

14. Because he protects beings from disputes regarding fields, he is a khattiya. The devatā speaks according to her own inclination. In 'among two-footed beings, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' four-footed beings, wives, and sons are included. In 'Buddhas, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' thoroughbreds, obedient wives, and submissive sons are included. In 'foremost among two-footed beings,' the rule 'foremost only among two-footed beings' is not intended, but rather 'indeed the foremost' is intended. Therefore, the Fully Enlightened One, arising among two-footed beings and others, is indeed the foremost of all, as there is none superior to him. This is the meaning here. Hence it is said, 'But when he arises…' and so on. Because he knows cause and non-cause, he is a thoroughbred. 'Make him take it up': Make the wild beast take it up in such a way that water will not wet it. Some read 'disobedience.' 'Listening attentively' means being responsive and receptive to instruction.

Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta is concluded.

5. Saṇamānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Saṇamāna Sutta

15. Ṭhite majjhanhiketi pubbaddhaṃ nikkhamitvā aparaddhaṃ appatvā ṭhitamajjhanhe. Sannisīvesūti parissamavinodanatthaṃ sabbaso sannisīdantesu. Da-kārassa hi va-kāraṃ katvā niddeso. Tenāha “sannisinnesu vissamamānesū”ti. Sabbasattānanti sabbesañca āhārūpajīvitasattānaṃ [V 1.0070] ghammatāpane santattakāyānaṃ iriyāpathadubbalyakāloti ṭhānādiiriyāpathassa asamatthakālo. Saṇati viyāti saddaṃ karoti viya, yathā taṃ aññampi mahāvanaṃ vakkhamānanayena. Tenāha “tappaṭibhāgaṃ nāmeta”nti chiddaveṇupabbānanti randhajātakīcakamahāveḷupabbānaṃ. Dutiyakaṃ sahāyaṃ alabhantī anabhiratiparitassanāya evamāha. Anappakaṃ sukhanti vipulaṃ uḷāraṃ vivekasukhaṃ.

15. 'At midday standing' means when midday is established, having passed the forenoon and not yet reached the afternoon. 'When they have settled down' refers to when all are sitting down completely for the purpose of dispelling fatigue. The instruction is given having changed the letter 'd' to a 'v'. Hence it is said: 'when they are seated and resting.' 'Of all beings' means: for all beings who subsist on food, whose bodies are scorched by the heat, it is a time of weakness of posture, a time of being unable to maintain postures such as standing. 'It seems to resound' means it seems to make a sound, just as another great forest does, in the way that will be described. Hence it is said: 'that is its counterpart.' 'Of hollow bamboo joints' means of the joints of large hollow bamboos that have developed holes. Not finding a second companion, out of discontent and fear, he spoke thus. 'Not insignificant happiness' means abundant, sublime happiness of seclusion.

Ekavihāratāya suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa. Tena kāyavivekaṃ dasseti. Aniccānupassanādīhi niccasaññādippahānena santacittassa. Tena cittavivekaṃ dasseti. Saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanato bhikkhuno ubhayavivekasampannassa, tato [M 1.0079] eva uttariṃ manussadhammato ratiṃ lābhino. Amānusī ratīti bhāvanārati. Puratoti purimabhāge. Pacchatoti pacchimabhāge. Aparoti añño. Puratoti vā anāgate, anāgataṃ ārabbhāti attho. Pacchatoti atīte atītaṃ ārabbha paṭipattiyā vibādhanato. Paroti kodho cittapaṭidussanatāya. Na paroti aparo, lobho, so ce na vijjati. Etena anāgatappajappanāya atītānusocanāya ca abhāvaṃ dasseti. Atīva phāsu bhavatīti nīvaraṇajeṭṭhakassa kāmacchandassa vigamena vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa jhānassa vasena ativiya phāsuvihāro hoti. Ekassa vasato vaneti taṇhādutiyikābhāvena ekassa araññe vivekavāsaṃ vasato. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paṭhamagāthāyaṃ vuttasadisameva.

Of one who has entered an empty dwelling for the sake of solitude; by this, he shows bodily seclusion. Of one whose mind is peaceful through the abandonment of perceptions of permanence, etc., by means of the contemplation of impermanence, etc.; by this, he shows mental seclusion. Of the monk who sees danger in the cycle of existence, who is endowed with both kinds of seclusion, and who for that very reason gains a delight that surpasses the human state. That non-human delight is the delight in meditation. 'Before' refers to the former part. 'After' refers to the latter part. 'Another' refers to something else. Or, 'before' means in the future, that is, concerning the future. 'After' refers to the past, because practice is hindered by being concerned with the past. 'Another' refers to anger, because it corrupts the mind. 'Not another' means there is no other, namely greed; if that does not exist. By this is shown the absence of projecting about the future and lamenting over the past. 'He becomes exceedingly at ease': with the removal of sensual desire, the chief of the hindrances, and with the hindrances suppressed, by means of jhāna there is an exceedingly comfortable abiding. 'Of one dwelling alone in the forest' means of one dwelling in seclusion in the wilderness, without craving as a companion. 'The rest is just as it was' means what remains to be said here is similar to what was said in the first verse.

Saṇamānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṇamāna Sutta is concluded.

6. Niddātandīsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Niddātandī Sutta

16. Pacchime māse pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajānoti ettakaṃ pāṭhaṃ saṅkhipitvā “niddaṃ okkamitā”ti vuttaṃ. Kiriyāmayacittehi avomisso bhavaṅgasoto abyākataniddā. Sā hi khīṇāsavānaṃ uppajjanārahā, tassā pubbabhāgāparabhāgesu…pe… uppannaṃ thinamiddhaṃ idhādhippetā niddā, sā akhīṇāsavānaṃ yebhuyyena aniyatakālā, tabbidhuraniyatasabbhāvaṃ dassento “aticchāta…pe… āgantukaṃ ālasiya”nti āha. Kāyālasiyapaccayā vīriyassa paṭipakkhabhūtā cattāro akusalakkhandhā tandī nāma. Tandīti sabhāvaniddeso. Tandiyanāti ākāraniṃddeso. Tandīmanatāti tandībhūtacittatā. Ālasyanti alasabhāvāharaṇaṃ. Ālasyāyitattanti alasabhāvappatti. Kāyavijambhanāti kāyassa vināmanā. Akusalapakkhā ukkaṇṭhitatāti akusalapakkhiyā [V 1.0071] anabhirati. Bhattakilamathoti yathāvuttassa bhattavatthukassa āhārassa vasena sarīre uppajjanakakhedo. Upakkiliṭṭhoti paññāya dubbalīkaraṇena upakkiliṭṭhacitto. Cittassa asamāhitattā nivāritapātubhāvo. Ariyamaggassa jotanaṃ nāma uppajjanamevāti āha “na jotati[M 1.0080], na pātubhavatīti attho”ti. Na hi ariyamaggo jotiajotināmo pavattati.

16. 'In the last month of the hot season, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, having laid out his four-fold outer robe, he lies down on his right side, mindful and fully aware'—this much of the text is summarized as 'he succumbed to sleep.' The stream of the life-continuum, unmixed with functional consciousness, is indeterminate sleep. For that is fit to arise for those whose cankers are destroyed. The sloth and torpor that has arisen in its initial and later phases is the sleep intended here. For those whose cankers are not destroyed, that sleep is mostly of uncertain timing. To show its fixed nature, which is devoid of that, it is said: 'from being overly full… adventitious sloth.' The four unwholesome aggregates which are the opposite of energy, conditioned by bodily sloth, are called 'torpor.' 'Torpor' is the designation of its nature. 'Torpidity' is the designation of its mode. 'Torpid-mindedness' is the state of a torpid mind. 'Sloth' is the adoption of a slothful state. 'Slothfulness' is the attainment of a slothful state. 'Stretching the body' means bending the body. 'Discontent' means dissatisfaction with what belongs to the unwholesome side. 'Meal-fatigue' is the weariness arising in the body on account of the food from the meal as described. 'Defiled' means the mind is defiled by the weakening of wisdom. Its manifestation is prevented due to the mind's lack of concentration. The 'shining' of the noble path is simply its arising; hence it is said, 'it does not shine, meaning it does not appear.' For the noble path does not proceed by way of shining and not shining.

Maggasahajātavīriyenāti lokiyalokuttaramaggasahajātavīriyena. Missakamaggo hi idha adhippeto. Nīharitvāti nīharaṇahetu. Hetuattho hi ayaṃ tvā-saddo “paññāya cassa disvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.271) viya. Tena “maggo visujjhatī”ti vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. “Ariyamaggaṃ visujjhatī”ti keci paṭhanti.

“By the energy co-arisen with the path” means by the energy co-arisen with the mundane and supramundane paths. For here, the mixed path is intended. “‘Having removed’ means for the cause of removing.” The meaning of cause is intended here by the suffix -tvā, as in phrases like “having seen with wisdom” (MN 1.271). Thus, the statement “the path is purified” is supported. Some read it as “the noble path is purified.”

Niddātandīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Niddātandī Sutta is concluded.

7. Dukkarasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse on Difficult Deeds

17. Dukkhaṃ titikkhanti duttitikkhaṃ. Tañca dukkhamaṃ dussahanaṃ ārambhavasena dukkaraṃ, anuyuñjanavasena duttitikkhanti. Abyattenāti sāmaññassa upakārānupakāre dhamme jānanasamatthāya veyyattiyasaṅkhātāya paññāya abhāvato na byattena. Tenāha “bālenā”ti. Yasmiṃ dhamme sati samaṇoti vuccati, taṃ sāmaññanti āha “samaṇadhammo”ti. Imināti “dukkaraṃ duttitikkhañca, abyattena ca sāmañña”nti iminā gāthaddhena idaṃ dassetīti idaṃ idāni vuccamānaṃ atthajātaṃ dasseti. Abhidantanti abhibhavanadantaṃ, uparidantanti attho. So hi itaraṃ musalaṃ viya udukkhalaṃ visesato kassaci khādanakāle abhibhuyya vattati. Ādhāyāti nippīḷanavaseneva ṭhapetvā. Tāluṃ āhaccāti tālupadesamāhanitvā viya. Cetasāti kusalacittena. Cittanti akusalacittaṃ. Abhiniggaṇhitvāti yathā atisamudācāro na hoti, evaṃ vibādhanavasena niggahetvā. Āpāṇakoṭikanti pāṇakoṭipariyosānaṃ, parijīvanti attho. Sambādhetīti sambādho, antarāyiko. Bahū parissayāti ayoniso kāmavitakkādivasena.

17. They endure suffering that is hard to endure. And that suffering is difficult to bear, difficult to do by way of exertion, and hard to endure by way of repeated engagement. 'By an unskilled one' means not by a skilled one, due to the absence of the wisdom called 'skill,' which is capable of knowing the beneficial and unbeneficial qualities of asceticism. Therefore, he said, 'by a fool.' That quality, in the presence of which one is called an ascetic, is asceticism; he says, 'the duty of an ascetic.' By this—'hard to do and hard to endure, and for the unskilled, asceticism'—by this half-verse, he shows this collection of meanings that is now being explained. 'Abhidantaṃ' means an overpowering tooth, that is, an upper tooth. For it overcomes the other like a pestle over a mortar, especially when eating something. 'Ādhāya' means having placed by way of pressing down. 'Striking the palate' means as if having struck the region of the palate. 'With the mind' means with a wholesome mind. 'Mind' means an unwholesome mind. 'Having thoroughly restrained' means having restrained by way of suppression, so that there is no excessive conduct. 'Until the end of life' means ending at the tip of life; the meaning is 'they survive.' 'It obstructs' means an obstruction, a hindrance. 'Many dangers' means by way of unwise consideration, such as sensual thoughts and so on.

Pajjati cittametthāti padaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ. Iriyāpathaṃ eva padaṃ iriyāpathapadaṃ.

'The mind proceeds to this' (pajjati cittaṃ ettha) is a 'base' (padaṃ), an object. The posture itself is the 'base' (padaṃ), hence 'posture-base' (iriyāpathapadaṃ).

Gīvā [M 1.0081] cattāro pādāti gīvapañcamāni. Samodahanti vā samodhānahetūti ayamettha atthoti āha – “samodahitvā vā”ti, sammā odhāya anto pavesetvāti attho. Sake ārammaṇakapāleti gocarajjhattaṃ vadati. Samodahanti samodahanto. Anissitoti tebhūmakadhammesu kañcipi [V 1.0072] dhammaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhābhinivesavasena anissito. Avihiṃsamāno vihiṃsānimittānaṃ pajahanena. Ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitenāti sīlabyasanato uddharaṇarūpe saṇṭhitena, karuṇāyuttenāti attho. Tenāha “kāruññataṃ paṭiccā”ti.

'Neck and four legs' means with the neck as the fifth. 'They compose themselves' or 'for the cause of composure'—this is the meaning here, he says—'or having composed oneself,' the meaning is 'having properly placed and brought inside.' 'In their own object-bowl' refers to being within one's own pasture. 'Samodahanti' means 'they compose themselves'; 'samodahanto' means 'one who is composing himself.' 'Unattached' means not depending on any phenomenon among the three planes of existence by way of adherence through craving and views. 'Not harming' means by abandoning the signs of harming. 'Established in the nature of lifting up' means established in the form of rescuing from the ruin of virtue; the meaning is, endowed with compassion. Therefore, he says, 'on account of compassion.'

Dukkarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Difficult Deeds is concluded.

8. Hirīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discourse on Conscience

18. Nisedhetīti nivāreti pavattituṃ na deti. Pucchati devatā. Apaharantoti apanento, yathā sabbena sabbaṃ akkosavatthu na hoti, evaṃ pariharantoti attho. Bujjhati sārathividhaṃ. Attani nipātaṃ na deti, ājānīyo hi yuttaṃ pajānāti. Abhūtena abhūtakkosena parimutto nāma natthi bālānañca janānaṃ parāpavāde yuttapayuttabhāvato. Tenāha bhagavā –

18. 'Restrains' means prevents, does not allow to proceed. The deity asks. 'Removing' means taking away, so that no grounds for abuse remain at all; thus, 'avoiding' is the meaning. He understands the way of a charioteer. He does not allow it to fall upon himself, for a thoroughbred knows what is yoked. There is no one, indeed, who is freed from false abuse, for among foolish people, in disparaging others, they do not discern what is suitable or unsuitable. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

“Nindanti tuṇhimāsīnaṃ, nindanti bahubhāṇinaṃ;

Mitabhāṇimpi nindanti, natthi loke anindito”ti. (dha. pa. 227);

“They censure one who sits silent, they censure one who speaks much; they censure also one who speaks in moderation. There is no one in the world uncensured.”

Tanuyāti vā katipayā. Tenāha “appakā”ti. Sadā satāti hirinisedhabhāve kāraṇavacanaṃ. Pappuyyāti patvā adhigantvā. Vānato nikkhantattā nibbānaṃ, asaṅkhatadhātu.

'Tanu' means few. Therefore, he says, 'few.' 'Always mindful' is a statement of the cause for the state of being restrained by conscience. 'They reach' means having attained, having realized. Nibbāna, the unconditioned element, is so-called because it has emerged from craving.

Hirīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Conscience is concluded.

9. Kuṭikāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discourse on Huts

19. Antoti kucchiabbhantare. Vasanaṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti vasanabhāvena. Kulapaveṇinti kulācāraṃ kulatantiṃ. Santānakaṭṭhenāti kulasantatiyā bandhanabhāvena[M 1.0082]. Evaṃ sabbapadehi pucchitatthassa anujānanavasena “ekaṃsavacane nipāto”ti vuttaṃ. Āpādikā posikā mātucchā mahāpajāpati mātā evāti katvā “pahāya pabbajitattā”ti avisesato vuttaṃ. Pahāya pabbajitattā natthīti ānetvā sambandho. Puna mātukucchivāsādīnaṃ abhāvavacaneneva vaṭṭamhi bandhanassa abhāvo dīpito hotīti na gahito. Ayaṃ kira devatā yathā puthujjanā buddhānaṃ guṇe na jānanti, evaṃ na jānāti, tasmā “mayā sannāhaṃ bandhitvā”tiādimāha.

19. 'Inside' means in the interior of the belly. 'By way of being a dwelling place' means by the state of dwelling. 'A lineage tradition' means family custom, family continuity. 'By way of continuity' means by the state of being bound by family continuity. Thus, by way of assenting to the meaning inquired by all these terms, it is said, 'a particle in a definitive statement.' The one who brings up, the one who fosters, the maternal aunt, Mahāpajāpatī, is indeed the mother—having considered this, 'because of having renounced and gone forth' is stated without distinction. The connection is made by supplying 'is not' to 'because of having renounced and gone forth.' Furthermore, by the very statement of the absence of dwelling in the mother's womb and so on, the absence of bondage in the round of existence is shown; thus it is not taken. It is said that this deity, just as ordinary people do not know the virtues of the Buddhas, so she does not know; therefore, she said, 'having bound armor,' and so on.

Kuṭikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Huts is concluded.

10. Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discourse on Samiddhi

20. Tapanabhāvena [V 1.0073] tapanodakattā tapodāti tassa rahadassa nāmaṃ. Tenāha “tattodakassa rahadassā”ti. Tatoti nāgabhavane udakarahadato tapodā nāma nadī sandati. Sā hi nadī bhūmitalaṃ ārohati. “Edisā jātā”ti vacanaseso. Petalokoti lohakumbhinirayā idhādhippetāti vadanti. Rahadassa pana ādito pabbatapādavanantaresu bahū petā viharanti, svāyamattho petavatthupāḷiyā lakkhaṇasaṃyuttena ca dīpetabbo. Yatāyanti yato rahadato ayaṃ. Sātodakoti madhurodako. Setodakoti parisuddhodako, anāvilodakoti attho. Tatoti tapodānadito.

20. Because of its heating nature and because it has hot water, the name of that lake is Tapodā. Therefore, it is said, 'of the lake with hot water.' From that water-lake in the Nāga's dwelling, a river named Tapodā flows. Indeed, that river rises to the surface of the earth. The remainder of the statement is, 'it has become such.' 'The world of ghosts'—they say that here the Lohakumbhī hells are intended. Moreover, from the origin of the lake, many ghosts dwell in the forest areas at the foot of the mountains; this meaning should be explained by the Petavatthu Pāḷi and the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta. 'Yatāyanti' means 'from which lake this comes.' 'Sātodaka' means 'having sweet water.' 'Setodaka' means 'having pure water,' the meaning being 'water without turbidity.' 'Tato' means 'from the Tapodā river.'

Samiddhoti avayavānaṃ sampuṇṇatāya saṃsiddhiyāva sammā iddho. Tenāha “abhirūpo”tiādi. Padhāne sammasanadhamme niyutto, taṃ vā ettha atthīti padhāniko. Senāsanaṃ suṭṭhapitadvāravātapānaṃ, tesaṃ pidahanena utuṃ gāhāpetvā.

'Samiddhi' means rightly prosperous by the completeness of his limbs and by his accomplishment. Therefore, it is said, 'handsome,' and so on. 'Devoted to striving' means engaged in striving, in the practice of insight, or one who possesses that here. 'A dwelling with well-placed doors and windows': by closing them, having caused the climate to be controlled.

Pubbāpayamānoti nhānato pubbabhāge viya vodakabhāvaṃ āpajjamāno gamento. Avattaṃ paṭikkhipitvā vattaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha…pe… na otaritabba”nti paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbadisāpalokanaṃ yathā nhāyanaṭṭhānassa manussehi vivittabhāvajānanatthaṃ. Khāṇuādivavatthāpanaṃ cīvarādīnaṃ ṭhapanatthaṃ udakasamīpeti [M 1.0083] adhippāyo. Ukkāsanaṃ amanussānaṃ apagamanatthaṃ. Avakujjaṭṭhānaṃ taṅkhaṇepi uparimakāyassa ujukaṃ avivaṭakaraṇatthaṃ. Cīvarapiṭṭheyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ yattha vā tattha vā aṭṭhapetvā. Udakanteti udakasamīpe. Sinnaṭṭhānanti sedagatapadeso. Pasāretabbaṃ tassa sukkhāpanatthaṃ. Saṃharitvā ṭhapanaṃ puna sukhena gahetvā nivāsanatthaṃ. Nābhippamāṇamattaṃ otaraṇaṃ tāvatā udakapaṭicchādilakkhaṇappattato. Vīciṃ anuṭṭhāpentenātiādi saṃyatakāritādassanaṃ. Nivāsanaṃ parikkhipitvāti antaravāsakaṃ kaṭippadesassa yathā parito hoti, evaṃ khipitvā parivasitvā.

'Making oneself ready beforehand' means going, attaining a state of being without water, as it were, in the part before bathing. First, 'There... one should not enter' is said in order to reject improper conduct and show proper conduct. Looking around in all directions is for the purpose of ascertaining that the bathing place is secluded from people. Establishing a stump or the like is for placing robes and other belongings near the water; this is the intention. Clearing the throat is for the purpose of making non-human beings depart. Bending forward is for the purpose of keeping the upper body straight and unexposed even at that moment. The robe should be placed on the back of the robe itself, not just put down anywhere. 'At the water's edge' means near the water. 'The place of bathing' refers to the area where sweat has gone. It should be spread out for the purpose of drying it. Gathering and placing it aside is for the purpose of easily taking it again and wearing it. Entering the water should be only up to the measure of the navel, as by that much the characteristic of being covered by water is attained. 'Not stirring up waves' and so on is a demonstration of restrained conduct. 'Wrapping the lower garment around' means having thrown and worn the inner robe so that it is around the waist area.

Sarīravaṇṇopi vippasīdi sammadeva bhāvanānussatimpi vindantassāti adhippāyo. Samanaṃ niggahetunti kilesavasaṃ gataṃ attano cittaṃ niggaṇhituṃ. Kāmūpanītāti kāmaṃ upagatacittā. Atha vā kilesakāmena there upanītacittā.

The radiance of the body also became perfectly clear for one who obtains even right mindfulness of development—this is the meaning. 'To restrain the ascetic' means to restrain one's own mind, which has fallen under the sway of defilements. 'Led by sensual desire' means having a mind that has gone to sensual pleasures. Alternatively, it means having a mind led to the elder by the defilement of desire.

Aparibhuñjitvāti ananubhotvā. Anubhavitabbanti atthato āpannamevāti āha “pañcakāmaguṇe”ti[V 1.0074]. Bhikkhasīti yācasi. Tañca bhikkhācariyavasenāti āha “piṇḍāya carasī”ti. Kāmaparibhogagarugamanakālo nāma visesato paṭhamayobbanāvatthāti āha “daharayobbanakālo”ti. Obhaggenāti majjhe saṃbhaggakāyena. Jiṇṇakāle hi sattānaṃ kaṭiyaṃ kāyo obhaggo hoti.

'Not having enjoyed' means not having experienced. 'It should be experienced' means it is indeed implied in meaning—thus he says, 'the five strands of sensual pleasure.' 'You beg' means you ask. And that by way of the alms-round—thus he says, 'you wander for alms.' The time when one is heavily given to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is especially the first stage of youth—thus he says, 'the time of youth.' 'With a broken body' means with a body broken in the middle. For in old age, the body of beings is broken at the waist.

Voti nipātamattaṃ “ye hi vo ariyā”tiādīsu viya. Sattānanti sāmaññavacanaṃ, na manussānaṃ eva. Dehanikkhepananti kaḷevaraṭṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ. Natthi etesaṃ nimittanti animittā, “ettakaṃ ayaṃ jīvatī”tiādinā sañjānananimittarahitāti attho. Na nāyareti na ñāyanti. Ito paranti ettha paranti aññaṃ kālaṃ. Tena orakālassapi saṅgaho siddho hoti. Paramāyuno orakāle eva cettha paranti adhippetaṃ tato paraṃ sattānaṃ jīvitassa abhāvato. Vavatthānābhāvatoti kālavasena vavatthānābhāvato. Vavatthānanti cettha paricchedo veditabbo, na asaṅkarato vavatthānaṃ, nicchayo vā. Abbudapesītiādīsu abbudakālo pesikālotiādinā kāla-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Kāloti idha pubbaṇhādivelā adhippetā. Tenāha pubbaṇhepi hītiādi[M 1.0084]. Idheva dehena patitabbanti sambandho. Anekappakāratoti nagare jātānaṃ gāme, gāme jātānaṃ nagare, vane jātānaṃ janapade, janapade jātānaṃ vanetiādinā anekappakārato. Ito cutenāti ito gatito cutena. Idha imissaṃ gatiyaṃ. Yante yuttagoṇo viyāti yathā yante yuttagoṇo yantaṃ nātivattati, evaṃ kālo gatipañcakanti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

'Vo' is merely a particle, as in phrases like 'ye hi vo ariyā.' 'Sattānaṃ' is a general term, not referring exclusively to humans. 'Dehanikkhepananti' means the place where the corpse is laid down. 'Natthi etesaṃ nimittanti' means they are without signs, that is, devoid of any sign for knowing, such as 'this one will live so long,' and so forth. 'Na nāyareti' means they are not known. Here, 'paraṃ' in 'ito paraṃ' means another time. Thereby, the inclusion of even a shorter period is established. In this context, 'paraṃ' is intended to mean a time shorter than the maximum lifespan, because beyond that there is no life for beings. 'Vavatthānābhāvatoti' means due to the absence of delimitation by time. 'Vavatthānanti' here should be understood as delimitation, not as non-confusion or certainty. In 'abbudapesītiādīsu,' the word 'kāla' should be connected separately to each, as in 'abbudakālo,' 'pesikālo,' and so forth. Here, 'kālo' is intended to mean a time of day, such as the morning. Hence it is said, 'even in the morning,' and so forth. The connection is: 'the body falls right here.' 'Anekappakāratoti' means in various ways: those born in a city die in a village, those born in a village die in a city, those born in a forest die in the countryside, those born in the countryside die in a forest, and so forth. 'Ito cutenāti' means having passed away from this existence. 'Idha' means here, in this state of existence. 'Yante yuttagoṇo viyāti': just as an ox yoked to a machine does not go beyond the machine, so too time does not go beyond the five destinies; this is how the application of the simile should be understood.

Ayaṃ kāloti ayaṃ maraṇakālo. Pacchime kāleti pacchime vaye. Tisso vayosīmāti. Paṭhamādikā tisso vayassa sīmā atikkantena. Purimānaṃ hi dvinnaṃ vayānaṃ sabbaso sīmā atikkamitvā pacchimassa ādisīmaṃ atikkanto tathā vutto. “Ayañhi samaṇadhammo…pe… na sakkā kātu”nti vatvā tamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “tadā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gaṇhitunti pāḷito atthato ca hadaye ṭhapanavasena gaṇhituṃ. Paribhuñjitunti vuttadhammapariharaṇasukhaṃ anubhavituṃ. Ekassa kathanato paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ suttaṃ vā ussāreti, tasmiṃ niṭṭhite itaro dhammakathiko taṃyeva vitthārento dhammaṃ katheti, ayaṃ sarabhāṇadhammakathā. Suttageyyānusārena yāva pariyosānā ussāraṇaṃ sarabhaññadhammakathā. “Mā maṃ kālo upaccagā”ti vadanto “samaṇadhammassa karaṇassa ayaṃ me kālo”ti katheti, tato paro “pacchimavayo añño kālo”ti katheti. “Kālaṃ vohaṃ…pe… tasmā abhutvā bhikkhāmī”ti vadanto attanā kataṃ paṭipattiñca sahetukaṃ sānisaṃsaṃ katheti.

'Ayaṃ kālo' means 'this is the time,' that is, 'this is the time of death.' 'Pacchime kāle' means 'in the final time,' that is, 'in the final age.' 'Tisso vayosīmā' means 'the three age limits.' This refers to one who has passed the three age limits beginning with the first. For having completely passed the limits of the first two ages and having passed the initial limit of the last age, he is thus called. Having stated, 'This is indeed the ascetic's duty… it cannot be done,' to explain that meaning in detail, 'tadā hi' and so forth is said. 'Gaṇhituṃ' means to grasp both the text and the meaning by placing them in the heart. 'Paribhuñjituṃ' means to experience the happiness of practicing the Dhamma as taught. When one person first recites a verse or a discourse, and when that is finished, another Dhamma speaker elaborates on that very topic—this is a connected Dhamma talk (sarabhāṇadhammakathā). Reciting according to the prose and verse sections of the discourse up to the conclusion is a recital-connected Dhamma talk (sarabhaññadhammakathā). Saying, 'May time not pass me by,' he speaks, 'This is my time for practicing the ascetic's duty.' Then, further, he speaks, 'The final age is another time.' Saying, 'I have known the time… therefore, not having enjoyed, I beg,' he explains the practice he has undertaken along with its cause and benefit.

Taṃ [V 1.0075] gāravakāraṇaṃ sandhāya. Etanti “atha kho sā devatā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā”ti etaṃ vuttaṃ. Daharo tvantiādimāha lobhābhibhūtatāya adhigatattā. Sabbasampattiyuttoti bhogasampadā parivārasampadāti sabbasampattīhi yutto. Alaṅkāraparihāranti alaṅkārakaraṇaṃ. Anikkīḷitāvīti akīḷitapubbo. Kīḷanañcettha kāmānaṃ paribhogoti āha “abhuttāvī”ti. Akatakāmakīḷoti akatakāmānubhavanappayogo. Sayaṃ attanā eva dissantīti sandiṭṭhā, sandiṭṭhā eva sandiṭṭhikā, attapaccakkhato sandiṭṭhikā. Pakaṭṭho kālo patto etesanti kālikā, te kālike.

This is stated with reference to the reason for reverence. This means what was said: 'Then that deity, having stood firmly on the ground.' 'Daharo tvan'ti' and so forth was said because he (the deity) understood that he (the youth) was overcome by greed. 'Sabbasampattiyutto' means endowed with all prosperities, namely, the prosperity of wealth and the prosperity of a retinue. 'Alaṅkāraparihāra' means the act of adorning. 'Anikkīḷitāvī' means one who has not sported before. And here, 'sport' is the enjoyment of sensual pleasures—thus he says, 'abhuttāvī' (one who has not enjoyed). 'Akatakāmakīḷo' means one who has not made the effort to experience sensual pleasure. 'Sandiṭṭhā' means directly visible to oneself; 'sandiṭṭhikā' is the same as 'sandiṭṭhā'; 'sandiṭṭhikā' means directly witnessed by oneself. 'Kālikā' means those for whom the excellent time has arrived; thus, 'kālike'.

Cittānantaranti [M 1.0085] icchitacittānantaraṃ, icchiticchitārammaṇākāreti attho. Tenevāha “cittānantaraṃ icchiticchitārammaṇānubhavanaṃ na sampajjatī”tiādi. Cittānantaraṃ laddhabbatāyāti anantaritasamādhicittānantaraṃ laddhabbaphalatāya. Samohitesupīti sambhatesupi. Sampannakāmassāti samiddhakāmassa. Cittakārā rūpalābhena, potthakārā paṭimākārakā, rūpakārā dantarūpakaṭṭharūpa-loharūpādikārakā. Ādisaddena nānārūpavesadhārīnaṃ naṭādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Sesadvāresūti ettha gandhabbamālākārasūpakārādayo vattabbā.

'Cittānantaraṃ' means immediately after a desired thought; the meaning is the desired object and its aspect. Therefore, he says, 'The experiencing of a desired object does not occur immediately after the thought,' and so forth. 'Cittānantaraṃ laddhabbatāya' means because the fruit is attainable immediately after the mind of uninterrupted concentration. 'Samohitesupi' means even when gathered. 'Sampannakāmassa' means for one whose sensual desires are fulfilled. 'Cittakārā' are painters; 'potthakārā' are image-makers; and 'rūpakārā' are those who make forms from ivory, wood, metal, and so forth. By the word 'ādi' (etc.) are included various performers like actors who wear diverse costumes. Regarding the remaining sense-doors, perfumers, garland-makers, cooks, and so forth should be mentioned.

Soti samiddhitthero. Samohitasampattināti saṅgāhabhogūpakaraṇasampattinā. Pattabbadukkhassāti kāmānaṃ āpajjanarakkhaṇavasena laddhabbassa kāyikacetasikadukkhassa. Upāyāsassāti daḷhaparissamassa viratassa. “Vissātassā”ti keci. “Paccavekkhaṇañāṇenā”ti keci paṭhanti. Asukasmiṃ nāma kāle phalaṃ hotīti evaṃ udikkhitabbo nassa kāloti akālo. Etthāti etesu navasu lokuttaradhammesu. Ehipassavidhinti “ehi passā”ti evaṃ pavattavidhivacanaṃ. Upanetabboti vā upaneyyo, so eva opaneyyiko. Viññūhīti vidūhi paṭividdhasaccehi. Te ekaṃsato ugghaṭitaññūādayo hontīti āha “ugghaṭitaññūādīhī”ti. “Paccatta”nti etassa patiattanīti bhummavasena attho gahetabboti āha “attani attanī”ti.

'So' refers to the elder Samiddhi. 'Samohitasampattinā' means with the prosperity of collected enjoyments and requisites. 'Pattabbadukkhassa' refers to the physical and mental suffering to be obtained by way of acquiring and guarding sensual pleasures. 'Upāyāsassa' means of one who has ceased from strong exertion. Some say 'vissātassa.' Some read 'paccavekkhaṇañāṇena.' 'Akālo' means it is not a time that can be looked forward to, as in 'at such and such a time the fruit will be'; thus, it is timeless. 'Ettha' means in these nine supramundane states. 'Ehipassavidhi' is a term for the method expressed as 'come and see.' 'Upanetabbo' or 'upaneyyo' means 'to be led to'; that itself is 'opaneyyiko.' 'Viññūhi' means by the wise, by those who have penetrated the truths. They are certainly those of quick understanding and so on—thus he says, 'by those of quick understanding and so on.' The meaning of 'paccattaṃ' should be understood in the locative sense as 'pati attani'—thus he says, 'attani attani' (in each self).

Sabbapadehi sambandhoti “kathaṃ ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo, kathaṃ akāliko”tiādinā sabbehi paccekaṃ sambandho veditabbo.

'Sabbapadehi sambandho' means that the connection with all terms should be understood individually with each one, such as with 'How is the danger here greater? How is it timeless?' and so on.

Navoti taruṇo na ciravasso. Ye bhikkhunovādakalakkhaṇappattā, te sandhāya “vīsativassato paṭṭhāya thero”ti vuttaṃ. Idha sāsanaṃ nāma sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ piṭakattayanti āha “dhammena [V 1.0076] hī”tiādi. Tattha dhammena vinayo ettha vinā daṇḍasatthehīti dhammavinayo. Dhammāya vinayo ettha na āmisatthanti dhammavinayo. Dhammato vinayo na adhammatoti dhammavinayo. Dhammo vā bhagavā dhammassāmī dhammakāyattā, tassa dhammasaññitassa satthu vinayo, na takkikānanti dhammavinayo. Dhamme vinayo na adhamme vinayo. Dhammo ca so yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne satte apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti, sabbe saṃkilesato vinetīti vinayo cāti dhammavinayo. Tenāha “ubhayampetaṃ sāsanasseva nāma”nti.

'Navo' means young, not of long standing. With reference to those who have attained the characteristics qualifying them to admonish nuns, it is said, 'an elder is one from twenty years onwards.' Here, the Dispensation, which comprises the threefold training and the three baskets, is what is meant—thus he says, 'by the Dhamma,' and so forth. In this context, 'Dhamma-Vinaya' means: the discipline is by means of the Dhamma, that is, without rods and weapons. Or, it is the discipline for the sake of the Dhamma, not for the sake of material gain. Or, it is the discipline that is from the Dhamma, not from non-Dhamma. Or, the Dhamma is the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, on account of his Dhamma-body; it is the discipline of that Teacher, who is designated as Dhamma, not that of the logicians. Or, it is discipline in the Dhamma, not in non-Dhamma. Or, it is the Dhamma because it upholds beings who practice as instructed, preventing them from falling into states of woe; and it is the Vinaya because it disciplines one from all defilements—thus, 'Dhamma-Vinaya.' Therefore, he says, 'both of these are indeed names for the Dispensation.'

Dhammavinayoti [M 1.0086] dhammena yutto vinayoti dhammavinayo ājaññaratho viya. Dhammo ca vinayo cāti vā dhammavinayo, taṃ dhammavinayaṃ. Dhammavinayānañhi satthubhāvavacanato dhammavinayattasaṃsiddhi dhammavinayānaṃ aññamaññaṃ visesanato. Abhidhammepi vinayavacananti dhammavinayadvayasiddhi, desitapaññattavacanato dhammavinayasiddhi. Dhammo catudhā desito sandassana-samādāpana-samuttejana-sampahaṃsanavasena, vinayo catudhā paññatto sīlācārato parājitavasena. Dhammacariyā sakavisayo, vinayapaññatti buddhavisayo. Pariyāyena desito dhammo, nippariyāyena paññatto vinayo. Dhammadesanā adhippāyatthappadhānā, vinayapaññatti vacanatthappadhānā. Paramatthasaccappadhāno dhammo, sammutisaccappadhāno vinayo. Āsayasuddhipadhāno dhammo, payogasuddhipadhāno vinayo.

“Dhamma-Vinaya” means Vinaya endowed with Dhamma, like a thoroughbred chariot. Or, “Dhamma and Vinaya”—that is the Dhamma-Vinaya. The perfect establishment of the state of Dhamma-Vinaya is from the statement of their being the Teacher's teachings, and by the Dhamma and Vinaya distinguishing each other. Even in the Abhidhamma, there is a statement of Vinaya—thus the establishment of the two, Dhamma and Vinaya, is accomplished. The Dhamma-Vinaya is established from the statement of what is taught and what is prescribed. The Dhamma is taught in four ways: in terms of showing, instilling, rousing, and gladdening. The Vinaya is prescribed in four ways: in terms of conduct, behavior, and offenses causing defeat. The practice of Dhamma is one's own domain, while the prescriptions of Vinaya are the Buddha's domain. The Dhamma is taught by implication, while the Vinaya is prescribed without implication. The teaching of Dhamma emphasizes the intended meaning, while the prescriptions of Vinaya emphasize the literal meaning. The Dhamma has ultimate truth as its focus, while the Vinaya has conventional truth as its focus. The Dhamma emphasizes purity of underlying disposition, while the Vinaya emphasizes purity of application.

Kiriyadvayasiddhiyā dhammavinayasiddhi. Dhammena hi anusāsanasiddhi, vinayena ovādasiddhi. Dhammena dhammakathāsiddhi, vinayena ariyatuṇhībhāvasiddhi. Sāvajjadvayaparivajjanato dhammavinayasiddhi. Dhammena hi visesato pakatisāvajjapariccāgasiddhi, vinayena paññattisāvajjapariccāgasiddhi. Gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇaguṇadvayasiddhi. Bahussutasutapasannadvayato pariyatti-pariyāpuṇana-dhammavihāra-vibhāgato dhammadharavinayadharavibhāgato ca dhammavinayadvayasiddhi, saraṇadvayasiddhiyā dhammavinayadvayasiddhi. Idha sattānaṃ duvidhaṃ saraṇaṃ dhammo attā ca. Tattha dhammo suciṇṇo saraṇaṃ. “Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”nti (theragā. 303; jā. 1.10.102; 1.15.385) hi vuttaṃ. Sudanto attāpi saraṇaṃ “attā hi attano nātho”ti (dha. pa. 160, 380) vacanato. Tena vuttaṃ “saraṇadvayasiddhiyā dhammavinayasiddhī”ti. Tattha yatassa dhammasiddhi, yato ca vinayasiddhi, tadubhayaṃ dassento āha – “dhammena hettha dve piṭakāni vuttāni, vinayena vinayapiṭaka”nti. Adhunā āgato idāneva na cirasseva upagato.

The establishment of the Dhamma and Vinaya is through the establishment of two activities. For through the Dhamma is the establishment of instruction, and through the Vinaya, the establishment of admonition. Through the Dhamma is the establishment of Dhamma-talk, and through the Vinaya, the establishment of noble silence. The establishment of the Dhamma and Vinaya is from the avoidance of two kinds of blameworthy deeds. For through the Dhamma is especially the establishment of abandoning what is naturally blameworthy, and through the Vinaya, the establishment of abandoning what is blameworthy by prescription. The establishment of the Dhamma and Vinaya is also through the establishment of two qualities—common and uncommon—for both householders and the ordained. The establishment of the two, Dhamma and Vinaya, is from the two qualities of being greatly learned and faithful in what is heard, from the distinction regarding the mastery of the scriptures, study, and dwelling in the Dhamma, and from the distinction between an upholder of the Dhamma and an upholder of the Vinaya. The establishment of the Dhamma and Vinaya is also through the establishment of the twofold refuge. Here, beings have a twofold refuge: the Dhamma and the self. Among these, the well-practiced Dhamma is a refuge. For it is said: “Indeed, the Dhamma protects one who lives by the Dhamma.” The well-controlled self is also a refuge, as stated: “For one is indeed one’s own refuge.” Therefore, it is said: “The establishment of the Dhamma and Vinaya is through the establishment of the twofold refuge.” Herein, showing both from what the establishment of the Dhamma arises and from what the establishment of the Vinaya arises, he says: “Through the Dhamma, two Piṭakas are spoken of here, and through the Vinaya, the Vinaya Piṭaka.” Newly arrived, just now, not long ago approached.

Mahante [V 1.0077] ṭhāne ṭhapetvāti mahesakkhatādassanatthaṃ attano parivārena mahantaṭṭhāne ṭhapitabhāvaṃ pavedetvā. Mahatiyāti upasaṅkamanavandanādivacanāpajjanavasena samāciṇṇāya. Sabbepi kira nisīdantā taṃ ṭhānaṃ ṭhapetvāva nisīdanti. Thirakaraṇavasenāti daḷhīkaraṇavasena. Ayaṃ kira devatā ñāṇasampannā mānajātikā, tasmā nāyaṃ mānaṃ appahāya [M 1.0087] mama desanaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ sakkotīti mānaniggaṇhanatthaṃ ādito duviññeyyaṃ kathento bhagavā “akkheyyasaññino”tiādinā tāya ñātumicchitakāmānaṃ kālikādibhāvaṃ, dhammassa ca sandiṭṭhikādibhāvaṃ vibhāvento dve gāthā abhāsi.

“Having placed in a great position”: this is for the purpose of showing great influence, by announcing the fact that he was placed in a great position by his retinue. “With great”: this refers to its being frequented by way of approaching, paying respects, uttering suitable words, and so on. Indeed, it is said that all who sit down, do so only after setting that place aside. “By way of making firm”: this means by way of strengthening. This deity, it is said, is endowed with knowledge and is of a proud nature. Therefore, she cannot penetrate my teaching without abandoning pride. Thus, for the purpose of subduing her pride, the Blessed One, at first speaking in a way difficult to understand, beginning with “Perceiving what can be expressed,” analyzed the temporal nature and so forth for those who wished to know from her, and the immediately visible nature and so forth of the Dhamma, and spoke two verses.

Akkheyyatoti gihiliṅgapariyāyanāmavisesādivasena tathā tathā akkhātabbato. Tenāha “kathānaṃ vatthubhūtato”ti. Etesanti sattānaṃ. Patiṭṭhitāti pavattitā āsattā. Pañcannaṃ kāmasaṅgādīnaṃ vasena āsattā hontu, itaresaṃ pana kathanti? Aniṭṭhaṅgatopi hi “idaṃ nu kho”tiādinā kaṅkhato tattha āsatto eva nāma avijahanato, tathā vikkhepagato vikkhepavatthusmiṃ, anusayānaṃ pana āsattabhāve vattabbameva natthi. Maccuno yoganti, maccubandhanaṃ, maraṇadhammatanti attho. Yasmā apariññātavatthukā anatītamaraṇattā maccunā yathāruci payojetabbā, tattha tattha uparūpari ca khipitāya āṇāya abbhantare eva honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “payogaṃ…pe… āgacchantī”ti. Yasmā tebhūmakā dhammā kamanīyaṭṭhena kāmā, nesampi kālassa laddhabbatāya kālikatā idha akkheyyavacanena paveditā. Tenāha – “evamimāya gāthāya kālikā kāmā kathitā”ti. Sabbepi tebhūmakā dhammā kamanīyā, yasmā ca kālikānaṃ kāmānaṃ tathāsabhāvatā kathitā. Ayampi gāthā tadatthameva dīpetīti imāya te kathitā eva honti. Ye ca sattā pañcasu khandhesu diṭṭhitaṇhādivasena patiṭṭhitā “itthī, puriso, ahaṃ, mamā”ti ca abhinivisiya kāme paribhuñjanti, te maraṇaṃ nātivattanti. Evampettha kāmānaṃ kālikattho kathitoti āha “kālikā kāmā kathitā”ti.

“Akkheyya” (what can be expressed): because it is to be expressed in various ways, such as by way of gender, case, synonyms, specific names, and so on. Hence it is said: “because it is the basis of speech.” “Of these” means of beings. “Established” means engaged, attached. Let them be attached by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure and so on, but what about the others? For even one who is inclined toward the undesirable, doubting with thoughts like “What could this be?” is indeed attached there by not letting go. Similarly, one who is distracted is attached to the object of distraction. As for the latent tendencies, however, there is nothing to be said about their state of attachment. “The yoke of Death” means the bondage of death, the state of being subject to death; this is the meaning.
