Because, with the objects not fully understood and death not transcended, they are to be employed by Death as he pleases, and because they are within the command hurled again and again, therefore it is said: “they come under the sway… and so on.” Because the phenomena of the three realms are “kāmā” (pleasures) in the sense of being desirable, and since they are subject to time, their temporality is declared here by the word “akkheyya.” Hence it is said: “Thus, in this verse, temporal pleasures are spoken of.” All phenomena of the three realms are desirable. And since the true nature of temporal pleasures has been explained, and this verse also illuminates that very meaning, they are indeed spoken of by this verse. Those beings who are established in the five aggregates through views, craving, and so on, clinging with notions like “woman, man, I, mine,” and who indulge in sensual pleasures, do not transcend death. In this way, the temporal meaning of pleasures is explained here. Therefore, it is said: “temporal pleasures are spoken of.”

Ayaṃ ñātapariññāti rūpārūpadhamme lakkhaṇādito ñāte katvā paricchindanapaññā. Tenāha “evaṃ ñātaṃ katvā”tiādi. Padaṭṭhānaggahaṇeneva cettha tesaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ paccayo gahitoti paccayapariggahassapi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tīreti tuleti vīmaṃsati. Dvācattālīsāya ākārehīti iminā matthakappattaṃ mahāvipassanaṃ dasseti. Te pana ākārā visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāya vuttanayena veditabbā. “Aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādinā vipassanākkhaṇepi ekadesena pahānaṃ labbhateva, anavasesato pana pahānavasena pahānapariññaṃ dassento [V 1.0078] āha “aggamaggena [M 1.0088] …pe… ayaṃ pahānapariññā”ti. Tathā ca āha “evaṃ tīhi pariññāhī”tiādi.

This is comprehension of the known (ñāta-pariññā): the wisdom that discerns and defines material and immaterial phenomena after having known them by way of their characteristics and so on. Here, by the very grasping of the proximate cause, the condition of those material and immaterial phenomena is grasped; thus, the inclusion of the comprehension of conditions (paccaya-pariggaha) should also be seen. It assesses, weighs, and investigates. By “by means of forty-two aspects,” it shows the great insight (mahā-vipassanā) that has reached its peak. Those aspects, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Path of Purification). By the phrase “Through the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence,” and so on, abandonment is indeed obtained to some extent even at the moment of insight. However, showing comprehension as abandonment by way of complete abandonment, it is said: “by the supreme path… this is comprehension as abandonment.” And thus it is said: “in this way, by these three kinds of comprehension,” and so on.

Akkhātāranti akkhātabbaṃ, na akkheyyakaṃ. Tenāha “kammavasena kāraka”ntiādi. Kārakanti ca sādhanamāha. Na maññatīti vā maññanaṃ nappavatteti akkhātāranti khīṇāsavaṃ. Atha vā tañhi tassa na hotīti taṃ kāraṇaṃ tassa khīṇāsavassa na hoti na vijjati, yena diṭṭhitaṇhādikāraṇena akkheyyaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ “tisso”ti vā “phusso”ti vā “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā abhinivissa vadeyyāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Manussanāgādīhi pūjanīyattā “yakkho”ti sabbadevānaṃ sādhāraṇavacananti devadhītāpi “yakkhī”ti vuttā. Akkheyyanti pahānapariññāya pahānamaggo, tassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ nibbānampi gahitaṃ. Na maññatīti khīṇāsavassa assa phalappattīti āha “navavidho lokuttaradhammo kathito”ti.

“Akkhātāraṃ” (the declarer) means what is to be declared, not what is expressible (akkheyyaṃ). Hence it is said: “the agent by way of action,” and so on. And by “agent” is meant the means of accomplishment. “He does not conceive” means he does not give rise to conceiving regarding the declarer, that is, the Arahant. Alternatively, because that cause does not exist for him—that cause is not found for that Arahant, by which, due to causes such as views and craving, he might cling to and speak of the five aggregates, which are expressible, as “Tissa,” or “Phussa,” or “a woman,” or “a man.” Thus, the meaning here should be understood. Because they are worthy of veneration by humans, nāgas, and others, “yakkha” is a common term for all deities; thus, even a female deity is called a “yakkhī.” By “akkheyyaṃ” (the expressible) is meant the path of abandoning through comprehension as abandonment; its object, Nibbāna, is also included. “He does not conceive”: this refers to the Arahant and his attainment of the fruit. Thus, it is said: “The ninefold supramundane Dhamma has been taught.”

Visesīti visesajātiādivasena seyyoti attho. Tesu gahitesūti tesu seyyamānādīsu tīsu mānesu gahitesu. Tayo seyyamānā, tayo sadisamānā, tayo hīnamānā gahitāva honti. So puggaloti so appahīnamaññanapuggalo. Teneva mānena hetubhūtena. Upaḍḍhagāthāyāti purimaddhena pana vatthukāmā vuttāti āha “kālikā kāmā kathitā”ti.

“Visesī” means superior, by way of distinguished birth and so on; this is the meaning. “When those are taken” means when those three conceits—superior, equal, and inferior—are taken. Three conceits of superiority, three conceits of equality, and three conceits of inferiority have indeed been taken. “That person” refers to the individual who has not abandoned conceiving. By that very conceit as the cause. “By half a verse” means that in the first half, however, sensual pleasures as objects were spoken of. Hence he says: “Temporal desires have been discussed.”

Vidhīyati visadisākārena ṭhapīyatīti vidhā, koṭṭhāso. Kathaṃvidhanti kathaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ, kena pakārena pavattitanti attho. Vidahanato hīnādivasena vividhenākārena dahanato upadhāraṇato vidhā, māno. Mānesūti nimittatthe bhummaṃ, mānahetūti attho. Na calatīti na vedhati attano parisuddhapakatiṃ avijahanato.

“Vidhā” means a portion, as it is established in a dissimilar manner; a section. “How constituted” means how it is established, in what way it proceeds; this is the meaning. “Vidhā” is conceit, from distinguishing, from burning in diverse ways such as inferior and so on, and from conceiving. “Among conceits” is the locative case in the sense of a sign, meaning, caused by conceit; this is the meaning. “It does not waver” means it does not tremble, from not abandoning its own pure nature.

Paññā “saṅkhā”ti āgatā, paññāti yoniso paṭisaṅkhānaṃ. Saṅkhāyakoti saṅkalanapaduppādanādi-piṇḍagaṇanāvasena gaṇako papañcasaṅkhāti mānādipapañcabhāgā. Te te dhammā sammā yāthāvato saṅkhāyanti upatiṭṭhanti etāyāti saṅkhā, paññā. Ekaṃ dvetiādinā saṅkhānaṃ gaṇanaṃ paricchindananti saṅkhā, gaṇanā. Saṅkhāyati bhāgaso kathīyatīti saṅkhā[M 1.0089], koṭṭhāso. Saṅkhānaṃ satto puggalotiādinā saññāpananti saṅkhā, rattotiādi paṇṇatti. Khīṇāsavo jahi pajahi rāgādīnaṃ suppahīnattā. Navabhedaṃ pabhedato, saṅkhepato tividhamānanti attho. Navavidhanti vā pāṭhe navabhedattā antarabhedavasena navavidhanti attho. Paccayavisesehi itthibhāvādivisesehi visesena [V 1.0079] mānīyati gabbho etthāti vimānaṃ, gabbhāsayo. Na upagacchīti na upagamissati. Tenāha “anāgatatthe atītavacana”nti. “Nājjhagā”ti hi atītaṃ “na gamissatī”ti etasmiṃ atthe. Chindi ariyamaggasatthena. Olokayamānā upapattīsu. Sattanivesanesūti sattānaṃ upapajjaṭṭhānesu. Lokuttaradhammameva kathesi arahattassa paveditattā.

Wisdom is called “saṅkhā”; wisdom is wise reflection. “Saṅkhāyako” refers to a reckoner who calculates by way of summation, derivation of terms, and the like; “papañca-saṅkhā” means the divisions of proliferation, such as conceit. Those various phenomena are rightly and truly reckoned and are present by means of this; hence, “saṅkhā,” wisdom. Counting as one, two, and so on, or delimiting by enumeration—this is “saṅkhā,” calculation. Being spoken of in parts—this is “saṅkhā,” a portion. Making known by designations such as “a being,” “a person,” and the like—this is “saṅkhā,” a designation such as “dyed” and so on. The one whose taints are destroyed has abandoned, has forsaken, due to the complete abandonment of lust and the like. It is ninefold by way of its divisions; in brief, the meaning is threefold conceit. Alternatively, in the reading “ninefold,” because it is ninefold by way of internal divisions, the meaning is “ninefold.” The embryo is especially esteemed herein due to particular conditions, such as the particularities of the female state and so on; thus, the womb is a “vimāna,” the abode of the embryo. “He did not approach” means he will not approach. Therefore, it is said: “a past tense word with a future meaning.” For “nājjhagā” is past tense, with the meaning of “he will not go.” He cut it with the sword of the noble path. Observing among rebirths. “In the abodes of beings” means in the places where beings are reborn. He spoke only of the supramundane Dhamma, because arahantship was proclaimed.

“Gāthāya atthaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti attha-saddo āharitvā vattabbo. Aṭṭhaṅgikamaggavasenapīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Satisampajaññaṃ nāma kusaladhammānuyoge kāraṇanti āha “dasakusalakammapathakāraṇa”nti.

The word 'meaning' should be supplied and spoken thus: “It is proper to explain the meaning of the verse.” Here too, in connection with the eightfold path, this is the same method. He said that mindfulness and clear comprehension are the cause for application to wholesome states, hence the words “the cause of the ten wholesome courses of action.”

Aṭṭhaṅgikamaggavasena ca gāthāatthavacane ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno vitthāra-nayo. Tasmiṃ kira ṭhāneti tasmiṃ kira devatāya pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjanaṭṭhāne. Devatāya ñāṇaparipākaṃ oloketvā anupubbiyā kathāya saddhiṃ sāmukkaṃsikadesanā mahatī dhammadesanā ahosi. Ñāṇaṃ pesetvāti satthudesanāya anussaraṇavasena pattavisuddhipaṭipāṭipavattaṃ bhāvanāñāṇaṃ bandhitvā. Sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāyāti satthudesanāvilāsena attano ca paripakkañāṇattā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ patvā. Evamāhāti evaṃ “pāpaṃ na kayirā”tiādippakārena gāthamāha. Aṅgaṃ na hoti, ājīvo yathā kuppamāno vācākammantavasena kuppati, tathā sampajjamānopīti. So vācākammantapakkhiko, tasmā taggahaṇena gahitova hoti. Vāyāmasatisamādhayo gahitā samādhikkhandhasaṅgahato. Sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappā gahitā paññākkhandhasaṅgahato. Antadvayavivajjanaṃ gahitaṃ sarūpenevāti adhippāyo. Itītiādi nigamanaṃ.

And by way of the Noble Eightfold Path, in explaining the meaning of the verse, this is the detailed method now being stated. In that place, indeed—that is, in the place where the question asked by the deity was answered. Having observed the maturity of the deity's knowledge, along with a gradual discourse, there was a great teaching of the Dhamma, an elevated teaching. Having directed knowledge—that is, having established the meditative knowledge, which proceeds in the order of purification attained by way of recollecting the Teacher’s teaching. Established in the fruit of stream-entry—that is, having attained the first fruit through the grace of the Teacher’s teaching and the maturity of one’s own knowledge. Thus he spoke—thus, in the manner of “Do no evil,” etc., he spoke the verse. It is not a factor, because livelihood, just as when it is corrupt it is so by way of speech and action, so too when it is perfected. It pertains to the category of speech and action; therefore, it is included by the mention of those. Effort, mindfulness, and concentration are included, being comprised in the aggregate of concentration. Right view and right intention are included, being comprised in the aggregate of wisdom. The avoidance of the two extremes is included by its very nature—this is the meaning. Thus, and so forth—this is the conclusion.

Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta is concluded.

Nandanavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nandana Chapter is concluded.

3. Sattivaggo

3. The Chapter on the Spear

1.Sattisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Satti Sutta

21. Desanāsīsanti [M 1.0090] desanāpadesalakkhaṇavacananti adhippāyo. Omaṭṭhoti adhomukhaṃ katvā dinnappahāro. Iminā eva pasaṅgena pahāre vibhāgato dassetuṃ “cattāro hī”tiādi vuttaṃ[V 1.0080]. Upari ṭhatvāti hatthiādīnaṃ upari ṭhatvā. Adhomukhaṃ dinnappahāroti khaggakaravālādīnaṃ adhomukhaṃ katvā pahatapahāro. Ummaṭṭho vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo. Vividhappahāro vimaṭṭho. “Omaṭṭho gahito”ti vatvā tasseva gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “so hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Duggandhakimiādīnaṃ vasena antodoso. Mañcena saddhiṃ bandhitvāti yasmiṃ mañce vaṇikapuggalo nipanno, tattha taṃ subandhaṃ katvā pādaṭṭhānaṃ uddhaṃ karontehi sīsaṭṭhānaṃ adho kātabbaṃ. Tenāha “adhosiro kātabbo”ti. Paribbajeti pavatteyya. Sā pana pavatti bhāvanāvihārena yuttāti āha “vihareyyā”ti.

21. The meaning is that it is a word indicating the characteristics of the teaching's main point. “Omaṭṭho” means a blow delivered downwards. By this very connection, to show the classification of blows, “four indeed” and so on is stated. “Standing above” means standing above elephants and the like. “A blow delivered downward” means a blow struck with swords, daggers, and the like, having turned them downward. “Ummaṭṭho” should be understood as the opposite of what was stated. “Vimaṭṭho” is a blow of various kinds. Having said, “Omaṭṭho was taken,” the reason for that taking is explained by saying, “for indeed” and so on. The internal defect is due to worms and the like that cause foul odors. “Bound together with the bed” means that where a merchant is lying on a bed, there, having made him well-fastened, while raising the foot end, the head end should be put downward. Hence it is said, “the head should be lowered.” “Paribbajeti” means ‘should proceed.’ But that proceeding is connected with abiding in development; hence it is said, ‘should abide.’

Sallassa ubbahanaṃ sallubbahanaṃ. Atthaṃ parittakaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā upamākārassa vikkhambhanappahānassa adhippetattā. Tenāha “punappuna”ntiādi. Anubandhova hoti sati paccaye uppajjanārahato devatāya kāmarāgappahānassa jotitattā. Nanu bhagavatā anāgāmimaggena desanā niṭṭhāpetabbāti? Na, itarissā ñāṇabalānurūpadesanāya pavattetabbato. Veneyyajjhāsayānukulañhi dhammaṃ dhammassāmī desetīti.

The extraction of the dart is ‘sallubbahana.’ The simile stands with a limited meaning, since abandonment by suppression is intended. Hence it is said, “again and again,” etc. There is indeed a connection, because it illuminates the abandonment of sensual desire by the deity, who is fit for it to arise when a condition is present. Now, should not the Blessed One have concluded the teaching with the path of the non-returner? No, because the teaching should proceed in accordance with the strength of the other's knowledge. For the Master of the Dhamma teaches the Dhamma in a way suitable to the inclinations of those to be trained.

Sattisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Satti Sutta is concluded.

2. Phusatisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Phusati Sutta

22. Kammaṃ aphusantanti kammaphassaṃ aphusantaṃ, kammaṃ akarontanti attho. Vipāko na phusatīti vipākaphasso na phusati, vipāko na uppajjateva kāraṇassa abhāvato. Evaṃ byatirekamukhena kammavaṭṭena vipākavaṭṭaṃ sambandhaṃ katvā atthaṃ vatvā idāni kevalaṃ kammavaṭṭavasena atthaṃ vadanto “kammamevā”tiādimāha. Tattha nākaroto kariyatīti kammaṃ akubbato na kayirati, anabhisandhikatakammaṃ nāma natthīti attho. Idāni [M 1.0091] tamevatthaṃ anvayato dassetuṃ “phusantañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatoti phusanahetu. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Vuttamevatthaṃ sakāraṇaṃ katvā pariveṭhitavasena vibhūtaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “tasmā phusanta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Dhammatāti kārakasseva kammavipākānubandho, nākārakassāti ayaṃ kammavipākānaṃ sabhāvo.

22. “Not touching action” means not touching action-contact, that is, one does not perform the action. “The result does not touch” means result-contact does not touch; the result simply does not arise due to the absence of a cause. Thus, having explained the meaning by way of contrast, connecting the round of results with the round of actions, now stating the meaning solely in terms of the round of actions, he says, “action alone,” etc. Here, “for the non-doer, it is not done” means for one who does not perform an action, it is not done; there is no such thing as an action done without intention—this is the meaning. Now, to show this same meaning by way of affirmation, “touching and,” etc., is stated. Here, ‘from that’ means from the cause of touching. The rest is as previously explained. To clarify the stated meaning with its cause, making it evident in a comprehensive manner, “therefore, touching,” etc., is stated. ‘The nature of things’ means that the connection of action and result follows only the doer, not the non-doer—this is the intrinsic nature of action and result.

Pacceti upagacchati anubandhati. Pāpanti pāpakaṃ kammaṃ phalañca. Ayañca attho araññe luddakassa uyyojanāya sunakhehi parivāriyamānassa bhikkhuno bhayena rukkhaṃ āruḷhassa [V 1.0081] cīvare luddassa upari patite tassa sunakhehi khāditvā māritavatthunā dīpetabboti.

“Follows” means approaches, pursues, accompanies. “Evil” means unwholesome action and its result. And this meaning should be illustrated by the story of the monk who, out of fear, climbed a tree in the forest when surrounded by dogs set on him by a hunter, and whose robe fell on the hunter, resulting in the dogs tearing him apart and killing him.

Phusatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Phusati Sutta is concluded.

3. Jaṭāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta

23. Yena atthena taṇhā “jaṭā”ti vuttā, tamevatthaṃ dassetuṃ “jāliniyā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā hi aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritapabhedā attano avayavabhūtā eva jālā etissā atthīti jālinīti vuccati. Idānissā jaṭākārena pavattiṃ dassetuṃ “sā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rūpādīsu ārammaṇesūti tassā pavattiṭṭhānamāha rūpādichaḷārammaṇavinimuttassa taṇhāvisayassa abhāvato. Heṭṭhupariyavasenāti kadāci rūpārammaṇe kadāci yāva dhammārammaṇā, kadāci dhammārammaṇe kadāci yāva rūpārammaṇāti evaṃ heṭṭhā ca upari ca pavattivasena. Desanākkamena cettha heṭṭhupariyatā veditabbā, kāmarāgādivasenapi ayamattho veditabbo. Saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikabhāvato aparāparuppatti ettha saṃsibbananti āha “punappunaṃ uppajjanato saṃsibbanaṭṭhenā”ti. Idaṃ yena sambandhena jaṭā viyāti jaṭāti jaṭātaṇhānaṃ upamūpameyyatā, taṃdassanaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – yathā jālinī veḷugumbassa sākhā, tāsaṃ sañcayādayo ca attano avayavehi saṃsibbitā vinaddhā “jaṭā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ taṇhāpi saṃsibbanasabhāvenāti.

23. To show the meaning by which craving is called “jaṭā” (tangle), it is said “jālinī” (net-like). For this craving, divided into one hundred and eight modes of activity, has its own nets—its own components—and thus is called “jālinī.” Now, to show how it operates in the form of a tangle, it is said, “For it…” Here, “among sense objects such as forms, etc.” indicates the basis for its operation, because craving has no scope beyond the six sense objects. “By way of lower and higher” means sometimes arising with a form as its object, sometimes with any of the others up to mental phenomena, and sometimes with a mental phenomenon as its object, then back down to a form—thus, it operates by alternating between lower and higher. In the order of the teaching, this alternation between lower and higher should be understood. The same meaning can also be understood in terms of sensual lust, etc. Due to the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena, their repeated arising is here called “interweaving.” Hence, it is said, “Because it arises again and again, it has the nature of being interwoven.” This shows the relationship of simile and object of simile between the tangle and craving. The meaning here is this: Just as the net-like branches of a bamboo thicket, their clusters and shoots, are interwoven and entangled with their own parts and are called a “tangle,” so too is craving by its very nature of being interwoven.

Ime [M 1.0092] sattā “mama ida”nti pariggahitaṃ attanibbisesaṃ maññamānā abbhantarimaṃ karonti. Abbhantaraṭṭho ca anto-saddoti sakaparikkhāresu uppajjanamānāpi taṇhā “antojaṭā”ti vuttā. Pabbajitassa pattādi, gahaṭṭhassa hatthiādi sakaparikkhāro. Attāti bhavati ettha abhimānoti attabhāvo, upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Sarīranti keci. “Mama attabhāvo sundaro, asukassa viya mama attabhāvo bhaveyyā”tiādinā sakaattabhāvādīsu taṇhāya uppajjanākāro veditabbo. Attano cakkhādīni ajjhattikāyatanāni, attano ca paresañca rūpādīni bāhirāyatanāni, paresaṃ sabbāni vā. Saparasantatipariyāpannāni vā cakkhādīni ajjhattikāyatanāni, tathā rūpādīni bāhirāyatanāni. Parittamahaggatabhavesu pavattiyāpi taṇhāya antojaṭābahijaṭābhāvo veditabbo. Kāmabhavo hi kassacipi kilesassa avikkhambhitattā katthacipi avimutto ajjhattaggahaṇassa visesapaccayoti “ajjhattaṃ anto”ti [V 1.0082] ca vuccati, tabbipariyāyato rūpārūpabhavo “bahiddhā bahī”ti ca. Tenāha bhagavā – “ajjhattasaṃyojano puggalo, bahiddhāsaṃyojano puggalo”ti (a. ni. 2.37).

These beings, thinking “this is mine,” grasp it as their own and make it internal. The meaning of ‘internal’ is ‘within,’ and thus even the craving that arises regarding one’s own possessions is called “internal tangle.” For a monk, his bowl and so forth; for a layperson, his elephant and so forth—these are their own possessions. 'Selfhood' (attabhāvo) is so called because conceit arises in it; it is the five aggregates of clinging. Some say it is the body. The manner in which craving arises regarding one’s own selfhood—such as thinking, “my selfhood is beautiful,” or “may my selfhood be like that one’s”—should be understood. One’s own eye and so forth are the internal sense bases, and one’s own and others’ forms and so forth are the external sense bases—or all of another’s. Alternatively, the eye and other internal sense bases pertaining to one’s own or another’s continuum, and similarly, forms and other external sense bases. The nature of craving as internal or external entanglement should also be understood through its occurrence in the limited and exalted planes of existence. The sense-sphere existence is a specific condition for internal grasping since no defilements have been suppressed in anyone, and no one is liberated anywhere; thus, it is called “internal” and “within.” In contrast, the form and formless realms are called “external” and “without.” Therefore, the Blessed One said: “A person bound internally, a person bound externally” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.37).

Visayabhedena pavattiākārabhedena anekabhedabhinnampi taṇhaṃ jaṭābhāvasāmaññena ekanti gahetvā “tāya evaṃ uppajjamānāya jaṭāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā pana pajāti vuttasattasantānapariyāpannā eva hutvā punappunaṃ taṃ jaṭentī vinandhantī pavattatīti āha “jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā”ti. Tathā hi paramatthato yadipi avayavabyatirekena samudāyo natthi, ekadeso pana samudāyo nāma na hotīti avayavato samudāyaṃ bhinnaṃ katvā upamūpameyyaṃ dassento “yathā nāma veḷujaṭādīhi…pe… saṃsibbitā”ti āha. Imaṃ jaṭanti sambandho. Tīsu dhātūsu ekampi asesetvā saṃsibbanena tedhātukaṃ jaṭetvā ṭhitaṃ. Tenassā mahāvisayataṃ vijaṭanassa ca sudukkarabhāvamāha. Vijaṭetuṃ ko samatthoti iminā “vijaṭaye”ti padaṃ sattiatthaṃ, na vidhiatthanti dasseti.

Although craving is divided into many kinds by the division of its objects and the division of its modes of occurrence, it is taken as one due to the commonality of its nature as a tangle. Thus, it is said, “By that very tangle arising in this way.” Moreover, this generation, being included in the continuum of beings as described, again and again entangles and binds it; hence it is said, “The generation is tangled by the tangle.” Indeed, in the ultimate sense, although there is no whole apart from its components, still, a part is not called a whole. Separating the whole from its components, he illustrates the comparison by saying, “Just as with a tangle of bamboo, etc., … it is interwoven.” The connection is to “this tangle.” Without leaving out even one of the three realms, by interweaving, it stands having tangled the three-realm existence. Thus, he speaks of its vast scope and the extreme difficulty of disentangling it. With “Who is capable of disentangling it?” he shows that the word “disentangle” has the meaning of ability, not a command.

Evaṃ “antojaṭā”tiādinā puṭṭho athassa bhagavā tamatthaṃ vissajjento “sīle patiṭṭhāyā”tiādimāha. Ettha sīleti kusalasīle. Taṃ pana pātimokkhasaṃvarādibhedesu parisuddhameva icchitabbanti āha “catupārisuddhisīle”ti.

Thus, when asked about “internal tangle” and so on, the Blessed One, explaining the meaning, said, “Established in virtue,” and so on. Here, “virtue” refers to wholesome virtue. That, however, is intended to be entirely pure in its divisions such as the Pātimokkha restraint and so forth, and is thus called “virtue of fourfold purity.”

Narati [M 1.0093] netīti naro, puriso. Kāmaṃ itthīpi taṇhājaṭāvijaṭane samatthā atthi, padhānameva pana sattaṃ dassento “naro”ti āha yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana avibhāgena puggalapariyāyo ayanti dassetuṃ “naroti satto”ti vuttaṃ. Vipākabhūtāya saha paññāya bhavatīti sapañño. Tāya hi ādito paṭṭhāya santānavasena bahulaṃ pavattamānāya ayaṃ satto savisesaṃ sapaññoti vattabbataṃ arahati. Vipākapaññāpi hi santānavisesena bhāvanāpaññuppattiyā upanissayapaccayo hoti ahetukadvihetukānaṃ tadabhāvato. Kammajatihetukapaṭisandhipaññāyāti kammajāya tihetukapaṭisandhiyaṃ paññāyāti evaṃ tihetukasaddo paṭisandhisaddena sambandhitabbo, na paññāsaddena. Na hi paññā tihetukā atthi. Paṭisandhito pabhuti pavattamānā paññā “paṭisandhiyaṃ paññā”ti vuttā taṃmūlakattā, na paṭisandhikkhaṇe pavattā eva.

A man is called “naro” because he rejoices (narati) and leads (neti). Indeed, a woman too is capable of disentangling the tangle of craving, but to show the principal type of being, he says “naro,” just as it is said “the Teacher of gods and men.” In the commentary, however, to indicate that this is a designation for a person without distinction, it is said “naro means a being.” He is called “sapañño” (possessing wisdom) because he exists with wisdom that is the result of past actions. For from the very beginning, due to that wisdom occurring abundantly throughout the continuity of existence, this being deserves to be specifically called “sapañño.” For resultant wisdom, through a distinction in the continuity, is a decisive support condition for the arising of developed wisdom; this is absent for those without roots or with two roots. “Kammajatihetukapaṭisandhipaññāya” means wisdom in a triple-rooted rebirth-linking born of kamma. Thus, the term “tihetuka” (triple-rooted) should be connected with the term “paṭisandhi” (rebirth-linking), not with the term “paññā” (wisdom). For there is no wisdom that is triple-rooted. The wisdom that arises continuously from rebirth-linking onwards is called “wisdom at rebirth-linking” because it is rooted in that, not because it occurs only at the very moment of rebirth-linking.

Cinteti ārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyatīti cittaṃ, samādhi. So hi sātisayaṃ upanijjhānakicco. Na hi vitakkādayo vinā samādhinā tamatthaṃ sādhenti, samādhi pana tehi vināpi [V 1.0083] sādhetīti. Paguṇabalavabhāvāpādanena paccayehi cittaṃ, attasantānaṃ cinotītipi cittaṃ, samādhi. Paṭhamajjhānādivasena cittavicittatāya iddhividhādicittakaraṇena ca samādhi cittanti vināpi paropadesenassa cittapariyāyo labbhateva. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana citta-saddo viññāṇe niruḷhoti katvā vuttaṃ “cittasīsena hettha aṭṭha samāpattiyo kathitā”ti. Yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi jānātīti paññā. Sā yadipi kusalādibhedato bahuvidhā, “bhāvaya”nti pana vacanato bhāvetabbā idhādhippetāti taṃ dassento “paññānāmena vipassanā kathitā”ti. Yadipi kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ ātāpanaṃ, taṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnampi attheva, ātappasaddo viya pana ātāpa-saddo vīriye eva niruḷhoti āha “ātāpīti vīriyavā”ti. Yathā kammaṭṭhānaṃ tāya paññāya parito harīyati pavattīyati, evaṃ sāpi tadatthaṃ yogināti āha “pārihāriyapaññā”ti. Abhikkamādīni sabbakiccāni sātthakasampajaññādivasena paricchijja netīti sabbakiccapariṇāyikā.

It thinks, it contemplates the object—that is the mind (citta); this is concentration (samādhi). For it has the function of supreme contemplation. Indeed, initial thought and the like cannot accomplish that purpose without concentration, but concentration accomplishes it even without them. Also, it accumulates its own continuity—thus, it is the mind; this is concentration. Because of the mind’s diversity through the first jhāna and so on, and by performing wonders like psychic powers, concentration is called “mind”—even without another's instruction, this synonym for “mind” is established. In the commentary, however, because the word “citta” is established in the sense of consciousness, it is said: “Here, the eight attainments are discussed under the heading of ‘citta.’” It knows things in their various aspects according to their true nature—that is wisdom (paññā). Although wisdom is of many kinds, such as wholesome and so forth, here it is intended as what should be developed, as indicated by the word “develop”; thus, it is stated: “Vipassanā (insight) is spoken of under the name of paññā (wisdom).” Although the burning away of defilements is a meaning also of right view and the like, the word “ātāpa” (ardor), like the word “ātappa,” is established only in the sense of energy; thus, it is said: “One who is ātāpī (ardent) is energetic.” Just as the meditation subject is carried around and made to proceed by that wisdom, so too is that wisdom for that purpose for the yogi—hence it is called “pārihāriya-paññā” (wisdom that carries along). It directs all activities—such as going forward—by assessing them with appropriate purpose and clear comprehension—thus, it is the guide of all activities.

Yasmā puggalādhiṭṭhānena gāthā bhāsitā, tasmā puggalādhiṭṭhānameva upamaṃ dassento “yathā nāma puriso”tiādimāha. Tattha sunisitanti suṭṭhu [M 1.0094] nisitaṃ, ativiya tikhiṇanti attho. Satthassa nisitatarabhāvakaraṇaṃ nisānasilāyaṃ, bāhubalena cassa ukkhipananti ubhayampetaṃ atthāpannaṃ katvā upamā vuttāti tadubhayaṃ upameyyaṃ dassento “samādhisilāyaṃ sunisitaṃ…pe… paññāhatthena ukkhipitvā”ti āha. Samādhiguṇena hi paññāya tikkhabhāvo. Yathāha “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071). Vīriyañcassā upatthambhakaṃ paggaṇhanato. Vijaṭeyyāti vijaṭetuṃ sakkuṇeyya. Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya hi vattamānāya yogāvacaro taṇhājaṭaṃ vijaṭetuṃ samattho nāma. Vijaṭanañcettha samucchedavasena pahānanti āha – “sañchindeyya sampadāleyyā”ti.

Since the verse was spoken with reference to a person, therefore, to illustrate that very reference to a person, he begins with “Just as a man,” etc. Here, “well-sharpened” means well sharpened; the meaning is extremely sharp. The sharpening of the sword is done on the whetstone, and lifting it is done by the strength of the arm—both these meanings are implied in the simile. To show both of these as the objects of comparison, he says, “on the whetstone of concentration, well-sharpened… lifted by the hand of wisdom.” For it is through the quality of concentration that wisdom becomes sharp, as it is said: “One who is concentrated understands things as they really are” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071). And energy is its support, by way of uplifting it. “Could disentangle” means would be able to disentangle. For when insight leading to emergence is functioning, the meditator is indeed capable of disentangling the tangle of craving. And here, the disentangling is abandonment by way of eradication, thus he says: “would sever, would completely cleave.”

Maggakkhaṇe panesa vijaṭeti nāma, aggaphalakkhaṇe sabbaso vijaṭitajaṭo nāma. Tenāha “idānī”tiādi. Yasmā jaṭāya vijaṭanaṃ ariyamaggena, tañca kho nibbānaṃ āgamma, tasmā taṃ sandhāyāha “jaṭāya vijaṭanokāsa”nti. Yattha pana sā vijaṭīyati, taṃ dassetuṃ “yattha nāmañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Paṭighaṃ rūpasaññā cā”ti gāthāsukhatthaṃ sānunāsikaṃ katvā niddeso, “paṭigharūpasaññā”ti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭighasaññāvasena kāmabhavo gahito kāmabhavapariyāpannattā tāya. Pathavīkasiṇādirūpe saññā rūpasaññā. Ubhayatthāpi saññāsīsena cittuppādasseva gahaṇaṃ. Bhavasaṅkhepenāti bhavabhāvena saṅkhipitabbatāya, bhavalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattāti attho. Rūpe vā virajjanavasena ca vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyā idha rūpasaññāti vuttā[V 1.0084], evampettha arūpabhavassa ca gahitatā veditabbā. “Nāmañca rūpañcā”ti anavasesato nāmarūpaṃ gahitanti arūpabhava-asaññabhavānampettha gahaṇaṃ siddhanti apare. Pariyādiyanaṭṭhāneti pariyādiyanakāraṇe sabbaso khepananimitte nibbāne. Tenāha “nibbānaṃ…pe… dassito hotī”ti.

At the moment of the path, one is called 'one who disentangles'; at the moment of the highest fruition, one is called 'one whose tangle is completely disentangled.' Therefore, he says, “Now,” etc. Because the disentangling of the tangle is by the noble path, and that is based on Nibbāna, therefore, referring to that, he says, “the occasion for the disentangling of the tangle.” To indicate where it is disentangled, it is said, “where name and form,” etc. The phrase “paṭighaṃ rūpasaññā ca” is stated with a nasalized ending for the sake of the verse's ease; what is meant is “perceptions of resistance and form.” The sense-sphere existence is taken by way of the perception of resistance, because it is comprised within that existence. Perception of form in the earth kasiṇa, etc., is perception of form. In both cases, it is the arising of consciousness itself that is taken, with “perception” as the leading term. By “summarized as existence” is meant that it is to be summarized by the nature of existence; that is, it has a single characteristic, the characteristic of existence. Or, “perception of form” is stated here by way of dispassion towards form; thus, in this context, the inclusion of the formless existence should also be understood. Others say that because “name and form” is taken without remainder, the inclusion of the formless existence and the non-percipient existence is also established here. By “in the place of exhaustion” is meant in Nibbāna, which is the cause of exhaustion, the basis for complete destruction. Therefore, he says, “Nibbāna… is shown.”

Jaṭāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta is concluded.

4. Manonivāraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Manonivāraṇa Sutta

24. Evaṃladdhikāti sabbathāpi cittuppatti sadukkhā, sabbathāpi acittakabhāvo seyyo, tasmā yato kutoci cittaṃ nivāretabbanti evaṃdiṭṭhikā[M 1.0095]. Soti satto. Aniyyānikakathaṃ katheti ayoniso cittanivāraṇaṃ vadantī. Saṃyatabhāvaṃ āgatanti rāgavisevanādito sammadeva saṃyatabhāvaṃ otarabhāvaṃ. Dhammacariyāvasena hi pavattamāne citte natthi īsakampi rāgādivisevanaṃ, na tassa sampati āyatiñca koci anattho siyā, tasmā taṃ mano sabbato anavajjavuttito na nivāretabbaṃ. Tenāha “dānaṃ dassāmī”tiādi. Yato yatoti yato yato sāvajjavuttito ayonisomanasikārato. Tanti mano nivāretabbaṃ anatthāvahattā.

24. By 'those of such a doctrine' is meant those who hold the view that any arising of consciousness is always painful, and a state of being without consciousness is always better; therefore, the mind should be restrained from wherever it arises. 'He' refers to a being. He speaks talk that does not lead to liberation, advocating unwise restraint of the mind. By 'having attained restraint' is meant the state of having rightly entered into restraint from excessive indulgence in lust, etc. For when the mind is proceeding by way of Dhamma practice, there is not even the slightest excessive indulgence in lust, etc., nor would any harm befall it now or in the future. Therefore, that mind should not be restrained from any blameless activity. Thus, he says, “I will give,” etc. By 'from wherever' is meant from whatever blameworthy activity or unwise attention. That mind should be restrained because it brings harm.

Manonivāraṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Manonivāraṇa Sutta is concluded.

5. Arahantasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Arahanta Sutta

25. Katāvīti katavā, pariññādikiccaṃ katvā niṭṭhapetvā ṭhitoti attho. Tenāha “catūhi maggehi katakicco”ti. Svāyamattho arahantiādisaddasannidhānato viññāyati. Evaṃ “ahaṃ vadāmī”tiādiākārena pucchati.

25. By 'one who has done' is meant one who has done, having completed the task of full understanding, etc., and remains so. Therefore, he says, “one who has completed the task through the four paths.” This meaning is understood from the proximity of the words “arahant,” etc. Thus, he asks about the manner of speech, such as 'I speak,' etc.

Khandhādīsu kusaloti khandhāyatanādīsu salakkhaṇādīsu ca samūhādivasena pavattiyañca cheko yathābhūtavedī. Upaladdhinissitakathanti attupaladdhinissitakathaṃ hitvā. Vohārabhedaṃ akarontoti “ahaṃ paramatthaṃ jānāmī”ti lokavohāraṃ bhindanto avināsento loke lokasamaññameva nissāya “ahaṃ, mamā”ti vadeyya. Khandhā bhuñjantītiādinā vohārabhedaṃ, tattha ca ādīnavaṃ dasseti.

By 'skillful in the aggregates, etc.' is meant one who is expert and knows things as they truly are in the aggregates, sense bases, etc., in their characteristics, etc., and in their occurrence by way of groups, etc. By 'talk dependent on acquisition' is meant abandoning talk dependent on the acquisition of a self. By 'not breaking convention' is meant not breaking or destroying worldly convention by saying, “I know the ultimate truth,” but rather, relying on worldly designations in the world, one would say, “I,” “mine.” Through phrases like “the aggregates experience,” etc., he shows the breaking of convention and the danger therein.

Māno nāma diṭṭhiyā samadhuro. Tathā hi dutiyamaggādīsu sammādiṭṭhiyā pahānābhisamayassa [V 1.0085] paṭivipaccanīke paṭipattisiddhi. Tenāha “yadi diṭṭhiyā vasena na vadati, mānavasena nu kho vadatīti cintetvā”ti. Vidhūpitāti santāpitā ñāṇagginā daḍḍhā. Te pana viddhaṃsitā nāma hontīti āha “vidhamitā”ti. Mamaṅkārādayo mayanti sattasantāne sati pavattanti etenāti mayo, maññanā. Mayo eva mayatāti āha “mayatanti maññana”nti.

Conceit is of the same nature as wrong view. For indeed, in the second path and so on, the accomplishment of practice is contrary to the abandonment and realization associated with right view. Therefore, he says, having considered: 'If he does not speak by way of view, does he then speak by way of conceit?' By 'scorched' is meant heated and burned by the fire of knowledge. But they are indeed called 'destroyed,' hence he says, 'dispersed' (vidhamitā). Mayo is that by which possessiveness and the like proceed when there is a continuum of a being; it is conceiving (maññanā). He says that mayo itself is mayatā: 'mayataṃ is conceiving.'

Arahantasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Arahanta Sutta is concluded.

6. Pajjotasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Pajjota Sutta

26. Divārattinti [M 1.0096] na ādicco viya divā eva, na candimā viya rattiṃ eva, atha kho divā ca rattiñca. Tattha tatthāti yattha yattha sampajjalito, tattha tattheva padese, na ādicco viya candimā viya sakalaṃ mahādisaṃ disantarāḷañca. Ñāṇānubhāvena uppannāloko ñāṇālokoti vadanti. “Idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti pubbe me, bhikkhave, ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi ñāṇaṃ udapādi paññā udapādi vijjā udapādi āloko udapādī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 15; paṭi. ma. 2.30) pana vacanato maggo ñāṇāloko. “Tamo vihato, āloko uppanno”ti (ma. ni. 1.386; pārā. 12) vā vacanato vijjattayāloko ñāṇāloko. Paṭhamābhisambodhiyaṃ viya sañjātapītivipphāro, visesato ratanaghare samantapaṭṭhānavicinane sañjātapītivasena uppannasarīrobhāso vā pītiāloko. Tattheva uppannapasādavasena sañjātaālokova pasādāloko. Dhammacakkapavattane “aññāsi vata, bho, koṇḍañño”ti uppannapasādālokoti ca vadanti. Sabbattheva satthu dhammadesanā sattānaṃ hadayatamaṃ vidhamantī dhammakathāāloko. Sabbopi buddhānaṃ pātubhāvā uppanno ālokoti iminā sāvakānaṃ desanāya sañjātadhammālokopi buddhānubhāvoti dasseti.

26. By 'day and night' is meant not like the sun, which shines only by day, nor like the moon, which shines only by night, but rather both day and night. By 'there, there' is meant that wherever it blazes forth, right there in that very spot, not like the sun or moon, which illuminate the entire great region and the intermediate directions. They call the light that arises through the power of knowledge 'the light of knowledge.' But according to the saying: '“This is suffering, the noble truth”—previously, monks, with regard to things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, understanding arose, light arose' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081; Mahāvagga 15; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.30), the path is the light of knowledge. Or, according to the statement, 'Darkness is dispelled, light has arisen' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.386; Pārāyana 12), the light of the three knowledges is the light of knowledge. The light of joy is like the suffusion of rapture that arose at the first full awakening, or especially the bodily radiance that arose by way of the joy that arose during the investigation of the Conditional Relations in the Jewel House. The light of confidence is the light that arose right there by way of arisen confidence. And at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, when it was said, 'Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood,' they also call the light that arose from this confidence the light of confidence. In all cases, the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, which dispels the darkness in the hearts of beings, is the light of Dhamma-talk. By this phrase, 'all light that arises from the appearance of the Buddhas,' he shows that even the light of Dhamma that arises from the teaching of the disciples is due to the power of the Buddhas.

Pajjotasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pajjota Sutta is concluded.

7. Sarasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sara Sutta

27. Saraṇato avicchedavasena pavattanato khandhādīnaṃ paṭipāṭi sarā. Tenāha “ime saṃsārasarā”ti. Kutoti kena kāraṇena, kimhi vā? Tenāha “kiṃ āgammā”ti? Na patiṭṭhāti paccayābhāvato. Āpotiādinā pāḷiyaṃ catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ appatiṭṭhānāpadesena tattha kāmarūpabhavānaṃ abhāvo dassito. Tadubhayābhāvadassanena heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva arūpabhavassapi [V 1.0086] abhāvo dassitova hoti, yathārutavasena vā ettha attho veditabbo. Yasmā purimā dve gahitā, gahitañca atthaṃ pariggahetvāva pacchimattho pavattoti.

27. The succession of aggregates and so on is called 'streams' (sarā) because they flow continuously without interruption. Hence it is said, 'These are the streams of saṃsāra.' 'Kuto' (from where?) means 'for what reason, or on what?' Hence it is said, 'Relying on what?' They do not stand firm due to the absence of conditions. In the Pāli text, by indicating the non-establishment of the four great elements through terms like 'water' (āpo), the absence of the realms of desire and form is shown there. By showing the absence of both, the absence of the formless realms is also demonstrated in the same way as previously stated, or the meaning here should be understood according to the expressed meaning. Since the first two are taken, the latter meaning proceeds only after grasping the meaning that has been taken.

Sarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sarasutta is concluded.

8. Mahaddhanasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Mahaddhana Sutta

28. Nidhīyatīti [M 1.0097] nidhānaṃ. Nidhātabbataṃ gataṃ nihitanti attho. Muttasārādīti muttāmaṇiveḷuriyapavāḷarajatajātarūpādi. Suvaṇṇarajatabhājanādīti ādi-saddena kahāpaṇa-dhaññakoṭṭhabhaṇḍādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tampi hi niccaparibbayavasena bhuñjīyatīti “bhogo”ti vuccati. Aññamaññaṃ abhigijjhantīti aññamaññassa santakaṃ abhigijjhanti. Tenāha “patthentī”ti. Analaṅkatāti na alaṃ pariyattanti evaṃ katacittā, atricchatāmahicchatāhi abhibhūtā. Tenāha “atittā apariyattajātā”ti. Ussukkajātesūti taṃtaṃkicce sañjātaussukkesu. Nānākiccajātesūti nānāvidhakiccesu, sañjātanānākiccesu vā. Vaṭṭagāmikapasutena vaṭṭasotaṃ anusarantesu. Taṇhānivāsatāya gehantipi agārantipi vuccatīti āha “mātugāmena saddhiṃ geha”nti. Virājiyāti hetuatthadīpakaṃ padanti āha “virājetvā”ti, tvā-saddopi cāyaṃ hetuatthoti.

28. 'Nidhīyati' (is deposited) means 'nidhāna' (a treasure). It means 'nihita' (deposited), having reached the state of being deposited. 'Muttasārādi' (pearls, etc.) means pearls, gems, beryl, coral, silver, gold, etc. 'Suvaṇṇarajatabhājanādi' (gold and silver vessels, etc.) includes, by the word 'ādi' (etc.), coins, grain, various goods, and so on. These too are called 'bhoga' (wealth) because they are enjoyed through constant consumption. 'Aññamaññaṃ abhigijjhanti' (they covet one another) means they covet the possessions of one another. Hence it is said, 'patthenti' (they long for). 'Analaṅkatā' (unadorned) means their minds are not contented, being overwhelmed by excessive greed and great desire. Hence it is said, 'atittā apariyattajātā' (unsatisfied, insatiable). 'Ussukkajātesu' (those who have become eager) means those who have become eager in their respective tasks. 'Nānākiccajātesu' (those who have become engaged in various tasks) means those engaged in various tasks, or those who have become engaged in various tasks. Being devoted to the course of the round, they follow the stream of the round. Because craving dwells in the home, it is called 'geha' (home) or 'agāra' (house). Hence it is said, 'the home with women' (gehaṃ mātugāmena saddhiṃ). 'Virājiyā' (having become dispassionate) is a word indicating a causal meaning. Hence it is said, 'virājetvā' (having become dispassionate), and this suffix '-tvā' also indicates a causal meaning.

Mahaddhanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahaddhana Sutta is concluded.

9. Catucakkasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Catucakka Sutta

29. Iriyā vuccati kāyena kattabbakiriyā, tassā pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato iriyāpatho, gamanādi. Taṃ aparāparappavattiyā cakkaṃ. Tenāha “catucakkanti catuiriyāpatha”nti. Navadvāranti karajakāyo adhippeto. So ca kesādiasuciparipūroti āha “puṇṇanti asucipūra”nti. Taṇhāya saṃyuttanti taṇhāsahitaṃ. Tena na kevalaṃ sabhāvato eva, atha kho nissitadhammo ca asuciṃ dasseti. Mātukucchisaṅkhāte asucipaṅke jātattā paṅkajātaṃ, kesādiasucipaṅkajātattā ca paṅkajātaṃ. Yātrāti apagamo. Tena sabhāvato nissitadhammato ca asucisabhāvato kāyato kathaṃ apagamo siyāti pucchati. Tenāha “etassā”tiādi.

29. 'Iriyā' (deportment) is called the activity to be performed by the body, and 'iriyāpatha' (posture)—such as walking, etc.—is its basis of occurrence. That is a wheel due to its continuous motion. Hence it is said, 'catucakkaṃ' (four wheels) means the four postures. 'Navadvāra' (nine-doored) refers to the body born of kamma. And it is full of impurities from hair onwards. Hence it is said, 'puṇṇaṃ' (full) means 'asucipūra' (full of impurities). 'Taṇhāya saṃyuttaṃ' (connected with craving) means accompanied by craving. Thus, it shows impurity not only by its very nature, but also as a dependent phenomenon. Because it is born in the impure mire described as the mother's womb, it is 'paṅkajātaṃ' (born from mire), and because it is born from the impure mire of hair, etc., it is 'paṅkajātaṃ'. 'Yātrā' (journey) means departure. Therefore, it asks how there can be departure from the body, given its impure nature both inherently and as a dependent phenomenon. Hence it is said, 'etassā' (of this), etc.

Nahanaṭṭhena bandhanaṭṭhena naddhīti upanāho idhādhippetoti āha “naddhinti upanāha”nti. So pana ito pubbakāle kodhoti āha “pubbakāle”tiādi[M 1.0098]. Pāḷiniddiṭṭheti upanāhaiccādike [V 1.0087] idha pāḷiyaṃ niddiṭṭhe kilese ṭhapetvā avasesā diṭṭhivicikicchādayo satta kilesā dummocayatāya varattā viyāti varattāti veditabbā. Ārammaṇaggahaṇasabhāvato eko evesa dhammo, pavatti-ākārabhedena pana icchanaṭṭhena patthanaṭṭhena icchā, lubbhanaṭṭhena gijjhanaṭṭhena lobhoti vutto. Paṭhamuppattikāti ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe, vāre vā paṭhamaṃ uppannā. Aparāparuppattikoti punappunaṃ uppajjamānako. Aladdhapatthanā appaṭiladdhavatthumhi āsatti lobho. Uppāṭetvāti sasantānato uddharitvā.

By the meaning of tying and binding, 'naddhi' (binding) is intended here as 'upanāha' (resentment). Hence it is said, 'naddhi' means 'upanāha'. But that, in a former time, is anger (kodha). Hence it is said, 'in a former time,' etc. 'Pāḷiniddiṭṭhe' (expounded in the Pāli) means that, setting aside the defilements expounded here in the Pāli, such as 'upanāha' (resentment), the remaining seven defilements—such as wrong view and doubt—are to be understood as 'varattā' (thongs) because they are hard to release, like thongs. By nature of grasping an object, this is indeed a single phenomenon, but due to differences in modes of activity, it is called 'icchā' (desire) by the meaning of wishing and longing, and 'lobha' (greed) by the meaning of being greedy and craving. 'Paṭhamuppattikā' (first arising) means arising first in a single object or instance. 'Aparāparuppattiko' (repeatedly arising) means arising again and again. 'Aladdhapatthanā' (longing for what is not obtained) is 'lobha' (greed), an attachment to an unobtained object. 'Uppāṭetvā' (having uprooted) means having removed it from one's own continuum.

Catucakkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Catucakka Sutta is concluded.

10. Eṇijaṅghasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Eṇijaṅgha Sutta

30. Eṇimigassa viyāti eṇimigassa jaṅghā viya. Avayavīsambandhe hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Piṇḍimaṃsassa parito samasaṇṭhitattā suvaṭṭītajaṅgho. Kisanti thūlabhāvapaṭikkhepaparājotanā, na suṭṭhu kisabhāvadīpanaparāti āha “athūlaṃ samasarīra”nti. Ātapena milātanti tapasā milātakāyaṃ indriyasantāpanabhāvato. Tenevāha – “tapo milāta”ntiādi, tathā cāha pāḷiyaṃ “appāhāraṃ alolupa”nti. Yathā “vīrassa bhāvo vīriya”nti vīrabhāvena vīriyaṃ lakkhīyati, evaṃ vīriyasambhavena vīrabhāvoti āha “vīranti vīriyavanta”nti. “Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive”ti (theragā. 983; mi. pa. 6.5.10) dhammasenāpativuttaniyāmena parimitabhojitāya appāhāratā bhojane mattaññutā. “Mitāhāra”nti vatvā puna paricchinnakālabhojitāyapi appāhārataṃ dassento “vikāla…pe… parittāhāra”nti āha. Catūsu paccayesu loluppavirahitaṃ bodhimūle eva sabbaso loluppassa pahīnattā. “Catūsu paccayesū”ti hi imināva sabbattha loluppavigamo dīpitovāti. Rasataṇhāpaṭikkhepo vā esa “appāhāra”nti vatvā “alolupa”nti vuttattā. “Sīhaṃ vā”ti ettha ekacarasaddo viya iva-saddo atthato “nāga”nti etthāpi ānetvā, sambandhitabboti [M 1.0099] āha – “ekacaraṃ sīhaṃ viya, ekacaraṃ nāgaṃ viyā”ti. Ekacarā appamattā ekīkatāya.

30. 'Eṇimigassa viya' (like a black antelope) means like the shank of a black antelope. This is indeed a genitive expression for the relation of a whole to its parts. The shank is well-rounded because the flesh is evenly formed all around. 'Kisaṃ' (lean) indicates a rejection of thickness, not a thorough description of thinness. Hence it is said, 'athūlaṃ samasarīraṃ' (not thick, evenly proportioned). 'Ātapena milātaṃ' (withered by heat) means the body is withered by ascetic practice, due to the scorching of the faculties. Therefore, it is said, 'tapo milātaṃ' (withered by ascetic practice), etc. Similarly, in the Pāli, it is said, 'appāhāraṃ alolupaṃ' (eating little, free from greed). Just as 'the state of a hero is heroism' (vīrassa bhāvo vīriyaṃ), heroism is characterized by the state of a hero, so too the state of a hero arises from energy. Hence it is said, 'vīraṃ' (heroic) means 'vīriyavantaṃ' (endowed with energy). According to the rule stated by the General of the Dhamma, 'Having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water' (Theragāthā 983; Milindapañha 6.5.10), eating little is moderation in food due to eating a limited amount. Having said 'mitāhāra' (moderate eater), he further shows 'eating little' also through eating at a limited time, saying, 'at the wrong time... etc. ...eating little.' He is free from greed regarding the four requisites—because greed is entirely abandoned at the root of enlightenment. Indeed, by 'catūsu paccayesu' (regarding the four requisites) alone, the absence of greed in all respects is demonstrated. Or this is the rejection of craving for tastes, because having said 'appāhāra' (eating little), it is stated as 'alolupa' (free from greed). Here, in the phrase 'or a lion' (sīhaṃ vā), the word 'like' (iva), just as the word 'solitary' (ekacara), should be supplied in meaning and also connected to 'elephant' (nāgaṃ). Hence it is said: 'solitary like a lion, solitary like an elephant' (ekacaraṃ sīhaṃ viya, ekacaraṃ nāgaṃ viya). Those who wander alone are heedful because of their solitude.

Pañcakāmaguṇavasena rūpaṃ gahitaṃ tesaṃ rūpasabhāvattā. Manena nāmaṃ gahitaṃ manassa nāmasabhāvattā. Avinibhuttadhammeti avinābhāvadhamme gahetvā. Ādi-saddena āyatanadhātuādayo gahitā. Kāmaguṇaggahaṇena hettha rūpabhāvasāmaññena pañca vatthūni gahitāneva honti, manogahaṇena dhammāyatanaṃ, evaṃ dvādasāyatanāni gahitāni honti. Iminā nayena dhātuādīnampi [V 1.0088] gahitatā yojetabbā. Tenāha “pañcakkhandhādivasenapettha bhummaṃ yojetabba”nti. Etthāti pāḷiyaṃ. Kāmavatthu bhummaṃ.

Form is grasped through the five strands of sensual pleasure because of their nature as form. Name is grasped by the mind because of the mind's nature as name. 'Avinibhuttadhamme' (inseparable phenomena) means having grasped inseparable phenomena. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the sense bases, elements, and so on are included. Here, by mentioning the strands of sensual pleasure, the five physical objects are indeed grasped as having the general nature of form. By mentioning the mind, the mind-object base is grasped—thus, the twelve sense bases are grasped. In this way, the inclusion of elements and so on should also be applied. Hence it is said, 'Here, the basis should be applied according to the five aggregates, etc.' 'Ettha' (here) refers to the Pāli text. The object of sensual pleasure is the basis.

Eṇijaṅghasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Eṇijaṅgha Sutta is concluded.

Sattivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sattivagga is concluded.

4. Satullapakāyikavaggo

4. The Satullapakāyika Chapter

1. Sabbhisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sabbhi Sutta

31. Sataṃ sādhūnaṃ saraṇagamanasīlādibhedassa dhammassa ullapanato, attano vā pubbenivāsānussatiyā tassa dhammassa ullapanato kathanato satullapā, devatā, tāsaṃ kāyo samūho, tattha bhavāti satullapakāyikā. Tenāha “sataṃ dhamma”ntiādi. Samādānavasena ullapetvā, na vaṇṇanākathanamattena tatrāti tasmiṃ tāsaṃ devatānaṃ satullapakāyikabhāve. Idaṃ vatthūti idaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Samuddavāṇijāti saṃyattikā. Khittasaravegenāti jiyāmuttasarasadisavegena, sīghaoghenāti attho. Uppatatīti uppāto. Uppāte bhavaṃ byasanaṃ uppātikaṃ. Patiṭṭhāti hitapatiṭṭhā. Paraloke hitasukhāvahaṃ abhayakāraṇaṃ. Jaṅghasatanti manussasataṃ. Jaṅghāsīsena hi manusse vadati sahacāribhāvato. Aggahesi pañcasīlāni. Āsannānāsannesu āsannasseva paṭhamaṃ vipaccanato “āsannakāle gahitasīlaṃ nissāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Ghaṭāvasenāti samūhavasena.

31. 'Satullapā' means those deities who proclaim the Dhamma—the Dhamma distinguished by such things as taking refuge and good conduct of the good, or the Dhamma they proclaim by recollecting their own past lives. 'Devatā' refers to deities, and 'kāyo' means their assembly. Hence, they are called 'Satullapakāyikā.' Therefore, it is said, 'the Dhamma of the good,' etc. They proclaim by undertaking it, not merely by speaking in praise of it; thus, in that state, those deities are Satullapakāyikā. 'This is the reason' means this is the cause. 'Samuddavāṇijā' refers to seafarers. 'Khittasaravegena' means with the speed of a released arrow, that is, with a swift current. 'Uppatati' means arising; an upheaval. 'Uppātikaṃ' refers to the calamity arising from an upheaval. 'Patiṭṭhāti' means a beneficial foundation—a cause of safety bringing welfare and happiness in the next world. 'Jaṅghasataṃ' means a hundred humans. For one speaks of humans by 'jaṅghāsīsa' due to association. 'Aggahesi' means he undertook the five precepts. 'Āsannānāsannesu' means that between the near and the not-near, for the near the ripening comes first—hence it is said, 'relying on the precepts undertaken at a time of nearness.' 'Ghaṭāvasena' means by way of a group.

Sabbhīti [M 1.0100] sādhūhi. Te hi saparahitasādhanato pāsaṃsatāya santaguṇatāya ca santoti vuccati. Te pana yasmā paṇḍitalakkhaṇehi samannāgatā honti, tasmā “paṇḍitehī”ti āha. Samāsethāti saṃvasethāti ayamettha adhippāyoti āha “sabbairiyāpathe”tiādi. Mittasanthavanti mettisandhānaṃ. Sattānaṃ hitesitālakkhaṇā hi metti, sā ca ñāṇasahitā ñāṇapubbaṅgamāvāti mittasanthavo asaṃkiliṭṭho, itaro saṃkiliṭṭhoti āha “na kenaci saddhiṃ kātabbo”ti. Saddhammanti diṭṭhadhammikādihitāvahaṃ sundaradhammaṃ. Seyyoti hitavaḍḍhanatādi vuttanti āha “vaḍḍhī”ti.

'Sabbhīti' means 'with the good.' For they are called 'good' because they accomplish the welfare of both themselves and others, and because of their praiseworthiness and peaceful qualities. Since they are endowed with the characteristics of the wise, it is said, 'with the wise.' 'Samāsethāti' means 'associate with'—the meaning here is, as stated, 'in all modes of conduct,' etc. 'Mittasanthava' means a bond of loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is characterized by desiring the welfare of beings, and when it is accompanied by knowledge, or preceded by knowledge, it is 'undefiled friendship'; the other is 'defiled'—hence it is said, 'not to be made with just anyone.' 'Saddhamma' means the beautiful Dhamma that brings benefit in this life and so on. 'Seyyo' means increase of welfare, etc., is meant—hence it is said, 'increase.'

Sataṃ sādhūnaṃ, paṇḍitānanti ayamettha attho. Tappaṭiyogavisayattā añña-saddassa vuttaṃ “aññato [V 1.0089] andhabālato”ti. Sokanimittaṃ sokakāraṇaṃ uttarapadalopena idha sokasaddena gahitanti āha “sokavatthūna”ntiādi. Sokavatthūni nāma corādayo acchindanādivasena paresaṃ sokakaraṇato. Sokānugatā sokappattā.

'Of the good, of the wise,' this is the meaning here. Due to its being the opposite domain, the word 'another' is mentioned: 'from another, from the blind and foolish.' The sign of sorrow, the cause of sorrow, is here understood by the word 'sorrow' through the elision of the latter word, as stated: 'the bases of sorrow,' etc. The bases of sorrow are such as thieves and others, who cause sorrow to others by robbing and the like. 'Sokānugatā' means attained by sorrow (sokappattā).

Therassāti saṃkiccattherassa. Attano bhaginiyā jeṭṭhattā “tumhe”ti āha. Ayaṃ “idha corā paṭipajjiṃsū”ti amhe tiṇāyapi na maññatīti cintetvā ekacce “mārema na”nti āhaṃsu. Karuṇāya ekacce “vissajjemā”ti āhaṃsu. Mantetvāti bhāsetvā.

Of the elder—this refers to Saṃkicca Thera. Because his sister was older, he addressed her as 'you' (plural). Some, thinking, 'Though we have appeared here as thieves, this one does not regard us even as grass,' said, 'Let us kill him.' Out of compassion, others said, 'Let us release him.' 'Mantetvā' means 'having spoken.'

Ahu ahosi, bhūtapubbanti attho. Araññasmiṃ brahāvaneti tādise brahāvane, mahāraññe nivāsīti attho cetoti byādho. Kūṭānīti vākurādayo. Oḍḍetvāti sajjetvā. Sasakanti pelakaṃ ubbiggāti bhītatasitā. Ekarattinti ekaratteneva. Dhanajānīti paribbayavasena addhikehi laddhabbadhanato hāni, “samaṇampi nāma hanti, kiṃ amhesu lajjissatī”ti addhikānaṃ anāgamanato ekadivasaṃ laddhabbaparibbayampi na labhissantīti adhippāyo.

'Ahu' means 'it was,' the meaning is 'it was in the past.' 'Araññasmiṃ brahāvaneti' means 'in such a great forest,' the meaning is 'dwelling in a great wilderness.' 'Ceta' means the hunter. 'Kūṭāni' means snares and the like. 'Oḍḍetvā' means 'having prepared.' 'Sasakaṃ' means a young animal; 'ubbiggā' means 'frightened, terrified.' 'Ekarattiṃ' means 'in just one night.' 'Dhanajāni' means a loss of wealth, a loss of the wealth to be obtained from travelers by way of payment. The meaning is that because travelers will not come, thinking, 'They even kill an ascetic, what shame will they have towards us?', they will not obtain even the daily payment they should receive.

Ñātayopi mātāpitubhātubhaginiādike ñātake. Te kira adhimuttassa bhaginiyā santikaṃ upagacchantā antarāmagge tena samāgatā, adhimutto [M 1.0101] saccavācaṃ anurakkhanto corabhayaṃ tesaṃ nārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ “tesampī”tiādi. Taṃ nissāya pabbajitattā “adhimuttasāmaṇerassa santike”ti vuttaṃ, na upasampadācariyo hutvā. Tenāha “attano antevāsike katvā”ti. Saccānurakkhaṇena anuttaraguṇādhigamena ca ñātimajjhe virocati.

Relatives—mother, father, brother, sister, and other kin. It is said that they, going to the presence of Adhimutta's sister, met him along the way. Adhimutta, guarding his truthful speech, did not announce to them the danger from thieves. Hence it is said: 'for them as well,' etc. Because they went forth relying on him, it is said: 'in the presence of Adhimutta the novice,' not because he had become their preceptor for higher ordination. Therefore, it is said: 'having made them his pupils.' By guarding the truth and attaining unsurpassed qualities, he shines among his relatives.

Sātatanti satataṃ. Sa-saddassa hi idha sābhāvo yathā “sārāgo”tiādīsu. Sātabhāvo vā sātatanti āha “sukhaṃ vā”ti. Kāraṇenāti tena tena kāraṇena. Sabbāsaṃ tāsaṃ vacanaṃ subhāsitaṃ, bhagavato pana ukkaṃsagataṃ subhāsitameva. Svāyamattho taṃtaṃgāthāpadeneva viññāyatīti taṃ nīharitvā dassetuṃ “na kevala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tena sappurisūpasaṃsevasaddhammābhiyogo yathā sattānaṃ vaḍḍhiyā paññāpaṭilābhassa ekantikaṃ kāraṇaṃ, evaṃ sokapaccaye sati visokabhāvassa, ñātimajjhe sobhāya, sugatigamanassa, ciraṃ sukhaṭṭhānassa, vaṭṭadukkhamocanassapi aññāsādhāraṇaṃ hotīti vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Sātataṃ' means 'constantly.' For here, the word 'sa' becomes 'sā,' as in 'sārāgo' (with passion), etc. Or, 'sātataṃ' means 'a state of pleasure,' hence it is said 'or pleasure' (sukhaṃ vā). 'Kāraṇena' means 'by this and that reason.' All those words are well-spoken, but the Blessed One's words, being supreme, are truly well-spoken. This meaning is understood from the very wording of the respective verses; therefore, to show this by extracting it, it is said, 'not only,' etc. Thus, it should be understood that just as associating with good people and devotion to the true Dhamma is a certain cause for the growth of beings and the acquisition of wisdom, so too is it an extraordinary cause for the state of being without sorrow when there is a condition for sorrow, for shining among relatives, for going to a good destination, for long-lasting happiness, and for release from the suffering of the round.

Sabbhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sabbhi Sutta is concluded.

2. Maccharisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Macchari Sutta

32. Pamajjanākārena [V 1.0090] pavattā anupaladdhi pamādo. Tena ekantato satirahitā hontīti vuttaṃ “sativippavāsalakkhaṇenā”ti. Diṭṭhivicikicchādayo cettha pamādeneva saṅgahitā. Idāni yathā macchariyanimittañca pamādanimittañca dānaṃ na dīyati, taṃ dassetuṃ “ekacco hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parikkhayaṃ gamissatīti bhogaparihāniṃ gamissati. Khiḍḍādīti ādi-saddena maṇḍanavibhūsanachaṇanakkhattakiccabyasanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Yasadāyakanti kittiyasassa parivārayasassa ca dāyakaṃ. Sirīdāyakanti sobhaggadāyakaṃ. Sampattidāyakanti kulabhogarūpabhogasampadāhi sampattidāyakaṃ. Puññanti vā idha puññaphalaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “evamidaṃ puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.80) viya. Atthi dānassa phalanti ettha deyyadhammassa anavaṭṭhitataṃ bahulasādhāraṇataṃ, taṃ pahāya gamanīyataṃ[M 1.0102], tabbisayāya pītiyā sāvajjataṃ, dānadhammassa anaññasādhāraṇataṃ anugāmikataṃ, tabbisayāya pītiyā anavajjataṃ, lobhādipāpadhammānaṃ vinodanaṃ, sesapuññānaṃ upanissayañca jānantenāti vattabbaṃ.

32. Negligence (pamādo) is non-apprehension that proceeds in the manner of heedlessness. Through it, one becomes completely devoid of mindfulness; therefore, it is said to be 'characterized by the absence of mindfulness' (sativippavāsalakkhaṇena). Here, wrong views (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā), etc., are included under negligence. Now, to illustrate how a gift is not given because of stinginess (macchariya) and negligence (pamāda), it is said, 'a certain person' (ekacco hi), etc. 'Will lead to loss' (parikkhayaṃ gamissati) means it will lead to the decline of wealth. 'Play, etc.' (khiḍḍādi): by the word 'etc.' (ādi), this includes adornment, decoration, festivals, auspicious occasions, and ruinous activities. 'A giver of fame' (yasadāyaka) means a giver of renown and a retinue. 'A giver of splendor' (sirīdāyaka) means a giver of beauty. 'A giver of prosperity' (sampattidāyaka) means a giver of prosperity through the accomplishments of family, enjoyments, and form. Here, 'merit' (puñña) should be understood as the fruit of merit, as in passages like, 'Thus this merit grows' (Dī. Ni. 3.80). Regarding 'There is fruit in giving' (atthi dānassa phalaṃ), it should be stated by one who knows the following: the unstable nature of the gift, its commonness to many, the necessity of relinquishing it when one departs, the faultiness of delight concerning it; and the uncommon nature of the act of giving, its following after the giver, the faultlessness of delight concerning it, the removal of unwholesome states like greed, and its being a supporting condition for other merits.

Taṃyeva bālanti yo maccharī, tameva. Adānasīlā bālā. Ekacco dhanassa paribhogaparikkhayabhayena attanāpi na paribhuñjati atilobhaseṭṭhi viyāti āha “idhalokaparalokesū”ti.

'That very fool' means: he who is miserly, that very one. Fools are those who are ungenerous. A certain person, fearing the exhaustion of their wealth through use, does not even enjoy it themselves—like a very greedy merchant; thus it is said, 'in this world and the next.'

Yasmā ekacco adānasīlo puriso addhike disvā passantopi na passati, tesaṃ kathaṃ suṇantopi na suṇoti, sayaṃ kiñci na katheti, adātukamyatāthambhe baddho hoti, tasmā tattha mataliṅgāni upalabbhantiyevāti āha “adānasīlatāya maraṇena matesū”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dānamattameva gahetvā matenassa samataṃ dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dānasīlassa pana amataliṅgāni vuttavipariyāyato veditabbāni. Vajanti puthutte ekavacanaṃ, tasmā vacanavipallāsena vuttanti āha “saha vajantā”ti. Dānasīlādidhammo purātano, na ajjatanoti sanantano, so etesu atthīti sanantanā, paṇḍitā, tesaṃ dhammāti tesaṃ vasenapi dhammo sanantanoti āha “sanantanānaṃ vā paṇḍitānaṃ esa dhammo”ti. Appasmimpi deyyadhamme sati eke dānaṃ dadanti, eke na dadanti maccharibhāvā. Sahassadānasadisāti ekāpi dakkhiṇā pariccāgacetanāya uḷārabhāvato sahassadānasadisā hoti.

Since a certain person of ungenerous character, even when seeing a traveler, does not see, and though hearing their words, does not listen, nor speaks anything himself—being bound by the pillar of unwillingness to give—therefore, the signs of the dead are indeed found in him. Thus it is said: 'among the dead by the death of ungenerous character.' In the commentary, however, taking just the matter of giving to show his equality with the dead, it is said: 'Just as...' etc. But for one of generous character, the signs of the deathless are to be understood as the opposite of what was said. 'Vajanti' is plural, but the meaning is singular; therefore, it is said with a change of number: 'going together.' The quality of generosity and similar virtues is ancient, not of today—thus it is eternal. It exists in them, the wise, who are thus eternal; it is their Dhamma, and through their influence, the Dhamma is eternal. Thus it is said: 'Or, this is the Dhamma of the eternal wise ones.' Even when there is little to be given, some give gifts, while others do not, due to stinginess. 'Equal to a thousand gifts' means that because the intention of relinquishment is sublime, even a single offering becomes equal to a thousand gifts.

Duranugamanoti asamaṅginā anugantuṃ dukkaro. Ananugamanañcassa dhammassa apūraṇamevāti āha [V 1.0091] “duppūro”ti. “Dhammaṃ care”ti ayaṃ dhammacariyā gahaṭṭhassa vasena āraddhāti āha “dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ caratī”ti. Tenāha “dārañca posa”nti. Samuñjakanti kassakehi attanā kātabbaṃ katvā visaṭṭhadhaññakaraṇato khale uñchācariyavasena samuñjaniādinā chaḍḍitadhaññasaṃharaṇaṃ. Tenāha “yo api…pe… samuñjakaṃ caratī”ti. Etenāti satasahassasahassayāgiggahaṇena dasannampi bhikkhukoṭīnaṃ piṇḍapāto dassito hoti. “Dinno”ti padaṃ ānetvā yojanā. Dasannaṃ vā kahāpaṇakoṭīnaṃ piṇḍapātoti dasannaṃ kahāpaṇakoṭīnaṃ viniyuñjanavasena sampāditapiṇḍapāto. Tayidaṃ satasahassaṃ [M 1.0103] sahassayāgīnaṃ dānaṃ ettakaṃ hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Samuñjakaṃ carantopīti samuñjakaṃ caritvāpi, samuñjakacaraṇahetūti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Dāraṃ posentopi dhammaṃ carati, appakasmiṃ dadantopi dhammaṃ caratīti yojanā. Tathāvidhassāti tādisassa tathādhammacārino yā dhammacariyā, tassā kalampi nagghanti ete sahassayāgino attano sahassayāgitāya. Yaṃ tena daliddenātiādi tassevatthassa vivaraṇaṃ. Sabbesampi tesanti “sataṃsahassānaṃ sahassayāgina”nti vuttānaṃ tesaṃ sabbesampi. Itaresanti “tathāvidhassā”ti vuttapurisato aññesaṃ. Dasakoṭisahassadānanti dasakoṭisaṅkhātaṃ tato anekasahassabhedatāya sahassadānaṃ.

'Difficult to follow' means: difficult for one who is not endowed with the necessary qualities to follow. And not following this Dhamma is indeed its non-fulfillment; hence it is said, 'difficult to fulfill.' 'Practice the Dhamma'—this practice of Dhamma is undertaken with respect to a householder; hence it is said, 'he practices the Dhamma of the tenfold path of wholesome actions.' Hence it is said, 'He supports his wife.' 'Gleaning' means: after the farmers have done what is to be done by them and have released the grain, it is the gathering of grain discarded on the threshing floor by way of gleaning with a broom and so on. Hence it is said, 'Even one who... gleans...' By this—that is, by the mention of a hundred thousand thousand-sacrificers—the almsfood for ten million bhikkhus is shown. The word 'given' should be supplied for the construction. Or, 'the almsfood of ten million kahāpaṇas' means the almsfood prepared by disbursing ten million kahāpaṇas. This gift of a hundred thousand thousand-sacrificers amounts to this much; so it is said. 'Even while gleaning' means: having gleaned, or because of the act of gleaning. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases. 'While supporting his wife, he practices the Dhamma,' and 'while giving from what little he has, he practices the Dhamma'—this is the construction. 'Of such a one' means: of such a person who practices the Dhamma in that way, that practice of Dhamma—not even a fraction of it do these thousand-sacrificers equal with their thousand-sacrificing. 'What is given by that poor man,' etc., is the explanation of that same meaning. 'Of all of them' means: of all of those who are spoken of as 'a hundred thousand thousand-sacrificers.' 'Of others' means: of others than the person spoken of as 'of such a one.' 'A gift of ten crore-thousands' means a gift counted as ten crores, which, due to its division into many thousands, is a thousand-gift.

“Kalaṃ nagghatī”ti idaṃ tesaṃ dānato imassa dānassa uḷāratarabhāvena vipulatarabhāvena vipulataraphalatāya vuttanti āha “kathaṃ nu kho etaṃ mahapphalataranti jānanattha”nti. Paccayavisesena mahattaṃ gatoti mahaggato, uḷāroti attho. Tenāha “vipulassetaṃ vevacana”nti. Samenāti ñāyena, dhammenāti attho. Visameti na same macchariyalakkhaṇappatte. Chetvāti pīḷetvā. Taṃ pana pīḷanaṃ pothananti dassento “pothetvā”ti āha. Assumukhāti tintaassumukhasammissā paraṃ rodāpetvā. Mahādānanti yathāvuttaṃ bahudeyyadhammassa pariccajanena mahantadānaṃ. Uppattiyā aparisuddhatāyāti ajjhāsayassa deyyadhammagavesanāya ca suddhatāya malīnattā. Itaraṃ dhammacariyāya nibbattitadānaṃ. Parittadānanti parittassa deyyadhammassa vasena parittadānaṃ. Attano uppattiyā parisuddhatāyāti ajjhāsayassa deyyadhammagavesanāya ca visuddhatāya. Evantiādimāhāti “evaṃ sahassānaṃ sahassayāgina”nti avoca. Tattha sahassānanti sataṃsahassānaṃ. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ sataggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

'Is not worth a fraction'—this is said because this gift is more sublime, more abundant, and more fruitful than their gift, for the purpose of knowing, 'How then is this more fruitful?' 'Of great value' (mahaggato) means having become great through a distinction of conditions; the meaning is 'sublime.' Hence it is said, 'This is a synonym for abundant.' 'Justly' means by the right method, that is, righteously. 'Unjustly' means not justly, possessed of the characteristic of stinginess. 'Having cut' means having oppressed. To show that this oppression is striking, it is said, 'having struck.' 'With tearful faces' means having made others weep, mingled with wet, tearful faces. 'A great gift' means a great gift through the relinquishment of many things to be given, as was said. 'Due to the impurity of its origin' means because of the impurity of one's disposition and in seeking things to be given. The other is the gift produced by righteous conduct. 'A small gift' means a gift that is small on account of the smallness of the thing to be given. 'Due to the purity of its own origin' means because of the purity of one's disposition and in seeking things to be given. Thus he spoke, saying, 'Thus of a thousand thousand-sacrificers.' Therein, 'of a thousand' means 'of a hundred thousand.' The word 'hundred' was not included for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. The rest is as previously explained.

Maccharisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Macchari Sutta is completed.

3. Sādhusuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sādhu Sutta

33. Udānaṃ [V 1.0092] udānesīti pītivegena uggiritabbatāya udānaṃ uggiri uccāresi. Tayidaṃ yasmā pītisamuṭṭhāpitaṃ vacanaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “udāhāraṃ udāharī”ti[M 1.0104]. Yathā pana taṃ vacanaṃ “udāna”nti vuccati, taṃ dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saddhāyāti ettha ya-kāro hetuattho. Pariccāgacetanāya hi saddhā visesapaccayo assaddhassa tadabhāvato. Pi-saddo vuttatthasampiṇḍanattho. “Sāhū”ti padaṃ sādhusaddena samānatthaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathanti dānayuddhānaṃ vipakkhasabhāvāti adhippāyo. Etaṃ ubhayanti dānaṃ yuddhanti idaṃ dvayaṃ. Jīvitabhīrukoti jīvitavināsabhīruko. Khayabhīrukoti bhogakkhayassa bhīruko. Vadantoti jīvite sālayataṃ, tato eva yujjhane asamatthataṃ pavedento. Chejjanti hatthapādādichedo. Ussahantoti vīriyaṃ karonto. Evaṃ bhoge rakkhissāmīti tathā bhoge aparikkhīṇe karissāmīti. Vadantoti idha bhogesu lobhaṃ, tato eva dātuṃ asamatthataṃ pavedento. Evanti evaṃ jīvitabhoganirapekkhatāya dānañca yuddhañca samaṃ hoti. Saddhādisampannoti saddhādhammajīvitāvīmaṃsāsīlādiguṇasamannāgato. So hi deyyavatthuno parittakattā appakampi dadanto attano pana cittasampattiyā khettasampattiyā ca bahuṃ uḷārapuññaṃ pavaḍḍhento bahuvidhaṃ lobha-dosa-issā-macchariya-diṭṭhivicikicchādibhedaṃ tappaṭipakkhaṃ abhibhavati, tato eva ca taṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “maccheraṃ maddati”cceva vuttaṃ, tassa pana ujuvipaccanīkabhāvato.

33. He uttered an exclamation (udānaṃ udānesi) means: because it should be uttered with a surge of joy, he uttered and pronounced an exclamation. Since this is speech produced by joy, it is said, 'he uttered an utterance (udāhāraṃ udāharī).' To show how that speech is called an 'exclamation' (udāna), it is said, 'as indeed,' and so forth. Here, in 'saddhāya,' the 'ya' has the meaning of cause. For faith is a special condition for the intention to relinquish, because one without faith lacks it. The word 'pi' serves to summarize the stated meaning. The word 'sāhū' should be understood as synonymous with 'sādhu.' 'How?' The intention is that generosity and battle are of opposite natures. 'Both' refers to these two: generosity and battle. 'Fearful of life' means fearful of the loss of life. 'Fearful of loss' means fearful of the depletion of wealth. By 'saying,' it means declaring their attachment to life and, because of that, their inability to fight. 'Cut off' means the severing of hands, feet, etc. 'Strive' means making an effort. Thus, by saying, 'We will protect our wealth' and 'We will make our wealth inexhaustible,' they declare their greed for wealth and, consequently, their inability to give. Thus, through indifference toward life and wealth, generosity and battle are equal. 'Endowed with faith and other such qualities' means possessing qualities such as faith, righteous living, investigation, morality, and so on. For even when giving little due to the scarcity of offerings, such a person, through the excellence of their mind and the field of merit, greatly increases abundant, noble merit, overcoming various opposing states such as greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, wrong views, and doubt. Hence, it becomes greatly fruitful and of great benefit. In the commentary, however, it is simply stated, 'he crushes stinginess,' due to its being the direct opponent.

Paratthāti paraloke. Ekasāṭakabrāhmaṇavatthu anvayavasena, aṅkuravatthu byatirekavasena vitthāretabbaṃ.

By 'in the next world' (parattha), it means in the other world. The story of the single-cloth Brahmin should be elaborated by way of positive example, and the story of Aṅkura by way of negative example.

Dhammo laddho etenāti dhammaladdho, puggalo. Aggiāhitapadassa viya saddasiddhi daṭṭhabbā. “Uṭṭhānanti kāyikaṃ vīriyaṃ, vīriyanti cetasika”nti vadanti. Uṭṭhānanti bhoguppāde yuttapayuttatā. Vīriyanti tajjo ussāho. Yamassa āṇāpavattiṭṭhānaṃ. Vetaraṇimpi itare niraye ca atikkamma. Te pana abbudādīnaṃ vasena avīciṃ dasadhā katvā avasesamahāniraye sattapi āyuppamāṇabhedena tayo tayo katvā ekatiṃsāti vadanti. Sañjīvādinirayasaṃvattanassa kammassa tikkhamajjhamudubhāvena tassa āyuppamāṇassa tividhatā vibhāvetabbā. Apare pana “aṭṭha mahānirayā soḷasa ussadanirayā ādito cattāro sitaniraye ekaṃ katvā satta sitanirayāti evaṃ ekatiṃsa mahānirayā”ti [M 1.0105] vadanti. Mahānirayaggahaṇato ādito cattāro sitanirayā eko nirayo katoti.

The Dhamma is obtained through this, thus 'dhammaladdho,' a person. The grammatical derivation should be understood like that of the word 'aggiāhita.' 'Exertion is physical energy, energy is mental,' they say. Exertion refers to being properly engaged in the production of wealth. Energy is the effort born of that engagement. That is the place where Yama's commands are issued. Having crossed the Vetaraṇī and the other hells as well. They say that, having divided Avīci into ten parts based on Abbuda and so forth, and having made the remaining seven great hells into three each according to differences in lifespan, there are thirty-one. The threefold nature of its lifespan should be understood as being due to the strong, medium, and weak nature of the kamma that leads to rebirth in the Sañjīva hell and so forth. Others, however, say: 'There are eight great hells, sixteen Ussada hells; from the beginning, the four cold hells are made into one, thus there are seven cold hells—in this way, there are thirty-one great hells.' Because of the inclusion of the great hells, the four cold hells from the beginning are made into one hell.

Tesanti [V 1.0093] vicinitvā gahitapaccayānaṃ. Pañcanavutipāsaṇḍabhedā papañcasūdanisaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbā. Tatthāti tesu dvīsu vicinanesu. Dakkhiṇāvicinanaṃ āha, upamānāni hi nāma yāvadeva upameyyatthavibhāvanatthāni. Etena sukhettagahaṇatopi dakkhiṇeyyavicinanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By 'for those' (tesaṃ), it means for those whose requisites have been accepted after examination. The ninety-five sectarian divisions should be understood in the way described in the Papañcasūdanī commentary. By 'therein' (tattha), it means in these two examinations. He speaks of the examination of offerings; for similes are indeed only for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of that which is to be compared. By this, from the taking of the 'good field,' the examination of worthy recipients should also be understood.

Pāṇesu saṃyamoti iminā dasavidhampi kusalakammapathadhammaṃ dasseti. Yathā hi “pāṇesu saṃyamo”ti iminā sattānaṃ jīvitāvoropanato saṃyamo vutto, evaṃ tesaṃ sāpateyyāvahārato paradārāmasanato visaṃvādanato aññamaññabhedanato pharusavacanena saṅghaṭṭanato niratthakavippalapanato parasantakābhijjhānato ucchedacintanato micchābhinivesanato ca saṃyamo hotīti. Tenāha “sīlānisaṃsaṃ kathetumāraddhā”ti. Pharusavacanasaṃyamo panettha sarūpeneva vutto.

By 'restraint towards living beings,' the tenfold wholesome course of action is shown.
