Just as 'restraint towards living beings' refers to restraint from depriving beings of life, so too is there restraint from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, from idle chatter, from covetousness for others' possessions, from ill will, and from wrong views. Therefore, it is said: 'He began to speak of the benefits of virtue.' Here, restraint from harsh speech is stated in its own form.

Parassa upavādabhayenāti pāpakiriyahetu parena attano vattabbaupavādabhayena. Upavādabhayāti upavādabhayanimittaṃ. “Kathaṃ nu kho amhe pare na upavadeyyu”nti āsīsantā pāpaṃ na karonti. Dhammapadamevāti asaṅkhatadhammakoṭṭhāso eva seyyo seṭṭho. Yasmā sabbasaṅkhataṃ aniccaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammaṃ, tasmā tadadhigamāya ussāho karaṇīyoti dasseti. Pubbasaddo kālavisesavisayoti āha “pubbe ca kassapabuddhādikālepī”tiādi. Puna akālaviseso apāṭiyekko bhummatthavisayovāti āha “sabbepi vā”tiādi. Tattha sabbepi vāti ete sabbepi kassapabuddhādayo lokanāthā santo nāma vūpasantasabbakilesasantāpā santasabbhūtaguṇattā.

By 'out of fear of others' blame,' it means out of fear of reproach to be spoken by others because of one's own evil doing. By 'fear of blame,' it means the cause consisting of fear of blame. Wishing, 'How might others not blame us?' they do not commit evil. By 'the Dhamma-path itself,' it means just the unconditioned element of the Dhamma is better, superior. Because all conditioned things are impermanent, have the nature of decay, have the nature of vanishing, have the nature of dispassion, have the nature of cessation, he shows that effort should therefore be made to realize that. The word 'before' refers to a specific time, as he said, 'even in the time of Kassapa Buddha and the like,' and so on. Again, it is not specific to time but is general, referring to the meaning of the locative case, as he said, 'or all indeed,' and so forth. There, 'all indeed' means all those lords of the world, Kassapa Buddha and the like, are peaceful, namely, those whose fever of all defilements is quenched, possessing the quality of being peaceful to all beings.

Sādhusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sādhu Sutta is concluded.

4. Nasantisuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Nāsanti Sutta

34. Kamanīyānīti [M 1.0106] kantāni. Tato eva etāni iṭṭhārammaṇāni sukhārammaṇāni rūpādīni, te pana vatthukāmā, tadārammaṇakilesakāmā vā. “Na santi kāmā manujesū”ti desanāsīsametaṃ, nicchayena kāmā aniccāyeva. Maccu dhīyati etthāti maccudheyyaṃ. Na puna āgacchati ettha taṃ apunāgamanaṃ. Apunāgamanasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ anupagacchanato. Nibbānaṃ hītiādi vuttassevatthassa vivaraṇaṃ. Baddhoti paṭibaddhacitto. Pamattoti vossaggapamādaṃ āpanno.

34. 'Kamanīyāni' means desirable. From that very fact, these forms and so forth are agreeable objects, pleasant objects; but these are either sensual objects (vatthukāmā) or defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāmā) related to those objects. 'There are no sensual pleasures among humans' is the main point of this teaching; for sensual pleasures are certainly impermanent. 'Death is placed here,' thus it is the 'realm of death' (maccudheyyaṃ). That state of not returning here again is 'non-returning.' [One remains in the realm of death] because of not attaining Nibbāna, which is designated as 'non-returning.' 'Nibbāna is...' etc., is an elaboration of the meaning already stated. 'Bound' means with an attached mind. 'Heedless' means one who has fallen into the heedlessness of abandonment.

Taṇhāchandato [V 1.0094] jātaṃ tassa visesapaccayattā. Icchitaṃ hanatīti aghaṃ, dukkhaṃ. Idha pana anavasesapariyādānavasena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhanti. Chandavinayā aghavinayoti hetunirodhena hi phalanirodho, evaṃ saupādisesanibbānaṃ vatvā aghavinayā dukkhavinayoti anupādisesanibbānaṃ vadati.

Born from craving and desire, due to its being a specific condition for it. 'It destroys what is desired' (icchitaṃ hanati), thus it is 'misery' (aghaṃ), that is, suffering. Here, however, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering in the sense of being completely and unreservedly consumed. 'The subduing of desire is the subduing of misery' means that by the cessation of the cause, there is cessation of the result; thus, having spoken of Nibbāna with residue, he speaks of Nibbāna without residue as 'the subduing of misery, the subduing of suffering.'

Citrānīti kilesakāmāpi vedanādiṭṭhisampayogabhedena honti, ākārabhedena ca atthi savighātāvighātāti tato visesetuṃ “ārammaṇacittānī”ti vuttaṃ. Saṅkappitarāgoti subhādivasena saṅkappitavatthumhi rāgo. Kilesakāmo kāmoti vutto tassevidha visesato kāmabhāvasiddhito. Pasūrasuttena vibhāvetabbo “na te kāmā”tiādinā tassa vatthumhi āgatattā. Idāni tamatthaṃ saṅkhepeneva vibhāvento “pasūraparibbājako hī”tiādimāha. Na te kāmā yāni citrāni loketi te ce kāmā na honti, yāni loke citrāni rūpādiārammaṇāni. Vedesīti kevalaṃ saṅkapparāgañca kāmaṃ katvā vadesi ce. Hehintīti bhaveyyunti attho. Suṇanto saddāni manoramāni, satthāpi te hehiti kāmabhogīti paccekaṃ gāthā, idha pana saṃkhipitvā dassitā. Dhīrā nāma dhitisampannāti āha “paṇḍitā”ti.

‘Diverse’ (citrāni): even defilement-desires (kilesakāmā) are distinguished by their association with feelings, views, and so forth, and by their mode, there being those with and without vexation; to distinguish them from that, it is said ‘diverse sense-objects’ (ārammaṇacittāni). ‘Lust of thought’ (saṅkapparāgo) means lust for an object conceived as beautiful, and so forth. Defilement-desire is called ‘desire’ (kāma) because its nature as desire is specifically established here. This should be clarified by the Pasūra Sutta, beginning with ‘Those are not desires,’ as it is found in that text. Now, explaining that meaning briefly, he says, ‘the wanderer Pasūra,’ and so on. ‘Those are not desires, which are diverse in the world’ means: those diverse objects in the world, such as forms and so forth, are not desires. ‘You declare’ (vedesi) means: if you say, having made mere lust of thought into desire. ‘Would be’ (hehinti) means ‘they would be.’ ‘Hearing delightful sounds, the Teacher too would be an enjoyer of sensual pleasures’—these are separate verses, but here they are shown in summary. The wise (dhīrā) are so called because they are endowed with fortitude (dhiti); for this he says ‘the learned’ (paṇḍitā).

Tassāti yo pahīnakodhamāno sabbaso saṃyojanātigo nāmarūpasmiṃ asajjanto rāgādikiñcanarahito, tassa. Mogharājā nāma thero bāvarībrāhmaṇassa paricārakānaṃ soḷasannaṃ aññataro. Yathānusandhiṃ appatto sāvasesa-attho, kiñci vattabbaṃ atthīti adhippāyo[M 1.0107]. Sabbaso vimuttattāva devamanussā namassanti, ye taṃ paṭipajjanti. Tesaṃ kiṃ hoti? Kiñcipi na siyāti ayamettha atthaviseso? Dasabalaṃ sandhāyevamāha ukkaṭṭhaniddesena. Anupaṭipattiyāti paṭipattiṃ anugantvā paṭipajjanena. Namassanti taṃ pūjenti.

‘To him’ (tassa) means to him who has abandoned anger and pride, has completely gone beyond all fetters, is not clinging to name-and-form, and is free from impediments such as lust. The elder named Mogharājā was one of the sixteen attendants of the brahmin Bāvarī. ‘Not having reached the proper connection’ (yathānusandhiṃ appatto) means the meaning is incomplete; the intention is that there is something more to be said. Because he is entirely liberated, gods and humans venerate him. As for those who undertake that practice, what becomes of them? Is the special meaning here that nothing at all would happen? Referring to the Ten-Powered One, he speaks thus with an exalted designation. ‘By following the practice’ (anupaṭipattiyā) means by practicing in accordance with the path. ‘They venerate him’ (namassanti) means they honor him.

Catusaccadhammaṃ jānitvāti tena paṭividdhaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivijjhitvā. Tathā ca buddhasubuddhatāya nibbematikā hontīti āha “vicikicchaṃ pahāyā”ti. Tato paraṃ pana anukkamena aggamaggādhigamena saṅgātigāpi honti. Asekkhadhammapāripūriyā pasaṃsiyā viññūnaṃ pasaṃsāpi hontīti.

‘Having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths’ means having penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths that was penetrated by him. Thus, because of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, they become free from doubt; hence it is said, ‘having abandoned doubt.’ Furthermore, by successively attaining the highest path, they also transcend attachment. By perfecting the qualities of the non-learner, they become praiseworthy and are also praised by the wise.

Nasantisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nāsanti Sutta is concluded.

5. Ujjhānasaññisuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Ujjhānasaññi Sutta

35. Ujjhānavasena [V 1.0095] pavattā saññā etesaṃ atthi, ujjhānavasena vā sañjānantīti ujjhānasaññī. Kārayeti katānaṃ pariyantaṃ kārayeti attho. Pariyantakāritanti paricchinnakāritaṃ parimitavacananti attho. Paṃsukūlādipaṭipakkhanayena pattuṇṇadukulādi vuttaṃ. Nāmaṃ gahitanti etena “ujjhānasaññikā”ti ettha ka-saddo saññāyanti dasseti.

35. ‘Ujjhānasaññī’ means one for whom there is perception that proceeds by way of fault-finding, or one who perceives by way of fault-finding. ‘Kārayeti’ means to cause what has been done to reach its limit. ‘Pariyantakāritaṃ’ means causing it to be clearly defined, meaning limited speech. By way of being the opposite of rag-robes and so forth, woolen cloth, fine linen, and so forth are mentioned. ‘The name is taken’ (nāmaṃ gahitaṃ): by this, it is shown that the syllable ‘ka’ in ‘ujjhānasaññikā’ is in the sense of perception (saññā).

Aññenākārena bhūtanti attanā pavediyamānākārato aññena asuddhena ākārena vijjamānaṃ upalabbhamānaṃ attānaṃ. Vañcetvāti palambhetvā. Tassa kuhakassa. Taṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ paribhuñjanaṃ. Parijānantīti tassa paṭipattiṃ paricchijja jānanti. Kārakoti sammāpaṭipattiyā kattā, sammāpaṭipajjitāti attho.

‘Existing in another way’ (Aññenākārena bhūtaṃ) means one’s self existing or being found in an impure manner, different from the manner declared by oneself. ‘Deceiving’ (Vañcetvā) means deluding. ‘Of that deceiver’ (Tassa kuhakassa). This refers to that person's enjoyment of the four requisites. ‘They fully understand’ (Parijānanti) means they discern and know his practice. ‘The doer’ (Kārako) means the one who acts with right practice; the meaning is, one who has practiced rightly.

Idanti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ, ayanti attho. Dhammānudhammapaṭipadāti nibbānadhammassa anucchavikatāya anudhammabhūtā paṭipadā. Paṭipakkhavidhamane asithilatāya daḷhā. Bhāsitamattena ca savanamattena cāti ettha ca-saddo visesanivattiattho. Tena bhāsitassa sutassa ca sammāpaṭipattivisesaṃ nivatteti. Lokapariyāyanti lokassa parividhamanaṃ uppādanirodhavasena saṅkhārānaṃ parāvuttiṃ. Tenāha “saṅkhāralokassa udayabbaya”nti. Svāyamattho saccapaṭivedheneva hotīti āha “catusaccadhammañca aññāyā”ti[M 1.0108]. Evaṃ na kubbantīti attani vijjamānampi guṇaṃ anāvīkaronto “yathā tumhe vadatha, evaṃ na kubbantī”ti avijjamānataṃ byākarotīti attho.

‘This’ (Idaṃ) is said by way of gender inversion; the meaning is ‘this’ (ayaṃ). ‘Practice in accordance with the Dhamma’ (Dhammānudhammapaṭipadā) refers to the practice that is suitable for the Dhamma of Nibbāna, being a secondary Dhamma. It is firm due to being unyielding in destroying the opposing side. In ‘by mere speech and mere hearing,’ the word ‘and’ (ca) has the meaning of eliminating distinction. By that, it negates any special quality of right practice in what is merely spoken and heard. ‘The way of the world’ (Lokapariyāya) means the destruction of the world, that is, the turning around of conditioned phenomena by way of arising and cessation. Hence it is said, ‘the rise and fall of the conditioned world.’ This meaning is realized only through the penetration of the truths; thus it is said, ‘and having understood the Dhamma of the Four Truths.’ ‘Thus, they do not do’ (Evaṃ na kubbanti) means: not revealing even the virtue present in oneself, declaring its absence by saying, ‘I do not do as you say.’

Akārakamevāti dosaṃ akārakameva. Accayassa paṭiggaṇhanaṃ nāma adhivāsanaṃ, evaṃ so desakena desiyamāno tato vigato nāma hoti. Tenāha “paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatū”ti.

‘Only a non-doer’ (Akārakameva) means the fault is only a non-doer. ‘Accepting the transgression’ (Accayassa paṭiggaṇhanaṃ) means forbearance; thus, being admonished by the instructor, he is said to be rid of it. Therefore, it was said, ‘Let him accept’ (paṭiggaṇhātu) means ‘let him forgive’ (khamatu).

Sabhāvenāti sabhāvato. Ekasadisanti paresaṃ cittācāraṃ jānantampi ajānantehi saha ekasadisaṃ karontā. Paratoti pacchā. Kathāya uppannāyāti “kassaccayā na vijjantī”tiādikathāya pavattamānāya “tathāgatassa buddhassā”tiādinā buddhabalaṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ dīpetvā. Khamissāmīti accayadesanaṃ paṭiggaṇhissāmi. Tappaṭiggaho hi idha khamananti adhippetaṃ, satthā pana sabbakālaṃ khamo eva.

‘By nature’ (Sabhāvena) means by intrinsic quality. ‘Equal in one respect’ (Ekasadisaṃ) means making oneself one and the same with those who do not know the conduct of others’ minds, even though one knows it. ‘Later’ (Parato) means afterward. ‘When a discussion arises’ (Kathāya uppannāya) means during the discussion which began with ‘whose offenses do not exist,’ etc., having revealed the Buddha’s power and majesty with phrases like ‘of the Tathāgata, the Buddha.’ ‘I will forgive’ (Khamissāmi) means I will accept the confession of the transgression. For here, acceptance of that is intended as forgiveness, but the Teacher is always forgiving.

Kopo [V 1.0096] antare citte etassāti kopantaro. Doso garu garukātabbo assāti dosagaru. “Paṭimuccatī”ti vā pāṭho, ayameva attho. Accāyikakammanti sahasā anupadhāretvā kiriyā. No cidhāti no ce idha. Idhāti nipātamattaṃ. Apagataṃ apanītaṃ. Doso no ce siyā, tena pariyāyena yadi aparādho nāma na bhaveyyāti. Na sammeyyuṃ na vūpasameyyuṃ. Kusaloti anavajjo.

‘One whose anger is internal’ (Kopantaro) means anger is in the inner mind of this one. ‘One for whom the fault is grave’ (Dosagaru) means the fault is grave, it should be taken gravely by him. Alternatively, the reading ‘he is released’ (Paṭimuccati) conveys the same meaning. ‘Urgent action’ (Accāyikakammaṃ) means acting hastily without deliberation. ‘Not if here’ (No cidhā) means ‘not if here’ (no ce idha); ‘here’ (idha) is just a particle. ‘Gone away, removed’ (Apagataṃ apanītaṃ): if there were no fault, by that means, if no such thing as an offense existed. ‘They would not be calmed, they would not subside.’ ‘Skillful’ (Kusalo) means blameless.

Dhīro satoti padadvayena vaṭṭachindaṃ āha. Ko niccameva paṇḍito nāmāti atthoti “kassaccayā”tiādikāya pucchāgāthāya attho. Dīghamajjhimasaṃvaṇṇanāsu tathāgata-saddo vitthārato saṃvaṇṇitoti āha “evamādīhi kāraṇehi tathāgatassā”ti. Buddhattādīhīti ādi-saddena “bodhetā pajāyā”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97) niddese āgatakāraṇāni saṅgayhanti. Vimokkhaṃ vuccati ariyamaggo, tassa anto aggaphalaṃ, tattha bhavā paṇṇatti, tassā vasena. Evaṃ buddhabalaṃ dīpeti. Idāni khittaṃ saṅkhepena saṃharāpitaṃ hotīti dasseti.

By the two words ‘wise’ (dhīro) and ‘mindful’ (sato), he speaks of the cutter of the round of existence. The meaning of the question verse beginning with ‘Whose transgressions...?’ (kassaccayā) is: ‘Who is always called wise?’ In the long and middle-length commentaries, the word ‘Tathāgata’ is extensively explained; hence it is said, ‘For such reasons of the Tathāgata,’ etc. By ‘Buddhahood and so on’ (Buddhattādīhi), the reasons mentioned in the exposition beginning with ‘awakener of beings’ (Mahāni. 192; Cūḷani. Pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97) are included. The Noble Path is called liberation; its end is the highest fruit, and the designation arises there, by means of that. Thus, the power of the Buddha is revealed. Now, it shows that what was scattered has been briefly collected.

Ujjhānasaññisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ujjhānasaññisutta is concluded.

6. Saddhāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Saddhāsutta

36. Tatvassāti [M 1.0109] o-kārassa va-kārādesaṃ a-kārassa ca lopaṃ katvā niddesoti āha “tato assā”ti. “Tatassā”ti vā pāṭho, tatoti ca saddhāhetūti attho. Nānupatantīti na vattanti. Pamādaṃ karontīti pamajjanti, micchā paṭipajjantīti attho. Lakkhaṇānīti aniccādilakkhaṇāni. Upanijjhāyatīti upecca ñāṇacakkhunā pekkhati, anupassatīti attho. Āgatakiccanti āhatakiccaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Sādhetīti asammohapaṭivedhavasena nipphādeti, tathalakkhaṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ upanijjhāyatīti ayamattho maggepi vattabbo tena vinā asammohapaṭivedhassa asambhavato. Kasiṇārammaṇassāti idaṃ lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Akasiṇārammaṇasamāpattiyopi hi santīti. Yathā ca kasiṇārammaṇāni aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ avasesānañca tadārammaṇānaṃ paccavekkhaṇavasena cittānaṃ, evaṃ tena tāni ārammaṇāni gahitānīti “kasiṇārammaṇassa”icceva vuttaṃ. Paramaṃ uttamaṃ sukhanti vattabbato paramasukhaṃ arahattaṃ.

36. ‘Tatvassāti’—by substituting ‘va’ for ‘o’ and eliding ‘a,’ the explanation is given as ‘tato assā.’ Alternatively, the reading ‘tatassā’ is also possible, where ‘tato’ means ‘due to faith.’ ‘Nānupatanti’ means they do not occur. ‘Pamādaṃ karonti’ means they are negligent, meaning they act wrongly. ‘Lakkhaṇāni’ refers to characteristics such as impermanence. ‘Upanijjhāyati’ means observing closely with the eye of wisdom, contemplating, meaning observing repeatedly. ‘Āgatakicca’ means a task that has been brought about; or this is the reading. ‘Sādheti’ means he accomplishes it by way of the penetration of non-delusion. The meaning is that he contemplates the characteristic of cessation, which is the truth of cessation; this meaning should also be stated regarding the path, for without it, the penetration of non-delusion is impossible. ‘Kasiṇārammaṇassa’—this is a term denoting a characteristic. For even attainments without kasiṇa objects exist. Just as the kasiṇa objects are the objects of the eight attainments and of the remaining minds by way of reviewing those objects, so too are those objects grasped by him—hence ‘kasiṇārammaṇassa’ is said. ‘Paramaṃ uttamaṃ sukha’—because it should be said that the highest happiness is arahantship.

Saddhāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saddhāsutta is concluded.

7. Samayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Samayasutta

37. Udānaṃ [V 1.0097] paṭiccāti ukkākaraññā jātisambhedaparihāranimittaṃ attano vaṃsaparisuddhaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ pītiudāhāraṃ paṭicca gottavasena “sakkā”ti laddhanāmānaṃ. Yadi ekopi janapado, kathaṃ bahuvacananti āha “ruḷhīsaddenā”ti. Akkharacintikā hi īdisesu ṭhānesu yutte viya saliṅgavacanāni icchanti, ayamettha ruḷhī yathā “avantī kurū”ti, tabbisesane pana janapadasadde jātisaddatāya ekavacanameva. Aropimeti kenaci na ropime.

37. ‘On account of an inspired utterance’ (Udānaṃ paṭicca): This refers to those who obtained the name ‘Sakyas’ by lineage, on account of an utterance of joy spoken, relying on the purity of their own lineage, as a sign for avoiding the mixing of castes by King Ukkāka. If it is one country, how is the plural used? He says, ‘by a conventional term’ (ruḷhīsaddena). For grammarians, in such cases, prefer words agreeing in gender and number, as in ‘Avantī, Kurū.’ However, when specifying, the word ‘janapada’ as a class noun is only in the singular. ‘Aropime’ means it should not be attributed by anyone.

Āvaraṇenāti setunā. Bandhāpetvāti paṇḍupalāsapāsāṇamattikakhaṇḍādīhi āliṃ thiraṃ kārāpetvā. Sassāni kārentīti jeṭṭhamāse kira ghammassa balavabhāvena himavante himaṃ vilīyitvā sanditvā anukkamena rohiṇiṃ nadiṃ pavisati, taṃ bandhitvā sassāni kārenti. “Jātiṃ [M 1.0110] ghaṭṭetvā kalahaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsū”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “koliyakammakarā vadantī”ti āha. Niyuttaamaccānanti tasmiṃ sassaparipālanakamme niyojitamahāmattānaṃ.

‘By a barrier’ (Āvaraṇena) means by a dam. ‘Having had it dammed’ (Bandhāpetvā) means having caused a strong embankment to be built with dry leaves, stones, lumps of clay, and so forth. ‘They cultivate crops’ (Sassāni kārenti): it is said that in the month of Jeṭṭha, due to the intense heat, the snow melts in the Himalayas, flows down, and gradually enters the Rohiṇī River, and having dammed it, they cultivate crops. To make the briefly stated meaning of ‘Stirring up lineage pride, they increased the quarrel’ clearer, he said, ‘The Koliyan laborers say...’ ‘Of the appointed ministers’ (Niyuttaamaccānaṃ) refers to the high officials assigned to the task of managing those crops.

Tīṇi jātakānīti “kuṭhārihattho puriso”tiādinā phandanajātakaṃ (jā. 1.13.14 ādayo) “duddubhāyati bhaddante”tiādinā duddubhajātakaṃ, (jā. 1.4.85 ādayo) “vandāmi taṃ kuñjarā”tiādinā laṭukikajātakanti (jā. 1.5.39 ādayo) imāni tīṇi jātakāni. Dve jātakānīti –

‘Three birth stories’ (Tīṇi jātakāni): ‘A man with an axe in hand,’ and so forth, refers to the Phandana Jātaka (Jā. 1.13.14 ff.); ‘There is a ‘dud-dubha’ sound, venerable sir,’ and so forth, refers to the Duddubha Jātaka (Jā. 1.4.85 ff.); ‘I salute you, O elephant,’ and so forth, refers to the Laṭukika Jātaka (Jā. 1.5.39 ff.)—these are the three birth stories. ‘Two birth stories’ (Dve jātakāni):—

“Sādhu sambahulā ñātī, api rukkhā araññajā;

Vāto vahati ekaṭṭhaṃ, brahantampi vanappati”nti. –

“Good are many relatives, even trees born in the forest; the wind overthrows even a great forest tree.”

Ādinā rukkhadhammajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.74).

By this beginning, this refers to the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka (Jā. 1.1.74).

“Sammodamānā gacchanti, jālamādāya pakkhino;

Yadā te vivadissanti, tadā ehinti me vasa”nti. (jā. 1.1.33) –

“Birds go together harmoniously, carrying the net; when they quarrel, then they will come into my power.” (Jā. 1.1.33)

Ādinā sammodamānajātakanti imāni dve jātakāni.

By this beginning, this refers to the Sammodamāna Jātaka. These are the two Jātakas.

“Attadaṇḍā [V 1.0098] bhayaṃ jātaṃ, janaṃ passatha medhagaṃ;

Saṃvegaṃ kittayissāmi, yathā saṃvijitaṃ mayā”ti. (su. ni. 941) –

“Fear is born of wielding the rod; look at people fighting. I will tell of the agitation, as it was felt by me.” (Su. ni. 941)

Ādinā attadaṇḍasuttaṃ.

By this beginning, this refers to the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

Tenāti bhagavatā. Kalahakaraṇabhāvoti kalahakaraṇassa atthibhāvo. Mahāpathaviyā mahagghe khattiye kasmā nāsethāti dassetvā kalahaṃ vūpasametukāmo bhagavā pathaviṃ nidassanabhāvena gaṇhīti dassento “pathavī nāma kiṃ agghatī”tiādimāha. Aṭṭhāneti akāraṇe. Veraṃ katvāti virodhaṃ uppādetvā. Taṃtaṃpalobhanakiriyāya parakkamantiyo “ukkaṇṭhantū”ti sāsanaṃ pesenti. Kuṇāladaheti kuṇāladahatīre patiṭṭhāya. Pucchitaṃ kathesi anukkamena kuṇālasakuṇarājassa pucchāpasaṅgena kuṇālajātakaṃ (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) kathessāmīti. Anabhiratiṃ vinodesi itthīnaṃ dosadassanamukhena kāmānaṃ ādīnavokārasaṃkilesavibhāvanavasena. Purisapurisehīti kosajjaṃ viddhaṃsetvā purisathāmabrūhanena uttamapurisehi no bhavituṃ vaṭṭatīti uppannacittā[M 1.0111]. Avissaṭṭhasamaṇakammantā apariccattakammaṭṭhānābhiyogāti attho. Nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatīti bhagavā cintesīti yojanā.

'Tena' means by the Blessed One. 'Kalahakaraṇabhāva' means the existence of quarrelsomeness. Wishing to pacify the quarrel, the Blessed One, having shown, 'Why should you destroy the great Kshatriyas over the great earth?', took the earth as an illustration, saying, 'What is the earth worth?' and so forth. 'Aṭṭhāne' means for no reason. 'Veraṃ katvā' means having stirred up opposition. Those striving to tempt others with various allurements send the message, 'Let them become discontented!' 'Kuṇāladahe' means having stood on the shore of the Kuṇālada Lake. He spoke what was asked; in due course, in connection with the question about Kuṇāla, the king of birds, he would narrate the Kuṇāla Jātaka (Jā. 2.21. Kuṇāla Jātaka). He dispelled discontent by way of showing the faults of women, explaining the dangers, drawbacks, and defilements of sensual pleasures. 'Purisapurisehi' refers to those who, having dispelled laziness and strengthened manly vigor, were of the mind that it is not fitting to be inferior to the best of men. 'Avissaṭṭhasamaṇakammantā' means unrelinquished application to meditation subjects. 'Nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati' means 'It is fitting to sit down'—this is the connection, meaning the Blessed One thought this.

Paduminiyanti padumavane. Vikasiṃsu guṇagaṇavibodhena. Ayaṃ imassa…pe… na kathesīti iminā sabbepi te bhikkhū tāvadeva paṭipāṭiyā āgatattā aññamaññassa lajjamānā attanā paṭiladdhavisesaṃ bhagavato nārocesunti dasseti. Khīṇāsavānantiādinā tattha kāraṇamāha.

'Paduminiyaṃ' means in the lotus forest. They blossomed with the awakening of their virtues. By 'This one... and so forth... did not speak,' it is shown that all those monks, having arrived in due order and feeling ashamed before one another, did not reveal to the Blessed One the special attainment they had gained. The reason for this is stated there, beginning with 'Those whose taints are destroyed,' and so forth.

Osaṭamatteti bhagavato santikaṃ upagatamatte. Ariyamaṇḍaleti ariyapuggalasamūhe. Pācīnayugandharaparikkhepatoti yugandharapabbatassa pācīnaparikkhepato, na bāhirakehi vuccamānaudayapabbatato. Rāmaṇeyyakadassanatthanti buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitattā visesato ramaṇīyassa lokassa ramaṇīyabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Ullaṅghitvāti uṭṭhahitvā. Evarūpe khaṇe laye muhutteti yathāvutte candamaṇḍalassa uṭṭhitakkhaṇe uṭṭhitavelāyaṃ uṭṭhitamuhutteti uparūparikālassa vaḍḍhitabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Osaṭamatte' means just as they came near the Blessed One. 'Ariyamaṇḍale' refers to the assembly of noble individuals. 'Pācīnayugandharaparikkhepato' means from the eastern boundary of Mount Yugandhara, not from Mount Udaya as it is called by outsiders. 'Rāmaṇeyyakadassanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of seeing the charming nature of the world, which is especially charming because it is adorned by the arising of a Buddha. 'Ullaṅghitvā' means having risen up. 'Evarūpe khaṇe laye muhutte' means at such a moment, at such a time, at such an instant. This was said to show the progressive increase of the successive periods of time, referring to the moment the moon's disk arose, the time of its rising, and the instant of its rising, as has been stated.

Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ jātiādivasena bhagavato anurūpaparivārabhāvaṃ dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Mahāsammatassa vaṃse uppannotiādi kulavaṃsasuddhidassanaṃ. Khattiyagabbhe jātoti idaṃ satipi jātivisuddhiyaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ vasena avisuddhatā siyāti tesampi “avisuddhatā natthi imesa”nti [V 1.0099] visuddhidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Satipi ca gabbhavisuddhiyaṃ katadosena missakattā arajjārahatāpi siyāti “tampi natthi imesa”nti dassanatthaṃ “rājapabbajitā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

To show that those monks were a suitable retinue for the Blessed One by way of birth and so forth, he said, 'therein,' and so forth. 'Born in the lineage of Mahāsammata,' and so forth, shows the purity of family lineage. 'Born in a Khattiya womb'—this was said to show their purity, for even though there is purity of birth, there might be impurity on account of the parents, and to show that 'for these there is no such impurity.' And even though there is purity of the womb, they might be unworthy of kingship because of being associated with one who has committed an offense; to show that 'that too is not the case for them,' 'those who have gone forth from royal families,' and so forth, is stated.

Sāmantāti samīpe. Caliṃsūti uṭṭhahiṃsu. Kosamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ saddantaraṃ, “saddasavanaṭṭhānameva saddantara”nti apare. Tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesūti jambudīpe kira ādito mahantāni tesaṭṭhi nagarasahassāni uppannāni, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyāha “tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesū”ti. Tāni pana sampiṇḍetvā satasahassato paraṃ navasahassādhikāni asītisahassāni. Navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesūti navasatasahassādhikesu [M 1.0112] navutisatasahassesu doṇamukhesu. Doṇamukhanti ca mahānagarassa āyuppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pādanagaraṃ vuccati. Chanavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesūti chakoṭisatasahassaadhikesu navutikoṭisatasahassapaṭṭanesu. Tambapaṇṇidīpādichapaṇṇāsāya ratanākaresu. Evaṃ pana nagara-doṇamukhapaṭṭana-ratanākarādibhāvena kathanaṃ taṃtaṃadhivatthāya vasantīnaṃ tāsaṃ devatānaṃ bahubhāvadassanatthaṃ. Yadi dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā sannipatitā. Atha kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “dasahi ca lokadhātūhī”ti? Vuttanti āha “dasasahassa…pe… adhippeta”nti. Tena sahassilokadhātu idha “ekā lokadhātū”ti veditabbā.

'Sāmanta' means in the vicinity. 'Caliṃsu' means they arose. 'Saddantara' is a place at the distance of a kosa; others say, 'a saddantara is simply a place where sound can be heard.' 'Tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesu' refers to the sixty-three thousand great cities that first arose in Jambudīpa, then a second time, and a third time. Referring to this, he said, 'thrice sixty-three thousand cities.' However, when combined, they total one hundred and eighty-nine thousand. 'Navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesu' refers to ninety-nine hundred thousand doṇamukha towns, meaning ninety hundred thousand doṇamukhas augmented by nine hundred thousand. A 'doṇamukha' is said to be a subordinate town that is the source of revenue and establishment for a great city. 'Chanavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesu' refers to ninety-six trillion paṭṭana cities, meaning ninety trillion paṭṭanas augmented by six trillion. In Tambapaṇṇi Island and the other fifty-six jewel mines. This description by way of cities, doṇamukha towns, paṭṭana cities, jewel mines, and so forth is for the purpose of showing the great number of those deities dwelling in those respective locations. If deities assembled from ten thousand world-systems, then why does the Pāli text say, 'from ten world-systems'? It is explained: 'Ten thousand... is intended.' Therefore, a thousand-fold world-system here should be understood as 'one world-system.'

Lohapāsādeti sabbapaṭhamakate lohapāsāde. Brahmaloketi heṭṭhime brahmaloke. Yadi tā devatā evaṃ nirantarā hutvā sannipatitā, pacchā āgatānaṃ okāso eva na bhaveyyāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yathā kho panā”tiādi.

'Lohapāsāde' refers to the brazen palace that was the very first to be built. 'Brahmaloke' refers to the lower Brahma world. Considering the objection that if those deities had gathered so densely, there would be no space left for those who arrived later, he said, 'But indeed...' and so forth.

Suddhāvāsakāye uppannā suddhāvāsakāyikā. Tāsaṃ pana yasmā suddhāvāsabhūmi nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “suddhāvāsavāsīna”nti. Āvāsāti āvāsaṭṭhānabhūtā. Devatā pana orambhāgiyānaṃ itaresañca saṃyojanānaṃ samucchinnaṭṭhena suddho āvāso vihāro etesanti suddhāvāsā. Mahāsamāgamaṃ ñatvāti mahāsamāgamaṃ gatāti ñatvā.

Those born in the Suddhāvāsa realm are called Suddhāvāsakāyikā. And since the Suddhāvāsa plane is their dwelling place, it is therefore said, 'of the dwellers of Suddhāvāsa.' 'Āvāsā' means being dwelling places. Moreover, the deities are called Suddhāvāsā because a pure dwelling and abode belong to them through the cutting off of the lower fetters and other fetters. 'Knowing the great assembly' (mahāsamāgamaṃ ñatvā) means having known that the great assembly had gathered.

Puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otari aññattha okāsaṃ alabhamāno. Evaṃ sesāpi. Maṇivammanti indanīlamaṇimayaṃ kavacaṃ. Buddhānaṃ abhimukhabhāgo buddhavīthi, sā yāva cakkavāḷā uttarituṃ na sakkā. Mahatiyā buddhavīthiyāvāti buddhānaṃ santikaṃ upasaṅkamantehi tehi devabrahmehi valañjitabuddhavīthiyāva.

He descended at the eastern edge of the world-sphere, finding no space elsewhere. So too the others. 'Maṇivamma' means an armor made of sapphire gems. The area facing the Buddhas is the Buddha-avenue, which cannot be traversed up to the world-sphere. 'By the great Buddha-avenue' (Mahatiyā buddhavīthiyā) means by the Buddha-avenue frequented by those gods and brahmas when approaching the presence of the Buddhas.

Samiti [V 1.0100] saṅgati sannipāto samayo, mahanto samayo mahāsamayoti āha “mahāsamūho”ti. Pavaddhaṃ vanaṃ pavananti āha “vanasaṇḍo”ti. Devaghaṭāti devasamūhā. Samādahaṃsūti samāhitaṃ lokuttarasamādhiṃ suṭṭhu appitaṃ akaṃsu. Tathā samāhitaṃ pana samādhinā niyojitaṃ nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “samādhinā yojesu”nti. Sabbesaṃ gomuttavaṅkādīnaṃ dūrasamussāritattā attano…pe… akariṃsu. Vinayati asse etehīti nettāni, yottāni. Avīthipaṭipannānaṃ assānaṃ vīthipaṭipādanaṃ rasmiggahaṇena hotīti “yottāni gahetvā acodento”ti vatvā taṃ pana acodanaṃ avāraṇamevāti āha “acodento avārento”ti.

Samiti, saṅgati, sannipāto, samayo all mean assembly; a great assembly is a mahāsamaya, thus it is said, 'a great multitude.' 'Pavana' is from 'pavaddhaṃ vanaṃ' (a great forest); thus it is said, 'a forest grove.' 'Devaghaṭā' means an assembly of gods. 'They composed themselves' (samādahaṃsu) means they well applied themselves to concentrated, supramundane concentration. And since being thus composed is called being yoked by concentration, it is said, 'they yoked with concentration.' Because all crookedness, like that of cow's urine, etc., was far removed from their own... they acted. 'Nettāni' are so called because one guides horses with them; also 'yottāni.' For horses not proceeding on the track, guiding them onto the track is done by taking hold of the reins; thus, having said, 'taking the reins without urging them on,' and since that non-urging is simply not hindering, he said, 'without urging on, without hindering.'

Yathā [M 1.0113] khīlaṃ bhittiyaṃ, bhūmiyaṃ vā ākoṭitaṃ dunnīharaṇaṃ, yathā ca palighaṃ nagarappavesanivāraṇaṃ, yathā ca indakhīlaṃ gambhīranemi sunikhātaṃ dunnīharaṇaṃ, evaṃ rāgādayo sattasantānato dunnīharaṇā nibbānanagarappavesanivāraṇā cāti te “khīlaṃ palighaṃ indakhīla”nti ca vuttā. Ūhaccāti uddharitvā. Taṇhāejāya abhāvena anejā. Paramasantuṭṭhabhāvena cātuddisattā appaṭihatacārikaṃ caranti. Buddhacakkhu-dhammacakkhu-dibbacakkhu-samantacakkhu-pakaticakkhūnaṃ vasena pañcahi cakkhūhi. Sudantā kutoti āha “cakkhutopī”ti. Chandādīhīti chandādīnaṃ vasena na gacchanti na vattanti. Na āgacchanti anuppādanato. Āgunti aparādhaṃ.

Just as a stake hammered into a wall or into the ground is hard to pull out, just as a bar is a hindrance to entering a city, and just as an indakhīla—a pillar sunk deep with a strong base—is hard to remove, so too are lust and other defilements hard to remove from the continuum of beings, acting as barriers to entering the city of Nibbāna. Thus they are called 'stake, bar, indakhīla.' 'Ūhacca' means having uprooted. 'Anejā' (unagitated) is because of the absence of craving's agitation. They wander unimpeded due to being perfectly content. With five eyes: that is, with the Buddha-eye, Dhamma-eye, divine-eye, all-seeing eye, and the physical eye. Why are they 'well-tamed' (sudantā)? It is said, 'even with regard to the eye.' They do not go or turn in accordance with desire and the like. They do not come, because of non-arising. 'Āgu' means a fault.

Sabbasaṃyogāti vibhattilopena niddeso, sabbe saṃyogeti attho. Visajjāti visajjitvā. Evampīti imāyapi gāthāya vasena “āguṃ na karotī”ti pade.

'Sabbasaṃyogā' (all bonds) is a designation by elision of the case ending; the meaning is 'all bonds.' 'Visajjā' (having released) means having abandoned. 'Evampi' (even so) refers to the phrase 'does not commit a fault' (āguṃ na karoti) in this verse as well.

Gatāseti gatā eva. Na gamissanti pariniṭṭhitasaraṇagamanattā. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanañhettha adhippetaṃ. Tenāha “nibbematikasaraṇagamanena gatā”ti. Te hi niyamena apāyaṃ na gamissanti, devakāyañca paripūressanti. Ye pana lokiyena saraṇagamanena buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā, na te gamissanti apāyaṃ, sati ca paccayantarasamavāye pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ devakāyaṃ paripūressantīti. Tenāha so brahmā “ye keci buddhaṃ…pe… paripūressantī”ti.

'Gatāse' (they have gone) means they have indeed gone. They will not go to another state of existence because their act of going for refuge is perfected. Here, the supramundane going for refuge is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'They have gone with a refuge-taking that is free from doubt.' For they will certainly not go to the lower realms and will fulfill the host of devas. But those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge with a mundane going-for-refuge will not go to the lower realms, and when a combination of other conditions is present, they will abandon the human body and fulfill the host of devas. Therefore, that Brahmā said: 'Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge… will fulfill the host of devas.'

Samayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samaya Sutta is concluded.

8. Sakalikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Sakalika Sutta

38. Tanti uyyānaṃ saṅkhaṃ gatanti sambandho. Dhanunā sarena gahanti pothayanti bādhentīti dhanuggahā. Taṃ sampaṭicchīti tassā silāya heṭṭhābhāgena uggantvā sampaṭicchi. Satthu puññānubhāvena [V 1.0101] upahatattā sayampi paripatantī vātaṃ upatthambheti. Abhihani satthārā anāvajjitattā. Tañca kho kammaphalavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tato eva tato paṭṭhāya bhagavato aphāsu jātanti etenapi upādiṇṇakasarīre nāma aniṭṭhāpi samphassakā patanti eva tathārūpena kammunā katokāseti dasseti. Ayaṃ [M 1.0114] vihāroti gijjhakūṭavihāro. Ujjaṅgalo na kattabbaparo. Visamoti bhūmibhāgavasena visamo. Sivikākārena sajjito mañco eva mañcasivikā.

38. The connection is: the text is reckoned as a park. Those who seize, strike, and oppress with bow and arrow are called archers. 'He received it' means he received it as it came up from the lower part of that stone. Because it was checked by the Teacher’s power of merit, even as it was falling by itself, the wind supported it. It struck because it was not adverted to by the Teacher. But this should be seen as due to the force of kamma. 'From that very moment, discomfort arose for the Blessed One'—this also shows that even unpleasant contacts indeed befall an acquired body when an opportunity is made by such kamma. 'This dwelling' refers to the Vulture Peak Monastery. 'Ujjaṅgala' means not suitable for cultivation. 'Visama' (uneven) means uneven in terms of the ground. A bed arranged like a palanquin is called a palanquin-bed.

Bhusāti daḷhā. Dukkhāti dukkhamā duttitikkhā. Kharāti kakkasā. Kaṭukāti aniṭṭhā. Asātāti na sātā appiyā. Na appetīti na upeti. Na appāyantīti na khamanti. Vedanādhivāsanakhantiyā satisampajaññayuttattā sabbasattaṭṭhitāhārasamudayavatthujātassa ādīnavanissaraṇānaṃ pageva suppaṭividitattā yathā samudācāro cittaṃ nābhibhavati, evaṃ sammadeva upaṭṭhāpitasatisampajaññattā vuttaṃ “vedanādhivāsana…pe… hutvā”ti. Apīḷiyamānoti abādhiyamāno. Kāmaṃ aniṭṭhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho tāya apīḷiyamāno nāma natthi, pariññātavatthukattā pana tassā vase avattamāno “avihaññamāno”ti vutto. Tenāha “samparivattasāyitāya vedanānaṃ vasaṃ agacchanto”ti.

'Bhusā' (strong) means firm. 'Dukkhā' (painful) means causing suffering, difficult to endure. 'Kharā' (rough) means coarse. 'Kaṭukā' (bitter) means undesirable. 'Asātā' (disagreeable) means not agreeable, unpleasant. 'Na appeti' (it does not please) means it does not come to be. 'Na appāyanti' (they are not satisfied) means they do not endure. Because of patience in enduring feelings, being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and because the danger and escape regarding all phenomena that are the cause for the sustenance of beings are already well-penetrated, the mind is not overwhelmed by whatever conduct arises. Thus, because of rightly established mindfulness and clear comprehension, it is said, 'enduring feelings... having become...' 'Apīḷiyamāno' (unoppressed) means unafflicted. Indeed, there is no one touched by an undesirable feeling who can be called 'unoppressed' by it; but because the matter is fully understood, one does not come under its sway and is thus said to be 'unvexed.' Therefore, it is said: 'Not coming under the sway of feelings that turn about and lie in wait.'

Sīhaseyyanti ettha sayanaṃ seyyā, sīhassa viya seyyā sīhaseyyā, taṃ sīhaseyyaṃ. Atha vā sīhaseyyanti seṭṭhaseyyaṃ uttamaseyyaṃ. Svāyamattho aṭṭhakathāyameva āgamissati. “Vāmena passena sentī”ti evaṃ vuttā kāmabhogiseyyā. Dakkhiṇapassena sayāno nāma natthi dakkhiṇahatthassa sarīraggahaṇādiyogakkhamato. Purisavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti dukkhuppattito. Ayaṃ sīhaseyyāti ayaṃ yathāvuttā sīhaseyyā. Tejussadattāti iminā sīhassa abhītabhāvaṃ dasseti. Bhīrukajātikā hi sesamigā attano āsayaṃ pavisitvā utrāsabahulā santāsapubbakaṃ yathā tathā sayanti, sīho pana abhirukabhāvato satokārī bhikkhu viya satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva sayati. Tenāha “dve purimapāde”tiādi. Purimapādeti dakkhiṇapurimapāde vāmassa purimapādassa ṭhapanavasena dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā. Pacchimapādeti dve pacchimapāde. Vuttanayeneva idhāpi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ṭhitokāsasallakkhaṇaṃ abhīrukabhāveneva. Sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvātiādinā vuttasīhakiriyā anutrāsapabujjhanaṃ viya abhīrukabhāvasiddhā dhammatāvasenevāti veditabbā. Sīhavijambhitavijambhanaṃ ativelaṃ ekākārena ṭhapitānaṃ sarīrāvayavānaṃ [M 1.0115] gamanādikiriyāsu yoggabhāvāpādanatthaṃ. Tikkhattuṃ sīhanādanadanaṃ appesakkhamigajātapariharaṇatthaṃ.

In the term 'sīhaseyya' (the lion's posture), 'seyyā' means lying down; 'sīhaseyyā' is a posture like that of a lion; thus, 'sīhaseyyaṃ.' Alternatively, 'sīhaseyyā' means the best posture, the supreme posture. This meaning will be found in the commentary itself. 'Lying on the left side' is said to be the posture of one who indulges in sensual pleasures. There is no lying on the right side for them, because the right hand is fit for the task of grasping the body and so on. And this is stated from a man's perspective. They cannot lie on one side because of the arising of pain. This is the lion's posture—this, as described, is the lion's posture. 'Tejussadattā' (abounding in majesty) indicates the lion's fearless nature. For other animals of a timid nature enter their lairs and lie down however they can, full of terror and preceded by fear. But the lion, being fearless, lies down only after establishing mindfulness, like a monk who acts with mindfulness. Therefore, it is said, 'the two front paws,' and so on. 'Front paws' means having placed the two front paws in one place by setting the right front paw on the left front paw. 'Hind paws' means the two hind paws. Here too, the placing in one place should be understood in the way described. The marking of its standing place is due to its fearlessness. As for the lion's actions mentioned, beginning with 'having raised its head,' such as awakening without terror, they should be understood as established by its fearless nature, simply by the force of its disposition. The lion's stretching and yawning is for the purpose of making the limbs of the body, which have been kept in one position for a very long time, fit for activities such as walking. The roaring of the lion's roar three times is for the purpose of driving away animals of little power.

Seti [V 1.0102] abyāvaṭabhāvena pavattati etthāti seyyā, catutthajjhānameva seyyā catutthajjhānaseyyā. Kiṃ panettha taṃ catutthajjhānanti? Ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ. Tato hi vuṭṭhahitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anukkamena aggamaggaṃ adhigantvā tathāgato jātoti. “Tayidaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, na seyyā, tathāpi yasmā ‘catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā samanantaraṃ bhagavā parinibbāyī’ti mahāparinibbāne (dī. ni. 2.219) āgataṃ. Tasmā lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpatti eva tathāgataseyyā”ti keci. Evaṃ sati parinibbānakālikāva tathāgataseyyāti āpajjati; na ca tathāgato lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpajjanabahulo vihāsi. Aggaphalavasena pavattaṃ panettha catutthajjhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha yathā sattānaṃ niddupagamalakkhaṇā seyyā bhavaṅgacittavasena hoti, sā ca nesaṃ paṭhamaṃ jātisamanvayā yebhuyyavuttikā, evaṃ bhagavato ariyajātisamanvayaṃ yebhuyyavuttikaṃ aggaphalabhūtaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ tathāgataseyyāti veditabbā. Sīhaseyyā nāma seṭṭhaseyyāti āha “uttamaseyyā”ti.

One lies down ('seti') or proceeds ('pavattati') in an untroubled state ('abyāvaṭabhāvena') herein ('ettha'); thus it is a 'seyyā' (lying-down state). The fourth jhāna itself is the 'seyyā,' the fourth-jhāna-seyyā. What here is that fourth jhāna? It is the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing. For it was after emerging from that, developing insight, and gradually attaining the supreme path that he became the Tathāgata. Some say: 'This is called the basis, not the seyyā. Nevertheless, because it is stated in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16), "Having emerged from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One immediately attained final Nibbāna," therefore the mundane attainment of the fourth jhāna is the Tathāgata’s seyyā.' If this were so, it would follow that the Tathāgata’s seyyā is only at the time of his final Nibbāna; but the Tathāgata did not dwell frequently attaining the mundane fourth jhāna. Here, the fourth jhāna should be understood as that which occurs by virtue of the supreme fruition. Just as for beings the 'seyyā,' characterized by the onset of sleep, occurs by way of the life-continuum consciousness, and this is for them the primary state connected with birth and of general occurrence, so too for the Blessed One, the fourth jhāna—which is connected with noble birth, is of general occurrence, and constitutes the supreme fruition—should be understood as the Tathāgata’s seyyā. The lion’s posture is the best posture; thus it is called 'the supreme posture.'

“Kālaparicchedaṃ katvā yathāparicchedaṃ uṭṭhahissāmī”ti evaṃ tadā manasikārassa akatattā pāḷiyaṃ “uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasikaritvā”ti na vuttanti āha “uṭṭhānasaññanti panettha na vutta”nti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “gilānaseyyā hesā”ti. Sā hi cirakālappavattikā hoti.

Because attention of the kind, 'Having set a time limit, I will rise at the designated time,' was not made on that occasion, it is not stated in the Pāḷi text as 'having attended to the perception of rising.' Thus he says, 'Here, "perception of rising" is not mentioned.' He states the reason for this: 'For this is the lying-down posture of a sick person.' For that tends to be of long duration.

Visuṃ visuṃ rāsivasena anāgantvā ekajjhaṃ puñjavasena āgatattā vuttaṃ “sabbāpi tā”ti. Tenāha “sattasatā”ti. Vikāramattampīti vedanāya asahanavasena pavattanākāramattampi. Susammaṭṭhakañcanaṃ viyāti sammaṭṭhasusajjitasuvaṇṇaṃ viya.

Because they did not come separately in individual groups, but arrived together as a mass, it is said, 'all of them.' Therefore, it is said 'seven hundred.' 'Even a mere alteration' (vikāramattampi) means just the mode of occurrence due to the inability to endure the feeling. 'Like well-burnished gold' means like gold that is well-burnished and beautifully prepared.

Dhammālapananti asaṅkhārikasamuppannasabhāvālapanaṃ. Samullapitañhi ākārasamānavacanametaṃ. Nāgo viya vāti pavattatīti nāgavo. Tassa bhāvo nāgavatā. Vibhattilopena hesa niddeso, mahānāgahatthisadisatāyāti attho. Byattuparicaraṇaṭṭhenāti byattaṃ uparūpari attano kiriyācaraṇena. Ājānīyoti sammāpatitaṃ dukkhaṃ sahanto [M 1.0116] attanā kātabbakiriyaṃ dhīro hutvā nitthārako. Kāraṇākāraṇajānanenāti niyyānikāniyyānikakaraṇañātatāya. Tenevaṭṭhenāti appaṭisamaṭṭheneva. “Mutto moceyya”ntiādi dhuravāhaṭṭhena. Nibbisevanaṭṭhenāti rāgādivisavigatabhāvena.

'Discourse on Dhamma' (dhammālapanā) means the discourse on the nature that arises spontaneously without prompting. For this is a word similar in form to 'samullapita' (spoken together). Just as an elephant (nāgo) moves (vāti), so it is called 'nāgavo.' Its state is 'nāgavatā.' This is a description by the elision of a case ending, meaning 'the state of being similar to a great elephant.' 'By way of skilled attendance' means being skilled through repeated performance of one's own actions and conduct. 'Ājānīya' refers to one who, enduring suffering that has rightly come, is a wise deliverer who completes the task that must be done by himself. 'By knowing cause and non-cause' means knowing causes that lead out and causes that do not lead out. 'By that very meaning' means precisely by an unequalled meaning. 'Freed, he would free,' etc.—this is in the sense of bearing the yoke. 'By way of being free from poison' means being in a state free from the poison of lust and so on.

Aniyamitāṇattīti anuddesikaṃ āṇāpanaṃ. Sāmaññakatopi samādhisaddo pakaraṇato idha visesatthoti āha “samādhinti arahattaphalasamādhi”nti. Paṭippassaddhivasena sabbakilesehi suṭṭhu [V 1.0103] vimuttanti suvimuttaṃ. Abhinataṃ nāma ārammaṇe abhimukhabhāvena pavattiyā. Apanataṃ apagamanavasena pavattiyā, vimukhatāyāti attho. Lokiyajjhānacittaṃ viya vipassanā viya ca sasaṅkhārena sappayogena tadaṅgappahānavikkhambhanapahānavasena ca vikkhambhetvā na adhigataṃ na ṭhapitaṃ, kiñcarahi kilesānaṃ sabbaso chinnatāyāti āha “chinnattā vataṃ phalasamādhinā samāhita”nti. Atikkamitabbanti ācārātikkamavasena laṅghitabbaṃ. Sā pana laṅghanā āsādanā ghaṭṭanāti āha “ghaṭṭetabba”nti.

An 'unrestricted command' (aniyamitāṇatti) is an instruction without a specific object. Although the word 'samādhi' is general, here, due to the context, it has a specific meaning; thus, he said, 'samādhi means the samādhi of the fruit of arahantship.' 'Well-liberated' (suvimuttaṃ) means completely liberated from all defilements by way of pacification. 'Inclined' (abhinataṃ) means proceeding with a forward tendency towards the object. 'Averted' (apanataṃ) means proceeding by way of moving away, that is, with aversion. It is not attained or established by suppression—as is done with mundane jhāna consciousness or insight meditation through conditioning and application, or by way of abandonment by substitution and abandonment by suppression—but rather, it is because the defilements are completely cut off. Thus, he said, 'truly, the bond being cut off, he is composed by the samādhi of fruition.' 'What is to be transcended' (atikkamitabbaṃ) means what is to be transgressed by way of misconduct. That transgression, however, is an assault, a striking; thus, he said, 'it must be struck against'.

Pañcavedā nāma – iruvedo, yajuvedo, sāmavedo, āthabbaṇavedo, itihāso cāti evaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ vedānaṃ. “Cara”nti vacanavipallāsena vuttanti āha “carantā”ti, tapantāti attho. Hīnattarūpāti hīnādhimuttikatāya nihīnacittasabhāvā. Vimuttikatāya abhāvato nibbānaṅgamā na honti. Arahattādhigamakammassa abhabbatāya parihīnatthā. Ajjhotthaṭāti abhibhūtā. Tādiseheva sīlehīti gosīlādīhi. Baddhāti samādapetvā pavattanavasena anubaddhā. Lūkhaṃ tapanti attakilamathānuyogaṃ. Taṃ pana ekadesena dassento “pañcātapatāpana”ntiādimāha. “Evaṃ paṭipannassa mokkho natthi, evaṃ paṭipannassa vaṭṭato mutti atthī”ti vadantī sā attato sāsanassa niyyānabhāvo kathito nāma hotīti āha “sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ kathentī”ti. Ādinti gāthādvayaṃ.

The five Vedas are named—the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, and Itihasa; thus, of the Vedas with Itihasa as the fifth. 'Cara,' due to a verbal inversion, is said as 'carantā,' meaning 'they torment themselves.' 'Of inferior nature' (hīnattarūpā) means having a base state of mind due to inferior inclinations. Because they lack liberation, they do not lead to Nibbāna. They are deficient due to their inability for the action of attaining arahantship. 'Overwhelmed' (ajjhotthaṭā) means overpowered. 'By such virtues' refers to virtues like those of a cow. 'Bound' (baddhā) means bound by way of having undertaken and continuing the practice. 'They practice harsh austerity' means they engage in self-mortification. To illustrate this partially, it is said, 'the fivefold self-tormenting practices,' and so on. That speech of theirs, saying, 'For one who practices thus, there is no liberation; for one who practices thus, there is release from the cycle,' is called a declaration by oneself of the teaching's nature of leading out. Thus, it is said, 'proclaiming the teaching's nature of leading out.' 'Etc.' refers to the two verses.

Sakalikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sakalika Sutta is concluded.

9. Paṭhamapajjunnadhītusuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Sutta on Pajjunna's Daughter

39. Cātumahārājikassāti [M 1.0117] cātumahārājikakāyikassa. Dhammo anubuddhoti catusaccadhammo pariññeyyādibhāvassa anurūpato buddho. Paccakkhamevāti parapattiyā ahutvā attapaccakkhameva katvā jānāmi. Dhammaṃ garahantā nāma saddadosavasena vā atthadosavasena vā garaheyyunti taṃ dassento “hīnakkhara…pe… kotivā”ti āha. Sā pana “tesaṃ vigarahā dummedhatāya mahānatthāvahāvā”ti dassentī devatā āha “dummedhā upenti roruva”nti. Visuṃ hotīti avīcimahānirayato visuṃ eva hoti. Khantiyāti ñāṇakhantiyā. Upasamenāti rāgādīnaṃ sabbaso vūpasamena. Tenāha “ruccitvā”tiādi.

39. 'Of the Four Great Kings' (cātumahārājikassa) means belonging to the assembly of the Four Great Kings. 'The Dhamma is understood' (dhammo anubuddho) means the Dhamma of the Four Truths is understood in accordance with its nature of being what is to be fully understood, etc. 'Directly' (paccakkhameva) means: I know by making it my own direct experience, not by way of another's attainment. 'Those who disparage the Dhamma' would disparage it based on faults in wording or faults in meaning. To illustrate this, it is said: 'inferior letters... up to the extreme.' Then, to show that 'their disparagement, due to foolishness, brings great harm,' the deity said: 'the foolish go to Roruva.' 'It is separate' (visuṃ hoti) means it is completely separate from the Avīci great hell. 'With patience' (khantiyā) means with the patience of wisdom. 'With pacification' (upasamena) means with the complete subsiding of lust and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'having approved,' etc.

Paṭhamapajjunnadhītusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Sutta on Pajjunna's Daughter is concluded.

10. Dutiyapajjunnadhītusuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Pajjunna's Daughter

40. Buddhañca [V 1.0104] dhammañca namassamānāti buddhasubuddhataṃ dhammasudhammatañca ñatvā tadubhayaṃ namassamānā. Yasmā buddhe ca dhamme ca pasanno saṅghe ca pasanno eva hoti tassa suppaṭipattiyā vijānanato, tasmā so attho gāthāya ca-saddasaṅgahitoti dassento “ca-saddena saṅghañcā”ti āha atthavatiyoti lokiyalokuttaraatthasaṅgahitā lokiyakusalalokuttaramaggasaṅgaṇhanato. Yaṃ dhammaṃ sā abhāsīti yaṃ tumhākaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitā, sā mahākokanadā attano balānurūpaṃ abhāsi. Bahunāti nānappakārena. Pariyāyenāti kāraṇena. Tādisoti tathārūpo tathāpaṭividdhasacco atthadhammādīsu kusalo ekekaṃ padampi udāharaṇahetunigamanāni nīharanto ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti. Tenāha “ayaṃ bhagavā”tiādi. Etena ativiya vitthārakkhamo sugatadhammoti dasseti. Pariyāpuṭanti parivattitaṃ. Evaṃ vitthārakkhamaṃ [M 1.0118] dhammaṃ yasmā devadhītā “saṃkhittamatthaṃ lapayissāmī”ti avoca, tasmā vuttaṃ “tassattha”ntiādi.

40. ‘Paying homage to the Buddha and the Dhamma’ means, having known the Buddha’s superb enlightenment and the Dhamma’s excellent quality, paying homage to both. Since one who has faith in the Buddha and the Dhamma also has faith in the Sangha, due to understanding its good practice, this meaning is included in the verse by the word ‘and.’ Thus, it is said: ‘by the word “ca” (and), the Sangha is also included.’ ‘Meaningful’ means it includes worldly and supramundane benefits, as it encompasses wholesome worldly states and the supramundane path. ‘The Dhamma she spoke’ means: having penetrated your Dhamma, she, Mahākokanadā, stood therein and spoke according to her ability. ‘In many ways’ means in various forms. ‘By way of’ (pariyāyena) means by reason. ‘Such’ means one of that kind—who has penetrated the truth in such a way, skilled in meaning, Dhamma, etc., who, bringing forth examples, reasons, and conclusions for each single word, indicates, teaches, proclaims, sets forth, clarifies, analyzes, and makes it plain. Therefore, it is said: ‘this Blessed One,’ etc. By this, it shows that the Sugata’s Dhamma is exceedingly capable of being expanded. ‘Mastered’ (pariyāpuṭaṃ) means recited. Since the deity said, ‘I will speak the meaning in brief,’ even though the Dhamma is so capable of being expanded, it is said: ‘its meaning,’ etc.

Dutiyapajjunnadhītusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Sutta on Pajjunna's Daughter is concluded.

Satullapakāyikavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of the Satullapa Group is concluded.

5. Ādittavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Burning

1. Ādittasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on the Burning

41. Sīsanti desanāpadeso, desanāya aññesupi vattabbesu kassacideva sīsabhāgena apadisanaṃ. Tenāha “rāgādīhī”tiādi. Dānenāti attano santakassa paresaṃ pariccajanena. Taṃ pana pariccajanaṃ cetanāya hotīti āha “dānacetanāyā”ti dānapuññacetanāti dānamayā puññacetanā dāyakasseva hoti taṃsantatipariyāpannattā. Nīhatabhaṇḍakanti ādittagehato bahi nikkhāmitaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ. Etanti “dinnaṃ hotī”tiādivacanaṃ. Adinneti dānamukhe aniyuñjite bhoge. “Antenā”ti jīvitassa anto adhippetoti āha “maraṇenā”ti. Mamāti pariggahitattā pariggahā, bhogā. Tepi kenaci ākārena vināsaṃ anupagatā maraṇena pahīyanti [V 1.0105] nāmāti vuttaṃ “corādīnaṃ vasena avinaṭṭhabhoge”ti. Sobhanā aggabhūtā rūpādayo etthāti saggo, taṃ saggaṃ.

41. ‘Head’ (sīsaṃ) is a section of the teaching; it is the designation of something by its principal part, even when there are other things to be said in the teaching. Hence it is said, ‘by lust, etc.’ ‘By giving’ means relinquishing one’s own possessions to others. That relinquishing, however, occurs through intention; thus it is said, ‘through the intention of giving.’ The meritorious intention of giving, that is, the merit-making intention consisting of giving, belongs to the giver alone because it is included in their continuum. ‘Goods carried out’ refers to goods carried out from a burning house. ‘This’ means the statement, ‘what is given,’ etc. ‘Not given’ refers to wealth not applied at the opportunity for giving. ‘By the end’ means the end of life is intended; hence it is said, ‘by death.’ ‘Mine’ refers to possessions, wealth, because they are acquired. Even those which have not undergone destruction in any way are indeed abandoned through death; hence the statement, ‘wealth not destroyed by thieves, etc.’ Heaven (sagga) is so called because beautiful and supreme forms, etc., are there; that heaven.

Ādittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sutta on the Burning is concluded.

2. Kiṃdadasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sutta on What to Give

42. Dve tīṇi bhattāni abhutvāti dve tayo vāre bhattāni abhuñjitvā. Uṭṭhātuṃ na sakkotīti uṭṭhātumpi na sakkotī, pageva aññaṃ sarīrena kātabbakiccaṃ dubbalabhāvato. Dubbalopi hutvāti bhuñjanato pubbe dubbalo hutvā balasampanno hoti. Evaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca āhārassa sarīre balavataṃ āha. Yasmā annado [M 1.0119] dāyako paṭiggāhakassa balado hoti, tasmā so āyatiṃ attano sarīre balado avināsavasena balassa rakkhako ca hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “balaṃ kho pana datvā balassa bhāgī hotī”ti (a. ni. 5.37) sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Surūpopīti abhirūpopi. Virūpo hotīti bībhaccharūpo kopīnassa acchannattā. Idañca yānanti sāmaññato vuttaṃ. Upāhanāti sarūpato dasseti. Adukkhappatto hutvā yāti vattati etenāti yānanti chattādīnampi yānabhāvo vutto. Tenāha “yānado sukhado hotī”ti. Cakkhudo nāma hoti cakkhunā kātabbakicce sahakārīkāraṇabhāvato dīpassa.

42. ‘Not having eaten two or three meals’ means not having eaten meals two or three times. ‘Unable to rise’ means unable even to rise, let alone perform any other bodily task, on account of weakness. ‘Though weak’ means that though one is weak before eating, one becomes possessed of strength after eating. Thus, he spoke of the strength of food for the body both by contrast and by sequence. Since the giver of food is a giver of strength to the recipient, therefore, in the future, he becomes a giver of strength to his own body and a protector of strength by way of its non-perishing. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘By giving strength, one becomes a partaker of strength’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.37); this same principle applies to the remaining phrases. ‘Pleasing in appearance’ means beautiful in appearance. ‘Ugly’ means repulsive in appearance due to the private parts not being covered. And this ‘vehicle’ (yāna) is said generally. ‘Footwear’ he shows specifically. ‘A vehicle’ (yāna) is that by which one goes and proceeds without experiencing suffering; by this, the nature of a vehicle is stated even for umbrellas and so forth. Therefore, it is said: ‘The giver of a vehicle is a giver of comfort.’ One is called a ‘giver of an eye’ because of a lamp's nature as a cooperative cause in the function to be performed by the eye.

“Sabbesaṃyeva balādīnaṃ dāyako hotī”ti saṅkhepato vuttaṃ atthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “dve tayo gāme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nisajjādivasena patissayitabbato patissayo, vihāro. Pakkhittaṃ viya hoti parissamassa vinoditattā. Bahi vicarantassāti patissayaṃ alabhitvā bahi vivaṭaṅgaṇe vicarantassa. Jhāyatīti jhāyantaṃ hoti, kilamatīti attho. Sītuṇhādivirodhipaccayavasena sasantāne visabhāgasantati, tabbipariyāyato sabhāgasantati veditabbā. Sukhaṃ nāma dukkhapaccayaparihārato sukhapaccayuppannato ca hoti, tadubhayaṃ patissayavasena labhatīti dassento “bahi vicarantassa pāde”tiādimāha. Dhammapītisukhanti dhammapaccavekkhaṇena uppannapītisukhaṃ. Upasamasukhanti kilesānaṃ vūpasamena pavattasukhaṃ. Nivātaṃ pihitavātapānaṃ patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya ṭhitassa andhakāro hotīti vuttaṃ “kūpe otiṇṇo viya hotī”ti. Tenāha “mañcapīṭhādīni na paññāyantī”ti. Tayidaṃ bahisamāpannaparissamadosena, na ca patissayadosena. Tenāha “muhutta”ntiādi.

To explain in detail the meaning briefly stated as ‘he is the giver of all strengths, and so forth,’ it is said, ‘two or three villages,’ and so on. A ‘shelter’ (patissaya) is that which is to be relied upon by way of sitting, and so forth; it is a dwelling. It is as if one is settled, because it dispels exertion. ‘For one wandering outside’ means for one who, not obtaining a shelter, wanders in an open space. ‘He is consumed’ (jhāyati) means he is exhausted; the meaning is ‘he toils.’ Due to opposing conditions like heat and cold, there is a dissimilar continuity in one's own mental stream; a similar continuity should be understood as its opposite. Happiness is so-called because it arises from the avoidance of conditions for suffering and from the arising of conditions for happiness; to show that both are obtained through reliance on a shelter, it is said, ‘for one wandering outside, the feet,’ and so on. ‘The happiness of joy in the Dhamma’ is the joy and happiness arising from reflecting on the Dhamma. ‘The happiness of peace’ is the happiness that arises from the calming of defilements. For one who has entered a shelter sheltered from the wind with closed windows and, having shut the door, stands there, there is darkness; it is said, ‘it is like one who has descended into a well.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘the bed, chair, and so forth, are not discernible.’ This is due to the fault of exertion experienced outside, not the fault of the shelter. Hence, it is said, ‘for a moment,’ and so on.

Na [V 1.0106] marati etenāti amaraṇaṃ, nibbānādhigamādayo. Tassa dānaṃ dhammūpadeso, taṃ deti. Tenāha “yo dhammaṃ anusāsatī”ti. Tayidaṃ dhammānusāsanaṃ kathaṃ hotīti āha “aṭṭhakatha”ntiādi. Aṭṭhakathaṃ kathetīti avivaṭapāṭhassa pāḷiyā atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ karotīti attho. Anadhītino pana pāḷiṃ vāceti. Tattha tattha gataṭṭhāne pucchitapañhaṃ vissajjeti, ayaṃ tāva ganthadhuro, paṭipattivāsadhure pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhati, ubhayesampi [M 1.0120] dhammassavanaṃ karoti. Sabbadānanti yathāvuttaāmisadānaṃ abhayadānaṃ. Dhammadānanti dhammadesanā. Dhammaratīti samathavipassanādhamme abhirati. Dhammarasoti saddhammasannissayaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ.

‘One does not die by this,’ thus it is ‘deathlessness’ (amaraṇaṃ), such as the attainment of Nibbāna, and so forth. The gift of that is the teaching of the Dhamma; that he gives. Therefore, it is said, ‘who instructs in the Dhamma.’ How does this instruction in the Dhamma occur? He said, ‘commentary,’ and so on. ‘He expounds the commentary’ means he explains the meaning of the Pāli whose text is unexplained. For one who has not studied, he recites the Pāli. Here and there, in various places, he answers questions that are asked. This, for a start, is the vocation of study. As for the vocation of the practice-dwelling, he explains the meditation subject. He makes both kinds of people listen to the Dhamma. ‘The gift of all’ refers to the material gifts and the gift of fearlessness as previously mentioned. ‘The gift of the Dhamma’ is the teaching of the Dhamma. ‘Delight in the Dhamma’ is delight in the Dhamma of serenity and insight. ‘The taste of the Dhamma’ is joy and gladness dependent on the true Dhamma.

Kiṃdadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kiṃdada Sutta is concluded.

3. Annasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Anna Sutta

43. Patthentīti pihenti. Yatthassa upagamanaṃ loke pākaṭataraṃ ahosi, te udāharaṇavasena dassento “cittagahapatisīvalittherādike viyā”ti āha. Annanti annasaññito catubbidhopi paccayo. Sabbepi dāyake ekajjhaṃ gahetvā sāmaññato ekavasena “dāyakamevā”ti vuttaṃ, yathā cāha “ko nāma so yakkho, yaṃ annaṃ nābhinandatī”ti? Tattha yakkhoti satto. Sāmaññajotanā ca nāma yasmā puthuatthavisayā, tasmā “ye naṃ dadanti saddhāya, vippasannena cetasā. Tameva annaṃ bhajatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha ma-kāro padasandhikaro, te evāti attho. Dāyakaṃ apariccajanameva anugacchati cakkaṃ viya kubbaraṃ.

43. ‘Patthenti’ means they desire. Showing by way of example those for whom its benefit became more evident in the world, he said, 'like the householder Citta, the Elder Sīvali, and so on.' ‘Anna’ means the fourfold requisite, which is designated as ‘anna’. Having taken all the donors together, it is said generally in the singular, ‘the donor indeed,’ just as it is said: ‘What being is there who does not rejoice in food?’ There, ‘yakkho’ means a being. And since a general explanation has a domain of various meanings, it is therefore said: ‘Those who give it with faith, with a serene mind, that very food attends them.’ There, the letter ‘m’ is for euphonic combination; the meaning is ‘te eva’ (them indeed). Not abandoning the donor, it follows, like a wheel follows the pole of a cart.

Annasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anna Sutta is concluded.

4. Ekamūlasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Ekamūla Sutta

44. Patiṭṭhaṭṭhena avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃ mūlaṃ etissāti ekamūlā. Taṃ ekamūlaṃ. Yathā saṃyojanīyesu assādānupassanāvasena taṇhāsamuppādo, evaṃ taṇhābhibhavavasena anavabodhoti avijjā taṇhāya mūlaṃ, taṇhā ca avijjāya mūlaṃ. Ayañhi nayo upanissayatāvasena vutto, sahajātavasena cāyaṃ aññamaññaṃ mūlabhāvo pākaṭoyeva. Idha pana imissaṃ gāthāyaṃ adhippetā “ekamūla”nti sā taṇhā. Tattha yā bhavataṇhā, sā sassatadiṭṭhivasena āvaṭṭati parivattati, vibhavataṇhā [M 1.0121] ucchedadiṭṭhivasena, evaṃ dvirāvaṭṭaṃ. Sahajātakoṭiyāti sahajātakoṭiyāpi, pageva sammuyhaṃ āpannassa pana vattamānāya taṇhāya balavabhāvena malīnatā siyā. Upanissayakoṭiyāti upanissayakoṭiyāva sahajātakoṭiyā asambhavato. Pattharaṇaṭṭhānāti vitthatā hutvā pavattiṭṭhānabhūmi[V 1.0107]. Tenāha “tesu sā pattharatī”ti. Samuddanaṭṭhena samuddo. Uttarituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya patāya alaṃ pariyattoti pātālo, ayaṃ pana pātālo viyāti pātālo. Tenāha “appatiṭṭhaṭṭhenā”ti. Agādhagambhīratāyāti attho.

44. By the meaning of foundation, that which has a single root reckoned as ignorance is ‘single-rooted’ (ekamūlā). That is the single root. Just as craving arises through the contemplation of gratification in things that fetter, so non-comprehension, which is ignorance, arises through the overpowering of craving; thus, ignorance is the root of craving, and craving is the root of ignorance. This principle is stated by way of dependence; but by way of co-arising, this mutual root-condition is indeed evident. Here, however, in this verse, the intended ‘single root’ is craving. Therein, craving for existence revolves and turns through the view of eternalism, and craving for non-existence through the view of annihilationism—thus, a twofold revolving. ‘By way of co-arising’ means even by way of co-arising; how much more so for one who has fallen into delusion might there be defilement due to the strong nature of present craving. ‘By way of dependence’ means only by way of dependence, because it is impossible by way of co-arising. 'Pattharaṇaṭṭhāna' means the place of expansion, the ground for spreading and occurring. Hence it is said, 'therein it spreads.' 'Samuddo' means ocean by the meaning of swelling up. 'Pātālo' means the abyss, being incapable of being crossed and sufficient for falling into; but this is like an abyss, hence ‘abyss’. Hence it is said, 'by the meaning of being without foundation.' The meaning is 'due to unfathomable depth.'

Ekamūlasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ekamūla Sutta is concluded.

5. Anomasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Anoma Sutta

45. Anomanāmanti anūnanāmaṃ. Guṇanemittikāni eva hi bhagavato nāmāni. Guṇānañcassa paripuṇṇatāya anūnanāmanti āha “sabbaguṇasamannāgatattā”tiādi. Apica tathā tevijjo, chaḷabhiññotiādīni nāmāni anomanāmāni na honti paricchinnavisayattā, bhagavato pana satthā, sabbaññū, sammāsambuddhotiādīni nāmāni anomanāmāni nāma mahāvisayattā anūnabhāvato. Tenāha “avekallanāma”nti. Khandhantarādayoti khandhavisesādike. Ñāṇena yāthāvato araṇīyaṭṭhena atthe. Anvayapaññādhigamāyāti lokuttarapaññāpaṭilābhāya. Paṭipadanti samathavipassanāpaṭipadaṃ. Kilesakāmānaṃ vasena allīyitabbaṭṭhena kāmā eva ālayo. Atītakāleyeva kamanataṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ “kamamāna”nti. Na etarahi tadabhāvatoti āha “atītaṃ pana upādāya idaṃ vutta”nti. Mahānubhāvatādinā mahantānaṃ.

45. ‘Anomanāmanti’ means ‘a name without deficiency.’ The Blessed One's names are indeed based on his virtues. And because his virtues are complete, it is called a name without deficiency, as he said, ‘due to being endowed with all virtues,’ and so on. Furthermore, names like 'tevijjo' (possessor of the threefold knowledge) and 'chaḷabhiñño' (possessor of the sixfold higher knowledge) are not names without deficiency because their scope is limited. But names of the Blessed One like 'satthā' (Teacher), 'sabbaññū' (All-knowing), and 'sammāsambuddho' (Perfectly Self-Enlightened) are indeed names without deficiency because their scope is vast and they are without deficiency. Hence, it is said, 'avekallanāma' (a name without incompleteness). 'Khandhantarādayoti' refers to distinctions among aggregates and so forth. ‘Atthè’ means in the meaning, which is to be correctly understood by knowledge in the sense of non-conflict. 'Anvayapaññādhigamāyāti' means for the attainment of consequential wisdom, that is, for the acquisition of supramundane wisdom. 'Paṭipadanti' refers to the path of serenity and insight. Sensual pleasures themselves are the abode of clinging, in the sense that they are to be clung to by means of defilements and sensual desires. The term ‘kamamāna’ is used with reference to enjoyment in the past. It is not so now, due to the absence of that; hence he said, ‘this is stated with reference to the past.’ ‘Mahantānaṃ’ means of the great ones, due to their great power and so forth.

Anomasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anoma Sutta is concluded.

6. Accharāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Accharā Sutta

46. “Accharāgaṇasaṅghuṭṭha”nti gāthā devaputtena yenādhippāyena gāyitā, so anupubbikathāya vinā na paññāyatīti taṃ āgamanato paṭṭhāya [M 1.0122] kathento “ayaṃ kira devaputto”tiādimāha. Tattha sāsaneti imasseva satthusāsane. Kammākammanti kammavinicchayaṃ. Atthapurekkhāratāya appakiccatāya ca sallahukavuttiko. Sayanassa koṭṭhāsoti divasaṃ purimayāmañca bhāvanānuyogavasena kilantakāyassa samassāsanatthaṃ seyyāya upagamanabhāgo anuññāto.

46. 'Resounding with a host of nymphs'—the verse was sung by the devaputta with a certain intention, which is not understood without a gradual explanation. Therefore, explaining it starting from his arrival, he said, 'This devaputta, it seems...' and so on. Here, 'in the teaching' refers to this very Teacher's dispensation. 'Kammākamma' means the discernment of action. Due to his focus on the goal and having few duties, he lived lightly. 'The portion for sleeping' means: for the sake of resting the body wearied through devotion to meditation during the day and the first watch, the part of going to bed was permitted.

Abbhantareti kucchiyaṃ bhattassa parittatāya satthakavātāti tikkhabhāvena satthakā viya kantanakā vātā. Dhurasmiṃyevāti kilesamārena yuddhe eva. Vimuttāyatanasīse ṭhatvā dhammaṃ desento vā. Upanissayamandatāya aparipakkañāṇatāya āsavakkhayaṃ appatto kālaṃ katvāti yojanā. Upari ṭhitanti parikkhārabhāvena dibbadussūpari ṭhitaṃ. Tatheva aṭṭhāsīti tāhi tathā vuttepi [V 1.0108] yathā tato pubbe, tatheva aṭṭhāsi. Suvaṇṇapaṭṭanti nibbuddhe paṭijinitvā laddhabbasuvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ. Vītikkamassa akatattā asambhinneneva sīlena. Yasmā tasmiṃ satthu santikaṃ āgacchante tāpi tena saddhiṃ āgamaṃsu tasmā “accharāsaṅghaparivuto”ti vuttaṃ.

'Within' means in the belly, due to the small amount of food; 'winds like knives' means winds that cut like knives due to their sharpness. 'At the very yoke' means in the very battle with Māra of the defilements. Or, standing at the summit of the sphere of liberation while teaching the Dhamma. The connection is: because of weak supporting conditions and immature knowledge, he passed away without having attained the destruction of the taints. 'Stood above' means stood above the celestial cloth as an adornment. 'He stood just so' means even when spoken to thus by them, he stood just as he had before. 'A golden plaque' means the golden plaque to be obtained for having refuted a non-Buddha. Because no transgression was committed, with virtue unbroken. Since they also came with him when he was coming into the Teacher's presence, it is said, 'surrounded by a host of nymphs.'

Saṅghositanti saṅgamma ghositaṃ, tattha tattha accharānaṃ gītasaddavasena ghositaṃ. Pisācagaṇaṃ katvā vadati acchandarāgatāya. Niyāmacittatāyāti sammattaniyāme ninnacittatāya. Garubhāvenāti tāsaṃ vase avattanato garuṭṭhānabhāvena. Yātrāti nibbānaṃ pati yātrā. Taṃ pana vaṭṭato niggamanaṃ hotīti āha “kathaṃ niggamanaṃ bhavissatī”ti.

'Proclaimed together' means proclaimed having come together, proclaimed in various places by means of the sound of the nymphs' songs. He speaks of them as a band of ghouls due to his own lack of desire and passion. 'Due to a mind on the fixed course' means due to a mind inclined to the fixed course of rightness. 'Due to being weighty' means due to being of honorable standing, from not falling under their power. 'Journey' means the journey to Nibbāna. But that is an escape from the round; thus he said, 'How will there be an escape?'

Atisallekhatevāti ativiya kilesānaṃ sallekhitavuttiko. Akatābhinivesassāti bhāvanamananuyuttassa anāraddhavipassakassa. Kārakassāti sugatovādakārakassa sammāpaṭipajjato. Suññatāvipassananti suññatādīpanaṃ vipassanaṃ duccaritataṇhāya dūrīkaraṇena ekavihāritāya. Eko maggo assāti lokuttaramaggo eva assa anāgato, pubbabhāgamaggo pana kataparicayoti attho.

'Indeed one of extreme effacement' means one whose practice is the extreme effacement of defilements. 'Of one who has not made a resolve' means of one not devoted to meditation, who has not undertaken insight. 'Of a doer' means of one who acts on the Sugata's advice, who practices rightly. 'Insight into emptiness' means insight that illuminates emptiness, by dwelling alone through the removal of misconduct and craving. 'One path remains for him' means the supramundane path has not yet come for him, but the preliminary path has been practiced—this is the meaning.

Kāyavaṅkādīnanti kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ abhāvato samucchindanena anupalabbhanato. Natthi ettha bhayaṃ, asmiṃ vā adhigate puggalassa natthi bhayanti [M 1.0123] abhayaṃ nāma. Saṃsārakantāraṃ atikkamitvā nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ khemaṃ amataṭṭhānaṃ gamane sugatasārathinā susajjitayānabhāvato ratho akūjanoti aṭṭhaṅgiko maggova adhippeto. Dhammato anapetatāya aparāparuppattiyā ca dhammacakkehi.

'Of bodily crookedness, etc.' means due to the absence of bodily misconduct, etc., as they are not found, having been eradicated. 'There is no fear here,' or for a person who has attained this there is no fear, thus it is called 'fearless.' Having crossed the wilderness of saṃsāra, for going to the safe, deathless state called Nibbāna, the chariot is 'noiseless' because it is a vehicle well-prepared by the Sugata as charioteer—here the Noble Eightfold Path is intended. By the wheels of Dhamma, due to their not departing from the Dhamma and their successive arising.

Ottappampi gahitameva avinābhāvā. Apālamboti avassayo. Parivāroti parikkhāro abhisaṅkharaṇato. Maggassa karaṇaṭṭhāne dhammo tappariyāpannā sammādiṭṭhi. Aniccādivasenāti aniccānupassanādivasena. Sodhitesu vajjhamānesu. Bhūmiladdhavaṭṭanti bhūmiladdhasaṅkhātaṃ vaṭṭaṃ. Tattha vipassanāya pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato pañcakkhandhā bhūmi nāma, vaṭṭamayakammabhāvato tattha uppajjanārahaṃ kilesajātaṃ bhūmiladdhavaṭṭaṃ. Parijānamānāti paricchindanavasena samatikkamavasena jānamānā paṭivijjhantī.

Moral shame is also included due to their inseparability. 'Support' means reliance. 'Retinue' means equipment, because of its preparation. In the place where the path is made, the Dhamma is right view, which is included therein. 'By way of impermanence, etc.' means by way of contemplation of impermanence, etc. When they are being purified, being struck down. 'The round obtained on the ground' means the round called 'obtained on the ground.' Therein, the five aggregates are called 'ground' because they are the place where insight proceeds; the mass of defilements fit to arise there, due to being kamma that consists of the round, is 'the round obtained on the ground.' 'Fully understanding' means knowing by way of delimiting, by way of overcoming, and by way of penetrating.

Kasmā devaputto sotāpattiphaleyeva patiṭṭhāsi, nanu ca sā desanā bhagavatā catumaggappadhānabhāvena pavattitāti āha “yathā hī”tiādi.

Why was the devaputta established only in the fruit of stream-entry, when that teaching was delivered by the Blessed One with the four paths as its principal feature? Hence it is said, 'Just as,' etc.

Accharāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Accharā Sutta is concluded.

7. Vanaropasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vanaropa Sutta

47. Kesanti [V 1.0109] sāmivasena vuttakasaddo “dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannā”ti ettha paccattabahuvacanavasena pariṇāmetabbo. Atthavasena hi vibhattivipariṇāmo. Ke janāti ettha vā vuttakesaddo sīhavilokananayena ānetvā yojetabboti āha “ke dhammaṭṭhā, ke sīlasampannā”ti? Pucchatīti iminā tattha kāraṇamāha. Phalādisampattiyā āramanti ettha sattāti ārāmo. Ārāme ropenti nipphādentīti ārāmaropā. Vanīyati chāyāsampattiyā bhajīyatīti vanaṃ. Tattha yaṃ upavanalakkhaṇaṃ vanaṃ, taṃ ārāmaggahaṇeneva gahitanti tapovanalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ dassento “sīmaṃ parikkhipitvā”tiādimāha. Visameti udakacikkhallena visame padese. Pānīyaṃ pivanti etthāti papā, taṃ papaṃ. Udakaṃ pīyati etthāti vā papā. Taḷākādīti ādi-saddena mātikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

47. 'Ke santi': the word 'ke' is spoken in a general sense and should be changed to the nominative plural in the phrase 'those established in Dhamma, endowed with virtue.' For a change of case-ending occurs according to the meaning. Or, in the phrase 'what people?', the word 'ke' should be brought forward and connected by the lion's glance method; thus it is said: 'Who are established in Dhamma? Who are endowed with virtue?' By 'he asks,' he states the reason for that. 'Park' (ārāma) is so called because beings delight (āramanti) there due to the attainment of fruits and so on. 'Park-planters' (ārāmaropā) are those who plant and produce in a park. 'Grove' (vana) is so called because it is desired (vanīyati) or frequented (bhajīyati) for its abundance of shade. Therein, the grove characterized as an ornamental grove is included by the term 'park'; showing the grove characterized as a hermitage, he said, 'having enclosed a boundary,' etc. 'On uneven ground' means in an uneven place with water and mud. 'A watering place' (papā) is where they drink (pivanti) drinking water; that is a papā. Or, a papā is where water is drunk (pīyati). In 'tanks and the like,' the word 'like' includes a watercourse.
