It is said that this person, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, practiced the ascetic life for many thousands of years but did not produce any distinction. To explain the reason for this, it is said, 'due to the abundance of defilements,' etc. 'Of one entirely pure' means: of one who is completely pure, wholly undefiled in every way, in such a manner as is conducive to distinction. 'Composed in virtue' means: just as virtue, being progressively developed, is conducive to distinction and partakes of penetration, so too are they those whose minds are rightly composed, whose minds are well-endowed. Being such, they are endowed with it; thus he says 'possessing them.' 'Established in nature' means: being trainees, they are established in their nature with an unshakeable quality by means of the Dhamma they have realized. The Blessed One said, 'Satisfaction brings happiness,' for the purpose of raising a subsequent question, thinking, 'When satisfaction is mentioned by me, the devaputta will say, "Satisfaction is hard to obtain."' One gone forth, dwelling at the foot of a tree or in the open, is called one who has embraced homelessness. But how is this said of one dwelling in a lodging? He says, 'in the seven-storied palace,' etc. 'Contentment with the four requisites' means: the contentment with the four requisites that is perfected through application to meditation. He shows that satisfaction is attained through this calming of the mind. 'By the development of the calming of the mind' means: by the development that pacifies the defilements of the mind. The connection is to be made as: 'the mind delights' in the development that brings about the special calming of the mind by causing a state of non-indulgence in the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth.

Ettha ca indriyūpasamena cittasamādhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti indriyabhāvanāya cittasamādhānassa akārakānaṃ dūrīkaraṇato. Adhicittasamādhānena catupaccayasantoso savisesaṃ parisuddho paripuṇṇo ca hoti paccayānaṃ alābhalābhesu pariccāgasabhāvato. Vuttanayena pana santuṭṭhassa yathāsamādinnaṃ sīlaṃ visujjhati pāripūriñca upagacchati, tathābhūto catusaccakammaṭṭhāne yutto maggapaṭipāṭiyā sabbaso kilese samucchindanto nibbānadiṭṭho hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “ye rattindiva”ntiādinā. Kiṃ na gacchissanti? Gamissantevāti ariyamaggabhāvanaṃ pahāya sammāpaṭipattiyā dukkarabhāvaṃ sandhāya sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Tenāha “ayaṃ pana duggamo bhagavā visamo maggo”ti.

Here, through the calming of the senses, the concentration of the mind becomes complete, because the cultivation of the senses removes that which hinders the mind's concentration. Through higher mental concentration, contentment with the four requisites becomes especially pure and completely fulfilled, due to the nature of relinquishment regarding the gain and loss of those requisites. Moreover, in the manner stated, the morality undertaken by one who is content is purified and reaches full perfection. One in such a state, engaged in the four truths as a basis for meditation, by cutting off all defilements completely through the progression of the path, becomes one who has seen Nibbāna—this meaning is shown by the passage beginning, “Those who day and night…” Why will they not go? They will indeed go—thus, he speaks with doubt, referring to the difficulty of right practice, as if giving up on the development of the noble path. Therefore he said, “But this path, Blessed One, is difficult and uneven.”

Tattha [M 1.0146] keci “ayaṃ panāti devaputto. So hi bhagavato ‘ariyā gacchantī’ti vacanaṃ sutvā ‘duggamo bhagavā’tiādimāhā”ti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati. Yasmā “saccameta”nti evamādipi tasseva vevacanaṃ katvā dassitaṃ, tasmā “yena maggena ariyā gacchantī”ti tumhehi vuttaṃ, ayaṃ pana “duggamo bhagavā visamo maggo”ti āha devaputto. Ariyamaggo kāmaṃ kadāci atidukkhā paṭipadātipi vuccati, tañca kho pubbabhāgapaṭipadāvasena, ayaṃ pana atīva sugamo sabbakilesaduggavivajjanato kāyaduccaritādivisamassa rāgādivisamassa ca dūrīkaraṇato na visamo. Tenāha “pubbabhāgapaṭipadāyā”tiādi. Assāti ariyamaggassa. Ariyamaggassa hi adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ paribundhitabbabhāgena bahū parissayā hontīti. Evaṃ vuttoti “duggamo visamo”ti ca evaṃ vutto.

Therein, some say: “This, however, is a devaputta. For having heard the Blessed One’s statement, ‘The noble ones go,’ he said, ‘This path, Blessed One, is difficult,’ and so forth.” That is not correct. Because statements such as, “This is true,” are also shown to be expressions of that same speaker. Therefore, you said, “By which path the noble ones go,” but this devaputta said, “This path, Blessed One, is difficult and uneven.” Indeed, the noble path is sometimes called a practice of extreme difficulty, but that is in terms of the preliminary practice. This path, however, is very easy because it avoids the difficulty of all defilements, and it is not uneven because it removes the unevenness of bodily misconduct and the unevenness of lust and so forth. Therefore, it is said, “in terms of the preliminary practice,” and so on. ‘Its’ refers to the noble path. For the noble path has many perils due to the part that must be cultivated, such as the training in higher virtue and so on. ‘Thus spoken’ means spoken of as ‘difficult’ and ‘uneven.’

Avaṃsirāti anuṭṭhahanena adhobhūtauttamaṅgā. Kusalaṅgesu hi sammādiṭṭhi uttamaṅgā sabbaseṭṭhattā[V 1.0129], tañca anariyā patanti na uṭṭhahanti micchāpaṭipajjanato. Tenāha “ñāṇasirenā”tiādi. Anariyamaggeti micchāmagge. Tenāha “visame magge”ti. Taṃ magganato anariyā ariyānaṃ maggato apāpuṇanena pariccattā hutvā apāye sakalavaṭṭadukkhe ca patanti. Svevāti svāyaṃ anariyehi kadācipi gantuṃ asakkuṇeyyo maggo ariyānaṃ visuddhasattānaṃ sabbaso samadhigamena samo hoti. Kāyavisamādīhi samannāgatattā visame sattakāye tesaṃ sabbasova pahānena sabbattha samāyeva.

‘Headlong’ (avaṃsirā) means with the highest part brought low due to not rising up. For among the wholesome factors, right view is the highest part due to its being the best of all; and the ignoble fall from it, not rising up because of wrong practice. Therefore, it is said, “with the head of wisdom,” and so on. ‘On the ignoble path’ (anariyamagge) means on the wrong path. Therefore, it is said, “on the uneven path.” By treading that path, the ignoble, being bereft of the path of the noble ones through not attaining it, fall into the states of woe and into all the suffering of the cycle of existence. ‘For them’ (sveva) means: this very path, which an ignoble one is never able to travel, is level for the noble ones, for purified beings, through its complete attainment. For them, in the uneven group of beings possessed of bodily unevenness and so on, through the complete abandonment of all that, they are even in every respect.

Kāmadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kāmada Sutta is concluded.

7. Pañcālacaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Pañcālacaṇḍa Sutta

88. Sambādheti sampīḷitataṇhākilesādinā sauppīḷatāya paramasambādhe. Ativiya saṅkāraṭṭhānabhūto hi nīvaraṇasambādho adhippeto. So hi duggahano tasmiṃ asati kāmaguṇasambādho anavasaro eva seyyathāpi mahākassapādīnaṃ. Okāsanti jhānassetaṃ nāmaṃ nīvaraṇasambādhābhāvato. Asambādhabhāvena hi jhānaṃ idha “okāso”ti vuttaṃ, tañca kho accantāsambādhaṭṭhānatāya vipassanāpādakatāya[M 1.0147]. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “avindī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avindīti vindi paṭilabhi. Bhūrimedhasoti mahāpañño, sapaññoti attho. Abujjhīti bujjhi paṭivijjhi. Paṭilīno hutvā seṭṭho, paṭilīnānaṃ vā seṭṭhoti paṭilīnaseṭṭho. Mānussayavasena unnatabhāvato paṭilīno nāma pahīnamāno. Paṭilabhiṃsūti kāmaguṇasambādhepi “ime kāmaguṇā mādisānaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? Te abhibhuyya nibbānappattiyā sammāsatiṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Tena sampayuttena lokuttarasamādhināpi suṭṭhu samāhitā.

88. ‘In confinement’ (sambādhe) means in extreme confinement, due to being greatly oppressed by oppressive craving, defilements, and so on. The confinement of the hindrances, which is like a refuse heap, is indeed intended. That is difficult to overcome; in its absence, the confinement of sensual pleasures has no opportunity, just as for Mahākassapa and others. ‘Opportunity’ (okāsa) is a name for jhāna, due to the absence of the confinement of the hindrances. Here, jhāna is called ‘opportunity’ because of its unconfined nature, and also because it is a state of complete non-confinement and is a basis for insight. Thus, in the Pāli text, it is said, “he found” (avindī), and so on. There, ‘he found’ means he found, he obtained. ‘Of vast wisdom’ (bhūrimedhaso) means of great wisdom; the meaning is ‘wise.’ ‘He understood’ (abujjhī) means he understood, he penetrated. ‘The best of the withdrawn’ (paṭilīnaseṭṭho) means the best, having withdrawn; or, the best among the withdrawn. ‘Withdrawn’ (paṭilīno) means one who has abandoned pride, due to the loftiness of the human state. ‘They obtained’ (paṭilabhiṃsu) means that even in the confinement of sensual pleasures, thinking, “What can these sensual pleasures do to those like us?” and overcoming them, they obtained right mindfulness for the attainment of Nibbāna. They were also well-concentrated with the associated supramundane concentration.

Ayaṃ kira devaputto ito purimavāre attabhāve paṭhamajjhānalābhī hutvā tato cavitvā brahmakāyikāsu nibbattitvā tattha jhānasukhaṃ anubhavitvā tato cuto idāni kāmabhave nibbatto, tasmā taṃ jhānaṃ sambhāvento “tādisassa nāma jhānasukhassa lābhī bhagavā”ti tena guṇena bhagavantaṃ abhitthavanto “sambādhe vatā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi. Athassa bhagavā yathā nāma aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanasatasahassubbedhasinerupabbatarājaṃ upādāya sāsapo na kiñci hoti, evaṃ anantāparimeyyabuddhaguṇe upādāya rūpāvacarapaṭhamajjhānaṃ na kiñci hotīti dassento “ye sati”ntiādinā anuttaraguṇādhigamaṃ pavedesi. Tattha satinti vipassanāsatiyā saddhiṃ ariyamaggasatiṃ. Susamāhitāti lokiyasamādhinā ceva lokuttarasamādhinā ca suṭṭhu samāhitā. Te [V 1.0130] hi accantaṃ susamāhitā, na jhānamattalābhino akuppadhammattā. Keci “kammante susamāhitā”ti pāṭhaṃ vatvā “maggasamāhitā”ti atthaṃ vadanti.

This devaputta, it is said, in a previous existence had attained the first jhāna. Then, having passed away from there, he was reborn among the Brahmā deities, and after experiencing the bliss of jhāna there, he passed away and was now reborn in the sensual realm. Thus, esteeming that jhāna and praising the Blessed One with that quality, saying, “The Blessed One is an attainer of such jhāna bliss,” he spoke the verse beginning, “In confinement, indeed…” Then the Blessed One, to show that the first jhāna of the form realm is nothing compared to the infinite and immeasurable qualities of a Buddha—just as a mustard seed is nothing compared to Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, which is 168,000 yojanas in height—declared his supreme attainment with the words beginning, “Those who are mindful…” Here, ‘mindful’ (sati) means insight-mindfulness together with noble path-mindfulness. ‘Well-concentrated’ (susamāhitā) means well-concentrated with both mundane and supramundane concentration. Indeed, they are extremely well-concentrated, not merely attainers of jhāna, because of their unshakeable nature. Some, stating the reading is ‘kammante susamāhitā’ (well-concentrated in work), give the meaning ‘concentrated on the path.’

Pañcālacaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pañcālacaṇḍa Sutta is finished.

8. Tāyanasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Tāyana Sutta

89. Atītajātiyaṃ sayaṃkāravasena tāya diṭṭhiyā uppāditattā pubbe titthakaro. Tenāha “diṭṭhi uppādetvā”ti. Apare āhu “ayaṃ me satthāti gahaṇavasena titthakaro assa atthīti pubbe titthakaro, atītattabhāve titthakarasāvako”ti. Te “diṭṭhiṃ uppādetvāti [M 1.0148] tassa satthuno diṭṭhiṃ ādāya gahetvāti attho”ti vadanti. Titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo tabbinimuttassa micchāvādassa abhāvato. Titthe niyuttāti titthikā, te eva titthiyāti vuttā ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā. Tassāti yathāvuttassa kalyāṇakammassa. Nissandenāti phalabhāvena. Vīriyappaṭisaṃyuttāti vīriyadīpanāti attho.

89. Because in a past life he generated that view by his own action, he was previously a founder of a sect (titthakaro). Therefore, it is said, “having generated a view.” Others say: “He was previously a sectarian in the sense that he had a sectarian teacher, by way of grasping, ‘This is my teacher’; in a past existence, he was a disciple of a sectarian teacher.” They say the meaning of ‘having generated a view’ is ‘having taken up and grasped the view of that teacher.’ ‘Sect’ (tittha) refers to the sixty-two views, because there is no wrong teaching apart from them. Those engaged in a sect are titthikā (sectarians); they are also called titthiyā by changing the ‘ka’ to a ‘ya’. ‘Of that’ refers to the wholesome kamma as mentioned. ‘As an outflow’ (nissandena) means by way of result, that is, by way of fruition. ‘Connected with energy’ (vīriyappaṭisaṃyuttā) means showing forth energy; this is the meaning.

Aniyamitaāṇattīti aniyamavidhānaṃ aniyamavasena vidhivacanaṃ. Taṇhāsotanti taṇhāppabandhanaṃ. Nīharāti samehi pajaha. Ekattanti ekaggaṃ. Tenāha “jhāna”nti. Upapajjatīti na uppajjati na pāpuṇātīti āha “na paṭilabhatī”ti. Na osakkeyyāti na saṅkocaṃ āpajjeyya. Gharāvāsato paribbajanaṃ parito apagamoti paribbajo. Pabbajitavatasamādānassa adaḷhatāya ca tattha ca asakkaccakiriyāya sithilagahitā. Atirekanti pabbajjāya purimakālatopi adhikaṃ. Uparīti uparūpari. Dukkaṭaṃ akatameva seyyoti duccaritaṃ nāma sabbena sabbaṃ akatameva hitāvahaṃ.

‘An unfixed injunction’ (aniyamitaāṇatti) means an unfixed regulation, a statement of a rule in an unfixed way. ‘The stream of craving’ (taṇhāsotaṃ) means the continuity of craving. ‘Remove’ (nīhara) means abandon with equanimity. ‘Oneness’ (ekattaṃ) means one-pointedness. Therefore, it is said, ‘jhāna.’ ‘Is not suitable’ (na upapajjati) means is not born, does not attain; it is said to mean ‘does not obtain.’ ‘One should not draw back’ (na osakkeyya) means one should not shrink back. ‘Wandering’ (paribbajo) means a complete going forth from the household life. ‘Loosely grasped’ (sithilagahitā) refers to the lack of firmness in undertaking the renunciate's vows and to careless practice therein. ‘Exceedingly’ (atirekaṃ) means more than, even more than the time before renunciation. ‘Above’ (upari) means higher and higher. ‘A wrong deed is better not done’ (dukkaṭaṃ akatameva seyyo) means that misconduct is entirely better not done at all, as it is not conducive to welfare.

Yaṃ kiñcīti yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ. Sithilaṃ katanti asakkaccakāritāya sithilaṃ katvā pavattitaṃ. Evarūpamevāti evarūpaṃ parāmaṭṭhasāmaññasadisameva pacchānutāpacariyādipaṭibhāgato. Saṃkiliṭṭhameva taṇhāsaṃkilesaupakkiliṭṭhattā. Āsaṅkitaparisaṅkitantiādito samantatopi parehi saṅkitaṃ. Brahmacariyassa ādi ādibrahmacariyaṃ, tattha niyuttāti ādibrahmacariyikā, maggabrahmacariyassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāti attho. Tenāha “maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtā”ti. Pubbapadhānabhūtāti paṭhamārambhabhūtā.

"Yaṃ kiñci" means whatever action it may be. "Sithilaṃ kataṃ" means done carelessly, performed in a lax manner because of being done without due care. "Evarūpameva" means just like that, similar to the general characteristic that is grasped, in terms of being a counterpart to remorseful conduct and so forth. "Saṃkiliṭṭhameva" means thoroughly defiled because of being defiled by the defilement of craving. "Āsaṅkitaparisaṅkitaṃ" means suspected by others from the beginning and from all sides. The beginning of the holy life is the initial holy life; those devoted to that are called those engaged in the initial holy life, meaning the preliminary practice for the path of the holy life. Hence it is said, "they are the initial stage of the path of the holy life." "Pubbapadhānabhūtā" means being the initial undertaking.

Tāyanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tāyana Sutta is concluded.

9. Candimasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Candima Sutta

90. Vimāne [V 1.0131] gahite taṃnivāsīpi gahito hotīti vuttaṃ “candavimānavāsī devaputto”ti. Sabbadhīti sabbasmā duggaṭṭhānā vippamuttosi bhagavā tvaṃ, tasmā mayhampi ito sambādhaṭṭhānato vippamokkhaṃ karohīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “tassa me saraṇaṃ bhavā”ti. Lokānukampakāti sabbassa [M 1.0149] lokassa anuggahā, tasmā tuyhampi etassapi candassa. Tādisā evāti samānā eva. Pamuñcasīti pamuñcittha. Tenāha “atītatthe vattamānavacana”nti.

90. When a celestial mansion is seized, its resident is also seized; thus it is said, "the devaputta dwelling in the moon mansion." By "sabbadhī" it is meant: You, Blessed One, are freed from all difficult situations; therefore, may you also bring about my release from this confined place—this is the intention. Hence it is said, "Be my refuge." By "lokānukampakā" is meant compassion for the whole world; therefore, for you also and for this moon. By "tādisā eva" is meant just the same. By "pamuñcasī" is meant "pamuñcittha." Hence it is said, "a present tense verb used in the sense of the past."

Candimasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Candima Sutta is concluded.

10. Sūriyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sūriya Sutta

91. Andhabhāvakaraṇeti lokassa andhakaraṇetipi apare. Tenāha “tamasī”ti. Virocatīti vijjotati. Kāmaṃ devaputtavasena paṭhamaṃ devatā uddhaṭā, rāhuno pana payogo tassa vimāneti āha “maṇḍalīti maṇḍalasaṇṭhāno”ti. Vadati tadā mukhena gahitattā. Mukhena gahaṇañcettha “gilī”ti adhippetaṃ, na ca ajjhoharaṇanti āha “gilīti vadatī”ti. Idāni tassa mukhena gahaṇasamatthataṃ dassetuṃ “rāhussa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sotiādi tassa candimasūriyānaṃ gahaṇakāraṇadassanaṃ. Adhivatthā devatāti candimasūriyānaṃ paricārakadevatā. Veganti javaṃ. So hi kenaci abhimukhaṃ atidunnivāro kammaniyāmasiddho. Matthakanti kaṇṭhassa uparimadesaṃ. Keci “sīsamatthakamevā”ti vadanti. Nikkhameyya vegassa tikkhasīghathāmabhāvato. Ākaḍḍhitvāti attano gamanadisābhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā. Nanti rāhuṃ. Uddhaṃ ullaṅghetukāmampi onameyya. Padadvayenapi so mahāsarīro mahābalo, candimasūriyānaṃ pana gamanavego tena sabbathāpi dunnivāriyovāti dasseti. Vimānenāti candaggahe candavimānena, sūriyaggahe sūriyavimānena ubhinnampi vimānena saheva. Amāvāsiyañhi dve vimānāni yojanamattantaritāni hutvā saheva pavattanti. Yadi dvepi devaputtā sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā, atha kasmā sūriyasutte eva “pajaṃ mama”nti vuttaṃ, na candasutteti? “So ca kira na cirasseva tato cavitvā aññattha nibbatto, aññā eva ca devatā tattha vasi, yasmiṃ candaggahe bhagavā taṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi, na tathā sūriyo, aparabhāge pana tatthapi kālena kālaṃ rāhuggaho hotī”ti vadanti.

91. By "andhabhāvakaraṇe" is meant causing darkness to the world; others say it means causing blindness. Hence it is said, "tamasī." By "virocati" is meant it illuminates. Although first the deity was mentioned in the form of a devaputta, Rāhu’s attack is on his mansion; hence it is said, "maṇḍalīti maṇḍalasaṇṭhāno." By "vadati": he speaks at that time because he has been seized by the mouth. And here, this seizing by the mouth is what is meant by "gilī," but it is not actual swallowing; hence it is said, "gilīti vadatī." Now, to show his ability to seize with his mouth, "rāhussa hī," etc., is said. The phrase beginning with "so" shows the reason for seizing the moon and sun. By "adhivatthā devatā" are meant the attendant deities of the moon and sun. By "vegaṃ" is meant swiftness. Indeed, he is exceedingly difficult for anyone to restrain directly, being established by the fixed order of kamma. By "matthakaṃ" is meant the region above the throat. Some say it means only the top of the head. He might emerge due to the sharp, swift, and forceful nature of his speed. By "ākaḍḍhitvā" is meant dragging them toward his own direction of movement. By "naṃ" is meant Rāhu. Even if he wishes to leap upward, he would bend them down. It is shown that although he is great-bodied and mighty, even with two feet, the speed of the movement of the moon and sun is entirely difficult for him to resist. By "vimānena" is meant with the moon’s mansion during a lunar eclipse, and with the sun’s mansion during a solar eclipse—with both mansions together. For, on the new moon day, the two mansions, being a yojana apart, move together. If both devaputtas had attained the fruit of stream-entry, then why in the Sūriya Sutta is it said "pajaṃ mama," but not in the Canda Sutta? They say: "Indeed, not long after, he passed away from there and was reborn elsewhere, and another deity dwelt there, at which lunar eclipse the Blessed One spoke that verse; it was not so for the sun. In a later period, however, from time to time an eclipse by Rāhu occurred there too."

Sūriyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sūriya Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Anāthapiṇḍikavaggo

2. The Anāthapiṇḍika Chapter

1. Candimasasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Candimasa Sutta

92. Pabbatataṭā [V 1.0132][M 1.0150] sandamāno tathārūpo nadīnivattanapadesopi sambādhaṭṭhānatāya kaccho viyāti āha “pabbatakacchepī”ti. Paṭipakkhadūrībhāvena seṭṭhaṭṭhena ca eko udetīti ekodi, ekaggatā. Tasmiṃ yogato ekaggacittā idha ekodī. Paṭipakkhato attānaṃ nipayanti visodhentīti nipakā, paññavanto. Tenāha “ekaggacittā cevā”tiādi. Kāyādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ sātisayāya satiyā sarantīti satā. Tenāha “satimanto”ti. Sotthiṃ gamissantīti yathāvuttapadese magā sotthimanupaddavena vattissanti, evaṃ jhānalābhino sotthiṃ kilesehi anupaddutā vattissanti. Ayaṃ kira devaputto brahmaloke nibbānasaññī, tasmā evamāha. Bhagavā “ayaṃ devaputto anibbānagāmī samāno nibbānagāmisaññī, handassa nibbānagāmino dassemī”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Catunnaṃ oghānaṃ, saṃsāramahoghasseva vā paratīrabhāvato paratīranti nibbānaṃ. Ambuni jāto ambujo, maccho. Suttajālaṃ chinditvā macchā viya kilesajālaṃ bhinditvā gamissantīti.

92. By "pabbatakacchepi" is meant a place where the river turns back, flowing down from the mountain slope, being a confined area like a marsh. By "ekodi" it is meant that being far from opposition and supreme in meaning, it arises alone; it means one-pointedness. Those with one-pointed mind, because of their meditation, are "ekodī" here. By "nipakā" is meant those who purify themselves by repelling opposition, meaning those endowed with wisdom. Hence it is said, "with one-pointed mind," and so forth. By "satā" is meant those who remember the object, whether body or otherwise, with surpassing mindfulness. Hence it is said, "the mindful ones." By "sotthiṃ gamissanti" it is meant that just as deer in the aforementioned place will live safely and unmolested, so too will those who attain jhāna live safely, unmolested by the defilements. This devaputta, it seems, perceived the idea of Nibbāna in the Brahma-world, hence he spoke thus. The Blessed One thought, "This devaputta, though not going to Nibbāna, perceives himself as going to Nibbāna. Come, let me show him those who do go to Nibbāna," and so he spoke the second verse. By "paratīraṃ" is meant Nibbāna, because it is the far shore of the four floods, or of the great flood of saṃsāra itself. By "ambuja" is meant that which is born in the water, a fish. Just as fish, having broken through the fishing net, go forth, so too will they, having broken through the net of defilements, go forth.

Candimasasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Candimasa Sutta is concluded.

2. Veṇḍusuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Veṇḍu Sutta

93. Payirupāsiyāti payirupāsahetu. Sikkhantīti tissopi sikkhā sikkhanti. Siṭṭhipadeti kilesānaṃ sāsanato vaṭṭadukkhaparittāsanato ca siṭṭhisaññite yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjitabbato pade, saddhammeti attho. Tenāha “anusiṭṭhipade”ti. Tattha anusiṭṭhīti saddhammo. Kāleti yuttapattakāle. Appamādonāma samathavipassanābhāvanā.

93. By "payirupāsiyā" is meant for the purpose of attending. By "sikkhanti" is meant they train in the threefold training. By "siṭṭhipade" is meant in the path, called "siṭṭhi" because of disciplining defilements and deliverance from the suffering of the round, which is to be practiced as instructed; the meaning is the good Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, "anusiṭṭhipade." Here, by "anusiṭṭhi" is meant the good Dhamma. By "kāle" is meant at the fitting time. "Appamāda" means the development of serenity and insight.

Veṇḍusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Veṇḍu Sutta is concluded.

3. Dīghalaṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta

94. Tatheva [M 1.0151] paññāyīti dīghalaṭṭhitveva paññāyi, tathāsamaññā eva ahosi.

94. By "Tatheva paññāyi" is meant he was known as Dīghalaṭṭhi; such was his designation.

Dīghalaṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta is concluded.

4. Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nandana Sutta

95. Natthi [V 1.0133] etassa āvaṭṭaṃ āvaraṇanti anāvaṭaṃ. Rukkho vā pabbato vāti sattānaṃ pakaticakkhussa āvaraṇabhūto rukkho viya pabbato viya ca abhibhavituṃ samattho ñeyyāvaraṇo natthi. Kathaṃvidhanti kathaṃsaṇṭhitaṃ, kathaṃpakāraṃ vā. Dukkhanti vaṭṭadukkhaṃ.

95. By "anāvaṭaṃ" is meant: "Natthi etassa āvaṭṭaṃ āvaraṇaṃ" (There is no turning back for him, no obstruction). By "Rukkho vā pabbato vā" is meant there is no obstruction of knowledge capable of overpowering him, like a tree or a mountain which are obstacles to the natural sight of beings. By "Kathaṃvidhaṃ" is meant of what structure, or of what manner. By "Dukkhaṃ" is meant the suffering of the round.

Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nandana Sutta is concluded.

5. Candanasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Candana Sutta

96. Heṭṭhāti kāmabhave. Tattha hi paribbhamantassa patiṭṭhā dullabhā yebhuyyena tattha sattā nimuggā eva honti, tasmā heṭṭhā appatiṭṭho saṃsāro. Uparīti mahaggatabhave. Tattha hi nibbattassa nibbānaṃ āruhituṃ ālambanā dullabhā, jhānābhiratiyā tattheva nikanti tesaṃ balavatī hoti, tasmā upari anālambano saṃsāro. Pesitattoti nibbānaṃ pati pesitacitto. Tayo kammābhisaṅkhārāti puññābhisaṅkhārādayo tayo abhisaṅkhārā. Tena “nandīpubbako kammabhavo”ti vatvā “nandiṃ janetvā”ti vutto. Kāmasaññāsīsena kāmacchandassa gahaṇaṃ, kāmacchandapamukhāni ca orambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni gahitānīti āha “kāmasaññāgahaṇena pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanānī”ti. Rūpabhavo rūpaṃ bhavapadalopena. Rūpabhavaggahaṇena cettha sesabhavassapi gahaṇaṃ. Tassa saṃyojanaggahaṇena pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni gahitāni. Mahogheti [M 1.0152] saṃsāramahoghe. Tesanti kāmabhavādīnaṃ gahaṇena bhavabhāvena tadekalakkhaṇatāya. Arūpabhavo gahito lakkhaṇahāranayena. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

96. ‘Below’ refers to the realm of sensual existence. There, for one wandering in it, a foothold is hard to find; for the most part, beings there are submerged, therefore the cycle of existence below is without a foothold. ‘Above’ refers to the sublime existence. There, for one reborn in it, a support for ascending to Nibbāna is hard to find; their delight in meditative absorption is strong, causing them to cling to that very state. Therefore, the cycle of existence above is without support. ‘Sent forth’ means one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna. ‘The three kamma-formations’ are the three formations beginning with the meritorious one. Therefore, having said, ‘Kamma-existence is preceded by delight,’ it is said, ‘having generated delight.’ By the term ‘sensual perception,’ the grasping of sensual desire is meant, and the five lower fetters, headed by sensual desire, are included. Hence it is said, ‘By the grasping of sensual perception, the five lower fetters are meant.’ ‘Existence of form’ is a shortened form of ‘the existence of form.’ Here, by mentioning the existence of form, the remaining existences are also included. By mentioning its fetters, the five higher fetters are included. ‘The great flood’ is the great flood of saṃsāra. Of these, by grasping the sensual existence and so on, they are taken as having a single characteristic due to their nature as existence. The formless existence is included by the method of characteristic inference. The rest is easily understood.

Candanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Candana Sutta is concluded.

6. Vāsudattasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Vāsudatta Sutta

97. Chaṭṭhaṃ heṭṭhā devatāsaṃyuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttatthameva.

97. The sixth has the same meaning as stated previously in the commentary on the Devatāsaṃyutta.

Vāsudattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vāsudatta Sutta is concluded.

7. Subrahmasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Subrahma Sutta

98. Subrahmāti tassa devaputtassa nāmaṃ. Tassa satthu santikūpasaṅkamanassa kāraṇaṃ dassento [V 1.0134] “so kirā”tiādimāha. Tadeva sokaṃ tassa devaputtassa aṭṭhuppatti. Accharāsaṅghaparivutoti sahassamattena accharāsaṅghena parivuto. Nandanakīḷikanti nandanavanakīḷikaṃ. Hatthaṃ āgacchatīti hatthagayhupago hoti. Ganthentīti ettha mālāveṭhanampi khiḍḍāpasutatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññathā pupphāniyeva tāya tāya cittassa vasena mālābhāvena hatthaṃ upagacchantīti. Upacchedakakammavasenāti tasmiṃ devaloke āyusese sati eva tassa pana upaghātakassa laddhokāsassa pāpakammassa vasena. “Pahāro”ti divasassa tatiyo bhāgo vuccati, tasmā ekappahārenevāti ekavelāyamevāti attho.

98. ‘Subrahmā’ is the name of that devaputta. To show the reason for his approaching the Teacher, it is said, ‘He, it is said,’ and so on. That very sorrow was the origin of the story of that devaputta. ‘Surrounded by a host of nymphs’ means surrounded by a host of about a thousand nymphs. ‘Sporting in Nandana’ means sporting in the Nandana Grove. ‘Comes to hand’ means it comes within reach of the hand. ‘Binding’: here, it should be understood that this is the winding of garlands, due to being intent on play. Otherwise, the flowers themselves, according to this or that inclination of the mind, come to hand in the form of garlands. ‘Due to a destructive kamma’: while there was still a remainder of life in that deva world, it was due to the power of a destructive evil kamma that had found its opportunity. ‘A pahāra’: the third part of the day is called a pahāra; therefore, ‘in a single pahāra’ means at a single time.

Piyavatthukasokenāti piyavatthunimittakena sokena. Ruppamānoti pīḷiyamāno. Sattame divaseti manussagaṇanāya sattame divase. Tatthevāti tasmiṃyeva niraye nibbattitabbaṃ iminā tāhi ca saheva pubbe tassa pāpakammassa katattā. Ruppīti cittasantāsaṃ āpajji. Niddhamitunti nīharituṃ apanetuṃ. Satthu santikaṃ gantvāti tāhi pañcasatāhi accharāhi saddhiṃ bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā.

‘By sorrow based on a dear object’ means by sorrow caused by a dear object. ‘Being vexed’ means being afflicted. ‘On the seventh day’ means on the seventh day by human reckoning. ‘In that very place’ means one will be reborn in that very hell because of having previously committed that evil deed together with them. ‘Was vexed’ means experiencing mental terror. ‘To dispel’ means to drive out or remove. ‘Having gone to the Teacher’s presence’ means going to the Blessed One’s presence together with those five hundred nymphs.

Idanti [M 1.0153] attano cittaṃ dasseti āsannapaccakkhabhāvato. Niccanti sadā. Svāyaṃ niccattho adhippāyavasena gahetabboti tattha pahātabbaṃ gahetabbañca dassento “devaloke”tiādimāha. Na gahetabbo hetupavattito pubbe tassa utrāsassa abhāvato. Tesūti dukkhesu. Tāni hi hetupaccayehi kattabbato gāthāyaṃ “kicchesū”ti vuttāni. Kicchesūti vā kicchanimittaṃ. Yāsañhi payogavipattīnaṃ vasenassa tāni dukkhāni uppajjeyyuṃ, taṃnimittanti attho. Tā hi assa payogavipattiyo gativipattiyo satthu santikaṃ upagamanena hāyeyyuṃ. Nibbattānaṃ diṭṭhānīti nibbattānaṃ vasena diṭṭhāni dukkhāni. Tesu ca dukkhesu. Sabbattha nimittatthe bhummaṃ. Ḍayhamāno viya cittasantāpena.

‘This’ indicates one's own mind due to its being near and directly perceptible. ‘Constantly’ means always. This meaning of ‘constantly’ should be understood according to the intention; showing what should be abandoned and what should be taken up, ‘in the deva world,’ and so on, is stated. It should not be understood as having a prior cause, because previously there was no such dread. ‘In these’ refers to sufferings. Since these are brought about by causes and conditions, they are called ‘in difficulties’ in the verse. Or ‘in difficulties’ means the cause of difficulty. The meaning is that those sufferings arise due to failure of effort. Those failures of effort and wrong destinies would be abandoned by approaching the Teacher. ‘Of the reborn, seen’ means sufferings seen by way of the reborn. And in those sufferings. Everywhere, the locative case is in the sense of a cause. As if burning with mental torment.

Cattāripi saccāni bujjhati paṭivijjhatīti bodhi, satiādidhammasāmaggī, tasmā bojjhā bodhito. Sā pana bodhi bhāvanākāreneva pavattati, aññatrasaddayogena ca “bojjhā”ti nissakkavacananti tadatthaṃ dassento muñcitvāpadaṃ apekkhitvā “bojjhaṅgabhāvana”nti āha. Tapoguṇanti dhutadhammamāha. So hi taṇhāloluppassa tapanato tapo, sayaṃ guṇasabhāvattā guṇasannissayato ca guṇanti. Tenāha “dhutaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ tapoguṇa”nti. Sabbe saṅkhāragatā nissajjīyanti etthāti sabbanissaggo, asaṅkhatadhātūti āha “sabbanissaggāti nibbānato”ti.

‘Enlightenment’ (bodhi) is so called because one awakens to and penetrates the four truths; it is the harmony of mental factors beginning with mindfulness. Therefore, from ‘bodhi’ comes ‘bojjhā’ (factors of enlightenment). That enlightenment proceeds only in the manner of development, and by connection with another word, ‘bojjhā’ is a term indicating escape. To show that meaning, with reference to the word ‘having been released,’ he said, ‘the development of the factors of enlightenment.’ ‘The quality of austerity’ refers to the ascetic practices. For it is ‘austerity’ (tapo) from tormenting the greed of craving, and it is a ‘quality’ (guṇa) because it has a virtuous nature and is a basis for virtue. Therefore, he said, ‘the quality of austerity known as the ascetic factors.’ ‘Where all conditioned things are relinquished,’ thus it is ‘total relinquishment,’ the unconditioned element. Thus he said, ‘from total relinquishment’ means from Nibbāna.

Indriyasaṃvarova [V 1.0135] paṭhamaṃ veditabbo paṭipattikkamavasena tasseva paṭhamattā. Taṃ pana paṭipattikkamaṃ dassetuṃ “indriyasaṃvare hī”tiādimāha. Nippariyāyato maggapariyāpannā eva bojjhaṅgāti āha “sahavipassanāya bojjhaṅge”ti. Tassāti tathābhāvena tassa yogino. Yasmā devaputtassa satthā taṃ gāthaṃ vatvā upari ca saccāni pakāsesi, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhagavā catusaccavasena desanaṃ vinivattesī”ti. Devaputto sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahīti kāmaṃ tasseva visesādhigamo idhāgato, pañcasatamattāhi pana accharāhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahīti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106) “so desanāpariyosāne pañcahi accharāsatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya taṃ sampattiṃ thāvaraṃ katvā devalokameva agamāsī”ti.

Restraint of the senses should be understood first, as it is the first step in the order of practice. To illustrate that order of practice, it is said, ‘For in restraint of the senses,’ and so on. The enlightenment factors are included in the path in a definitive manner; hence it is said, ‘the enlightenment factors together with insight.’ ‘His’ refers to that yogī in that state. Since the Teacher, after reciting that verse to the devaputta, further revealed the truths, it is said, ‘the Blessed One concluded the teaching by way of the four truths.’ The devaputta became established in the fruit of stream-entry—indeed, his special attainment is mentioned here. However, it should be understood that he became established in the fruit of stream-entry along with five hundred nymphs. Therefore, it is said in the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.373; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.106): ‘At the conclusion of the teaching, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry along with five hundred nymphs and, having made that attainment firm, returned to the deva world.’

Subrahmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Subrahma Sutta is concluded.

8. Kakudhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Kakudha Sutta

99. “Nandāmī”ti [M 1.0154] vutte nandī nāma pabbajitassa malanti codetukāmo devaputto “nandasī”ti pucchi. Athassa bhagavā taṃ paṭikkhipanto “kiṃ laddhā”ti? Āha. Tena “tayā mama adhippetanandiyā idha paccayo eva natthi, kuto sā nandī”ti dasseti. Tenāha “tuṭṭhi nāmā”tiādi. Atha devaputto nandiyā asati sokena bhavitabbaṃ, soko ca pabbajitassa malanti codento āha “tena hi, samaṇa, socasī”ti. Bhagavā tampi paṭikkhipanto “kiṃ jīyitthā”tiādimāha. Kiṃ maṃ jinātīti attho?

99. When it was said, ‘I delight,’ the devaputta, wishing to object that delight is a defilement for one who has gone forth, asked, ‘Do you delight?’ Then the Blessed One, rejecting that, asked, ‘Having gained what?’ By this, he shows, ‘For the delight you have in mind for me, there is no cause here—so whence that delight?’ Therefore, he said, ‘Contentment is called…’ Then the devaputta, objecting that if there is no delight there must be sorrow, and sorrow too is a defilement for one who has gone forth, said, ‘Well then, recluse, do you sorrow?’ The Blessed One, rejecting that as well, said, ‘What was lost?’ The meaning is, ‘What conquers me?’

Yadi te nandisokā na santi hāsavatthuno lābhassa jāniyā ca abhāvato, ekavihārino pana aratiyā bhavitabbanti āha – “kacci taṃ ekamāsīnaṃ, aratī nābhikīratī”ti. Tasmimpi bhagavatā paṭikkhitte atha nesampi nandisokāratīnaṃ abhāve kāraṇaṃ pucchanto “kathaṃ tva”nti gāthamāha? Athassa bhagavā taṃ kāraṇaṃ pavedento “aghajātassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha aghajātassāti aghe jātassa. Tenāha “vaṭṭadukkhe ṭhitassā”ti. Jātataṇhassa appahīnataṇhassa vaṭṭadukkhaṃ āgatameva kāraṇassa appahīnattā. Tasseva hi kāraṇassa appahīnataṃ dassento “dukkhī sukhaṃ patthayatīti hi vutta”nti āha. Dukkhappavattiyā sāpi taṇhāppavatti tena dassitā. Itītiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ nigamanavasena dasseti.

If for you there are no joys and sorrows due to the absence of a basis for laughter and of loss of gain, yet for one dwelling alone, discontent should arise—thus he said: “Surely, as you sit alone, does discontent not overwhelm you?” When that was rejected by the Blessed One, then, regarding the absence of joy, sorrow, and discontent, he asks for the reason, speaking the verse, “How then?” Then the Blessed One, explaining that reason, spoke the verse: “For one born into misery.” Therein, “for one born into misery” means born in misery. Therefore, it is said: “For one established in the suffering of the cycle.” For one in whom craving has arisen, for one with unabandoned craving, the suffering of the cycle has indeed come because the cause has not been abandoned. Indeed, to show the non-abandonment of that very cause, it is said: “One who suffers longs for happiness.” Through the occurrence of suffering, the occurrence of craving is also shown. Thus, by way of conclusion, the very meaning that has been stated is shown.

Kakudhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kakudha Sutta is concluded.

9. Uttarasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Uttara Sutta

100. Navamanti [V 1.0136] uttarasuttaṃ heṭṭhā devatāsaṃyuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttatthameva.

100. The ninth is the Uttara Sutta, whose meaning has already been explained in the Commentary on the Devatāsaṃyutta.

Uttarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Uttara Sutta is concluded.

10. Anāthapiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Anāthapiṇḍika Sutta

101. Dasame [M 1.0155] kāmaṃ devatāsaṃyuttepi “idaṃ hi taṃ jetavana”ntiādinā imā eva gāthā āgatā. Tattha “aññatarā devatā”ti nidānaṃ āropitaṃ. Heṭṭhā āgatanayattā eva hi potthakesu na likhitaṃ, idha pana devaputtasaṃyutte “anāthapiṇḍiko devaputto”ti nidāne nigame ca āgataṃ, tattha devaputtena satthu vuttappakāraguṇapavedanavasena vuttaṃ. Satthā pana bhikkhūnaṃ tamatthaṃ pavedento “aññataro devaputto”ti āha. Tathā pavedane pana kāraṇaṃ dassento “ānandattherassā”tiādimāha. Anumānabuddhiyāti anumānañāṇassa. Ānubhāvappakāsanatthanti baladīpanatthaṃ.

101. In the tenth, indeed, in the Devatāsaṃyutta too, these very verses appear, beginning with “This is indeed that Jetavana.” There, the introduction is set up as “a certain deity.” Indeed, because it follows the method already presented, it is not written in the books. Here, however, in the Devaputtasaṃyutta, it appears in the introduction and the conclusion as “the devaputta Anāthapiṇḍika,” where it was spoken by the devaputta by way of proclaiming the qualities of the Teacher of the kind that had been described. The Teacher, however, explaining that matter to the bhikkhus, said, “a certain devaputta.” And showing the reason for explaining it thus, he said, “of the Elder Ānanda,” and so on. “By inferential intelligence” means of inferential knowledge. “To reveal his power” means to demonstrate his strength.

Anāthapiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anāthapiṇḍika Sutta is concluded.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

3. Nānātitthiyavaggo

3. The Chapter on Various Sectarians

1. Sivasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Siva Sutta

102. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhamanti tatiyavagge paṭhamasuttaṃ. Vuttatthameva heṭṭhā satullapakāyikavagge paṭhamasutte.

102. The first of the third chapter means the first sutta in the third chapter. The meaning is as stated previously in the first sutta of the Satullapakāyika group.

Sivasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Siva Sutta is concluded.

2. Khemasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Khema Sutta

103. Paṭhamaṃyevāti jarāmaraṇādibhāvato pageva. Balavacintanaṃ cintetīti yathā sākaṭiko ajānitvā visame magge sakaṭaṃ pājento akkhe chinne patikātuṃ avisahanto dukkhī [V 1.0137] dummano balavacintanaṃ cinteti, mahantaṃ cittasantāpaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ adhammavādī maccumukhaṃ patto balavacittasantāpaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā dhammacariyāya nappamajjitabbanti.

103. ‘Even at first’ means even before the state of aging, death, and so on. ‘He thinks a strong thought’ means: just as a cart driver, not knowing the path is uneven, drives his cart, and when the axle is broken, being unable to repair it, he becomes miserable and dejected and thinks a strong thought, experiencing great mental torment; so too an adherent of a wrong teaching, having reached the mouth of death, experiences strong mental torment. Therefore, one should not be heedless in the practice of the Dhamma.

Khemasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Khema Sutta is concluded.

3. Serīsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Serī Sutta

104. Yaṃ [M 1.0156] dānaṃ demīti yaṃ deyyadhammaṃ parassa demi. Tassa pati hutvāti tabbisayaṃ lobhaṃ suṭṭhu abhibhavanto tassa adhipati hutvā demi tena anākaḍḍhanīyattā. “Na dāso na sahāyo”ti vatvā tadubhayaṃ anvayato byatirekato dassetuṃ “yo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dāso hutvā deti taṇhāya dāsabyassa upagatattā. Sahāyo hutvā deti tassa piyabhāvāvissajjanato. Sāmī hutvā deti taṇhādāsabyato attānaṃ mocetvā abhibhuyya pavattanato. Sāmiparibhogasadisā hetassāyaṃ pavattatīti.

104. ‘The gift I give’ means the thing-to-be-given that I give to another. ‘Having become its master’ means: having thoroughly overcome greed regarding that object, I give as its lord, because of not being drawn back by it. After saying “not as a slave, not as a friend,” in order to show both of these positively and negatively, “for one who…” and so on is said. One gives as a slave because one has fallen into the state of slavery to craving. One gives as a friend because of not relinquishing the state of fondness for it. One gives as a master because one acts having freed oneself from slavery to craving and having overcome it. For this occurs similarly to the enjoyment of a master.

Atha vā yo dānasīlatāya dāyako puggalo, so dāne pavattibhedena dānadāso dānasahāyo dānapatīti tippakāro hotīti dasseti. Tadassa tippakārataṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “yo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dātabbaṭṭhena dānaṃ, annapānādi. Tattha yaṃ attanā paribhuñjati taṇhādhipannatāya, tassa vase vattanato dāso viya hoti. Yaṃ paresaṃ dīyati, tatthapi annapānasāmaññena idaṃ vuttaṃ “dānasaṅkhātassa deyyadhammassa dāso hutvā detī”ti. Sahāyo hutvā deti attanā paribhuñjitabbassa paresaṃ dātabbassa ca samasamaṭṭhapanena. Pati hutvā deti sayaṃ deyyadhammassa vase avattitvā tassa attano vase vattāpanato.

Alternatively, it is shown that a person who is a giver by nature of generosity is of three kinds according to the different ways of acting in giving: a slave of giving, a friend of giving, and a master of giving. To show this threefold nature by analyzing it, “for one who…” and so on is said. A gift, in the sense of what is to be given, is food, drink, and so on. Therein, regarding what one enjoys oneself, because of being overcome by craving, one is like a slave by being under its control. Regarding what is given to others, there too, this is said in the general sense of food and drink: “one gives having become a slave to the thing-to-be-given, which is known as a gift.” One gives as a friend by placing on an equal footing what is to be enjoyed by oneself and what is to be given to others. One gives as a master by not being under the control of the thing-to-be-given oneself, but by making it be under one's own control.

Aparo nayo – yo attanā paṇītaṃ paribhuñjitvā paresaṃ nihīnaṃ deti, so dānadāso nāma tannimittanihīnabhāvāpattito. Yo yādisaṃ attanā paribhuñjati, tādisameva paresaṃ deti, so dānasahāyo nāma tannimittanihīnādhikabhāvavissajjanena sadisabhāvāpattito. Yo attanā nihīnaṃ paribhuñjitvā paresaṃ paṇītaṃ deti, so dānapati nāma tannimittaseṭṭhabhāvappattito. Kammasarikkhako hi vipāko, tasmā devaputto “dānapatī”ti vadanto “ahaṃ tādiso ahosi”nti dasseti.

Another way: one who enjoys what is excellent himself and gives what is inferior to others is called a slave of giving, because of incurring an inferior state on account of that. One who gives to others the same kind of thing that he enjoys himself is called a friend of giving, because by abandoning the states of inferior and superior on account of that, he attains a state of similarity. One who enjoys what is inferior himself and gives what is excellent to others is called a master of giving, because of attaining a superior state on account of that. For the result is similar to the deed; therefore the devaputta, saying “master of giving,” shows “I was of that kind.”

“Catūsu dvāresu dānaṃ dīyitthā”ti pāḷiyaṃ saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “tassa kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dānanti yiṭṭhaṃ, tañca kho sabbasādhāraṇavasena katanti āha “samaṇa [V 1.0138] …pe… yācakāna”nti. Pabbajjūpagatāti [M 1.0157] yaṃ kiñci pabbajjaṃ upagatā. Bhovādinoti jātimattabrāhmaṇe vadati. Nālattha buddhasuññattā tadā lokassa. Duggatāti dukkhajīvikakappakā kasiravuttikā. Tenāha “daliddamanussā”ti. Kasivāṇijjādijīvikaṃ anuṭṭhātuṃ asamatthā idha “kapaṇā”ti adhippetāti āha “kāṇakuṇiādayo”ti. Pathāvinoti addhikā. Vanibbakāti dāyakānaṃ guṇakittanakammaphalakittanavasena yācakā seyyathāpi naggādayo. Tenāha “iṭṭhaṃ dinna”ntiādi. Pasatamattanti vīhitaṇḍulādivasena vuttaṃ. Sarāvamattanti yāgubhattādivasena. Yathā gāmalābho gāme uppajjanako āyalābho, evaṃ tattha dvāralābhoti āha “tattha uppajjanakasatasahasse”ti. Mahantataraṃ dānaṃ adaṃsu aññassapi dhanassa viniyogaṃ gatattā. Taṃ sandhāyāti taṃ mahantataraṃ dānaṃ kataṃ sandhāya. Rañño hi tattha dānaṃ itthāgārassa dānena mahatā abhibhūtaṃ viya paṭinivattaṃ hotīti āha “paṭinivattī”ti. Kocīti bhummatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Tenāha “katthacī”ti. Anekavassasahassāyukakāle tassa uppannattā asītivassasahassāni so rājā dānamadāsīti.

To elaborate on the meaning stated briefly in the Pāḷi text, “A gift should be given at the four gates,” the words “For him, it is said,” and so on are stated. ‘A gift’ means an offering, and it was made in a way common to all; hence it is said, “for recluses … beggars.” ‘Those who have gone forth’ means those who have undertaken any kind of going forth. ‘Those who say ‘bho’’ refers to brahmins merely by birth. He did not attain because at that time the world was empty of a Buddha. ‘The unfortunate’ means those with a miserable livelihood, those living with difficulty. Hence it is said, “destitute people.” Those unable to make a living by farming, trade, and so on are here intended by ‘the wretched’; hence it is said, “the blind, the lame, and so on.” ‘Wayfarers’ means travelers. ‘Mendicants’ are beggars who praise the qualities of donors and the fruit of their actions, such as naked ascetics and others. Hence it is said, “what was desired was given,” and so on. ‘A handful’ is said in the sense of husked rice and so on. ‘A bowlful’ is said in the sense of rice-gruel, cooked rice, and so on. Just as village-gain is income arising in the village, so too there is gate-gain; hence it is said, “hundreds of thousands arising there.” They gave a greater gift because the wealth was also applied to other uses. The phrase ‘referring to that’ means referring to that greater gift having been made. For the king’s gift there was, as it were, turned back, being surpassed by the great gift of the women’s quarters; hence it is said, “it turned back.” The word `koci` is a singular form in the locative sense. Hence it is said, “somewhere.” Because he arose at a time when the lifespan was many thousands of years, that king gave gifts for eighty thousand years.

Serīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Serī Sutta is concluded.

4. Ghaṭīkārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta

105. Catutthaṃ heṭṭhā devatāsaṃyuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttatthameva.

105. The fourth has the same meaning as explained previously in the commentary on the Devatāsaṃyutta.

Ghaṭīkārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta is concluded.

5. Jantusuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Jantu Sutta

106. Ye vinaye apakataññuno saṃkilesikesu vodāniyesu dhammesu na kusalā yaṃ kiñci na kārino vippaṭisārabahulā. Tesaṃ anuppannañca uddhaccaṃ uppajjati, uppannañca bhiyyobhāvaṃ vepullaṃ āpajjatīti āha “akappiye kappiyasaññitāya…pe… uddhaccapakatikā”ti. Sārābhāvena tucchattā ca naḷo viyāti naḷo, mānoti āha “unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā”ti. Tenāha “uṭṭhitatucchamānā”ti. Māno hi seyyassa seyyoti [M 1.0158] sadisoti ca pavattiyā visesato tuccho. Cāpallenāti capalabhāvena, taṇhāloluppenāti attho. Mukhakharāti mukhena pharusā, pharusavādinoti attho. Vikiṇṇavācāti visaṭavacanā, samphappalāpatāya apariyantavacanā. Tenāha “asaṃyatavacanā”tiādi. Caṇḍasote baddhanāvāsadisāti etena anavaṭṭhitakiriyataṃ dasseti. Yena samannāgatā sattā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhātuṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā na [V 1.0139] sakkonti, ito cito ca vicaranti. Anavaṭṭhitacittāti ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe na avaṭṭhitacittā. Vivaṭaindriyāti asaṃvutacakkhādiindriyā.

106. Those who are unversed in the Vinaya, unskilled in defiling and purifying states, doing nothing whatsoever, and abounding in remorse—for them, restlessness, if unarisen, arises, and if arisen, it attains greater abundance and fullness. Thus it is said: “By perceiving the unallowable as allowable… of a restless nature.” Due to its lack of essence and its hollowness, like a reed, it is called “reed” (naḷa); conceit (māna), it is said, is “unnaḷa,” meaning “a risen reed” (uggatanaḷā). Therefore, it is said: “risen with hollow conceit” (uṭṭhitatucchamānā). For conceit is especially hollow in its tendency to consider itself superior or equal to what is superior. By “fickleness” (cāpallena) is meant “fickle nature” (capalabhāvena), that is, “greediness due to craving” (taṇhāloluppena). By “harsh-mouthed” (mukhakharā) is meant “harsh of mouth” (mukhena pharusā), that is, “speaking harsh words” (pharusavādino). By “scattered speech” (vikiṇṇavācā) is meant “dispersed words” (visaṭavacanā), that is, “endless words due to frivolous chatter” (samphappalāpatāya apariyantavacanā). Therefore, it is said: “unrestrained in speech,” and so forth. By “like a boat tied in a swift current” (caṇḍasote baddhanāvāsadisā) is shown their “unstable actions” (anavaṭṭhitakiriyataṃ). Beings endowed with this cannot stand or sit in one place, but wander here and there. By “unsteady mind” (anavaṭṭhitacittā) is meant “a mind not steady on one object” (ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe na avaṭṭhitacittā). By “unrestrained senses” (vivaṭaindriyā) is meant “uncontrolled senses such as the eye” (asaṃvutacakkhādiindriyā).

Guṇakathāya saddhiṃ kathiyamāno nigguṇassa aguṇo pākaṭo hoti jātimaṇisamīpe ṭhitassa viya kācamaṇino doso. Sukhajīvinoti sukhe ṭhitā. Yathā dāyakānaṃ subharaṃ hoti, evaṃ sukhena akicchena pavattajīvikā. Tenāha “pubbe bhikkhū”tiādi.

When discussing virtues, the faults of the unvirtuous become evident, like the flaws of a glass gem near a natural jewel. By “living at ease” (sukhajīvino) is meant “established in comfort” (sukhe ṭhitā). Just as it is easy for donors to support them, so their livelihood proceeds easily, without difficulty. Therefore, it is said: “formerly, monks,” and so forth.

Attano rucivasena gāmakiccaṃ netīti gāmaṇi, te pana hīḷento vadati “gāmaṇikā”ti. Vissajjetvāti sativossaggavasena vissajjetvā kilesamucchāyāti mahicchāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāmucchāya. Sīlavantānaṃyeva hi duppaṭipattiṃ sandhāya devaputto vadati. Vattabbayuttakeyevāti ovādena mayā anuggahetabbameva. Chaḍḍitakāti pariccattā ācariyupajjhāyādīhi. Tato eva anāthā appatiṭṭhā. Petāti vigatajīvitā matā. Yathā petā, tatheva honti attahitāsamatthatāya viññūnaṃ jigucchitabbatāya ca.

One who manages village affairs according to their own preference is called a “village headman” (gāmaṇi); but speaking disparagingly, one says “gāmaṇikā.” By “having dismissed” (vissajjetvā) is meant “having dismissed by way of relinquishing mindfulness” (sativossaggavasena vissajjetvā); by “intoxication by defilements” (kilesamucchāya) is meant “intoxication by craving, which is called great desire” (mahicchāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāmucchāya). Indeed, the deva’s son speaks with reference only to the misconduct of the virtuous. By “only those worthy of being spoken to” (vattabbayuttakeyeva) is meant “they should indeed be favored by my advice” (ovādena mayā anuggahetabbameva). By “abandoned” (chaḍḍitakā) is meant “rejected by teachers, preceptors, and so forth” (ācariyupajjhāyādīhi). Therefore, they are truly helpless and without support. By “the departed” (petā) is meant “departed from life, dead” (vigatajīvitā matā). Just as the departed are, so they are, due to their inability to achieve their own welfare and their being despised by the wise.

Jantusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jantu Sutta is concluded.

6. Rohitassasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta

107. Ekokāseti cakkavāḷassa pariyantasaññite ekasmiṃ okāse. Bhummanti “yatthā”ti idaṃ bhummavacanaṃ, sāmaññato vuttampi “so lokassa anto”ti vacanato visiṭṭhavisayameva hoti. “Na jāyati na mīyatī”ti vatvā puna “na cavati na upapajjatī”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “idaṃ aparāparaṃ…pe… gahita”nti. Padagamanenāti padasā gamanena. Saṅkhāralokassa antaṃ sandhāya vadati upari saccāni pakāsetukāmo. Saṅkhāralokassa hi anto nibbānaṃ.

107. By “in one location” (ekokāse) is meant “in a single space at the perceived limit of the universe” (cakkavāḷassa pariyantasaññite ekasmiṃ okāse). By `bhumma` is meant that this word `yatthā` (where) is a locative expression (bhummavacanaṃ); even though spoken generally, on account of the statement “that is the end of the world,” it becomes a specific subject. Having said “is not born, does not die,” why then is it said “does not cease, is not reborn”? He says: “This is stated successively… grasped.” By “by going on foot” (padagamanena) is meant “by going step by step” (padasā gamanena). He speaks with reference to the end of the world of formations, wishing to reveal the truths further on. For the end of the world of formations is Nibbāna.

Daḷhaṃ [M 1.0159] thiraṃ dhanu etassāti daḷhadhanvā. So eva daḷhadhammoti vutto. Tenāha “daḷhadhanū”ti. Uttamappamāṇenāti sahassathāmappamāṇena. Dhanusippasikkhitatāya dhanuggaho, na dhanuggahamattenāti āha “dhanuggahoti dhanuācariyo”ti. “Dhanuggaho”ti vatvā “sikkhito”ti vutte dhanusikkhāya sikkhitoti viññāyati, sikkhā ca ettake kāle samatthassa ukkaṃsagato hotīti āha “dasa dvādasa vassāni dhanusippaṃ sikkhito”ti. Usabhappamāṇepīti vīsatiyaṭṭhiyo usabhaṃ, tasmiṃ usabhappamāṇe padese. Vālagganti vāḷakoṭiṃ. Katahatthoti [V 1.0140] paricitahattho. Katasarakkhepoti vivaṭasarakkhepapadesadassanavasena sarakkhepakatāvī. Tenāha “dassitasippo”ti. “Katasippo”ti keci. Asanti etenāti asanaṃ, kaṇḍo. Tālacchāyanti tālacchādiṃ, sā pana ratanamattā, vidatthicaturaṅgulā vā.

Because he has a strong, firm bow, he is “strong-bowed” (daḷhadhanvā). He is also called “strong-bowed” (daḷhadhammo). Therefore, it is said: “strong-bowed” (daḷhadhanū). By “by the highest measure” (uttamappamāṇena) is meant “by the measure of a thousand strengths” (sahassathāmappamāṇena). Because he is trained in the art of the bow, he is a “bowman” (dhanuggaho), not merely by virtue of holding a bow; thus it is said: “a bowman (dhanuggaho) is a bow-master (dhanuācariyo).” Having said “bowman” (dhanuggaho) and then “trained” (sikkhito), it is understood that he is trained in the discipline of the bow, and the training of one so capable in that time is considered supreme; thus it is said: “trained in the art of the bow for ten or twelve years.” By “even in the measure of an usabha” (usabhappamāṇepī) is meant “an usabha is twenty rods (yaṭṭhi), in that place of an usabha’s measure.” By “the tip of a hair” (vālagganti) is meant “the point of a hair” (vāḷakoṭiṃ). By “a practiced hand” (katahattho) is meant “a hand accustomed to it” (paricitahattho). By “a skilled marksman” (katasarakkhepo) is meant “one who has become skilled in archery by demonstrating the place of a clear arrow-shot” (vivaṭasarakkhepapadesadassanavasena sarakkhepakatāvī). Therefore, it is said: “one who has demonstrated the art” (dassitasippo). Some say “one who has mastered the art” (katasippo). By `asanaṃ` (arrow) is meant “that by which they are not” (asanti etena), i.e., a shaft (kaṇḍo). By “the shade of a palm tree” (tālacchāyaṃ) is meant “the covering of a palm tree” (tālacchādiṃ), and it is the size of a gem, or a span and four fingers.

Puratthimasamuddāti ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷe puratthimasamuddā. Samuddasīsena puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiṃ vadati. Pacchimasamuddoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Nippapañcatanti adandhakāritaṃ. Sampatteti tādisena javena gacchantena sampatte. Anotatteti etthāpi “sampatte”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandho, tathā “nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā”ti etthāpi. Tadāti yadā so lokantagavesako ahosi, tadā. Dīghāyukakāloti anekavassasahassāyukakālo. Cakkavāḷalokassāti sāmaññavasena ekavacanaṃ, cakkavāḷalokanti attho. Imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe nibbatti pubbaparicariyasiddhāya nikantiyā. Sasaññimhi samanaketi na rūpadhammamattake, atha kho pañcakkhandhasamudāyeti dasseti. Samitapāpoti samucchinnasaṃkilesadhammo.

By “from the eastern ocean” (puratthimasamuddā) is meant “from the eastern oceans in one universe” (ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷe puratthimasamuddā). By “head of the ocean” (samuddasīsena), he speaks of the eastern boundary of the universe. By “the western ocean” (pacchimasamuddo), here too, the same method applies. By “without proliferation” (nippapañcataṃ) is meant “not acting slowly” (adandhakāritaṃ). By “having reached” (sampatte) is meant “having reached by going with such speed” (tādisena javena gacchantena sampatte). By “Anotatta” (anotatte), here too, the word “reached” (sampatte) is brought in to connect, and likewise in “having chewed the tooth-stick of the Nāga creeper” (nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā). By “then” (tadā) is meant “when he was a seeker of the world’s end, then” (yadā so lokantagavesako ahosi, tadā). By “the time of a long lifespan” (dīghāyukakālo) is meant “the time of a lifespan of many thousands of years” (anekavassasahassāyukakālo). By “of the universe-world” (cakkavāḷalokassa) is meant the singular form is used in a general sense; the meaning is “the universe-world” (cakkavāḷalokaṃ). In this very universe he was born, due to a desire perfected by previous service. By “in this with perception and mind” (sasaññimhi samanake) is shown that it is not merely in material phenomena, but rather in the collection of the five aggregates. By “one whose evil is stilled” (samitapāpo) is meant “one whose defiling states are utterly destroyed” (samucchinnasaṃkilesadhammo).

Rohitassasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta is concluded.

7-8. Nandasuttanandivisālasuttavaṇṇanā

7-8. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta and the Nandivisāla Sutta

108-109. Nandasuttavisālasuttāni sattamaaṭṭhamāni heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitarūpattā vuttatthāneva.

108-109. The Nanda Sutta and the Visāla Sutta, the seventh and eighth, are as previously explained, their meaning being as stated.

Nandasuttanandivisālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nanda Sutta and the Nandivisāla Sutta is concluded.

9. Susimasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Susima Sutta

110. Tuyhampi [M 1.0160] noti tuyhampi nu, nu-saddo pucchāyaṃ, tasmā vaṇṇaṃ kathetukāmo pucchatīti adhippāyo. Na vaṭṭatīti na yujjati, kathitoti kathetuṃ āraddho, tenāha “matthakaṃ na pāpuṇātī”ti. Tameva matthakāpāpuṇanaṃ dassetuṃ “so hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Satisampajaññāyogato gorūpasīlo, mūḷho khalitapañño, gorūpassa viya sīlaṃ etassāti hi gorūpasīlo. Sabhāgo ekarūpacittatāya. Ariyānaṃ sabhāgatā nāma guṇavantavasenāti āha “aññamaññassa guṇesu pasīditvā”ti. Soḷasavidhaṃ paññanti mahāpaññādikā cha, nava anupubbavihārasamāpattipaññā, āsavakkhayapaññāti imaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ paññaṃ. Tesaṭṭhi sāvakasādhāraṇañāṇānipi ettheva saṅgahaṃ samosaraṇaṃ gacchanti.

110. `Tuyhampi no` means `tuyhampi nu`. The particle `nu` is used in a question; thus, the intention is that he asks, wishing to speak in praise. `Na vaṭṭati` means it is not suitable. `Kathito` means he has begun to speak; therefore it is said, 'he does not reach the summit.' To illustrate this very failure to reach the summit, `so hī` and so on is stated. Due to a lack of application of mindfulness and clear comprehension, he is of bull-like behavior—confused, with impaired wisdom, for `gorūpasīlo` means one whose behavior is like that of a bull. `Sabhāgo` (of the same kind) is due to having a similar state of mind. The similarity of the noble ones is in terms of virtuous qualities, as it is said, 'being pleased with each other's virtues.' `Soḷasavidhaṃ paññaṃ` (sixteenfold wisdom) means this sixteenfold wisdom: the six kinds beginning with great wisdom, the nine wisdoms of the progressive meditative attainments, and the wisdom of the destruction of the taints. Here, the sixty-three types of knowledge common to disciples also find inclusion and convergence.

Ānandāti [V 1.0141] theraṃ āha. Ācāroti cārittasīlamāha. Gocaroti gocarasampatti. Vihāroti samāpattivihāro. Abhikkamotiādinā iriyāpathavihāraṃ. Tuyhampīti pi-saddena bhagavatā attānaṃ ādiṃ katvā tadaññesaṃ viññūnaṃ sabbesaṃ therassa ruccanasabhāvo dīpitoti dassento “mayhaṃ ruccatī”tiādimāha. Tattha satipi ānandattherassapi asītiyā mahātherānaṃ antogadhabhāve “asītiyā mahātherānaṃ ruccatī”ti vatvā “tuyhampi ruccatī”ti vacanaṃ tena dhammasenāpatino vaṇṇaṃ kathāpetukāmatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The word `Ānanda` refers to the elder. `Ācāra` refers to morality as conduct. `Gocara` means excellence of range. `Vihāra` refers to the dwelling of attainment. `Abhikkama` and so on refers to the dwelling in the modes of deportment. `Tuyhampi` (to you too)—with the particle `pi,` showing that the Blessed One, beginning with himself as the first, indicates the elder's agreeable nature to all the wise, he says, 'It pleases me,' and so on. Here, even though the Elder Ānanda was included among the eighty great elders, by saying, 'It pleases the eighty great elders,' and then, 'It pleases you too,' this statement should be seen as the desire to have the General of the Dhamma praised.

Sāṭakantareti nivatthavatthantare. Laddhokāsoti nibbuddhaṃ karonto sāṭakantare laddhaṃ gahetuṃ laddhāvasaro. Labhissāminoti labhissāmi vata. Dīpadhajabhūtanti satayojanavitthiṇṇaṃ jambudīpassa dhajabhūtaṃ. Puggalapalāpeti antosārābhāvato palāpabhūte puggale haranto. Bālatāyāti rucikhantiādiabhāvatāya. Dosatāyāti dussakabhāvena. Mohenāti mahāmūḷhatāya. Keci pana “bālo bālatāyāti mūḷhatāya pakatibālabhāvena na jānāti. Mūḷho mohenāti sayaṃ abālo samānopi yadā mohena pariyuṭṭhito hoti, tadā mohena na jānāti, ayaṃ padadvayassa viseso”ti vadanti. Vipallatthacittoti yakkhummādena pittummādena vā viparītacitto.

'The garment's edge' means the inner garment, the garment underneath. 'Having found an opportunity' means, having made an opening in the garment's edge, he found an opportunity to take what was placed there. 'I will get it' means, indeed, I will obtain it. 'Being a banner of the island' means it became a banner for Jambudīpa, which spans a hundred leagues. 'Carrying a worthless person' refers to carrying persons who are like chaff because of the absence of inner essence. 'Due to foolishness' means due to the absence of taste, inclination, and so on. 'Due to fault' means due to being difficult to manage. 'Due to delusion' means because of great ignorance. Some, however, explain: 'A fool due to foolishness' means he does not know because of his foolish nature. 'A deluded one due to delusion' means even if he is not naturally foolish, when he is overcome by delusion, he does not know due to delusion—this is the distinction between the two terms. 'With a deranged mind' means his mind is distorted due to spirit possession or bilious disorder.

“Catūsu [M 1.0161] kosallesū”ti vuttaṃ catubbidhaṃ kosallaṃ pāḷiyā eva dassetuṃ “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo samudayato atthaṅgamato assādato ādīnavato nissaraṇato ca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ dhātukusalo. Vuttanayena āyatanesu kusalo āyatanakusalo. Avijjādīsu dvādasapaṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu kusalo paṭiccasamuppādakusalo. “Idaṃ imassa phalassa ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ, idaṃ aṭṭhānaṃ akāraṇa”nti evaṃ ṭhānañca ṭhānato, aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānato ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalo. Yo pana imesu dhātuādīsu pariññābhisamayādivasena nissaṅgagatiyā paṇḍāti laddhanāmena ñāṇena ito gato pavatto, ayaṃ paṇḍito nāma.

'In the four skills,' it is said to show the fourfold skill precisely from the Pāli text; hence, 'this has been said' and so on was stated. Herein, one who understands the eighteen elements as they actually are—in terms of their arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape—is skilled in the elements. In the manner stated, one skilled in the sense bases is skilled in the sense bases. One skilled in the twelve links of dependent origination, starting with ignorance, is skilled in dependent origination. One who understands as it actually is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, knowing, 'This is the basis and cause for this result; this is an impossibility and not a cause,' is skilled in what is possible and impossible. Moreover, one who, through full understanding and realization in regard to these elements and so on, with detachment as his mode of progress, by means of knowledge that has obtained the name 'wisdom,' has gone and proceeded from here—such a one is called wise.

Mahantānaṃ atthānaṃ pariggaṇhanato mahatī paññā etassāti mahāpañño. Sesapadesupi eseva nayoti āha “mahāpaññādīhi samannāgatoti attho”ti. Nānattanti yāhi mahāpaññādīhi samannāgatattā thero “mahāpañño”tiādinā kittito, tāsaṃ mahāpaññādīnaṃ idaṃ nānattaṃ ayaṃ vemattatā. Yassa kassaci visesato arūpadhammassa mahattaṃ nāma kiccasiddhiyā veditabbanti tadassa kiccasiddhiyā dassento “mahante sīlakkhandhe pariggaṇhātī”tiādimāha. Tattha hetumahantatāya paccayamahantatāya nissayamahantatāya pabhedamahantatāya kiccamahantatāya phalamahantatāya ānisaṃsamahantatāya ca sīlakkhandhassa mahantabhāvo [V 1.0142] veditabbo. Tattha hetū alobhādayo. Paccayā hirottappasaddhāsativīriyādayo. Nissayā sāvakabodhipaccekabodhisammāsambodhiniyatatā, taṃsamaṅgino ca purisavisesā. Pabhedo cārittādivibhāgo. Kiccaṃ tadaṅgādivasena paṭipakkhassa vidhamanaṃ. Phalaṃ saggasampadā nibbānasampadā ca. Ānisaṃso piyamanāpatādi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.8-9) ākaṅkheyyasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 1.64 ādayo) ca āgatanayena veditabbo. Iminā nayena samādhikkhandhādīnampi mahantatā yathārahaṃ niddhāretvā veditabbā. Ṭhānāṭṭhānādīnaṃ pana mahantabhāvo mahāvisayatāya veditabbo. Tattha ṭhānāṭṭhānānaṃ mahāvisayatā bahudhātukasuttādīsu āgatanayena, vihārasamāpattīnaṃ samādhikkhandhe niddhāritanayena veditabbā. Ariyasaccānaṃ sakalasāsanasaṅgaṇhanato saccavibhaṅge [M 1.0162] (vibha. 189 ādayo) taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāsu (vibha. aṭṭha. 189 ādayo) āgatanayena; satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 355 ādayo) taṃsaṃvaṇṇanādīsu (vibha. aṭṭha. 355 ādayo) ca āgatanayena; sāmaññaphalānaṃ mahato hitassa mahato sukhassa mahato atthassa mahato yogakkhemassa nipphattibhāvato santapaṇītanipuṇaatakkāvacarapaṇḍitavedanīyabhāvato ca; abhiññānaṃ mahāsambhārato mahāvisayato mahākiccato mahānubhāvato mahānipphattito ca; nibbānassa madanimmadanādimahatthasiddhito mahantatā veditabbā. Pariggaṇhātīti sabhāvādito paricchijja gaṇhāti jānāti paṭivijjhatīti attho. Sā panāti mahāpaññatā.

Because he encompasses great things, great wisdom belongs to him—thus he is called 'great in wisdom.' The same principle applies to the other terms as well, hence it is said, 'endowed with great wisdom and so forth'—this is the meaning. 'Diversity' means this: it is the diversity and variety of those qualities, such as great wisdom, on account of being endowed with which the elder is praised with terms like 'great in wisdom.' The greatness of any specific immaterial quality should be understood by its success in its function. To illustrate this success in its function, he said, 'He encompasses the great aggregate of virtue,' and so on. Here, the greatness of the aggregate of virtue should be understood in terms of greatness in seven ways: (1) by cause, (2) by condition, (3) by support, (4) by divisions, (5) by function, (6) by fruit, and (7) by benefits. Among these, the causes are non-greed and so forth. The conditions are moral shame, moral dread, faith, mindfulness, energy, and so on. The supports are the certainty of discipleship, individual enlightenment, and perfect enlightenment, as well as the exceptional individuals associated with these. The divisions are classifications such as virtuous conduct. The function is the destruction of opposing factors by way of their respective antidotes. The fruit is the attainment of heavenly bliss and the attainment of Nibbāna. The benefits include being dear and agreeable, and so on. This is a summary here; however, the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method found in the Visuddhimagga and in suttas like the Ākaṅkheyya. In the same way, the greatness of the aggregates of concentration and so on should be determined and understood as appropriate. However, the greatness of the possible and impossible and so on should be understood in terms of their vast scope. Here, the vast scope of the possible and impossible is to be understood according to the method found in suttas like the Bahudhātuka, while the vast scope of the dwelling-attainments is to be understood according to the method determined in the aggregate of concentration. The greatness of the Noble Truths should be understood from their comprehensive inclusion of the entire teaching, as found in the Saccavibhaṅga and its commentaries; the greatness of the foundations of mindfulness and so on should be understood from the Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga and its commentaries; the greatness of the fruits of recluseship lies in their accomplishment of great benefit, great happiness, great welfare, and great security from bondage, as well as their being peaceful, refined, subtle, beyond the reach of logic, and knowable by the wise; the greatness of the direct knowledges lies in their great accumulation, vast scope, great function, great power, and great accomplishment; the greatness of Nibbāna lies in its achievement of the great purpose—the destruction of intoxication and so forth. 'He encompasses' means he grasps by distinguishing according to intrinsic nature, knows, and penetrates—this is the meaning. 'But that' refers to great wisdom.

Puthupaññāti ettha nānākhandhesu ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti ayaṃ rūpakkhandho nāma…pe… ayaṃ viññāṇakkhandho nāmāti evaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Tesu ekavidhena rūpakkhandho, ekādasavidhena rūpakkhandho, ekavidhena vedanākkhandho, bahuvidhena vedanākkhandho, ekavidhena saññākkhandho, saṅkhārakkhandho, viññāṇakkhandhoti evaṃ ekekassa khandhassa ekavidhādivasena atītādivasenapi nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Tathā idaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ nāma…pe… idaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ nāmaṃ. Tattha dasāyatanā kāmāvacarā, dve catubhūmakāti evaṃ āyatanānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Nānādhātūsūti ayaṃ cakkhudhātu nāma…pe… ayaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu nāma. Tattha soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve catubhūmakāti evaṃ dhātunānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati, taṃ upādiṇṇadhātuvasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ paccekabuddhānañhi dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānañca upādiṇṇadhātūsu eva nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Tañca kho ekadesamattato, na nippadesato, anupādiṇṇakadhātūnaṃ pana nānākaraṇaṃ na jānanti eva. Itarasāvakesu vattabbameva natthi, sabbaññubuddhānaṃyeva pana imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannattāva imassa rukkhassa khandho seto hoti, imassa kāḷo, imassa maṭṭho, imassa [V 1.0143] bahalattaco, imassa tanuttaco, imassa pattaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena evarūpaṃ; imassa pupphaṃ nīlaṃ pītakaṃ lohitakaṃ odātaṃ, sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ; phalaṃ khuddakaṃ mahantaṃ dīghaṃ vaṭṭaṃ susaṇṭhānaṃ maṭṭhaṃ [M 1.0163] pharusaṃ sugandhaṃ madhuraṃ tittakaṃ ambilaṃ kaṭukaṃ kasāvaṃ; kaṇṭako tikhiṇo atikhiṇo ujuko kuṭilo tambo lohito odāto hotīti dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati.

Here, regarding 'diverse wisdom,' knowledge occurs by discerning the diversity in the aggregates: 'This is called the form aggregate'... up to... 'this is called the consciousness aggregate.' Thus, knowledge occurs by discerning the diversity of the five aggregates. Among these, the form aggregate is of one kind; the form aggregate is of eleven kinds; the feeling aggregate is of one kind; the feeling aggregate is of many kinds; the perception aggregate is of one kind; the formations aggregate; and the consciousness aggregate. Thus, knowledge occurs by discerning the diversity of each aggregate in terms of its being of one kind, etc., and in terms of its being past, etc. Similarly, 'This is called the eye-base'... up to... 'this is called the mind-object base.' Among these, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere, and two belong to the four planes. Thus, knowledge occurs by discerning the diversity of the bases. Regarding the diverse elements: 'This is called the eye-element'... up to... 'this is called the mind-consciousness element.' Among these, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere, and two belong to the four planes. Thus, knowledge occurs by discerning the diversity of the elements. It should be understood that this is stated in terms of the clung-to elements. For the knowledge of Paccekabuddhas and the two chief disciples occurs only in the clung-to elements by discerning their diversity. And that too, only partially, not completely. They do not know the diversity of the unclung-to elements at all. For other disciples, there is nothing to be said. But for the Omniscient Buddhas alone, due to the prominence of this or that element, knowledge occurs by discerning the diversity of elements, such as: 'The trunk of this tree is white, of that one black, of another smooth, of another thick-skinned, of another thin-skinned; the leaf of this one is of such a color and shape; the flower of this one is blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, foul-smelling; the fruit of this one is small, large, long, round, well-formed, smooth, rough, fragrant, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, astringent; the thorn of this one is sharp, very sharp, straight, crooked, copper-colored, reddish, white.'

Atthesūti rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu. Nānāpaṭiccasamuppādesūti ajjhattabahiddhābhedato ca saṇṭhānabhedato ca nānappabhedesu paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu. Avijjādiaṅgānañhi paccekaṃ paṭiccasamuppādasaññitāti. Tenāha saṅkhārapiṭake “dvādasa paccayā dvādasa paṭiccasamuppādā”ti. Nānāsuññatamanupalabbhesūti nānāsabhāvesu niccasārādivirahato suññasabhāvesu, tato eva itthipurisaattaattaniyādivasena anupalabbhesu sabhāvesu. Ma-kāro hettha padasandhikaro. Nānāatthesūti atthapaṭisambhidāvisayesu paccayuppannādibhedesu nānāvidhesu atthesu. Dhammesūti dhammapaṭisambhidāvisayesu paccayādinānādhammesu. Niruttīsūti tesaṃyeva atthadhammānaṃ niddhāraṇavacanasaṅkhātāsu niruttīsu. Paṭibhānesūti atthapaṭisambhidādīsu visayabhūtesu “imāni idamatthajotakānī”ti tathā tathā paṭibhānato patiṭṭhānato paṭibhānānīti laddhanāmesu ñāṇesu. Puthu nānāsīlakkhandhesūtiādīsu sīlassa puthuttaṃ nānattañca vuttameva. Itaresaṃ pana vuttanayānusārena suviññeyyattā pākaṭameva. Yaṃ pana abhinnaṃ ekameva nibbānaṃ, tattha upacāravasena puthuttaṃ gahetabbanti āha “puthu janasādhāraṇe dhamme samatikkammā”ti. Tenassa idha madanimmadanādipariyāyena puthuttaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti.

Regarding 'in the objects': in objects such as form, etc. Regarding 'in the diverse dependent originations': in the various kinds of factors of dependent origination, due to the distinction between internal and external, and due to the distinction in structure. For the factors beginning with ignorance are each designated as dependent origination. Therefore, it is said in the Saṅkhāra Piṭaka: 'Twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations.' Regarding 'in the various emptinesses that cannot be apprehended': in natures that are diverse and empty due to the absence of permanence, essence, etc., and thus in natures that cannot be apprehended as male, female, self, or belonging to self. Here, the letter 'm' serves as a word-connector. Regarding 'in the various meanings': in the diverse kinds of meanings classified as conditioned, etc., which are the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning. Regarding 'in the phenomena': in the various phenomena such as conditions, etc., which are the domain of the analytical knowledge of phenomena. Regarding 'in the expressions': in the expressions, which are designated as the clarifying terms for those very meanings and phenomena. Regarding 'in the insights': in the knowledges that are called 'insights' because they appear and are established in various ways, such as 'these illuminate such-and-such meanings,' which are the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning, etc. Regarding 'in the widely diverse aggregates of virtue, etc.': the multiplicity and diversity of virtue have already been explained. The rest, however, are evident, being easily understood according to the method already stated. However, regarding Nibbāna, which is undifferentiated and singular, multiplicity is taken figuratively, as it is said: 'having transcended the phenomena common to ordinary people.' Thus, here its multiplicity is shown through terms such as 'dispelling intoxication,' etc.

Evaṃ visayavasena paññāya mahattaṃ puthuttañca dassetvā idāni sampayuttadhammavasena hāsabhāvaṃ, pavattiākāravasena javanabhāvaṃ, kiccavasena tikkhādibhāvañca dassetuṃ “katamā hāsapaññā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha hāsabahuloti pītibahulo. Sesapadāni tassa vevacanāni. Sīlaṃ paripūretīti haṭṭhapahaṭṭho udaggudaggo hutvā pītisahagatāya paññāya pātimokkhasīlaṃ ṭhapetvā hāsanīyatarasseva visuṃ gahitattā itaraṃ tividhaṃ sīlaṃ paripūreti. Pītisomanassasahagatā hi paññā abhirativasena tadārammaṇe phullitā vikasitā viya vattati, na upekkhāsahagatā. Sīlakkhandhaṃ samādhikkhandhantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Therotiādinā abhinīhārasiddhā therassa hāsapaññatāti dasseti.

Having thus shown the greatness and diversity of wisdom by way of its objects, now, to show its joyful nature by way of associated phenomena, its swiftness by way of its mode of occurrence, and its sharpness, etc., by way of its function, it is said, 'What is joyful wisdom?' and so on. Herein, 'abounding in joy' means abounding in gladness. The remaining terms are synonyms for that.
