'He fulfills virtue': being delighted and elated, with wisdom accompanied by joy, he fulfills the other threefold virtue, setting aside the Pātimokkha virtue, since that which is even more worthy of joy is taken separately. For wisdom accompanied by joy and gladness operates, delighting in its object, as if blossoming and flourishing, not so when accompanied by equanimity. The same method applies to 'the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,' etc. By 'the Elder,' etc., it is shown that the Elder's joyful wisdom is accomplished through resolution.

Sabbaṃ [M 1.0164] rūpaṃ aniccalakkhaṇato khippaṃ javatīti rūpakkhandhaṃ aniccanti sīghavegena pavattiyā paṭipakkhadūrībhāvena pubbābhisaṅkhārassa sātisayattā indena visaṭṭhavajiraṃ viya lakkhaṇaṃ [V 1.0144] paṭivijjhantī adandhāyantī rūpakkhandhe aniccalakkhaṇaṃ vegena paṭivijjhati, tasmā sā javanapaññā nāmāti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāvasena javanapaññaṃ dassetvā balavavipassanāvasena dassetuṃ “rūpa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khayaṭṭhenāti yattha yattha uppajjati, tattha tattheva khaṇeneva bhijjanato khayasabhāvato. Bhayaṭṭhenāti bhayānakato. Asārakaṭṭhenāti attasāravirahato niccasārādivirahato ca. Tulayitvāti tulābhūtāya vipassanāya tulayitvā. Tīrayitvāti tāya eva tīraṇabhūtāya tīretvā. Vibhāvayitvāti yāthāvato pakāsetvā pañcakkhandhaṃ vibhūtaṃ katvā pākaṭaṃ katvā. Rūpanirodheti rūpakkhandhassa nirodhabhūte nibbāne ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena. Idāni sikhāppattavipassanāvasena javanapaññaṃ dassetuṃ puna “rūpa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāvasenā”ti keci.

All form, due to its impermanent characteristic, swiftly passes away. Thus, the meaning is that this wisdom, without faltering, swiftly penetrates the impermanent characteristic in the aggregate of form, like a thunderbolt released by Indra, due to the rapidity of its occurrence, the absence of opposing forces, and the overwhelming influence of past formations. Therefore, it is called swift wisdom. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Having thus shown swift wisdom by way of insight focused on characteristics, now, to show it by way of strong insight, 'form,' etc., is stated. Herein, 'in the sense of destruction' means that wherever it arises, there and then it instantly disintegrates due to its destructive nature. 'In the sense of danger' means it is fearful. 'In the sense of being insubstantial' means it lacks any essence, being devoid of self-essence and permanent essence, etc. 'Having weighed' means having weighed with insight as the scale. 'Having examined' means having judged with that same insight which serves as judgment. 'Having discerned' means having revealed it as it truly is, making the five aggregates clear and evident. Regarding 'the cessation of form': by way of tendency, inclination, and leaning towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the aggregate of form. Now, to illustrate swift wisdom through insight that has reached its peak, 'form,' etc., is again stated. Some say, 'by way of insight leading to emergence.'

Ñāṇatikkhabhāvo nāma savisesaṃ paṭipakkhasamucchindane veditabboti “khippaṃ kilese chindatīti tikkhapañño”ti vatvā te pana kilese vibhāgena dassento “uppannaṃ kāmavitakka”ntiādimāha. Tikkhapañño khippābhiñño hoti, paṭipadā cassa na calatīti āha “ekasmiṃ āsane cattāro ca ariyamaggā adhigatā hontī”tiādi. Thero cātiādinā dhammasenāpatino tikkhapaññatā sikhāppattāti dasseti.

The sharpness of wisdom is to be understood as the distinguished eradication of opposing factors. Having said, 'One who quickly cuts off defilements is sharp in wisdom,' he then shows those defilements in detail, saying, 'arisen sensual thought,' etc. One with sharp wisdom is quick in direct knowledge, and his practice does not falter. Therefore, it is said, 'In one sitting, the four noble paths are attained,' etc. By 'the Elder,' etc., it is shown that the sharp wisdom of the General of the Dhamma has reached its peak.

“Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā”ti yāthāvato dassanena saccasampaṭivedho ijjhati, na aññathāti kāraṇamukhena nibbedhikapaññaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbasaṅkhāresu ubbegabahulo hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ubbegabahuloti vuttanayena sabbasaṅkhāresu abhiṇhappavattasaṃvego. Uttāsabahuloti ñāṇuttāsavasena sabbasaṅkhāresu bahuso utrastamānaso. Tena ādīnavānupassanamāha. Ukkaṇṭhanabahuloti iminā pana nibbidānupassanamāha, aratibahulotiādinā tassā eva aparāparuppattiṃ. Bahimukho sabbasaṅkhārato bahibhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ uddissa pavattañāṇamukho, tathā [M 1.0165] vā pavattitavimokkhamukho. Nibbijjhanaṃ nibbedho, so etissā atthi, nibbijjhatīti vā nibbedhā, sā eva paññā nibbedhikā. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

The thorough understanding of truth is accomplished by seeing as it really is that 'all conditioned things are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, compounded, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation,' and not otherwise. To show the penetrative wisdom by way of its cause, it is said, 'one is greatly distressed by all formations,' etc. Herein, 'greatly distressed' means the constantly occurring sense of urgency regarding all formations, in the manner described. 'Full of dread' means having a mind frequently terrified toward all formations by way of the dread of knowledge. Through this, the contemplation of danger is indicated. 'Full of disenchantment' indicates the contemplation of aversion here. 'Full of aversion,' etc., indicates the successive arising of that same state. 'Outward-turned' means having knowledge directed towards Nibbāna, which is external to all formations, or having a liberation doorway thus directed. The act of penetrating is penetration; this wisdom possesses it. Or, because it penetrates, it is a penetrator. That very wisdom is penetrative. As for what is not analyzed here in terms of meaning, it should be easily understood from the method explained earlier.

Appicchoti santaguṇaniguhanatāti attani vijjamānānaṃ bāhusaccadhutadhammasīlādiguṇānañceva paṭivedhaguṇassa ca niguhanaṃ, paṭiggahaṇe ca mattaññutāti eteneva pariyesanaparibhogamattaññutāpi vuttā hoti. Tīhi santosehīti catūsu paccayesu paccekaṃ tīhi santosehi[V 1.0145], sabbe pana dvādasa. Paṭisallīnena vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ na saṅgaṇikārāmānaṃ. Nekkhammābhiratānanti pabbajjaṃ upagatānaṃ. Parisuddhacittānaṃ vigatacittasaṃkilesānaṃ. Paramavodānappattānaṃ aṭṭhasamāpattisamadhigamena ativiya vodānaṃ visuddhiṃ pattānaṃ. Kilesupadhiādīnaṃ abhāvato nirupadhīnaṃ. Phalasamāpattivasena sabbasaṅkhāravinissaṭattā visaṅkhāraṃ nibbānaṃ. Upagatānaṃ, imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ lābhī pavivitto “pakārehi vivitto”ti katvā. Samāsajjanaṃ parisinehuppādo saṃsaggo, savanavasena uppajjanakasaṃsaggo savanasaṃsaggo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Samullapanaṃ ālāpasallapanaṃ. Saṃsaggavatthunā iminā tassa paribhogo paribhogasaṃsaggo.

‘Of few wishes’ (appiccho) means concealing one’s good qualities, that is, the concealment of virtues present in oneself, such as extensive learning, ascetic practices, moral conduct, and the virtue of penetration; and moderation in accepting offerings. By this, moderation in seeking and using requisites is also stated. ‘With threefold contentment’ (tīhi santosehi) means with three kinds of contentment for each of the four requisites, making twelve in all. ‘Those in seclusion’ (paṭisallīna) means those whose bodies are established in seclusion, not delighting in company. ‘Those who rejoice in renunciation’ (nekkhammābhirata) means those who have gone forth into homelessness. ‘Those with purified minds’ (parisuddhacitta) means those whose mental defilements have vanished. ‘Those who have attained supreme purity’ (paramavodānappatta) means those who, through the attainment of the eight attainments, have attained exceedingly pure purification. ‘Those who are free from substrata’ (nirupadhi) means those who are without substrata, due to the absence of defilements, substrata, etc. ‘Those who have reached the unconditioned, Nibbāna’ (visaṅkhāraṃ nibbānaṃ upagata) means those who, by way of fruition attainment, are entirely released from all conditioned formations, having reached the unconditioned, Nibbāna. One who has gained these three kinds of seclusion is secluded, having been ‘secluded in various ways’. ‘Association’ (samāsajjana) means the arising of affection through close contact, which is association. The association that arises by way of hearing is ‘association by hearing’ (savanasaṃsagga). The same method applies to the rest. ‘Conversation’ (samullapana) means friendly talk and chatter. His usage by means of this basis of association is ‘association by usage’ (paribhogasaṃsagga).

Āraddhavīriyoti ettha vīriyārambho nāma vīriyassa paggaṇhanaṃ paripuṇṇakaraṇaṃ. Taṃ pana sabbaso kilesānaṃ niggaṇhananti dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Odhunanavattāti kilesānaṃ yassa kassaci sāvajjassa odhunanavasena vattā. Tenāha “bhikkhūna”ntiādi. Otiṇṇaṃ nāma vajjaṃ ajjhācaritanti ārocitaṃ. Anotiṇṇaṃ anārocitaṃ. Tantivasenāti pāḷidhammavasena, yuttasaddassa vasenāti attho. Pāpe lāmake puggale dhamme ca garahati jigucchatīti pāpagarahī. Tenāha “pāpapuggale”tiādi. Ekadassīti ekabhavadassī, idhalokamattadassī diṭṭhadhammikasukhamattāpekkhī. Samantāti samantato, parito me katthaci mā ahūti yojanā.

‘One with aroused energy’ (āraddhavīriyo) here means the commencement of energy, namely, the exertion and full accomplishment of energy. To show that this entirely suppresses defilements, he said the passage beginning with ‘therein’. ‘One who behaves by shaking off’ (odhunanavattā) means one who behaves by way of shaking off any blameworthy thing. Hence he said, ‘for the bhikkhus,’ and so on. ‘Fallen into’ (otiṇṇaṃ) means a fault that has been committed and declared. ‘Not fallen into’ (anotiṇṇaṃ) means undeclared. ‘By way of the text’ (tantivasena) means according to the Pāli Dhamma; the meaning is according to the usage of the appropriate word. ‘One who censures evil’ (pāpagarahī) means one who censures and despises wicked, base individuals and things. Hence he said, ‘wicked individuals,’ and so on. ‘Seeing only one’ (ekadassī) means seeing only one existence, seeing only this present world, concerned only with happiness in this visible life. ‘Completely’ (samantā) means from all sides, all around; the construction is: ‘May there be nothing for me anywhere’.

Soḷasahi padehīti soḷasahi koṭṭhāsehi. Akuppanti kenaci akopanīyaṃ. Ayaṃ dhammasenāpatino guṇakathā satthu vacanānusārena dasasahassacakkavāḷabyāpinī [M 1.0166] ahosi, taṃ dassetuṃ “eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Catubbidhā vaṇṇanibhā pātubhavi uḷārapītisomanassasamuṭṭhānattā. Suṭṭhu obhāsatīti subho. Obhāsasampattiyā maṇino bhaddakatāti āha “subhoti sundaro”ti. Jātimā parisuddhaākarasamuṭṭhitattā. Kuruvindajātiādijātivisesopi maṇi ākaraparisuddhamūlako evāti āha “jātisampanno”ti. Dhovanādiparikammenāti catūsu pāsāṇesu dhovanadosanīharaṇatāpanasaṇhakaraṇādiparikammena. Rattakambalassa vasena sabhāvavaṇṇasiddhiyā veḷuriyamaṇi ativiya sobhatīti āha “paṇḍukambale nikkhitto”ti. Nikkhanti bhaṇḍamāha. Tañca appakena suvaṇṇena kataṃ bhaṇḍaṃ na sobhati sobhāvipulenāti āha “atirekapañcasuvaṇṇena katapiḷandhana”nti. Suvaṇṇanti pañcadharaṇassa samaññā, tasmā pañcavīsatisuvaṇṇasāriyā vicittaābharaṇaṃ idha “nikkha”nti adhippetaṃ. Tañhi vipulaṃ na parittakaṃ. Mahājambusākhāya pavattanadiyanti mahājambusākhāya heṭṭhā sañjātanadiyaṃ. Taṃ kira ratanaṃ rattaṃ. Sukusalena…pe… sampahaṭṭhanti suṭṭhu kusalena suvaṇṇakārena ukkāya tāpetvā sammā [V 1.0146] pahaṭṭhaṃ majjanādivasena sukataparikammaṃ. Dhātuvibhaṅgeti dhātuvibhaṅgasutte. Katabhaṇḍanti ābharaṇabhāvena kataṃ bhaṇḍaṃ.

‘With sixteen facets’ (soḷasahi padehi) means with sixteen sections. ‘Unshakable’ (akuppaṃ) means not to be shaken by anything. This account of the virtues of the General of the Dhamma, in accordance with the Teacher’s words, pervaded ten thousand world-systems. To show this, the passage beginning with ‘thus’ was stated. A fourfold radiance appeared, arising from sublime joy and happiness. ‘Shining brightly’ (subho) means it shines very brightly. Because of the excellence of its radiance, the goodness of the gem, he said, ‘subho means sundaro (beautiful)’. ‘Of excellent birth’ (jātimā) means originating from a completely pure mine. Even a gem of a special variety, such as the Kuruvinda, has the purity of its mine as its basis; hence it is said, ‘endowed with birth’ (jātisampanno). ‘By processing, etc.’ (dhovanādiparikammena) means by the process of washing, removing flaws, heating, smoothing, etc., on four stones. He said, ‘placed on a pale blanket’ (paṇḍukambale nikkhitto), because a beryl gem shines exceedingly when its natural color is perfected by means of a red blanket. ‘Nikkha’ refers to an ornament. And an ornament made with a little gold does not shine as one made with abundant gold does; hence it is said, ‘an ornament made with more than five suvaṇṇas’. ‘Suvaṇṇa’ is a designation for five dharaṇas; therefore, a variegated ornament worth twenty-five suvaṇṇas is what is meant here by ‘nikkha’. That is abundant, not small. ‘In the river flowing from the great Jambu branch’ (mahājambusākhāya pavattanadiyaṃ) means in the river that arose beneath the great Jambu branch. It is said that this jewel is red. ‘Skillfully… well-wrought’ (sukusalena…pe… sampahaṭṭhaṃ) means heated with a blowpipe by a very skillful goldsmith, well-beaten, and well-finished by means of polishing and other processes. ‘In the Dhātuvibhaṅga’ (dhātuvibhaṅge) means in the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta. ‘A finished article’ (katabhaṇḍaṃ) means an article made into an ornament.

Nātiucco nātinīco taruṇasūriyo nāma. Satthārā ābhatavaṇṇo ubbhataguṇoti attho. Neva maraṇaṃ abhinandatīti attanopi maraṇaṃ neva abhinandati attavinipātassa sāvajjabhāvato. Bodhisatto pana paresaṃ atthāya attano attabhāvaṃ pariccajati karuṇāvasena, evaṃ vosajjanaṃ paramatthapāramīpāripūriṃ gacchatīti sāvakā na tathā kātuṃ sakkā sikkhāpadato. Na jīvitaṃ pattheti jīvitāsāya samucchinnattā. Divasasaṅkhepanti ajja tvaṃ idaṃ nāma kammaṃ karohi, idaṃ te vetananti divasabhāgena paricchinnaṃ vetanaṃ. Tādiso hi bhatako divasakkhayameva udikkhati, na kammaniṭṭhānaṃ. Nibbisaṃ bhatako yathāti vetanaṃ bhatiṃ icchanto kālakkhayaṃ udikkhanto bhatakapuriso viya.

The young sun is neither too high nor too low. The meaning is: praised by the Teacher, of excellent qualities. ‘He does not delight in death’ (neva maraṇaṃ abhinandati) means he does not delight even in his own death, because self-destruction is blameworthy. A Bodhisatta, however, out of compassion, gives up his own existence for the sake of others. Such relinquishment leads to the fulfillment of the ultimate perfections. Disciples, however, cannot do so because of the training precepts. ‘He does not long for life’ (na jīvitaṃ pattheti) because his craving for life is eradicated. ‘The day’s reckoning’ (divasasaṅkhepaṃ) refers to a wage limited by a portion of the day, as in: ‘Today you must do this work, this is your wage.’ For such a hired worker looks only to the day’s end, not to the completion of the work. ‘Like a hired worker seeking wages’ (nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā) means like a hired man who, desiring his wage, looks forward to the end of his time.

Susimasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Susima Sutta is completed.

10. Nānātitthiyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Disciples of Various Sectarians

111. Nānātitthiyasāvakāti [M 1.0167] puthutitthiyānaṃ sāvakā. Chinditeti hatthacchedādivasena chede. Māriteti māraṇe. Na pāpaṃ samanupassatīti kiñci pāpaṃ atthīti na passati, paresañca tathā pavedeti. Vissāsanti vissatthabhāvaṃ. “Katakammānampi vipāko natthī”ti vadanto katapāpānaṃ akatapuññānañca vissatthataṃ nirāsaṅkataṃ janeti.

111. ‘Disciples of various sectarians’ means the disciples of various sectarians. ‘In cutting’ means in cutting by way of severing hands and so forth. ‘In killing’ means in the act of killing. ‘He does not see evil’ means he does not see that any evil exists, and he proclaims the same to others. ‘Confidence’ means a state of trust. By saying, ‘There is no result even for deeds done,’ he generates confidence and fearlessness in those who have done evil and have not done merit.

Tapojigucchāyāti tapasā acelavatādinā pāpato jigucchanena, “pāpaṃ virājayāmā”ti acelavatādisamādānenāti attho. Tasmiñhi samādāne ṭhitena saṃvarena saṃvutacitto samannāgato pihito ca nāma hotīti “susaṃvutatto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cattāro yāmā bhāgā catuyāmā, catuyāmā eva cātuyāmā. Bhāgattho hi idha yāma-saddo yathā “rattiyaṃ paṭhamo yāmo”ti. So panettha bhāgo saṃvaralakkhaṇoti āha “cātuyāmena susaṃvuto”ti, catukoṭṭhāsena saṃvarena suṭṭhu saṃvutoti attho. Paṭikkhittasabbasītodakoti paṭikkhittasabbasītudakaparibhogo. Sabbena pāpavāraṇena yuttoti sabbappakārena saṃvaralakkhaṇena pāpavāraṇena samannāgato. Dhutapāpoti sabbena nijjaralakkhaṇena pāpavāraṇenapi dhutapāpo. Phuṭṭhoti aṭṭhannampi kammānaṃ khepanena vikkhepappattiyā kammakkhayalakkhaṇena sabbena pāpavāraṇena phuṭṭho, taṃ phusitvā ṭhito. Na niguhantoti na niguhanahetu diṭṭhasute tatheva kathento.

‘By austerity and revulsion’ means by revulsion from evil through asceticism such as the practice of nakedness; the meaning is by undertaking practices such as nakedness with the thought, ‘We shall get rid of evil.’ For one established in such an undertaking, with a mind restrained by restraint, is said to be endowed and protected; hence it is said, ‘well-restrained in self,’ etc. Four ‘yāmas’ are four parts; four parts are ‘cātuyāma.’ Here the word ‘yāma’ has the meaning of a part, as in ‘the first yāma (watch) of the night.’ Here that part has the characteristic of restraint, thus he says, ‘well-restrained by the fourfold restraint (cātuyāma),’ meaning well-restrained by the four-portioned restraint. ‘One who has rejected all cold water’ means one who has rejected the use of all cold water. ‘Endowed with all prevention of evil’ means endowed with every kind of prevention of evil, which is characterized by restraint. ‘One who has shaken off evil’ means one who has shaken off evil also by means of the all-round prevention of evil which is characterized by the wearing away of kamma. ‘Touched’ means touched by the all-round prevention of evil which is characterized by the destruction of kamma, through the exhaustion and dissipation of the eight kinds of kamma; one stands having touched that. ‘Not concealing’ means speaking of what is seen and heard just as it is, not for the sake of concealment.

Nānātitthiyānaṃyeva [V 1.0147] upaṭṭhākoti paravādīnaṃ sabbesaṃyeva titthiyānaṃ upaṭṭhāko, tesu sādhāraṇavasena abhippasanno. Koṭippattāti mokkhādhigamena samaṇadhamme pattabbamariyādappattā.

‘A supporter of various sectarians’ means a supporter of all sectarians who hold other views, being impartially devoted to them. ‘Having reached the limit’ means having reached the boundary of what is to be attained in the ascetic life through the attainment of liberation.

Sahacaritamattenāti sīhanādena saha vassakaraṇamattena. Sīhena sīhanādaṃ nadantena saheva siṅgālena attano siṅgālaravakaraṇamattena. Kotthukoti khuddakakotthu. Āsaṅkitasamācāroti attanā ca parehi ca āsaṅkitabbasamācāro. Sappurisānanti buddhādīnaṃ.

‘By mere association’ means by the mere act of making a sound along with the lion’s roar. It is the mere making of its own jackal-howl by a jackal at the same time as a lion roars its lion’s roar. ‘Kotthu’ means a small jackal. ‘Of suspicious behavior’ means behavior that is to be suspected by oneself and by others. ‘Of the virtuous’ means of the Buddhas and others.

Tassāti vegabbharissa devaputtassa. Sarīre anuāvisīti sarīre anupavisitvā viya āvisi. Adhimuccīti yathā gahitassa vasena cittaṃ na vattati, attano eva vase vattati, evaṃ adhiṭṭhahi. Āyuttāti dassanena saṃyuttā[M 1.0168]. Pavivekiyanti kappakavatthabhuñjanasenāsanehi pavivittabhāvaṃ. Tenāha “te kirā”tiādi. Rūpe niviṭṭhāti cakkhurūpadhamme abhiniviṭṭhā. Tenāha “taṇhādiṭṭhīhi patiṭṭhitā”ti. Devalokapatthanakāmāti devalokasseva abhipatthanakāmā. Maraṇadhammatāya mātiyā. Tenāha “mātiyāti maccā”ti. Paralokatthāyāti parasampattibhāvāya lokassa atthāya.

‘Of that’ means of the deva’s son Vegabbhara. ‘He entered into the body’ means he possessed it as if having entered the body. ‘He was resolved’ means he determined thus: the mind does not proceed according to what is grasped, but proceeds only under its own power. ‘Engaged’ means connected by seeing. ‘Seclusion’ means the state of being secluded in regard to suitable requisites, food, and lodging. Hence he said, ‘They, it is said,’ etc. ‘Fixed on form’ means fixated on the phenomena of eye and form. Hence he said, ‘Established by craving and views.’ ‘Desiring the deva world’ means desiring only the deva world. ‘Through the mother, who is subject to death.’ Hence he said, ‘“mātiyā” means mortals (maccā).’ ‘For the sake of the other world’ means for the benefit of the world, for the sake of a future state of success.

Pabhāsavaṇṇāti pabhāya samānavaṇṇā. Kesaṃ pabhāyāti āha “candobhāsā”tiādi. Sajjhārāgapabhāsavaṇṇā indadhanupabhāsavaṇṇāti paccekaṃ yojanā. Āmo āmagandho etassa atthīti āmisaṃ. Vadhāyāti viddhaṃsituṃ. Rūpāti rūpāyatanādirūpidhammā.

‘Of the color of light’ means having a color similar to light. To the question, ‘Whose light?,’ he says, ‘like the light of the moon,’ and so on. ‘Having the color of the light of sajjhu resin’ and ‘having the color of the light of Indra’s bow’—the construction is with each term separately. That which has a raw smell (āmagandha) is ‘material bait’ (āmisaṃ). ‘For destruction’ means to destroy. ‘Forms’ means material phenomena such as the form-base and so on.

Rājagahasamīpappavattīnaṃ rājagahiyānaṃ. “Seto”ti kelāsakūṭo adhippetoti āha “setoti kelāso”ti. Kenaci na ghaṭṭetīti aghaṃ, antalikkhanti āha “aghagāmīnanti ākāsagāmīna”nti. Udakaṃ dhīyati etthāti udadhi, mahodadhi. Vipuloti vepullapabbato. Himavantapabbatānanti himavantapabbatabhāgānaṃ. Buddho seṭṭho sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanādīhi sabbaguṇehi.

‘Rājagahasamīpappavattīnaṃ’ means belonging to those dwelling near Rājagaha. ‘Seto’ refers to the Kelāsa peak, hence it is said, ‘Seto means Kelāsa.’ ‘Aghaṃ’ means not struck by anything, hence unhindered; it is said, ‘Aghagāmīnaṃ means ākāsagāmīnaṃ (sky-goers).’ ‘Udadhi’ means water is held here, thus the ocean, the great ocean. ‘Vipulo’ means Vepulla Mountain. ‘Himavantapabbatānaṃ’ means of the parts of the Himavanta mountain. The Buddha is supreme in all virtues such as morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Nānātitthiyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Disciples of Various Sects is completed.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Chapter is completed.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Connected Discourses.

Devaputtasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meanings in the Commentary on the Devaputta Saṃyutta is completed.

3. Kosalasaṃyuttaṃ

3. The Kosala Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Daharasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Dahara Sutta

112. Bhagavatā [V 1.0148][M 1.0169] saddhiṃ sammodīti bhagavato guṇe ajānanto kosalarājā attano khattiyamānena kevalaṃ bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Paṭhamāgate hi satthari tassa sammoditākāraṃ dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā khamanīyādīni pucchantoti yathā bhagavā “kacci te, mahārāja, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā tena raññā saddhiṃ paṭhamaṃ pavattamodo ahosi pubbabhāsitāya, tadanukaraṇena evaṃ sopi rājā bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosīti yojanā. Taṃ pana samappavattamodanaṃ upamāya dassetuṃ “sītodakaṃ viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sammoditanti saṃsanditaṃ ekībhāvanti sammodanakiriyāya samānataṃ ekarūpataṃ, khamanīyanti “idaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ dukkhabahulatāya sabhāvato dussahaṃ, kacci khamituṃ sakkuṇeyya”nti pucchati. Yāpanīyanti paccayāyattavuttikaṃ cirapabandhasaṅkhātāya yāpanāya kacci yāpetuṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ. Sīsarogādiābādhābhāvena kacci appābādhaṃ. Dukkhajīvikābhāvena kacci appātaṅkaṃ. Taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇe uṭṭhānasukhatāya kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ. Tadanurūpabalayogato kacci balaṃ. Sukhavihārasambhavena kacci phāsuvihāro atthīti tattha tattha kacci-saddaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo. Balavappattā pīti pītiyeva. Taruṇapīti pāmojjaṃ. Sammodanaṃ janeti karotīti sammodanīyaṃ. Sammoditabbato sammodanīyanti imaṃ pana atthaṃ dassento “sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato”ti āha. Saritabbabhāvatoti anussaritabbabhāvato. “Saraṇīya”nti vattabbe dīghaṃ katvā “sāraṇīya”nti vuttaṃ.

112. ‘Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodī’ means the Kosalan king, not knowing the virtues of the Blessed One, exchanged greetings with the Blessed One solely out of his own warrior pride. To illustrate his manner of greeting when first meeting the Teacher, it is said, ‘as follows.’ ‘As when asking about well-being and so on’ means just as the Blessed One first engaged in conversation with that king by saying, ‘I hope, great king, you are well, I hope you are comfortable,’ and so on—similarly, that king also exchanged greetings with the Blessed One in the same manner. This is the explanation. To illustrate this mutual exchange of greetings, it is said, ‘like cool water,’ and so on. Here, ‘sammoditaṃ’ means coming together, unification, homogeneity, achieving sameness through the act of greeting, becoming one in form. ‘Khamanīyaṃ’—he asks, meaning, ‘This body-machine with its four wheels and nine gates is inherently difficult to endure due to its abundance of suffering. I hope you can bear it.’ ‘Yāpanīyaṃ’ means, ‘Can you sustain yourself, dependent on the conditions, reckoned as continuous maintenance?’ ‘Appābādhaṃ’ means free from ailments like headaches and so on. ‘Appātaṅkaṃ’ means free from the suffering of livelihood. ‘Lahuṭṭhānaṃ’ means capable of quick exertion in performing various duties due to the pleasure of exertion. ‘Balaṃ’ means possessing strength in accordance with the appropriate power. ‘Phāsuvihāro’ means is there a comfortable way of living? In each case, the word ‘kacci’ should be connected to understand the meaning. ‘Balavappattā pīti’ is simply joy. ‘Taruṇapīti’ is delight. ‘Sammodanīyaṃ’ means it generates or creates greeting. To show this meaning, that 'sammodanīyaṃ' derives from 'that which is fit to be greeted,' he says, 'because of its fitness to be greeted.' ‘Saritabbabhāvato’ means from the state of being worthy of recollection. Though it should be said as ‘saraṇīya,’ it is lengthened and said as ‘sāraṇīya.’

Suyyamānasukhatoti āpāthamadhurataṃ āha, anussariyamānasukhatoti vimaddaramaṇīyataṃ. Byañjanaparisuddhatāyāti sabhāvaniruttibhāvena tassā kathāya vacanacāturiyamāha, atthaparisuddhatāyāti atthassa nirupakkilesataṃ. Anekehi pariyāyehīti anekehi kāraṇehi. Adiṭṭhattāti [V 1.0149][M 1.0170] upasaṅkamanavasena adiṭṭhattā. Guṇāguṇavasenāti guṇavasena gambhīrabhāvaṃ vā aguṇavasena uttānabhāvaṃ vā. Ovaṭṭikasāraṃ katvāti ovaṭṭikāya gahetabbasāravatthuṃ katvā. Lokanissaraṇabhavokkantipañhanti lokato nissaṭabhāvapañhañceva ādito bhavokkamanapañhañca. Satthu sammāsambuddhataṃ pucchanto hi “kiṃ bhavaṃ gotamo sabbalokato nissaṭo, sabbasattehi ca jeṭṭho”ti? Pucchati nāma. Yathā hi satthu sammāsambuddhatāya lokato nissaṭatā viññāyati, evaṃ sabbasattehi jeṭṭhabhāvato seṭṭhabhāvato. Svāyamattho aggapasādasuttādīhi (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34) vibhāvetabbo. Kathaṃ pana sambuddhatā viññāyatīti? Aviparītadhammadesanato. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanādīsu (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.124) vuttanayena veditabbo.

‘Suyyamānasukhatā’ means the sweetness at first hearing. ‘Anussariyamānasukhatā’ means the delight upon reflection. ‘Byañjanaparisuddhatāya’ means skill in speech due to the natural expression of meaning in words; ‘atthaparisuddhatāya’ refers to the meaning being free from defilement. ‘Anekehi pariyāyehi’ means by many reasons. ‘Adiṭṭhattā’ means not having been seen due to not approaching. ‘Guṇāguṇavasena’ means either depth due to virtue or shallowness due to lack of virtue. ‘Ovaṭṭikasāraṃ katvā’ means having taken the essential point from the opening. ‘Lokanissaraṇabhavokkantipañha’ refers both to the question of being liberated from the world and the question of transcending existence from the beginning. For one who asks about the Teacher’s perfect enlightenment, it is as if asking, ‘Is the venerable Gotama liberated from the entire world, and is he the foremost among all beings?’ Just as the Teacher’s perfect enlightenment is understood by his liberation from the world, so too is his preeminence and superiority understood from his being the foremost among all beings. This meaning should be clarified by the Aggapasādasutta and others (Itivuttaka 90; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34). But how is perfect enlightenment understood? By teaching the Dhamma without distortion. This is the summary here; however, the detailed explanation should be understood in the way described in the commentaries on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 1.124).

Rājā satthu aviparītadhammadesanaṃ ajānanto tato evassa sammāsambodhiṃ asaddahanto “vuḍḍhataresupi cirapabbajitesu sammāsambuddhabhāve alabbhamāne tabbiparīte kathaṃ labbheyyā”ti maññamāno “kiṃ pana bhavaṃ gotamo”tiādiṃ vakkhati. Rājā attano laddhiyā na pucchati attano sammukhā tehi asammāsambuddhabhāvasseva paṭiññātattā. Yasmā te musāvāditāya attano upaṭṭhākādīnaṃ “buddhā maya”nti paṭijāniṃsu, tasmā vuttaṃ “loke mahājanena gahitapaṭiññāvasena pucchatī”ti. Svāyamattho āgamissati. Buddhasīhanādanti buddhānaṃ eva āveṇikaṃ sīhanādaṃ. Kāmaṃ maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, sambodhiñāṇe pana gahite taṃ atthato gahitameva hotīti vuttaṃ “sabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhātaṃ sammāsambodhi”nti.

The king, not understanding the Teacher's undistorted teaching of the Dhamma, and thus not believing in his Perfect Self-Enlightenment, thought, "Even among the very old who have long gone forth, the state of Perfect Self-Enlightenment is not found—how then could it be attained in the opposite case?" and so he will say, "But what about the venerable Gotama?" etc. The king does not ask based on his own doctrine, because they themselves had declared in his presence that they were not Perfectly Self-Enlightened. Since they, being speakers of falsehood, declared, "We are Buddhas," to their own attendants and the like, it is said, "He asks based on the declaration accepted by the great mass of people in the world." This meaning will come later. The Buddha's lion's roar means the lion's roar unique to the Buddhas. Although the knowledge of omniscience is the proximate cause for path-knowledge, when enlightenment-knowledge is grasped, that is in effect grasped as its meaning; thus it is said, "Perfect Self-Enlightenment, which is called the knowledge of omniscience."

Pabbajjūpagamanenāti yāya kāyaci pabbajjāya upagamanamattena samaṇā, na samitapāpatāya. Jātivasenāti jātimattena brāhmaṇā, na bāhitapāpatāya. Pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅghoti pabbajitasamūhatāmattena saṅgho, na niyyānikadiṭṭhivisuddhasīlasāmaññavasena saṃhatattāti adhippāyo. Etesaṃ atthīti etesaṃ sabbaññupaṭiññātānaṃ parivārabhūto atthi. Svevāti pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto eva. Keci pana “pabbajitasamūhavasena. Saṅghino, gahaṭṭhasamūhavasena gaṇino”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ gaṇe eva loke saṅghasaddassa niruḷhattā. Ācārasikkhāpanavasenāti acelakavatacariyādi-ācārasikkhāpanavasena. Pākaṭāti saṅghīādibhāvena [M 1.0171] pakāsitā. “Appicchā”ti vatvā tattha labbhamānaṃ appicchataṃ dassetuṃ “apicchatāya vatthampi na nivāsentī”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi tesu sāsanikesu viya santaguṇaniguhanā appicchā labbhatīti. Yasoti kittisaddo. Taranti etena saṃsāroghanti evaṃ sammatattā titthaṃ vuccati laddhīti [V 1.0150] āha “titthakarāti laddhikarā”ti. Sādhusammatāti “sādhū”ti sammatā, na sādhūhi sammatāti āha “santo…pe… puthujjanassā”ti.

"By approaching the state of going forth" (pabbajjūpagamanena) means that they are ascetics merely by adopting some form of going forth, not because they have pacified evil. "By birth" (jātivasena) means that they are brahmins merely by birth, not because they have cast out evil. "The Saṅgha designated as an assembly of those gone forth" (pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅgho) means that it is a Saṅgha merely by being an assembly of those gone forth, not because they are united by a liberating view, purified virtue, and commonality. "They have this" (etesam atthīti) means that these claimants to omniscience have a retinue. "That very one" (sveva) means merely the one designated as an assembly of those gone forth. Some, however, say, "By way of an assembly of those gone forth, they are a Saṅgha; by way of an assembly of householders, they are a group." That is merely their opinion, for in the world, the term 'Saṅgha' is established for a group only. "By teaching conduct" (ācārasikkhāpanavasena) refers to teaching practices such as the conduct of the naked ascetics. "Manifest" (pākaṭā) means made evident by their status as having a group, etc. Having said "of few wishes," to show the few-wishedness found among them, it is said, "They do not even wear a garment due to their lack of desire." For among them, unlike among those of the true teaching, few wishes are not found through concealing good qualities. "Fame" (yaso) is the word for renown. Because it is considered that "one crosses the flood of saṃsāra by this," a doctrine is called a ford (titthaṃ); hence, he says, "ford-makers" (titthakarā) are "doctrine-makers" (laddhikarā). "Deemed good" (sādhusammatā) means deemed "good," not deemed good by the good; thus he says, "by the good...by the ordinary person."

Kappakolāhalanti kappato kolāhalaṃ, “kappuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti devaputtehi ugghositamahāsaddo. Imeti pūraṇādayo. Buddhakolāhalanti devatāhi ghositaṃ buddhakolāhalaṃ. Payirupāsitvāti purisasutiparamparāya sutvā. Cintāmaṇivijjā nāma paracittajānāpanavijjā. Sā kevaṭṭasutte “maṇikā”ti āgatā, ādi-saddena gandhārisambhavavijjādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha gandhāriyā vikubbanaṃ dasseti. Attabhāveti sarīre. Rājusmāti rājatejo.

"Kappa uproar" (kappakolāhalaṃ) means the uproar about the aeon, the great sound proclaimed by the devas, saying, "There will be an aeon's arising." "These" (ime) refers to Pūraṇa and others. "Buddha uproar" (buddhakolāhalaṃ) means the Buddha uproar proclaimed by the devas. "Having attended upon" (payirupāsitvā) means having heard through a lineage of men. "The jewel-lore" (cintāmaṇivijjā) is a knowledge that makes known the thoughts of others. It is called "jewel" (maṇikā) in the Kevaṭṭa Sutta, and the term "etc." includes the Gandhārī spell and others. There, it shows a transformation through Gandhārī. "In his own body" (attabhāve) means in the body. "Royal splendor" (rājusmā) means the king's radiance.

Sukkadhammoti anavajjadhammo nikkilesatā. Idaṃ gahetvāti idaṃ parammukhā “mayaṃ buddhā”ti vatvā attano sammukhā “na mayaṃ buddhā”ti tehi vuttavacanaṃ gahetvā. Evamāhāti “yepi te, bho gotama…pe… navo ca pabbajjāyā”ti evaṃ avoca. Attano paṭiññaṃ gahetvāti “na mayaṃ buddhā”ti tesaṃ attano purato pavattitaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā. Īdise ṭhāne kiṃ-saddo paṭisedhavācako hotīti vuttaṃ “kinti paṭikkhepavacana”nti, kasmā paṭijānātīti attho?

"Pure Dhamma" (sukkadhammo) means blameless Dhamma, freedom from defilements. "Taking this" (idaṃ gahetvā) means taking this statement made by them: behind one's back, they say, "We are Buddhas," but in one's presence, they say, "We are not Buddhas." "Thus he said" (evam āha) refers to the words, "Those, Master Gotama... newly gone forth." "Taking their own declaration" (attano paṭiññaṃ gahetvā) means taking their declaration made in his presence, "We are not Buddhas." Here, the word "what" (kiṃ) serves as a term of denial; thus it is said, "the word 'kiṃ' is a word of refusal." The meaning is: "Why does one claim?"

Na uññātabbāti na garahitabbā. Garahattho hi ayaṃ u-saddo. “Daharo”ti adhikatattā vakkhamānattā ca “khattiyoti rājakumāro”ti vuttaṃ. Urasā gacchatīti urago, yo koci sappo, idha pana adhippetaṃ dassetuṃ “āsīviso”ti āha. Sīlavantaṃ pabbajitaṃ dasseti sāmaññato “bhikkhū”ti vadanto. Idha pana yasmā “bhavampi no gotamo”tiādinā bhagavantaṃ uddissa kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, tasmā bhagavā attānaṃ abbhantaraṃ akāsi. Yadipi viseso sāmaññajotanāya vibhāvito hoti, saṃsayuppattidīpakaṃ noti vuttaggahaṇaṃ pana taṃ paricchijjatīti. Tenāha “desanākusalatāyā”tiādi. Idāni avaññāparibhave payogato vibhāvetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha acittīkatākāravasena avaññāya pākaṭabhāvo, vambhanavasena paribhavassāti adhippāyena [M 1.0172] kāyapayogavasena avaññā dassitā, vacīpayogavasena paribhavo, ubhayaṃ pana ubhayatthāpi pabhedato gahitaṃ, avaññaparibhavānaṃ dvinnampi ubhayattha pariggaho. Taṃ sabbampīti taṃ avaññādi sabbampi. Catūsupi taṃ na kātabbameva sampati āyatiñca anatthāvahattā.

"Not to be despised" (na uññātabbā) means not to be blamed. Indeed, this syllable 'u-' has the meaning of blame. "Youthful" (daharo) means being superior and to be explained later, hence it is called "a prince of the warrior caste." "Moving on the chest" (urasā gacchati) means a serpent (urago), any snake; but here, to specify the intended meaning, it is called "a viper" (āsīviso). It indicates a virtuous renunciant in general by the term "bhikkhu." Here, however, because he began the discussion by addressing the Blessed One with "Even our Master Gotama," the Blessed One included himself in the matter. Although a specific case is clarified by indicating a general one, this does not give rise to doubt, for the aforementioned inclusion defines it. Therefore, he says, "skill in teaching," etc. Now, to elaborate on the application in terms of contempt and humiliation, it is stated, "And here," etc. In that context, the obviousness of contempt is due to acting without respect, and humiliation is by way of disparagement; thus contempt is shown through bodily action, and humiliation through verbal action. However, both are taken in both respects according to the distinction, for both contempt and humiliation are included in both. All of that—that is, all contempt and the rest—should certainly not be done in any of the four cases, since it brings harm both now and in the future.

Tadatthadīpanāti tassa ādito vuttassa atthassa dīpanā. Visesatthadīpanāti tato visiṭṭhatthadīpanā[V 1.0151]. Khettānaṃ adhipatīti khattiyoti niruttinayena saddasiddhi veditabbā. Khettato vivādā satte tāyatīti khattiyoti lokiyā kathayanti. “Mahāsammato, khattiyo, rājā”ti evamāgatesu imesu dutiyaṃ. Akkharanti samaññā. Sā hi udayabbayābhāvato “na kadāci kharatīti akkhara”nti vuttā. Tenāha “nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti. Jātisampannanti sampannajātiṃ ativisuddhajātiṃ. Tīṇi kulānīti brāhmaṇavessasuddakulāni. Atikkamitvāti attano jātisampattiyā abhibhavitvā.

"The explanation of its meaning" (tadatthadīpanā) is the elucidation of the meaning stated from the beginning. "The explanation of the distinctive meaning" (visesatthadīpanā) is the elucidation of a meaning more distinguished than that. "Lord of the fields" (khettānaṃ adhipatīti) is to be understood as "khattiya," according to the method of etymology. Worldly people say, "He protects beings from disputes over fields; thus he is a khattiya." Among these terms when they occur—"Mahāsammata, khattiya, rājā"—this is the second. "Akkharā" (akkharaṃ) means a designation. For it is said, "Because it does not decay since there is no origination and dissolution, it is called 'akkhara' (indestructible)." Hence it is said, "Name and lineage do not decay." "Endowed with birth" (jātisampannaṃ) means one of accomplished birth, of exceedingly pure birth. "The three clans" (tīṇi kulāni) are the brahmin, vessa, and sudda clans. "Having transcended" (atikkamitvā) means having surpassed by the accomplishment of one's own birth.

Kevalaṃ nāmapadaṃ vuttaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ apekkhatevāti āha “ṭhānaṃ hīti kāraṇaṃ vijjatī”ti. Uddhaṭadaṇḍenāti samantato ubbhatena daṇḍena sāsanena, balavaṃ upakkamaṃ garukaṃ rājānampi. Taṃ khattiyaṃ parivajjeyyāti khattiyaṃ avaññāparibhavakaraṇato vajjeyya. Tenāha “na ghaṭṭeyyā”ti.

"Only the noun is spoken, the verb is indeed expected," thus he says, "because there is a cause, namely, a place." "With an upraised stick" (uddhaṭadaṇḍena) means with a stick raised all around, with a strong and severe command, a heavy punishment even for kings. "One should avoid that Khattiya" (taṃ khattiyaṃ parivajjeyya) means one should avoid the Khattiya, refraining from causing disrespect and humiliation. Therefore, he said, "one should not provoke."

Uragassa ca nānāvidhavaṇṇaggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ vadati “yena yena hī”tiādinā. Bahubhakkhanti mahābhakkhaṃ sabbabhakkhakhādakaṃ. Pāvakaṃ sodhanatthena asuddhassapi dahanena. Soti maggo. Kaṇho vattanī imassāti kaṇhavattanī. Mahanto aggikkhandho hutvā. Yāvabrahmalokappamāṇoti kappavuṭṭhānakāle araññe agginā gahite kālantare eva kaṭṭhatiṇarukkhādisambhavoti dassetuṃ “jāyanti tattha pārohā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha.

The reason for the various colors of the serpent is explained by the phrase "yena yena hi," etc. "Bahubhakkhanti" means a great eater, a devourer of all. "Pāvakaṃ" means purifying by burning even the impure. "Soti" is the path. "Kaṇhavattanī" means it has a black path. Having become a great mass of fire. "Yāvabrahmalokappamāṇoti" refers to the extent up to the Brahma world: to show that at the time of the aeon's arising, when the forest is seized by fire, in due time, wood, grass, trees, etc., originate, he says, "there," etc., showing what is stated in the Pali text by the phrase "jāyanti tattha pārohā" (sprouts arise there).

Ḍahituṃ na sakkoti paccakkosanādinā. Vinassanti samaṇatejasā vināsitattā. “Na tassā”ti ettha na-kāraṃ “vindare”ti ettha ānetvā sambandhitabbanti [M 1.0173] āha “na vindantī”ti. Vatthumattāvasiṭṭhoti ṭhānameva nesaṃ avasissati, sayaṃ pana sabbaso saha dhanena vinassantīti attho.

One cannot burn him by means of recrimination and so on. They perish, destroyed by the ascetic's power. He said that in "Na tassā," the negative particle "na" is brought to "vindare" and connected; hence, it means "na vindantī." "Vatthumattāvasiṭṭhoti" means only the site remains for them; but they themselves, along with their wealth, perish completely.

“Sammadeva samācare”ti ettha yathā rājādīsu sammā samācareyya, taṃ vibhāgena dassento “khattiyaṃ tāvā”tiādimāha. Taṃ suviññeyyameva. Tisso kulasampattiyoti khattiya-brāhmaṇagahapati-mahāsālakulāni vadati. Pañca rūpibrahmaloke, cattāro arūpībrahmaloketi evaṃ nava brahmaloke kammabhavavibhāgena, sesānaṃ gaṇanānaṃ upapattibhavavibhāgena.

"Sammadeva samācare" means one should act rightly towards kings and others, as explained in detail by "khattiyaṃ tāva" and so on. This is easily understood. "The three kinds of family fortune" (tisso kulasampattiyo) refer to the families of warriors, brahmins, and wealthy householders and great clans. Five abodes in the form Brahma world and four in the formless Brahma world make up the nine Brahma worlds, classified by karmic existence, while the remaining calculations are classified by rebirth existence.

Abhikkantanti ativiya kamanīyaṃ. Sā panassā kantatā ativiya iṭṭhatāya manavaḍḍhanatāya [V 1.0152] sobhanatāyāti āha “atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ atisundaranti attho”ti. “Abhikkanta”nti vacanaṃ apekkhitvā napuṃsakaniddeso, vacanaṃ pana bhagavato dhammadesanāti tathā vuttaṃ. Atthamattadassanaṃ vā etaṃ, tasmā atthavasena liṅgavibhattivipariṇāmo veditabbo. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo.

"Abhikkantaṃ" (abhikkantaṃ) means exceedingly lovely. That loveliness of it is because of being exceedingly desirable, greatly pleasing to the mind, and exceedingly beautiful; thus he said, "it means exceedingly liked, exceedingly agreeable, exceedingly beautiful." Considering the word "Abhikkanta," the neuter gender is indicated; but the utterance is the Blessed One's teaching, therefore it is said thus. Or this is merely showing the meaning, therefore the alteration of gender and case should be understood according to the meaning. The same method applies to the second term as well.

Adhomukhaṭhapitanti kenaci adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Heṭṭhāmukhajātanti sabhāveneva heṭṭhāmukhaṃ jātaṃ. Ugghāṭeyyāti vivaṭaṃ kareyya. Hatthe gahetvāti “puratthābhimukho uttarābhimukho vā gacchā”tiādīni avatvā hatthe gahetvā nissandehaṃ katvā “esa maggo”ti evaṃ vatvā “gacchā”ti vadeyya. Kāḷapakkhacātuddasīti kāḷapakkhe cātuddasī. Nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyyāti ādheyyassa anādhārabhūtaṃ bhājanaṃ tassa ādhārabhāvāpādanavasena ukkujjeyya. Aññāṇassa abhimukhattā heṭṭhāmukhajātatāya saddhammavimukhaṃ, tato eva adhomukhabhāvena asaddhamme patitanti evaṃ padadvayaṃ yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ, na yathāsaṅkhayaṃ. Kāmaṃ kāmacchandādayopi paṭicchādakā, micchādiṭṭhi pana savisesaṃ paṭicchādikāti āha “micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchanna”nti. Tenāha bhagavā – “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 1.310). Sabbāpāyagāmimaggo kummaggo “kucchito maggo”ti katvā. Sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhatāya micchādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha micchattadhammā micchāmaggo. Teneva hi tadubhayapaṭipakkhataṃ sandhāya “saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sappiādisannissayo padīpo na tathā ujjalo, yathā telasannissayoti [M 1.0174] telapajjotaggahaṇaṃ. Etehi pariyāyehīti etehi nikkujjitukkujjanapaṭicchannavivaraṇādiupamopamitabbappakārehi.

‘Placed upside down’ means placed upside down by someone. ‘Naturally facing downward’ means by its very nature it is born facing downward. ‘Should reveal’ means should make it open. ‘Taking by the hand’ means without saying, ‘Go facing east or north,’ and so on, taking one by the hand, making it free from doubt, saying, ‘This is the path,’ and thus saying, ‘Go.’ ‘The fourteenth of the dark fortnight’ means the fourteenth day in the dark fortnight. ‘Should turn upright what is overturned’ means one should turn upright a vessel that is not a receptacle for what is to be placed in it, thereby making it a receptacle. Due to facing ignorance and being naturally downward-facing, one is turned away from the True Dhamma; and thus, by being upside-down, one falls into the false Dhamma—thus, these two pairs of terms should be connected appropriately, not sequentially. Although sensual desire and so on are also concealers, wrong view is especially a concealer; hence it is said, ‘concealed by the thicket of wrong view.’ Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘Monks, I declare wrong view to be the foremost fault’ (AN 1.310). The path leading to all states of woe is the wrong path, being a ‘corrupt path.’ Due to their direct opposition to right view and so on, wrong view and so on—the eight wrong states—constitute the wrong path. For this very reason, with reference to the opposition to both, it is said, ‘by one who makes manifest the path to heaven and liberation.’ A lamp dependent on ghee and so on is not as bright as one dependent on oil—hence, the taking of an oil lamp as an example. ‘By these methods’ means by these ways of comparison through similes, such as overturning and turning upright, concealing and revealing, and so on.

Pasannākāranti pasannehi kātabbaṃ sakkāraṃ. Saraṇanti paṭisaraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ. Ajjatāti ajjāti padassa vaḍḍhanamattaṃ hettha tā-saddo yathā “devatā”ti. Pāṇehi upetanti pāṇehi saha saraṇaṃ upetaṃ. “Yāva me pāṇā dharanti, tāva saraṇaṃ gatameva maṃ dhāretū”ti āpāṇakoṭikaṃ attano saraṇagamanaṃ pavedeti. Tenāha “yāva me”tiādi. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘The manner of the faithful’ means the honor to be done by the faithful. ‘Refuge’ means reliance, final resort. ‘Ajjatā’ is merely an extension of the word ‘ajja’ (today); the suffix ‘-tā’ here is like in ‘devatā’ (deity). ‘Endowed with life’ means gone for refuge together with life. ‘As long as my life-breaths endure, so long may you hold me as one who has gone for refuge’—thus, one declares one’s going for refuge to last until the very end of life. Therefore, it is said, ‘as long as my,’ and so on. Whatever is not explicitly analyzed here in meaning is nevertheless easily understood.

Daharasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dahara Sutta is concluded.

2. Purisasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Purisa Sutta

113. Purimasutteti purimasuttadesanāyaṃ. Tattha hi upasaṅkamantavelāya satthu guṇe ajānanto [V 1.0153] kevalaṃ sammodanaṃ karoti. Desanaṃ sutvā pana satthu guṇe ñatvā saraṇaṅgatattā idha imasmiṃ samāgame abhivādesi pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandi. Attānaṃ adhi ajjhattaṃ, avijahena attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattadhammā ajjhattaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahaṇavasena, bhummatthe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Kāmañcāyaṃ ajjhattasaddo gocarajjhattavisayajjhattaajjhattajjhattesu pavattati. Te panettha na yujjantīti vuttaṃ “niyakajjhatta”nti, niyakasaṅkhātaajjhattadhammesūti attho. Tenāha “attano santāne”ti. Lubbhanalakkhaṇoti gijjhanalakkhaṇo, ārammaṇe daḷhaggahaṇasabhāvoti attho. Dussanalakkhaṇoti kujjhanalakkhaṇo, byāpajjanasabhāvoti attho. Muyhanalakkhaṇoti aññāṇalakkhaṇo, ārammaṇe sabhāvasammohabhāvoti attho. Viheṭhentīti atthanāsanaanatthuppādanehi vibādhenti. Tato eva yathā saggamaggesu na dissati, evaṃ karontīti āha “nāsenti vināsentī”ti. Attani sambhūtāti santāne nibbattā.

113. ‘In the former sutta’ means in the discourse of the former sutta. There, at the time of his approach, not knowing the Teacher’s virtues, he merely offers a friendly greeting. But having heard the teaching, known the Teacher’s virtues, and gone for refuge, here in this assembly he paid homage, bowing down with the fivefold prostration. ‘Internally’ (ajjhattaṃ) is from ‘adhi’ (concerning) and ‘attānaṃ’ (oneself); it refers to phenomena that occur concerning oneself, with reference to oneself, without abandoning oneself, by way of grasping them as a unity; and this is a term for the individual in the locative sense. Although this term ‘ajjhatta’ is used for the internal sense-sphere, the internal sense-object, and the internal of the internal, these are not applicable here. Thus it is said, ‘one’s own internal,’ meaning, in the internal phenomena designated as one’s own. Therefore, it is said, ‘in one’s own continuity.’ ‘The characteristic of greed’ means the characteristic of avidity; the meaning is that it has the nature of grasping an object firmly. ‘The characteristic of hatred’ means the characteristic of anger; the meaning is that it has the nature of malevolence. ‘The characteristic of delusion’ means the characteristic of ignorance; the meaning is that it has the nature of confusion about an object’s intrinsic nature. ‘They harass’ means they oppress by destroying what is beneficial and producing what is not beneficial. For that very reason, they act in such a way that one is not seen on the paths to heaven; thus it is said, ‘they destroy, they annihilate.’ ‘Arisen in oneself’ means produced in one’s continuity.

Purisasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Purisa Sutta is concluded.

3. Jarāmaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Jarāmaraṇa Sutta

114. Aññatra [M 1.0175] jarāmaraṇāti jarāmaraṇena vinā. Jarāmaraṇavirahito jāto nāma atthi nu khoti pucchati. Pāḷiyaṃ jātassāti paccatte sāmivacanaṃ. Mahāsālāti iminā ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā “mahāsālā”ti vuttanti dasseti yathā “puratthiyoti pulatthiyo”ti. Mahāsārappattāti mahantaṃ vibhavasāraṃ pattā. Koṭisataṃ dhanaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. “Kumbhaṃ nāma dasa ambaṇānī”ti vadanti. Issarāti vibhavissariyena issarā. Suvaṇṇarajatabhājanādīnanti ādi-saddena vatthaseyyāvasathādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Asādhāraṇadhanānaṃ nidhānagatattā “anidhānagatassā”ti vuttaṃ. Tuṭṭhikaraṇassāti pāsādasivikādisukhasādhanassa.

114. ‘Apart from aging and death’ means without aging and death. The question is: ‘Is there anyone born who is devoid of aging and death?’ In the Pāli, ‘jātassa’ is a genitive used in the sense of the individual. ‘Mahāsālā’: this shows that ‘mahāsālā’ is said by changing the letter ‘r’ to ‘l’, just as ‘puratthiyo’ becomes ‘pulatthiyo.’ ‘Having attained great substance’ means having attained a great substance of wealth. A hundred crores of wealth; or this is the reading. They say, ‘A kumbha is ten ambaṇas.’ ‘Lords’ means lords by reason of their lordship over wealth. ‘Of golden and silver vessels, etc.’: by the word ‘etc.’ are included clothing, bedding, dwellings, and so on. Because uncommon wealth is put into a treasury, the term ‘of that which has not gone into a treasury’ is used. ‘Of that which causes delight’ means of the means for happiness, such as palaces, palanquins, and so on.

Ārakā kilesehīti niruttinayena saddasiddhimāha. Ārakāti ca sabbaso samucchinnattā tehi dūreti attho. Rāgādīnaṃ hatattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvato, anuttaradakkhiṇeyyatādipaccayā ca arahaṃ. Kāmañcāyaṃ saṃyuttavaṇṇanā, abhidhammanayo eva pana nippariyāyoti āha “cattāro āsavā”ti brahmacariyavāsanti maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ. Vuṭṭhāti vuṭṭhavanto. Catūhi maggehi karaṇīyanti paccekaṃ catūhi maggehi kattabbaṃ pariññāpahānasacchikiriyabhāvanābhisamayaṃ. Evaṃ gataṃ soḷasavidhaṃ hoti. Osīdāpanaṭṭhena bhārā viyāti bhārā. Tenāha “bhārā have pañcakkhandhā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.22). Attapaṭibaddhatāya attano avijahanato paramatthadesanāya ca paramattho arahattaṃ. Kāmañcāyamattho sabbasamiddhisasantatipariyāpanno anavajjadhammo [V 1.0154] sambhavati akuppasabhāvā, aparihānadhammesu pana aggabhūte arahatte sātisayo, na itaresūti “arahattasaṅkhāto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Orambhāgiyuddhambhāgiyavibhāgaṃ dasavidhampi bhavesu saṃyojanaṃ kilesakammavipākavaṭṭapaccayo hutvā nissarituṃ appadānavasena bandhatīti bhavasaṃyojanaṃ. Satipi hi aññesaṃ tappakkhiyabhāvena vinā saṃyojanāni tesaṃ tappaccayabhāvo atthi, bhavaniyāmo orambhāgiyuddhambhāgiyasaṅgahitoti taṃtaṃbhavanibbattakakammaniyāmo ca hoti, na ca upacchinnasaṃyojanassa katānipi kammāni bhavaṃ nibbattentīti tesaṃyeva saṃyojanaṭṭho daṭṭhabbo. Sammā [M 1.0176] kāraṇehi jānitvāti ñāyena dukkhādīsu so yathā jānitabbo; tathā jānitvā, pubbakālakiriyāvimuttā hi aparakālakiriyā ca yathā sambhavati, taṃ dassetuṃ “maggapaññāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

He is ‘far’ (ārakā) from the defilements; thus, he states the derivation of the word by way of etymology. And ‘far’ means he is distant from them because they are completely cut off. He is an ‘arahant’ because he has destroyed (hata) lust and so on, because of the absence of secret (raha) evil-doing, and because he is worthy (araha) of requisites such as the unsurpassed offering. Although this is the commentary on the Saṃyutta, the Abhidhamma method is the definitive one; hence it states, ‘the four taints.’ ‘Living the holy life’ means living the holy life of the path. ‘He has emerged’ (vuṭṭhāti) means those who have emerged. ‘To be done by the four paths’ means the comprehension of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development, which is to be done by each of the four paths. Thus, it becomes sixteenfold. Because they have the meaning of weighing down, they are like burdens (bhārā viya), thus they are called ‘burdens’ (bhārā). Therefore, it is said: ‘The five aggregates are indeed burdens,’ and so on (SN 3.22). The ultimate goal (paramattho) is arahantship, because it is connected to oneself, because it does not abandon oneself, and because it is the ultimate meaning in the teaching. And although this meaning—a blameless state, unshakeable in nature—is found throughout the continuity of all achievements, it is exceptional in arahantship, which is the highest of the imperishable states, but not in the others; hence it is said, ‘designated as arahantship,’ and so on. The tenfold fetter of existence, divided into the lower and higher parts, is called the ‘fetter of existence’ because it binds one by becoming a condition for the round of defilements, kamma, and results in various existences, and by not allowing an opportunity to escape. For even when other states are present, without the fetters, which are on their side, they have no status as a condition for them. The regulation of existence is comprised of the lower and higher fetters, and it is also the regulation of kamma that produces this or that existence. But for one whose fetters are cut off, even kammas that have been done do not produce existence. Thus, the function of a fetter should be seen only in them. ‘Having known rightly by means’ means having known suffering and so on by the proper method, as it should be known. In order to show how, having known thus, a later action is free from a former action, as is possible, it is said, ‘by the wisdom of the path,’ and so on.

Bhijjanasabhāvo khaṇāyattattā. Nikkhipitabbasabhāvo maraṇadhammattā. Ayaṃ kāyo usmāyuviññāṇāpagamo chaḍḍanīyadhammo, yasmiṃ yaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ, taṃ tassa santānagatavippayuttanti katvā vattabbataṃ arahatīti āha “khīṇāsavassa hi ajīraṇadhammopi atthī”tiādi. Tenāha bhagavā “imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññapemi lokasamudayañca lokanirodhañcā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45). Assa khīṇāsavassa, “jīraṇadhamma”nti yathāvuttaṃ ajīraṇadhammaṃ ṭhapetvā jīraṇadhammaṃ dassento “tesaṃpāyaṃ kāyo bhedanadhammo”ti evamāha. Jaraṃ pattasseva hissa bhedananikkhipitabbatāniyate atthe suttadesanā pavattā. Atthassa uppatti aṭṭhuppatti, sā etassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattiko. Kira-saddo anussavattho, tena anussavāgatoyamattho, na aṭṭhakathāgatoti dīpeti. Tenāha “vadantī”ti. Yenāyaṃ attho hetunā aṭṭhuppattiko, taṃ dassetuṃ “sivikasālāyaṃ nisīditvā kathita”nti vuttaṃ. “Viharati jetavane”ti nidānavacanena yathā na virujjhati, tathā veditabbaṃ. Nanu imassa suttassa pucchāvasiko nikkhepoti? Saccametaṃ, suttekadesaṃ pana sandhāya aṭṭhuppattikatāvacanaṃ. Keci pana “yānaṃ āruhitvā rājā āgato, rañño ārohanīyarathaṃ dassetvā vutta”ntipi vadanti.

Its nature is to break up, because it is dependent on the moment. Its nature is to be discarded, because it is subject to death. This body, devoid of heat, the life-faculty, and consciousness, is a thing to be cast away—it is fit to be said that whatever is established in it is disconnected from its continuity. Thus, it is said, ‘Even for one whose cankers are destroyed, there is still the nature of not decaying,’ and so on. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘In this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, I make known the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world,’ and so on (SN 1.107; AN 4.45). For him whose cankers are destroyed, showing the nature of decay, having set aside the nature of non-decay as stated, he thus says, ‘For them, this body is of a breaking nature.’ For him who has attained old age, the sutta teaching proceeds with the definite meaning that breaking and being discarded are inevitable. The arising of a meaning is ‘aṭṭhuppatti’; one for whom this exists is ‘aṭṭhuppattiko’. The word ‘kira’ is in the sense of tradition; therefore, this meaning has come by tradition, not from the commentary, thus it indicates. Therefore, it is said, ‘they say.’ To show the reason why this meaning is occasioned by a specific incident, it is said, ‘spoken while seated in the Sivika hall.’ It should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict the introductory words, ‘He dwells in Jetavana.’ Now, is not the exposition of this sutta based on a question? This is true, but the statement about it being occasioned by a specific incident refers to a portion of the sutta. Some, however, say, ‘Having mounted a vehicle, the king arrived, and it was spoken after showing the king’s royal chariot.’

Sarīre pheṇapiṇḍasame kiṃ vattabbaṃ? Sabbhi saddhinti sādhūhi saha pavedayanti. Na hi kadāci sādhūnaṃ sādhūhi saha kattabbā honti, tasmā sīdanasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ bhijjanappattattā nibbānaṃ sabbhīti vuccati. Purimapadassāti “satañca dhammo na jaraṃ upetī”ti padassa. Kāraṇaṃ dassento byatirekavasena. Sataṃ dhammo nibbānaṃ kilesehi saṃsīdanabhijjanasabhāvo na hoti, tasmā taṃ āgamma jaraṃ na upeti. Kilesā pana tannimittakā, [V 1.0155] evamayaṃ vuttakāraṇato jaraṃ na upetīti. Tenāha “ida”ntiādi. Sundarādhivacanaṃ vā etaṃ “sabbhī”ti padaṃ apāpatādīpanato, sabbhidhammabhūtanti [M 1.0177] attho. Tenāha “virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34), na tena dhammena samatthi kiñcī”ti (khu. pā. 6.4; su. ni. 227) ca.

What is to be said of the body, which is like a lump of foam? `Sabbhi saddhiṃ` means they make it known together with the good. Indeed, for the good there is never anything to be done with the good. Therefore, because it is the attainment of the breaking of defilements which have a nature of sinking, Nibbāna is called `sabbhi`. Regarding the previous phrase, ‘the Dhamma of the good does not age,’ the reason is explained by way of contrast. The Dhamma of the good, Nibbāna, is not of the nature of sinking or breaking due to defilements; therefore, having come to it, aging does not approach. But defilements are the cause of that aging; thus, for the reason stated, aging does not approach. Therefore, it is said, ‘this,’ etc. Alternatively, the term ‘sabbhi’ is a beautiful expression because it indicates faultlessness, meaning ‘having become the Dhamma of the good.’ Hence it is said, ‘dispassion is declared the highest among them’ (Itivuttaka 90; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34), and ‘there is nothing equal to that Dhamma’ (Khuddakapāṭha 6.4; Sutta Nipāta 227).

Jarāmaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jarāmaraṇasutta is concluded.

4. Piyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Piyasutta

115. Rahasi gatassāti janasambādhato apakkantassa. Nilīnassa teneva janavivekena ekamantaṃ nisajjāya ekībhāvena paṭisallīnassa viya. Tenāha “ekībhūtassā”ti. Sabbaññubhāsitaṃ karonto āha tassa vacanaṃ “evameta”nti sampaṭicchitvā tassa vacanaṃ tathāpaccanubhāsanto. Antakenādhipannattā eva khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇādi mānusaṃ bhavaṃ jahato. Anuganti anugataṃ, tameva anugāmīti attho. Nicayanti uparūpari vaḍḍhiyā nicitabhūtaṃ. Samparāyikanti samparāya hitaṃ.

115. `Rahasi gatassa` means of one who has departed from the crowd. `Nilīnassa` refers to one who is as if absorbed in seclusion, by that very seclusion from people, by sitting in a solitary place, in a state of being alone. Hence it is said, `ekībhūtassa`. Making it an utterance of the Omniscient One, having accepted his words with ‘So it is,’ he spoke, repeating his words thus. Because of being overcome by the Ender, one abandons human existence, including fields, land, gold, and silver, etc. `Anuganti` means ‘followed’; the meaning is ‘a follower.’ `Nicayanti` means what has become heaped up by growing again and again. `Samparāyikaṃ` means what is beneficial for the future life.

Piyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Piyasutta is concluded.

5. Attarakkhitasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Attarakkhitasutta

116. Pīdahananti saṃyamanaṃ. Kammapathabhedaṃ appattassāti supinakālo viya pavattimattatāya kammapathavisesaṃ agatassa. Kammassāti akusalakammassa. Saṃvaranti saṃvarabhāvaṃ dasseti, itarassa pana saṃvarabhāvo purimehi tīhi padehi dassitovāti. Ottappampi gahitameva tadavinābhāvato. Na hi pāpajigucchanaṃ pāpautrāsarahitaṃ, utrāso vā pāpajigucchanarahito atthīti.

116. `Pīdahanaṃ` means restraint. `Kammapathabhedaṃ appattassa` means for one who has not attained a specific path of action, merely existing as a process, like the state of dreaming. `Kammassa` refers to unwholesome action. `Saṃvaraṃ` shows the state of restraint; but for the other, the state of restraint is already shown by the preceding three terms. Moral dread is also included, due to its inseparability. For there is no loathing of evil without dread of evil, nor is there dread of evil without loathing of evil.

Attarakkhitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Attarakkhitasutta is concluded.

6. Appakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Appakasutta

117. Uḷārasaddo [M 1.0178] seṭṭhe bahuke ca dissatīti āha “paṇīte ca bahuke cā”ti. Mānamajjanenāti mānavasena madappattiyā. Atikkamanti sādhumariyādavītikkamalakkhaṇaṃ dosaṃ. Kūṭo pāso.

117. The word `uḷāra` is seen in the sense of both excellent and abundant, hence it is said, ‘refined and abundant.’ `Mānamajjanena` means due to arrogance and attainment of intoxication. `Atikkamaṃ` refers to the fault characterized by overstepping the boundaries of the good. `Kūṭo` means a snare.

Appakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Appakasutta is concluded.

7. Aḍḍakaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Aḍḍakaraṇasutta

118. Yasmā [V 1.0156] kāmanimittaṃ satto sampajānamusā bhāsati, tasmā kāmā tassa patiṭṭhā paccayo kāraṇanti āha “kāmahetū”tiādi. Bhadramukhasīsena viṭaṭubhaṃ bhadropacārena upacaratīti attho, vinicchayo karīyati etthāti aḍḍakaraṇaṃ, vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ. Khippanti kūṭaṃ, macchakhippantipi vaṭṭati. Oḍḍitanti oḍḍanavasena phalaṃ pāpitaṃ.

118. Because a being, on account of a sensual object, speaks falsehood knowingly, therefore sensual pleasures are his foundation, condition, and cause—hence it is said, ‘because of sensual pleasure,’ etc. `Bhadramukhasīsena` means that one approaches a rogue with fair conduct. `Aḍḍakaraṇaṃ` is where a judgment is made, a place of judgment. `Khippaṃ` means a trap; it also applies to a fish trap. `Oḍḍitaṃ` means brought to fruition by way of setting a snare.

Aḍḍakaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Aḍḍakaraṇasutta is concluded.

8. Mallikāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Mallikāsutta

119. “Kasmā pucchatī”ti? Pucchākāraṇaṃ codetvā samudayato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “ayaṃ kira mallikā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mālārāmaṃ gantvāti attano pitu mālārāmaṃ rakkhaṇatthañceva avasesapupphaggahaṇatthañca gantvā. Kāsigāmeti kāsiraṭṭhassa gāme. So kira gāmo mahākosalarājena attano dhītuyā patigharaṃ gacchantiyā pupphamūlatthāya dinno, taṃnimittaṃ. Bhāgineyyena ajātasattunā. Tassāti rañño pasenadissa. Sāti mallikā. Nivattitunti tassā dhammatāya nivattituṃ tassā vacanaṃ paṭikkhipituṃ. Nevajjhagāti vattamānatthe atītavacananti āha “nādhigacchatī”ti. Puthu attāti tesaṃ sattānaṃ attā.

119. ‘Why does she ask?’ Having raised the question of the reason for asking, ‘This, it seems, is Mallikā,’ and so on, was said to show it from the origin onward. `Having gone to the flower garden` means having gone to her father's flower garden both to guard it and to collect the remaining flowers. `In a village of Kāsi` means in a village of the Kāsi kingdom. It is said that village was given by King Mahākosala to his daughter when she was going to her husband's house for the price of flowers; that is the reason. By Ajātasattu, the nephew. `His` means of King Pasenadi. `She` means Mallikā. `Nivattituṃ` means to refute, that is, to turn back from her principle, to reject her words. `Nevajjhagā` is a past tense word used in the present sense; thus he says, `nādhigacchati` (he does not find). `Puthu attā` means the self of those beings.

Mallikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mallikāsutta is concluded.

9. Yaññasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Yaññasutta

120. Thūṇanti [M 1.0179] yaññūpatthambhaṃ. Upanītāni yaññaṃ yajituṃ ārambhāya. Ettāvatāti “idha, bhante…pe… rudamānā parikammāni karontī”ti ettakena pāṭhena. Sanniṭṭhānanti “naṃ itthiṃ labhissāmi nu kho, na nu kho labhissāmī”ti nicchayaṃ avindanto na ñāyanto. Pheṇuddehakanti yathā yattha kuthite pheṇaṃ uddehati na upadhīyati, evaṃ anekavāraṃ pheṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā. Taṃ divasanti tasmiṃ raññā niddaṃ alabhitvā dukkhaseyyadivase. Ālokaṃ oloketvāti lohakumbhimukhavaṭṭisīse patte tattha mahantaṃ ālokaṃ oloketvā. Attāno vacanaṃ rañño pavattiñāpanatthaṃ. Mahāsaddo udapādi “evarūpaṃ yaññaṃ rājā kārāpetī”ti. Vattukāmo ahosi, vattuñca pana avisahanto “sa” iti vatvā lohakumbhiyaṃ nimuggo. Imaṃ gāthaṃ vattukāmo ahosīti ayaṃ panettha sambandho. Esa nayo sesapadadvayepi. Dhammabheriṃ carāpesuṃ “koci [V 1.0157] kañci pāṇaṃ mā hanatū”ti. So itthisāmiko puriso sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi attano upanissayasampattiyā sattu ca desanāvilāsasampattiyā, rājā pana mahābodhinirujjhanasabhāvattā kiñci visesaṃ nādhigacchi.

120. 'Thūṇa' means the pillar of the sacrifice. 'Prepared' means brought for the purpose of performing the sacrifice. 'Thus far' refers to this passage: 'Here, venerable sir... weeping, they perform the preliminary rites.' 'Determination' means not finding a decision, not knowing: 'Shall I obtain that woman or not?' 'Foam-raising' means just as foam, where it is agitated, rises and does not settle, so too, having raised foam many times. 'That day' means on that day of painful lying down when the king could not get sleep. 'Having looked at the light' means having seen a great light in the bowl placed on the rim of the iron pot's mouth. His own words were for the purpose of making the king aware of the event. A great cry arose: 'The king is having such a sacrifice performed.' He wanted to speak, but being unable to speak, he said 'sa' and sank into the iron pot. He intended to recite this verse—this is the connection here. The same principle applies to the remaining two phrases as well. They had the drum of the Dhamma proclaimed: 'Let no one kill any living being.' That man, the husband of the woman, became established in the fruit of stream-entry due to the attainment of his own supporting conditions and the Teacher's excellence in delivering the teaching; but the king, due to his nature being one of obstructing great enlightenment, did not attain any distinction.

Saṅgahavatthūnīti lokassa saṅgahakāraṇāni. Nipphannasassato navabhāge kassakassa datvā raññaṃ ekabhāgaggahaṇaṃ dasamabhāgaggahaṇaṃ. Evaṃ kassakā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā sassāni sampādentīti āha “sassasampādane medhāvitāti attho”ti. Tato orabhāge kira chabhāgaggahaṇaṃ jātaṃ. Chamāsikanti channaṃ channaṃ māsānaṃ pahonakaṃ. Pāsetīti pāsagate viya karoti. Vācāya piyassa piyakarassa kammaṃ vācāpeyyaṃ. Sabbaso raṭṭhassa iddhādibhāvato khemaṃ. Nirabbudaṃ coriyābhāvato. Idañhi raṭṭhaṃ acoriyaṃ niraggaḷanti vuccati apārutagharabhāvato.

The bases of beneficence mean the causes for benefiting the world. When the crops are ripe, giving nine parts to the farmer, the king takes one part—this is the taking of the tenth part. Thus, the farmers, being joyful and content, cultivate the crops well. Hence it is said: 'Wise is he in the production of crops,' which is the meaning. Then, in later times, it is said that the taking of a sixth part arose. 'Six-monthly' means sufficient for six months at a time. 'Pāseti' means to act as if caught in a snare. 'Vācāpeyya' means the action of one who is dear by speech, who does what is dear. In every way, the kingdom is secure through prosperity and so on. 'Freedom from disturbance' means due to the absence of theft. For this kingdom is called 'free from theft, without bolts,' because its houses remain unbarred.

Uddhaṃmūlakaṃ katvāti ummūlaṃ katvā. Dvīhi pariyaññehīti mahāyaññassa pubbabhāge pacchā ca pavattetabbehi dvīhi parivārayaññehi. Sattavīsati…pe… nassāti sattavīsādhikānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pasusatānaṃ dvāvīsatiyā assādīhi ca saṭṭhiadhikadvisataāraññakapasūhi ca saddhiṃ sampiṇḍitānaṃ pana [M 1.0180] navādhikachasatapasūnaṃ māraṇena bheravassa pāpabhīrukānaṃ bhayāvahassa. Tathā hi vadanti –

'Having uprooted it from the base' means having completely uprooted it. 'With two surrounding sacrifices' refers to the two attendant sacrifices that should be performed before and after the great sacrifice. 'Twenty-seven... perished' means by the killing of six hundred and nine animals—namely, three hundred and twenty-seven domestic animals, along with twenty-two horses and the like, and two hundred and sixty wild animals—which was terrifying, bringing fear to those who are afraid of evil. For thus they say—

“Chasatāni niyujjanti, pasūnaṃ majjhime hani,

Assamedhassa yaññassa, adhikāni navāpi cā”ti.

Six hundred animals are yoked; in the middle sacrifice they are slain, for the horse sacrifice, and nine more as well.

Sammanti yugacchidde pakkhipitabbadaṇḍakaṃ. Pāsentīti khipanti. Saṃhārimehīti sakaṭehi vahitabbehi yūpehi. Pubbe kira eko rājā sammāpāsaṃ yajanto sarassatinadītīre pathaviyā vivare dinne nimuggoyeva ahosi. Andhabālabrāhmaṇā gatānugatigatā “ayaṃ tassa saggagamanamaggo”ti saññāya tattha sammāpāsayaññaṃ paṭṭhapenti. Tena vuttaṃ “nimuggokāsato pabhutī”ti. Ayūpo appakadivaso yāgo, sayūpo bahudivasaṃ sādheyyo satrayāgo. Mantapadābhisaṅkhatānaṃ sappimadhūnaṃ vājamiti samaññā, hiraññasuvaṇṇagomahiṃ sādisattarasakadakkhiṇassa. Sāragabbhakoṭṭhāgārādīsu natthettha aggaḷanti niraggaḷo. Tattha kira yaññe attano sāpateyyaṃ anavasesato anigūhitvā niyyātīyati. Mahārambhāti bahupasughātakammā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vividhā yattha haññare”ti vakkhamānattā “mahākiccā”ti attho vutto, idha “mahārambhāti papañcavasena ajeḷakā”tiādi vuttanti “bahupasughātakammā”ti attho vutto. Nirārambhāti [V 1.0158] etthāpi vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Anugataṃ kulanti anukulaṃ, kulānugatanti attho veditabbo. Tenāha “yaṃ niccabhattādi…pe… attho”ti.

'Samma' means the stick to be placed in the hole of the yoke. 'Pāsenti' means they throw. 'Saṃhārima' means with posts to be carried by carts. Formerly, it is said, a certain king, while performing the Sammāpāsa sacrifice on the banks of the Sarasvatī River, sank into a fissure that had opened in the ground. Blind and foolish brahmins, following the way of their predecessors, thought, 'This is the path to heaven for him,' and established the Sammāpāsa sacrifice there. Hence it is said, 'from the place of sinking onwards.' A sacrifice of few days is 'ayūpa' (without a post); a 'satrā' sacrifice to be accomplished over many days is 'sayūpa' (with a post). 'Vāja' is a designation for clarified butter and honey consecrated with mantras, and for the seventeen-fold offering including gold, silver, cows, and buffaloes. In the treasury, storerooms, and other places, there is no bolt—hence 'niraggaḷa' (without a bolt). There, it is said, in that sacrifice, one gives away all of one’s possessions without remainder and without concealment. 'Mahārambhā' means an act involving the slaughter of many animals. However, in the commentary, because it will be explained that 'various beings are slain there,' the meaning 'great undertaking' is given. Here, since it is said, '“Mahārambhā” refers to goats and sheep, etc., due to elaboration,' the meaning 'an act involving the slaughter of many animals' is given. 'Nirārambhā' should also be understood in the manner explained. 'Anugataṃ kulaṃ' means 'anukulaṃ' (of good family); the meaning should be understood as 'following the family tradition.' Therefore, it is said, 'That which is constant alms-giving, etc., ... is the meaning.'

Yaññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Yaññasutta is concluded.

10. Bandhanasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bandhana Sutta

121. Idanti “idha, bhante”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ. Te bhikkhū ārocesunti sambandho. Tesūti tesu raññā bandhāpitamanussesu. Sukatakāraṇanti sukāraṇakiriyaṃ ārocesuṃ, na kevalaṃ tesaṃ manussānaṃ bandhāpitabhāvaṃ[M 1.0181]. Idāni tamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “rañño kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhavaṅkoti aṭṭhaṃso. Antogharacārinoti antepuravāsino.

121. The word 'idaṃ' refers to the expression beginning 'Here, venerable sir,' and so forth. The connection is: 'those bhikkhus informed.' 'Among them' refers to those people imprisoned by the king. 'The reason being a good deed' means they reported the doing of a meritorious act, not merely the fact that those people had been imprisoned. Now, to explain that matter in detail, what begins with 'It is said that the king...' was stated. 'Aṭṭhavaṅka' means having eight parts. 'Living in the inner house' refers to those dwelling in the inner palace.

Ukkaṭṭheti yuddhe. Mantīsūti guttamantīsu. Akutūhalanti saññataṃ. Piyanti piyāyitabbaṃ. Annapānamhi madhure abhutte uppanne. Attheti atthe kicce jāte thiranti na kathenti kāyabalamattena apanetuṃ sakkuṇeyyattā. Suṭṭhu rattarattāti ativiya rattā eva hutvā rattā. Sārattenāti sārabhāvena sārabhāvasaññāya. Ohārinanti heṭṭhā haraṇasīlanti āha “catūsu apāyesu ākaḍḍhanaka”nti. Sithilanti sithilākāraṃ, na pana sithilaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “duppamuñca”nti.

'Ukkaṭṭheti' (praises) means in battle. 'Mantīsu' means among those with guarded counsel. 'Akutūhala' means restrained. 'Piya' means to be cherished. The phrase is: 'when sweet food and drink arise but are not consumed.' 'Atthe' means when a purpose or duty has arisen. 'Thira' (firm) means they do not speak of it, as they are capable of removing it merely by bodily strength. 'Suṭṭhu rattarattā' means having become exceedingly impassioned, they are impassioned. 'Sārattena' means by its essential nature, by the perception of its essential nature. 'Ohārin' means having the nature of dragging down; it is said to be 'that which drags one into the four states of loss.' 'Sithila' (slack) means slack in appearance, but not truly slack. Therefore, the Blessed One said it is 'hard to release.'

Bandhanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Bandhana Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Sattajaṭilasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sattajaṭila Sutta

122. Pubbārāmasaṅkhāteti sāvatthinagarassa pubbadisāya katattā pubbārāmeti saṅkhaṃ gate. Tatrāti “migāramātuyā pāsāde”ti tasmiṃ saṃkhittavacane. Ayaṃ idāni vuccamānā anupubbikathā ādito paṭṭhāya anukkamakathā. Patthanaṃ akāsi tassa bhagavato aggupaṭṭhāyikaṃ ekaṃ upāsikaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ ākaṅkhantī. Meṇḍakaputtassāti meṇḍakaseṭṭhiputtassa. Mātiṭṭhāne [V 1.0159] ṭhapesi tassā upakāraṃ garubhāvañca disvā. Tāya kārite pāsādeti tāya mahāupāsikāya mahālatāpasādhanaṃ vissajjetvā navahi koṭīhi karīsamatte bhūmibhāge kārite sahassagabbhapaṭimaṇḍite pāsāde.

122. 'Pubbārāma' (Eastern Park) is so called because it was built to the east of the city of Sāvatthī, thus it came to be designated 'Eastern Park.' 'There' refers to the concise expression 'at Migāramātā’s mansion.' This gradual discourse now being spoken is a sequential discourse from the very beginning. She made a wish, desiring that position, after seeing a certain female lay follower who was the chief attendant of that Blessed One. 'Of Meṇḍakaputta' means of the son of the merchant Meṇḍaka. He established her in the position of a mother, seeing her assistance and her dignity. 'In the mansion built by her' refers to the mansion, adorned with a thousand chambers, built by that great female lay follower on a plot of land the size of a karīsa with nine crores, after she had given up her Mahālatā ornament.

Parūḷhakacchāti parūḷhakacchalomā. Kamaṇḍalughaṭikādiṃ pabbajitaparikkhāraṃ. Naggabhogganissirikānanti naggānañceva bhoggānañca nissirikānañca. Te hi anivatthavatthatāya naggā ceva, acelakavatādinā bhoggasarīratāya bhoggā, sobhārahitatāya nissirikā ca. Attanā diṭṭhasutaṃ [M 1.0182] paṭicchādetvā na katheyyunti akāraṇametaṃ tesaṃ raññā payuttacarapurisabhāvato. Evaṃ kate pana te “aññepi pabbajitā atthīti ayaṃ jānātī”ti maññeyyunti kohaññacitto evaṃ akāsīti sakkā viññātuṃ. Tathā hi tenatthena aparitosamāno “apicā”tiādimāha.

'Parūḷhakaccha' means having overgrown armpit hair. The phrase refers to: a water pot, a small pot, and other requisites of a renunciant. 'Of the naked, crooked, and wretched' means of those who are naked, crooked, and wretched. For they were naked due to not wearing clothes; they were crooked due to having crooked bodies from vows such as nakedness; and they were wretched due to being devoid of beauty. That she should conceal what she had seen and heard herself and not speak of it—this was not the reason, due to their being spies employed by the king. However, had she done so, they might have thought, 'This one knows that there are other renunciants,' and thus it could be understood that she acted with a deceitful mind. Indeed, being dissatisfied with that meaning, he said what begins with 'Moreover...'

Kāsikacandananti ujjalacandanaṃ. Taṃ kira vaṇṇavasena samujjalaṃ hoti pabhassaraṃ, tadatthameva naṃ saṇhataraṃ karonti. Tenāha “kāsikacandananti saṇhacandana”nti. Vaṇṇagandhatthāyāti vaṇṇasobhatthañceva sugandhabhāvatthañca. Vaṇṇagandhatthāyāti chavirāgakaraṇatthañceva sugandhatthāya ca. “Gihinā”tiādīhi padehi evaṃ pamādavihārinā tayā arahanto duviññeyyāti dasseti.
