'Kāsika sandalwood' means 'radiant sandalwood'. It is said to be very radiant and luminous because of its color, and for that very reason they make it even smoother. Hence, it is said, 'Kāsika sandalwood' means 'smooth sandalwood'. 'For the sake of color and fragrance' means both for the sake of beauty of color and for the sake of good fragrance. 'For the sake of color and fragrance' means both for the sake of making the skin radiant and for the sake of good fragrance. With the words 'by a householder,' and so forth, it shows that arahants are hard to discern by one who lives thus heedlessly.

Saṃvāso nāma idha kālena upasaṅkamananti dassento “upasaṅkamantenā”ti āha. Kāyavācāhi asaṃyatenapi saṃyatākāro, asaṃvutindriyenapi saṃvutindriyākāro. Pariggahessāmīti vīmaṃsissāmi “parisuddhaṃ nu kho, no”ti. Sappaññenāti sīlapariggaṇhanapaññāya sappaññena. Jānituṃ na sakkoti sabhāvassa sato sīlassa anupadhāraṇato.

'Association' here means 'visiting from time to time'; thus, by saying 'by visiting,' he shows this. Even with unrestrained body and speech, there is the appearance of being restrained; even with unrestrained faculties, there is the appearance of having restrained faculties. 'I will examine' means 'I will investigate whether it is pure or not'. 'By one with wisdom' means 'by one with wisdom that discerns virtue'. He is unable to know the true nature of the existing virtue, because of not discerning it.

Kathanenāti aparāparaṃ kathanena. Tathā hi vakkhati “ekaccassa hī”tiādi. Ariyavohāroti diṭṭhādilakkhaṇena voharito “diṭṭhaṃ adiṭṭha”ntiādinā pavuttasaddavohāro. Tassa pana kāraṇameva gaṇhanto “ettha cetanā”ti āha. Esa nayo anariyavohārepi. Paramatthato hi saccavācādayo musāvādādayo cetanālakkhaṇāti. Paññattivohāro tathā tathā voharitabbato evamāha “saṃvohārena kho, mahārāja, soceyyaṃ veditabba”nti.

'By speaking' means by speaking consecutively. For thus he will say, 'For some, indeed...' and so on. 'Noble expression' refers to the verbal expression spoken with the characteristic of 'seen,' etc., such as 'seen, unseen,' and so on. But taking only the cause of that, he says, 'Here, intention...' This method applies even to ignoble expression. For in the ultimate sense, truthful speech and false speech, and so forth, are characterized by intention. Regarding conventional expression, because it is to be expressed in such and such a way, he said, 'By conversation, O king, purity is to be known'.

Ñāṇathāmoti ñāṇaguṇabalaṃ, yena ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānādinā accāyikakiccakaraṇīyāni niṭṭhāpeti. Saṃkathāyāti atthavīmaṃsanavasena pavattāya sammākathāya. Uppilavati lahukabhāvato. Heṭṭhācarakāti [V 1.0160] avacarakā. Ye anupavisitvā paresaṃ rahassavīmaṃsanavasena pavattā, tesu ocarakavohāroti vuttaṃ “carā hī”tiādi.

'Strength of knowledge' means 'the power of the quality of knowledge', by which urgent tasks are accomplished through readiness of wit in a situation and other means. 'By conversation' means 'by proper conversation that proceeds by way of examining the meaning'. 'It floats' means it floats up because of lightness. 'Spies' means secret agents. Regarding those who, having entered, engage in secret investigations of others, the designation 'spy' is used, as it is said: 'For they are spies,' and so on.

Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānenāti vaṇṇena vā saṇṭhānena vā vaṇṇapokkharatāya vā saṇṭhānasampattiyā vā. Sujāno pesalo vissaseti yojanā. Lahukadassanenāti [M 1.0183] parittadassanena vijjukena viya. Parikkhārabhaṇḍakenāti pabbajitaparikkhārabhūtena bhaṇḍakena. Lohaḍḍhamāsoti lohamayo upaḍḍhagghanakamāso.

'By color and form' means either by color or by form, or by the excellence of color or the accomplishment of form. The application is: 'easy to know, amiable, inspires confidence'. 'With slight seeing' means 'with fleeting seeing, like lightning'. 'With a bundle of requisites' means 'with a bundle of goods that are requisites for a renunciant'. 'An iron half-māsaka' means 'a māsaka of half value made of iron'.

Sattajaṭilasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sattajaṭila Sutta is concluded.

2. Pañcarājasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Pañcarāja Sutta

123. Rūpāti rūpasaṅkhātā kāmaguṇā. Te pana nīlādivasena anekabhedabhinnāpi rūpāyatanattā cakkhuviññeyyataṃ nātivattantīti āha “nīlapītādibhedaṃ rūpārammaṇa”nti. To-saddopi dā-saddo viya kālattho hotīti āha “yatoti yadā”ti. Manaṃ āpayati vaḍḍhetīti manāpaṃ, manoramaṃ. Manāpanipphattitanti tassa puggalassa manasā piyāyitaṃ, tassa aggabhāvena pariyantaṃ paramaṃ koṭiṃ katvā pavattitanti attho. Puggalamanāpanti ārammaṇasabhāvaṃ acintetvā puggalassa vasena manāpabhāveneva iṭṭhatāya iṭṭhanti. Sammutīti samaññā. Puggalamanāpaṃ nāma saññāvipallāsavasena viparītampi gaṇhāti itarasabhāvatoti āha “yaṃ ekassa…pe… iṭṭhaṃ kanta”nti. Idāni taṃ jivhāviññeyyavasena yojetvā dassento “paccantavāsīna”ntiādimāha. Idaṃ puggalamanāpanti idaṃ yathāvuttaṃ jivhāviññeyyaṃ viya aññampi evaṃjātikaṃ tena tena puggalena manāpanti gahetabbārammaṇaṃ puggalamanāpaṃ nāma.

123. 'Forms' refers to forms reckoned as sensual qualities. Though these are divided into many kinds, such as blue, yellow, etc., being the form sphere, they do not transcend what is cognizable by the eye. Hence, it is said, 'form as an object, differentiated as blue, yellow, etc.' The particle 'to' is like the particle 'dā,' indicating time. Thus, it is said, 'yato means yadā' (when). 'Manāpaṃ' means what pleases and increases the mind—what is delightful. 'The accomplishment of the agreeable' refers to what is loved by that person's mind, meaning it proceeds having made the ultimate extreme, the highest point, by virtue of its supreme nature. 'Personally agreeable' means that, without considering the intrinsic nature of the object, it is desired for its agreeableness on account of the person. 'Convention' means designation. What is called 'personally agreeable' can also be grasped as its opposite due to perceptual distortion, because of the nature of another. Hence, it is said, 'What is pleasing, lovely, and desirable to one...' Now, connecting this to what is cognizable by the tongue, he shows this, saying: 'For those living on the borders...' etc. 'This personally agreeable' means that this object to be grasped as agreeable by this or that person—like the aforementioned things cognizable by the tongue, and any other thing of this kind—is called 'personally agreeable'.

Loke paṭivibhattaṃ natthi, vibhajitvā dassanena lokena madhurajātenapi paṭivibhattaṃ katvā gahetuṃ na sakkuṇeyyāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “vibhajitvā pana dassetabba”nti. Dibbakappampīti devalokapariyāpannasadisampi amanāpaṃ upaṭṭhāti uḷārapaṇītārammaṇaparicayato. Majjhimānaṃ pana…pe… vibhajitabbaṃ tesaṃ manāpassa manāpato, amanāpassa amanāpato upaṭṭhānato. Tatthapi iṭṭhāniṭṭhaparicchedo nippariyāyato evaṃ veditabboti dassento āha “tañca paneta”ntiādi. Tañca panetaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kāmāvacarajavanesu akusalassa vasena yebhuyyena [M 1.0184] pavattatīti katvā tattha “rajjati dussatī”ti akusalasseva pavatti dassitā. Sesakāmāvacarassapi vasena pavatti labbhateva. Tathā hi taṃ appaṭikūlepi paṭikūlākārato, paṭikūlepi [V 1.0161] appaṭikūlākārato pavattatīti. Vipākacittaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ paricchindati, na sakkā vipākaṃ vañcetunti. Kusalakammaṃ hi ekantato iṭṭhameva, akusalakammañca aniṭṭhameva, tasmā tattha uppajjamānaṃ vipākacittaṃ yathāsabhāvato pavattatīti.

The meaning is that there is no inherent division in the world; even if one were to show it divided, the world would not be able to grasp it as divided, even in the case of pleasant things. Therefore, it is said, 'Yet it should be shown by division.' Even something like a divine thing, similar to what is included in the world of the devas, appears disagreeable due to familiarity with superior and refined objects. But for those of middling faculties... it should be divided, because for them what is agreeable appears as agreeable, and what is disagreeable appears as disagreeable. Here too, to show that the distinction between what is desirable and undesirable should be understood without ambiguity, it is said, 'And yet this...' etc. And yet, this object, being desirable or undesirable, mostly occurs in the impulsive consciousnesses of the sensual sphere by way of unwholesome states. Therefore, there, 'one is impassioned or repelled' shows the occurrence of unwholesome states. The occurrence by way of other sensual-sphere consciousnesses is also obtained. For it occurs with a repulsive aspect even toward what is not repulsive, and with a non-repulsive aspect even toward what is repulsive. Resultant consciousness distinguishes between the desirable and undesirable—one cannot deceive the result. Wholesome kamma is entirely desirable, and unwholesome kamma is entirely undesirable. Therefore, the resultant consciousness that arises in that case proceeds according to its true nature.

Yaṃ pana sammohavinodaniyaṃ “kusalakammajaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, taṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena sobhanaṃ akusalakammajampi ekaccānaṃ sattānaṃ iṭṭhanti anuññātaṃ siyā. Kusalakammajaṃ pana sabbesaṃ iṭṭhamevāti vadanti. Tiracchānagatānaṃ kesañci manussarūpaṃ amanāpaṃ, yato te disvāva palāyanti. Manussā ca devatānaṃ rūpaṃ disvā bhāyanti, tesampi vipākaviññāṇaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha kusalavipākameva uppajjati, tādisassa pana puññassa abhāvā na tesaṃ tattha abhirati hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kusalakammajassa pana aniṭṭhassa abhāvo viya akusalakammajassa sobhanassa iṭṭhassa abhāvo vattabbo. Hatthiādīnampi hi akusalakammajaṃ manussānaṃ akusalavipākasseva ārammaṇaṃ, kusalakammajaṃ pana pavatte samuṭṭhitaṃ kusalavipākassa, iṭṭhārammaṇena vomissakattā appakaṃ akusalakammajaṃ bahulaṃ akusalavipākuppattiyā kāraṇaṃ na bhavissatīti sakkā vattuṃ. Idāni tameva vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇavavatthānaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kiñcāpi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tayidaṃ sammutimanāpasaṃvibhāgatthaṃ vuttaṃ, idha pana na tathā vibhattanti āha “bhagavā panā”tiādi.

However, regarding the statement in the Sammohavinodanī, 'there is no undesirable thing born of wholesome kamma,' this should be seen as a mere illustration. By this, it would be admitted that for some beings, even a beautiful thing born of unwholesome kamma is desirable. But they say that what is born of wholesome kamma is desirable for everyone. For some animals, the human form is disagreeable, since they flee upon seeing it. And humans become frightened upon seeing the forms of deities; yet, for them too, the resultant consciousness arising in relation to that form is indeed a wholesome result. However, it should be understood that due to the absence of such merit, they do not find delight in it. The idea that there are no undesirable things born of wholesome kamma is to be denied, just as the idea that there are no beautiful and desirable things born of unwholesome kamma is to be denied. For, in the case of elephants and so on, what is born of their unwholesome kamma is an object for the unwholesome result of humans, while what is born of wholesome kamma, arisen in the course of existence, is an object for a wholesome result. Because of being mixed with desirable objects, it can be said that a small amount born of unwholesome kamma will not be a cause for the arising of much unwholesome result. Now, to clarify this very distinction between desirable and undesirable objects based on their results, it is said: 'Even though...' etc. This was stated for the purpose of distinguishing what is conventionally agreeable, but here it is not classified in that way, as it is said: 'The Blessed One, however...' etc.

So upāsako candanaṅgalagāme jātattā “candanaṅgaliko”ti paññāyati, “candanavilāso”ti keci. Tassa upāsakassa paṭibhānaṃ udapādīti yojanā. Te rājāno hatappabhe hatasobhe disvāti sambandho. Udakābhisitteti udakena abhisiñcite. Aṅgāre viyāti aṅgārakkhaṇe viya.

That lay follower, having been born in the village of Candanaṅgala, is known as 'Candanaṅgalika'; some call him 'Candanavilāsa.' The application is that an inspiration arose in that lay follower. The connection is: 'the kings saw them deprived of splendor and beauty.' 'Sprinkled with water' means sprinkled with water. 'Like embers' means like embers at that instant.

Kālassevāti pageva. Avigatagandhaṃ taṅkhaṇavikasitatāya. Īdisaṃ vacananti “acchādesī”ti evarūpaṃ vacananti.

'Early' means in the morning. 'With fragrance not faded' means due to having bloomed at that very moment. 'Such a speech' means a speech of this sort: 'he covered'.

Pañcarājasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pañcarājasutta is finished.

3. Doṇapākasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Doṇapāka Sutta

124. “Doṇapākakura”nti [M 1.0185] ettha vibhattilopaṃ katvā niddesoti āha “doṇapākaṃ kura”nti. Doṇassāti catunnaṃ āḷhakānaṃ, soḷasanāḷīnanti attho. Tadupiyanti tadanurūpaṃ, tassa [V 1.0162] vuttaparimāṇassa anucchavikanti attho. Pubbeti taṃdivasato purimataradivasesu. Balavāti mahā. Bhattapariḷāhoti bhattasammadahetuko. Assa rañño ubhosu passesu gahitatālavaṇṭā bījanti yamakatālavaṇṭehi. Phāsuvihāranti bhojane mattaññutāya laddhabbasukhavihāraṃ. Bhojanamattaññū hi sukhavihāro hoti. Tenāha “tanukassa bhavanti vedanā, saṇikaṃ jīrati āyu pālaya”nti.

124. In 'Doṇapākakura,' the explanation is given as 'doṇapākaṃ kura,' the case ending having been elided. A doṇa means four āḷhakas, that is, sixteen nāḷīs. 'Tadupiya' means corresponding to that, fitting for that stated measure. 'Pubbe' means on days earlier than that day. 'Balavā' means great. 'Bhattapariḷāho' means the feverishness caused by intoxication from food. For this king, on both sides, they fan him with palm-leaf fans, that is, with paired palm-leaf fans. 'Phāsuvihāra' means the comfortable abiding to be obtained through moderation in eating. For one who is moderate in eating indeed abides comfortably. Therefore, it is said: 'For one who is lean, sensations are mild; slowly does he age, protecting his life.'

Tanukassāti tanukā assa puggalassa, bhuttapaccayā visabhāgavedanā na hontīti attho. Saṇikanti mandaṃ mudukaṃ, aparissayamevāti attho. Jīratīti paribhuttāhāro paccati. Āyupālayanti nirodho avedano jīvitaṃ rakkhanto. Atha vā saṇikaṃ jīratīti so bhojane mattaññū puggalo parimitāhāratāya saṇikaṃ cirena jīrati jaraṃ pāpuṇāti jīvitaṃ pālento.

'Tanukassa' means for that person who is lean; the meaning is that disagreeable feelings do not arise on account of food. 'Saṇikaṃ' means slowly, gently, that is, without danger. 'Jīrati' means the consumed food is digested. 'Āyupālayanti' means protecting life, a cessation without feeling. Alternatively, 'saṇikaṃ jīrati' means that person, being moderate in eating, ages slowly, over a long time, on account of his limited food intake, reaching old age while preserving his life.

Pariyāpuṇitvāti ettha yathā sabbaṃ so pariyāpuṇi, tato parañca yathā paṭipajji, taṃ dassetuṃ “raññā saddhi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tāvatake taṇḍule hāreyyāsi tadupiyañca byañjananti ānetvā sambandho.

Regarding 'Pariyāpuṇitvā,' to show how he fully mastered everything and thereafter practiced it, the phrase 'with the king,' etc., is stated. The phrase 'Tāvatake taṇḍule hāreyyāsi tadupiyañca byañjanaṃ' is to be connected by supplying 'bringing.'

Purisabhāgo esāti majjhimena purisena bhuñjitabbabhāgo eso, yadidaṃ nāḷikodanamattaṃ. Sallikhitasarīratāti bhamaṃ āropetvā ullikhitassa viya sabbapariḷāhavūpasamassa puthulatāpagatasarīrassa. Sīlaṃ samparāyikatthoti vuttaṃ, kuto panettha sīlanti āha “bhojane”tiādi. Sīlaṅgaṃ nāma hotīti catupārisuddhisīlassa avayavo eko bhāgo hoti.

'Purisabhāgo eso' means this is the portion to be eaten by an average man, namely, a measure of a nāḷika of rice. 'Sallikhitasarīratā' means like one whose body has been scraped by applying a lathe, all feverishness having subsided, and the grossness of the body having departed. It is said that virtue is for the benefit of the future life; but where is virtue here? He says, 'in eating,' etc. 'Sīlaṅgaṃ' means it is a component, one part, of the fourfold purification virtue.

Doṇapākasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Doṇapāka Sutta is concluded.

4. Paṭhamasaṅgāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Saṅgāma Sutta

125. Vedena [M 1.0186] ñāṇena īhati iriyatīti vedehī, kosalarājabhaginī ajātasattuno mātā, sā kira sampajaññajātikā. Tenāha “paṇḍitādhivacana”nti, cattāri aṅgāni etissanti caturaṅginī. Dvinnaṃ rajjānanti kāsikarajjamagadharajjānaṃ antare, so pana gāmo kāsikarajjo.

125. 'Vedehī' means one who strives and acts with knowledge; she was the sister of the king of Kosala and the mother of Ajātasattu. It is said that she was of a nature endowed with full awareness. Therefore, it is said to be 'a term for the wise.' 'Caturaṅginī' means possessing four constituents. 'Between the two kingdoms' means between the kingdoms of Kāsi and Magadha; however, that village belonged to the kingdom of Kāsi.

Pāpāti lāmakā nihīnācārā. Mejjati siniyhatīti metti, sā etesu atthīti mittā. Saha ayanti pavattantīti sahāyā. Sampavaṅkanti suṭṭhu onataṃ. Jayakāraṇaṃ disvā āha, tathā [V 1.0163] hi “ajja imaṃ rattiṃ dukkhaṃ setī”ti kālaparicchedavasena vuttaṃ. Verighāto nāma veripuggale satīti āha “veripuggalaṃ labhatī”ti.

'Pāpā' means low and of base conduct. One is affectionate (`mejjati`, `siniyhati`), hence `metti` (friendship). Those in whom this exists are `mittā` (friends). They go (`ayanti`) and proceed (`pavattanti`) together (`saha`), hence they are `sahāyā` (companions). 'Sampavaṅkanti' means thoroughly bent down, that is, humble. Seeing the cause of victory, he said, 'Indeed, tonight he will sleep in suffering'—this was said with reference to a specific period of time. The term 'verighāto' (slaying of enemies) applies when there is an enemy person; thus it says, 'he gets an enemy person.'

Paṭhamasaṅgāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Saṅgāma Sutta is concluded.

5. Dutiyasaṅgāmasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Second Saṅgāma Sutta

126. Suṇāthāti “vatvā”ti vacanaseso. Upakappatīti sambhavati. Sayhaṃ hotīti kātuṃ sakkā hoti. “Yadā caññe”ti ca-kāro nipātamattanti āha “yadā aññe”ti. Vilumpantīti vināsaṃ acchindanaṃ karonti. Vilumpīyatīti viluttaparasantakassa asakattā puggalo diṭṭhadhammikaṃ kammaphalaṃ paṭisaṃvedento viya sayampi parena vilumpīyati, dhanajāniṃ pāpuṇāti. “Kāraṇa”nti hi maññatīti pāpakiriyaṃ attano hitāvahaṃ kāraṇaṃ katvā maññati. Jayanto puggalo “idaṃ nāma jināmī”ti maññamāno sayampi tato parājayaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ghaṭṭetāranti pāpakammavipākaṃ. Kammavivaṭṭenāti kammassa vivaṭṭanena, paccayalābhena laddhāvasarena vivaṭṭetvā vigamitena kammenāti attho.

126. Regarding 'Suṇātha,' the omitted word is 'vatvā' (having said). 'Upakappati' means it is possible. 'Sayhaṃ hoti' means it is possible to do. Regarding 'Yadā caññe,' the particle 'ca' is merely a particle; hence it is said, 'yadā aññe.' 'Vilumpanti' means they cause destruction and seizure. 'Vilumpīyati' means that a person who has plundered the property of others, because it is not his own, as if experiencing the result of his kamma in this very life, is himself plundered by others and suffers loss of wealth. 'Kāraṇanti hi maññati' means he considers his evil deed to be a beneficial cause for himself. A conquering person, thinking, 'I have conquered this,' himself undergoes defeat on that account. 'Ghaṭṭetāraṃ' means the result of evil kamma. 'Kammavivaṭṭena' means by the unfolding of kamma; that is, by the kamma that has turned around and departed, having found its opportunity through the acquisition of conditions.

Dutiyasaṅgāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Saṅgāma Sutta is concluded.

6. Mallikāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta

127. Ekaccāti [M 1.0187] paṇḍitā sapaññā. Seyyāti varā. Gāthāsukhatthaṃ sasurasaddalopaṃ katvā “sassudevā”ti vuttanti āha “sassusasuradevatā”ti. Disājeṭṭhakāti catūsupi disāsu jeṭṭhakasīsena hi lokaṃ vadati. Tādisāyāti tathārūpāya medhāvitādiguṇavuttiyā. Subhariyāyāti sukhettabhūtāya sundaritthiyāti attho.

127. 'Ekaccā' means some wise ones, endowed with wisdom. 'Seyyā' means the best, the excellent. For the sake of the verse's euphony, the word 'sasura' having been elided, it is said 'sassudevā,' meaning 'mother-in-law, father-in-law, and deities.' 'Disājeṭṭhakā' means that the world speaks of him as chief and head in all four directions. 'Tādisāya' means of such a kind, by reason of qualities like intelligence and so forth. 'Subhariyā' means she is like a fertile field, that is, a beautiful woman.

Mallikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta is concluded.

7. Appamādasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Heedfulness

128. Samadhiggayhāti sammā ativiya gahetvā, ñāyena visesato gaṇhitvā. Kārāpakaappamādoti tiṇṇaṃ puññakiriyavatthūnaṃ pavattakaappamādo. Samavadhānanti samavarodhaṃ antogadhaṃ. Upakkhepanti bahi ahutvā pakkhipitabbataṃ. Sesapadajātāni viya ava…pe… dhammā sappadesattā. Appamāde samodhānaṃ gacchanti tassa nippadesattā. Aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ mahantaṃ sesadhammānaṃ [V 1.0164] appamādo. Paṭilābhakaṭṭhenāti adhigamahetutāya. Lokiyopi samānoti kāmāvacaropi samāno. Mahaggatānuttarānaṃ pubbabhāge pavattaappamādo hi idhādhippeto.

128. ‘Samadhiggayha’ means to take up thoroughly and rightly, to grasp in a special way according to principle. ‘Kārāpaka-appamāda’ refers to the heedfulness that initiates the three bases of meritorious action. ‘Samavadhāna’ means complete inclusion, being contained within. ‘Upakkhepa’ means being fit to be placed inside, not being outside. The remaining terms… the qualities, like the rest, are specifically located. They converge in heedfulness because it is non-localized. Heedfulness is supreme, the best, the greatest of the remaining qualities. ‘Paṭilābhakaṭṭhena’ means by way of being a cause for attainment. Even mundane states are included, even those belonging to the sense-sphere. For the heedfulness that occurs in the preliminary stages of the exalted and unsurpassed is what is intended here.

Pasaṃsanti paṇḍitāti yojanā. Appamādassa pāsaṃsabhāve ekantato kattabbatāya pana “etānī”tiādinā kāraṇaṃ āha. Imissā yojanāya “puññakiriyāsū”ti padassa “appamatto”ti iminā sambandho. Yasmā paṇḍitā appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, yasmā ca puññakiriyāsu appamatto ubho atthe adhiggaṇhāti, tasmā āyuādīni patthayantena appamādova kātabboti. Dutiyayojanāya pana paṇḍitā appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti. Kattha? Puññakiriyāsu. Kasmāti ce? Appamattotiādi. Tenāha “yasmā…pe… attho”ti. Atthapaṭilābhāti diṭṭhadhammikādihitapaṭilābhā.

‘The wise praise it’—this is the connection. However, regarding the absolute necessity of practicing heedfulness due to its being praised, the reason is stated beginning with ‘these’. In this connection, the phrase ‘puññakiriyāsu’ (in meritorious deeds) is related to the word ‘appamatto’ (heedful). Since the wise praise heedfulness, and since the heedful one grasps both advantages in meritorious deeds, therefore, one who desires long life and so forth should practice only heedfulness. In the second connection, however, the wise praise heedfulness. Where? In meritorious deeds. Why? Because of being heedful, and so on. Therefore, it is said, ‘since…the meaning’. ‘Atthapaṭilābha’ means the gaining of benefits such as those in this very life and so on.

Appamādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Heedfulness is concluded.

8. Kalyāṇamittasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on a Good Friend

129. Sīlādiguṇasamannāgato [M 1.0188] kalyāṇo bhaddako mitto etassāti kalyāṇamitto, tassa dhammo kalyāṇamittasseva svākhāto nāma hoti sutvā kattabbakiccassa sādhanato. Tenāha “atthaṃ pūretī”ti. Itarassāti pāpamittassa. Tenāti atthapūraṇena. Etanti “so ca kho kalyāṇamittassā”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ. Desanādhammoti pariyattidhammo. So hi kalyāṇamittato paccakkhato laddhabbo, itare tadupanissayā paccattapurisakārehi, tena laddhabbo kalyāṇamittoti evamattho gahetabbo. Sāvakabodhisattavasena hesā desanā āgatā. Na hi sesabodhisattānaṃ paropadesena payojanaṃ atthi.

129. He who has a good and excellent friend endowed with virtues such as morality is a 'kalyāṇamitto' (one with a good friend). The teaching of such a good friend is called 'well-proclaimed' because upon hearing it, the duties that need to be done are accomplished. Therefore, it is said, ‘He fulfills the purpose’. 'Of the other' means of a bad friend. 'By that' means by the fulfillment of the purpose. 'This' refers to the statement, 'and this is for one with a good friend'. 'Desanādhamma' (the teaching-Dhamma) means the scriptural Dhamma. For that is to be obtained directly from a good friend; others obtain it through their own personal effort, relying on that as a support. Thus, the meaning should be understood as: 'a good friend is to be obtained.' This teaching is given in terms of a disciple-bodhisattva, for other bodhisattvas have no need for instruction from another.

Upaḍḍhaṃ kalyāṇamittatoti brahmacariyaṃ carantassa upaḍḍhaguṇo kalyāṇamittato laddhabbo. Upaḍḍhaṃ paccattapurisakāratoti itaraṃ upaḍḍhaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭipajjantassa attano purisakārato. Lokepi pākaṭoyamattho “ācariyato upaḍḍhaṃ, paccattapurisakārato upaḍḍhaṃ laddhabbā tevijjatā”ti, tasmā thero tathā cintesi. Nippadesanti anavasesato. Tatoti kalyāṇamittato. Upaḍḍhaṃ āgacchatīti upaḍḍhaguṇo paṭipajjantaṃ upagacchati. Bahūhi purisehi. Vinibbhogo vivecanaṃ natthi ekajjhaṃ atthassa vivecetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā. Esāti paratoghosapaccattapurisakārato ca sijjhamāno attho. Ettakanti ettako bhāgo. Yadi na sakkā laddhuṃ, atha kasmā upaḍḍhanti vuttanti āha “kalyāṇamittatāyā”tiādi. Sammādiṭṭhiādīsu na sakkā laddhuṃ. Asakkuṇeyye [V 1.0165] sakalampi na sambhavati paratoghosamattena tesaṃ asijjhanato, padhānahetubhāvadīpanatthaṃ pana “sakalamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Pubbabhāgapaṭilābhaṅganti pubbabhāge paṭiladdhabbakāraṇaṃ kalyāṇamittassa upadesena vinā tena uttari visesato aladdhabbato. Atthatoti paramatthato. “Kalyāṇamittaṃ…pe… cattāro khandhā”ti vatvā sutvāti attho. Te pana sīlādayo saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannāti āha “saṅkhārakkhandhotipi vadantiyevā”ti.

‘Half [of the holy life depends on] good friendship’ means that for one practicing the holy life, half the benefit is to be gained from good friendship. ‘Half [from] one’s own personal effort’ means that the other half, knowledge, is to be attained by one’s own personal effort while practicing. This meaning is also well-known in the world: ‘Half is to be gained from the teacher, and half from one’s own personal effort—thus, the threefold knowledge is attained.’ Therefore, the elder thought in this way. ‘Nippadesa’ means completely, without remainder. ‘From that’ means from good friendship. ‘Half comes’ means half the benefit approaches one who practices. ‘By many people’—there is no separation or distinction, because of the inability to discern the meaning all at once. ‘This’ means the meaning that is accomplished both through the voice of another and one’s own personal effort. ‘Ettaka’ means this much, this portion. If it cannot be attained, then why is it called ‘half’? It is said, ‘Because of good friendship,’ and so on. In right view and other factors, it cannot be attained. If it is unattainable, the whole cannot be accomplished merely by the words of others, since they alone do not bring about their success. But to emphasize the importance of being the main cause, it is said, ‘the whole indeed’. ‘Pubbabhāgapaṭilābhaṅga’ means the cause to be attained in the preliminary stage, for without the instruction of a good friend, further distinction cannot be achieved by it. ‘Atthato’ means in the ultimate sense. Having said, ‘A good friend… the four aggregates,’ and having heard it—this is the meaning. But those virtues, etc., are included in the aggregate of formations—thus it is said, ‘They also speak of the aggregate of formations’.

Māhevanti mā aha evanti chedo, ahāti nipātamattaṃ, māti paṭisedhe nipāto. Tenāha “mā evaṃ abhaṇī”ti. “Māhevaṃ ānandā”ti [M 1.0189] vadato bhagavato imasmiṃ ṭhāne tādisassa nāma te, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaguṇe sevato vattuṃ yuttaṃ ayāthāvatoti dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa yathābhūtaguṇakittanamukhena paṭikkhepo yuttoti dassento “bahussuto”tiādimāha. Idanti idaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavā āhāti sambandho. Sakalameva hīti ettha hi-saddo hetuattho. Tena “māheva”nti tassa paṭikkhepassa kāraṇaṃ jotitaṃ, na sarūpato vuttaṃ. “Kalyāṇamittasseta”ntiādinā pana taṃ sarūpato dassitanti āha “idāni…pe… ādimāhā”ti. Pāṭikaṅkhitabbanti icchanaṭṭhena pāṭikaṅkhitabbaṃ, na paṭikaṅkhānimittenāti āha “avassaṃbhāvīti attho”ti.

‘Māhevaṃ’ is analyzed as ‘mā aha evaṃ’; ‘aha’ is merely a particle; ‘mā’ is a particle of prohibition. Therefore, it is said, ‘Do not speak thus’. When the Blessed One said, ‘Do not speak thus, Ānanda,’ it was because for one like you, Ānanda, who associates with the qualities of a good friend, it is not proper to speak in a way that is not in accordance with reality. Showing that this rejection was fitting by declaring the true qualities of the keeper of the Dhamma treasury, he said, ‘one who has heard much,’ and so on. ‘Idaṃ’ (this) refers to the statement made by the Blessed One—this is the connection. ‘Sakalameva hi’—here, the word ‘hi’ has the meaning of reason. By this, the reason for that rejection, ‘māhevaṃ,’ is illuminated, not stated explicitly. But with ‘Kalyāṇamittassetaṃ’ (this is of the good friend), and so on, it is shown explicitly; hence it is said, ‘now…and so on…the beginning is said’. ‘Pāṭikaṅkhitabba’ (should be expected) means it should be expected in the sense of what is desirable, not by means of a sign of expectation; hence it is said, ‘the meaning is inevitable’.

Idhāti antogadhāvadhāraṇapadaṃ, idhevāti attho. Imasmiṃyeva hi sāsane ariyamaggabhāvanā, na aññattha. Ādipadānaṃyevāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vākye ādito eva vuttasammādiṭṭhiādipadānaṃyeva. Sammādassanalakkhaṇāti catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ pariññābhisamayādivasena sammadeva dassanasabhāvā. Sammāabhiropanalakkhaṇoti nibbānasaṅkhāte ārammaṇe sampayuttadhamme sammadeva āropanasabhāvo. Sammāpariggahaṇalakkhaṇāti musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato pariggāhakasabhāvā sammāvācā siniddhabhāvena sampayuttadhamme sammāvācāpaccayaṃ subhāsitasotārañca puggalaṃ pariggaṇhātīti sammāpariggahaṇalakkhaṇā. Yathā kāyikakiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sayañca samuṭṭhahanaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hoti, tathā sammākammanta saṅkhātā viratipīti samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇā daṭṭhabbā, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhāpanaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā, jīvitappavattiyā ājīvasseva vā suddhi vodānaṃ. Yathā uppannuppannānaṃ vajjānaṃ dhammena pahānānuppādaatthalābhādiparivuḍḍhi hoti, evaṃ sampayuttānaṃ paggahaṇasabhāvoti sammāpaggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Kāyavedanācittadhammesu subhasukhaniccaattagāhānañca vidhamanavasena sammāpatiṭṭhānasabhāvāti sammāupaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ sammā samādahanaṃ [V 1.0166] ekaggatākaraṇaṃ sabhāvo etassāti sammāsamādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi. Tīṇi kiccāni honti paṭipakkhadhammesu[M 1.0190], ārammaṇadhammesu, sampayuttadhammesu ca ekasmiṃyeva khaṇe pavattivisesabhūtāni. Idāni tāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “seyyathida”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Saddhinti iminā “aññehī”ti vuttakilesā micchādiṭṭhiyā saha ekaṭṭhā vā anekaṭṭhā vāti dasseti. Pajahati pahāya naṃ paṭivijjhati. Nirodhanti nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati.

‘Idha’ (here) is a word indicating inclusion within, meaning ‘right here.’ For it is within this very teaching that the noble path is developed, not elsewhere. ‘Ādipadānaṃyeva’ (of the very first terms) means that in each statement, only the terms beginning with right view, mentioned from the outset, are intended. The characteristic of right seeing is the nature of seeing rightly due to the direct comprehension of the four noble truths through complete understanding and realization. The characteristic of right resolve is the nature of properly inclining the associated states toward the object designated as Nibbāna. The characteristic of right speech is the nature of proper embracing, being the opposite of the harsh and non-embracing nature of false speech and so on, due to their function of deception and so on. Right speech, by its gentle nature, embraces the associated states, the condition for right speech, and the person who hears well-spoken words; thus it has the characteristic of right embracing. Just as bodily action initiates something to be done, and is itself an arising and an exertion, so too right action, known as abstinence, should be seen as having the characteristic of initiating. Or, it is the uplifting of associated states, an initiating, like the lifting of a burden by bodily action. It is the purity and cleansing of livelihood, or the continuation of life, for a living being or for the associated states. Just as, through the Dhamma, there is growth in the abandonment of arisen faults, the non-arising of others, and the attainment of benefits, and so on, so too right effort has the characteristic of right exertion, being the nature of uplifting the associated states. The characteristic of right mindfulness is the nature of proper establishment by way of dispelling the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self in body, feeling, mind, and phenomena. The characteristic of right concentration is the nature of properly composing the associated states and making them one-pointed. There are three functions, being distinct types of activity occurring in a single moment, in relation to opposing qualities, object qualities, and associated qualities. Now, to illustrate them in essence, ‘that is to say’ and so on is stated. ‘Saddhiṃ’ (together with) here indicates whether the defilements mentioned as ‘others’ are of one nature or of many natures, along with wrong view. ‘Pajahati’ (abandons)—having abandoned it, one penetrates it. ‘Nirodha’ (cessation)—one makes Nibbāna the object and penetrates it through realization and direct knowledge.

Na kevalaṃ maggadhammā vuttanayeneva, atha kho aparenapi nayena veditabbāti dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Nānākhaṇā punappunaṃ uppajjanato. Nānārammaṇā aniccānupassanādibhāvato. Ekakkhaṇā sakideva uppajjanato. Ekārammaṇā nibbānavisayattā. Cattāri nāmāni labhati pariññābhisamayādivasena pavattiyā. Tīṇi nāmāni labhati kāmasaṅkappādīnaṃ pahānavasena pavattiyā. Paṭipakkhapahānavasena hissa nāmattayalābho. Esa nayo sesesupi. Viratiyopi honti cetanāyopi pubbabhāgepi vikkhambhanavasena pavattanato. Maggakkhaṇe pana viratiyova paṭipakkhasamucchindanassa maggakiccattā. Na hi cetanā maggasabhāvā. Sammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasenāti catubbidhasammappadhānacatubbidhasatipaṭṭhānavasena cattāri nāmāni labhati anuppannākusalānuppādanādīnaṃ kusalānañca vaḍḍhanato. Pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepīti yathā pubbabhāge paṭhamajjhānādivasena nānā. Evaṃ maggakkhaṇepi. Na hi ekopi ca maggasamādhi paṭhamajjhānasamādhiādināmāni labhati sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ viya kiccavasena bhedābhāvato. Tenāha “maggakkhaṇepi sammāsamādhiyevā”ti.

“Not only should the path factors be understood in the way already stated, but they should also be known by another method.” Thus, showing this, he begins with “furthermore” (apicā). Of different moments, because they arise repeatedly. Of various objects, because of the nature of impermanence contemplation, etc. Of a single moment, because they arise only once. Of a single object, because their domain is Nibbāna. They acquire four names by way of their occurrence in terms of full understanding, realization, etc. They acquire three names by way of their occurrence in terms of abandoning sensual thoughts, etc. For it, there is the gaining of three names by way of abandoning opposing states. This is the method for the rest as well. Abstinences and volitions also occur in the preliminary stage by way of suppression. But at the moment of the path, only the abstinences perform the function of cutting off opposing states, because this is the function of the path. For volition is not intrinsic to the path. By way of the fourfold right efforts and the fourfold foundations of mindfulness, they acquire four names because of the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, etc., and the increase of wholesome states. In the preliminary stages as well as at the moment of the path—just as in the preliminary stages, they are various according to the first jhāna, etc., so too at the moment of the path. For not even a single path concentration acquires names like the first jhāna concentration, etc., because there is no distinction by way of function, unlike right view, etc. Hence it is said, “At the moment of the path, it is only right concentration.”

Ñatvā ñātabbāti sambandho. Vuddhi nāma vepullaṃ bhiyyobhāvo punappunaṃ uppādo evāti āha “punappunaṃ janetī”ti. Abhinibbattetīti abhivaḍḍhaṃ pāpento nibbatteti. Vivittatāti vivittabhāvo. So hi vivecanīyato viviccati, yaṃ viviccitvā ṭhitaṃ, tadubhayampi idha vivittabhāvasāmaññena “vivittatā”ti vuttaṃ. Tesu purimo vivecanīyato viviccamānatāya viviccanakiriyāya samaṅgī dhammasamūho tāya eva viviccanakiriyāya vasena vivekoti gahito. Itaro sabbaso tato vivittasabhāvatāya. Tattha yasmiṃ dhammapuñje sammādiṭṭhi pavattati, taṃ yathāvuttāya viviccamānatāya vivekasaṅkhātaṃ nissāyeva pavattati, itaraṃ pana taṃninnatātaṃārammaṇatāhīti vuttaṃ “vivekaṃ nissitaṃ, viveke vā nissita”nti.

The connection is: 'having known, it is to be known.' Growth means abundance, increase, and repeated arising itself; thus it is said, “produces repeatedly.” Abhinibbatteti means “it brings forth, causing to grow.” Seclusion means the state of being secluded. For it is separated from what should be separated, and whatever stands having been separated—both are here called “seclusion” by the general term for the state of being separated. Among these, the former, being a collection of states endowed with the act of separating by being separated from what should be separated, is taken as “seclusion” by way of that very act of separating. The latter is so by being entirely of a nature separated from that. Here, the aggregate of states wherein right view occurs, occurs depending on what is called “seclusion” by way of the aforementioned state of being separated. The other, however, is said to be “dependent on seclusion, or dependent in seclusion” by way of being inclined towards that and having that as its object.

Yathā [M 1.0191] vā vivekavasena pavattaṃ jhānaṃ “vivekaja”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ vivekavasena pavattā sammādiṭṭhi [V 1.0167] “vivekanissitā”ti daṭṭhabbā. Nissayo ca vipassanāmaggānaṃ vasena maggaphalānaṃ veditabbo. Asatipi tāsaṃ pubbāparabhāve “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti ettha paccayānaṃ samuppādanaṃ viya abhinnadhammādhārā nissayabhāvanā sambhavanti. Tassa tadaṅga-samucchedanissaraṇavivekanissitataṃ vatvā paṭippassaddhivivekanissitatāya avacanaṃ ariyamaggabhāvanāya vuccamānattā. Bhāvitamaggassa hi ye sacchikātabbā dhammā. Tesaṃ kiccaṃ paṭippassaddhiviveko. Ajjhāsayatoti “nibbānaṃ sacchikarissāmī”ti mahantaajjhāsayato. Yadipi hi vipassanākkhaṇe saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ, saṅkhāresu pana ādīnavaṃ suṭṭhu, disvā tappaṭipakkhe nibbāne ninnatāya ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissito hoti, uṇhābhibhūtassa puggalassa sītaninnacittatā viya. Keci pana “yathā sabhāvato, yathā ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitatā, evaṃ paṭippassaddhivivekanissitatāpi siyā”ti vadanti. Yadaggena hi nibbānaninnatā siyā, tadaggena phalaninnatāpi siyā “kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihareyya”nti ajjhāsayasampattiyā bhāvato. Yasmā pahānavinayo viya rāganirodhopi idhādhippetavivekena atthato nibbisiṭṭho, tasmā vuttaṃ esa nayo virāganissitādīsūti. Tenāha “vivekatthā eva hi virāgādayo”ti.

Just as the jhāna that occurs by way of seclusion is called “born of seclusion,” so too should right view, which occurs by way of seclusion, be regarded as “dependent on seclusion.” And dependence should be understood by way of insight and path, and by way of path and fruit. Even if there is no before-and-after sequence for them, just as the arising of conditions is spoken of in “dependent origination,” so too, the development of dependence, supported by non-different phenomena, is possible. Having stated its dependence on seclusion by abandonment-by-substitution, by eradication, and by escape, the non-statement of dependence on seclusion by tranquility is because it is being spoken of in terms of the cultivation of the noble path. For one who has developed the path, the function of the phenomena to be realized is the seclusion of tranquility. Ajjhāsayato means “by inclination,” because of the great inclination, “I will realize Nibbāna.” Indeed, even at the moment of insight, though the mind has formations as its object, yet having clearly seen the danger in formations, one is dependent on the seclusion of escape by inclination, by being inclined towards Nibbāna, its opposite, like the mind of a person overcome by heat inclining towards coolness. Some, however, say, “Just as there is dependence on the seclusion of escape by nature and by inclination, so too could there be dependence on the seclusion of tranquility.” For to the extent that there is inclination towards Nibbāna, to that extent there is also inclination towards the fruit, because of the existence of the fulfillment of inclination, thinking, “When, indeed, shall I dwell having attained that sphere?” Because abandoning and subduing, and also the cessation of lust, are in meaning not distinct from the seclusion intended here, therefore it is said: “This is the method in ‘dependent on dispassion,’ etc.” Hence it is said: “For dispassion and so on have seclusion as their meaning.”

Vossaggasaddo pariccāgattho pakkhandanattho cāti vossaggassa duvidhatā vuttā. Vossajjanañhi pahānaṃ, vissaṭṭhabhāvena nirāsaṅkapavatti ca, tasmā vipassanākkhaṇe tadaṅgavasena, maggakkhaṇe samucchedavasena paṭipakkhassa pahānaṃ vossaggo, tathā vipassanākkhaṇe taṃninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe ārammaṇakaraṇena vissaṭṭhasabhāvatā vossaggoti veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha “tattha pariccāgavossaggo”tiādi. Ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhīti ayaṃ missakavasena vuttā sammādiṭṭhi. Yathāvuttena pakārenāti tadaṅgappahānasamucchedappahānapakārena taṃninnatadārammaṇakaraṇappakārena ca.

The term “vossagga” is said to have a twofold meaning: the meaning of relinquishment and the meaning of leaping forward. For vossajjana is abandonment, and it is unhesitating occurrence by way of a released state. Therefore, at the moment of insight, the abandonment of the opposing factor by way of substitution, and at the moment of the path, by way of eradication, is vossagga. Similarly, at the moment of insight, by way of being inclined towards that, and at the moment of the path, by making it the object, the nature of being released should be understood as vossagga. Therefore, it is said, “Therein, vossagga as relinquishment,” etc. This right view: this right view is stated in a mixed way. By the aforementioned manner: by the manner of abandonment by substitution and abandonment by eradication, and by the manner of being inclined towards that and making that the object.

Pubbe vossaggavacanasseva atthassa vuttattā āha “sakalena vacanenā”ti. Pariṇamantaṃ vipassanākkhaṇe, pariṇataṃ maggakkhaṇe. Pariṇāmo nāma idha paripākoti āha “paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcā”ti. Paripāko ca āsevanalābhena laddhasāmatthiyassa kilese pariccajituṃ [M 1.0192] nibbānaṃ pakkhandituṃ tikkhavisadabhāvo. Tenāha “aya”ntiādi. Esa nayoti yvāyaṃ nayo “vivekanissita”ntiādinā sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ vutto, sesesu sammāsaṅkappādīsupi eseva nayo, evaṃ tattha netabbanti attho. Paṭiccāti nissāya. Jātisabhāvāti jāyanasabhāvā. Sakaloti anavaseso, sabboti attho. Na koci maggo sāvaseso hutvā sambhavati. Heṭṭhime magge uppanne [V 1.0168] uparimo uppanno eva nāma anantarāyena uppajjanato. Vavassaggattheti vacasāyatthe. Vaṇṇayantīti guṇavaṇṇanavasena vitthārenti.

Because the meaning of the word ‘vossagga’ was stated previously, he says “with the entire utterance.” Transforming at the moment of insight, transformed at the moment of the path. Transformation here means maturation; therefore, he says “maturing and matured.” And maturation is the state of keenness and clarity of one who has gained capability through the attainment of repeated practice, for abandoning defilements and leaping forward to Nibbāna. Hence it is said, “this” and so on. This is the method: the method stated in right view with “dependent on seclusion,” etc., is the very same method in the remaining right thought, etc.; this is the meaning of “it should be applied there.” Paṭicca means “relying upon.” Jātisabhāva means “the nature of arising.” Sakala means “without remainder,” the meaning is “all.” No path arises with any remainder. When the lower path has arisen, the higher one is as good as arisen, because of its arising without interval. Vavassaggattheti means “in the sense of the word.” Vaṇṇayanti means “they elaborate by way of describing virtues.”

Kalyāṇamittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kalyāṇamittasutta is finished.

9. Paṭhamaaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the First Discourse on One Who is Childless

130. Diva-saddo divā-saddo viya divasapariyāyo, tasmā visesanabhāvena vuccamāno divasaddo atthavisesaṃ dīpetīti āha “divasassa divā”tiādi. Saṃ vuccati dhanaṃ, tassa patīti sampati, dhanasāmiko, tassa hitāvahattā sāpateyyanti āha “sāpateyyanti dhana”nti. Tassa gehe katākatabhaṇḍassa atibahubhāvato vimhayappatto rājā “ko pana vādo”ti āha. Kāḷalohaṃ nāma ayophalaṃ. Kacchapādirūpehipi sovaṇṇādīni ṭhapenti. Sakuṇḍakabhattanti sakuṇḍehi vā sathusehi vā pakkabhattaṃ. Bilaṅgaṃ vuccati dhaññabilaṅgaṃ, āranālantipi vuccati, taṃ dutiyaṃ assāti bilaṅgadutiyaṃ. Tañhi kañjito nibbattattā kañjikaṃ nāma. Tīhi pakkhehi vatthakhaṇḍehi katanivāsanaṃ tipakkhavasanaṃ. Tenāha “tīṇi…pe… nivāsana”nti.

130. The word 'diva' is a synonym for 'day', like the word 'divā'. Therefore, when used as a qualifier, the word 'diva' indicates a specific meaning; thus it is said: 'divasassa divā' and so on. 'Saṃ' is called wealth; its master is 'sampati', the owner of wealth. Because it brings benefit, it is called 'sāpateyya'; thus it is said: 'sāpateyya is wealth'. Due to the great abundance of goods, both finished and unfinished, in his house, the king, astonished, said, 'What more is there to say?' 'Kāḷalohaṃ' is iron plate. They also store gold and other valuables in forms such as tortoises. 'Sakuṇḍakabhattaṃ' means cooked rice with bran or with chaff. 'Bilaṅgaṃ' refers to grain-gruel, also called 'āranālaṃ'. That which has it as a second dish is bilaṅgadutiyaṃ. Because it is produced from sour rice-gruel, it is called 'kañjikaṃ'. A lower garment made from three panels of cloth is 'tipakkhavasanaṃ'. Therefore, it is said: 'three... etc.... lower garment'.

Asanto nīco purisoti asappurisoti āha “lāmakapuriso”ti. Kammassa nibbattabhāvena otaraṇatāya phalaṃ aggaṃ nāma, uparibhūmigatattā uddhaṃ aggaṃ assāti uddhaggikaṃ. Dakkhiṇanti dānamāha. Saggo nāma kāmabhavūpapattibhavo, tassa nibbattanato “saggassa hitā”ti vuttaṃ. Tatrupapattijananatoti tatra upapattiyā jananato, uppādanatoti attho.

An untrue, base person is an ignoble person (asappurisa); thus it is said, 'a wretched person'. The fruit is called 'foremost' (aggaṃ) because of its arrival by way of the arising of kamma. It is 'upward-leading' (uddhaggikaṃ) because its summit is upward, having gone to a higher plane. 'Dakkhiṇā' refers to a gift. Heaven (saggo) is the realm of rebirth in the desire realm; because it generates that, it is said to be 'for the welfare of heaven'. 'Generating rebirth there' means generating, producing rebirth there—that is the meaning.

Setaṃ [M 1.0193] udakaṃ etissāti setodakā. So yena bhāvena yattha pākaṭataro hutvā dissati, taṃ dassetuṃ “vīcīnaṃ bhinnaṭṭhāne”ti āha. Sukhotaraṇaṭṭhānatāya kaddamādidosavirahato ca sundaratitthā. Taṃ apeyyamānanti taṃ udakaṃ kenaci aparibhuñjiyamānaṃ. Attanā kattabbakiccakaroti attanā kātabbakammasaṅkhātakiccakaro, paribhogavasena ceva saṅgahetabbasaṅgaṇhanavasena ca niyojakoti attho. Kusalakiccakaroti attanā kātabbapuññakaro.

It has white water, thus it is Setodakā. To show the manner in which and the place where it appears more prominent, it is said, 'at the place where the waves break'. It is a beautiful ford because it is a place easy to cross and is free from faults such as mud. 'That it is not being drunk' means that water is not being consumed by anyone. 'One who does the duties to be done by oneself' means one who does the tasks called 'work to be done by oneself'; the meaning is one who applies oneself both by way of consumption and by way of collecting what should be collected. 'A doer of skillful deeds' means one who performs meritorious acts to be done by oneself.

Paṭhamaaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on One Who is Childless is finished.

10. Dutiyaaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Second Discourse on One Who is Childless

131. Piṇḍapātenāti [V 1.0169] sahayoge karaṇavacanaṃ. Paṭipādanaṃ tena saha yojananti āha “piṇḍapātena saddhiṃ saṃyojesi, piṇḍapātaṃ adāsīti attho”ti. “Paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā”ti vuttaṃ, pāḷiyaṃ pana “kaṇājakaṃ bhuñjati bilaṅgadutiya”nti. Taṃ taṃ pavattitaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idāni “imassa seṭṭhissa kassaci samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā dethā”ti vacanaṃ na sutapubbaṃ, yasmā paccekabuddhā nāma attano guṇānubhāvehi loke pākaṭā sañjātā eva honti, tasmā seṭṭhibhariyāya “na yassa vā tassa vā”tiādi cintitaṃ. Tathā hi tesaṃ dentāpi sakkaccaṃ yebhuyyena paṇītameva denti. Nāsāpuṭaṃ pahari attano ānubhāvena. So luddhatāya “bahu vata dhaññaṃ mamassā”ti cittaṃ saṃyametuṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto.

131. 'With almsfood'—this is the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment. It means 'connecting along with that,' as it is said, 'he joined it with almsfood, meaning he gave almsfood.' Though it is stated, 'having eaten excellent food,' in the Pāli text it says, 'he eats broken rice with sour gruel as a second course.' This should be understood as spoken generally according to what has occurred. Now, the statement from this treasurer, 'Give to some ascetic or brahmin,' was unheard of before, because Paccekabuddhas are indeed naturally manifest and known in the world by the power of their own virtues. Therefore, the treasurer's wife thought, 'not to just anyone,' and so on. Indeed, even when giving to them, people usually give excellent food respectfully. He struck his nostril by his own power. He, due to greed, being unable to restrain and steady his mind, thought, 'Indeed, much grain is mine.'

Vippaṭisāruppannākāraṃ dassetuṃ “varameta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Imassa samaṇassa piṇḍapātaṃ dehī”ti vadato na ekāya eva javanavīthiyā vasena atthasiddhi. Atha kho tattha ādito pavattajavanavāropi atthi majjhe pavattajavanavāropi, taṃ sandhāyāha “pubbapacchimacetanāvasenā”ti. Ekā cetanā dve paṭisandhiyo na detīti ettha sāketapañhavasena nicchayo veditabbo. Cuddasannaṃ cetanānaṃ pubbe puretaraṃ katattā purāṇaṃ.

To show the manner in which regret arises, it is said, 'better this,' and so on. When one says, 'Give almsfood to this ascetic,' the purpose is not accomplished by way of a single process of apperception alone. Rather, there is an occasion of apperception occurring at the beginning and an occasion of apperception occurring in the middle. Referring to that, it is said, 'by way of the preceding and succeeding volitions.' A single volition does not give two rebirth-linkings—here, the determination should be understood by way of the question in the Sāketa Sutta. Of the fourteen volitions, the earlier is old because it was done previously.

Parigayhatīti [M 1.0194] pariggahoti āha “pariggahitaṃ vatthu”nti. Anvāya upanissāya jīvantīti anujīvino. Sabbametanti dhanadhaññādisabbaṃ etaṃ yathāvuttapariggahavatthuṃ. Nikkhippagāminanti nikkhipitabbatāgāminaṃ. Nikkhipitabbasabhāvaṃ hotīti āha “nikkhippasabhāva”nti. Pahāya gamanīyanti ayamettha atthoti āha “pariccajitabbasabhāvamevā”ti.

'Because it is grasped, it is a grasping,' he said, 'the object is grasped.' 'Dependents'—those who live following and relying on something. 'All this'—all this wealth, grain, etc., all this aforementioned object of grasping. 'Tending towards being laid aside' means that which is destined to be laid aside. 'Of a nature to be laid aside' means it is of a nature to be laid aside. 'To be abandoned and gone from'—this is the meaning here, as he said, 'of the very nature of being relinquished.'

Dutiyaaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Childless is concluded.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Persons

132. “Nīce [V 1.0170] kule paccājāto”tiādi appakāsanabhāvena tamatīti tamo, tena tamena yuttoti tamo puggalo vuccati, taṃyogato puggalassa tabbohāro yathā “maccherayogato macchero”ti. Tasmā tamoti appakāsanabhāvena tamo tamabhūto andhakāro viya jāto, andhakārattaṃ vā pattoti attho. Vuttalakkhaṇaṃ tamameva paramparato ayanaṃ gati niṭṭhā etassāti tamaparāyaṇo, tamaparāyaṇataṃ vā pattoti attho. Ñāyenapi tamaggahaṇena khandhatamova kathito, na andhakāratamo. Khandhatamoti ca sampattirahitā khandhapavattiyeva daṭṭhabbā. “Ucce kule paccājāto”tiādi pakāsanabhāvena jotetīti joti, tena jotinā yuttotiādi sabbaṃ tame vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Itare dveti jotitamaparāyaṇo jotijotiparāyaṇoti itare dve puggale.

132. "Born in a low family" and so on—due to a state of not shining forth, it is 'darkness' (tamo). One endowed with that darkness is called a 'dark person' (tamo puggalo). From that association, the person receives that designation, as in "one associated with stinginess is called stingy." Therefore, 'darkness' means one who, due to a lack of shining forth, has become dark, like darkness, or has attained a state of obscurity. He for whom that darkness with the stated characteristic is the ultimate destination, the path, and the final end, is 'one destined for darkness' (tamaparāyaṇo), meaning one who has attained a state of being destined for darkness. Even by reasoning, with the term 'darkness,' it is the darkness of the aggregates that is spoken of, not physical darkness. And 'darkness of the aggregates' should be understood as merely the continuation of aggregates devoid of attainment. "Born in a high family" and so on—because it shines with a state of radiance, it is 'light' (joti). One endowed with that light, and so on—all this should be understood in the same way as explained for darkness. The other two means the other two persons: the one who is light but destined for darkness (joti-tamaparāyaṇo) and the one who is light and destined for light (joti-jotiparāyaṇo).

Veṇuvettādikehi peḷādikārakā vilīvakārakā. Migamacchādīnaṃ nisādanato nesādā, māgavikamacchabandhādayo. Rathesu cammena hananakaraṇato rathakārā cammakārā vuttā. “Pu” iti karīsassa nāmaṃ, taṃ kusenti apanentīti pukkusā, pupphachaḍḍakā. Dubbaṇṇoti virūpo. Okoṭimakoti [M 1.0195] ārohābhāvena heṭṭhimakoṭiko, rassakāyoti attho. Tenāha “lakuṇḍako”ti. Laku viya ghaṭikā viya ḍeti pavattatīti hi lakuṇḍako, rasso. Kaṇati nimīlatīti kāṇo. Taṃ panassa nimīlanaṃ ekena akkhinā dvīhipi vāti āha “ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā”ti. Kuṇanaṃ kuṇo, hatthavekallaṃ, so etassa atthīti kuṇī. Khañjo vuccati pādavikalo. Heṭṭhimakāyasaṅkhāto sarīrassa pakkho padeso hato assāti pakkhahato. Tenāha “pīṭhasampī”ti. Padīpe padīpane etabbaṃ netabbanti padīpeyyaṃ, telakapallādiupakaraṇaṃ. Vuttanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Those who make baskets and the like from bamboo and rattan are basket-makers. From snaring deer, fish, and so on, they are hunters—hunters, fish-binders, and the like. Because they do the striking with leather on chariots, chariot-makers are called leather-workers. 'Pu' is a name for dung; those who remove it are 'pukkusā,' refuse-removers or flower-sweepers. 'Dubbaṇṇa' means deformed. 'Okoṭimako' means one of the lowest end due to a lack of height; the meaning is short of stature. Therefore, it is said, 'lakuṇḍako' (a dwarf). For one who moves like a club or a small pot is a 'lakuṇḍako,' a short person. 'Kāṇo' is one who squints or closes an eye. But this closing of his may be with one eye or with both, thus it is said: 'blind in one eye or blind in both eyes.' 'Kuṇanaṃ' is a crippled state; 'kuṇo' is a defect of the hand; one who has this is 'kuṇī.' 'Khañjo' is said of one who is disabled in the foot. 'Pakkhahato' is one whose side—a part of the body—is afflicted. Therefore, it is said, 'pīṭhasampī' (one who moves by means of a stool). 'Padīpeyyaṃ' is that which should be brought for lighting a lamp; it is the equipment such as an oil pot. 'Vuttaṃ' means 'stated in the commentary.'

Āgamanavipattīti āgamanaṭṭhānavasena vipatti āgamo etthāti katvā. Pubbuppannapaccayavipattīti paṭhamuppannapaccayavasena vipatti. Caṇḍālādisabhāvā hissa mātāpitaro paṭhamuppannapaccayā, paṭhamuppattiyā vā paccayā, tehevassa vipatti eva, na sampatti. Pavattapaccayavipattīti pavatte sukhapaccayavipatti. Tādise nihīnakule uppannopi koci vibhavasampanno [V 1.0171] siyā, ayaṃ pana duggato durūpo hoti. Ājīvupāyavipattīti ājīvanupāyavasena vipatti. Sukhena hi jīvikaṃ pavattetuṃ upāyabhūtā hatthisippādayo imassa natthi, pupphachaḍḍakasilākoṭṭanādikammaṃ pana katvā jīvikaṃ pavatteti. Tenāha “kasiravuttike”ti. Attabhāvavipattīti upadhivipatti. Dukkhakāraṇasamāyogoti kāyikacetasikadukkhuppattiyā paccayasamodhānaṃ. Sukhakāraṇavipattīti sukhapaccayaparihāni. Upabhogavipattīti upabhogasukhassa vināso anupaladdhi. Joti ceva jotiparāyaṇabhāvo ca sukkapakkho.

The failure in arrival means failure due to the place of arrival, considering that arrival is there. The failure of previously arisen conditions means failure due to the conditions that arose first. For his parents, being of a nature such as outcastes, are the first arisen conditions, or the conditions for his first arising—from them there is only failure for him, not success. The failure of present conditions means the failure of conditions for happiness in the present. Even if someone born in such a low family could become wealthy, this one is wretched and misshapen. The failure in means of livelihood means failure by way of the means of livelihood. Indeed, he lacks skills such as elephant training, which are means to maintain a comfortable life, but instead makes a living by doing work such as sweeping away discarded flowers or breaking stones. Hence it is said, "one who lives with difficulty." The failure in personal existence means failure in the substratum of existence. Association with causes of suffering means the conjunction of conditions for the arising of bodily and mental suffering. The failure in causes of happiness means the decline of conditions for happiness. The failure in enjoyment means the destruction or non-attainment of the happiness of enjoyment. Both light and the state of being destined for light belong to the bright side.

Dasahi akkosavatthūhīti lakkhaṇavacanaṃ etaṃ yathā “yadi me byādhitā honti, dātabbamidamosadha”nti, tasmā dasahi akkosavatthūhi, tattha vā yena kenaci paribhāsatīti attho. Ekaggacittoti dānaṃ dātuṃ apekkhitatāya samāhitacitto.

'With the ten grounds for abuse'—this is a descriptive statement, as in, "If there are sick people for me, this medicine should be given." Therefore, the meaning is: he reviles him with the ten grounds for abuse, or with any one of them. 'Single-minded' means having a concentrated mind due to the expectation of giving a gift.

Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Persons is concluded.

2. Ayyikāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ayyikā Sutta

133. Jarājiṇṇāti [M 1.0196] jarāya jiṇṇā. Tena pākaṭajarāya matthakappattimāha. Vayovuḍḍhāti vayasā vuḍḍhā. Tena pacchimavayassa osakkasampavattiṃ vadati. Jātimahallikāti jātimahattagatā. Cirakālaṃ atikkantāti dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe vītivattā. Vayo-saddo sādhāraṇavacanopi jiṇṇasaddasannidhānato osānavayaṃ eva vadatīti āha “pacchimavayaṃ sampattā”ti. Ayyikāti mātāmahiṃ sandhāya vadati. Hatthī eva ratanabhūto hatthiratananti āha “satasahassagghanakenā”tiādi. Sabbāni tānīti kumbhakārabhājanāni, tehi saddhiṃ sattasantānassa pamāṇaṃ dassento “tesu hī”tiādimāha, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

133. 'Worn out by old age'—worn out by old age. By this, he indicates arrival at the culmination of manifest old age. 'Advanced in years'—advanced in age. By this, he speaks of the decline and progression of the final stage of life. 'Very old by birth'—having attained greatness of age by birth. 'Having passed a long time'—having lived through two or three royal cycles. He says that although the word 'age' is a general term, because of its proximity to the word 'aged,' it refers specifically to the final age, thus: 'having reached the final stage of life.' 'Grandmother'—he speaks referring to the maternal grandmother. The elephant itself is the jewel, the elephant-jewel—hence it is said, 'with a value of one hundred thousand,' etc. 'All those'—the potter's vessels. To show the measure of the seven generations along with them, he says, 'among them,' etc.; this is easily understood.

Ayyikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ayyikā Sutta is concluded.

4. Issattasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Issatta Sutta

135. Aṭṭhuppattikoti ettha kā assa aṭṭhuppatti? Titthiyānaṃ bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca alābhāya ayasāya parisakkanaṃ. Taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “bhagavato kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā taṃ sabbadisāsu yamakamahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā mahāoghaṃ viya sabbā pāramiyo “imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ dassāmā”ti sampiṇḍitā viya lābhasakkāramahoghaṃ nibbattayiṃsu. Tato tato annapānayānavatthamālāgandhavilepanādihatthā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo āgantvā – “kahaṃ bhagavā, kahaṃ [V 1.0172] devadevo narāsabho lokanātho”ti bhagavantaṃ pariyesanti, sakaṭasatehipi paccaye āharitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā samantā gāvutappamāṇampi sakaṭadhurena sakaṭadhuraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti ceva anuvattanti ca andhakavindabrāhmaṇādayo viya. Sabbaṃ khandhake (mahāva. 282) tesu tesu suttesu ca āgatanayena veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca bhagavato, evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassapi. Vuttampi – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvara…pe… parikkhārānaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghopi kho”tiādi (udā. 38), tathā “yāvatā kho, cunda, etarahi [M 1.0197] saṅgho vā gaṇo vā loke uppanno, nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ ekaṃ saṅghampi ekaṃ gaṇampi samanupassāmi evaṃ lābhaggayasaggappattaṃ, yatharivāyaṃ, cunda, bhikkhusaṅgho”ti (dī. ni. 3.176). Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena. Nijjhattinti saññattiṃ. Nanti kathaṃ.

135. What is the occasion for this 'aṭṭhuppatti' here? It is the sectarians' striving for the loss and dishonor of the Blessed One and the Sangha of bhikkhus. To explain this in detail, it is said, 'Indeed, the Blessed One...' and so on. Just as a great twin rain cloud arose in all directions, like a mighty flood, all the perfections seemed to gather together, as if declaring, 'We will show our result in this very existence,' and thus generated a great flood of gain and honor. From here and there, khattiyas, brahmins, and others, with food, drink, vehicles, cloths, garlands, perfumes, and ointments in hand, came searching for the Blessed One, asking, 'Where is the Blessed One? Where is the god of gods, the bull among men, the protector of the world?' Bringing offerings in hundreds of carts, and not finding an opportunity, they stood all around, cart-yoke to cart-yoke for even a distance of a gāvuta, both standing and waiting, like the Andhakavinda brahmins and others. All of this should be understood according to the method that has come in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga. 282) and in those various suttas. Just as it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Sangha of bhikkhus. It was also said: 'At that time, the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, worshipped, venerated, and obtained robes...pe...requisites, and so too was the Sangha of bhikkhus...' (Udāna. 38), as well as 'As far as, Cunda, any Sangha or group has arisen in the world at this time, I do not see, Cunda, any other single Sangha or group that has attained to such an extent of gain, honor, and esteem, as this Sangha of bhikkhus' (Dīgha Nikāya. 3.176). Thus, in the manner now being spoken of. 'Nijjhatti' means a declaration. 'Na' means how?

Evaṃ pucchituṃ ayuttaṃ titthiyānaṃ kathā mahājanasannipāte niyyātitā hotīti. Tasmiṃ dātabbaṃ, cittappasādamattena dentepi hi puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati. Ārocitaṃ attanoti adhippāyo. Bhagavāti satthu āmantanaṃ. Cittaṃ nāma yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānaṃ nigaṇṭhā…pe… pasīdati pasannassāti adhippāyo. Pubbe avisesato deyyadhammassa dātabbaṭṭhānaṃ nāma pucchitaṃ, idāni tassa mahapphalabhāvakaro dakkhiṇeyyavisesoti āha “aññaṃ tayā paṭhamaṃ pucchitaṃ, aññaṃ pacchā”ti. Sallakkhehi etaṃ. Pacchimaṃ purimena saddhiṃ ānehīti adhippāyo. Pucchitassa nāma pañhassa kathanaṃ mayhameva bhāro. Samupabyūḷhoti ekato senāya rāsivasena sampiṇḍitoti attho. Tenāha “rāsibhūto”ti. Asikkhitoti sattaṭṭhasaṃvaccharāni dhanusippena sikkhito. Dhanusippaṃ sikkhitvāpi koci katahattho na hoti, ayaṃ pana asikkhito na katahattho, poṅkhānupoṅkhabhāvoyeva byāmamuṭṭhibandho. Tiṇapuñjamattikāpuñjādīsūti ādi-saddena paṃsupuñjavālukapuñjasāraphalakaayoghanādike saṅgaṇhāti. Akataparicayoti tesaṃ santikā vijjhanaṭṭhena akataparicayo. Rājarājamahāmattādike upecca asanaṃ upāsanaṃ, na kataṃ upāsanaṃ etenāti akatūpāsano. Asikkhitatādinā bhīrubhāvena vā kāyassa chambhanaṃ saṅkampanaṃ uttāso etassa atthīti chambhīti āha “pavedhitakāyo”ti.

To ask in this way is not fitting for the sectarians—their discussion was brought forward in a great assembly. One should give to him; for merit increases even when giving with mere mental confidence. The intention is that it was announced by oneself. "Bhagavā" is an address to the Teacher. The mind, it is said, proceeding according to conditions... the Nigaṇṭhas... becomes confident; this is the meaning for one who is confident. Previously, the place where gifts should be given was asked about without specification; now, the distinction of the recipient that makes it greatly fruitful is stated: "One thing was asked by you first, another afterward." Consider this. The meaning is to bring the latter in conjunction with the former. The explanation of the question asked is indeed my burden. "Samupabyūḷho" means gathered together in one place like an army or a heap—this is the meaning. Hence it is said, "formed into a mass." "Unskilled"—not trained in archery for seven or eight years. Even after training in archery, some are not skilled, but this one is untrained, not skilled—his drawing and holding of the fist is merely arrow after arrow. In heaps of grass, piles of clay, and so on—the word "and so on" includes heaps of dust, sand, hardwood planks, and iron masses. "Unaccustomed"—unfamiliar with piercing them due to lack of practice. Not having approached kings, great ministers, and others for attendance—thus, "unaccustomed to attendance." Due to being untrained and so on, or because of timidity, his body trembles and shakes, and he is terrified—this is the meaning of "chambhī." Hence it is said, "his body quakes."

Dakkhiṇeyyatāya adhippetattā “arahattamaggena kāmacchando pahīno hotī”ti āha. Accantappahānassa icchitattā tatiyeneva kukkuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti paṭighasampayogaṃ. Asekkhassa ayanti asekkhaṃ, sīlakkhandho. Tayidaṃ na aggaphalaṃ sīlameva adhippetaṃ, atha kho yaṃ kiñci asekkhasantāne pavattaṃ sīlaṃ, lokuttaro eva na adhippeto sikkhāya jātattā, evaṃ vimuttikkhandhopīti[V 1.0173]. Sekkhassa esoti vā, apariyositasikkhattā sayameva sikkhatīti vā sekkho, catūsu maggesu [M 1.0198] heṭṭhimesu ca tīsu phalesu sīlakkhandho. Upari sikkhitabbābhāvato asekkho. Vuḍḍhippatto sekkhoti asekkho. Aggaphalabhūto sīlakkhandho vucceyya, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vipassakassa sīlassa adhippetattā tathā attho vutto. Sabbatthāti “asekkhenā”tiādīsu. Ettha ca yathā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā missakā adhippetā, evaṃ vimuttikkhandhāpīti tadaṅgavimuttiādayopi veditabbā, na paṭippassaddhivimutti eva.

Because worthiness of offerings is intended, it is said, "Sensual desire is abandoned by the path of Arahantship." Due to the desire for complete abandonment, remorse connected with aversion is abandoned by the third path. This is the non-learner's virtue aggregate. This is not to say that only the virtue that is the supreme fruit is intended; rather, whatever virtue occurs in the continuum of a non-learner is intended. The supramundane itself is not intended, because it is born of training. Thus, the liberation aggregate is also to be understood in this way. Or, it belongs to the learner; because training is not yet completed, one trains oneself—thus, a learner's virtue aggregate pertains to the four lower paths and the three fruits. The non-learner is one who has nothing further to train. Having reached maturity, the learner becomes a non-learner. The virtue aggregate that has become the supreme fruit could be mentioned, but in the commentary, because the virtue of a vipassanā practitioner is intended, the meaning is stated accordingly. In all cases—such as in "by the non-learner." Here, just as the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom are intended as mixed, so too should the liberation aggregate be understood to include momentary liberation and others, not only liberation by tranquillization.

Yena sippena issāso hoti, taṃ issattanti āha “ususippa”nti. Yassā vāyodhātuyā vasena sarīraṃ sañjātathāmaṃ hoti, taṃ balapaccayaṃ sandhāyāha “balaṃ nāma vāyodhātū”ti. Samappavattito hi visamappavattinivārakadhātu balaṃ nāma, tena tato aññaṃ balarūpaṃ nāma natthi.

By whatever skill one becomes an archer, that is called "archery," namely "the skill of the arrow." Referring to that element of wind by which the body becomes strong, which is the cause of strength, it is said, "Strength is the wind element." For the element that prevents uneven movement and promotes even movement is called strength; there is no other form of strength besides that.

Yasmā arahā eva ekantato sorato, tassa bhāvo soraccanti āha “soraccanti arahatta”nti. Ete dveti khanti soraccanti ete dve dhammā. Pānīyaṃ pivanti etthāti papā, yo koci jalāsayo yaṃ kiñci pānīyaṭṭhānanti āha “caturassapokkharaṇīādīnī”ti. Udakavikūlādīsu kamanti atikkamanti etehīti saṅkamanāni, setuādīni. Setukaraṇayuttaṭṭhāne setuṃ, caṅkamanakaraṇayuttaṭṭhāne caṅkamanaṃ, maggakaraṇayuttaṭṭhāne maggaṃ kareyyāti ayamettha adhippāyo. Tenāha “paṇṇāsā”tiādi.

Because the Arahant is entirely gentle, his state is called gentleness—thus it is said, "Gentleness is Arahantship." These two—patience and gentleness—are these two qualities. They drink water here—thus it is a watering place. Any water reservoir, any place for water, is called "a four-sided lotus pond and so on." They go or pass over places like uneven banks of water by means of these—thus they are crossings, such as bridges and the like. In a place suitable for making a bridge, one should make a bridge; in a place suitable for making a promenade, one should make a promenade; in a place suitable for making a road, one should make a road—this is the meaning here. Therefore, it is said, "fifty," and so on.

Bhikkhācāravattanti ariyānaṃ hitaṃ vattapaṭipattiṃ. Dentopīti pi-saddena akhīṇāsavassa dentopīti imamatthaṃ dasseti yassa kassacipi dentenapi kammaphalaṃ saddahitvā vippasannacitteneva dātabbattā. Thanayanti idaṃ tassa mahāmeghabhāvadassanaṃ, yo hi mahāvassaṃ vassati, so gajjanto vijjummālaṃ vissajjento pavassati. Abhisaṅkharitvā samodhānetvāti khādanīyassa vividhajātiyāni sampiṇḍetvā. Tenāha “rāsiṃ katvā”ti.

The practice of going for alms is the beneficial conduct of the noble ones. Even when giving—the particle "pi" here indicates the meaning that even when giving to one whose taints are not extinguished, one should give with faith in the result of kamma and with a serene mind, because it should be given to anyone whatsoever. Thundering—this illustrates its state of being like a great cloud. For when a great rain pours down, it thunders, sending forth flashes of lightning as it showers. Having prepared and combined—this refers to consolidating various kinds of edible food. Hence it is said, "having made a heap."

Pakiraṇaṃ nāma vikiraṇampi hoti anekatthattā dhātūnanti āha “vikiratī”ti. Pakiranto viya vā dānaṃ detīti iminā guṇakhettameva apariyesitvā karuṇākhettepi mahādānaṃ pavattetīti dasseti. Tena “pakiretī”ti [M 1.0199] vadantena bhagavatā aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ āgatatitthiyavādena appaṭisedhitatāpi dīpitā hoti. Puññadhārāti puññamayadhārā puññābhisandā. Sinehayantīti thūladhārenapi sinehena siniddhaṃ karontī. Kiledayantīti allabhāvaṃ pāpayantī. Yathāyaṃ puññadhārā [V 1.0174] dātāraṃ anto sineheti pūreti abhisandeti, evaṃ paṭiggāhakānampi anto sineheti pūreti abhisandeti. Tenevāha “dadaṃ piyo hoti bhajanti naṃ bahū”tiādi (a. ni. 5.34) evaṃ santepi “dātāraṃ abhivassatī”ti vuttattā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dāyakavaseneva “sinehetī”ti vuttaṃ, yasmā vā paṭiggāhakassa sinehuppatti āmisanissitāti dāyakavaseneva vuttaṃ.

The term 'pakiraṇa' also means scattering or dispersal, due to the diversity of meanings of the verbal roots; hence it is said, 'he scatters.' Or, just as one who scatters gives gifts, this shows that without scrutinizing for a field of merit, he sets forth great generosity even in the field of compassion. Therefore, when the Blessed One says, 'he scatters,' it also indicates the non-rejection of the heretical view that had arisen on that occasion. 'Puññadhārā' means a stream made of merit, a flood of merit. 'Sinehayantī' means making moist with a thick stream of affection. 'Kiledayantī' means causing a state of wetness. Just as this stream of merit inwardly moistens, fills, and floods the giver, so too does it inwardly moisten, fill, and flood the recipients. Therefore, it is said, 'the giver becomes dear, many associate with him,' and so on (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.34). Even so, because it is said that 'it rains upon the giver,' in the commentary the term 'sinehetī' is used with reference to the donor. Or, since the arising of affection in the recipient is dependent on material things, it is spoken of with reference to the donor.

Issattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Issatta Sutta is finished.

5. Pabbatūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Pabbatūpama Sutta

136. Khattiyāti abhisekappattā. Issariyamado kāmagedho. Pathavimaṇḍalassa mahantatā taṃnivāsinaṃ anuyantatāti sabbamidaṃ yathicchitassa rājakiccassa sukhena samijjhanassa kāraṇakittanaṃ. Yādise rājakicce ussukkaṃ āpanno, taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “esa kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Antaragamanānīti tiṇṇaṃ nirantaragamanānaṃ antarantarā gamanāni. Corā cintayiṃsūti eko antarabhogiko rājāparādhiko pañcasatamanussaparivāro coriyaṃ karonto vicarati, te sandhāya vuttaṃ.

136. “Khattiyā” refers to those who have attained consecration. The intoxication of dominion; the greed for sensual pleasures. The vastness of the earth and the allegiance of its inhabitants—all this is mentioned as a reason for the easy accomplishment of the king’s duties as he wishes. To show in detail what kind of royal duty he was diligent in, “this, indeed,” etc., was said. “Antaragamanāni” means journeys in between the three uninterrupted journeys. “The thieves thought”—this refers to a certain official, guilty of offenses against the king, who wandered about committing thievery with a following of five hundred men. This was said with reference to them.

“Ayuttaṃ te kata”nti sacāhaṃ vakkhāmīti yojanā. Dhuravihāreti rathassa dhuraṃ viya nagarassa dhurabhūte vihāre. Santhambhitunti vissāsabhāvena upaṭṭhātuṃ. Saddhāyikoti saddhāya ayitabbo, saddheyyoti attho. Tenāha “saddhātabbo”ti. Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbo. Abbhasamaṃ puthulabhāvena. Nippothentoti nimmaddento. Saṇhakaraṇīyaṃ atisaṇhaṃ pisanto nisadapoto viya pisanto.

“If I were to say, ‘You have done what is unsuitable,’” is the connection. “Dhuravihāra” means a monastery that is the main support of the city, like the yoke of a chariot. “Santhambhitum” means to attend with confidence. “Saddhāyiko” means one who should be approached with faith; the meaning is trustworthy. Therefore, it is said, “worthy of faith.” “Paccayiko” means one who should be approached with trust. “Abbhasamaṃ” means like a cloud, because of its extensive size. “Nippothento” means crushing down. “Saṇhakaraṇīyaṃ” means grinding very finely, like a small grinding stone grinds.

Dhammacariyātiādittampi sīsaṃ celañca ajjhupekkhitvā sammāpaṭipatti eva kātabbā tassā eva paraloke patiṭṭhābhāvato. Ācikkhāmīti kathemi, kathento ca yathā tamatthaṃ sammadeva rājā jānāti, evaṃ jānāpemīti[M 1.0200]. Nipphatti yuddhena kātabbaatthasiddhi. Visinoti bandhati yathādhippetaṃ cittaṃ etenāti visayo, samatthabhāvo. Mantasampannāti sampannarājamantā. Mahāamaccāti mahosadhādisadisā nītisatthachekā amaccapurisā. Upalāpetunti paresaṃ antare virodhatthaṃ saṅgaṇhituṃ.

Even if one's head and robe are on fire, one should disregard them and still practice rightly, for that alone is one's foundation in the next life. “Ācikkhāmi” means I declare, I speak, and while speaking, I make the king know the matter as it truly is. “Nipphatti” means the accomplishment of the purpose to be achieved by battle. “Visinoti” means 'it binds'; “visayo” is that by which the desired mind is bound, hence it is a sphere or domain, a state of capability. “Mantasampannā” means possessing accomplished royal counsel. “Mahāamaccā” refers to great ministers like Mahosadha, skilled in the science of policy. “Upalāpetum” means to win over others in order to create discord among them.

Dveyeva pabbatāti pabbatasadisā dveyeva gahitā. Rājovādeti rājovādasutte. Āgatāva tattantiyā [V 1.0175] anurūpatthaṃ. Vilumpamānāti iti-saddo ādiattho. Vipattīti bhogaparihānādivināso. Hatthiyuddhādīhi jarāmaraṇaṃ jinituṃ na sakkā sattassa avisayabhāvato. Yena pana jinituṃ sakkā, taṃ dassento bhagavā “buddhe…pe… nivesaye”ti āha. Ratanattaye hi saddhā niviṭṭhā mūlajātā patiṭṭhitā ekantato jarāmaraṇavijayāya hoti. Tenāha “tasmā saddha”nti.

“There are only two mountains” means only two things similar to mountains are taken. “Rājovāde” refers to the Rājovāda Sutta. The word “āgatā” has a meaning suitable for that textual passage. “Vilumpamānā”—the word “iti” here has the sense of “etcetera.” “Vipatti” means destruction, such as loss of possessions, and so on. Through elephant fights and the like, it is impossible to conquer old age and death, since that is outside a being's domain. But showing by what it can be conquered, the Blessed One said, “In the Buddha… one should establish…” For faith, entered into, rooted, and established in the Triple Gem, leads definitively to the conquest of old age and death. Therefore he said, “Therefore, faith…”

Pabbatūpamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pabbatūpama Sutta is concluded.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Chapter is concluded.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya

Kosalasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of Hidden Meanings in the Commentary on the Kosala Saṃyutta is concluded.

4. Mārasaṃyuttaṃ

4. The Māra Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Tapokammasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Tapokamma Sutta

137. Uruvelāya [V 1.0176][M 1.0201] samīpe gāmo uruvelagāmo, taṃ uruvelagāmaṃ abhimukhabhāvena sammadeva sabbadhamme bujjhatīti abhisambodhi, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tena samannāgatattā ca bhagavā abhisambuddhoti vuccati. Tassa pañcacattālīsāya vassesu ādito pannarasa vassāni paṭhamabodhi, idha pana sattāhabbhantarameva adhippetanti āha “abhisambuddho hutvā antosattāhasmiṃ yevā”ti. Asukhabhāvena aññehi kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā dukkaraṃ karotīti dukkarakāro, so eva itthiliṅgavasena dukkarakārikā. Tāya mutto vatamhīti cintesi. Yadi evaṃ kasmā taṃ lokanātho chabbassāni samanuyuñjati? Kammapīḷitavasena. Vuttañhetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.39.92-94) –

137. The village near Uruvelā is Uruvelagāma. Facing that village of Uruvelā, he rightly awakened to all phenomena—this is supreme enlightenment, the knowledge of omniscience.
