Because he was endowed with that, the Blessed One is called “the Supremely Enlightened One.” Of his forty-five years, the first fifteen years are the “first enlightenment.” Here, however, the period within seven days is intended, hence it is said: “Having become supremely enlightened, just within seven days.” Because it is difficult to do, being unable to be done by others due to its unpleasant nature, he is a “doer of the difficult.” That very word in the feminine gender is Dukkarakārikā. He reflected, “By that, I am freed from my vow.” If so, why did the Lord of the World practice it for six years? Due to being oppressed by kamma. For this is stated in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Theragāthā 1.39.92-94):

“Avacāhaṃ jotipālo, sugataṃ kassapaṃ tadā;

Kuto nu bodhi muṇḍassa, bodhi paramadullabhā.

“Then I, Jotipāla, spoke to the Sugata Kassapa: ‘Whence can there be enlightenment for this shaveling? Enlightenment is supremely hard to gain.’”

“Tena kammavipākena, acariṃ dukkaraṃ bahuṃ;

Chabbassānuruvelāyaṃ, tato bodhimapāpuṇiṃ.

“By the result of that kamma, I performed many difficult austerities; for six years at Uruvelā, then I attained awakening.”

“Nāhaṃ etena maggena, pāpuṇiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ;

Kummaggena gavesissaṃ, pubbakammena vārito”ti.

“I did not attain the supreme enlightenment by this path; I sought by a wrong path, prevented by former kamma.”

Māretīti vibādheti. Vipattiādisaṃyojanañhi sādhūnaṃ paramatthato maraṇaṃ saccapaṭivedhamāraṇattā, pāpatarattā pāpatamoti pāpimā. Sā cassa pāpatamatā pāpavuttitāyāti āha “pāpe [V 1.0177] niyutto”ti. Adhipatīti kāmādhipati. Appahīnakāmarāge attano vase vattetīti vasavattī. Tesaṃyeva kusalakammānaṃ antaṃ karotīti antako. Vaṭṭadukkhato aparimuttapaccayattā namuci. Mattānaṃ pamattānaṃ bandhūti pamattabandhu.

“Māreti” means he kills or obstructs. For fetters such as failure are, in the ultimate sense, death for the virtuous, because they cause the death of the penetration of the truth. Because he is more evil, he is the most evil, hence Pāpimā (the Evil One). And this state of being most evil is due to his evil conduct, hence it is said, “devoted to evil.” “Adhipati” means lord of sensual pleasures. Because he makes those who have not abandoned sensual lust subject to his power, he is called Vasavattī (the Controller). He brings an end to those very wholesome kammas, hence Antaka (the Ender). Because he is a condition for not being freed from the suffering of the round of rebirth, he is called Namuci. He is a kinsman to the intoxicated and heedless, hence Pamattabandhu (the Kinsman of the Heedless).

Tapokammāti [M 1.0202] attakilamathānuyogato. Aparaddhoti virajjhasi. “Aparādho”tipi atthi, soyeva attho. Kāyakilamathaṃ anuyuñjanto yebhuyyena amaratthāya anuyuñjati, so ca kammavādīhi anuyuñjiyamāno devatthāya siyāti āha “amarabhāvatthāyā”ti. Sabbaṃ tapanti sabbaṃ attaparitāpanaṃ. Atthāvahaṃ na bhavati bodhiyā anupāyattā. Kiñcassāti kiñci siyāti attho. Phiyārittaṃva dhammanīti dhammaṃ vuccati vaṇṇu, so idha “dhamma”nti vutto, dhammani vaṇṇupadeseti attho. Tenāha “araññe”ti. Ubhosu passesu phiyāhi ākaḍḍheyya ceva arittehi uppīḷeyya ca.

“Tapokamma” means due to the practice of self-mortification. “Aparaddho” means you fail. There is also “aparādho,” which has the same meaning. One who engages in bodily mortification mostly does so for the sake of deathlessness, and when engaged in by advocates of kamma, it may be for the sake of becoming a deva, hence it is said, “for the sake of a state of deathlessness.” “Sabbaṃ tapanti” means all self-torment. It is not beneficial because it is not a means to enlightenment. “Kiñcassa” means “something might be.” Regarding 'dhammanī': `dhamma` is called `vaṇṇu` (a leather thong), and that is what is meant here by 'dhamma'; the meaning is 'in the place of the thong'. Therefore, it is said, “in the forest.” On both sides, one would be pulled by poles and pressed by rudders.

Sammāvācākammantājīvā gahitā maggasīlassa adhippetattā. Samādhino hi gahaṇena sammāvāyāmasatisamādhayo gahitā upakārabhāvato. Paññāyāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Bujjhati etenāti bodho. Maggoti āha “bodhāyāti maggatthāyā”ti. Kathaṃ pana maggaṃ maggatthāya bhāvetīti āha “yathā hī”tiādi. Tena yathā yāgupacanārambho yāvadeva yāguattho, evaṃ maggabhāvanārambho maggādhigamatthāyāti dasseti. Ārambhoti ca ariyamaggabhāvanāya bandhāpanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci pana “magganti ariyamaggaṃ, bodhāyāti arahattasambodhāya, evañca katvā ‘pattosmi paramasuddhi’nti idampi vacanaṃ samatthita”nti vadanti, apare pana “sabbaññutaññāṇasambodhāyāti. So hi sabbasmāpi bodhito uttaritaro”ti. Nihato nibbisevanabhāvaṃ pāpito. Tenāha “parājito”ti.

Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are included, as they are intended as path virtue. For by the inclusion of concentration, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are included because they are aids. As for wisdom, the same principle applies here. “Bodho” means awakening through this. He says “maggo” (path) means “for enlightenment,” that is, “for the purpose of the path.” How then does one develop the path for the purpose of the path? He says, “just as,” etc. Thus, just as the preparation for cooking gruel is solely for the sake of gruel, so the undertaking of path development is for the attainment of the path. The undertaking should be seen as binding oneself to the development of the noble path. Some, however, say, “the path means the noble path; for enlightenment means for the sake of arahantship-enlightenment, and having done so, this statement ‘I have attained the highest purity’ is also justified.” Others, however, say, “for the sake of omniscient knowledge-enlightenment, for that is superior to all enlightenment.” “Nihato” means struck down, brought to a state of non-adherence. Therefore, he says, “vanquished.”

Tapokammasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tapokamma Sutta is concluded.

2. Hatthirājavaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Hatthirājavaṇṇa Sutta

138. Andhabhāvakāraketi pacurajanassa cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇena andhabhāvakārake. Mahātameti mahati tamasi. Pāsāṇaphalake mahācīvaraṃ sīse ṭhapetvāti etena taṃ phalakaṃ apassāya nisinnoti dasseti[M 1.0203]. Padhānanti bhāvanaṃ. Pariggaṇhamānoti sabbaso gaṇhanto avissajjento, bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto anupubbasamāpattiyo phalasamāpattiñca manasikarontoti attho. Tenāha “nanu cā”tiādi. Ariṭṭhakoti ariṭṭhakavaṇṇo. Tenāha “kāḷako”ti.

138. “Andhabhāvakārake” means in causing blindness by preventing the arising of eye-consciousness in many people. “Mahātame” means in great darkness. “Pāsāṇaphalake mahācīvaraṃ sīse ṭhapetvā” indicates that he sat without relying on that slab, having placed a large robe on his head. “Padhānaṃ” means development. “Pariggaṇhamāno” means fully grasping, not letting go, engaging in development, and attending to the successive attainments and the fruition attainment. Therefore it is said, “Nanu ca,” and so forth. “Ariṭṭhako” means of the color of ariṭṭhaka. Therefore it is said, “kāḷako.”

Dīghamaddhānanti [V 1.0178] cirataraṃ kālaṃ. Saṃsaranti āsādanādhippāyena sañcaranto, alaṃ tuyhaṃ etena nippayojananti adhippāyo. Na hi tena mārassa kāci atthasiddhīti.

“Dīghamaddhānaṃ” means a very long time. “Saṃsaranti” means wandering, moving about with the intention of harming; the meaning is, “This is enough for you; it is useless.” For by that, Māra achieves no purpose.

Hatthirājavaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Hatthirājavaṇṇa Sutta is concluded.

3. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Subha Sutta

139. Susaṃvutāti maggasaṃvarena suṭṭhu saṃvutā. Supihitāti suṭṭhu pihitā. Vasānugāti kāyādidvāravasānugā vasavattino na honti. Baddhacarāti paṭibaddhacariyāti.

139. “Susaṃvutā” means well-restrained by the restraint of the path. “Supihitā” means well-covered. “Vasānugā” means not following the sway of the sense doors, beginning with the body; they are not under their power. “Baddhacarā” means one whose conduct is bound.

Subhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Subha Sutta is concluded.

4. Paṭhamamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the First Mārapāsa Sutta

140. Upāyamanasikārenāti aniccādīsu aniccādito manasikaraṇena. Upāyavīriyenāti anuppannākusalānaṃ anuppādanāya vidhinā pavattavīriyena. Kāraṇavīriyenāti anuppannānuppādanādiatthassa kāraṇabhūtena vīriyena. Anuppannapāpakānuppādanādiatthāni hi vīriyāni yadatthaṃ honti, taṃ atthaṃ sādhentiyevāti etassa atthassa dīpako sammā-saddo. Yonisosammāsaddena hi upāyakāraṇatthadīpakataṃ sandhāya “upāyavīriyena kāraṇavīriyenā”ti vuttaṃ. Arahattaphalavimutti ukkaṭṭhaniddesena. Mārena “mayhaṃ kho, bhikkhave”tiādikaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ sutvā vuttaṃ “arahattaṃ patvāpi na tussatī”tiādi.

140. “Upāyamanasikārena” means by skillful attention, that is, by attending to impermanence and so forth as impermanent and so forth. “Upāyavīriyena” means by effort with means, that is, the effort that proceeds by method for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. “Kāraṇavīriyena” means by causal effort, that is, the effort that is the cause for the purpose of preventing the arising of the unarisen, and so forth. For the efforts that exist for the purpose of preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and so forth, do indeed accomplish that purpose, and the word 'sammā' is the revealer of this meaning. For it is with reference to the clarifying function of the words 'yoniso' and 'sammā' regarding the meaning of 'means' and 'cause' that it is said 'by skillful effort, by causal effort'. The liberation of arahantship is by way of an excellent designation. Hearing the Blessed One's words, “Mayhaṃ kho, bhikkhave,” and so forth, Māra said, “Even having attained arahantship, he is not satisfied,” and so forth.

Kilesapāsenāti [M 1.0204] kilesamārassa upāyabhūtena. Kilesamāro hi satte kāmaguṇapāsehi nibandhati, na pana sayameva. Tenāha “ye dibbā kāmaguṇasaṅkhātā”tiādi. Mārabandhaneti kilesamārassa bandhanaṭṭhāne, bhavacāraketi attho. Na me samaṇa mokkhasīti idaṃ māro “anuttarā vimutti anuppattā, vimuttā sabbapāsehī”ti ca bhagavato vacanaṃ asaddahanto vadati saddahantopi vā “evamayaṃ paresaṃ sattānaṃ mokkhāya ussāhaṃ na kareyyā”ti attano kohaññe ṭhatvā vadati.

“Kilesapāsena” means by that which is the means of the defilement-Māra. For the defilement-Māra binds beings with the snares of sensual qualities, but not by himself. Therefore it is said, “ye dibbā kāmaguṇasaṅkhātā,” and so forth. “Mārabandhane” means in the place of bondage of the defilement-Māra, that is, in the prison of existence. “Na me samaṇa mokkhasi”—this is Māra speaking, disbelieving the Blessed One's words, “The unsurpassed liberation has been attained, freed from all snares,” or, even believing, he speaks, standing in his own deceit, saying, “Thus, this one should not exert himself for the liberation of other beings.”

Paṭhamamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Mārapāsa Sutta is concluded.

5. Dutiyamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Second Mārapāsa Sutta

141. Anupubbagamanacārikanti [V 1.0179] gāmanigamarājadhānīsu anukkamena gamanasaṅkhātaṃ cārikaṃ. Evaṃ hi gatesūti evaṃ tumhesu bahūsu ekajjhaṃ gatesu.

141. “Anupubbagamanacārikaṃ” means the wandering characterized by sequential travel through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. “Evaṃ hi gatesū” means when many of you have gone together in this way.

Ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ etassāti ādikalyāṇaṃ, tathā sesesu. Sāsanassa ādi sīlaṃ mūlakattā. Tassa samathādayo majjhaṃ sāsanasampattiyā vemajjhabhāvato. Phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ tadadhigamato uttari karaṇīyābhāvato. Sāsane sammāpaṭipatti nāma paññāya hoti, tassā ca sīlaṃ samādhi ca mūlanti āha “sīlasamādhayo vā ādī”ti. Yasmā paññā anubodhapaṭivedhavasena duvidhā, tasmā tadubhayaṃ gaṇhanto “vipassanāmaggā majjha”nti āha. Paññānipphatti phalakiccaṃ, nibbānasacchikiriyā pana sammāpaṭipattiyā pariyosānaṃ tato paraṃ kattabbābhāvatoti āha “phalanibbānāni pariyosāna”nti. Phalaggahaṇena hi saupādisesanibbānaṃ gayhati, itarena itaraṃ, tadubhayavasena paṭipattiyā osānanti āha “phalanibbānāni pariyosāna”nti. “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ, diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.369) vacanato sīladiṭṭhujukatāya matthakabhūtā vipassanā, tadadhiṭṭhānā sīlasamādhīti ime [M 1.0205] tassa sāsanassa mūlanti āha “sīlasamādhivipassanā vā ādī”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

It is good in the beginning, hence 'ādikalyāṇaṃ,' and similarly in the rest. The beginning of the Dispensation is virtue, as it is the root. Its middle consists of serenity and so forth, being the middle part of the Dispensation's attainment. The fruits and Nibbāna are the culmination, as there is nothing further to be done after their attainment. Right practice in the Dispensation arises through wisdom, and its roots are virtue and concentration—therefore it is said, 'virtue and concentration are the beginning.' Since wisdom is twofold—by way of understanding and penetration—therefore, including both, it is said, 'insight and the paths are the middle.' The accomplishment of wisdom is the function of the fruit, while the realization of Nibbāna is the conclusion of right practice, as there is nothing further to be done thereafter—therefore it is said, 'the fruits and Nibbāna are the culmination.' For by the mention of 'fruit,' Nibbāna with residue is implied, and by the other, the Nibbāna without residue; thus, by way of both, the practice reaches its end—therefore it is said, 'the fruits and Nibbāna are the culmination.' As stated in the passage, 'Therefore, bhikkhu, purify the beginning in wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Virtue well-purified and straight view' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.369), insight, which is supreme by virtue of purified virtue and straightened view, and virtue and concentration, which are its foundation—these are the roots of that Dispensation—therefore it is said, 'virtue, concentration, or insight are the beginning.' The rest is as explained.

Kiñcāpi avayavavinimutto samudāyo natthi, yesu pana avayavesu samudāyarūpena apekkhitesu gāthāti samaññā, taṃ tato bhinnaṃ viya katvā dassento “catuppadikagāthāya tāva paṭhamapādo”tiādimāha. Pañcapadachappadānaṃ gāthānaṃ ādipariyosānaggahaṇena itare dutiyādayo tayo cattāro vā majjhanti avuttasiddhamevāti na vuttaṃ. Ekānusandhikasuttassāti idaṃ bahuvibhāgaṃ yathānusandhinā ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, itarassa pana teyeva desetabbadhammavibhāgena ādimajjhapariyosānabhāgā labbhanti. Nidānanti kāladesakaparisādi-apadisanalakkhaṇādiko attho. Idamavocāti iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena tadavasesanigamanapāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Anekānusandhīkassa saha nidānena paṭhamo anusandhi ādi. Saha nigamanena pacchimo pariyosānaṃ, itarena majjhimantiādimajjhapariyosānāni veditabbāni.

Although there is no aggregate apart from its parts, the designation 'verse' is applied to those parts when they are regarded in the form of an aggregate. To show this as if distinct from that, he says, 'First, the first line of a four-line verse,' and so forth. For five-line and six-line verses, by taking the beginning and end, the remaining three or four lines in the middle are implicitly understood, and thus it is not stated. Regarding a sutta with a single connection, this is said referring to a sutta that has a single connection throughout its many divisions; but for another kind of sutta, the beginning, middle, and end sections are discernible by the division of the teachings to be expounded. 'Nidāna' means the meaning characterized by the indication of time, place, assembly, and so forth. In 'Idamavocāti,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'beginning.' By this, it includes the remaining concluding passage. For a sutta with many connections, the first connection together with the nidāna is the beginning; the last together with the concluding passage is the end, and the others are the middle; thus are the beginning, middle, and end to be understood.

Sātthakanti atthasampattiyā sātthakaṃ katvā. Sabyañjananti byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Sampatti ca nāma paripuṇṇabyañjanatāti āha “byañjanehi…pe… desetā”ti. Sakalaparipuṇṇanti [V 1.0180] sabbaso paripuṇṇaṃ sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhapāripūriyā. Nirupakkilesaṃ diṭṭhimānādiupakkilesābhāvato. Avisesato tisso sikkhā sakale sāsane bhavanti. Dhammoti pana brahmacariyaṃ vā sandhāya vuttaṃ “katamesānaṃ kho, bhante, buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ brahmacariyaṃ ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ahosī”tiādīsu (pārā. 18) viya. Dukūlasāṇiyā paṭicchannā viya, na tu pākāraselādipaṭicchannā viya. Tena dhammaniruttiyā sakalakilesānaṃ pahānānubhāvaṃ vadati. Alābhaparihāniyā, na laddhaparihāniyā. Aḍḍhuḍḍhānīti pañcasatādhikāni tīṇi pāṭihāriyasahassāni. Sātanti sukhaṃ.

"Sātthaka" means making it meaningful by the accomplishment of the meaning. "Sabyañjana" means making it well-phrased by the accomplishment of the phrasing. And 'accomplishment' means the completeness of the phrasing—therefore he says, 'with phrasing... a teacher.' "Sakalaparipuṇṇa" means entirely complete by the fulfillment of the five aggregates of Dhamma, beginning with virtue. "Nirupakkilesa" means due to the absence of defilements such as wrong view and conceit. Without distinction, the three trainings are present in the entire Dispensation. 'Dhamma,' however, is said referring to the holy life, as in passages like, 'For which, venerable sir, of the Blessed Buddhas was the holy life long-established?' and so forth (Pārā. 18). Like one covered by a cloth of fine linen or hemp, not like one covered by walls, rocks, and so forth. By this explanation of Dhamma, he speaks of the power of abandoning all defilements. "Alābhaparihāniyā" means by the decline of non-acquisition, not by the decline of what has been acquired. "Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni" refers to three thousand five hundred miracles. "Sāta" means happiness.

Dutiyamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra's Snare is concluded.

6. Sappasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Snake

142. Surākārakānanti [M 1.0206] piṭṭhasurāyojanakānaṃ. Kosalānaṃ issaroti kosalo, kosalarājassa ayanti kosalikā. Paribhogapātīti bhattaparibhojanatthāya pāti paribhogapāti. Kammāruddhanapaṇāḷiyāti kammāruddhanapaṇāḷimukhe. Dhamamānāyāti dhamiyamānāya. Taṃ pana yasmā bhastavātehi pūritaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā “bhastavātena pūriyamānāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Niyāmabhūmiyanti bhagavato paṭisallānaṭṭhāne sañcarantaṃ māraṃ maṃsacakkhunāva disvā. Tenāha “vijjulatālokenā”ti.

142. 'Makers of liquor' means those who prepare liquor from flour. 'The ruler of the Kosalans' is the Kosalan; 'belonging to the king of Kosala' are the Kosalans. 'A bowl for use' means a bowl for the purpose of eating a meal. 'At the blacksmith’s furnace-pipe' means at the mouth of the blacksmith’s furnace-pipe. 'Being blown' means being fanned. But since it is indeed filled with the wind from the bellows, therefore it is said, 'being filled by the wind from the bellows.' 'On the ground of certainty' means: having seen with the physical eye Māra wandering in the Blessed One's place of seclusion. Therefore he said, 'with the light of lightning.'

Seyyatthāyāti seyyānisaṃsāya. Tenāha “ṭhassāmī”tiādi. Attasaññatoti attabhāvena saṃyato. Tenāha “saṃyatattabhāvo”ti. Taṃsaṇṭhitassāti tasmiṃ hatthapādakukkuccarahite buddhamunismiṃ avaṭṭhitassa. Vossajja careyya tattha soti iminā bhagavā taṃ byākaramāno vibhiṃsitā buddhānaṃ kiṃ karissati bhayābhāvato? Kevalaṃ pana anaṭṭhavalikaṃ uppīḷento viya tvameva āyāsaṃ āpajjissasīti māraṃ santajjeti.

'For the sake of lying down' means for the benefit of lying down. Hence he said, 'I will stand,' etc. 'Restrained in self' means restrained in one's own person. Hence he said, 'one of restrained being.' 'Established in him' means established in that Buddha-sage, who is free from scruples about hands and feet. By this—'Let go and wander there'—the Blessed One, explaining it, frightens Māra, saying: 'What can he do to the Buddhas who have shattered delusion, since they are fearless? You alone, like one squeezing a useless twisted rope, will come to fatigue.'

Bheravāti avītarāgānaṃ bhayajanakā. Tatthāti taṃnimittaṃ. Phaleyyāti bhijjeyya. Sattisallanti sattisaṅkhātaṃ puthusallaṃ. Urasmiṃ cārayeyyunti phāsuṃ vijjhituṃ ṭhapeyyuṃ uggireyyuṃ. Khandhupadhīsūti khandhasaṅkhātesu upadhīsu. Tāṇaṃ karonti nāmāti tato bhayanimittato attano tāṇaṃ karonti nāma.

'Terrifying' means fear-producing for those who are not free from lust. 'There' means on that account. 'Would split' means would be broken. 'A spear-dart' means a large dart reckoned as a spear. 'They would apply to the chest' means they would place it to pierce a rib, they would hurl it. 'In the aggregates as attachments' means in the attachments reckoned as the aggregates. 'They make a shelter indeed' means they indeed make a shelter for themselves from that cause of fear.

Sappasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Snake is finished.

7. Supatisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Sleeping Well

143. Utugāhāpanatthaṃ [V 1.0181] dhovitvā, na rajojallavikkhālanatthaṃ. Tenāha “buddhānaṃ panā”tiādi. Dhotapādake geheti dhotapādehi akkamitabbake. Vattabhedo nāma natthi dhammassāmibhāvato. Vattasīse [M 1.0207] ṭhatvā dhovanti aññesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanatthaṃ. Soppapariggāhakenāti ettha soppaṃ nāma niddāya antarantarā pavattakiriyamayacittappavattirahitā nirantarabhavaṅgasantatīti taṃ sabhāvato payojanato kālaparicchedato pariggāhakaṃ upariniddesasatisampajaññaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “soppapariggāhakena satisampajaññenā”ti. Keci pana “niddāsoppanā”ti vadanti, taṃ bhagavato soppaṃ hīḷento vadati.

143. Having washed for the purpose of regulating the temperature, not for the purpose of washing off dust and dirt. Therefore he said, 'But for the Buddhas,' etc. 'Taking the washed-feet-place' means that which is to be stepped upon by washed feet. There is indeed no breach of duty, because he is the master of the Dhamma. Standing at the head of the observance, they wash so that others may follow their example. 'With that which delimits sleep': Here, 'sleep' is the uninterrupted stream of the life-continuum, devoid of the activity of mind consisting of processes occurring in between sleep. That which 'delimits' it—by its nature, by its purpose, and by its time-limit—is said with reference to the mindfulness and clear comprehension mentioned above. Thus the meaning is: 'with mindfulness and clear comprehension that delimits sleep.' Some, however, say 'sleep and drowsiness,' but that is said by one who disparages the Blessed One's sleep.

Kiṃ nūti etthaṃ kinti hetunissakke paccattavacananti āha “kasmā nu supasī”ti? Dubbhago vuccati nissiriko bhinnabhago, so pana matasadiso visaññisadiso ca hotīti āha “mato viya visaññī viya cā”ti.

Regarding 'Kiṃ nu': here 'kiṃ' is a personal expression indicating a cause, without a doubt. He says, 'Why do you sleep?' 'Unfortunate' is said of one who is without splendor, whose fortune is broken. And such a one is like the dead and like one who is unconscious; hence he said, 'like the dead and like the unconscious.'

Ādināti ādi-saddena “bāhirassa upādāya aṭṭhārasā”tiādinā (vibha. 842) āgataṃ taṇhākoṭṭhāsaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha tattha visattatāyāti tammiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe visesato āsattabhāvena. Visassa dukkhanibbattakakammassa hetubhāvato visamūlatā visaṃ vā dukkhadukkhādibhūtavedanā mūlaṃ etassāti visamūlā, taṇhā. Tassa rūpādikassa dukkhassa paribhogo, na amatassāti visaparibhogatā. Katthaci netunti katthaci bhave sabbathā netuṃ? Parikkhayāti sabbaso khīṇattā. Tuyhaṃ kiṃ etthāti sabbupadhiparikkhayā suddhassa mama paṭipattiyaṃ tuyhaṃ kiṃ ujjhāyanaṃ? Kevalaṃ vighātoyeva teti dasseti.

'Beginning': with the word 'beginning,' it includes the portion of craving that comes in the passage beginning 'the external eighteen based on clinging' (Vibh 842). 'By clinging there, there' means by being especially attached to this or that object. 'Poison-rooted': because it is the cause of kamma that produces suffering like poison, it is poison-rooted; or because suffering—that is, the feeling that is painful suffering, etc.—is its root, craving is poison-rooted. 'Enjoyment of poison' is the experiencing of that suffering related to forms, etc., not of the deathless. 'To lead anywhere' means to lead anywhere at all in any existence. 'From complete destruction' means from being totally exhausted. 'What is there for you in this?' means: 'Since all attachments are completely destroyed, what complaint do you have about my pure practice? It is merely vexation for you'—this he shows.

Supatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Sleeping Well is finished.

8. Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Rejoicing

144. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānatthameva.

144. The eighth is simply of plain meaning.

Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Rejoicing is finished.

9. Paṭhamaāyusuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Longevity

145. Paṇṇāsaṃ [V 1.0182][M 1.0208] vā vassāni jīvati vassasatato upari seyyathāpi thero anuruddho. Saṭṭhi vā vassāni seyyathāpi thero bākulo. Paṭiharitvā paccanīkabhāve sātaṃ sukhaṃ etassāti paccanīkasāto, tabbhāvo paccanīkasātatā, tāya. Abhibhavitvā abhāsi paṭivacanaṃ jānamānova.

145. 'One lives for fifty years or over a hundred years,' like the Elder Anuruddha; 'or for sixty years,' like the Elder Bākula. 'By means of contrary pleasantness': one for whom there is pleasure and happiness in a contrary state is 'one with contrary pleasantness'; the state of that is 'contrary pleasantness'; by that. 'Overcoming, he spoke a reply,' just as one who knows.

Na hīḷeyya na jiguccheyya. Evanti so dārako viya kiñci acintento sappuriso careyya, evaṃ hissa cittadukkhaṃ na hotīti adhippāyo. Pajjalitasīso viya careyyāti yathā pajjalitasīso puriso aññaṃ kiñci akatvā tasseva vūpasamāya vāyameyya, evaṃ sappuriso āyuṃ parittanti ñatvā teneva nayena sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ aniccaṃ, aniccattā eva dukkhaṃ, anattāti vipassanampi otaritvā taṃ ussukkāpentopi saṅkhāravigamāya careyya paṭipajjeyya.

'One should not scorn, one should not loathe.' 'Thus': a good person should fare like a child, not thinking about anything; the intention is that in this way mental suffering does not arise for him. 'One should fare like one whose head is ablaze': just as a person whose head is on fire, doing nothing else, would strive only for its quenching, so too a good person, having known that life is short, should by that same method enter upon insight that all conditioned things are impermanent, and because of impermanence are suffering and not-self; and while striving at that, he should fare and practice for the cessation of conditioned formations.

Paṭhamaāyusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Discourse on Longevity is finished.

10. Dutiyaāyusuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Longevity

146. Nemīvāti nemisīsena cakkaṃ vadati. Kubbaraṃ anupariyāyatīti kubbaraṃ anuparivattati. Tathābhūto pana so taṃ ajahantovāti āha “na vijahatī”ti. Āyu anupariyāyatīti maccānaṃ āyu gatampi paccāgacchatīti bhagavato paṭāṇi hutvā vadati, bhagavā pana taṃ abhibhavitvā “accayanti ahorattā”tiādinā āyuno accayagamanamaraṇataṃyeva pavedesi.

146. ‘Like a wheel’s rim’ means he speaks of the wheel by its rim. ‘The hub revolves accordingly’ means the hub turns along with it. Though it is so, he says, ‘It does not abandon it.’ ‘Life revolves accordingly’—that the gone life of mortals returns—he speaks, taking a position contrary to the Blessed One. But the Blessed One, transcending this, declared through ‘Days and nights pass away’ and so forth, that the passing away of life is simply death.

Dutiyaāyusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Longevity is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Pāsāṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Rock

147. Pavijjhīti [V 1.0183][M 1.0209] pabbataṃ sabbato pavattento tato tato nissajji. Sakalanti sabbabhāgavantaṃ, nissesanti attho.

147. 'He hurled' means, causing the mountain to roll from all sides, he let it loose from here and there. 'Whole' means possessing all its parts; the meaning is 'without remainder.'

Pāsāṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Rock is concluded.

2. Kiṃnusīhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on 'What Now, Lion?'

148. Vicakkhukammāyāti vicakkhubhāvakāmatāya. Yathā sā bhagavato desiyamānaṃ dhammaṃ attano paññācakkhunā na passituṃ sakkoti, evaṃ kātuṃ kāmatāya. Tenāha “parisāyā”tiādi. Vināsetuṃ na sakkoti bheravārammaṇe bhāyanasseva abhāvato. Dasabalappattāti dasahi balehi samannāgatā.

148. ‘Blindness of action’ (vicakkhukammāya) means the desire for a state of blindness, in that she wanted to act in such a way that she would not be able to see the Dhamma being taught by the Blessed One with her eye of wisdom. Therefore, it is said, ‘In the assembly’ and so forth. She could not destroy it because of the absence of fear in the frightening object. ‘Attained the ten powers’ (dasabalappattā) means possessed of the ten powers.

Kiṃnusīhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kiṃnusīha Sutta is concluded.

3. Sakalikasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sakalika Sutta

149. Mandabhāvenāti jaḷabhāvena momūhabhāvenāti mahāmūḷhatāya. Kabbakaraṇena mattoti kabbakiriyāpasutatādivasena matto kabbaṃ katvā. Kimidaṃ soppasevāti idaṃ tava soppaṃ kimatthaṃ, purisena nāma purisattakarena bhavitabbaṃ, na soppatiyeva. Atthaṃ samāgantvāti paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ sammā āgantvā adhigantvā. Asaṅga…pe… natthi sabbaso siddhatthabhāvato. Jaggantoti jāgaranto puriso viya, na bhāyāmi bhayahetūnaṃ abhāvā. Nānutapanti sabbattha sabbadāpi vissaṭṭhabhāvato, māmanti mamaṃ. Gāthāsukhatthañhi dīghaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Ṭhitattāti uddesaparipucchāya paricchijjattā. Hāninti kassaci jāniṃ.

149. ‘Dullness’ (mandabhāvena) means dullness (jaḷabhāvena); ‘great delusion’ (momūhabhāvena) means great delusion (mahāmūḷhatāya). ‘Intoxicated by poetic composition’ (kabbakaraṇena matto) means intoxicated by being devoted to the act of poetic composition and so forth, having composed poetry. ‘What is this sleep of yours?’ (kimidaṃ soppasevā) means, ‘What is this sleep of yours for? A man should indeed act like a man, not just sleep.’ ‘Having rightly attained the goal’ (atthaṃ samāgantvā) means having rightly attained the ultimate goal, Nibbāna. ‘Unattached’ (asaṅga)… and so forth… means there is no attachment because of the attainment of complete purpose. ‘Staying awake’ (jagganto) means like a person who is awake; ‘I do not fear’ (na bhāyāmi) because there is no cause for fear. ‘They do not grieve’ (nānutapanti) means not grieving anywhere or at any time, due to being free from all bonds. ‘Me’ (māmaṃ) means me (mamaṃ). Indeed, it is stated by making it long for the sake of metrical ease. ‘One with an established self’ (ṭhitattā) means being defined by way of exposition and questioning. ‘Loss’ (hāniṃ) means the loss of someone.

Sakalikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sakalika Sutta is concluded.

4. Patirūpasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Patirūpa Sutta

150. Anurujjhati [V 1.0184][M 1.0210] etenāti anurodho, rāgo. Virujjhati etenāti virodho, paṭigho. Tesu anurodhavirodhesu tannimittaṃ sajjati nāma saṅgaṃ karoti nāma, anurodhavirodhuppādanameva cettha sajjanaṃ. Yadaññamanusāsatīti yaṃ aññesaṃ anusāsanaṃ, taṃ tesaṃ hitesanaṃ anukampanaṃ, tasmā anukampake hitesake sammāsambuddhe anurodhavirodhe āropetvā vikampanatthaṃ micchā vadasīti.

150. ‘One is attracted by this’ (anurujjhati etena) means attraction (anurodha), that is, lust (rāga). ‘One is averse by this’ (virujjhati etena) means aversion (virodha), that is, hatred (paṭigha). In these attractions and aversions, one clings to their cause, meaning one forms attachments. Here, clinging is simply the arising of attraction and aversion. ‘When he instructs others’ (yadaññamanusāsati) means the instruction which is given to others, which is desiring their welfare and having compassion for them. Therefore, it is with the intent to cause doubt that one falsely accuses the Perfectly Enlightened One—who is compassionate and seeks the welfare of others—of attraction and aversion.

Patirūpasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Patirūpa Sutta is concluded.

5. Mānasasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Mānasasutta

151. Ākāse caranteti pañcābhiññe sandhāya vadati. Antalikkhe carantepi kiccasādhanato antalikkhacaro. Manasi jātoti mānaso. Taṃ pana manasantānasampayuttatāyāti āha “manasampayutto”ti.

151. ‘Moving in the sky’ (ākāse caranto) refers to one endowed with the five higher knowledges. One who moves in the intermediate space is a sky-walker (antalikkhacaro) because of the accomplishment of a task. ‘Born of mind’ (manasi jāto) means mental (mānaso). It is further explained as ‘associated with the mind’ (manasampayutto), due to its connection to the mental continuum.

Mānasasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mānasasutta is concluded.

6. Pattasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Patta Sutta

152. Pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ lakkhaṇādīni ceva samudayañca assādādīnavanissaraṇāni ca gahetvā sammā tesaṃ lakkhaṇādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ hotīti āha “pañca upādānakkhandhe ādiyitvā”ti. Ruppanavediyanasañjānanaabhisaṅkharaṇavijānanāni khandhānaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇāni. Ādi-saddena rasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni ceva samudayādīni ca saṅgaṇhāti. Dassetīti paccakkhato dasseti, hatthāmalakaṃ viya pākaṭe vibhūte katvā vibhāveti. Gaṇhāpetīti te dhamme manasā anupekkhite diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhe karonto uggaṇhāpeti. Samādānamhīti tattha atthassa sammadeva ādiyane khandhānañca sammasanavasena aññadhammavasena samādiyane. Paṭividdhaguṇenāti tāya desanāya, taṃ nissāya paccattapurisakārena ca tesaṃ paṭividdhaguṇena[M 1.0211]. Jotāpetīti tesaṃ cittasantānaṃ assaddhiyādikilesamalavidhamanena pabhassaraṃ karoti. Aṭṭhiṃ katvāti tāya desanāya pāpetabbaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā. Tenāha “ayaṃ no”tiādi. Kammakārakacittaṃ nāma otaraṇacittaṃ. “Yonisomanasikārapubbakaṃ vipassanācitta”nti [V 1.0185] keci. Ohitasotāti anaññavihitatāya dhammassavanāya appitasotā, tato eva tadatthaṃ ṭhapitasotā.

152. By taking the characteristics and so forth of the five aggregates of clinging, as well as their arising, and the allure, drawbacks, and escape from them, one correctly grasps their characteristics and so forth. Therefore, it is said, ‘having taken up the five aggregates of clinging’ (pañca upādānakkhandhe ādiyitvā). The essential characteristics of the aggregates are being afflicted (ruppana), feeling (vediyana), perceiving (sañjānana), forming (abhisaṅkharaṇa), and cognizing (vijānana). The term ‘and so forth’ (ādi-saddena) includes the function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), and their arising and so forth. ‘He shows’ (dasseti) means he reveals directly, making it clear and evident like a myrobalan fruit in the hand. ‘He makes them grasp’ (gaṇhāpeti) means he causes them to learn those phenomena by reflecting with the mind and thoroughly understanding them with insight. ‘In taking up’ (samādānaṃ) refers to correctly taking up the meaning there and also taking up the aggregates through thorough comprehension and through differentiation from other phenomena. ‘By the quality of having penetrated’ (paṭividdhaguṇena) means through that teaching, relying on it and personally realizing those qualities. ‘He illuminates’ (jotāpeti) means he makes their mental continuum bright by dispelling the stains of defilements such as lack of faith and so forth. ‘Having made firm’ (aṭṭhiṃ katvā) means firmly establishing the purpose and benefit to be achieved through that teaching. Therefore, it is said, ‘this is ours’ and so forth. ‘The mind of the worker’ (kammakārakacittaṃ) refers to the mind ready to absorb the teaching. Some say, ‘the insight mind preceded by wise attention’ (yonisomanasikārapubbakaṃ vipassanācittaṃ). ‘With ears intent’ (ohitasotā) means with ears fixed on listening to the Dhamma without being diverted elsewhere, thus establishing the purpose for listening.

Ete rūpādayo khandhe yañca saṅkhataṃ samiddhapaccayehi kataṃ, tañca “eso ahaṃ na homi, etaṃ mayhaṃ na hotī”ti passantoti yojanā. Khemo attāti khemattā, taṃ khemattaṃ. Tenāha “khemibhūtaṃ attabhāva”nti. Pariyesamānā mārasenā.

The construction is: one sees these aggregates of form and so forth, and whatever is conditioned, made by complete conditions, thus: ‘This I am not, this is not mine.’ ‘Secure in self’ (khemo attā) means security (khemattā), that security. Therefore, it is said, ‘the state of being secure in self’ (khemibhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ). The army of Māra is searching.

Pattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Patta Sutta is concluded.

7. Chaphassāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Chaphassāyatana Sutta

153. Sañjāyati etasmāti sañjāti, so eva sampayuttadhammo samosarati etthāti samosaraṇaṃ, so eva attho, tena sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhena. Bhayabheravaṃ saddanti bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, tadeva yassa kassaci bheravāvahattā bheravaṃ, devādisaddanti attho. Vigatavalāhake deve uppātavasena uppajjanakasaddo devadundubhi. Asanipātādisaddo asanipātasaddo. Undrīyatīti viparivattati. Loko adhimucchitoti atithaddhakāyo viya mucchaṃ āpanno. Mārassāti kilesamārassa. Ṭhānabhūtanti pavattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ.

153. ‘Origin’ (sañjāti) is so called because from this it originates. That very associated phenomenon converges here, thus it is ‘convergence’ (samosaraṇaṃ). This is the meaning; therefore, by the meaning of origin and convergence. ‘Sound of fear and terror’ means: ‘fear’ (bhayaṃ) is so called because one fears from this; that very thing is ‘terror’ (bheravaṃ) because it brings terror to anyone; this is the meaning of the sound of gods, etc. The sound that arises in the sky when the clouds have disappeared, due to an omen, is the divine drum. The sound of a lightning strike, etc., is the sound of a lightning strike. ‘It turns over’ (undrīyati) means it revolves. ‘The world is overwhelmed’ (loko adhimucchito) means it has fallen into a stupor, as if the body is extremely stiff. ‘Of Māra’ means of the Māra of defilements. ‘A place of establishment’ (ṭhānabhūtaṃ) means a place of establishment for the occurrence.

Chaphassāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chaphassāyatana Sutta is concluded.

8. Piṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Piṇḍa Sutta

154. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ñātimittakule. Pāhunakānīti pahitabbapaṇṇākārāni. Āgantukapaṇṇākārānīti āgantukānaṃ upagatānaṃ [M 1.0212] dātabbapaṇṇākārāni. Sayaṃcaradivaseti kumārakānañca kumārikānañca sayaṃ attanā caritabbachaṇadivase. Idāni tamatthaṃ vitthārato dassento “samavayajātigottā”tiādimāha. Samavayasamajātikasamagottāti paccekaṃ sama-saddo yojetabbo. Gottasamatā ca āvāhavivāhayogyatāvasena daṭṭhabbā, na ekagottatāvasena. Tato tato gāmato. Aññasmiṃ dātabbe asati. Chaṇavasena pahiṇituṃ sampāditaṃ pūvaṃ chaṇapūvaṃ. Tāsaṃ sampattiyāti tāsaṃ dānaṃ dhammassavanañcāti tassā duvidhāyapi sampattiyā.

154. ‘Here and there’ (tattha tatthā) means in each and every household of relatives and friends. ‘Guest offerings’ (pāhunakāni) means gifts to be sent. ‘Offerings for visitors’ (āgantukapaṇṇākārāni) means gifts to be given to those who have arrived as visitors. ‘On the day they go themselves’ (sayaṃcaradivase) means the festival day when young boys and girls should go by themselves. Now, explaining that matter in detail, it says, ‘of equal age, birth, and lineage,’ and so forth. ‘Of equal age, same birth, and same lineage’—the word ‘equal’ should be connected separately to each. And equality of lineage should be understood in terms of suitability for marriage, not merely being of one and the same lineage. ‘From here and there’ (tato tato) means from this village and that village. When there is nothing else to give. ‘Festival cakes’ (chaṇapūvaṃ) refers to cakes prepared to be sent for the festival. ‘For their attainment’ (tāsaṃ sampattiyā) means for their giving and listening to the Dhamma, that is, for the attainment of both kinds.

Ñāṇaṃ nāma āvajjanapubbakaṃ, tasmā ajānanassa “anāvajjanatāyā”ti kāraṇaṃ vatvā [V 1.0186] sesakāraṇaṃ vadanto “buddhāna”ntiādimāha. Upacārabhedanti buddhaṃ disvā manussehi kātabbaupacārassa bhindanaṃ. Bhinditunti vidhamituṃ.

Knowledge is preceded by adverting. Therefore, having stated ‘due to non-adverting’ as the reason for not knowing, it then states the remaining reason, ‘of the Buddhas,’ and so forth. ‘Breaking of homage’ (upacārabhedanaṃ) means the breaking of the homage that should be paid by people upon seeing the Buddha. ‘To break’ (bhindituṃ) means to dispel.

Bhagavā panāti panasaddo visesatthajotako. Tena na kevalaṃ bhagavā uppaṇḍanaṃ pariharanto taṃ gāmaṃ na puna pāvisi, atha kho māraṃ anukampantoti idaṃ visesaṃ joteti.

‘But the Blessed One’—here the particle ‘pana’ indicates a special meaning. By this, it indicates the special point that the Blessed One not only avoided that village, preventing ridicule, and did not enter it again, but also had compassion for Māra.

Janesīti apuññaṃ janesi, janento ca yathā tato āyatiṃ thirataraṃ mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ nipphajjissati, evaṃ nipphādesi. Āsajjananti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ. Kiñcati maddati abhibhavatīti kiñcananti āha “maddituṃ samattha”nti.

‘He generates’ (janesi) means he generated demerit, and by generating it, he brought it about such that in the future even greater and more lasting suffering would arise from it. In ‘assaulting’ (āsajjanaṃ), the ‘na’ here is merely a particle. ‘What crushes, what overcomes’ is ‘impediment’ (kiñcana), thus it is said ‘able to crush’.

Piṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Piṇḍa Sutta is concluded.

9. Kassakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Kassaka Sutta

155. Nibbānaṃ apadisitvāti nibbānaṃ nissāya nibbānaguṇe ārabbhāti attho. Haṭahaṭakesoti ito cito ca vikiṇṇattā ākulākulakeso. Cakkhusamphassaviññāṇāyatananti ettha yathā cakkhuggahaṇena phasso visesito, tena eva viññāṇāyatanaṃ. Tathā sati cakkhuviññāṇassa ca gahaṇaṃ āpajjeyyāti. Nanu cettha cakkhuggahaṇena visesitattā cakkhudvārikānaṃ sabbesaṃ viññāṇānaṃ gahaṇanti? Saccametaṃ, tañca kho paṭhamena cakkhuggahaṇenāti nāyaṃ doso. Bhavaṅgacittanti āvajjanāya anantarapaccayabhūtameva [M 1.0213] adhippetanti niyametvā dassetuṃ “sāvajjanaka”nti vuttaṃ, tasmā tadārammaṇampīti javanacittena saha tadārammaṇacittampi. “Viññāṇāyatana”nti ca vutte nimmalameva.

155. “Having pointed out Nibbāna” means relying on Nibbāna, with reference to the qualities of Nibbāna. “With disheveled hair” means with hair scattered here and there, hence very tangled. Regarding “the sphere of eye-contact-consciousness”: here, just as contact is specified by the term ‘eye,’ so too is the sphere of consciousness. If that were so, the inclusion of eye-consciousness would also result. But is it not the case that here, since it is specified by the term ‘eye,’ all consciousnesses of the eye-door are included? That is true, but this is by the first mention of ‘eye,’ so there is no fault. Regarding “life-continuum consciousness”: the term “with adverting” is stated in order to demonstrate definitively that only that which is the immediately preceding condition for adverting is intended; therefore, the registration consciousness is also included along with the impulsion consciousness. And when “sphere of consciousness” is stated, it is only a pure one.

“Cakkhū”ti avisesato vuttattā pana mārassa ayampi attho āpannoti dassetuṃ “yaṃ loke”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upakkavipakkanti cakkhupākarogena upari heṭṭhā ca sabbaso pakkaṃ kuthitaṃ. Eseva nayoti iminā yaṃ loke kuṭṭhakilāsagaṇḍakacchuādīhi upaddutaṃ vaṇapīḷakādivasena paggharantaṃ asuciṃ antamaso paramajeguccharūpampi, sabbaṃ taṃ taveva hotūti evamādiṃ apadisati.

Regarding “the eye”: since it is stated without specification, to show that this meaning also applies to Māra, “whatever in the world,” and so forth, is stated. “Afflicted and putrid” means completely festered and putrid above and below due to a disease ripening in the eye. “By this same method”: by this, it indicates that whatever in the world is afflicted by leprosy, skin eruptions, tumors, scabies, and so on, oozing as sores, boils, and the like, impure, even the most utterly disgusting forms—all that belongs to you alone, and so forth.

Yaṃ bhaṇḍakanti hiraññasuvaṇṇādikhettavatthādiupakaraṇaṃ gahaṭṭhā, pabbajitā ca yaṃ pattacīvarādiṃ “mama ida”nti abhinivisantāva vadanti, etesu pariggahatthesu ca tesaṃ pariggāhakapuggalesu [V 1.0187] ca te cittaṃ yadi atthi, tāni ārabbha tava cittaṃ yadi bhavati, evaṃ tvaṃ tattha baddho eva hosīti attho. Tenāha “na me samaṇa mokkhasī”ti.

Regarding “what goods”: householders refer to gold, silver, fields, land, and other implements, while renunciates refer to bowls, robes, and the like, saying, “This is mine,” while clinging to them. If your mind is present in these objects of possession or in the individuals who possess them, if your mind arises with reference to them, then in this way you are indeed bound there—this is the meaning. Therefore, he said, “You will not be freed from me, ascetic.”

Yaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ vadantīti yathāvuttaṃ upakaraṇaṃ loke bahujanā “mama ida”nti vadanti. Na taṃ mayhanti taṃ mayhaṃ na hoti, na tattha mama taṇhāvasena mamanti natthi. Na te ahanti ye puggalā ettha baddhā, tepi ahaṃ na homi, tattha me diṭṭhibaddho natthi. Na me maggampi dakkhasīti evaṃ sabbaso baddhābhāvena muttassa me gatamaggampi māra tvaṃ na dakkhasi na passissasi, ye bhavādayo tuyhaṃ visayā, tesu bhavayonigatiādīsu mayhaṃ gatamaggaṃ na passissasi bhavanissaṭṭhattāti.

Regarding “what they call possessions”: as mentioned, many people in the world say “This is mine” of such requisites. Regarding “that is not mine”: that is not mine; there is no “mine” there by way of craving. Regarding “nor are they I”: those individuals who are bound to these things, they also are not I; I have no bondage there through views. Regarding “you will not even see my path”: thus, being entirely free from bondage, Māra, you will not see, you will not perceive the path I have taken. In the realms of existence and so on, which are your domain—in those births, origins, destinations, and so on—you will not see the path I have taken, because I am released from existence.

Kassakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kassaka Sutta is concluded.

10. Rajjasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Rajja Sutta

156. Ahananti karaṇe paccattavacananti āha “ahanantenā”ti, paccatte eva vā paccattavacanaṃ, “ahananto hutvā”ti vacanasesena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ajinanti antogadhahetuatthaṃ [M 1.0214] vadatīti āha “parassa dhanajāniṃ akarontenā”ti. Akārāpentenāti parassa dhanajāniṃ akārentena. Asocantenāti bhogabyasanādivasena paraṃ asocantena. Kasmā bhagavā evaṃ cintesīti tattha kāraṇamāha “itī”tiādinā. Rajje vijite daṇḍakarapīḷiteti dhanadaṇḍādidaṇḍena ceva balinā ca bādhite.

156. Regarding `ahananto` (not striking): it is a first-person expression in the instrumental case, thus he says, “by not striking.” Or, it is simply a first-person expression, the intention being that the meaning is understood by supplying the rest of the phrase, “having become one who does not strike.” This same method applies to the remaining terms. Regarding `ajinanto` (not depriving): this is said to have the meaning of an implicit cause, thus he says, “by not causing loss of another’s wealth.” “By not having it caused” means by not causing another’s wealth to be lost. “By not causing sorrow” means not causing another to grieve on account of loss of wealth, calamity, and so on. Why did the Blessed One think thus? He states the reason with “Thus,” and so on. “In a conquered kingdom, oppressed by punishment and tribute” means oppressed by punishments such as fines, and by force.

Ijjhanakakoṭṭhāsāti cetovasibhāvādikassa sādhanakakoṭṭhāsā. Vaḍḍhitāti bhāvanāpāripūrivasena anubrūhitā. Punappunaṃ katāti bhāvanāya bahulīkaraṇena aparāparaṃ pavattitā. Yuttayānanti yathā yuttānaṃ ājaññarathānaṃ sārathinā adhiṭṭhitaṃ yathāruci pavattati, evaṃ yathārucipavattitaṃ gamitā. Patiṭṭhaṭṭhenāti adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena. Vatthukatāti sabbaso upakkilesasodhanena iddhivisayatāya patiṭṭhānabhāvato suvisodhitaparissayavatthu viya katā. Avijahitāti paṭipakkhadūrībhāvato subhāvitabhāvena taṃtaṃadhiṭṭhānayogyatāya na jahāpitā. Niccānubaddhāti tato eva niccaṃ anubaddhā viya katā. Suparicitāti suṭṭhu sabbabhāgena bhāvanānupacayaṃ gamitā. Avirādhitavedhihattho viyāti avirajjhanabhāvena virajjhanahattho viya. Suṭṭhu samāraddhāti bhāvanāuppattiyā sammadeva sampāditā. Cinteyyāti atthuddhāravasena cinteyya.

“Parts conducive to accomplishment” means the parts that bring about mastery over the mind and similar qualities. “Developed” means augmented by way of the fulfillment of cultivation. “Done again and again” means made to occur repeatedly through frequent cultivation. “A yoked vehicle” means made to proceed as desired, just as a chariot with thoroughbreds yoked, controlled by a charioteer, proceeds as he pleases. “In the sense of a foundation” means in the sense of a basis. “Made a basis” means made like a well-cleared site, being thoroughly purified from all defilements and established as a basis for the sphere of psychic power. “Not abandoned” means not given up, being suitable for each and every resolve due to being well-developed and far from opposition. “Constantly pursued” means made as if constantly followed for that very reason. “Well-acquainted” means brought to accumulation through cultivation well in every aspect. “Like an archer with an unerring hand” means like an archer who hits the mark due to the quality of not missing. “Well undertaken” means properly accomplished for the arising of cultivation. “One should reflect” means one should reflect by way of extracting the meaning.

Pabbatassāti [V 1.0188] pabbato assa. Pabbato assāti pabbato bhaveyya kīdisassāti āha “suvaṇṇassā”tiādi. Jātarūpassāti ātaparūpasampannassa. Dvikkhattumpi tāva mahantoti yattako so pabbato hoti, dvikkhattuṃ tattako. Ekassāti ekassapi puggalassa nālaṃ na pariyatto taṇhāya duppūraṇabhāvā. Evaṃ jānantoti evaṃ taṇhāya duppūraṇabhāvādīnavataṃ jānanto. Samaṃ careyyāti paravatthuparāmāsādiṃ vihāya kāyādīhi samameva paṭipajjeyya.

“Of a mountain” means a mountain might be his. “A mountain might be his”: if a mountain were his, of what kind would it be? Thus he says, “of gold,” and so on. “Of gold” means possessing the appearance of sunlight. “Even twice as large” means however large that mountain is, twice that large. “For one”: it is not enough, not sufficient even for one single person, due to the insatiable nature of craving. “Knowing thus” means knowing thus the danger in the insatiable nature of craving. “One should fare evenly” means that, having abandoned the misappropriation of others’ property and so on, one should conduct oneself evenly with body and so forth.

Dukkhaṃ taṇhānidānaṃ, taṇhā kāmaguṇanidānā, tasmā dukkhassa taṇhāpaccayakāmaguṇanidānattaṃ vuttaṃ. Tanti dukkhaṃ. Yatonidānaṃ hotīti yaṃnidānaṃ yaṃkāraṇaṃ taṃ pavattati. Evaṃ yo adakkhīti yo pariññātavatthuko evaṃ dukkhaṃ tassa nidānabhūte kāmaguṇe ca tathato paññācakkhunā passi. Kena kāraṇena nameyya? Taṃ kāraṇaṃ natthīti attho. Kāmaguṇaupadhinti kāmaguṇasaṅkhātaṃ upadhiṃ. Sajjati etthāti saṅgo eso, lagganametanti evaṃ [M 1.0215] viditvā. Tameva kāmābhibhūto nappaṭiseveyya na laggeyyāti evaṃ vinayāya vūpasamāya sikkheyyāti.

Suffering has craving as its source; craving has sensual qualities as its source. Therefore, it is said that suffering has as its source the sensual qualities which are a condition for craving. “That” refers to suffering. “From which source it is” means from whichever source, from whichever cause, it proceeds. “One who saw thus” means one who, having fully understood the matter, saw thus with the eye of wisdom suffering and the sensual qualities that are its source, as they really are. For what reason would he incline towards them? The meaning is that there is no such reason. “The substrate of sensual qualities” means the substrate called sensual qualities. “One is attached to this, thus it is attachment; it is a clinging”—having known it thus. One overcome by sensual pleasures should not indulge in it, should not cling to it; thus one should train for its removal, for its pacification.

Rajjasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Rajja Sutta is concluded.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Sambahulasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta

157. Jaṭācumbaṭakenāti sīse paṭimukkena jaṭākalāpena. Apariggahabrāhmaṇapabbajitā hi jaṭāya uñchācariyaṃ caranti. Udumbaradaṇḍañhi attaguttatthāya gahitaṃ tesaṃ appicchabhāvappakāsanaṃ. Tenāha “appicchabhāvappakāsanattha”nti. Sīsaṃ okampetvāti ettha ativiya sīsassa okampitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “hanukena uraṃ paharanto adhonataṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ. Jivhaṃ nīharitvāti lambanacālanavasena mukhato nikkhāmetvā. Tenāha “uddha”ntiādi. Tisākhanti tibhaṅgabhakuṭi viya nalāṭe jātattā nalāṭikaṃ. Tenāha “nalāṭe uṭṭhitaṃ valittaya”nti, tibhaṅgavalikaṃ nalāṭe katvāti attho. Attanova teleti attanova pāpakammanibbattake tele, pacitabbaṭṭhānageheti adhippāyo.

157. “With a coil of matted hair” means with a mass of matted hair worn on the head. For brahmin renunciates without possessions wander, gleaning their food, with matted hair. The udumbara staff, taken for self-protection, demonstrates their state of having few wishes. Hence it is said, “to show their state of having few wishes.” Regarding “shaking his head”: here, to show that the head was shaken excessively, it is described as “striking the chest with the chin, having bent down.” “Sticking out his tongue” means extending it from the mouth by letting it hang and move. Hence it is said, “upwards,” and so on. “Three-forked” refers to the three lines appearing on the forehead like a three-fold frown. Hence it is said, “the three wrinkles that arose on his forehead,” meaning having made a three-fold wrinkle on his forehead. “In his own oil” refers to the oil produced by his own evil kamma; the intention is, in the house that is the place where he must be cooked.

Sambahulasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sambahula Sutta is concluded.

2. Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta

158. Mayhaṃ [V 1.0189] lābhāti evarūpassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa satthussa paṭilābho, evarūpassa ca nāma niyyānikassa saddhammassa paṭilābho, evarūpānañca suppaṭipannānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ paṭilābho, ete mayhaṃ suladdhalābhā. Mayhaṃ suladdhanti yañcetaṃ mama niyyānikasāsane pabbajjā upasampadā, tasmiñca abhiratīti sabbañcetaṃ mayā suladdhaṃ. Yathā panassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko uppanno, taṃ dassetuṃ “so kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Caritānurūpavasena [M 1.0216] gahitaṃ mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Pāsādikanti pasādāvahaṃ. Evamahosīti “lābhā vata me”tiādinā evaṃ parivitakko ahosi. Nisinnasadisoti nisinno viya. Tasmiṃyeva ṭhāneti yasmiṃ ṭhāne nisinnaṃ māro upasaṅkami, tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne. Tassāti samiddhittherassa. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ sappāyanti kammaṭṭhānabhāvanāya anuyuñjanaṃ sappāyaṃ upakārāvahaṃ bhavissati.

158. "It is my gain" refers to obtaining such a Teacher, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; obtaining such a liberating true Dhamma; and obtaining such well-practicing companions in the holy life—these are gains well gained by me. "It is well gained by me" refers to my going forth and higher ordination in this liberating dispensation, and my delight in it—all this is well gained by me. To show the thought that arose in his mind, "so, it seems" etc., was said. The root meditation subject was taken according to his character. "Inspiring confidence" means producing faith. "Thus it was" refers to the thought, "truly, it is my gain," etc. "Like one seated" means as if seated. "In that very place" means in the very place where Māra approached him while he was seated. "His" refers to the elder Samiddhi. "Suitable for meditation" means that engaging in the development of the meditation subject will be suitable and helpful.

Mayhanti mayā. Sati ca paññā ca satipaññā, tā ariyamaggena jānanasamatthanabhāvena avabuddhā. Thero kira tadā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpesi. Kāmanti yathāruci. Keci “kāmaṃ karassūti āyasmato ‘kāmā’ti mārassa ālapana”nti vadanti. Vibhiṃsakārahānīti bhayānakārahāni. Rūpānīti vippakārāni. Vippakāratthopi hi rūpasaddo “rūpaṃ dasseti anappaka”ntiādīsu viya. Na kampessasīti samaṇadhammakaraṇato na calissasi.

"Mayhaṃ" means "by me." "Satipaññā" is mindfulness and wisdom, which are understood through the noble path as having the capability of knowing. It is said that the elder then made an effort in insight meditation. "Kāmaṃ" means 'as you wish.' Some say that "kāmaṃ karassu" is Māra’s address to the venerable one as "Kāma." "Vibhiṃsakārahāni" means frightening aspects. "Rūpāni" means diverse forms, for the word "rūpa" can also mean diversity, as in "he shows a form not insignificant," etc. "You shall not waver" means you shall not be shaken from performing the ascetic's duty.

Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta is finished.

3. Godhikasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Godhika Sutta

159. Pabbatassa passeti pabbatapāde upaccakāyaṃ. Samaye samaye laddhattā sāmayikaṃ. Tenāha “appitappitakkhaṇe paccanīkadhammehi vimuccatī”ti. Lokiyavimutti hi anaccantapahāyitāya samayavimutti nāma, lokuttaravimutti accantapahāyitāya asamayavimutti. Tāhi samannāgatā “samayavimuttā, asamayavimuttā”ti ca vuccanti. Yāva paṭhamajjhānanibbattanaṃ, tāva kasmā parihāyīti attho? Sābādhattāti sarogattā. Vātapittasemhavasenāti kadāci vātapittavasena, kadāci vātasemhavasena, ubhinnampi sannipātavasena. Anusāyikoti kāyaṃ anugantvā sayito, yāpyāmayabhāvena ṭhitoti attho. Samādhissāti samādhibhāvanāya. Upakārakadhamme utubhojanādike. Pūretunti samodhānetuṃ. Parihāyīti sarīrassa akallabhāvato.

159. "On the mountain's slope" means at the foot of the mountain, in the foothills. Because it is attained from time to time, it is called temporary. Therefore, it is said: "At the very moment of application, he is freed from opposing states." For mundane liberation, since it does not abandon completely, is called temporary liberation. Supramundane liberation, since it abandons completely, is called non-temporary liberation. Those endowed with these are called "temporarily liberated" and "non-temporarily liberated." Until the attainment of the first jhāna, why did he decline? This is the meaning: because of being afflicted—being diseased. Due to imbalances of wind, bile, and phlegm—sometimes due to wind and bile, sometimes due to wind and phlegm, or due to a combination of both. "Anusāyiko" means lying down following the body; the meaning is remaining in a state of manageable illness. "Samādhissa" refers to the cultivation of concentration. "Supportive conditions" include climate, food, and so on. "Pūretuṃ" means to bring together. "Parihāyi" means because of the body's unsuitability.

Āhareyyanti [V 1.0190][M 1.0217] jīvitaharaṇatthāya upaneyyaṃ. Nibaddhā gati hoti kevalaṃ brahmalokūpapattito, na sotāpannādīnaṃ viya paricchinnabhāvena. Tenāha “brahmaloke nibbattatī”ti.

"Āhareyyaṃ" means it should be brought forth for the purpose of taking life. One's destiny is fixed solely for arising in the Brahma world, not in a circumscribed way like that of stream-enterers and others. Therefore it is said, "he is reborn in the Brahma world."

Jalamānāti samuṭṭhitaniyataiddhiyā anaññasādhāraṇaparivārasampattiyā ca sadevake loke jalamānā. Maṃsacakkhu dibbacakkhu dhammacakkhu paññācakkhu samantacakkhūti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Ānubhāvadharāti acinteyyāparimeyyabuddhānubhāvasampannā. Ānubhāvapariyāyopi hi juti-saddo hoti “iddhijutibalavīriyūpapattī”tiādīsu (jā. 2.22.1589, 1595) viya. Anavasesato mānaṃ siyati samucchindatīti aggamaggo mānasaṃ. Tannibbattanā pana arahattassa mānasatā daṭṭhabbā. Sīlādīnīti anuttarasīlādīni. Sikkhamānoti sikkhāni bhāvento attano santāne uppādento. Na cittabhāvanā. Tenāha “sakaraṇīyo”ti. Janeti sattassa kāye, sadevake loketi attho. Vissutāti anaññasādhāraṇehi sīlādiguṇehi vissutā.

"Jalamānā" means shining forth in the world with its devas, with arisen, fixed psychic power and an unparalleled retinue and its accompanying wealth. "Cakkhumā" means possessing five eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Dhamma eye, the wisdom eye, and the universal eye. "Ānubhāvadharā" means endowed with the inconceivable and immeasurable majesty of a Buddha. The term "juti" (splendor) also signifies power, as in passages such as "iddhijutibalavīriyūpapattī" (Jā 2.22.1589, 1595). The supreme path is called `mānasaṃ` because it binds and cuts off conceit without remainder. Furthermore, the quality of being 'of the mind' of arahantship, produced by that, should be understood. "Sīlādīni" refers to unsurpassed virtues and so on. "Sikkhamāno" means developing the trainings, generating them within oneself. This does not refer to mental cultivation alone. Therefore, it is said, "one who has work to do." "Janeti" means it causes to arise in the body of a being; in the world with its devas, this is the meaning. "Vissutā" means renowned for unparalleled qualities such as morality.

Vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvāti uppannaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ paṭicca uppannaattakilamathaṃ anuppādanavasena vikkhambhetvā taṃyeva vedanaṃ pariggahetvā pavattavipassanā vīthimeva otaratīti katvā mūlakammaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ. “Samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyī”ti vatvā tassa pabhedaṃ vibhajitvā idhādhippetaṃ dassetuṃ “samasīsī nāma tividho hotī”tiādimāha. Iriyāpathavasena samasīsī iriyāpathasamasīsī. Esa nayo sesadvayepi.

"Having suppressed the feeling" means: having suppressed the self-torment that arose in dependence on the arisen painful feeling by preventing it from arising, and having grasped that very feeling, insight proceeds along the path—thus, it is called the root meditation subject. Having stated, "Becoming even-headed, one attains final Nibbāna," and having analyzed its divisions, to show what is intended here it is said: "Even-headedness is of three kinds," and so on. Even-headedness by way of posture is even-headedness in posture. The same method applies to the remaining two.

Iriyāpathakopanañcāti iriyāpathehi asamāyogo. Ekappahārenevāti ekavelāyameva. Parinibbānavasenāti anupādisesaparinibbānavasena, na kilesakkhayamattena. Etthāti etesu dvīsu nayesu. Evaṃ sati teneva iriyāpathena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā teneva iriyāpathena, ekasmiṃ antorogeyeva vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ patvā teneva rogena parinibbāyantā khīṇāsavā bahavopi samasīsino eva sambhaveyyuṃ. Tasmā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

"The disturbance of postures" refers to improper engagement with the postures. "At once" means in a single time. "By way of final Nibbāna" refers to final Nibbāna without residue, not merely the destruction of defilements. Here, in these two methods, this being so, if insight is established through a particular posture and arahantship is attained in that very posture, or if insight is established during a single illness and arahantship is attained, many perfected ones passing away from that same illness could be considered 'even-headed.' Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the stated method.

Sīsañcettha [M 1.0218] terasa – palibodhasīsaṃ taṇhā, bandhanasīsaṃ māno, parāmāsasīsaṃ diṭṭhi, vikkhepasīsaṃ uddhaccaṃ, kilesasīsaṃ avijjā, adhimokkhasīsaṃ saddhā, paggahasīsaṃ vīriyaṃ, upaṭṭhānasīsaṃ sati, avikkhepasīsaṃ samādhi, dassanasīsaṃ paññā, pavattisīsaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, gocarasīsaṃ vimokkho, saṅkhārasīsaṃ nirodhoti. Imesu terasasu sīsesu palibodhasīsādīni pavattisīsañca pariyādiyitabbāni, adhimokkhasīsādīni pariyādāyakāni, pariyādāyakaphalaṃ gocarasīsaṃ. Tañhi visayajjhattaṃ phalaṃ vimokkho, pariyādāyakassa maggassa phalassa ca ārammaṇaṃ [V 1.0191] saṅkhārasīsaṃ saṅkhāravivekabhūto nirodhoti pariyādiyitabbānaṃ pariyādāyakaphalārammaṇānaṃ saha viya saṃsiddhaṃ dassanena samasīsibhāvaṃ dassetuṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ terasa sīsāni vuttāni. Idha pana “apubbaṃ acarimaṃ āsavapariyādānañca hoti jīvitapariyādānañcā”ti (pu. pa. 16) vacanato tesu kilesapavattasīsānameva vasena yojanaṃ karonto “ettha ca pavattisīsa”ntiādimāha.

Here, there are thirteen heads—the head of hindrance is craving, the head of bondage is conceit, the head of grasping is wrong view, the head of distraction is restlessness, the head of defilement is ignorance, the head of resolution is faith, the head of effort is energy, the head of establishing is mindfulness, the head of non-distraction is concentration, the head of vision is wisdom, the head of continuity is the life faculty, the head of range is liberation, and the head of formations is cessation. Among these thirteen heads, the heads of hindrance, etc., up to the head of continuity, are to be overcome. The heads of resolution, etc., are the overcomers, and the fruit of the overcomer is the head of range. For that liberation is the fruit, the internal object. The object of the overcomer's path and its fruit is the head of formations—cessation, which is the seclusion from formations. To show the even-headedness by demonstrating the simultaneous accomplishment, as it were, of what is to be overcome, what overcomes, its fruit, and its object, thirteen heads are mentioned in the Paṭisambhidā. Here, however, based on the statement, "There is the unprecedented and non-subsequent destruction of the taints and also the destruction of life," the explanation is given with reference to the heads of defilement and continuity, saying, "Here, the head of continuity," etc.

Tattha pavattisīsaṃ pavattato vuṭṭhahanto maggo cutito uddhaṃ appavattikaraṇavasena yadipi pariyādīyati, yāva pana cuti, tāva pavattisabbhāvato “pavattisīsaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ cuticittaṃ khepetī”ti āha. Kilesapariyādānena pana maggacittena attano anantaraṃ viya nipphādetabbā paccavekkhaṇavārā ca kilesapariyādānasseva vārāti vattabbataṃ arahanti. “Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.78; saṃ. ni. 3.12) vacanato paccavekkhaṇaparisamāpanena kilesapariyādānaṃ samāpitaṃ nāma hoti, taṃ pana parisamāpanaṃ yadi cuticittena hoti, teneva jīvitaparisamāpanañca hotīti imāya vāracutisamatāya kilesapariyādānajīvitapariyādānānaṃ apubbācarimatā veditabbāti dassento “dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ ekato uppādo natthī”tiādimāha. Dvinnaṃ cittānanti cuticittamaggacittānaṃ. Tanti paccavekkhaṇaṃ paripuṇṇajavanacittānaṃ sattakkhattuṃ pavattiyā, aparipuṇṇānaṃ vā pañcakkhattuṃ pavattiyā. Kiñcāpi “eko vā dve vā”ti vuttaṃ yathā “ekaṃ vā dve vā tadārammaṇacittānī”ti, heṭṭhimantena pana dve pavattanti.

Here, although the path, arising from the process-head, is exhausted by way of causing non-arising upwards from cessation, yet since the process exists until cessation, it is said, 'The death consciousness exhausts the process-head, the life faculty.' However, with the exhaustion of defilements by the path consciousness, the reviewing moments that are to be generated immediately after itself are worthy of being called moments of the exhaustion of defilements. From the statement, 'When liberated, there is the knowledge, “I am liberated,”' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.78; Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.12), the exhaustion of defilements is considered completed with the completion of the reviewing. But if that completion occurs with the death consciousness, then the completion of life also occurs with it; thus, showing that the simultaneity of the exhaustion of defilements and the exhaustion of life should be understood by this sameness of the cognitive process and the moment of death, he says, 'There is no simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses,' and so on. 'Two consciousnesses' means the death consciousness and the path consciousness. 'That' means the reviewing, which occurs seven times for complete impulsion consciousnesses, or five times for incomplete ones. Although it is said, 'one or two,' as in 'one or two registration consciousnesses,' still, according to the lower method, two occur.

Uppāṭetvāti [M 1.0219] uddharitvāti attho. Anupādisesenāti anupādisesanibbānena.

Having pulled out means having uprooted. Without residue means with Nibbāna without residue.

Dhūmāyitattanti dhūmassa viya ayitabhāvaṃ pavattiākāraṃ. Dhūmasadisā valāhakā dhūmavalāhakā, timiravalāhakā, ye mahikā “timira”nti vuccanti. Appatiṭṭhitenāti patiṭṭhaṃ alabhantena. Itthambhūtalakkhaṇe etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, anuppattidhammenāti attho. Sati hi uppāde patiṭṭhitaṃ nāma siyā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yadeva tassa viññāṇassa appatiṭṭhānakāraṇaṃ, tadeva parinibbānakāraṇanti vuttaṃ “appatiṭṭhitakāraṇā”ti.

"The state of being smoky" means the state of being, or the manner of occurring, like smoke. Clouds similar to smoke are smoke-clouds, or dark clouds, which mists are called "gloom." "Without settling" means not obtaining a support. This is an instrumental case indicating a characteristic of being in such a state, meaning "by way of the nature of non-arising." For if arising occurs, there would be something called "established." However, in the commentary, it is stated that the very cause of that consciousness's non-settlement is the cause of its complete cessation—hence, "due to the cause of non-settlement."

Sokena phuṭṭhassāti “aphalo vata me vāyāmo jāto”ti sokena abhibhūtassa. Abhassathāti balavasokābhitunnassa satisammosā sithilaṃ gahitā bhassi patitā sā kacchā.

Afflicted by sorrow: for one overwhelmed by sorrow, thinking, "Alas, my effort has been fruitless." It slipped off: for one pierced by intense sorrow, due to confusion of mindfulness, the loosely held loincloth slipped and fell.

Godhikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Godhika Sutta is concluded.

4. Sattavassānubandhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sutta on the Seven-Year Pursuit

160. Yasmā [V 1.0192] kapilavatthuto nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya māro otārāpekkho lokanāthaṃ anubandhituṃ āraddho, tasmā vuttaṃ “pure bodhiyā chabbassānī”ti. Atigahetvāti anugantvā tassa yathāruci paṭipattiṃ anuvatto viya hutvā.

160. Since Māra, seeking an opportunity, began to follow the Lord of the World from the time he left Kapilavatthu, it is therefore said, "six years before enlightenment." Having followed: having gone after him, having become like one conforming to his practice according to his inclination.

Avajjhāyantoti pajjhāyanto. Jito vittaparājito asi nu. Pamāṇātikkantanti garutaraṃ.

Brooding: being dejected. Are you conquered, defeated by wealth? Exceeding measure: very heavy.

Khanitvā ummūletvā. Kāmāsavādīni pajahanto anāsavo.

Having dug up, having uprooted. Abandoning the taints of sensuality and so forth, one is taintless.

Pehīti apehi. Pāragāminoti pāraṅgamanasīlā. Tekāliko ayaṃ gāmi-saddoti āha “yepī”tiādi.

Go away: depart. Those who go to the far shore: those whose nature is to go to the far shore. This word 'gāmi' refers to all three times, thus he said, 'those who...' and so on.

Māravisūkānīti mārakaṇṭakāni kaṇṭakasadisāni mārassa durācārāni. Viruddhasevitāni virodhavasena tāsaṃyeva vevacanāni. Tāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “appamāyū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nibbejanīyāti nibbedadāyikā. Ukkaṇṭhanīyāti ukkaṇṭhavahā.

Māra's darts: Māra's thorns, that is, Māra's evil practices which are like thorns. Hostile practices: these are synonyms for those same things in the sense of opposition. To show them in their true form, 'not gladdening' and so on, is said. Causing revulsion: giving rise to revulsion. Causing distress: bringing about distress.

Vikappavasena [M 1.0220] veditabbo opammaparikappavisayattā tassa kiriyāpadassa. Tenāha “anuparigaccheyyā”ti. Etthāti etasmiṃ medavaṇṇavatthusmiṃ. Mudunti mudumadhurasaṃ vindeyyāma paṭilabheyyāma. Assādoti assādetabbo.

It should be understood in terms of conception, as that verb is within the scope of metaphorical conception. Therefore, he said, 'would go along.' Here: in this object with the appearance of fat. Soft: we might find, we might obtain a soft, sweet taste. A taste: it should be tasted.

Sattavassānubandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on the Seven-Year Pursuit is concluded.

5. Māradhītusuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sutta on Māra's Daughters

161. Cintesīti sokavasiko hutvā cintayi. Gaṇikārahatthiniyoti dīpakakareṇuyo. Ekasataṃ ekasatanti ekasataṃ ekasataṃ paccekaṃ sataṃ satanti attho. Tenāha “ekekaṃ sataṃ sataṃ katvā”ti. Kumārivaṇṇasatanti kumāritthīnaṃ attabhāvānaṃ sataṃ. Tā kira paṭhamaṃ kaññārūpena attānaṃ dassesuṃ. Anupagatapupphānañhi samaññā kaññāti. Puna yathāvuttakumārirūpena upagatapupphā hi kumārī. Puna vadhukārūpena. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “avijātavaṇṇasata”nti[V 1.0193]. Tatiyavāre yuvatirūpena. Vijātā hi itthī anatikkantamajjhimavayā yuvatī. Ettāvatā bālā taruṇī porīti tividhāsu itthīsu purimā dve dassitā, pariyosānavāresu manussajātikānaṃ manussitthiyova ruccantīti tena manussarūpena tā attānaṃ dassesuṃ.

161. He thought: he thought while being under the influence of sorrow. Female elephants like the Gaṇikāra flower: lamp-like female elephants. One hundred each: a hundred for each one, this is the meaning. Hence it is said, 'making one hundred each.' A hundred forms of maidens: a hundred embodiments of maidenly women. It is said that first they displayed themselves in the form of virgins. For the term 'virgin' (kaññā) refers to those who have not yet reached the flowering of youth. Then, in the form of maidens (kumārī) as described, for a maiden is one who has reached the flowering of youth. Then, in the form of a bride (vadhukā). This is referred to by the phrase 'a hundred forms of those who have not given birth.' In the third instance, in the form of a young woman (yuvatī). For a woman who has given birth but not yet passed middle age is a young woman. Thus far, among the three types of women—the girl, the young woman, and the mature woman—the first two have been shown. In the final instances, since human women are pleasing to those of human birth, they displayed themselves in human form.

Atthassa pattinti ekantato hitānuppattiṃ. Hadayassa santinti paramacittupasamaṃ. Kilesasenanti kāmaguṇasaṅkhātaṃ paṭhamaṃ kilesasenaṃ. Sā hi kilesasenā accharāsaṅghātasabhāvāpi paṭipatthayamānā piyāyitabbaicchitabbarūpabhāvato piyarūpasātarūpā nāma attano kiccavasena. Eko ahaṃ jhāyantoti gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya kilesasaṅgaṇikāya ca abhāvato eko asahāyo ahaṃ lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena nijjhāyanto. Anubujjhinti anukkamena maggapaṭipāṭiyā bujjhiṃ paṭibujjhiṃ. Tasmāti yathāvuttavivekasukhasamadhigamanimittaṃ. Akaraṇenāti mittasanthavassa akaraṇena. Sakkhīti sakkhibhāvo.

The attainment of the goal: the complete arising of benefit. The peace of the heart: the supreme pacification of the mind. The army of defilements: the first army of defilements, designated as the cords of sensual pleasure. For this army of defilements, even though it is of the nature of a host of nymphs, because it has a form that is to be cherished and wished for, is called 'pleasing forms, agreeable forms' according to its own function. I, alone, meditating: because of the absence of the company of a group and the company of defilements, I, alone, without a companion, am meditating by means of close contemplation of the characteristics. I understood: I understood, I awakened, gradually, by the sequence of the path. Therefore: as a cause for attaining the bliss of seclusion as stated before. By not doing: by not forming an intimacy with a friend. A witness: the state of being a witness.

Katamena [M 1.0221] vihārenāti jhānasamāpattīnaṃ katamena vihārena. Idha dutiyapadassa attho vissajjanagāthāvaṇṇanāyameva āvi bhavissati. Anāmantena “taṃ puggala”nti sammukhā ṭhitampi bhagavantaṃ asammukhā viya katvā vadati, kathaṃ tvanti attho.

By which abiding: by which abiding in the absorptions and attainments. Here, the meaning of the second line will become clear in the commentary on the reply verse itself. Without addressing him, he says 'that person,' treating the Blessed One, though standing face to face, as if he were not present. The meaning is 'how are you?'

“Avitakkajhāyī”ti vakkhamānattā ayamevettha kāyapassaddhi veditabbāti āha “catutthajjhānena assāsapassāsakāyassa passaddhattā passaddhakāyo”ti. Puññābhisaṅkhārādike kammābhisaṅkhāre. Kāmālayādīnaṃ abhāvato anālayo. Na saratīti na savati. Rāgavasena hi sattā saṃsāramanusavanti. Na thinoti na thinamiddhacitto. Mohavasena hi sattā thinamiddhaṃ āpajjantīti. Diyaḍḍhakilesasahassanti khuddakavatthuvibhaṅge (vibha. 842, 976) āgatesu aṭṭhasu kilesasatesu aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritāni apanetvā sesā paññāsādhikaṃ sataṃ kilesā, te brahmajāle (dī. ni. 1.31) āgatāhi dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīhi saha pañcapaññāsādhikaṃ sattasataṃ hoti; tā ca uppannānuppannabhāvena diguṇitā diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ dasādhikaṃ hoti; taṃ appakaṃ pana ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanupagaṃ na hotīti “diyaḍḍhakilesasahassa”nti vuttaṃ. Itaresaṃ atītādibhāvāmasanato aggahaṇaṃ pahānassa adhippetattā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ (dha. sa. anuṭī. nidānakathāvaṇṇanā) vuttanayena veditabbo. Paṭhamapadenāti “na kuppatī”ti iminā padena. Dutiyenāti “na saratī”ti padena. Tatiyenāti [V 1.0194] “na thino”ti padena. Nīvaraṇappahānena khīṇāsavataṃ dasseti, anavasesato nīvaraṇānaṃ accantappahānaṃ adhippetaṃ.

“One who meditates without thought-conception”: because this will be explained, it should be understood here that this refers to bodily tranquility; thus it is said: “Due to the fourth jhāna, the body of in-and-out breathing is calmed, thus the body is tranquil.” Regarding the volitional formations of merit and so forth, this refers to the volitional formations of action. Because there is no presence of sensual attachments and so forth, one is free from attachment. “Does not flow” means one does not drift. For beings drift through the cycle of existence due to lust. “Is not sluggish” means one’s mind is not affected by sloth and torpor. For beings fall into sloth and torpor due to delusion. “One and a half thousand defilements”: in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 842, 976), among the eight hundred defilements mentioned, excluding eight hundred that are driven by craving, the remaining one hundred and fifty defilements, together with the sixty-two views mentioned in the Brahmajāla (Dī. Ni. 1.31), make seven hundred and fifty-five. These, when doubled by their arisen and unarisen states, become one thousand five hundred and ten. This small amount, whether slightly less or more, is not included in the calculation—hence, it is called “one and a half thousand defilements.” The others are not included because abandonment is intended, which does not take into account their state as past and so forth. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Abhidhamma subcommentary (Dha. Sa. Anuṭī. Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā). By the first phrase: by the phrase “does not become agitated.” By the second: by the phrase “does not flow.” By the third: by the phrase “is not sluggish.” Through the abandonment of the hindrances, he shows the state of one whose taints are destroyed—the complete and final abandonment of the hindrances is intended.

Pañcadvārikakilesoghaṃ tiṇṇoti channaṃ dvārānaṃ vasena pavattanakilesoghaṃ taritvā ṭhito. Kāmoghadiṭṭhoghabhavoghaṭṭhakilesabhāvato “pañcoghaggahaṇena vā pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni veditabbānī”ti āha. Rūparāgādayo visesato na pañcadvārikāti vuttaṃ “chaṭṭhaggahaṇena pañcuddhambhāgiyāni veditabbānī”ti.

“Having crossed the flood of defilements of the five doors” means that one stands having crossed the flood of defilements that proceeds by way of the six doors. Because they are the defilements which are the floods of sensual desire, wrong view, becoming, and ignorance, it is said, “By the taking up of the five floods, the five lower fetters should be understood.” Because lust for form and the others are not specifically related to the five doors, it is said, “By the taking up of the sixth, the five higher fetters should be understood.”
