Maccurājassāti sambandhe sāmivacananti dassento “maccurājassa hatthato”ti āha. Nayamānānanti anādare sāmivacananti katvā vuttaṃ “nayamānesū”ti.

“Of the King of Death”: showing this is the genitive case indicating relationship, he said, “from the hand of the King of Death.” “Of those leading”: taking this as the genitive absolute, signifying disregard, it is said, “while they are leading.”

Ūhaccāti [M 1.0222] buddhaṃ nissāya. “Idamavocā”ti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetvāti etena saṃyuttesu ayaṃ nigamanapāḷi, heṭṭhā anāgatanayattā pana kesuci potthakesu na likhīyatīti dasseti. Daddallamānāti jajjakārassa hi daddakāraṃ katvā niddeso. Tenāha “ativiya jalamānā”ti. Nīharīti tāsaṃ kāyavacīvikāraṃ na manasikaronto tiṇāyapi amaññamānova anapekkheneva nīhari. Phalato bhaṭṭhanti phalasipāṭikato bhaṭṭhaṃ. Kuṇḍatiṇādigacchatūlaṃ poṭakitūlaṃ.

“Having approached” means relying on the Buddha. “This he said”: having concluded the teaching. By this, it is shown that this is the concluding passage in the Saṃyuttas, but it is not written in some books because this method has not been presented before. “Blazing”: this is a description made by forming “daddakāra” from “jajjakāra.” Hence he said, “exceedingly blazing.” “He led them out”: not paying attention to their bodily and verbal contortions, regarding them as less than grass, he led them out with indifference. “Fallen from the fruit” means fallen from the fruit’s pod. Fibre from shrubs such as kuṇḍa grass, and poṭaki cotton.

Māradhītusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Māradhītu Sutta is finished.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Mārasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Māra Saṃyutta is complete.

5. Bhikkhunīsaṃyuttaṃ

5. The Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta

1. Āḷavikāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Āḷavikā Sutta

162. Āḷaviyaṃ [V 1.0195][M 1.0223] jātāti āḷaviyaṃ vijāyitvā saṃvaḍḍhamānā. Tenāha “āḷavinagaratoyeva ca nikkhamma pabbajitā”ti. Dhanaṃ samādapetvāti cetiyassa rājā ekaṃ mukhaṃ, rājaputto ekaṃ, amaccānaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā senāpati ekaṃ, janapadānaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā seṭṭhi ekanti evaṃ catūsu mukhesu navakamme kayiramāne seṭṭhinā gahitamukhe kamme olīyamāne eko upāsako ariyasāvako pañca sakaṭasatāni yojāpetvā janapadaṃ gantvā “yo yaṃ dātuṃ ussahati hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā sattavidharatanaṃ vā haritālaṃ vā manosilaṃ vā, so dhanaṃ detū”ti samādapetvā yathāladdhaṃ paṭhamaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pesetvā “navakammaṃ niṭṭhita”nti sutvā ekakaṃ āgacchantaṃ antarāmagge corā palibundhitvā tato kiñcipi dhanaṃ alabhantā “sace naṃ muñcissāma, anatthaṃ no kareyyā”ti jīvitā voropesuṃ. Anaparādhe ariyasāvake aparādhakā te corā andhā jātā, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ “andhavana”nti paññāyitthāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Khīṇāsavānaṃ yasmā yattha katthaci cittaviveko hotiyeva upadhivivekassa siddhattā. Tasmā “kāyavivekatthinī”ti vuttaṃ.

162. “Born in Āḷavī” means having been born in Āḷavī and growing up there. Hence it is said, “Having gone forth from the city of Āḷavī, she was ordained.” “Having urged the collection of wealth” means: while renovation work was being carried out at the four entrances of the shrine—the king at one entrance, the prince at another, the general, being the chief of the ministers, at a third, and the treasurer, being the chief of the country-folk, at the fourth—the work at the entrance assigned to the treasurer was delayed. A noble lay disciple, having yoked five hundred carts, went to the countryside and urged, “Whoever is able to give gold, silver, the seven kinds of gems, orpiment, or realgar, let them give wealth.” Having sent the first of what was collected to the worksite, and hearing that “the renovation is complete,” he was returning alone when robbers waylaid him on the road. Finding no wealth on him, they thought, “If we release him, he might cause us trouble,” and so they took his life. Those robbers, offenders against an innocent noble disciple, became blind. Therefore, that place came to be known as “Andhavana” (the Blind Forest), as is said in the commentary. For those whose taints are destroyed, mental seclusion occurs wherever they are, since seclusion from the substrates of existence is already accomplished. Hence, it is said, “one who desires bodily seclusion.”

Nissaraṇanti nibbānaṃ sabbasaṅkhatassa nissaṭattā. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇenāti paccavekkhaṇañāṇena, pageva maggaphalañāṇehīti adhippāyo. Nibbānapadanti nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ dhammakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Vinivijjhanaṭṭhenāti hadayaṃ vinividdhena hadayamhi vijjhitvā dukkhuppādanena khandhānaṃ ete pañca kāmā sattisūlasadisā. Adhikuṭṭanabhaṇḍikāti āghātanaghaṭikā.

“Escape” is Nibbāna, because it is an escape from all that is conditioned. “With the knowledge of reviewing”: the meaning is, how much more so with the knowledges of the path and fruition. “The state of Nibbāna” means the portion of Dhamma designated as Nibbāna. “By way of piercing”: because they pierce the heart and produce suffering for the aggregates, these five sensual pleasures are like a spear and a stake. “The executioner’s block” means the executioner’s pot.

Āḷavikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āḷavikā Sutta is finished.

2. Somāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Somā Sutta

163. Ṭhānanti [V 1.0196] issariyaṭṭhānaṃ visayajjhattaṃ. Duppasahaṃ akampiyabhāvattā. Dvaṅgulapaññāyāti ettha itthiyo hi daharakumārikākālato paṭṭhāya [M 1.0224] odanapacanavidhiṃ anutiṭṭhantiyo ukkhaliyaṃ udakaṃ tāpetvā taṇḍule pakkhipitvā attano buddhiyā tesaṃ pākakālappamāṇaṃ paricchindituṃ tāni dabbiyā uddharitvāpi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānaggahaṇamattena pakkāpakkabhāvaṃ jānituṃ na sakkonti, kevalaṃ pana dvīhi aṅgulīhi uppīḷitakāle eva jānanti, tasmā dvīhaṅgulikehi dubbalapaññattā “dvaṅgulapaññā”ti vuccanti. Phalasamāpattiñāṇappavattikittanena catūsu saccesu asammohavihāro dīpito hotīti āha “ñāṇamhi vattamānamhīti phalasamāpattiñāṇe pavattamāne”ti. Vipassantassāti asammohapaṭivedhato visesena passantassa khandhapañcakameva saccābhisamayato pubbabhāge vipassantassa. Aññaṃ vāti itthipurisato aññaṃ vā kiñci vatthuṃ. “Ahaṃ asmī”ti mānadiṭṭhigāhataṇhāgāhavasena gahitavatthusmiṃ yevāti āha “ahaṃ asmīti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasenā”ti.

163. “Position” refers to a position of authority, an internal domain; it is “difficult to assail” because it is unshakeable. “With two-finger wisdom”: Here, women, from the time they are young girls, while observing the method of cooking rice, heat water in a pot and add the rice grains. Although they try to determine the cooking time by their own intelligence, even when they take the grains out with a ladle, they cannot discern whether they are cooked or uncooked merely by observing their color and shape. They only know when the grains are pressed between two fingers. Therefore, because of their weak wisdom dependent on two fingers, they are called “those with two-finger wisdom.” By mentioning the arising of the knowledge of fruition-attainment, the abiding in non-delusion regarding the four truths is illuminated, thus it is said: “when knowledge is present” refers to “when the knowledge of fruition-attainment is arising.” “For one who sees clearly”: this refers to one who sees distinctly through the penetration of non-delusion, one practicing insight on the five aggregates in the preliminary stage before the realization of the truths. “Or anything else” refers to any object apart from male or female. “‘I am’”: this refers only to an object grasped by way of the grasp of craving, conceit, and wrong view, hence it is said, “‘I am’ by way of craving, conceit, and wrong view.”

Somāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Somā Sutta is finished.

3. Kisāgotamīsuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta

164. “Kisāgotamī”ti ettha kā panāyaṃ kisāgotamī, kissa ayaṃ bhikkhunī hutvā samaṇadhammaṃ matthakaṃ pāpesīti tamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “pubbe kirā”tiādimāraddhaṃ. Aṅgārāvāti addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇaaṅgārā eva jātā. Dārusākanti addhamāsakena dāruṃ sākañca āharissāmīti antarāpaṇe antaravīthiṃ gatā.

164. “Kisāgotamī”: In this context, who is this Kisāgotamī, and why did this bhikkhunī bring the ascetic’s life to its culmination? To clarify this matter, the passage begins with “formerly, it is said.” “Like embers”: she was born with a complexion like embers, the color of burnt bricks. “Firewood and greens”: thinking, “I will bring firewood and greens with half a māsaka,” she went to an inner street in the market.

Siddhatthakanti sāsapaṃ. Sālāyanti anāthasālāyaṃ. Khuraggeyevāti khurasikhe eva, kesorohanakkhaṇe evāti attho.

“Mustard seed” means sāsapa. “In the hall” means in the charity hall. “Right on the razor’s edge” means right on the blade of the razor; that is, at the very moment of the lowering of the hair.

Ekamāsīti ettha ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Saṃhitāvasena ca purimapade vā rassattaṃ. Parapade vā dīghattanti āha “ekā āsī”ti. Bhāvanapuṃsakametaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”tiādīsu viya. Puttamaraṇaṃ antaṃ atītaṃ idāni puttamaraṇassa abhāvato. Tenevāha “puttamaraṇaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Purisaṃ gavesitunti yathā mayhaṃ purisagavesanā nāma sabbaso natthi, tathā eva puttagavesanāpi natthi, tasmā me puttamaraṇaṃ etadantaṃ, sabbesu khandhādīsu bhavādīsu ca taṇhānandiyā [V 1.0197] abhāvakathanena sabbasattesu taṇhā sabbaso [M 1.0225] visositā, tassāyeva kārakaavijjākkhandho padālitoti attano nikkilesataṃ pavedentī therī sīhanādaṃ nadīti.

Here, the letter 'ma' serves as a sandhi connector of words. Due to euphonic combination, there may be shortening in the preceding word or lengthening in the following word; hence it is said, 'ekā āsī.' This is a neuter form by usage, as in phrases like 'sat down to one side' and so on. The death of a son is an end that is past, for now the death of a son is absent. Therefore, she says, 'There is no such thing as the death of a son.' Just as there is absolutely no seeking of a man for me, so too there is no seeking of a son. Thus, for me, the death of a son is terminated at this very point. By stating the absence of delight in craving for all aggregates, existences, and so on, craving for all beings is entirely dried up. The aggregate of ignorance, its very cause, is split asunder—thus, the elder nun, proclaiming her own stainlessness, roars a lion's roar.

Kisāgotamīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta is concluded.

4. Vijayāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vijayā Sutta

165. Pañca aṅgāni etassāti pañcaṅgaṃ, pañcaṅgameva pañcaṅgikaṃ, tena pañcaṅgikena. Ātatantiādīsu ātataṃ nāma cammapariyonaddhesu bheriādīsu ekatalaṃ tūriyaṃ. Vitataṃ nāma ubhayatalaṃ. Ātatavitataṃ nāma tantibaddhavīṇādi. Susiraṃ vaṃsādi. Ghanaṃ sammādi. Tataādivisesopi ātatamevāti “cammapariyonaddhesū”ti visesanaṃ. Ekatalaṃ kumbhathūṇadaddarādi. Ubhayatalaṃ bherimudiṅgādi. Cammapariyonaddhaṃ sesaṃ tantibaddhaṃ sabbaṃ ātatavitataṃ nāma, gomukhīādīnampi ettheva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Vaṃsādīti ādisaddena saṅkhasiṅgānampi saṅgaho. Sammatāḷa-kaṃsatāḷa-silātāḷa-salākatāḷādi sammādi nāma. Tattha sammatāḷaṃ nāma daṇḍamayatāḷaṃ, kaṃsamayatāḷaṃ kaṃsatāḷaṃ, silāyaṃ ayopattena ca tāḷanatāḷaṃ. Sabbe kāmaguṇe. Uggharitapaggharitaṭṭhenāti upari gharaṇena ca vissandanena ca. Evanti “iminā pūtikāyenā”ti. Arūpaṭṭhāyinoti sattādhiṭṭhānenāyaṃ dhammadesanāti āha “sabbatthāti sabbesu rūpārūpabhavesū”ti. Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ rūpārūpabhavānaṃ gahitattā. Bhavabhāvasāmaññato, tadadhiṭṭhānato gahite kāmabhave. Avijjātamo vihato aggamaggena samugghātitattā.

165. Five factors belong to this, hence it is 'five-factored'; the five-factored itself is 'pañcaṅgika,' and by that 'pañcaṅgika.' In the terms like 'ātata,' 'ātata' refers to single-headed drums like the 'bheri' and other instruments covered with hide. 'Vitata' refers to double-headed ones. 'Ātatavitata' refers to stringed instruments like the lute. 'Susira' refers to bamboo flutes and the like. 'Ghana' refers to cymbals and similar instruments. Even though the distinction of 'tata' and others exists, 'ātata' itself is meant; thus the specification 'covered with hide.' Single-headed instruments include pot-drums, tambourines, and so forth. Double-headed instruments include drums like the 'bheri' and 'mudiṅga,' and so forth. The remaining hide-covered instruments and all stringed instruments are called 'ātata-vitata'; instruments like the 'gomukhī' should also be understood as included here. The term 'vaṃsādi' (bamboo flutes, etc.) includes conch shells and horns by means of the word 'ādi.' 'Sammādi' refers to cymbals such as 'sammatāḷa,' 'kaṃsatāḷa,' 'silātāḷa,' and 'salākatāḷa.' Among these, 'sammatāḷa' is a cymbal made of wood; 'kaṃsatāḷa' is a cymbal made of bronze; and 'silātāḷa' is a cymbal for striking on a stone and with an iron plate. 'All sensual pleasures.' The phrase 'uggharitapaggharitaṭṭhena' means 'by pouring from above and by trickling down.' The word 'evaṃ' (thus) means 'with this foul body.' The term 'arūpaṭṭhāyino' (established in the formless) is explained thus: this Dhamma teaching is established on the basis of beings; thus it says, 'everywhere means in all realms of form and formlessness.' Because these two, the form and formless realms, are taken up, and by the commonality of the state of existence and because it is their basis, the realm of sensual desire is also taken up. The darkness of ignorance is destroyed because it has been uprooted by the supreme path.

Vijayāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vijayā Sutta is concluded.

5. Uppalavaṇṇāsuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Uppalavaṇṇā Sutta

166. Aggato [M 1.0226] paṭṭhāyāti sabbaaggato pabhuti yāva mūlā antarāyuttaṃ sammadeva pupphitaṃ sālarukkhaṃ. Vaṇṇadhātusīsena vaṇṇadhātusampannaṃ dutiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ vadatīti āha “tayā sadisā aññā bhikkhunī natthī”ti. Pakhumasīsena akkhibhaṇḍaṃ vuccatīti āha “pakhumantarikāyanti dvinnaṃ akkhīnaṃ majjhe”ti. Nāsavaṃseti nāsavaṃsamūle. “Na passasī”ti vatvā adassane kāraṇaṃ āha “vasībhūtamhī”ti.

166. 'From the top' (aggato paṭṭhāya) means from the very top down to the root, the sal tree is fully in bloom, connected without interruption. With the phrase 'vaṇṇadhātusīsena' (by the heading 'color-element'), it refers to the second bhikkhunī, who is endowed with the color element, saying, 'There is no other bhikkhunī like you.' The term 'pakhumasīsa' refers to the organ of the eye; thus it says, 'pakhumantarikāyaṃ' means 'between the two eyes.' 'Nāsavaṃse' means at the root of the nose. Having said, 'You do not see,' the reason for not seeing is stated: 'because I have mastery (vasībhūtamhi).'

Uppalavaṇṇāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Uppalavaṇṇā Sutta is concluded.

6. Cālāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Cālā Sutta

167. Idanti [V 1.0198] idaṃ dassanaṃ. Gāhāpesīti samādāpesi “jātiṃ mā rocā”ti. Aññanti bandhavadhato aññaṃ chedanādiṃ. Nivesesīti pavisāpesi.

167. 'Idaṃ' (this) means this sight. 'Gāhāpesi' (she made to grasp) means she exhorted, saying, 'Do not approve of birth.' 'Aññaṃ' (other) means other than killing relatives, such as cutting off and so forth. 'Nivesesi' (she made to enter) means she caused to enter.

Cālāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cālā Sutta is concluded.

7. Upacālāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Upacālā Sutta

168. Punappunaṃ…pe… āgacchanti kāraṇassa asamūhatattā. Santāpito kilesasantāpehi. Agatīti avisayo.

168. 'Punappunaṃ…pe… āgacchanti' (again and again… they come back) because the cause has not been eradicated. 'Santāpito' (afflicted) means afflicted by the heat of the defilements. 'Agati' (no resort) means it is not their domain.

Upacālāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Upacālā Sutta is concluded.

8. Sīsupacālāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sīsupacālā Sutta

169. Samaṇisadisāti samaṇaliṅgassa dhāraṇena samaṇisadisā, kassacipi pāsaṇḍassa aruccanato monamaggassa appaṭipajjanato tava samaṇibhāvaṃ nānupassāmīti adhippāyo. Pāsaṃ ḍentīti pāsaṃ sajjenti, yathā [M 1.0227] tattha diṭṭhipāse sattānaṃ cittaṃ paṭimukkaṃ hoti, evaṃ sajjentīti attho. Tathābhūtā ca te sattānaṃ citte khittā viya hontīti āha “cittesu diṭṭhipāsaṃ khipantīti attho”ti. Pāse mocetīti diṭṭhipāse sattānaṃ cittasantānato nīharati dhammasudhammatāya. Tasmāti pāsamocanato pāsaṇḍoti na vuccati. “Ito bahiddhāyeva pāsaṇḍā hontī”ti vuttassa atthassa nigamanaṃ. Evañca katvā sabbepi bāhirakasamaye sandhāya cūḷasīhanādasutte “channavuti pāsaṇḍā”ti vuttaṃ. Pasīdantīti diṭṭhipaṅke saṃsārapaṅke ca pakārehi agādhā osīdanti.

169. 'Samaṇisadisā' (like a nun) means resembling a nun by wearing the outward signs of an ascetic. The meaning is: 'Because of your disapproval of any heretic and not practicing the path of silence, I do not perceive your state as a nun.' 'Pāsaṃ ḍenti' (they set snares) means they prepare snares; just as the minds of beings are ensnared in the snares of views, so they prepare them—this is the meaning. And being such, they are as if cast into the minds of beings; hence it is said, 'They cast the snares of views into minds—this is the meaning.' 'Pāse moceti' (he frees from snares) means he removes the snares of views from the mental continuum of beings through the excellence of the true Dhamma. Therefore, because of freeing from snares, one is not called a heretic. This is the conclusion of the meaning of the statement, 'Heretics exist only outside of this.' And thus, with reference to all external schools, it is said in the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, 'ninety-six heretics.' 'Pasīdanti' (they sink) means they sink down deeply and in various ways into the bottomless mire of views and the mire of saṃsāra.

Abhibhavitvāti sabbasaṃkilesappahānena abhibhuyya atikkamitvā. Ajitoti ajini avijayattā. Sabbāni akusalakammāni kusalakammāni ca khīṇāni etthāti sabbakammakkhayo, arahattaṃ. Upadhayo sammadeva khīyanti etthāti upadhisaṅkhayo, nibbānaṃ.

'Abhibhavitvā' (having overcome) means having overcome and transcended by abandoning all defilements. 'Ajito' (unconquered) means unconquered due to not being defeated. 'Sabbakammakkhayo' is where all unwholesome and wholesome kammas are destroyed; this is arahantship. 'Upadhisaṅkhayo' is where the substrates are completely destroyed; this is Nibbāna.

Sīsupacālāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sīsupacālā Sutta is concluded.

9. Selāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Selā Sutta

170. Kenidaṃ [V 1.0199] pakataṃ bimbanti idaṃ attabhāvasaññitaṃ bimbaṃ brahmā-visaṇupurisa-pajāpatiādīsu kena kataṃ nimmitaṃ nibbattitanti kattabbamohaṃ nāma kātukāmo pucchati. Aghanti aghavatthu. Tenāha “dukkhapatiṭṭhānattā”ti. Hetunirodhenāti taṇhāsaṅkhatassa hetuno anuppādanirodhena. Paccayavekallenāti tadavasiṭṭhakilesābhisaṅkhārādipaccayassa vekallabhāvena, apaccayabhāvūpagamanenāti attho.

170. 'By whom was this image made?' (Kenidaṃ pakataṃ bimbaṃ) —thus, desiring to create the delusion of a doer, one asks, 'by whom was this image, designated as a self, made, fashioned, produced among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Prajāpati, and so forth?' 'Agha' (suffering) means the basis of suffering. Therefore, he said, 'because it is the foundation of suffering (dukkhapatiṭṭhānattā).' 'Hetunirodhena' (by the cessation of the cause) means through the non-arising and cessation of the cause designated as craving. 'Paccayavekallena' (due to the lack of conditions) means due to the state of lacking the remaining conditions such as defilements and volitional formations; that is, by approaching the state of being without conditions. This is the meaning.

Selāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Selā Sutta is concluded.

10. Vajirāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Vajirā Sutta

171. Suddhasaṅkhārapuñjeti rūpārūpavibhāge kilesasaṅkhārasamūhe. Paramatthatoti sabhāvena. Yathā na hi sattasaññitasaṅkhārapuñjo nāma paramatthato [M 1.0228] upalabbhati, evaṃ tabbinimutto nāma koci na upalabbhati avijjamānattā. Vijjamānesūti yathāpaccayasampattiyā labbhamānesu. Tenākārenāti itthipurisādiākārena. Vavatthitesūti paccekaṃ paccayavisesasamuṭṭhitaṃ saṇṭhānavisesaṃ upādāya “puriso hatthī asso”tiādinā abhisaṅgato pavattesu. Sammutīti sattoti vohāro. Tenāha “samaññāmattamevā”ti. Pañcakkhandhadukkhanti pañcakkhandhasaññitaṃ dukkhaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ bhagavatā “saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (dī. ni. 2.387; ma. ni. 1.120; 3.373; vibha. 202) añño neva sambhoti yathāvuttadukkhato aññassa saṅkhatadhammassa abhāvato. Na nirujjhatīti tato aññaṃ na nirujjhati, uppādato hoti nirodhoti.

171. 'Suddhasaṅkhārapuñje' (in a heap of pure formations) means in the mass of formations of defilements, in the division of form and formless. 'Paramatthato' (in the ultimate sense) means by its intrinsic nature. Just as a heap of formations designated as a 'being' is not found in the ultimate sense, so too, anything apart from that is not found, due to its non-existence. 'Vijjamānesu' (in existing things) means in things that are found through the fulfillment of their respective conditions. 'Tenākārena' (by that form) means by a form such as male or female. 'Vavatthitesu' (in what is established) means in things that proceed from convention, such as 'a man, an elephant, a horse,' based on a particular configuration that has arisen from specific individual conditions. 'Sammuti' (convention) means the designation 'being.' Therefore, it is said: 'It is merely a designation.' 'Pañcakkhandhadukkhaṃ' (the suffering of the five aggregates) means the suffering designated as the five aggregates. For this was stated by the Blessed One: 'In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.' No other arises apart from the aforesaid suffering, since there is no other conditioned phenomenon. 'Na nirujjhati' (it does not cease) means nothing other than that ceases; from arising, there is cessation.

Vajirāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vajirā Sutta is concluded.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya

Bhikkhunīsaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of Hidden Meanings in the Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta is concluded.

6. Brahmasaṃyuttaṃ

6. The Brahma Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Brahmāyācanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Brahmā's Invitation Sutta

172. Parivitakko [V 1.0200][M 1.0229] udapādīti dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇahetuko dhammadesanāya appossukko uppajji. Ayaṃ parivitakko kasmā udapādi? Kattha ca udapādīti taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “sabbabuddhāna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha āciṇṇasamāciṇṇoti ācarito ceva ācarantehi ca sammadeva ācaritoti attho. Etena ayaṃ parivitakko sabbabuddhānaṃ paṭhamābhisambodhiyaṃ uppajjatevāti ayamettha dhammatāti dasseti. Tattha aṭṭhame sattāheti idaṃ sattamasattāhato paraṃ sattāhabbhantare uppannattā vuttaṃ, na pana itaresaṃ viya aṭṭhamassa nāma sattāhassa pavattitassa sabbhāvā. Sapaccaggheti mahagghe. “Paccagghe”ti vā pāṭho, abhinaveti attho. Selamayeti muggavaṇṇasilāmaye.

172. ‘A thought arose’ means that a disinclination to teach the Dhamma arose, caused by reflection on the profundity of the Dhamma. Why did this thought arise? And where did it arise? To clarify all this, the passage beginning with ‘for all Buddhas’ was commenced. Therein, ‘practiced and well-practiced’ means both practiced, and rightly practiced by those who practice. By this it is shown that this thought indeed arises for all Buddhas at the time of their first supreme enlightenment—this is the nature of things here. Therein, the phrase ‘in the eighth week’ is said because this arose within the week following the seventh week, not because an actual eighth week occurred as with the others. ‘Of great value’ means very costly. Alternatively, the reading is ‘new,’ the meaning of which is fresh. ‘Made of rock’ means made of stone the color of a green gram.

Paṭividdhoti sayambhuñāṇena “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā paṭimukhaṃ nibbijjhanavasena patto, yāthāvato avabuddhoti attho. Dhammoti catusaccadhammo tabbinimuttassa paṭivijjhitabbadhammassa abhāvato. Gambhīroti mahāsamuddo viya makasatuṇḍasūciyā aññatra samupacitaparipakkañāṇasambhārehi aññesaṃ ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho. Tenāha “uttānapaṭikkhepavacanameta”nti. Yo alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho, so ogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya sarūpato visesato ca passituṃ na sakkāti āha “gambhīrattāva duddaso”ti. Dukkhena daṭṭhabboti kicchena kenaci kadācideva daṭṭhabbo. Yaṃ pana daṭṭhumeva na sakkā, tassa ogāhetvā anu anu bujjhanako kadāci natthīti āha “duddasattāva duranubodho”ti. Dukkhena avabujjhitabbo avabodhassa dukkarabhāvato. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1115) suttapadaṃ vattabbaṃ. Santārammaṇatāya vā santo. Nibbutasabbapariḷāhatāya nibbuto. Attano paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nītoti [M 1.0230] vā paṇīto[V 1.0201]. Atittikaraṇaṭṭhena atappako sādurasabhojanaṃ viya. Tattha ca nirodhasaccaṃ santaṃ ārammaṇanti santārammaṇaṃ, maggasaccaṃ santaṃ santārammaṇañcāti santārammaṇaṃ, anupasantasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ saṅkhārānañca abhāvato santo. Nibbutasabbapariḷāhattā nibbuto. Santapaṇītabhāveneva tadatthāya asecanakatāya atappakatā daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha “idaṃ dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vutta”nti. Uttamañāṇassa visayattā na takkena avacaritabbo. Tato eva nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya saṇhasukhumasabhāvattā ca nipuṇo. Bālānaṃ avisayattā yathāvuttehi paṇḍitehi eva veditabboti paṇḍitavedanīyo. Ālīyanti abhiramitabbaṭṭhena sevīyantīti ālayā, pañca kāmaguṇā. Ālayanti allīyanti abhiramaṇavasena sevantīti ālayā, taṇhāvicaritāni. Ramantīti ratiṃ vindanti kīḷanti laḷanti. Ālayaratāti ālayaniratā.

‘Penetrated’ means attained by way of direct penetration through the knowledge of a self-enlightened one, as in ‘this is suffering,’ and so forth; the meaning is that it is understood as it truly is. The ‘Dhamma’ is the Dhamma of the Four Truths, since there is no other Dhamma to be penetrated apart from it. It is ‘deep’ like the great ocean, whose footing is unattainable by the knowledge of others—except by those with the requisites of accumulated and matured knowledge. Therefore it is said, ‘this is a statement rejecting the superficial.’ Because its footing is unattainable, it cannot be plunged into, and thus it cannot be seen in its own nature and in its specifics; hence it is said, ‘due to its depth, it is hard to see.’ ‘To be seen with difficulty’ means to be seen only with great effort, by a certain person, on a rare occasion. But as for that which cannot be seen at all, there is never anyone who awakens to it bit by bit after having plunged into it; hence it is said, ‘because it is hard to see, it is hard to comprehend.’ It is ‘to be comprehended with difficulty’ because comprehension is arduous. In this context, the sutta passage should be cited: ‘What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more difficult or harder to attain?’ (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1115). It is ‘peaceful’ because it has a peaceful object. It is ‘quenched’ because all fevers are extinguished. It is ‘excellent’ because it is brought to a state of preeminence by its own conditions. It is ‘never-satiating’ in the sense that one does not tire of it, like a delicious meal. And therein, the truth of cessation is a peaceful object, thus it is ‘that which has a peaceful object’; the truth of the path is peaceful and has a peaceful object, thus it is ‘that which has a peaceful object.’ It is ‘peaceful’ due to the absence of defilements and formations, which are unpeaceful in nature. It is ‘quenched’ because all fevers are extinguished. Precisely because of its peaceful and excellent nature, its quality of being never-satiating and unadulterated should be understood as being for that purpose. Hence it is said, ‘these two are spoken of with reference to the supramundane alone.’ It is not to be fathomed by reasoning because it is the domain of supreme knowledge. For that very reason, and because it is the sphere of refined knowledge and has a fine and delicate nature, it is ‘subtle.’ It is ‘to be known by the wise’ because it is not the domain of fools and is to be known only by the wise as described. ‘Attachments’ (ālayā) are so called because they are clung to (ālīyanti), that is, they are resorted to in the sense of being something to be delighted in; these are the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Attachments’ (ālayā) are so called because they cling (ālayanti), that is, they adhere and resort to by way of delighting; these are the activities of craving. ‘They delight’ (ramanti) means they find enjoyment, they play, they sport. ‘Delighting in attachments’ means devoted to attachments.

Ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāti ṭhānasaddaṃ sandhāya, atthako pana ṭhānanti ca paṭiccasamuppādo eva adhippeto. Tiṭṭhati phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti hi ṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayabhūtā avijjādayo. Imesaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, avijjādayo. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā yathā “devo eva devatā”. Idappaccayānaṃ vā avijjādīnaṃ attano phalaṃ pati paccayabhāvo uppādanasamatthatā idappaccayatā. Tena paramatthapaccayalakkhaṇo paṭiccasamuppādo dassito hoti. Paṭicca samuppajjati phalaṃ etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Padadvayenapi dhammānaṃ paccayaṭṭho eva vibhāvito. Tenāha “saṅkhārādipaccayānaṃ etaṃ adhivacana”nti. Saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayā saṅkhārādipaccayā, avijjādayo. Tesaṃ saṅkhārādipaccayānaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.572-573) vuttanayena veditabbo. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbanti sabbasaṅkhārasamathādiabhidheyyaṃ sabbaṃ atthato nibbānameva. Idāni assa nibbānabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti nibbānaṃ. Āgammāti paṭicca ariyamaggassa ārammaṇapaccayahetu. Sammantīti paṭippassaddhivūpasamavasena sammanti. Tathā santā ca savisesaṃ upasantā nāma hontīti āha “vūpasammantī”ti. Etena [M 1.0231] sabbe saṅkhārā sammanti etthāti sabbasaṅkhārasamatho, nibbānanti dasseti. Sabbasaṅkhāravisaṃyutte hi nibbāne sabbasaṅkhāravūpasamapariyāyo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto eva. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

With reference to the term ‘ṭhāna’ means with reference to the word ‘ṭhāna,’ but the intended meaning of ‘ṭhāna’ is dependent origination itself. For ‘ṭhāna’ is that on which the fruit stands by way of its dependent occurrence, namely, ignorance and other factors that serve as conditions for formations and so on. The conditions for these formations and so on are specific conditions (idappaccayā), namely, ignorance and other factors. Specific conditionality (idappaccayatā) is the specific conditions themselves, just as ‘devatā’ is ‘deva.’ Or, specific conditionality (idappaccayatā) is the state of being a condition for their own fruit, the capacity to produce, on the part of the specific conditions, namely ignorance and so on. By this, dependent origination is shown to have the characteristic of an ultimate condition. Dependent origination is so called because from this the fruit arises dependently. Even by these two words, the conditional nature of phenomena is clearly explained. Therefore, it is said: ‘This is a designation for the conditions of formations, etc.’ The conditions of formations, etc., are the ‘conditions of formations, etc.,’ namely, ignorance and so on. Of those conditions of formations, etc.... This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. Mahāṭī. 2.572–573). ‘The stilling of all formations,’ and so forth—all that is denoted by ‘the stilling of all formations,’ and so forth—is in meaning Nibbāna itself. Now, to show its nature as Nibbāna, it is said: ‘Because...’ and so on. That is Nibbāna. ‘Āgamma’ means ‘relying on,’ because it is the object-condition for the noble path. ‘Sammanti’ means they come to rest by way of pacification and subsiding. And being thus stilled, they are called ‘especially stilled’; thus it is said ‘they are fully stilled’ (vūpasammanti). By this, it is shown that ‘the stilling of all formations’ is Nibbāna, for ‘all formations come to rest therein.’ Indeed, in Nibbāna, which is disjoined from all formations, the aspect of the subsiding of all formations is stated in the commentary. The same method applies to the remaining phrases.

Upadhīyati ettha dukkhanti upadhi, khandhādayo. Paṭinissaṭṭhāti samucchedavasena pariccattā honti. Sabbā taṇhāti aṭṭhasatappabhedā sabbāpi taṇhā. Sabbe kilesarāgāti kāmarāgarūparāgādibhedā sabbepi kilesabhūtā rāgā, sabbepi vā kilesā idha “kilesarāgā”ti adhippetā, na lobhavisesā eva cittassa pariḷāhabhāvāpādanato. Yathāha “rattampi cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ[V 1.0202], duṭṭhampi cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ, mūḷhampi cittaṃ vipariṇata”nti (pārā. 271). Virajjantīti palujjanti vikkhambhanato sabbaso tena visaṃyuttabhāvato. Sabbaṃ dukkhanti jarāmaraṇādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ. Bhavena bhavanti tena tena bhavena bhavantaraṃ bhavanikantibhāvena saṃsibbati. Phalena vā saddhiṃ kammaṃ sataṇhasseva āyatiṃ punabbhavabhāvato. Tato vānato nikkhantaṃ tattha tassa sabbaso abhāvato. Ciranisajjācirabhāsanehi piṭṭhiāgilāyanatālugalasosādivasena kāyakilamatho ceva kāyavihesā ca veditabbā. Sā ca kho desanāya atthamajānantānaṃ apaṭipajjantānañca vasena, jānantānaṃ pana paṭipajjantānañca desanāya kāyaparissamopi satthu aparissamoyeva. Tenāha bhagavā – “na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vihesesī”ti (udā. 10). Tenevāha – “yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assā”ti. Ubhayanti cittakilamatho cittavihesā cāti ubhayampetaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi bodhimūle eva samucchinnattā. Anubrūhanaṃ sampiṇḍanaṃ. Soti apissūti nipāto. Vuddhippattā vā acchariyā anacchariyā, vuddhiatthopi hi -kāro hoti yathā “asekkhā dhammā”ti. Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ cattāri ca asaṅkhyeyyāni sadevakassa lokassa dhammasaṃvibhāgakaraṇatthameva pāramiyo pūretvā idāni samadhigatadhammarajjassa tattha appossukkatāpattidīpanatā gāthatthassa ca acchariyatā tassa vuddhippattīti veditabbaṃ. Atthadvārena hi gāthānaṃ anacchariyatā. Gocarā ahesunti upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Upaṭṭhānañca vitakketabbatāvāti āha “parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti.

Here, 'upadhi' (that in which suffering is deposited) refers to the aggregates and so forth. 'Paṭinissaṭṭhā' (abandoned) means they have been relinquished through complete eradication. 'Sabbā taṇhā' (all craving) refers to all craving in its one-hundred-and-eightfold variety. 'Sabbe kilesarāgā' (all defilements of lust) means all lusts that are defilements, such as sensual lust and form lust; or, all defilements are intended here by 'kilesarāgā,' not merely a specific greed, because it produces mental agitation. As it is said: 'The mind is corrupted by passion, corrupted by hatred, corrupted by delusion' (Pārā. 271). 'Virajjanti' (they fade away) means they are destroyed through suppression, or through being completely dissociated from them. 'Sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ' (all suffering) refers to all the suffering of the cycle of existence, such as aging and death. 'Bhavena bhavanti' (they come into being through existence) means that through delighting in becoming, one is bound to a future existence; or, for one with craving, action together with its fruit leads to future rebirth. 'Tato vānato nikkhantaṃ' (departed from that craving) means departed from it, due to its total absence there. From prolonged sitting and prolonged speaking, bodily fatigue and bodily distress, such as back pain and dryness of the palate and throat, are to be understood. And that fatigue is in the case of teaching those who do not understand the meaning or do not practice; but for those who understand and practice, even the Teacher's bodily exertion is no exertion at all. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'No dispute over the Dhamma has troubled me' (Udā. 10). For that reason, he also said: 'That which is teaching those who do not understand, that would be fatigue for me.' 'Ubhayanti' (both) refers to mental fatigue and mental distress—both of these are absent in the Buddhas because they were severed at the root of enlightenment. 'Anubrūhanaṃ' means a summary. 'So' is a particle, as is 'apissu'. 'Vuddhippattā vā acchariyā anacchariyā' means 'having attained growth, whether astonishing or not'; for the suffix '-kāra' can also have the meaning of 'growth', as in 'asekkhā dhammā' (the qualities of a non-learner). For a hundred thousand eons and four incalculable periods, he fulfilled the perfections for the sole purpose of sharing the Dhamma with the world, including the gods. That for him, who has now attained the sovereignty of the Dhamma, there was the revealing of an arising of little enthusiasm, and that the meaning of the verse is astonishing, should be understood as his attainment of growth. For, through their meaning, the verses are not astonishing. 'Gocarā ahesuṃ' (they became his domain) means they arose in his mind. And since arising is the state of being something to be reflected upon, it is said: 'They attained the state of being worthy of reflection.'

Yadi [M 1.0232] sukhāpaṭipadāva, kathaṃ kicchatāti āha “pāramīpūraṇakāle panā”tiādi. Evamādīni duppariccajāni dentassa. Ha-iti vā byattanti etasmiṃ atthe nipāto. “Ekaṃsatthe”ti keci. Ha byattaṃ, ekaṃsena vā alaṃ nippayojanaṃ evaṃ kicchena adhigatassa pakāsituṃ desitunti yojanā. Halanti vā alanti iminā samānatthapadaṃ “halanti vadāmī”tiādīsu viya. Rāgadosaphuṭṭhehīti phuṭṭhavisena viya sappena rāgena dosena ca phuṭṭhehi abhibhūtehi. Rāgadosānugatehīti rāgadosehi anubandhehi.

If it is the pleasant practice, how is it difficult? To this it is said, 'But at the time of fulfilling the perfections,' and so on, while giving such things that are difficult to relinquish. The particle 'ha' is in the sense of 'byattaṃ' (clearly). Some say it is in the sense of 'certainty'. The connection is: 'Ha' (clearly, or certainly), enough! It is useless to teach and declare what has been attained with such difficulty. Or, 'halaṃ' is a word with the same meaning as 'alaṃ', as in phrases like 'I say halaṃ,' and so on. 'Rāgadosaphuṭṭhehi' (struck by lust and hatred) means overwhelmed by lust and hatred, as if struck by the poison of a snake. 'Rāgadosānugatehi' (accompanied by lust and hatred) means pursued by lust and hatred.

Niccādīnanti niccādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vipallāsānaṃ. Evaṃgatanti evaṃ aniccantiādinā ākārena pavattaṃ bujjhitabbaṃ. Kāmarāgarattā ca bhavarāgarattā ca nīvaraṇehi nivutacittatāya diṭṭhirāgarattā viparītābhinivesena na dakkhanti yāthāvato dhammaṃ na paṭivijjhissanti. Sabhāvenāti aviparītasabhāvena. Evaṃ gāhāpetunti aniccantiādinā sabhāvena yāthāvato dhammaṃ jānāpetuṃ. Rāgadosaparetatāpi nesaṃ sammūḷhabhāvenevāti āha “tamokhandhena āvuṭā”ti.

'Niccādīnaṃ' refers to the four perversions (vipallāsas) of permanence, etc. 'Evaṃgataṃ' means it should be understood as proceeding in the way of impermanence, etc. Being impassioned with sensual lust and impassioned with lust for existence, their minds obstructed by the hindrances, and being impassioned with lust for views with perverse adherence, they will not see the Dhamma as it truly is, nor will they penetrate it. 'Sabhāvena' means by its true, non-perverted nature. 'Evaṃ gāhāpetuṃ' means to make them know the Dhamma as it truly is, by its nature of impermanence, etc. And that they are overcome by lust and hatred is due to their state of delusion; therefore it is said: 'They are enveloped by the mass of darkness.'

Dhammadesanāya [V 1.0203] appossukkatāpattiyā kāraṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kasmā panā”tiādinā sayameva codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Aññātavesenāti imassa bhagavato sāvakabhāvūpagamanena aññātavesena. “Aññataratāpasavesenā”ti keci, so panassa arahattādhigamaneneva vigaccheyya. Tividhaṃ kāraṇaṃ appossukkatāpattiyā paṭipakkhassa balavabhāvo, dhammassa gambhīratā, tattha ca bhagavato sātisayaṃ gāravanti taṃ dassetuṃ “tassa hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭipakkhā nāma rāgādayo kilesā sammāpaṭipattiyā antarāyakarattā. Tesaṃ balavabhāvato ciraparibhāvanāya sattasantānato dubbisodhiyatāya te satte mattahatthino viya dubbalapurisaṃ adhibhavitvā ajjhottharitvā anayabyasanaṃ āpādentā anekasatayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ sunicitaṃ ghanasannivesaṃ kaṇṭakaduggampi adhisenti. Dūrapabhedaducchejjatāhi dubbisodhiyataṃ pana dassetuṃ “athassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ca anto amaṭṭhatāya kañjiyapuṇṇā lābu, cirapārivāsikatāya takkabharitā cāṭi, snehatintadubbalabhāvena vasāpītapilotikā, telamissitatāya añjanamakkhitahattho dubbisodhanīyā vuttā. Hīnūpamā cetā rūpapabandhabhāvato acirakālikattā ca malīnatāya, kilesasaṃkileso eva pana dubbisodhanīyataro [M 1.0233] anādikālikattā arūpanissitattā ca. Tenāha “atisaṃkiliṭṭhā”ti.

To explain the reason for the lack of enthusiasm for teaching the Dhamma, the question 'Kasmā pana' (But why?) is raised by way of self-reproach. 'Aññātavesena' (disguised as another)—this refers to approaching the Blessed One’s disciples in an unrecognized guise. Some say 'aññataratāpasavesena' (disguised as an ascetic), but that would have ceased upon his attainment of arahantship. The threefold reason for the lack of enthusiasm—the strength of the opposition, the profundity of the Dhamma, and the supreme reverence of the Blessed One for it—is shown by the passage beginning, 'Tassa hi' (For indeed...). Here, the opposition refers to defilements such as lust, which obstruct right practice. Due to their strength, long cultivation in the mental continuity of beings, and their difficulty to purify, these defilements overpower weak individuals like a mad elephant, overwhelming them and leading them to ruin and misery. They dwell in even the dense, thorny thicket extending hundreds of leagues. To illustrate their difficulty to purify due to being hard to penetrate and destroy, the passage beginning 'Athassā' (Moreover...) is stated. Here, a gourd filled with fermented rice water is hard to clean due to the roughness of its inside; a pot filled with buttermilk is hard to clean due to long-standing residue; a cloth soaked in oil and grease is hard to clean due to its oily saturation; and a hand smeared with ointment is hard to clean due to its oiliness. These are inferior similes because they are bound to form and because their stain is not long-lasting. But the stain of the defilements is even harder to purify due to its beginningless nature and its reliance on the formless. Hence it is said, 'atisaṃkiliṭṭhā' (exceedingly defiled).

Yathā ca dubbisodhanīyataratāya, evaṃ gambhīraduddasaduranubodhānampi vuttaupamā hīnūpamāva. Gambhīropi dhammo paṭipakkhavidhamanena ñāṇena visadabhāvaṃ āpannena supākaṭo bhaveyya, paṭipakkhavidhamanaṃ pana sammāpaṭipattipaṭibaddhaṃ, sā saddhammassavanādhīnā, taṃ satthari dhamme ca pasādāyattaṃ. So garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ ajjhesanahetukoti paṇālikāya sattānaṃ dhammasampaṭipattiyā brahmāyācanānimittanti taṃ dassento “apicā”tiādimāha.

And just as the aforementioned similes are inferior with regard to the greater difficulty of purification, so too are they inferior with regard to the Dhamma being profound, difficult to see, and hard to understand. Even a profound teaching would become very clear by means of wisdom that has attained clarity by dispelling the opposition. But dispelling the opposition is bound up with right practice, which depends on hearing the true Dhamma. That, in turn, depends on confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma. That confidence is caused by the request of those worthy of respect. To show that, in due course, Brahmā's request is the sign for the beings' attainment of the Dhamma, he says 'Apicā' (Moreover), and so on.

Upakkilesabhūtaṃ appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ etassāti apparajaṃ, apparajaṃ akkhi paññācakkhu yesaṃ te taṃsabhāvāti katvā apparajakkhajātikāti imamatthaṃ dassento “paññāmaye”tiādimāha. Appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ yesaṃ taṃsabhāvā apparajakkhajātikāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Assavanatāti “sayaṃ abhiññā”tiādīsu viya karaṇe paccattavacananti āha “assavanatāyā”ti. Dasapuññakiriyavasenāti dānādidasavidhapuññakiriyavatthūnaṃ vasena. Tenāha “katādhikārā”tiādi. Papañcasūdaniyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.282) pana “dvādasapuññakiriyavasenā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ dānādīsu saraṇagamana-parahitapariṇāmanādipakkhipanavasena vuttaṃ.

The small amount of dust-like defilements such as lust is theirs—thus, 'apparajaṃ' (little dust). Those whose nature is to have the eye of wisdom with little dust are, because they are of that nature, called 'apparajakkhajātikā' (of a nature with little dust in the eye). To explain this meaning, it is said, 'paññāmaye' (in the wisdom-eye), and so on. Here, the meaning should be understood as follows: those whose nature is to have little dust of lust and other defilements in their eye of wisdom are called 'apparajakkhajātikā'. Regarding 'assavanatā' (from not hearing): this is a singular ablative used in the sense of the instrumental, as in phrases like 'sayaṃ abhiññā' (by oneself having directly known); thus it is said 'assavanatāya' (by not hearing). 'Dasapuññakiriyavasena' (by means of the ten meritorious actions) refers to the tenfold grounds of meritorious actions, such as giving and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'katādhikārā' (those who have made a foundation of merit), and so on. However, in the Papañcasūdanī (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary 1.282), it is stated as 'dvādasapuññakiriyavasena' (by means of the twelve meritorious actions). That is said by including additional factors such as going for refuge and dedicating merit to the welfare of others, and so on, within the categories of giving and the like.

Rāgādimalena samalehi pūraṇādīhi chahi satthārehi satthupaṭiññehi kabbaracanāvasena cintākaviādibhāve ṭhatvā takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ cintito. Te kira buddhakolāhalānussavena [V 1.0204] sañjātakutūhalaṃ lokaṃ vañcentā kohaññe ṭhatvā sabbaññutaṃ paṭijānantā yaṃ kañci adhammameva “dhammo”ti dīpesuṃ. Tenāha “te hi puretaraṃ uppajjitvā”tiādi. Apāpuretanti etaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti pihitaṃ nibbānamahādvāraṃ ariyamaggaṃ saddhammadesanāhatthena apāpura vivara.

By the six teachers, Pūraṇa and others, who were defiled with stains such as lust and were self-proclaimed teachers, standing as thinkers and poets by way of their compositions, they devised a teaching based on logic, followed by investigation, and of their own invention. It is said that, deceiving a world whose curiosity was aroused by the rumor of a Buddha, they established themselves in deceit, claimed omniscience, and taught whatever was non-Dhamma as 'Dhamma.' Therefore, it is said, 'They, having arisen earlier,' and so on. 'Apāpuretanti' means that he opened, he uncovered with the hand of the teaching of the true Dhamma, the noble path—the great door to Nibbāna—which had been closed since the disappearance of the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.

Selo pabbato ucco hoti thiro ca, na paṃsupabbato missakapabbato cāti āha “sele yathā pabbatamuddhanī”ti. Dhammamayaṃ pāsādanti lokuttaradhammamāha. So hi sabbaso pasādāvaho, sabbadhamme [M 1.0234] atikkamma abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādasadiso ca. Paññāpariyāyo vā idha dhamma-saddoti vuttaṃ “paññāmaya”nti. Sā hi abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādoti abhidhamme āgatā. Tathā cāha –

A rock mountain is high and firm, not a mountain of dust or a composite mountain; thus it is said, 'as on a rock at a mountain's summit.' 'The palace made of Dhamma' refers to the supramundane Dhamma, for it is altogether confidence-inspiring and, surpassing all things by its elevated nature, is like a palace. Alternatively, the word 'Dhamma' here is a synonym for wisdom; hence it is called 'made of wisdom.' For wisdom, due to its elevated nature, is called a palace, as stated in the Abhidhamma. And thus it is said—

“Paññāpāsādamāruyha, asoko sokiniṃ pajaṃ;

Pabbataṭṭhova bhūmaṭṭhe, dhīro bāle avekkhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 28);

Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the sorrowless one surveys the sorrowing crowd; as one on a mountain peak surveys those on the ground, so does the wise one survey the fools. (Dhp. 28);

Yathā hītiādīsu yathā ca pabbate ṭhatvā andhakāre heṭṭhā olokentassa purisassa khettakedārapāḷikuṭikāyo tattha sayitamanussā ca na paññāyanti anujjalabhāvato, kuṭikāsu pana aggijālā paññāyati samujjalabhāvato, evaṃ dhammapāsādamāruyha sattalokaṃ olokayato bhagavato ñāṇassa āpāthaṃ nāgacchanti akatakalyāṇā sattā, ñāṇagginā anujjalabhāvato anuḷārabhāvato ca rattiṃ khittā sarā viya honti, katakalyāṇā pana bhabbapuggalā dūre ṭhitāpi bhagavato āpāthaṃ āgacchanti paripakkañāṇaggitāya samujjalabhāvato uḷārasantānatāya himavantapabbato viya cāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

Just as, when a person stands on a mountain in the darkness and looks below, the fields, rice-paddies, dikes, and huts, as well as the people sleeping there, are not visible due to their lack of brightness, whereas the flames of fires in the huts are visible because they are blazing; similarly, when the Blessed One ascends the palace of the Dhamma and surveys the world of beings, those beings who have not done good do not come within the range of his knowledge because they do not glow with the fire of wisdom and are insignificant; they are like arrows shot at night. But those worthy individuals who have done good, even if they stand far away, come within the Blessed One’s range of vision because their wisdom is fully matured and blazing, and because of their eminent character—like the Himālaya mountain. Thus should the connection be understood.

Garuṭṭhānīyaṃ payirupāsitvā garutaraṃ payojanaṃ uddissa abhipatthanā ajjhesanā, sāpi atthato yācanāva hotīti āha “ajjhesananti yācana”nti. Padesavisayaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ ahutvā buddhānaṃyeva āveṇikabhāvato idaṃ ñāṇadvayaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti vuccatīti āha “imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ ‘buddhacakkhū’ti nāma”nti. Tiṇṇaṃ magggañāṇānanti heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ “dhammacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ catusaccadhammadassanamattabhāvato. Yato tāni ñāṇāni vijjūpamabhāvena vuttāni, aggamaggañāṇaṃ pana ñāṇakiccassa sikhāppattiyā dassanamattaṃ na hotīti “dhammacakkhū”ti na vuccati, yato taṃ vajirūpamabhāvena vuttaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “apparajakkhajātikā”ti ettha vuttanayena. Yasmā mandakilesā “apparajakkhā”ti vuttā, tasmā [V 1.0205] bahalakilesā “mahārajakkhā”ti veditabbā. Paṭipakkhavidhamanasamatthatāya tikkhāni sūrāni visadāni, vuttavipariyāyena mudūni. Saddhādayo ākārāti saddahanādippakāre vadati. Sundarāti kalyāṇā. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ pana “yesaṃ āsayādayo koṭṭhāsā [M 1.0235] sundarā, te svākārā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ imāya atthavaṇṇanāya aññadatthu saṃsandatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāraṇaṃ nāma paccayākāro, saccāni vā. Paralokanti samparāyaṃ. Taṃ dukkhāvahaṃ vajjaṃ viya bhayato passitabbanti vuttaṃ “paralokañceva vajjañca bhayato passantī”ti. Sampattibhavato vā aññattā vipattibhavo paralokoti vuttaṃ “para…pe… passantī”ti.

An aspiration and request aiming for a greater purpose, made after attending upon one worthy of reverence—this too, in essence, is a request. Hence it is said, '`Ajjhesanā` means a request.' Because there is no knowledge and vision with a limited scope for Buddhas, and because this pair of knowledges is unique to them alone, it is called the 'Buddha-eye.' Therefore, it is said, 'Indeed, these two knowledges have the name “Buddha-eye.”' The lower three path-knowledges are called the 'Dhamma-eye' because they consist merely of seeing the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Since those knowledges are described as being like lightning, the knowledge of the highest path, however, is not called the 'Dhamma-eye' because, having reached the peak of the function of knowledge, it is not mere seeing; for it is described as being like a diamond. 'By the stated method' means by the method stated in the phrase 'of a nature with little dust.' Because those with few defilements are called 'of little dust,' those with thick defilements should be understood as 'of much dust.' Due to their ability to destroy opposing states, the faculties are sharp, valiant, and clear; by the reverse of this, they are dull. 'The modes beginning with faith' refers to the types such as believing. '`Sundara`' means good. In the Sammohavinodanī, however, it is said, 'Those whose parts, such as inclination, are good, they are of good character.' This should be seen as corresponding with this explanation of the meaning. 'Cause' means the mode of condition, or the truths. 'The other world' means the future life. They see that fault which brings suffering with fear, thus it is said, 'they see the other world and fault with fear.' Or, because the state of misfortune is different from the state of attainment, the state of misfortune is called the 'other world,' as stated, 'they see the other... with fear.'

Ayaṃ panettha pāḷīti ettha “apparajakkhā”ti padānaṃ atthavibhāvane ayaṃ tassa tathābhāvasādhanapāḷi. Saddhādīnañhi vimuttaparipācakadhammānaṃ balavabhāvo tappaṭipakkhānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ dubbalabhāve sati hoti. Tesañca balavabhāvo saddhādīnaṃ dubbalabhāveti vimuttiparipācakadhammānaṃ savisesaṃ atthitānatthitāvasena apparajakkhā mahārajakkhātiādayo pāḷiyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.111) vibhajitvā dassitā “saddho puggalo apparajakkho”tiādinā. Khandhādayo eva lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko sampattibhavabhūto loko sampattibhavaloko, sugatisaṅkhāto upapattibhavo. Sampatti bhavati etenāti sampattisambhavaloko, sugatisaṃvattaniyo kammabhavo. Duggatisaṅkhātaupapattibhava-duggatisaṃvattaniyakammabhavā vipattibhavaloka-vipattisambhavalokā. Puna ekakadukādivasena lokaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “eko loko”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āhārādayo viya hi āhāraṭṭhitikā saṅkhārā sabbe lujjanaṭṭhena lokoti. Tattha eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikāti yāyaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya sabbesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paccayāyattavuttitā vuttā, tāya sabbo saṅkhāraloko eko ekavidho pakārantarassa abhāvato. Dve lokātiādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Nāmaggahaṇena cettha nibbānassa aggahaṇaṃ tassa alokasabhāvattā.

Here, in the explanation of the meaning of the words 'of little dust,' this is the Pāli text that establishes its being so. For the strength of the qualities that mature liberation, such as faith, exists when their opposing evil qualities are weak, and the strength of those evil qualities exists when faith and so on are weak. According to the presence or absence of distinction in these qualities that mature liberation, terms such as 'of little dust' and 'of much dust' are shown by way of division in the Pāli text (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.111), beginning with 'a faithful person is of little dust.' The aggregates and so forth are 'world' due to their nature of crumbling and dissolving. The world that is the plane of attainment-existence is the 'attainment-existence-world,' which is the rebirth-existence called a happy destiny. 'Attainment comes to be through this,' thus the 'attainment-source-world,' which is the kamma-existence leading to a happy destiny. The rebirth-existence called an unhappy destiny and the kamma-existence leading to an unhappy destiny are the 'misfortune-existence-world' and the 'misfortune-source-world.' Furthermore, to show the world divided by way of ones, twos, etc., it is said, 'one world,' and so on. For all formations, being sustained by nutriment, are 'world' due to their nature of crumbling. Therein, 'one world: all beings are sustained by nutriment' means that by this talk based on the individual, the dependent nature of all formations is stated; thereby the entire world of formations is one, of a single kind, due to the absence of any other kind. Similarly, the meaning of 'two worlds' and so forth should be understood in this way. Here, by the designation 'world,' Nibbāna is not included, because it is by nature not a world.

Nanu ca “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti ettha paccayāyattavuttitāya maggaphalānampi lokatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, pariññeyyānaṃ dukkhasaccadhammānaṃ idha “loko”ti adhippetattā. Atha vā na lujjati na palujjatīti yo gahito tathā na hoti, so lokoti taṃgahaṇarahitānaṃ lokuttarānaṃ natthi lokatā. Upādānānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Anurodhādivatthubhūtā lābhādayo aṭṭha [M 1.0236] lokadhammā. Dasāyatanānīti dasa rūpāyatanāni. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Vivaṭṭajjhāsayassa adhippetattā tassa ca sabbaṃ tebhūmakakammaṃ garahitabbaṃ vajjitabbañca hutvā upaṭṭhātīti vuttaṃ “sabbe abhisaṅkhārā vajjā, sabbe bhavagāmikammā vajjā”ti[V 1.0206]. Apparajakkhatādīsu pañcasu dukesu ekekasmiṃ dasa dasa katvā “paññāsāya ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni jānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā anvayato byatirekato ca saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ paropariyattaṃ jānātīti katvā tathā vuttaṃ. Ettha ca apparajakkhādibhabbādivasena āvajjentassa bhagavato te sattā puñjapuñjāva hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, na ekekā.

Now then, in the phrase 'sustained by nutriment,' does worldliness also apply to the paths and fruits due to their dependence on conditions? It does not, because here 'world' is intended to refer to the dhammas of the truth of suffering, which are to be fully understood. Alternatively, 'world' is that which is grasped as 'it does not crumble, it does not dissolve,' but is not in fact so; therefore, the supramundane states, being devoid of such grasping, have no worldly nature. The aggregates that have become objects of clinging are the clinging-aggregates. The eight worldly conditions, such as gain and loss, are the basis for conformity and opposition. 'The ten sense bases' means the ten material sense bases. The rest is easily understood. Because one's intention is for the rolling back of existence, all kamma pertaining to the three realms presents itself to one as reprehensible and to be avoided; thus it is said: 'All formations are to be avoided; all kamma leading to existence is to be avoided.' In the five pairs beginning with 'of little dust,' taking ten in each case, it is said, 'He knows these five faculties in fifty modes.' Alternatively, it is said thus because he knows the superiority and inferiority of the faculties such as faith both positively and negatively. And here, when the Blessed One adverts to beings according to their state—such as those with little dust, those who are capable, and so on—they appear to him in clusters, not one by one.

Uppalāni ettha santīti uppalinī. Uppalagacchopi jalāsayopi ca. Idha pana jalāsayo adhippetoti āha “uppalavane”ti. Yāni hi udakassa anto nimuggāneva hutvā pusanti vaḍḍhanti, tāni antonimuggaposīni. Dīpitānīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pakāsitāni, idheva vā “aññānipī”tiādinā dassitāni. Ugghaṭitaññūti ugghaṭanaṃ nāma ñāṇugghaṭanaṃ, ñāṇena ugghaṭitamatteneva jānātīti attho. Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritameva atthaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Niddesādīhi dhammābhisamayāya netabboti neyyo. Pajjati attho etenāti padaṃ, pajjate ñāyateti vā padaṃ, tadattho. Padaṃ paramaṃ etassa, na saccābhisambodhoti padaparamo.

‘Here there are lotuses,’ hence it is called Uppalinī. It refers to both a lotus clump and a water reservoir. Here, however, a water reservoir is intended, as stated by the term ‘in a lotus pond.’ Those that are nourished and grow while remaining submerged within the water are called ‘nourished while submerged.’ ‘Explained’ means clarified in the commentary, or shown here by such phrases as ‘and others.’ ‘One who understands upon disclosure’ (ugghaṭitaññū) means that ‘disclosure’ is the disclosure of knowledge; the meaning is that one understands merely upon the disclosure by knowledge. ‘One who understands the elaborated meaning’ (vipañcitaññū) is one who understands the meaning when it has been explained in detail. ‘One who is to be guided’ (neyya) is one who is to be led to the realization of the Dhamma through explanations and so on. A ‘word’ (pada) is that by which the meaning is approached, or a word is that by which the meaning is understood; that is its meaning. For this person, the word is supreme, and there is no full awakening to the truth, thus he is a padaparama (one for whom the word is supreme).

Udāhaṭavelāyāti udāhāre dhammassa uddese udāhaṭamatteyeva. Dhammābhisamayoti catusaccadhammassa ñāṇena saddhiṃ abhisamayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena saṃkhittena mātikāya ṭhapiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho puggalo “ugghaṭitaññū”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti saṃkhittena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho puggalo “vipañcitaññū”ti vuccati. Uddesatoti uddesahetu. Uddisantassa uddisāpentassa vāti attho. Paripucchatoti atthaṃ paripucchantassa. Anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hotīti anukkamena arahattappatti hoti. Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti tena attabhāvena maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā antamaso jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti. Ayaṃ vuccati padaparamoti ayaṃ puggalo chabbidhaṃ byañjanapadaṃ chabbidhaṃ atthapadanti idaṃ padameva paramaṃ assāti padaparamoti vuccatīti attho.

‘At the time of utterance’ means at the moment of merely uttering the Dhamma, at the exposition of the teaching. ‘Realization of the Dhamma’ means the realization of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, together with knowledge. ‘This is said’ means that a person who is capable of attaining arahantship by directing their knowledge according to the teaching when the matrix is laid down concisely—by the method beginning with ‘the four establishments of mindfulness’—is called an ugghaṭitaññū (one who understands upon disclosure). ‘This is said’ means that a person who is capable of attaining arahantship when the meaning is analyzed in detail after the matrix has been laid down concisely is called a vipañcitaññū (one who understands the elaborated meaning). ‘Through exposition’ means for the sake of exposition; that is, for one who expounds or causes another to expound. ‘Through questioning’ means for one who inquires into the meaning. ‘There is a gradual realization of the Dhamma’ means that the attainment of arahantship occurs step by step. ‘There is no realization of the Dhamma in that life’ means that with that individual existence, one is unable to bring forth the path or the fruit, or at the very least, jhāna or insight. ‘This is called a padaparama’ means that this person, for whom the sixfold verbal expression and the sixfold meaning expression—this very word—is supreme, is called a padaparama (one for whom the word is supreme); this is the meaning.

Vāsanā [M 1.0237] hotīti desanā phalavohārena vāsanā hotīti vuttā. Na hi kāci buddhānaṃ desanā niratthakā. Yeti ye duvidhe puggale. Vibhaṅge kammāvaraṇenāti pañcavidhena ānantariyakammena. Vipākāvaraṇenāti ahetukapaṭisandhiyā. Yasmā pana duhetukānampi ariyamaggapaṭivedho natthi, tasmā duhetukā paṭisandhipi vipākāvaraṇamevāti veditabbā. Kilesāvaraṇenāti niyatamicchādiṭṭhiyā. Assaddhāti buddhādīsu saddhārahitā. Acchandikāti kattukamyatāchandarahitā. Uttarakurukā manussā acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Duppaññāti bhavaṅgapaññāya parihīnā. Bhavaṅgapaññāya [V 1.0207] pana paripuṇṇāyapi yassa bhavaṅgacalanaṃ lokuttarassa paccayo na hoti, sopi duppañño eva nāma. Abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ okkamituṃ adhigantuṃ abhabbā. Na kammāvaraṇenātiādīni vuttavipariyāyena veditabbāni. Rāgacaritādiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paramatthadīpaniyaṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.43) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

‘There is an impression’ (vāsanā): the teaching is said to be an ‘impression’ by way of its result. Indeed, no teaching of the Buddhas is without purpose. ‘Those’ refers to those two kinds of individuals. In the Vibhaṅga, ‘by the obstruction of kamma’ means by the five kinds of heinous kamma. ‘By the obstruction of result’ means by rebirth without root-causes. However, since even for those with two root-causes there is no penetration of the noble path, rebirth with two root-causes should also be understood as an obstruction of result. ‘By the obstruction of defilements’ means by fixed wrong view. ‘Lacking faith’ means devoid of faith in the Buddha and so on. ‘Lacking desire’ means devoid of the desire to act. The humans of Uttarakuru have entered the state of lacking desire. ‘Unwise’ means deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum. However, even if one is fully endowed with the wisdom of the life-continuum, if the stirring of the life-continuum does not become a condition for the supramundane, such a person is still called unwise. ‘Incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states’ means they are incapable of entering, of attaining, the path designated as the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states. The phrases ‘not by the obstruction of kamma’ and so on should be understood in the opposite sense of what was stated. Regarding those with lustful natures and so forth, what should be said is to be understood according to the method explained in the Paramatthadīpanī, the subcommentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. Mahāṭī. 1.43).

Nibbānassa dvāraṃ pavisanamaggo vivaritvā ṭhapito mahākaruṇūpanissayena sayambhuñāṇena adhigatattā. Saddhaṃ pamuñcantūti attano saddhaṃ dhammasampaṭicchanayogyaṃ katvā vissajjentu, saddahanākārena naṃ upaṭṭhapentūti attho. Sukhena akicchena pavattanīyatāya suppavattitaṃ. Na bhāsiṃ na bhāsissāmīti cintesiṃ.

The door to Nibbāna, the path of entry, was opened and established because it was attained by self-originated knowledge, with great compassion as its basis. ‘Let them release faith’ means let them make their own faith suitable for receiving the Dhamma and send it forth; the meaning is, let them establish it in the manner of belief. ‘Well-promulgated’ because it could be set in motion easily and without difficulty. ‘I did not speak, nor will I speak,’ I thought.

Satthu santikaṃ upagatānaṃ devānaṃ brahmānañca tassa purato antaradhānaṃ nāma atiṭṭhananti āha “sakaṭṭhānameva gato”ti. Saddhindriyādi sammādiṭṭhiādiko dhammo eva vineyyasantāne pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ. Atha vā cakkanti āṇā. Dhammanti desanā. Atha vā atthadhammato anapetattā dhammañca taṃ pavattanaṭṭhena cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ. Dhammena ñāyena cakkantipi dhammacakkaṃ. Yathāha “dhammañca pavatteti cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, cakkañca pavatteti dhammañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammena pavattetīti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammacariyāya pavattetīti dhammacakka”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 2.40-41). Pavattesīti paṭṭhapesi.

The disappearance of the devas and Brahmās who had approached the Teacher from his presence, that is, their not remaining, is stated as: ‘He has gone to his own place.’ The Dhamma, beginning with the faculty of faith and right view, is the Dhamma-wheel in the sense that it turns in the mental continuum of those to be trained. Alternatively, ‘wheel’ means command; ‘Dhamma’ means the teaching. Or, because it is not separate from the meaning and the Dhamma, and because it is a wheel in the sense of setting in motion, it is the Dhamma-wheel. It is also the Dhamma-wheel because it is a wheel by means of the Dhamma, that is, by justice. As it is said: ‘He sets the Dhamma in motion and the wheel, hence the Dhamma-wheel; he sets the wheel in motion and the Dhamma, hence the Dhamma-wheel; he sets it in motion by means of Dhamma, hence the Dhamma-wheel; he sets it in motion by the practice of Dhamma, hence the Dhamma-wheel,’ and so on (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.40-41). ‘He set in motion’ means he established.

Brahmāyācanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Brahmāyācana Sutta is concluded.

2. Gāravasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Gārava Sutta

173. Ayaṃ [M 1.0238] vitakkoti ayaṃ “kintāhaṃ vihareyya”nti evaṃ pavattitavitakko. Aññasminti parasmiṃ. Attā na hotīti hi añño, paro. So panettha na yo koci adhippeto, atha kho garuṭṭhānīyo. Tenāha “kañci garuṭṭhāne aṭṭhapetvā”ti. Patissavati garuno “āmā”ti sampaṭicchatīti patisso, na patissoti appatisso. Patissayarahito garupassayarahitoti attho.

173. ‘This thought’ means this thought that arose thus: ‘How should I dwell?’ ‘In another’ means in someone else. For what is not self is indeed ‘another,’ ‘someone else.’ But here, this does not refer to just anyone, but rather to someone worthy of respect. Hence it is said, ‘having placed someone in a position of respect.’ One who accepts the teacher’s word with ‘Yes’ is responsive (patisso); one who is not is unresponsive (appatisso). ‘Devoid of responsiveness’ means devoid of reliance on a teacher; this is the meaning.

Sadevaketi avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho. Sadevakaggahaṇena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ pārisesañāyena itaresaṃ padantarehi saṅgahitattā, samārakaggahaṇena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ [V 1.0208] paccāsattiñāyena. Tattha hi māro jāto tannivāsī ca hoti. Sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ paccāsattiñāyeneva. “Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāyā”ti sāsanassa paccatthikasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ apaccatthikānaṃ asamitapāpānaṃ abāhitapāpānañca samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ teneva vacanena gahitattā. Kāmaṃ “sadevake”tiādivisesanānaṃ vasena sattavisayo lokasaddoti viññāyati tulyayogavisayattā tesaṃ. “Salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu pana atulyayogepi ayaṃ samāso labbhatīti byabhicāradassanato pajāgahaṇanti pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ. Devabhāvasāmaññena mārabrahmesu gahitesupi itarehi tesaṃ labbhamānavisesadassanatthaṃ visuṃ gahaṇanti dassento “māro nāmā”tiādimāha. Māro brahmānampi vicakkhukammāya pahotīti āha “sabbesa”nti. Uparīti uparibhāve. Brahmāti dasasahassibrahmānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tathā cāha “dasahi aṅgulīhī”tiādi. Idha dīghanikāyādayo viya bāhirakānampi ganthanikāyo labbhatīti āha “ekanikāyādivasenā”ti.

Regarding sadevake (with its devas): the analysis is by its parts; the meaning of the compound is the aggregate. By the term sadevake, the devas of the five sense-sphere realms are included by the principle of remainder, since the others are included by other terms. By the term samārake (with Māra), the devas of the sixth sense-sphere realm are included by the principle of proximity, for Māra is born and dwells there. By the phrase sabrahmake (with its Brahmās), the Brahmās beginning with the Brahmakāyika devas are included by the same principle of proximity. By ‘with its ascetics and brahmins, this generation’ (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya), the ascetics and brahmins hostile to the teaching are included. And this is merely an example, for those ascetics and brahmins who are not hostile, who have not stilled evil, and who have not abandoned evil, are also included by that very statement. Indeed, by means of qualifiers like sadevake, the term loka (world) is understood to refer to the world of beings, due to their having a domain of similar application. However, since in phrases like salomako sapakkhako (with fur, with wings) this type of compound is found even with an unequal application, this shows an exception; therefore, by the inclusion of pajā (generation), the world of beings is included by that word. Although Māra and Brahmā are included by the general characteristic of being a deva, to show the distinct qualities they possess compared to the others, they are mentioned separately; showing this, it says, ‘Māra is…’ and so on. Māra is capable of blinding even the Brahmās, hence it says ‘of all.’ ‘Above’ (uparī) means in a higher state. ‘Brahmā’ is said with reference to the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world system. And so it is said: ‘with ten fingers,’ and so on. Here, just as there are collections of texts like the Dīgha Nikāya, collections of external texts are also found; hence it is said ‘by way of a single collection,’ and so on.

Vatthuvijjādīti ādi-saddena vijjāṭṭhānāni saṅgahitāni. Yathāsakaṃ kammakilesehi pajātattā nibbattattā pajā, sattanikāyo. Tassā pajāya. Sadevamanussāyāti vā iminā sammutidevaggahaṇaṃ tadavasiṭṭhamanussalokaggahaṇañca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ bhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetvā idāni abhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetuṃ “apicetthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Lokavasena vuttāni “lokīyanti ettha kammakammaphalānī”ti [M 1.0239] katvā, pajāvasena “hetupaccayehi pajāyatī”ti katvā. Sīlasampannataranti ettha paripuṇṇasampannatā adhippetā “sampannaṃ sālikedāra”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.14.1) viya. Tenāha “adhikataranti attho”ti. Paripuṇṇampi “adhikatara”nti vattabbatamarahati. Sesesūti “samādhisampannatara”ntiādīsu.

'The science of sites, etc.'—here, by the word 'etc.,' the various branches of knowledge are included. 'Pajā' refers to the multitude of beings, because they are generated and produced by their respective kamma and defilements. For that populace. Or, by 'with devas and humans,' the inclusion of conventional devas and the inclusion of the remaining human world should be understood. Having thus explained the world by taking it in parts, now, to explain it by taking the world as a whole, the phrase 'furthermore, here' and so on was stated. It is said in terms of 'world' because 'herein kamma and its results are experienced'; and in terms of 'beings' because 'they are generated through causes and conditions.' 'More accomplished in virtue'—here, complete accomplishment is intended, as in phrases like 'a fully cultivated rice field' and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'The meaning is "greater."' Even what is complete is worthy of being called 'greater.' 'In the remaining cases' refers to phrases like 'more accomplished in concentration,' and so on.

Kāraṇantiādīsu kāraṇanti yuttiṃ. Atthanti aviparītatthaṃ. Vuḍḍhinti abhivuḍḍhinimittaṃ.

In the phrase 'reason, etc.,' 'reason' means logical reason. 'Meaning' means the non-perverted meaning. 'Growth' means the cause of growth.

Iminā vacanenāti imasmiṃ sutte anantaraṃ vuttavacanena. Na kevalaṃ imināva, suttantarampi ānetvā paṭibāhitabboti dassento “na me ācariyo atthī”tiādimāha. Ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.162) vuttameva. Saranti karaṇe etaṃ paccattavacananti āha “sarantenā”ti, saranti vā saraṇahetūti attho.

'By this statement' means by the words spoken immediately before in this discourse. Not only by this, but it should also be refuted by bringing in other discourses—showing this, he says, 'I have no teacher,' and so on. Here, what should be said has been stated in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya. Regarding 'saranti' (they remember), this is a word in the instrumental sense, hence he says 'by remembering'; or the meaning is 'it is a cause for remembering.'

Gāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Gārava Sutta is concluded.

3. Brahmadevasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Brahmadeva Sutta

174. Ekakoti [V 1.0209] vivekaṭṭhitatāya nissaṭo. Gaṇasaṅgaṇikābhāvo tassānena dīpito, kilesasaṅgaṇikābhāvo pana “appamatto”tiādīhi pakāsito. Pesitattoti nibbānaṃ pati pesitacitto. Sammadevāti ñāyeneva. So pana yadi āgamanato paṭṭhāya labbhati, vattabbameva natthi, atha paṭipadārambhato paṭṭhāya labbhati, evampi vaṭṭatevāti dassetuṃ “yathā vā tathā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aggamaggādhigamena asammohapaṭivedhassa sikhāppattattā maggadhammesu viya phaladhammesupi sātisayo asammohoti “sayaṃ abhiññā”ti vuttanti āha “sāmaṃ jānitvā”ti. Yathā jānanā panassa sacchikaraṇaṃ attapaccakkhakiriyāti “sacchikatvā”ti vuttanti āha “paccakkhaṃ katvā”ti. Tathā sacchikiriyā cassa vipassanāpaṭilābhoti “upasampajjā”ti vuttanti āha “paṭilabhitvā”ti. Etenāti “khīṇā jātī”tiādivacanena.

174. 'Alone' means one is released due to dwelling in seclusion. The absence of association with a group is indicated by this, while the absence of association with defilements is shown by such terms as ‘diligent.’ ‘One whose self is sent forth’ means one whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna. ‘Rightly’ means by the proper method. If this is attained from the moment of arrival, there is nothing to be said; but if it is attained from the beginning of the practice, this too is valid—to show this, the phrase ‘in whatever way’ and so on is stated. Through the attainment of the supreme path, the penetration of non-delusion reaches its peak; just as in the path-states, so too in the fruition-states, there is a surpassing non-delusion. Thus, it is said ‘having directly known by himself,’ which means, he says, ‘having known by himself.’ As for his knowing, it is the realization, the act of direct personal verification. Thus, it is said ‘having realized,’ which means, he says, ‘having made it directly evident.’ Likewise, his realization is the attainment of insight. Thus, it is said ‘having attained,’ which means, he says, ‘having gained.’ 'By this' means by such statements as ‘destroyed is birth.’

Jāti [M 1.0240] khīṇāti ettha jātisīsena tabbikāravanto khandhā vuttā. Pubbeva khīṇattāti maggādhigamanato pageva atītabhāveneva khīṇattā. Tattha anāgatesu. Vāyāmābhāvatoti avijjamānattā. Anāgatabhāvasāmaññaṃ gahetvā lesena vuttaṃ. Na paccuppannā vijjamānattāti saṃkiliṭṭhā ca maggabhāvanāti siyāti vacanaseso. Yathā ajātaphalataruṇarukkhamūle chinne āyatiuppajjanārahāni phalāni chedanapaccayā anuppajjamānāni naṭṭhāni nāma honti, evameva bhāvanāya asati uppajjanārahā kilesā tappaccayā jāti ca maggabhāvanāya sati na uppajjamānā pahīnāti vuccantīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “maggassa panā”tiādinā. Anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena ñāṇena khīṇarāgavasena.

Here, in 'birth is destroyed,' by the heading 'birth,' the aggregates that are subject to its modifications are meant. 'Because it was already destroyed beforehand' means because it was destroyed even before the attainment of the path, simply by having passed away. Therein, regarding future aggregates, 'due to the absence of effort' means because they are non-existent. This is stated allusively, taking the general state of the future. 'Not the present ones, because they exist'—the remainder of the statement is 'and because defiled states and the cultivation of the path might be.' Just as, when the root of a young tree that has not yet borne fruit is cut, the fruits that were liable to arise in the future do not arise due to the condition of being cut and are said to be destroyed, in the same way, the defilements that are liable to arise when there is no cultivation—and the birth dependent on them—are said to be abandoned because they do not arise when there is cultivation of the path. This meaning is shown by the passage beginning, ‘But as for the path...’ By way of the destruction of lust through the knowledge that attains the state of non-arising.

Soḷasakiccabhāvāyāti soḷasakiccatāya, soḷasavidhassa vā kiccassa bhāvāya uppādanāya. Pāḷiyaṃ sapadānanti sapadānacāro vutto bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesenāti āha “sapadānacāra”nti. Anukkammāti anatikkamitvā. Āhutipiṇḍanti juhitabbapiṇḍaṃ, juhanavasena aggimhi pakkhipitabbapāyāsapiṇḍanti adhippāyo. Bhūtabalikammanti tathā pakkhipitvā balikammakaraṇaṃ. Haritupalittanti allagomayena kataparibhaṇḍaṃ. Vanamālaparikkhittanti manoharāhi vanapupphamālāhi parikkhittaṃ. Dhūmakaṭacchūti dhūmapānaṃ. Sīlagandhanti sīlaṃ paṭicca uppannakittigandhaṃ. Ghāyamānassāti upagataṃ gaṇhantassa.

'For the state of sixteen duties' means for the sixteenfold nature of the duties, or for the production of the sixteen kinds of duties. In the Pāli, ‘sapadāna’ refers to ‘sapadānacāra’ (going from house to house for alms), which is stated with the designation of a neuter abstract noun; hence it is said ‘sapadānacāra’. ‘Anukkamma’ means without transgressing. ‘Āhutipiṇḍa’ means the offering-lump; the intended meaning is a lump of rice-milk to be thrown into the fire as an offering. ‘Bhūtabalikamma’ means performing the offering to beings by throwing it in that way. ‘Haritupalitta’ means an area prepared by smearing with fresh cow dung. ‘Vanamālaparikkhitta’ means surrounded by delightful garlands of forest flowers. ‘Dhūmakaṭacchu’ means smoking. ‘Sīlagandha’ means the fragrance of reputation that arises on account of virtue. ‘Ghāyamānassa’ means for one who is smelling, for one who is taking in what has approached.

Imamhā [V 1.0210] ṭhānāti imasmā manussānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānā, mahāpathavitalatoti adhippāyo. Sabbaheṭṭhimoti brahmapārisajjānaṃ vāsabrahmalokamāha. Brahmapatho nāma cattāri kusalajjhānāni brahmalokamaggabhāvato. Jīvitapatho nāma jīvitapavattiupāyabhāvato. “Bhuñjatu bhavaṃ mahābrahmā”ti vacanaṃ sandhāyāha “kiṃ jappasī”tiādi. Tiṇabījānīti sālitaṇḍulādīni. Goyūsanti khīraṃ jigucchanto vadati. Ayampi attho “netādiso brahmabhakkho”ti vadantena dīpitoti.

'From this place' means from this dwelling place of humans; the intended meaning is from the surface of the great earth. 'The very lowest' refers to the Brahmā world that is the abode of Brahmā’s retinue. The 'Brahmā path' refers to the four wholesome jhānas, because they are the path to the Brahmā world. The 'life path' refers to the means for the continuation of life.
