Sukhumāpi samānā dibbojā tena pāyasena missitā oḷārikasammissatāya sukhumavatthukānaṃ devānaṃ sukhadā na hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “goyūse panā”tiādinā. Paribhogavatthuno oḷārikatāya vā devānaṃ dukkaraṃ sammā pariṇāmetuṃ, dibbojāya garutarabhāvena manussānaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “na khvāha”ntiādi. Samāpatticittasamuṭṭhitā tejodhātu jhānānubhāvasantejitā tikkhatarā hotīti vuttaṃ “aṭṭha…pe… pariṇāmeyyā”ti. Bhagavato pana suddheneva pariṇamatīti vuttaṃ “pākatikenevā”ti, jhānānubhāvappattena jhānena vinā sabhāvasiddheneva.

'Upahaṭamatte' means just when the brahmin had brought it near, saying, 'May your reverence eat.' 'Nibbattitojameva' means only the produced essence, not taking it with its material basis, but the essence separated from its substance. 'Tena taṃ sukhumattaṃ gataṃ' means that the remnant of the oblation had become entirely subtle. This is said with reference to its being perceived in its former shape due to the non-grossness of the essence, not with reference to the grasping of the essence alone. For it cannot be grasped separately due to its inseparable nature; hence, even the deities grasp it along with its material basis. 'Manussānaṃ vatthu' refers to the physical body of humans. Due to the grossness of the material basis, their receptivity is not as sharp as the deities', and because of being mixed with divine essence, it does not undergo proper transformation. This meaning—that even though the divine essence is subtle, when mixed with that rice porridge, due to its gross mixture, it does not bring pleasure to deities with subtle material forms—is conveyed by 'goyūse panā' and so on. Or, due to the grossness of the consumable substance, it is difficult for deities to properly transform it, and for humans, it is difficult because of the greater weight of the divine essence. Therefore the Blessed One said, 'Indeed, I do not,' and so on. The fire element, arisen from the attainment-mind and intensified by the power of jhāna, becomes sharper—this is stated in 'aṭṭha…pe… pariṇāmeyyā.' But for the Blessed One, it is transformed by the pure element alone—this is stated by 'pākatikeneva,' meaning by that which is naturally perfected by its own nature, without jhāna or that which is attained through the power of jhāna.

“Appaharite”ti ettha appa-saddo “appiccho”tiādīsu viya abhāvatthoti āha “appahariteti aharite”ti. Pātisatepi pāyase. Na āluḷatīti na āvilaṃ hoti. Anāgantāva gaccheyya “attanāpi [M 1.0262] na paribhuñji, aññesaṃ na dāpesi, kevalaṃ pāyasaṃ nāsesī”ti domanassappatto.

Here, in 'appaharite,' the word 'appa' has the meaning of absence, as in 'appiccho' and so on; thus it is said, 'appaharite means aharite (without green vegetation).' Even when the rice porridge is thrown. 'Na āluḷati' means it does not become turbid. He would go away without having come, having become distressed that: 'He neither consumes it himself nor has it given to others; he simply destroys the rice porridge.'

Dāru [V 1.0229] samādahānoti dāruhariddi dārusmiṃ tassa dahanto. Yadītiādi dārujhāpanassa bahiddhabhāvasādhanaṃ asuddhahetūnaṃ paṭipakkhābhāvato tassa. Khandhādīsu kusalāti tesu sabhāvato samudayato atthaṅgamato assādato ādīnavato nissaraṇato jānanato chekā paṇḍitā. Ñāṇajotinti ñāṇamayaṃ jotiṃ. Jālemīti pajjalitaṃ karomi. Niccaṃ pajjalitaggi sabbatthakameva vigatasammohandhakāratāya ekobhāsabhāvato. Sabbaso vikkhepābhāvato niccasamāhitatto. Evaṃ vadatīti caritaṃ brahmacariyaṃ gahetvā carāmīti evaṃ vattamānaṃ viya vadati āsannataṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā.

'Dāru samādahāno' means one who, placing a fire-stick on the wood, kindles it. 'Yadītiādi' ('If,' etc.) is a proof of the external nature of fire-kindling, because for it there is an absence of opposition to impure causes. 'Kusalā' (skillful) in the aggregates and so forth means clever and wise in knowing them by their nature, origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape. 'Ñāṇajotiṃ' means the light consisting of knowledge. 'Jālemi' means 'I make it blaze.' The constantly blazing fire is indeed all-pervading, because the darkness of delusion has departed and because of its nature as a single radiance. Because of the utter absence of distraction, one's self is constantly composed. 'Evaṃ vadatī' (thus he speaks) means he speaks as if saying, 'Having undertaken it, I live the holy life,' placing its nearness in his heart.

Khāribhāroti khāribhārasadiso. Tenāha “yathā”tiādi. Khandhena vayhamānoti kāje pakkhipitvā khandhena vayhamāno. Pathaviyā saddhiṃ phuseti bhārassa garukabhāvena kājassa pariṇamanena. Mānena attano jātiādīni paggaṇhato aññassa tāni na sahatīti āha – “tattha tattha issaṃ uppādento”ti, tattha tattha jātiādimānavatthusmiṃ garutaraggahaṇena saṃsīdeyyāti adhippāyo. Kodho dhūmoti yathāpi bhāsuro aggi dhūmena upakkiliṭṭho, evaṃ kodhena upakkiliṭṭho. Ñāṇaggīti tassa kodho dhūmo. Musāvādova mosavajjaṃ. Yathā ñāṇe sati musāvādo natthi, evaṃ musāvāde sati ñāṇampīti tena taṃ nirodhitaṃ viya hotīti āha – “musāvādena paṭicchannaṃ ñāṇa”nti. Yathā sujāya vinā brāhmaṇānaṃ yāgo na ijjhati, evaṃ pahūtajivhāya vinā satthu dhammayāgo na ijjhatīti jivhā sujāpariyāyā vuttā. Joti ṭhiyati etthāti jotiṭṭhānaṃ vedi, yaṃ aggikuṇḍaṃ. Sattānaṃ hadayaṃ jotiṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇaggino tattha samujjalanato. Attāti cittaṃ “āhito ahaṃ māno etthā”ti katvā.

'Khāribhāro' means like a khāri load. Therefore it is said, 'yathā,' and so on. 'Khandhena vayhamāno' means being carried on the shoulder after being placed in the sling of a carrying pole. It touches the earth due to the heaviness of the load and the bending of the carrying pole. Through pride, one extolling one's own birth and other attributes cannot endure those of another; thus it is said, 'arousing envy here and there.' The intention is that one would sink due to excessively heavy grasping of the grounds for pride, such as birth, here and there. 'Kodho dhūmo' (anger is smoke) means: just as a blazing fire is defiled by smoke, so too is one defiled by anger. For the fire of knowledge, anger is the smoke. False speech is deceitful speech. Just as when there is knowledge, there is no false speech, so too when there is false speech, there is no knowledge; it is as if obstructed by it. Thus it is said, 'knowledge concealed by false speech.' Just as a sacrifice of the brahmins does not succeed without the sujā (sacrificial ladle), so too the Teacher’s Dhamma-sacrifice does not succeed without an abundant tongue; hence the tongue is called a synonym for the sujā. 'Jotiṭṭhānaṃ' is so called because 'the flame stands here'; it is the altar, which is the fire pit. The hearts of beings are the 'place of the flame' for the fire of knowledge, because it blazes up there. 'Attā' means the mind, because of the thought: 'The conceit "I am" is placed here.'

Dhammo rahadoti assaddhiyādiālasiyābhāvato kilesamalapakkhālanato paramagginibbutāvahanato ariyamaggadhammo anāvilo rahado. Heṭṭhupariyavālukāti viparivattitavālukā hutvā. Āluḷāti [M 1.0263] ākulajātā. Paṇḍitānaṃ pasatthoti paṇḍitānaṃ purato seṭṭho. Seṭṭhabhāvena santo pāsaṃso hutvā kilese bhindati samucchindatīti sabbhīti vuccati. Tenāha “uttamaṭṭhenā”ti. Tathā cāha bhagavā “maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho”ti (dha. pa. 273).

'Dhammo rahado' (the Dhamma is a lake) means the Dhamma of the noble path is a clear lake because of its freedom from faithlessness, laziness, and so on; because it washes away the stain of the defilements; and because it brings the extinguishing of the supreme fire. 'Heṭṭhupariyavālukā' means having sand that has been turned over. 'Āluḷā' means having become agitated. 'Paṇḍitānaṃ pasattho' (praised by the wise) means foremost in the presence of the wise. Because it is excellent (seṭṭhabhāvena santo), praiseworthy (pāsaṃso), and breaks and utterly cuts off the defilements (kilese bhindati samucchindati), it is called 'sabbhi' (a good person). Therefore it is said, 'in the highest sense.' And so the Blessed One said: 'Of paths, the eightfold is the best' (Dhp. 273).

Vacīsaccanti iminā “caturaṅgasamannāgatā vācā suparisuddhā hotī”ti sammāvācaṃ dasseti. Saccasaṃyamapadehi dassitā maggadhammā idha “dhammo”ti adhippetāti āha – “dhammoti iminā…pe… dassetī”ti. Maggasaccaṃ gahitaṃ anantaragāthāya anekehi visesetvā vuttattā. Atthatoti pubbaṅgamattādiatthato. Tāya hi sakiccaṃ karontiyā itare sabbepi tadanuvattikā [V 1.0230] honti. Taggatikattāti sammādiṭṭhiyā upakārakabhāvena tāya samānagatikattā. Ārammaṇañhi vitakkenāhaṭaṃ paññā vicinituṃ sakkoti. Tathā hi so paññākkhandhena saṅgahaṃ gato. Dhammoti sabhāvato samādhi gahito, itare dve tadupakārattā. Tathā hi “evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.13; ma. ni. 3.197; saṃ. ni. 5.378) samādhi “dhammo”ti vutto. Paramatthasaccaṃ gahitaṃ sabbesaṃ seṭṭhabhāvato. Yathāha – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34). Atthatoti tato eva paramatthato, anantaraṃ vuccamānānaṃ vā maggadhammānaṃ ārammaṇabhāvato. Pañcaṅgāni gahitāni tāsaṃ maggabhāvato. Tīṇi aṅgāni. Brahmacariyaṃ nāmāti etaṃ nibbānagāmi uttamaṭṭhena maggabrahmacariyaṃ nāma. Majjhe sitāti līnuddhaccādiantadvayavivajjanena majjhe majjhimapaṭipadābhāvanaṃ nissitā. Sassatucchedaggahaṇaṃ hettha padhānatāya nidassanamattaṃ. Seṭṭhappattīti seṭṭhabhāvappatti. Ta-kāro padasandhikaroti “sa ujubhūtesū”ti vattabbe majjhe ta-kāro padasandhikaro, “sa dujjubhūtesūti keci paṭhanti, tesaṃ da-kāro padasandhikaro. Sa-iti sundariko brāhmaṇo vuttoti katvā āha “sa tva”nti, so tvanti attho. Dhammo sāriyo paridhānabhūtā alaṅkārā etassāti dhammasārī. Atha vā dhammehi sāritavāti dhammasārī, tehi sāretvā ṭhitavāti attho. Tenāha “kusaladhammehī”tiādi.

'Truthfulness in speech'—by this, it shows right speech as 'speech endowed with four factors is perfectly pure.' The path-qualities indicated by the terms 'truth' and 'restraint' are here intended as 'Dhamma'—thus it is said: 'By this, Dhamma… it is shown.' The truth of the path is taken because it is spoken of with many distinctions in the immediately following verse. In meaning, from the meaning of being a precursor, etc. For when it performs its function, all the others also follow it. Because it has the same course—due to its supportive role for right view, it has the same course. For wisdom is able to investigate an object brought by thought. Thus, it is included in the aggregate of wisdom. As 'Dhamma', concentration is taken in its nature; the other two are its supports. For in passages like 'Thus, these Blessed Ones are of such Dhamma,' concentration is called 'Dhamma.' The ultimate truth is taken because of its supremacy over all. As it is said: 'Monks, as far as conditioned or unconditioned phenomena go, dispassion is declared the highest among them.' In meaning, from that very ultimate standpoint, or because it is the object of the path-qualities mentioned immediately after. Five factors are taken because they constitute the path. Three factors. 'The holy life' means this path leading to Nibbāna, which is called the holy life of the path in the supreme sense. 'Situated in the middle' means that by avoiding the two extremes of laxity and agitation, etc., one is based on the cultivation of the middle way. The grasping of eternalism and annihilationism here is merely an example due to its prominence. 'Attained the highest' means the attainment of the highest state. The letter 'ta' is a euphonic consonant. Where 'sa ujubhūtesu' should be said, the 'ta' in the middle is a euphonic consonant. Some read 'sa dujjubhūtesu'; for them, the 'da' is a euphonic consonant. 'Sa'—because Sundarika the brahmin was spoken of, it is said 'sa tvaṃ,' meaning 'so tvaṃ' (that you). 'Dhamma is the essence, the garments and ornaments for this one,' thus 'dhammasārī.' Or, 'one directed by the Dhamma' is 'dhammasārī,' meaning 'one who is established, having been directed by them.' Therefore, it is said: 'by wholesome qualities,' etc.

Sundarikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sundarika Sutta is finished.

10. Bahudhītarasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Bahudhītara Sutta

196. Samantatoti [M 1.0264] dakkhiṇavāmānaṃ vasena samantato. Ūrubaddhāsananti ūrūnaṃ bandhanavasena nisajjanaṃ. Dvinnaṃ ūrūnaṃ aññamaññabandhanavasena ābhujitākāraṃ sandhāyāha “ābhujitvāti bandhitvā”ti. Heṭṭhimakāyassa anujukaṃ ṭhapanaṃ nisajjāvacaneneva bodhitanti “ujuṃ kāya”nti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayoti āha “uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Taṃ pana ujukaṭṭhapanaṃ sarūpato payojanato ca dassetuṃ “aṭṭhārasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parimukhanti ettha pari-saddo abhisaddena samānatthoti āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purekkhatoti attho. Pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu viya. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho “suññatavimokkhamukha”ntiādīsu viya. Paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho hi niyyānaṭṭho, tasmā pariggahitaniyyānanti sabbathā gahitasammosaṃ pariccattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā paramaṃ satinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho. Chabbaṇṇā…pe… nisīdi brāhmaṇassa pasādasañjānanatthaṃ. Aṭavimukhā caramānāti gocaraṃ gaṇhantā.

196. 'All around' means on the right and left sides. 'Sitting with thighs bound' means sitting by way of binding the thighs. Referring to the posture of bending by way of binding the two thighs to each other, it says, 'having bent' means 'having bound.' That the lower body is not kept straight is understood by the very word 'sitting'; therefore, in 'straight body,' the word 'body' refers to the upper body. Thus it says, 'having kept the upper body straight.' To show this keeping straight, both in its nature and its purpose, it is said, 'eighteen,' etc. 'Around the mouth' (parimukhaṃ): here the word 'pari' has the same meaning as the word 'abhi'; thus it says, 'facing the meditation object.' The meaning is that, having averted the mind from external, diverse objects, one places only the meditation object before oneself. The meaning is 'grasping' (pariggaha), as in 'guide' (pariṇāyikā), etc. 'Mukha' has the meaning of 'exit', as in 'the entrance to the liberation of emptiness,' etc. For the meaning of 'exit' is the meaning of 'going out from the opposite'. Therefore, 'a grasped exit' means having established mindfulness that has completely abandoned confusion, and having brought to bear supreme vigilance in mindfulness. 'Of six colors…' etc., he sat down for the purpose of generating faith in the brahmin. 'Wandering facing the forest' means gathering alms-food.

Ajjasaṭṭhinti [V 1.0231] ajja channaṃ pūraṇī saṭṭhī divasavutti, ajja ādiṃ katvā cha divaseti attho. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Ajja chadivasamattakāti ajjato chaṭṭhadivasamattakā. Lāmakāti nihīnā nipphalā. Tenāha “tilakhāṇukā”tiādi.

'Ajjasaṭṭhi' means 'today is the sixth, completing six,' a period of days; the meaning is 'six days beginning from today.' And this is a locative of duration. 'Only six days today' means 'only the sixth day from today.' 'Inferior' means 'lowly, fruitless.' Therefore it is said: 'like sesame stalks,' etc.

Ussāhenāti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ pasārena abhibhavanena. Taṃ pana nesaṃ abhibhavanaṃ dassetuṃ “kaṇṇanaṅguṭṭhādīnī”tiādimāha.

'By exertion' means by spreading upwards and upwards, by overpowering. To show that overpowering of theirs, it says: 'the ear, the tail,' etc.

“Uppāṭakapāṇakā”ti tacaṃ uppāṭetvā viya khādakapāṇakā ūkāmaṅgulādayo.

'Creatures that tear' are those that bite as if tearing the skin, such as lice, mites, etc.

Kaḷārapiṅgalāti nikkhantapiṅgalakkhikā, kaḷārapiṅgalāti vā rattagattā ca piṅgalacakkhukā ca. Tilakāhatāti āhatatilakā, tilappamāṇehi bindūhi samantato santhatasarīrā.

'Kaḷārapiṅgalā' means having protruding tawny eyes, or 'kaḷārapiṅgalā' means having red bodies and tawny eyes. 'Tilakāhatā' means 'struck with spots,' having bodies covered all over with spots the size of sesame seeds.

Paṭigāthāhi brāhmaṇassa dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhesīti pakatiyā tassa attanā kathetabbaṃ dhammadesanaṃ pabbajjāguṇakittanavasena sattahi vaḍḍhesi. Pabbajitvāti [M 1.0265] iṇāyikānaṃ attano palibodhaṃ tathā tathā jānāpetvā pabbajitvā.

'With verses in reply, he enhanced the Dhamma teaching for the brahmin' means that he augmented the Dhamma teaching that was to be spoken by himself for him, by way of praising the virtues of going forth with seven verses. 'Having gone forth' means having gone forth after having informed the creditors in various ways about his own impediment.

Yathā ca tattha bhagavā paṭipajji, taṃ dassetuṃ “puna divase”tiādi vuttaṃ.

And to show how the Blessed One conducted himself there, it is said: 'Again on the next day,' etc.

Taṃ taṃ kulagharaṃ pesetvāti taṃ taṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa dhītaraṃ tassa tassānucchavikassa brāhmaṇassa dento taṃ taṃ kulagharaṃ pesetvā brāhmaṇadhamme garukaraṇābhāvato.

'Having sent her to this and that family' means that by giving that daughter of the brahmin to this and that suitable brahmin, he sent her to this and that family, due to not holding the brahminical custom in esteem.

“Naṭṭhe mate pabbajite, napuṃsakepi bhattari;

Itthiyā patiseṭṭhāya, na añño pati icchiyo”ti. –

“When the husband is lost, dead, gone forth, or impotent, no other husband is desired by a woman devoted to her husband.”

Ayañhi brāhmaṇadhammo. Ayyikaṭṭhāneti mātāmahiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi satthu cittārādhanavasenāti.

For this is the brahminical custom. 'In the position of a grandmother' means he placed her in the position of a maternal grandmother for the sake of pleasing the Teacher's mind.

Bahudhītarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bahudhītara Sutta is finished.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Chapter is finished.

2. Upāsakavaggo

2. The Chapter on Lay Followers

1. Kasibhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta

197. Dakkhiṇāgirisminti [V 1.0232] dakkhiṇāgirijanapade, tasmiṃ dakkhiṇāgirijanapade dakkhiṇāgirivihāre. Khandhesu ṭhapetvā yuge yottehīti yottarajjūhi yuttāni payojitāni icceva attho.

197. 'In Dakkhiṇāgiri' means in the Dakkhiṇāgiri country; in that Dakkhiṇāgiri country, in the Dakkhiṇāgiri monastery. 'Having placed the yokes on their shoulders with reins' just means 'yoked and harnessed with yoke-ropes'.

Paṭhamadivaseti vapanadivasesu paṭhamadivase āraddhadivase. Pañcaṅgānipi paripuṇṇāni, pageva itaraṅgānīti dassetuṃ “paripuṇṇapañcaṅgā”icceva vuttaṃ. Haritālamanosilāañjanehi uratthanādīsu ṭhapitattā ābhāya ujjalagattā. Avasesā balībaddā. Kilantagoṇaṃ mocetvā akilantassa yojanaṃ kilantaparivattanaṃ.

'On the first day' means on the first of the sowing days, the day of commencement. To show that the five factors are complete, let alone the other factors, it is said, 'complete with five factors.' Because orpiment, realgar, and collyrium were placed on their chests, humps, etc., their bodies were radiant with splendor. The remaining ones are the draught oxen. Releasing a tired ox and yoking an untired one is 'changing the tired one'.

Sīhakuṇḍalānīti sīhamukhakuṇḍalāni. Brahmaveṭhananti brahmuno veṭhanasadisaṃ, assanakhaveṭhanasadisanti attho.

'Lion-earrings' means lion-faced earrings. 'Brahma-turban' means 'like Brahma's turban'; the meaning is 'like a horse's hoof-turban'.

Buddhānaṃ [M 1.0266] kiccāni kālavasena vibhattāni pañca kiccāni bhavanti. Purebhattakiccanti bhattato pubbe buddhena kātabbakiccaṃ. Vītināmetvāti phalasamāpattiyā kālaṃ vītināmetvā. Kadāci ekotiādi tesaṃ tesaṃ vineyyānaṃ vinayanānurūpapaṭipattidassanaṃ. Pakatiyāti pakatibuddhavesena. Buddhānaṃ hi rūpakāyassa asītianubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍita-bāttiṃsamahāpurisa- lakkhaṇa-kāyappabhā-byāmappabhā-ketumālāvicittatā buddhaveso. Kadāci anekehi pāṭihāriyehi vattamānehīti iminā pāramīnaṃ nissandabhūtāni pāṭihāriyāni rucivaseneva pakāsanakāni bhavanti, na sabbadāti dasseti. Evañca katvā “indakhīlassa anto ṭhapitamatte dakkhiṇapāde”tiādivacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Bhagavato kāye pītarasmīnaṃ yebhuyyatāya “suvaṇṇarasasiñcanāni viyā”ti vatvā kāyamhi nīlādirasmīhi tahaṃ tahaṃ pītamissitaṃ sandhāya “vicitrapaṭaparikkhittāni viya cā”ti vuttaṃ. Madhurenākārena saddaṃ karonti tuṭṭharavaravanato.

The duties of the Buddhas are divided into five according to time. 'Purebhattakicca' refers to the duty the Buddha must perform before the meal. 'Vītināmetvā' means having passed the time in the attainment of fruition. 'Kadāci eko,' etc., refers to the display of conduct suitable for the training of various trainees. 'Pakatiyā' means by the natural manner of a Buddha. For the Buddhas, the natural manner consists of the physical body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics and the thirty-two marks of a great man, radiating light with a fathom-long aura, and variegated with a garland of rays. 'Kadāci anekehi pāṭihāriyehi vattamānehi'—by this, it is shown that the miracles, which are the natural results of the perfections, are displayed according to inclination, not always. And by doing so, statements like 'the right foot having been placed within the Indakhīla' are substantiated. Regarding the Blessed One’s body, since golden rays are predominant, it is said, 'like being sprinkled with liquid gold.' Yet, because blue and other rays are also mixed with the gold here and there on the body, it is described as 'as if wrapped in a variegated garment.' They produce sounds with a sweet quality, from their delightful, excellent sound.

Tatthāti [V 1.0233] vihāre. Gandhamaṇḍalamāḷeti hatthena kataparibhaṇḍe samosaritagandhapupphadāme maṇḍalamāḷe.

‘Tattha’ means in the monastery. ‘Gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe’ means in a circular pavilion, a decorative arrangement made by hand, where garlands of perfumes and flowers are gathered.

Upaṭṭhāneti pamukhe. “Ovadatī”ti vatvā tatthovādaṃ sāmaññato dassetuṃ, “bhikkhave”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sampattīti cakkhādiindriyapāripūri ceva hatthādisampadā ca. Samassāsitakāyo kilamathavinodanena. “Tañca kho samāpajjanenā”ti vadanti. Dutiyabhāgeti iminā aparabhāgaṃ tayo bhāge katvā tattha purimabhāgaṃ seyyanisajjāvasena samāpattīhi vītināmetīti dasseti. Lokanti rājagahādīsu yaṃ tadā upanissāya viharati, tattha aññattha vā bujjhanakaṃ vineyyasattalokaṃ buddhacakkhunā voloketi. Kālayuttanti tesaṃ indriyaparipākakālānurūpaṃ. Samayayuttanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Samayayuttanti vā tehi ājānitabbavisesapaṭilābhānurūpaṃ.

‘Upaṭṭhāne’ means in the forefront. Having said, 'He advises,' to show the advice there in general, 'bhikkhus,' etc., is said. 'Sampatti' means the completeness of faculties such as the eye, and the perfection of hands, etc. The body is refreshed by the dispelling of weariness. 'And that, indeed, is by means of attainment,' they say. By 'in the second part,' it is shown that, having divided the later part into three parts, he spends the first part of it in attainments by way of lying down and sitting. 'Lokaṃ' means he surveys with the Buddha-eye the world of beings to be awakened, whether in Rājagaha and other places where he is then dwelling in dependence, or elsewhere. 'Kālayuttaṃ' means suitable to the time of the maturing of their faculties. 'Samayayuttaṃ' is a synonym for that. Or, 'samayayuttaṃ' means suitable for their attainment of the special distinction that is to be known.

Paṭisallīnoti kālaparicchedaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ samāpanno. Adhippāyaṃ sampādento taṃ avirādhento, ajjhāsayānurūpanti attho.

‘Paṭisallīno’ means having entered into meditative attainment after determining a period of time. Fulfilling the intention, not failing in it; 'in accordance with one's inclination' is the meaning.

Sakala…pe… devatāyoti ettha lokadhātusākalyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na devatāsākalyaṃ. Na hi mahāsamaye viya sabbadā majjhimayāme dasasahassacakkavāḷe [M 1.0267] sabbattha sabbā devatā satthu samīpaṃ upagacchanti. Kilāsubhāvo kilamatho.

In the phrase 'sakala… devatāyo,' the entirety of the world-system should be understood, not the entirety of the deities. For not all deities from all ten thousand world-systems always approach the Teacher in the middle watch of the night, as they did during the Great Assembly. The state of being weary is exhaustion.

Vihāracīvaraparivattanavasenāti vihāre nivatthanivāsanaparivattanavasena. Ādiyitvāti pārupanavasena gahetvā. Tenāha “dhāretvā”ti. Bhikkhācāranti bhikkhatthaṃ caritabbaṭṭhānaṃ.

'Vihāracīvaraparivattanavasena' means by way of exchanging the lower garment worn in the dwelling. 'Ādiyitvā' means having taken for the purpose of wearing. Hence it is said, 'dhāretvā.' 'Bhikkhācāraṃ' means the place where one should wander for alms.

Atirocamānanti taṃ taṃ atikkamitvā samantato sabbadisāsu virocamānaṃ. Sarīrappabhanti attano sarīrappabhaṃ. Jaṅgamaṃ viya padumasaranti ratanamayakiñjakkhaṃ rajatamayakaṇṇikaṃ samantato samphullitakañcanapadumaṃ sañcārimasaraṃ viya. Gaganatalanti abbhamahikādiupakkilesavigamena suvisuddhaākāsatalaṃ viya. Tampi hi tārāgaṇakiraṇajālasamujjalatāya samantato virocati. Kanakasikharanti kanakagirisikharaṃ. Siriyā jalamānanti sabbaso anavajjāya sabbākārena paripuṇṇakāyatāya anaññasādhāraṇāya rūpakāyasiriyā samujjalaṃ, yassā rucirabhāvo viddhe vigatavalāhake puṇṇamāsiyaṃ paripuṇṇakalamanomamaṇḍalaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ atirocati, pabhassarabhāvo sahassaraṃsikiraṇatejojālasamujjalaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ abhibhavati, hemasamujjalabhāvo [V 1.0234] tadubhaye abhibhuyya pavattamānaṃ ekakkhaṇe dasasahassilokadhātuvijjotanasamattha-mahābrahmuno pabhāsamudayaṃ abhivihacca bhāsati tapati virocati.

'Atirocamānaṃ' means shining all around in every direction, surpassing this and that. 'Sarīrappabhaṃ' means his own bodily radiance. 'Jaṅgamaṃ viya padumasaraṃ' means like a moving pond with jeweled filaments, a silver pericarp, and fully bloomed golden lotuses all around. 'Gaganatalaṃ' means like the expanse of the sky, utterly pure due to the departure of defilements such as clouds and mist. For that too shines all around with the brilliance of the net of rays from the host of stars. 'Kanakasikharaṃ' means the peak of a golden mountain. 'Siriyā jalamānaṃ' means blazing with the glory of his physical form, which is entirely flawless, perfect in body in every way, and not shared by others; the delightful quality of which outshines the full, spotless, and pleasing orb of the moon on a clear, cloudless full-moon night; the luminous quality of which surpasses the sun's orb, resplendent with the blaze of its thousand-rayed splendor; the golden resplendence of which, surpassing both, shines, blazes, and is brilliant, excelling the arising of the radiance of a Great Brahmā, which is capable of illuminating ten thousand world-systems in a single moment.

Samantapāsādiketi samantato pasādāvahe. Tañca kho sabbaso saritabbatāyāti āha “pasādanīye”ti. Uttamadamathasamathamanuppatteti kāyavācāhi anuttaraṃ dantabhāvañceva anuttaraṃ cittavūpasamañca sampatte. Appasādenāti pasādābhāvena, pasādapaṭikkhepena vā assaddhiyena. Ubhayathāpi noti appasādo macchariyanti ubhayathāpi no eva, atha kho anattamanatāya upārambhādhippāyena apasādento, bhagavato mukhato kiñci desetukāmo vā evamāha. Tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “bhagavato panā”tiādimāha. Atittanti tittiṃ agacchantaṃ. Kammabhaṅganti kammahāniṃ.

'Samantapāsādike' means inspiring confidence all around. And because it should be remembered in every way, it is said to be 'pasādanīye.' 'Uttamadamathasamathamanuppattaṃ' means having attained the unsurpassed state of being tamed in body and speech, and the unsurpassed stilling of the mind. 'Appasādena' means through lack of confidence, or through rejection of confidence, through faithlessness. 'Ubhayathāpi no' means it is not in either way, that is, neither lack of confidence nor stinginess; rather, finding fault out of displeasure, or wishing to have the Blessed One teach something, he speaks thus. Showing the reason for this, he says, 'bhagavato pana,' etc. 'Atittaṃ' means not reaching satisfaction. 'Kammabhaṅgaṃ' means the ruin of the work.

Tikkhapañño esa brāhmaṇo, tathā hi na cirasseva arahattaṃ sacchikarissati. Kathāpavattanatthampi evamāha – “evaṃ ahaṃ imassa kañci dhammaṃ sotuṃ [M 1.0268] labhissāmī”ti. Veneyyavasenāti attano kasanakāribhāvakittanamukhena vinetabbapuggalavasena.

This brahmin is of sharp wisdom, for he will realize arahantship before long. He also speaks thus for the purpose of continuing the conversation, thinking: 'In this way, I will get to hear some Dhamma from him.' 'Veneyyavasena' means in the manner of a person to be trained, by way of praising his own state as a cultivator.

Oḷārikānīti pākatikāni. “Esa uttamadakkhiṇeyyo”ti sañjātabahumāno. Pāḷiyaṃ “yugaṃ vā naṅgalaṃ vā”ti vā-saddo avuttavikappattho. Tena bījādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, tasmā bījaṃ vā īsaṃ vā pariggahayottāni vāti ayamattho dassito hoti. Tathā hi bhagavā brāhmaṇassa paṭivacanaṃ dento “saddhā bīja”ntiādimāha. Pubbadhammasabhāgatāyāti paṭhamaṃ gahitadhammasabhāgatāya. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāruḷhameva gahetabbañca saddato atthāpattito vā idha daṭṭhabbaṃ. Buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo ayaṃ, yadidaṃ pasaṅgāgatadhammamukhena desanaṃ ārabhitvā veneyyavinayanaṃ.

'Oḷārikāni' means the ordinary ones. 'This is the supreme recipient of offerings'—thus much respect arose in him. In the Pāli, the word 'vā' in 'yugaṃ vā naṅgalaṃ vā' has the meaning of an unstated alternative. By this, it includes seeds and so on; therefore, the meaning 'seeds or a plow-shaft or reins for grasping' is shown. For indeed, the Blessed One, giving a reply to the brahmin, said, 'faith is the seed,' and so on. 'Pubbadhammasabhāgatāya' means by having a share in the Dhamma grasped previously. Whatever should be said here, that which is established in the commentary should be taken, and it should be understood here either from the letter of the text or by inference of meaning. This is the power of the Buddhas: that they begin a teaching through a topic that has arisen from the occasion and thereby train the trainable.

Ananusandhikāti pucchānusandhivasena ananusandhikā. Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena. Etthāti etissā desanāya. Soti bhagavā. Tassāti brāhmaṇassa. Anukampāyāti asabbaññū hi satipi anukampāya pucchitamatte tiṭṭheyya, tathā jānantopi ananukampako, bhagavā pana ubhayadhammapāripūriyā “idaṃ apucchita”nti aparihāpetvā katheti. Samūlantiādinā saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tattha bījassa kasiyā mūlabhāvo nānantariyato tappamāṇavidhānato cāti āha “tasmiṃ…pe… kattabbato”ti. Tena anvayato byatirekato ca [V 1.0235] bījassa kasiyā mūlabhāvaṃ vibhāveti. Kusalāti iminā akusalā tato aññathāpi karonti, taṃ pana appamāṇanti dasseti.

'Ananusandhikā' means not connected by way of a sequence of questions. 'Evaṃ' means in the manner now being spoken. 'Ettha' means in this teaching. 'So' refers to the Blessed One. 'Tassa' refers to the brahmin. 'Anukampāya'—for one who is not all-knowing, even if compassionate, would stop at what was asked; and one who knows but is uncompassionate would likewise. But the Blessed One, due to the perfection of both qualities, speaks without omitting anything on the grounds that 'this was not asked.' With 'samūlaṃ,' etc., he explains the meaning stated in brief, elaborating with 'tattha,' etc. There, the root-nature of the seed for cultivation is due to its being the immediate basis and because of the determination of its measure; thus he says, 'tasmiṃ… kattabbato.' Through this, both by way of affirmation and negation, he clarifies the root-nature of the seed for cultivation. 'Kusalā'—by this, he shows that the unskillful also act otherwise, but that is of no account.

Tassāti brāhmaṇassa bījaṭṭhāniyassa dhammassa ca upakārabhāvato. Dhammasambandhasamatthabhāvatoti tathā vuttadhammassa phalena sambandhituṃ yojetuṃ samatthabhāvato. Tapo vuṭṭhīti vuttavacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “ayaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kassakassa upakārassa bījassa anantaraṃ vuṭṭhi vuccamānā aṭṭhāne vuttā nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Bījassa vappakāle anurūpāya vuṭṭhiyā icchitabbato, tasmā avasāne majjhe vā vuccamānāya dhammasambandhasamatthatā tassā vibhāvitā na siyā. Attano avisayeti jhānādiuttarimanussadhamme. Pacchāpīti kasisambhārakathanato pacchāpi. Vattabboti ekantena vattabbo. Tadanantaraṃyevāti bījānantaraṃyeva. Vuccamānā vuṭṭhi samatthā hoti[M 1.0269], bījassa phalena sambandhane samatthāti dīpitā hoti anantaravacaneneva tassā āsannaupakārattadīpanato.

'Of that' refers to the Brahmin, and to the Dhamma which is in the position of a seed, due to its supportive nature. 'The ability to connect with the Dhamma' means the ability to connect and join the aforesaid Dhamma with its fruit. 'Austerity is rain' is said with reference to the aforesaid statement. To make clear the meaning stated in brief, 'for this is...' and so on is said. The rain, when mentioned immediately after the seed which is a support to the farmer, is not said out of place. Why? Because suitable rain is desired at the time of sowing the seed; therefore, if it were mentioned at the end or in the middle, its ability to connect with the Dhamma would not be made clear. 'Beyond one's own scope' refers to supramundane states such as the jhānas. 'Even afterwards' means even after the discussion of the requisites for ploughing. 'It should be stated' means it should be stated definitively. 'Immediately thereafter' means immediately after the seed. Rain, being mentioned, is capable; it is shown to be capable of connecting the seed with its fruit, because the immediately following statement reveals its nature as a proximate support.

Sampasādalakkhaṇāti pasīditabbe vatthusmiṃ sammadeva pasīdanalakkhaṇā. Okappanalakkhaṇāti saddheyyavatthuno evametanti pakkhandanalakkhaṇā. Mūlabījantiādīsu mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi bījagāmassa adhippetattā. Bhūtagāmo pana mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassāti mūlabījantiādinā veditabbo. Bījabījanti pañcamaṃ pana paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato virūhanasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bījasaddo tadatthasiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti tato nivattanatthaṃ ekena bīja-saddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “bījabīja”nti “dukkhadukkhaṃ rūparūpa”nti ca yathā. Evampi iminā atthena imassapi nippariyāyova bījabhāvoti dassento āha “taṃ sabbampi…pe… gacchatī”ti.

'The characteristic of clarity' is the characteristic of becoming perfectly serene regarding an object about which one should be serene. 'The characteristic of conviction' is the characteristic of leaping forward to a credible object, thinking, 'It is so.' In 'root-seed' and so on, the root itself is the seed, hence 'root-seed.' This is the method for the others as well, since the category of seeds is intended. But the category of plants should be understood by 'root-seed' and so on, meaning 'the root is its seed.' As for 'seed-seed,' the fifth: because it is a special cause for the production of a similar fruit when other conditions are present, the word 'seed' is established in the sense of an essential fruit capable of sprouting. Since, to accomplish that meaning, it is also applied in some cases to roots and so on, it is specified with an additional word 'seed'—'seed-seed'—in order to distinguish it from that usage, just as in 'suffering-suffering' or 'form-form.' Even so, showing that by this meaning, this too has a seed-nature without qualification, he said: 'All that... proceeds.'

Idāni kathañci vattabbe saddhāya opammatte bīje saddhāya bījabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “tattha yathā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Kāmaṃ saddhūpanisaṃ sīlaṃ, tathāpi samādhissa viya sabbesampi anavajjadhammānaṃ ādimūlabhāvato saddhāyapi patiṭṭhā hotīti āha “heṭṭhā sīlamūlena patiṭṭhātī”ti. Yasmā sabbasseva puggalassa saddhāvasena samathavipassanārambho, tasmā sā “upari samathavipassanaṅkuraṃ uṭṭhāpetī”ti vuttā. Tanti dhaññabījaṃ. Pathavirasaṃ āporasanti sasambhārapathavīāpesu labbhamānaṃ rasaṃ. Gahetvāti paccayaparamparāya gahetvā. Dhaññaparipākagahaṇatthanti dhaññaparipākanibbattiatthaṃ. Rasanti saddhāsīlamūlahetusamathavipassanābhāvanārasaṃ ādiyitvā. Ariyamagganāḷenāti ariyamaggasotena ariyaphaladhaññaparipākagahaṇatthanti ariyaphalameva [V 1.0236] dhanāyitabbato dhaññaṃ tassa nibbattiatthaṃ. Dhaññanāḷaṃ nāma kaṇḍassa nissayabhūto pacchimadeso, kaṇḍo tabbhantaro taṃnissayoyeva daṇḍo. Pasavo nāma pupphaṃ. Vuddhinti avayavapāripūrivasena vuddhiṃ. Virūḷhinti mūlasantānadaḷhatāya viruḷhataṃ. Vepullanti pattanāḷādīhi vipulabhāvaṃ. Khīraṃ janetvāti taruṇasalāṭukabhāvappattiyā taṇḍulassa bījassa bījabhūtaṃ khīraṃ uppādetvā. Esāti saddhā. Patiṭṭhahitvāti kammapathākammapathasammādiṭṭhisahitena ādito pavattasīlamattena patiṭṭhahitvā. Vuddhintiādīsu suparisuddhāhi sīlacittavisuddhīhi vuddhiṃ, diṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhīhi virūḷhiṃ. Maggāmaggapaṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīhi vepullaṃ patvā. Ñāṇadassanavisuddhikhīranti [M 1.0270] sādurasasuvisuddhibhāvato ñāṇadassanavisuddhisaṅkhātaṃ khīraṃ janetvā. Aneka…pe… phalanti anekapaṭisambhidā-anekābhiññāṇaparipuṇṇaṃ arahattaphalasīsaṃ nipphādeti.

Now, since faith should be spoken of, with the seed as a simile for faith, the passage 'therein, just as...' and so on was begun in order to reveal the seed-nature of faith. Granted, virtue has faith as its supporting condition, yet just as for concentration, because it is the initial root of all blameless qualities, faith too is a foundation; thus it is said, 'It is established below with the root of virtue.' Since for every individual the beginning of serenity and insight arises through faith, therefore it is said, 'It makes the sprout of serenity and insight grow above.' That is the grain seed. 'Earth-essence, water-essence' means the essence obtained from earth and water with their constituents. 'Having taken' means having taken through a succession of conditions. 'For the purpose of ripening the grain' means for the purpose of producing the ripened grain. 'Essence' refers to taking up the essence of the development of serenity and insight, which is rooted in faith and virtue. 'Through the stalk of the noble path' means through the stream of the noble path. 'For the purpose of ripening the noble fruit-grain' means for the purpose of producing the noble fruit, which, being desirable, is the grain. The 'grain-stalk' (nāḷa) is the final part which is the basis for the stem (kaṇḍa); the stem is its interior, and the main stalk (daṇḍo) is dependent on that. 'Offspring' (pasavo) refers to the flower. 'Growth' means growth through the completeness of the parts. 'Flourishing' means flourishing due to the firmness of the root system. 'Abundance' refers to the fullness through the expansion of leaves and stalks. 'Having produced milk' means having generated the milk that is the seed of the rice grain upon its reaching the state of a tender, unripe ear. 'This' refers to faith. 'Having been established' means having been established from the beginning with mere virtue, accompanied by right view concerning the path of action and non-action. In 'growth' and so on, growth is through the perfectly pure purities of virtue and mind; flourishing is through the purities of view and of overcoming doubt; abundance is attained through the purities of knowledge and vision of the path and not-path, and of the way. 'The milk of the purity of knowledge and vision' means having generated the milk called the purity of knowledge and vision, due to its delicious and very pure nature. 'Many... fruits' means it produces the pinnacle of the fruit of arahantship, complete with the many analytical knowledges and the many direct knowledges.

Bījakiccakaraṇatoti bījakiccassa karaṇato. Yañhi taṃsadisassa visadisassa ca attano phalassa patiṭṭhāpanasambandhananipphādanasaṅkhātaṃ bījassa kiccaṃ, tassa karaṇato nibbattanato “evaṃ saddhā bījakicca”nti vuttaṃ. Iminā anaññasādhāraṇaṃ saddhāya kusaladhammānaṃ bījabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sā cātiādinā tamevatthaṃ samattheti. Idāni tattha āgamaṃ dassento “saddhājāto”tiādimāha. Tena yathā sappurisūpanissayassa saddhammassavanassa ca, evaṃ anavasesāya sammāpaṭipattiyā saddhā mūlakāraṇanti dasseti.

'Because of performing the function of a seed' means because of performing the function of a seed. For the function of a seed is described as establishing, connecting, and producing its own fruit, whether similar or dissimilar; because of performing and accomplishing this, it is said, 'Thus, faith has the function of a seed.' By this, he shows that faith's nature as a seed for wholesome qualities is not shared by anything else. The phrase 'and that' and so on supports this very meaning. Now, presenting the scriptural authority for this, he says, 'born of faith,' etc. By this, he shows that just as for reliance on good people and listening to the true Dhamma, so too for the entire right practice, faith is the root cause.

Indriyasaṃvaro vīriyañca akusaladhamme, dukkarakārikā dhutaṅgañca akusaladhamme ceva kāyañca tapati vibādhatīti tapoti vuccati. Indriyasaṃvaro adhippeto vīriyassa dhorayhabhāvena gayhamānattā, itaresaṃ vuṭṭhibhāvassa anuyuñjamānattā. Ādi-saddena kalalaṅgāravuṭṭhiādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Samanuggahitanti upagataṃ. Viruhanāmilāyananipphattivacanehi dhaññabījasantānassa viya tesaṃ vuddhiyā saddhābījasantānassa tapovuṭṭhiyā ādimajjhapariyosānesu upakārataṃ dasseti.

Sense-restraint and effort burn up unwholesome states; difficult practice and ascetic observances burn up and torment both unwholesome states and the body—thus they are called 'austerity' (tapo). Sense-restraint is intended, since effort is included due to its nature as a beast of burden, and since the others are connected with the state of being rain. The term 'and so on' includes things like mud-rain and ember-rain. 'Supported' means approached. Through terms like 'sprouting,' 'withering,' and 'ripening,' it shows the supportive nature of the rain of austerity for the continuity of the seed of faith in the beginning, middle, and end, just as for the growth of the continuity of a grain-seed.

Purimapadesupīti api-saddena parapadesupīti attho daṭṭhabbo “hirī me īsā, mano me yotta”nti icchitattā, “sati me”ti ettha me-saddo ānetvā yojetabbo. Udakampi tāva dātabbaṃ hoti nadītaḷākādito ānetvā. Vīriyabalībadde catubbidhe yojetvā. Niccakālaṃ atthīti vacanaseso.

'Even in the earlier sections'—due to the word 'api,' the meaning should also be understood as 'in later sections,' as is intended in 'Shame is my pole, mind is my yoke.' In 'mindfulness is my...,' the word 'me' should be brought in and connected. First, even water must be given, bringing it from rivers, ponds, and so on. The four kinds of effort should be yoked like strong oxen. The remainder of the statement is, 'It exists at all times.'

Saha vipassanāya maggapaññā adhippetā amatapphalāya kasiyā adhippetattā. Vipassanā paññā [V 1.0237] cāti duvidhāpi paññā upanissayā hoti visiṭṭhabhāvato. Tenāha “yathā hī”tiādi. Paññāti pakārehi jānātīti paññā. Paññavataṃ paññā purato hoti yonisomanasikārassa visesapaccayabhāvato, sahajātādhipatīsu ca ukkaṭṭhabhāvato. Sirīti sobhaggaṃ. Sataṃ dhammā saddhādayo, anvāyikāti anugāmino. Īsābaddhā hotīti hirisaṅkhātaīsāya baddhā hoti[M 1.0271], paññāya kadāci appayogato manosīsena samādhi idha vuttoti āha “manosaṅkhātassa samādhiyottassā”ti. Samaṃ upanetvā bandhitvā baddharajjukattā samādhiyottaṃ. Ekato gamananti līnaccāraddhasaṅkhātaṃ ekapassato gamanaṃ vāreti. Majjhimāya vipassanāvīthiyā paṭipādanato kāyādīsu subhasukhaniccattabhāvavigamane paññāya visesapaccayā satīti vuttaṃ – “satiyuttā paññā”ti tassā sativippayogāsabbhāvato. Santatighanādīnaṃ ayaṃ viseso – purimapacchimānaṃ dhammānaṃ nirantaratāya ekībhūtānaṃ viya pavatti santatighanatā, ekasamūhavasena ekībhūtānamiva pavatti samūhaghanatā, dubbiññeyyakiccabhedavasena ekībhūtānamiva pavatti. Kiccaghanatā, ekārammaṇavasena ekībhūtānamiva pavatti ārammaṇaghanatā. Sabbesaṃ, sabbāni vā kilesānaṃ mūlasantānakāni sabba…pe… santānakāni. Anuppayogo hi attho. Padāletīti bhindati samucchindati. Sā ca kho “padāletī”ti vuttā lokuttarāva paññā anusayappahānassa adhippetattā. Santatighanādibhedanā pana lokiyāpi hoti vipassanāvasena ghanavinibbhogassa nipphādanato. Tenāha “itarā pana lokikāpi siyā”ti.

Together with insight, path-wisdom is intended, as it is intended for the cultivation leading to the deathless fruit. Both insight-wisdom and path-wisdom serve as a decisive support condition due to their distinguished nature. Hence it is said, “Just as…” and so on. “Wisdom” (paññā) is so called because it knows in various ways. For the wise, wisdom comes first due to its being a special condition for wise attention, and because it excels among the co-arisen dominants. “Splendor” (sirī) means magnificence. The qualities of the virtuous, such as faith, are “followers” (anvāyikā), meaning they accompany. “It is bound by the pole” (īsābaddhā hoti) means it is bound by the pole called moral shame (hiri). Here, concentration is sometimes mentioned as the mind’s pole due to the occasional non-application of wisdom. Hence it is said, “of the yoke of concentration, which is known as the mind.” It is called the yoke of concentration because it binds evenly, like a fastened rope. “Going to one side” (ekato gamanaṃ) prevents going to one extreme, which is characterized by sluggishness or over-exertion. Because it guides along the middle path of insight, wisdom is a special condition for the removal of the notions of beauty, pleasure, and permanence regarding the body, etc. Hence it is said, “wisdom yoked with mindfulness,” due to the impossibility of wisdom being separated from mindfulness. This is the distinction of continuity-compactness, etc.: continuity-compactness (santatighanatā) is the uninterrupted flow of preceding and succeeding phenomena, appearing as if unified. Mass-compactness (samūhaghanatā) is their appearance as a single mass due to their collective nature. Function-compactness (kiccaghanatā) is their appearance as unified due to the division of functions being hard to discern. Object-compactness (ārammaṇaghanatā) is their appearance as unified due to sharing a single object. All, or all the root-continuities of the defilements… their continuities. Non-application is indeed the meaning. “It shatters” (padāleti) means it breaks and utterly destroys. This wisdom, called “shattering,” is exclusively supramundane, as it is intended for the abandonment of latent tendencies. However, the breaking of continuity-compactness, etc., can also be mundane, as it accomplishes the dissolution of compactness through insight. Hence it is said, “but the other may also be mundane.”

Hirīyatīti lajjati, jigucchatīti attho. Tasmā “pāpakehi dhammehī”ti nissakkavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, hetumhi vā karaṇavacanaṃ. Ottappampi gahitameva, na hi lajjanaṃ nibbhayaṃ pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthīti. Rukkhalaṭṭhīti rukkhadaṇḍo. Tena padesena kasanato visesato naṅgalanti vuccatīti āha “īsā yuganaṅgalaṃ dhāretī”ti. Kāmaṃ paññārahitā hirī atthi, hirirahitā pana paññā natthevāti āha “hiri…pe… abhāvato”ti. Sandhiṭṭhāne kampanābhāvato acalaṃ. Thirabhāvena asithilaṃ. Hiripaṭibaddhapaññā paṭipakkhavasena ca asithilabhāvena ca acalā asithilāti āha “abbokiṇṇā ahirikenā”ti. Nāḷiyā minamānapuriso viya ārammaṇaṃ munāti paricchedato jānātīti mano. Manosīsenāti manaso apadesena. Taṃsampayuttoti iminā kuntasahacaraṇato puriso kunto viya manasahacaraṇasamādhi “mano”ti vuttoti dasseti. Sārathināti kassakena. So hi idha balībaddānaṃ sāraṇato pācanato “sārathī”ti adhippeto. Ekābandhananti ekābaddhakaraṇaṃ. Sakakicceti sakakiccena yutte. Tena hi īsādīsu [M 1.0272] yathārahaṃ bandhitvā ekābaddhesu katesu naṅgalesu kiccaṃ ijjhati, no aññathāti taṃ “sakakicce paṭipādetī”ti vuttaṃ. Avikkhepasabhāvenāti attano avikkhepasabhāvena[V 1.0238]. Bandhitvāti sahajātādipaccayabhāvena attanā sambandhitvā. Sakakicceti hirīādīhi yathāsakaṃ kattabbe kicce.

“One feels moral shame” (hirīyati) means one is ashamed, one is disgusted. Therefore, regarding “from evil qualities,” the ablative case should be understood, or the instrumental case in the sense of cause. Moral dread is also included, for there is no shame that is fearless, nor is there fear of evil that is shameless. “A wooden staff” (rukkhalatthī) means a wooden stick. Due to its use in plowing, it is specifically called a plow, hence it is said, “the pole supports the yoke and plough.” Although shame may exist without wisdom, wisdom is utterly absent without shame—thus it is said, “shame… due to its absence.” Because it does not waver in its joint, it is unshaken. Due to its firmness, it is not slack. Wisdom bound with shame is unshaken and not slack through opposition and unwavering firmness—thus it is said, “unmixed with shamelessness.” Like a person measuring with a reed, the mind (mano) knows the object by delimitation—thus it is called “mind.” “By the mind’s pole” (manosīsena) means by the mind’s designation. “Associated with that” (taṃsampayutta) indicates that just as a man is called a spearman from his association with a spear, so too is concentration, from its association with the mind, called “mind.” “By the charioteer” (sārathinā) refers to the plowman. For he is called “charioteer” here because he guides and urges the oxen. “Making one-bound” (ekābandhana) means making them bound as one. “In its own duty” (sakakicce) means engaged in its own duty. Thus, when the pole and other parts are properly bound together as one, the work of the plough succeeds—not otherwise—hence it is said, “it accomplishes its own duty.” “By its nature of non-distraction” (avikkhepasabhāvena) means by its own nature of non-distraction. “Having bound” (bandhitvā) means having connected with itself by way of co-nascence and other conditions. “In its own duty” (sakakicce) means in the duty to be performed by each—shame and the rest—as required.

Cirakatādimatthanti cirabhāsitampi atthaṃ. Sarati anussarati kāyādiṃ asubhādito nijjhāyati. Phāletīti padāleti. Pājenti gamentīti taṃ pājanaṃ. Idha imasmiṃ sutte “pācana”nti vuttaṃ ja-kārassa ca-kāraṃ katvā. Phālapācananti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā hi brāhmaṇa…pe… satī”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni tamatthaṃ vitthārato dassento “tattha yathā”tiādimāha. Naṅgalaṃ anurakkhati bhijjanaphālanato. Purato cassa gacchatīti assa naṅgalassa kassane bhūmiyā vilikhane purato gacchati pubbaṅgamā hoti. Gatiyoti pavattiyo. Samanvesamānāti saraṇavasena gavesamānā. Ārammaṇe vā kāyādike upaṭṭhāpayamānā asubhādivasena paññānaṅgalaṃ rakkhati. Sabhāvāsabhāvūpagame phālo viya naṅgalassa “ārakkhā”ti vuttā “sabbānatthato sati rakkhatī”ti katvā. Tathā hesā ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā. Cirakatacirabhāsitānaṃ asammussanavasena sati paññānaṅgalassa purato hotīti vatvā tassa puratobhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “sati…pe… no pamuṭṭhe”ti āha. Satipariciteti satiyā paṭṭhāpite. “Upaṭṭhāpite”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Saṃsīdituṃ na detīti sakiccakiriyāya saṃsīdanaṃ kātuṃ na deti. Kosajjasaṅkhātaṃ saṃsīdanaṃ kosajjasaṃsīdanaṃ.

“What was done long ago, etc.” refers to things done and also spoken long ago. “One remembers” (sarati) means one recollects; one contemplates the body and so on, beginning with the impure. “It splits” (phāleti) means it shatters. “They drive” (pājenti) means they make go, hence “driving” (pājana). Here, in this discourse, “pācana” is said by changing the letter ‘ja’ to ‘ca’. To explain the meaning of “ploughshare and goad” (phālapācana), it is said, “Just as a brahmin… mindfulness.” Now, to explain that meaning in detail, he says, “There, just as…” It protects the plow from breaking and splitting. “It goes before it” (purato cassa gacchati) means it goes before the plow in plowing, in furrowing the ground; it is the forerunner. “Courses” (gatiyo) means occurrences. “Investigating” (samanvesamānā) means searching by means of recollection. Or, by establishing the mind on objects such as the body, in terms of the impure and so on, it protects the plow of wisdom. Just as the ploughshare is protection for the plow when encountering suitable and unsuitable conditions, so too is mindfulness said to be “protection,” because “mindfulness protects from all harm.” Thus, its characteristic is protection. Having stated that mindfulness, by way of not forgetting what was done or spoken long ago, goes before the plow of wisdom, it is said, “Mindfulness… not forgotten,” to show its being in front. “Familiarized by mindfulness” (satiparicite) means established by mindfulness. There is also a reading as “upaṭṭhāpite,” the meaning is the same. “It does not allow sinking” means it does not allow sinking in the performance of its own task. The sinking of laziness is sinking that is characterized as laziness.

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttaṃ kāyikavācasikasaṃyamassa kathitattā. Āhāre udare yatoti paribhuñjitabbaāhāre saṃyatabhāvadassanena paribhuñjitabbatāya catūsupi paccayesu saṃyatabhāvo dīpitoti āha “āhāramukhenā”tiādi. Saṃyatabhāvo cettha paccayahetu anesanābhāvoti vuttaṃ “nirupakkilesoti attho”ti. Bhojanasaddo āhāraparibhoge niruḷhoti katvā vuttaṃ “bhojane mattaññutāmukhenā”ti. Paribhuñjanaṭṭhena pana bhojanasaddamukhenāti vutte adhippetattho labbhateva. Tenāti kāyaguttātiādivacanena. Na vilumpantīti “dīpetī”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandho.

The virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is spoken of because bodily and verbal restraint has been mentioned. Regarding “restrained in food, in the belly”: by showing restraint in food that is to be consumed, restraint in all four requisites is demonstrated, as stated: “through the entry-point of food,” etc. Here, this state of restraint regarding the requisites means the absence of improper seeking; hence it is said, “the meaning is without defilements.” The word “bhojana” is conventionally used in the sense of consuming nourishment, hence it is said, “through the entry-point of moderation in food.” Yet, by speaking of the word “bhojana” in the sense of consuming, the intended meaning is indeed obtained. Therefore, by the phrase “guarding the body,” etc., the connection with “they do not plunder” is made by supplying the word “demonstrates.”

Dvīhākārehīti [M 1.0273] adiṭṭhādīnaṃ adiṭṭhādivasena diṭṭhādīnañca diṭṭhādivasenāti evaṃ dvippakārehi. Avisaṃvādanaṃ avitathakathanaṃ. Chedanaṃ mūlappadese nikantanaṃ. Lunanaṃ yattha katthaci chedanaṃ. Uppāṭanaṃ ummūlanaṃ. Asitenāti dattena, lāyitenāti attho. Visaṃvādanasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇānaṃ, aṭṭhannaṃ anariyavohārānanti attho. Yathābhūtañāṇanti nāma rūpaparicchedakañāṇaṃ. Saccanti veditabbaṃ aviparītavuttikattā “chedakaṃ” chindanakaṃ. Niddānanti niddāyakaṃ. Idameva saccaṃ [V 1.0239] moghamaññanti diṭṭhi “diṭṭhisacca”nti vuccati. Dvīsu vikappesūti bhāvakattusādhanavasena dvīsu vikappesu. “Niddāna”nti upayogavaseneva attho.

“In two ways” (dvīhākārehi) means thus in two modes: regarding the unseen, etc., in the manner of the unseen, etc., and regarding the seen, etc., in the manner of the seen, etc. “Non-deception” (avisaṃvādanaṃ) means speaking what is not untrue. “Cutting” (chedanaṃ) means cutting at the root. “Mowing” (lunanaṃ) means cutting anywhere. “Uprooting” (uppāṭanaṃ) means pulling out by the roots. “By a sickle” (asitena) means by a scythe; the meaning is “by reaping.” Of the weeds known as deception, meaning, of the eight ignoble ways of speech. “Knowledge of things as they are” (yathābhūtañāṇa) is the knowledge that discerns name and form. “Truth” (saccaṃ) should be understood as that which has a non-perverted nature. “Cutting” (chedakaṃ) means that which cuts. “A weeding tool” (niddānaṃ) means that which weeds. The view, “This alone is truth, all else is vain,” is called “truth of view” (diṭṭhisacca). “In two alternatives” (dvīsu vikappesu) means in two alternatives based on derivation as an abstract noun and as an agent noun. “Niddāna” has the meaning of purpose alone.

Sīlameva “soracca”nti vuttaṃ “pāṇātipātādīhi suṭṭhu oratassa kamma”nti katvā. Saṅkhāradukkhādīnaṃ abhāvato sundarabhāvato sundare nibbāne ārammaṇakaraṇavasena ratattā surato, arahā. Tassa bhāvo soraccaṃ, arahattaṃ. Appamocanameva accantāya pamocanaṃ na hoti.

Virtue itself is called 'soracca,' because it is 'the action of one who has thoroughly abstained from killing living beings and so forth.' Because of the absence of the suffering of formations and the like, and because of its beautiful nature, one delights in the beautiful Nibbāna by way of making it an object—thus, one is a 'surata,' an Arahant. The state of that one is 'soracca,' Arahantship. A partial release is not an ultimate release.

Yadaggena vipassanāya paññāya taṃsahagatavīriyassa ca naṅgaladhorayhatā, tathāpavattakusalabhāvanāya ca kasibhāvo ca, tadaggena tato puretaraṃ pavattapaññāvīriyapāramīnaṃ naṅgaladhorayhatā, tathāpavattakusalabhāvanāya ca kasibhāvo veditabboti dassento “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Dhuraṃ vahatīti dhorayhaṃ. Yathāvuttaṃ ghananti asmimānādibhedaṃ ghanaṃ. Vahitabbā ādibhūtā dhurā etesaṃ atthīti dhurā, purimadhuravāhakā. Taṃmūlakā aparaṃ dhuraṃ vahantā dhorayhā. Dhurā ca dhorayhā ca dhuradhorayhaṃ ekattavasena. Vahantanti kasanena pavattantaṃ.

Showing that it should be understood that just as by the foremost wisdom of insight and the effort associated with it there is the state of being a yoke-bearer of the plough, and by the cultivation of wholesome qualities that have so arisen there is the state of farming, so by that foremost state, the perfections of wisdom and effort that occurred even before that have the state of being a yoke-bearer of the plough, and the cultivation of wholesome qualities that have so arisen has the state of farming, he said, 'Just as indeed,' and so forth. One who bears a yoke is a yoke-bearer. 'Firm,' as previously described, refers to the mass of conceit and other such things. Those for whom there are primary yokes to be borne are 'dhurā,' the carriers of the prior yoke. Rooted in that, those who bear a further yoke are 'dhorayhā.' 'Dhurā' and 'dhorayhā' become 'dhuradhorayha' by way of unity. 'Bearing' means proceeding by ploughing.

Kāmayogādīhi yogehi khemattā anupaddavattā. Taṃ nibbānaṃ adhikicca uddissa. Vāhīyati vipassanāya sahagataṃ. Abhimukhaṃ vāhīyati maggapariyāpannaṃ. Khettakoṭinti khettamariyādaṃ. Diṭṭhekaṭṭheti diṭṭhiyā sahajātekaṭṭhe pahānekaṭṭhe ca. Oḷāriketi uparimaggavajjhe upādāya vuttaṃ, aññathā dassanapahātabbāpi dutiyamaggavajjhehi oḷārikāti. Aṇusahagateti aṇubhūte. Idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe upādāya vuttaṃ. Sabbakilese avasiṭṭhasabbakilese pajahantaṃ anivattantaṃ gacchati puna pahātabbatāya abhāvato. Anivattantanti na nivattantaṃ, yathā nivattanaṃ na [M 1.0274] hoti, evaṃ gacchatīti attho. Tenāha “nivattanarahita”ntiādi. Etaṃ pana tava dhuradhorayhaṃ.

Because of security from the yokes of sensual desire and so forth, it is free from harm. That Nibbāna is the objective, the aim. It is borne along, accompanied by insight. It is borne along towards it, being included in the path. 'Khettakoṭi' means the boundary of the field. 'Diṭṭhekaṭṭha' means having a single function with view in arising together, and a single function in abandonment. 'Gross' is stated with reference to what is to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even what is to be abandoned by vision is gross in comparison with what is to be abandoned by the second path. 'Accompanied by the subtle' means experienced as subtle. This is stated with reference to what is to be abandoned by the lower paths. Abandoning all defilements, all remaining defilements, one goes without turning back, because there is nothing further to be abandoned. 'Not turning back' means not returning; the meaning is that one goes in such a way that there is no turning back. Hence it is said, 'devoid of turning back,' and so forth. This, indeed, is your yoke and yoke-bearer.

Evamesā kasīti yathāvuttassa paccāmasanaṃ. Tenāha “nigamanaṃ karonto”ti. Vuttasseva hi atthassa puna vacanaṃ. Paññānaṅgalena satiphālaṃ ākoṭetvāti paññāsaṅkhātena naṅgalena saddhiṃ satiphālassa ekābaddhabhāvakaraṇena ākoṭetvā. Kaṭṭhāti ettha “kasī”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ “kaṭṭhā kasī”ti. Kammapariyosānanti yathāvuttakasikammassa pariyosānabhūtaṃ. Yadipi pubbe “paññā me yuganaṅgala”ntiādinā attuddesikavasenāyaṃ amatapphalā kasi dassitā, mahākāruṇikassa pana bhagavato desanā sabbassapi sattanikāyassa sādhāraṇā evāti dassento “sā kho panesā”tiādimāha.

'Thus, this is the cultivation' is a review of what was stated. Therefore, it is said, 'while making a conclusion.' For it is a restatement of the meaning already spoken. 'Having struck the ploughshare of mindfulness with the plough of wisdom' means having struck it by making the ploughshare of mindfulness bound as one with the plough known as wisdom. Here, with 'kaṭṭhā,' the word 'kasī' should be brought in and connected as 'kaṭṭhā kasī' (the cultivation is completed). 'The end of the work' means the culmination of the work of cultivation as described. Although previously this cultivation with the deathless as its fruit was shown by way of self-reference with 'my wisdom is the yoke and plough,' and so forth, showing that the teaching of the Blessed One, the greatly compassionate one, is indeed common to the entire host of beings, he said, 'but this,' and so forth.

Divaseyevāti [V 1.0240] taṃdivase eva. Ādimāhāti ettha ādi-saddena kathāpariyosāne pāṭhapadeso gahitoti tadaññaṃ “evaṃ vutte”tiādipāṭhaṃ sandhāya “tato parañcā”ti āha.

'Divaseyeva' means on that very day. Here, in 'ādimāha,' by the word 'ādi' (beginning), a passage at the conclusion of the discourse is taken; referring to the other text beginning with 'when this was said,' he said, 'and after that.'

Kasibhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta is concluded.

2. Udayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Udaya Sutta

198. Etaṃ vuttanti “odanena pūresī”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ. “Gahetuṃ samattho nāma nāhosīti bhagavato adhiṭṭhānabalenā”ti vadanti. Taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vinetukāmatāya kira bhagavā tathā akāsi.

198. “This was said” means this statement, “he filled it with rice-gruel,” was uttered. “He was not able to take it”—they say this was due to the power of the Blessed One’s resolve. It is said that the Blessed One acted thus out of a desire to train that brahmin.

Upārambhabhayenāti parūpavādabhayena. Avatvāva nivatto “abbhāgatopi pāsaṇḍo vācāmattenapi na pūjetabbo”ti brāhmaṇadhamme vuttattā. Pakkantoti brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ avatvā pakkanto brāhmaṇassa na tāva ñāṇaṃ paripakkanti. Etaṃ vacanaṃ…pe… magamāsi “punappunañceva vapanti bīja”ntiādinā [M 1.0275] dhammaṃ kathetuṃ avassaṃ ākaṅkhanto. Pakārato kassatīti pakaṭṭhako, rasataṇhāya pakaṭṭhoti attho. Tenāha “rasagiddho”ti.

'For fear of reproach' means for fear of blame from others. He turned back without speaking, because it is said in the brahminical teaching: 'A visiting heretic should not be honored even with a mere word.' 'He departed' means he departed without speaking the Dhamma to the brahmin, because the brahmin's knowledge was not yet mature. This statement… and so on… he went on his way, necessarily desiring to teach the Dhamma beginning with 'they sow seed again and again.' 'One who ploughs in a special way is a pakaṭṭhaka'; the meaning is 'one who is drawn on by craving for tastes.' Therefore, it is said, 'greedy for taste'.

“Punappunañceva vapanti bīja”nti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhīti sambandho. Bījanti ca iti-saddo nidassanattho vā. Tena avayavena samudāyaṃ nidasseti. Osakkasīti saṅkocasi. Vuttanti vapanaṃ kataṃ. Tasmā vuttaṃ “alamettāvatā”ti. “Vassitvā”ti vuṭṭhiṃ pavattetvā.

The connection is that he began this teaching, 'They sow seed again and again.' In 'bījaṃ,' the particle 'iti' is illustrative. By that part, it indicates the whole. 'Osakkasi' means you withdraw. 'Vuttaṃ' means the sowing is done. Therefore, it is said, 'Enough of this.' 'Vassitvā' means having caused rain to fall.

Desanā…pe… dasseti brāhmaṇena vuttaṃ ayuttavacanaṃ parivaṭṭentopi divase divase bhikkhācariyā nāma bhikkhūnaṃ kāyagatā vuttīti. Khīraṃ hatthena nayantīti vā khīranikā. Kilamatīti taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇavasena khijjati. Phandatīti anatthasamāyogavasena vipphandati. Apunabbhavāyāti āyatiṃ anuppattiyā. Maggo nāmāti upāyo nāma nibbānaṃ, tasmiṃ laddhe punabbhavābhāvato. “Punappuna”nti vacanaṃ upādāya bījavapanādayo punappunadhammā nāma jātāti āha “soḷasa punappunadhamme desentenā”ti.

The teaching… and so on… shows that, even while turning aside the inappropriate words spoken by the brahmin, going for alms day after day is called the bodily sustenance of monks. 'One who carries milk by hand' is a milk-seller. 'One grows weary' means one is exhausted by way of performing various tasks. 'One throbs' means one trembles due to association with what is unbeneficial. 'For non-becoming again' means for non-arising in the future. 'The path' means the means to Nibbāna, because when that is attained, there is no more becoming again. Taking the word 'again and again,' he says that the sowing of seeds and so forth are called 'phenomena of repetition.' Thus, it is said, 'by the one teaching the sixteen phenomena of repetition.'

Udayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Udaya Sutta is concluded.

3. Devahitasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Devahita Sutta.

199. Udaravātehīti [V 1.0241] vātakatavijjhanatodanādivasena aparāparaṃ vattamānehi udaravātehi, tassa vā vikārehi. Nibaddhupaṭṭhākakāle pana dhammabhaṇḍāgārikova. Araññanti bhagavato bhikkhūnañca vasanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ tapovanaṃ. Taṃ niddhūmaṃ hoti udakatāpanassapi akaraṇato. Tasmāti yasmā tassa uṇhodakavikkiṇanacariyāya jīvikākappanaṃ hoti, tasmā.

199. 'By abdominal winds' means by abdominal winds that occur again and again by way of piercing, pricking, and similar pains caused by wind, or by their disorders. But at the time of being a constant attendant, he was indeed the treasurer of the Dhamma. 'The forest' means the ascetics' grove, which was the dwelling place for the Blessed One and the monks. It is smokeless because not even the heating of water is done. 'Therefore' means: since his livelihood is arranged through the practice of selling hot water, therefore.

Vattametaṃ tassa patikāratthaṃ parikathādīnampi kātuṃ labbhanato. Idāni tattha kāraṇampi savisayaṃ dassetuṃ “vaṇṇaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhagavā hi āyasmato upavāṇassa devahitabrāhmaṇassa taṃ sambhāvitaṃ bhavissati [M 1.0276] tikicchāpaṭiyattaṃ, tāya ca attano rogassa vūpasamanaṃ, tappasaṅgena ca devahitabrāhmaṇo mama santikaṃ āgantvā dhammassavanena saraṇesu sīlesu ca patiṭṭhahissatīti sabbamidaṃ ñatvā evaṃ “iṅgha me tvaṃ, upavāṇa, uṇhodakaṃ jānāhī”ti avoca. Āgamanīyappaṭipadaṃ pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ pubbabhāgappaṭipattiṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati anuttarimanussadhammattā. Sadevakena lokenāti anavasesato lokassa gahaṇaṃ. Phalavisesākaṅkhāya pūjetabbāti pūjanīyā, te eva idha “pūjaneyyā”ti vuttā. Tathā ādarena pūjetabbatāya sakkāriyā, ā-kārassa rassattaṃ, ri-saddassa ca re-ādesaṃ katvā “sakkareyyā”ti vuttaṃ. “Apacayeyyā”ti vattabbe ya-kāralopaṃ katvā “apaceyyā”ti vuttaṃ. Tesanti sadevakena pūjaneyyādīnaṃ. Haritunti netuṃ.

This is a duty for him for the sake of a remedy, since it is possible to engage in discussion and so forth. Now, to show the reason in that case, along with its scope, 'praise, indeed,' and so forth was said. Indeed, the Blessed One, knowing all this: that the prepared medicine for the Venerable Upavāṇa would be esteemed by the brahmin Devahita, that through it his own illness would be alleviated, and that, through confidence arising from that, the brahmin Devahita would come into his presence and, upon hearing the Dhamma, would be established in the refuges and virtues—knowing all this, he said, 'Come now, Upavāṇa, find out about some warm water for me.' It is fitting to speak of the practice leading to arrival, the preliminary practice, and the preliminary conduct, because it is a superhuman state. 'With the world including its devas' means the inclusion of the world without remainder. 'Worthy of honor' means they are to be honored with a desire for a special result; they are indeed called 'pūjaneyyā' here. Similarly, because they are to be honored with respect, they are 'sakkāriyā'; by shortening the long 'ā' and substituting 're' for the sound 'ri', 'sakkareyyā' is said. Where 'apacayeyyā' should be said, by eliding the 'y,' 'apaceyyā' is said. 'Of them' refers to those worthy of honor and so forth, together with the world including its devas. 'Harituṃ' means to lead.

Ettakenapīti upasaṅkamanādinā ettakena appamattakenapi katavattena ayaṃ kitti…pe… somanassajāto.

'Even by this much' means: even by this small duty performed, such as approaching and so forth, this fame… and so on… he became joyful.

Yajamānassāti deyyadhammaṃ dentassa. Dakkhiṇāya ijjhanaṃ nāma vipulaphalabhāvoti āha “mahapphalo hotī”ti. Viditanti paṭividdhapaccakkhakataṃ. Ājānātīti vutthabhavādiṃ pariyādāya jānāti paṭivijjhati. Jānitvāti cattāri saccāni maggapaṭipāṭiyā paṭivijjhitvā. Aggappattatāya katakiccataṃ patto. Brāhmaṇena attanā kato kāro ca bhagavato eva paccupaṭṭhātīti taṃ dassento “iminā khīṇāsave yajanākārena yajantassā”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Of the sacrificer’ means of the giver of the offering. The success of the offering is its abundant fruitfulness; hence, it is said, ‘it is of great fruit.’ ‘Understood’ means penetrated and directly realized. ‘Knows thoroughly’ means one knows, having encompassed the completed round of existence and so on, and penetrates it. ‘Having known’ means having penetrated the four truths in the order of the path. Having attained the highest, he has reached the state of having done what was to be done. The act done by the brahmin himself also presents itself to the Blessed One—showing this, it was said, ‘of one sacrificing in this manner to one whose cankers are destroyed.’”

Devahitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Devahita Sutta is concluded.

4. Mahāsālasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta

200. Yasmā [V 1.0242] tassa brāhmaṇassa anissayassa jiṇṇabhāvena visesato kāyo lūkho jāto, jiṇṇapilotikakhaṇḍehi saṅghaṭitaṃ pāvuraṇaṃ, tasmā “lūkhapāvuraṇo”ti padassa “jiṇṇapāvuraṇo”ti attho vutto. Pāṭiyekkanti puttesu ekameko ekamekāya vācāya visuṃ visuṃ.

200. Because for that brahmin, being without support and due to old age, his body had become especially coarse, and his outer robe was patched together from pieces of old rags, therefore the meaning of the word ‘coarse-robed’ is given as ‘old-robed.’ ‘Individually’ means each of the sons, with a single speech each, separately.

Sampucchanaṃ [M 1.0277] nāma idha sammantananti āha “saddhiṃ mantayitvā”ti. Nandissanti abhinandiṃ. Atītatthe hi idaṃ anāgatavacanaṃ. Tenāha “nandijāto…pe… ahosi”nti. Bhussantāti nibbhussanavasena ravantā.

Here, ‘inquiry’ is consultation; thus it says, ‘having consulted together.’ ‘They will rejoice’ means they rejoiced. For this future tense verb is used in the sense of the past. Therefore it is said, ‘joy arose… he was.’ ‘Making a noise’ means crying out resoundingly.

Vayogatanti pacchimavayaṃ upagataṃ. So pana yasmā purime dve vaye atikkamavasena gato. Pacchimaṃ ekadesato atikkamanavasena, tasmā vuttaṃ – “tayo vaye gataṃ atikkantaṃ pacchimavaye ṭhita”nti.

‘Reached old age’ means having reached the final stage of life. But since he has passed beyond the first two stages of life by way of transcending them, and has partially passed beyond the final stage by way of transcending it, therefore it is said: ‘Having gone beyond the three stages of life, having transcended them, he stands in the final stage of life.’

Nipparibhogoti jiṇṇabhāvena javaparakkamahāniyā aparibhogo na bhuñjitabbo. Khādanā apanīyatīti yavasaṃ adadantā tato nīharanti nāma. Theroti vuḍḍho.

‘Without use’ means that due to old age, with the loss of swiftness and vigor, he is without use, not to be made use of. ‘Fodder is taken away’ means that, not giving him fodder, they lead him out from there. ‘Elder’ means old.

Anassavāti na vacanakarā. Appatissāti patissayarahitā. Avasavattinoti na mayhaṃ vasena vattanakā. Sundarataroti upatthambhakāribhāvena sundarataro.

‘Uncompliant’ means not doing what is said. ‘Disrespectful’ means devoid of reverence. ‘Not under my control’ means not acting according to my will. ‘Better’ means better because it acts as a support.

Puratoti upatthambhakabhāvena purato katvā. Udake patiṭṭhaṃ labhati tattha patiṭṭhato thirapatiṭṭhabhāvato. Addhapatiṭṭho hi daṇḍo daṇḍadharapurisassa patiṭṭhaṃ labhāpeti.

‘In front’ means having placed it in front because it acts as a support. ‘He gains a foothold in the water’ means he obtains a footing there, from standing there, because of having a stable footing. For a staff that is half-established enables the person holding the staff to gain a footing.

Brāhmaṇiyoti attano brāhmaṇiyo. Pāṭiyekkanti “asukassa gehe asukassa gehe”ti evaṃ uddesikaṃ katvā visuṃ visuṃ. Mā niyyādehi, amhākaṃ ruccanaṭṭhānamevāti tava puttānaṃ gehesu yaṃ amhākaṃ ruccanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tatthameva gamissāmāti sabbesampi etesaṃ anuggahaṃ kātukāmo bhagavā evamāha.

‘Brahmin women’ means his own brahmin women. ‘Individually’ means, having made the designation ‘in so-and-so’s house, in so-and-so’s house,’ thus separately. ‘Do not assign us; only to the place that pleases us’ means ‘in your sons’ houses, whichever is a place that pleases us, to that very place we will go.’ Desiring to show favor to all of them, the Blessed One spoke thus.

Tato paṭṭhāyāti sotāpattiphalapaṭilābhato paṭṭhāya. Yadatthaṃ mayaṃ imassa brāhmaṇassa mahāsampattidānādinā [V 1.0243] anuggaho kato, so cassa puttaparijanassapi attho siddhoti satthā na sabbakālaṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa puttānaṃ gehaṃ agamāsi, te eva pana kālena kālaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā yathāvibhavaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ akaṃsūti adhippāyo.

‘From that time onward’ means from the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry. The purpose for which a favor was done by us to this brahmin by giving great wealth and so on, that purpose was also accomplished for his children and retinue; therefore, the Teacher did not always go to the houses of that brahmin’s sons, but they themselves, from time to time, went to the Teacher’s presence and offered respect and honor according to their means—this is the intention.

Mahāsālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta is concluded.

5. Mānatthaddhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Mānatthaddha Sutta

201. Mānena [M 1.0278] thaddhoti “ayaṃ kho”tiādinā paggahitena mānena thaddho bajjhitacitto thaddhaayosalāko viya kassacipi anonato. Na kiñci jānāti loke paṭisanthāramattassapi ajānanato.

201. ‘Stiff with pride’ means stiffened by the pride that is held, beginning with ‘This is…,’ his mind bound, like a rigid iron bar, unbending to anyone. ‘He knows nothing in the world’ is said because of his not knowing even a mere friendly welcome.

Abbhutavittajātāti sañjātaabbhutavittā. Vittaṃ vittīti ca tuṭṭhipariyāyā. Abhūtapubbāyāti yā tassā parisāya vitti tadā bhūtā, sā ito pubbe abhūtā. Tenāha “abhūta…pe… samannāgatā”ti. Assa puggalassāti anena puggalena. Apacitāti paramanipaccena pūjanīyasāmaññato tattha attano pakkhipanaṃ idha desanākosallaṃ.

‘Wondrous joy having arisen’ means for whom wondrous joy has arisen. ‘Vitta’ and ‘vitti’ are synonyms for satisfaction. ‘Unprecedented’ means that the joy that arose then for that assembly had not existed before this. Hence it is said, ‘unprecedented… endowed with.’ ‘Of this person’ means by this person. ‘Venerated’ means that here, the placing of oneself in a state of extreme humility, which is common towards one who is venerable, is due to his skill in teaching.

Mānatthaddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mānatthaddha Sutta is concluded.

6. Paccanīkasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Paccanīka Sutta

202. “Sabbaṃ seta”nti kenaci vutte tassa paccanīkaṃ karontasseva assa brāhmaṇassa. Vinetvāti vināsetvā. Suṇātīti atthoti “suṇātī”ti kiriyāpadaṃ āharitvā gāthāya attho veditabbo “jaññā subhāsita”nti vuttattā. Na hi asutvā desitaṃ jānituṃ sakkonti.

202. When someone says, ‘Everything is white,’ this refers to that brahmin who opposes him. ‘Having dispelled’ means having destroyed. The meaning is ‘he hears’; by supplying the verb ‘he hears,’ the meaning of the verse should be understood, because it is said, ‘He would know what is well-spoken.’ For one cannot know what is taught without having heard it.

Paccanīkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paccanīka Sutta is concluded.

7. Vanakammikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vanakammika Sutta

203. Vanakamme niyutto, kiriyamānena vanakammaṃ etassa atthīti vanakammiko. Imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍeti imasmiṃ evaṃmahante vanasaṇḍe. Na me vanasmiṃ karaṇīyamatthi yathā, “brāhmaṇa, tuyha”nti adhippāyo. Itaraṃ pana yaṃ mahākilesavanaṃ, taṃ maggañāṇapharasunā samādhimayasilāyaṃ [V 1.0244] sunisitena sabbaso [M 1.0279] ucchinnamūlaṃ, tato eva nibbanatho nikkilesagahano. Vivekābhiratiyā ekako abhirato paṭipakkhavigamena. Tenāha “aratiṃ…pe… jahitvā”ti.

203. Engaged in forest work; one for whom forest work is being done is a ‘forest-worker.’ ‘In this forest grove’ means in this very vast forest grove. The intention is: ‘There is nothing to be done by me in the forest, as there is for you, brahmin.’ But the other, the great forest of defilements, has been entirely uprooted by the axe of path-knowledge, well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration. From that, he is without a forest, free from the thicket of defilements. Delighting in seclusion, he delights alone, through the removal of opposing factors. Therefore it is said, ‘Having abandoned discontent… and so on.’

Vanakammikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vanakammika Sutta is concluded.

8. Kaṭṭhahārasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāra Sutta

204. Dhammantevāsikāti kiñcipi dhanaṃ adatvā kevalaṃ antevāsikā. Tenāha “veyyāvaccaṃ katvā sippuggaṇhanakā”ti. Gambhīrasabhāveti samantato dūrato gahanasacchannavipulatararukkhagacchalatāya ca, tadā himapiṇḍasinnabhāvena mayūrayānehi patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ca gambhīrabhāve.

204. ‘Pupils in the teaching’ means those who, without giving any wealth, are merely pupils. Hence it is said, ‘those who learn a craft after performing service.’ ‘In a profound state’ refers to the profound state due to being hidden from afar on all sides by a dense covering of very extensive trees, bushes, and creepers, and also due to the inability of peacocks to stand on their paths because of the slipperiness from the mass of snow at that time.

Bahubheraveti bahubhayānake. Aniñjamānenāti itthambhūtatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Atisundaraṃ vatāti evaṃ sante nāma araññe evaṃ niccalakāyo nisinno jhāyanto ativiya sundarañca jhānaṃ jhāyasīti vadati.

‘In a place of many terrors’ means in a place of many fears. ‘Unmoving’ is an instrumental case in the sense of being in such a state. ‘How very beautiful!’—he says: ‘Indeed, being in the forest, sitting thus with a motionless body and meditating, you are meditating on an exceedingly beautiful meditation.’

Accherarūpanti acchariyabhāvaṃ. Seṭṭhappattiyāti seṭṭhabhāvappattiyā.

‘A wonderful form’ means the state of being wonderful. ‘For the attainment of the best’ means for the attainment of the state of being the best.

“Lokādhipatisahabyataṃ ākaṅkhamāno”ti iminā brāhmaṇo lokādhipatisahayogaṃ pucchati, “kasmā bhava”ntiādinā pana tadaññavisesākaṅkhaṃ pucchatīti āha “aparenapi ākārena pucchatī”ti.

With ‘wishing for companionship with the lord of the world,’ the brahmin asks about union with the lord of the world. But with ‘why, sir?’ and so on, he asks about the desire for other distinctions than that; thus it says, ‘he asks in another manner as well.’

Kaṅkhāti taṇhā abhikkhaṇavasena pavattā. Anekasabhāvesūti rūpādivasena ajjhattikādivasena evaṃ nānāsabhāvesu ārammaṇesu. Assādarāgo lobho abhijjhāti nānappakārā. Sesakilesā vā diṭṭhimānadosādayo. Niccakālaṃ avassitā sattānaṃ avassayabhāvattā. Pajappāpanavasenāti pakārehi taṇhāyanavasena. Nirantāti antarahitā niravasesā.

‘Doubt’ means craving that proceeds by way of repetition. ‘In many natures’ means in various natural objects, such as forms and so on, internal and so on. Lust for delight, greed, and covetousness are of many kinds. Or the remaining defilements, such as wrong view, conceit, and aversion. Always clinging, because of the state of dependence of beings. ‘By way of longing’ means by way of craving in various modes. ‘Without interval’ means without a gap, without remainder.

Anupagamanoti anupādāno. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dīpeti, tassa hi vasena eva nānāsabhāvesu [V 1.0245] bhagavā samantacakkhunā passatīti “sabbe…pe… dassano”ti [M 1.0280] vuccati. Arahattaṃ sandhāyāha, tañhi nippariyāyato “anuttara”nti vuccati.

‘Not approaching’ means non-clinging.
