It reveals the knowledge of omniscience, for it is by means of that that the Blessed One sees in various natures with his all-seeing eye—thus he is called ‘the seer of all… and so on.’ This is said with reference to arahantship, for that is called ‘unsurpassed’ in the ultimate sense.

Kaṭṭhahārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāra Sutta is concluded.

9. Mātuposakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Mātuposaka Sutta.

205. Itoti manussattabhāvato. Paṭigantvāti abhigantvā. Sagge hi nibbattanto kammaphalena dhammatāvasena paṭisandhikālato paṭṭhāya abhirativasena abhiramati eva nāmāti.

205. ‘Ito’ means from the human state. ‘Paṭigantvā’ means having approached. Indeed, one who is reborn in heaven, by the result of kamma, as a natural consequence, from the time of rebirth onwards, certainly delights by way of extreme delight; such is the nature of things.

Mātuposakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mātuposaka Sutta is complete.

10. Bhikkhakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Bhikkhaka Sutta.

206. Virūpaṃ gandhaṃ pasavatīti visso, duggandho. Bāhitvāti attano santānato bahikatvā nīharitvā. Taṃ pana anavasesato pajahananti āha “aggamaggena jahitvā”ti. Saṅkhāyati sammadeva paricchindati etāyāti saṅkhā, ñāṇanti āha “saṅkhāyāti ñāṇenā”ti. Bhinnakilesattāti niruttinayena bhikkhusaddasiddhimāha.

206. ‘Visso’ is so called because it emits a foul smell; a bad odor. ‘Bāhitvā’ means having expelled and removed it from one's own continuum. But as to abandoning that completely, he says, ‘having abandoned it by the supreme path.’ ‘Saṅkhā’ is that by which one rightly reckons and delimits; it is knowledge. Thus he says, ‘by reckoning, by knowledge.’ Because the defilements are broken, he states the derivation of the word ‘bhikkhu’ according to the method of etymology.

Bhikkhakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhikkhaka Sutta is complete.

11. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta.

207. Paccetīti pattiyāyati saddahati. Tathābhūto ca tamatthaṃ nikāmento nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “icchati patthetī”ti. Sādhu, bhanteti ettha sādhu-saddo āyācanattho, na abhinandanatthoti “āyācamāno āhā”ti vatvā āyācane kāraṇaṃ dassento “therassa kirā”tiādimāha. Udakasuddhiko na ekaṃsena apāyūpago, laddhiyā pana [M 1.0281] sāvajjakilesabhūtabhāvato āyācati. Aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ apadisanto “apicā”tiādimāha. Phalabhūto attho etassāti atthavasaṃ, kāraṇanti āha “atthānisaṃsaṃ atthakāraṇa”nti. Papañcasūdaniyaṃ pana phaleneva araṇīyato attho, kāraṇanti katvā “attho eva atthavaso, tasmā dve atthavaseti dve atthe dve kāraṇānī”ti vuttaṃ.

207. ‘Pacceti’ means he trusts, he has faith. And being such, he is called one who desires that goal, as it is said, ‘he wishes, he desires.’ In ‘Sādhu, bhante,’ the word ‘sādhu’ has the meaning of a request, not of approval. Thus, having said ‘requesting, he said,’ he then shows the reason for the request by saying, ‘for the elder, it seems,’ and so on. One who believes in purification by water is not one who will invariably go to a woeful state, but he requests because his view is of a blameworthy and defiled nature. Pointing out another reason, he says, ‘moreover,’ and so on. ‘Atthavasaṃ’ means the purpose which is its fruit; the reason. Thus he says, ‘the benefit of the purpose, the reason for the purpose.’ But in the Papañcasūdanī, it is said that the purpose is to be attained through the fruit itself, taking it as the reason: ‘The purpose itself is the “atthavasa”; therefore, “two atthavasas” means two purposes, two reasons.’

Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta is complete.

12. Khomadussasuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary on the Khomadussa Sutta.

208. Evaṃladdhanāmaṃ [V 1.0246] piṇḍāya pāvisīti yojanā. Evamevanti kenaci animantitena sayameva upasaṅkamante. Aphāsukadhātukanti ayuttarūpaṃ. Sabhādhammanti sabhāya caritabbaṃ cārittadhammaṃ. Asañcāletvāti āsanato avuṭṭhāpetvā. Ujukameva āgacchati lokagganāyako bhagavā sabbasattuttamo attano uttaritarassa abhāvato lokassa apacitiṃ na dasseti. Ye sabbaso saṃkilese pajahanti, teva paṇḍite “santo”ti dasseti “ete”tiādinā.

208. Having thus gained a name, he entered for alms—this is the connection. ‘Evameva’ means approaching on one's own initiative, without being invited by anyone. ‘Aphāsukadhātukaṃ’ means of an unsuitable nature. ‘Sabhādhammaṃ’ means the customary conduct to be practiced in an assembly. ‘Asañcāletvā’ means without causing him to rise from his seat. The Blessed One, the foremost leader of the world, supreme among all beings, comes straightforwardly; due to the absence of one superior to himself, he does not show reverence to the world. Those who abandon all defilements completely, them alone he shows as the wise, the peaceful—this is shown by ‘these,’ and so on.

Khomadussasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Khomadussa Sutta is complete.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter is complete.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Brāhmaṇasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the hidden meaning in the Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta is complete.

8. Vaṅgīsasaṃyuttaṃ

8. The Connected Discourses with Vaṅgīsa

1. Nikkhantasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discourse on Renunciation

209. Āḷaviyanti [V 1.0247][M 1.0282] āḷavinagarasamīpe. Aggacetiyeti gotamakacetiyādīhi uttamacetiye. Taṃ kira bhūmirāmaṇeyyakabhāvena manuññatāya padhānayuttatādisampattiyā ca itaracetiyehi seṭṭhasammataṃ. Kappattherenāti “kappo”ti gottato āgatanāmo thero, sahassapurāṇajaṭilānaṃ abbhantare ayaṃ mahāthero. Ohīnakoti theresu gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhesu vihāre eva avahīnako ṭhito. Tattha kāraṇamāha “vihārapālo”tiādi. Samalaṅkaritvāti samaṃ alaṅkārena alaṅkaritvā. Kusalacittaṃ viddhaṃseti pavattituṃ appadānavasena. Etasminti etasmiṃ rāge uppanne. “Ekasmi”nti vā pāṭho, ekasmiṃ visabhāgavatthuke rāge uppanne. Dhammo vāti mama citte uppajjanakato añño dhammo vā. Yena kāraṇena paro anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā idāneva abhiratiṃ uppādeyya, taṃ kāraṇaṃ kuto labbhāti yojanā, taṃ kāraṇaṃ natthīti attho, tassa abhāvakāraṇavacanaṃ.

209. ‘Āḷaviyaṃ’ means near the city of Āḷavi. ‘Aggacetiye’ means at the foremost cetiya, which is supreme among the Gotamaka cetiya and others. It is said that this cetiya was considered superior to other cetiyas due to the pleasantness of the land, its charm, its suitability for striving, and other such excellences. ‘By the Elder Kappa’ means the elder whose name ‘Kappa’ came from his clan; this great elder was among the thousand ancient matted-hair ascetics. ‘Ohīnako’ means that when the elders had entered the village for alms, he remained behind in the monastery. There he states the reason: ‘the monastery guardian,’ and so on. ‘Samalaṅkaritvā’ means having adorned it completely with adornments. It destroys the wholesome mind by not giving it a chance to arise. ‘Etasmiṃ’ means when this lust has arisen. ‘Ekasmiṃ’ is an alternative reading, meaning when lust has arisen towards a single unsuitable object. ‘Dhammo vā’ means or another mental state than that which arises in my mind. The connection is: ‘By what reason could another dispel discontent and immediately produce delight? Where could that reason be found?’ The meaning is that there is no such reason; it is a statement about the absence of such a reason.

Anagāriyanti agāravirahato anagāraṃ pabbajjā. Tattha niyuttattā anagāriyaṃ ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā, pabbajitanti attho. Ādhāvantīti hadayaṃ abhibhavitvā dhāvanti. Uggatānanti uḷārānaṃ puttā. Tenāha “mahesakkhā rājaññabhūtā”ti. Uttamappamāṇanti sahassapalaṃ samantāti samantato. Parikireyyunti vijjheyyuṃ. Etasmā sahassāti yathāvuttā dhanuggahasahassato. Atirekatarā anekasahassā. Itthiyo olokanasitalapitaroditasare khipantiyo. Neva maṃ byādhayissanti neva maṃ nijjhāyissanti. “Byādhayissatī”ti pāṭhoti vuttaṃ “cāletuṃ na sakkhissatīti attho”ti. Dhamme samhīti sake santike patiṭṭhite sāsanadhamme. Tenāha “anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā”tiādi.

‘Anagāriyaṃ’ means the homeless state, renunciation, because it is devoid of a home. Because of being engaged in that, ‘anagāriyaṃ’ is formed by changing the ‘ka’ to ‘ya’; the meaning is ‘one who has gone forth.’ ‘Ādhāvanti’ means they run, overpowering the heart. ‘Uggatānaṃ’ means sons of the eminent. Hence it is said, ‘of great power, being of the warrior class.’ ‘Uttamappamāṇaṃ’ means a thousand palas. ‘Samantā’ means all around. ‘Parikireyyuṃ’ means they would pierce. ‘Etasmā sahassā’ means from the aforementioned thousand archers. ‘Atirekatarā’ means many thousands more. Women, casting cool, tearful glances and uttering sounds of weeping, would neither afflict me nor gaze at me. It is said that ‘Byādhayissati’ is a reading, the meaning of which is ‘will not be able to shake.’ ‘Dhamme samhi’ means in the Dhamma of the teaching established in one's own presence. Hence it is said, ‘having dispelled discontent,’ and so on.

Magganti “maggo”ti vattabbe liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “so hi nibbānassa pubbabhāgamagggo”ti.

‘Maggaṃ’ is stated with a change of gender where ‘maggo’ should be said. Hence it is said, “For that is the preliminary path to Nibbāna.”

Nikkhantasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Renunciation is complete.

2. Aratisuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Arati Sutta

210. Vihāragaruko [V 1.0248][M 1.0283] kiresa theroti etena thero attano saddhivihārikaṃ vaṅgīsaṃ ovadituṃ anavasaro. Tena antarantarā tassa cittaṃ rāgo anuddhaṃsetīti dasseti. Sāsane aratinti sīlaparipūraṇe samathavipassanābhāvanāya ca anabhiratiṃ. Kāmaguṇesu ca ratinti pañcasu kāmakoṭṭhāsesu assādaṃ. Pāpavitakkanti kāmasaṅkappaṃ. Sabbākārenāti sabbe tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchindanākārena. Yathā mahantaṃ araññaṃ vanathanti, evaṃ mahantaṃ kilesavanaṃ “vanatha”nti vuttaṃ.

210. It is said this elder was attached to his dwelling; thus, the elder had no opportunity to advise his co-resident Vaṅgīsa. This shows that, because of that, from time to time lust harassed his mind. ‘Discontent with the Dispensation’ means lack of delight in perfecting virtue and in the development of serenity and insight. ‘Delight in sensual pleasures’ means finding enjoyment in the five portions of sensuality. ‘Evil thought’ means sensual intention. ‘In every way’ means by all modes: by substitution of opposites, by suppression, and by eradication. Just as a great wilderness is called ‘vanatha,’ so too the great forest of defilements is called ‘vanatha.’

Pathaviñca vehāsanti bhummatthe paccattavacanaṃ, tasmā pathaviyaṃ ākāse cāti attho. Tenāha “pathaviṭṭhita”ntiādi. Jagatīti ca pathaviyā vevacanaṃ. Tenāha “antopathaviya”nti. Parijīratīti sabbbaso jaraṃ pāpuṇāti. Samāgantvāti ñāṇena samāgantvāti attho. Tenāha “mutattāti viññātattabhāvā”ti.

‘Pathaviñca vehāsaṃ’ is a case ending used in the sense of location; therefore, the meaning is ‘on the earth and in the sky.’ Therefore he says, ‘standing on the earth,’ and so on. ‘Jagatī’ is also a synonym for the earth. Hence, he says, ‘within the earth.’ ‘Parijīrati’ means it completely reaches decay. ‘Samāgantvā’ means ‘having come together with knowledge.’ Therefore he says, ‘“mutattā” means because of the state of having been understood.’

Paṭighapadena gandharasā gahitā ghānajivhānaṃ paṭihananavasena pavattanato. Mutapadena phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ gahitaṃ mutvā gahetabbato. Na lippatīti na makkhīyati.

By the term ‘resistance,’ smells and tastes are included because they function by striking against the nose and tongue. By the term ‘touched,’ tangible objects are included because they are to be apprehended by touching. ‘Na lippati’ means it is not smeared.

Saṭṭhi-saddo cha-saddena samānatthoti “saṭṭhinissitā”ti padassa “chaārammaṇanissitā”ti attho vutto. Puthū adhammavitakkāti rūpavitakkādivasena bahū nānāvitakkā micchāsaṅkappā. Janatāya niviṭṭhāti mahājane patiṭṭhitā. Tesaṃ vasenāti tesampi micchāvitakkānaṃ vasena. Na katthaci ārammaṇe. Kilesavaggagatoti kilesasaṅgaṇikaṃ upagato na bhaveyya, kilesavitakkā na uppādetabbāti attho. Duṭṭhullavacanaṃ kāmapaṭisaṃyuttakathā.

The word ‘sixty’ has the same meaning as the word ‘six’; hence, the phrase ‘dependent on sixty’ means ‘dependent on the six sense objects.’ ‘Puthū adhammavitakkā’ means many diverse wrong thoughts, wrong intentions, by way of thoughts of form, etc. ‘Janatāya niviṭṭhā’ means established among the great mass of people. ‘Tesaṃ vasena’ means through them, that is, through those wrong thoughts as well. Not on any object. ‘Kilesavaggagato’ means one should not have gone to the company of defilements; the meaning is that defiling thoughts should not be produced. ‘Duṭṭhullavacanaṃ’ refers to talk connected with sensuality.

Dabbajātikoti dabbarūpo. Nepakkenāti kosallena. Nibbānaṃ paṭiccāti asaṅkhatadhātuṃ ārammaṇavasena paṭicca. Parinibbānakālanti anupādisesanibbānakālaṃ.

‘Dabbajātiko’ means of a dull nature. ‘Nepakkena’ means with skillfulness. ‘Nibbānaṃ paṭicca’ means depending on the unconditioned element by way of object. ‘Parinibbānakālaṃ’ refers to the time of Nibbāna without remainder of aggregates.

Aratisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Arati Sutta is complete.

3. Pesalasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Pesala Sutta.

211. Etesanti [M 1.0284] etesaṃ mahallakānaṃ. Na pāḷi āgacchati appaguṇabhāvato. Na ca pāḷi [V 1.0249] upaṭṭhāti, ekāya pāḷiyā sati pāḷigatiyā tathā tathā upaṭṭhānampi nesaṃ natthīti vadati. Na aṭṭhakathāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sithiladhanitāditaṃtaṃbyañjanabuddhiṃ ahāpetvā uccāraṇaṃ padabyañjanamadhuratā. Atikkamitvā maññati aññe bhikkhū. Hīḷanavasena abhibhavitvā paṭibhānasutena attānaṃ pasaṃsati sambhāveti. Mānassa pavattitāya sahajātanissayādipaccayadhammā taṃsahabhudhammā. Mānavasena vippaṭisārī ahuvā. Mā ahosīti yojanā. Vaṇṇabhaṇananti parehi kiriyamānaṃ guṇābhitthavaṃ. Akhiloti pañcacetokhilarahito. Nissesaṃ navavidhanti navavidhampi mānaṃ kassaci ekadesassapi asesato. Vijjāyāti aggamaggavijjāya. Accantameva samitatāya vūpasamitatāya samitāvī.

211. ‘Etesaṃ’ means ‘of these elders’. The Pāli does not come to them due to their few good qualities. Nor does the Pāli present itself to them; even if there is a single Pāli text, the understanding of the Pāli does not arise in them in such and such a way, so it is said. ‘Not the commentary’—here, too, this same method applies. Sweetness of word and syllable is the utterance without abandoning the understanding of the respective syllables, such as lax and tense. He thinks he surpasses other monks. Overcoming them through disparagement, he praises and esteems himself by means of his ready wit. Due to the occurrence of conceit, the conditions such as co-nascence and dependence are states concomitant with it. He became remorseful on account of conceit. The construction is: ‘May it not have been so.’ ‘Vaṇṇabhaṇana’ means the extolling of virtues performed by others. ‘Akhila’ means devoid of the five mental barrennesses. ‘Nissesaṃ navavidhaṃ’ means the ninefold conceit in its entirety, without remainder, even in a single part of anyone. ‘Vijjāya’ means by the knowledge of the supreme path. Because of being utterly calmed, completely appeased, he is one who is calmed.

Pesalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pesala Sutta is concluded.

4. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

212. Rāgoti ettha āyasmato vaṅgīsassa rāgassa uppattiyā kāraṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “āyasmā ānando”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti ānandattheraṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetunti kāyavedanādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ satigocaraṃ. Asubhadukkhādito, rūpādiekekameva vā chaḷārammaṇaṃ aniccadukkhādito pariggaṇhituṃ paricchijja jānituṃ. Itthirūpārammaṇeti itthisantāne rūpasabhāve ārammaṇe.

212. ‘Rāgo’—here, to explain the cause for the arising of lust in the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, the passage beginning “the Venerable Ānanda” was spoken. ‘Taṃ’ refers to the Elder Ānanda. ‘Ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetuṃ’ means to grasp the object, the resort for mindfulness, which is differentiated as body, feeling, and so on; to grasp, delimit, and know each one of the six objects beginning with form from the perspective of the foul and suffering, or from the perspective of impermanence and suffering. ‘Itthirūpārammaṇe’ means in the object which is the nature of form in a woman’s continuity.

Nibbāpananti nibbāpayati etenāti nibbāpanaṃ. Vipallāsenāti asubhe “subha”nti vipallāsabhāvahetu. Rāgaṭṭhāniyanti rāguppattihetu. Iṭṭhārammaṇanti subhārammaṇaṃ. Ettha ca iṭṭhārammaṇasīsena tattha iṭṭhākāraggahaṇaṃ vadati. Tañhi vajjanīyaṃ. Paratoti avasavattanatthena aññato. Saṅkhārā hi “mā bhijjantū”ti icchitāpi bhijjanteva, tasmā te avasavattittā paro nāma, sā ca nesaṃ paratā aniccadassanena pākaṭā hotīti vuttaṃ “parato passāti aniccato passā”ti. Kāmaṃ vipassanā saṅkhāranimittaṃ na [M 1.0285] pariccajati saṅkhāre ārabbha vattanato, yesaṃ pana nimittānaṃ aggahaṇena animittāti gahituṃ arahati, taṃ dassetuṃ “niccādīnaṃ nimittāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Salakkhaṇa-sāmaññalakkhaṇa-dassanavasena mānassa dassanābhisamayo, vipassanāya pahānābhisamayo. “Maggenā”ti vadanti, maggeneva pana asammohato pariññāpaṭivedhavasena dassanābhisamayo, pahānapaṭivedhavasena pahānābhisamayo. Rāgādisantatāyāti rāgādīnaṃ samucchedavasena paṭippassaddhivasena vūpasametabbato santabhāvena.

‘Nibbāpana’ means that by which one extinguishes; thus, it is extinguishment. ‘Vipallāsena’ means because of the state of distortion, which is perceiving the foul as ‘lovely.’ ‘Rāgaṭṭhāniya’ means a cause for the arising of lust. ‘Iṭṭhārammaṇa’ means a desirable object. And here, under the heading of a desirable object, it speaks of grasping the feature of desirability. For that is to be avoided. ‘Parato’ means as other, in the sense of not being under one’s control. For formations, even when it is wished, “May they not break apart,” do indeed break apart. Therefore, because they are not under one’s control, they are called ‘other,’ and this otherness of theirs becomes manifest through seeing impermanence. Hence it is said, “One sees them as other means one sees them as impermanent.” Although insight does not abandon the sign of formations, since it proceeds in relation to formations, it is able to be taken as ‘signless’ by not grasping those signs. To show this, the passage beginning “the signs of permanence, etc.” was spoken. The breakthrough by seeing conceit occurs by way of seeing specific and general characteristics; the breakthrough by abandoning occurs by way of insight. Some say, “by the path.” But indeed, by the path itself, through non-delusion, the breakthrough by seeing occurs by way of the penetration of full understanding, and the breakthrough by abandoning occurs by way of the penetration of abandoning. ‘Rāgādisantatāya’ means by the peaceful state, because lust and so on are to be pacified by way of eradication and by way of tranquillization.

Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is concluded.

5. Subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Well-Spoken Sutta

213. Aṅgīyanti [V 1.0250] hetubhāvena āgamabhāvena avayavabhāvena vā ñāyantīti aṅgāni, kāraṇāni, avayavā vāti āha “aṅgehīti kāraṇehi, avayavehi vā”ti. Viratiyo subhāsitavācāya pubbaṃ patiṭṭhitā hontīti musāvādāveramaṇiādayo tassā visesahetūti āha “musāvādā…pe… kāraṇānī”ti. Yasmā ariyavohārā visesato cetanāsabhāvā, tasmā vacīsucaritasamudāyassa saccavācādayo aṅgabhūtāti āha “saccavacanādayo cattāro avayavā”ti. Nissakkavacananti hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ. Tenāha “samanuāgatā pavattā”ti. Vācā hi tāya viratiyā sammā anurūpato āgatā pavattāti “samannāgatā”ti vuccati. Karaṇavacananti sahayoge karaṇavacanaṃ. Tenāha “yuttā”ti. Sahajātāpi hi cetanā yathāsamādinnāya viratiyā sammā anurūpato yuttāti vattuṃ arahati.

213. ‘Aṅgīyanti’—they are known as ‘factors’ (aṅgāni) because they are understood by way of being causes, by way of being tradition, or by way of being constituents; thus they are causes or constituents. Hence it is said: ‘By factors (aṅgehi) means by causes, or by constituents.’ Because the abstinences are established beforehand as a foundation for well-spoken speech, abstaining from false speech and so on are its specific causes. Hence it is said: ‘Abstaining from false speech… are the causes.’ Because noble expressions are especially of the nature of intention, truthful speech and the like have become factors, being components of the collection of good verbal conduct. Hence it is said: ‘Truthful speech and the other three are the components.’ ‘Nissakkavacanaṃ’ is the ablative of cause. Therefore it is said: ‘Endowed, it proceeds.’ For speech, having arisen and proceeded rightly in accordance with that abstinence, is called ‘endowed’ (samannāgatā). ‘Karaṇavacanaṃ’ is the instrumental in the sense of association. Therefore it is said: ‘Joined’ (yuttā). For even the co-arisen intention is fit to be called ‘joined’ rightly and appropriately to the abstinence as it has been undertaken.

Samullapanavācāti saddavācā, sā vuccatīti vācā nāma. Viññatti pana vuccati etāyāti vācā nāma, tathā virati cetanāvācā. Na sā idha adhippetāti sā cetanāvācā viññattivācā viya idha imasmiṃ sutte na adhippetā “subhāsitā hotī”ti vacanato. Tenāha “abhāsitabbato”ti. Suṭṭhu bhāsitāti sammā ñāyena bhāsitā vacīsucaritabhāvato. Atthāvahatanti hitāvahakālaṃ pati āha. Kāraṇasuddhinti [M 1.0286] yonisomanasikārena kāraṇavisuddhiṃ. Dosābhāvanti agatigamanādidosābhāvaṃ. Rāgadosādivinimuttañhi taṃ bhāsato anurodhavirodhavivajjanato agatigamanaṃ dūrasamugghāṭitamevāti. Anuvādavimuttāti apavādavirahitā. Sabbākārasampattiṃ dīpeti, asati hi sabbākārasampatiyaṃ anuvajjatāpi.

‘Samullapanavācā’ means conversational speech; it is called speech because it is spoken. But communication (viññatti) is called speech because one communicates by it; similarly, abstinence is speech of intention. That is not meant here. That speech of intention, like speech as communication, is not meant here in this sutta, because of the phrase, “it is well-spoken.” Therefore it is said, “because it is not what is spoken.” ‘Well-spoken’ means spoken rightly, by the correct method, because of its being good verbal conduct. ‘Atthāvaha’ refers to bringing benefit at the appropriate time. ‘Kāraṇasuddhi’ means the purity of the cause through wise attention. ‘Dosābhāva’ means the absence of faults such as going on a wrong course. For one who speaks what is free from lust, hatred, and so on, because they avoid partiality and opposition, going on a wrong course is utterly uprooted. ‘Anuvādavimuttā’ means free from accusation. This shows accomplishment in all aspects, for if there were no accomplishment in all aspects, there would be blameworthiness.

Kiñcāpi pubbe dhammādhiṭṭhānā desanā āraddhā, puggalajjhāsayato pana puggalādhiṭṭhānāya…pe… vacanametaṃ. Kāmañcettha “aññataraniddosavacana”nti avisesato vuttaṃ, “dhammaṃyeva bhāsatī”tiādinā pana adhammadosādirahitāya vācāya vuccamānattā idhāpi subhāsitā vācā adhippetāti. “Subhāsitaṃyevā”ti avadhāraṇena nivattitaṃ sarūpato dasseti “no dubbhāsita”nti iminā. Tenāha “tasseva vācaṅgassa paṭipakkhabhāsananivāraṇa”nti. Paṭiyogīnivattanattho hi eva-saddo, tena pisuṇavācāpaṭikkhepo dassito. “Subhāsita”nti vā iminā catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritaṃ gahitanti “no dubbhāsitanti iminā micchāvācappahānaṃ dīpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbavacīsucaritasādhāraṇavacanañhi subhāsitanti. Tena parabhedanādikaṃ asabbhādikañca bodhisattānaṃ vacanaṃ apisuṇādivisayanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhāsitabbavacanalakkhaṇanti bhāsitabbassa [V 1.0251] vacanassa sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ dīpetīti ānetvā sambandho. Yadi evaṃ nanu abhāsitabbaṃ paṭhamaṃ vatvā bhāsitabbaṃ pacchā vattabbaṃ yathā “vāmaṃ muñca, dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhā”ti āha “aṅgaparidīpanatthaṃ panā”tiādi.

Although the teaching was at first established on the Dhamma, this statement is established on the person, on account of the individual’s disposition. And although it is stated here without distinction as “a certain faultless speech,” because it is spoken of as speech free from faults such as being contrary to the Dhamma, with phrases like “he speaks only the Dhamma,” here too well-spoken speech is intended. By the emphasis in “well-spoken indeed,” it shows by exclusion its own nature with the phrase “not ill-spoken.” Hence it is said: “the prevention of speaking the opposite of that very factor of speech.” For the word ‘eva’ has the meaning of excluding the counterpart; by it, the rejection of divisive speech is shown. Or, by “well-spoken,” the fourfold good verbal conduct is included; thus it is said that by “not ill-spoken,” it shows the abandonment of wrong speech. For “well-spoken” is a term common to all good verbal conduct. Therefore, the speech of bodhisattvas, which is not for the dividing of others and is not unseemly, should be understood as being in the domain of non-divisive speech and so on. ‘The characteristic of speech that should be spoken’ means it shows the intrinsic characteristic of speech that should be spoken; this is the connection to be supplied. If so, should not what is not to be spoken be stated first, and what is to be spoken be stated afterwards, as in “release the left, take the right”? To this it is said, “But for the purpose of clarifying the factors,” and so on.

Paṭhamenāti “subhāsita”nti padena. Dhammato anapetanti attano paresañca hitasukhāvahadhammato anapetaṃ. Mantāvacananti mantāya pavattetabbavacanaṃ. Paññavā avikiṇṇavāco hi na ca anatthāvahaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati. Itarehi dvīhīti tatiyacatutthapadehi. “Imehi khotiādīnīti karaṇe etaṃ upayogavacana”nti keci. Taṃ vācanti yathāvuttaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ. Yañca vācaṃ maññantīti sambandho. Aññeti ito bāhirakā ñāyavādino akkharacintakā ca. “Paṭiññāhetuudāharaṇūpanayanigamanāni avayavā vākyassā”ti vadanti. Nāmādīhīti nāmākhyātapadehi. Liṅgaṃ itthiliṅgādi vacanaṃ ekavacanādi. Paṭhamādi vibhatti atītādi kālaṃ. Kattā sampadānaṃ [M 1.0287] apādānaṃ karaṇaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ kammañca kārakaṃ. Sampattīhi samannāgatanti ete avayavādike sampādetvā vuttaṃ. Taṃ paṭisedhetīti taṃ yathāvuttavisesampi vācaṃ “imehi kho”ti vadanto bhagavā paṭisedheti. Kho-saddo hettha avadhāraṇattho. Tenāha “avayavādī”tiādi. Yā kāci asabhāvaniruttilakkhaṇā. Sā milakkhubhāsā. Sīhaḷakenevāti sīhaḷabhāsāya pariyāpannena vacanena. Arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti saṃsāre ativiya sañjātasaṃvegā tannissaraṇe ninnapoṇamānasā hutvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

‘Paṭhamena’ means ‘by the word “well-spoken.”’ ‘Dhammato anapetaṃ’ means not deviating from the Dhamma that brings welfare and happiness to oneself and others. ‘Mantāvacana’ means speech to be guided by counsel. A wise person, whose speech is not scattered, does not speak words that are unbeneficial. ‘Itarehi dvīhi’ means by the other two, i.e., by the third and fourth lines. ‘Imehi kho’ and so on—some say this is a word of instrumental case usage. That speech is the fourfold speech as described. The connection is, ‘And whatever speech they deem.’ ‘Aññe’ refers to those outside, proponents of logic and theorists of letters. They say: ‘Statement, reason, example, application, and conclusion are the parts of a sentence.’ ‘Nāmādīhi’ refers to nouns and verbs. ‘Gender’ refers to feminine gender, etc.; ‘number’ to singular number, etc. ‘First case, etc.’ refers to the nominative case, etc.; ‘past tense, etc.’ refers to past tense, etc. ‘Agent, receiver, ablative, instrument, locative, and object’ are the grammatical cases. ‘Sampattīhi samannāgata’—this is said after having assembled these components as the beginning parts. ‘He refutes that’—the Blessed One refutes even that speech with the aforementioned distinctions by saying, ‘by these indeed.’ Here, the particle ‘kho’ has an emphatic meaning. Hence it is said, ‘proponents of parts,’ and so on. Whatever lacks the characteristics of natural expression—that is barbarian language. ‘Sīhaḷakeneva’ means in words that are entirely Sinhalese. ‘Arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu’—being exceedingly stirred by saṃsāra, their minds inclined toward release from it, they roused their insight and attained arahantship through the path of practice.

Pātova phullitakokanadanti pātova saṃphullapadumaṃ. Bhijjiyateti nibbhijjiyati nibbhiggo jāyati. Manussattaṃ gatāti manussattabhāvaṃ upagatā.

‘Pātova phullitakokanada’ means ‘at dawn, the lotus fully blossoms.’ ‘Bhijjiyati’ means ‘it becomes broken up, destroyed.’ ‘Manussattaṃ gatā’ means ‘they reached the state of being human.’

Buddhantareti buddhuppādantare dvinnaṃ buddhuppādānaṃ antarā. Tadā hi paccekabuddhānaṃ sāsane, na buddhasāsane dippamāne.

‘Buddhantara’ means the interval between the arising of two Buddhas, the period between the appearance of two Buddhas. For then, it is the dispensation of the Paccekabuddhas, not the Buddha’s dispensation which is shining brightly.

Jarāya parimadditanti yathā hatthacaraṇādiaṅgāni sithilāni honti, cakkhādīni indriyāni savisayaggahaṇe asamatthāni honti, yobbanaṃ sabbaso vigataṃ, kāyabalaṃ apagataṃ, satimatidhitiādayo vippayuttā, pubbe attano ovādapaṭikarā puttadārādayopi apasādakā, parehi vuṭṭhāpanīyasaṃvesanīyatā punadeva bālabhāvappatti ca honti, evaṃ jarāya sabbaso vimadditaṃ. Etanti sarīraṃ vadati. Milātachavicammanissitanti jiṇṇabhāvena appamaṃsalohitattā milātehi [V 1.0252] gatayobbanehi dhammehi sannissitaṃ. Ghāsamāmisanti ghāsabhūtaṃ āmisaṃ maccunā gilitvā viya patiṭṭhapetabbato. Kesalomādinānākuṇapapūritaṃ. Tato eva asucibhājanaṃ etaṃ. Sabbathāpi nissāratāya kadalikkhandhasamaṃ.

Crushed by old age: meaning, just as limbs like hands and feet become slack, faculties like the eyes are unable to grasp their objects, youth is completely gone, bodily strength has departed, mindfulness, intelligence, and fortitude are lost, even one's own children and spouse, who once heeded advice, now become disrespectful, and one is fit to be raised up and laid down by others, and even returns to a childlike state—thus, it is completely crushed by old age. This refers to the body. Covered with withered skin: meaning, due to its decrepit state, having little flesh and blood, it is associated with the withered qualities of departed youth. A lump of flesh: meaning, it is a lump of flesh that serves as food, because it is to be established as if swallowed by death. It is filled with various impurities like hair and nails; therefore, it is a vessel of impurity. In every way, due to its lack of essence, it is like a plantain trunk.

Anucchavikāhīti sammāsambuddhassa anurūpāhi. Na tāpeyyāti cittañca kāyañca na tāpeyya. Tāpanā cettha sampati āyati ca visādanā. Na bādheyyāti “nābhibhaveyyā”ti padassa atthadassanaṃ. Apisuṇavācāvasenāti sabbaso pahīnapisuṇavācatāvasena. Pāpānīti lāmakāni nikiṭṭhakāni. Tenāha “appiyānī”tiādi. Anādāyāti aggahetvā.

Anucchavikāhi: meaning, fitting for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. It does not afflict: meaning, it does not torment the mind and body. Here, torment is both present and future affliction. It does not oppress: this shows the meaning of the phrase “it does not overwhelm.” By abstaining from divisive speech: meaning, by completely abandoning divisive speech. Evil deeds: meaning, base and contemptible acts. Hence it is said, “unpleasant,” etc. Not taking up: meaning, not taking.

Sādhubhāvenāti [M 1.0288] niddosamadhurabhāvena. Amatasadisāti sadise tabbohāroti, kāraṇe vāyaṃ kāriyavohāroti āha “nibbānāmatapaccayattā vā”ti. Paccayavasena hi sā tadā dassanappavatti. Cariyāti cārittaṃ. Porāṇā nāma paṭhamakappikā, buddhādayo vā ariyā.

By good nature: meaning, by way of a faultless and sweet nature. Like the deathless: meaning, the term is used for what is similar, or this is a term for the effect based on the cause; thus it is said, “or because it is a condition for the deathless (Nibbāna).” For indeed, the arising of that vision is dependent on conditions. Conduct: meaning, virtuous conduct. The ancients: meaning, those of the first age, or the noble ones such as the Buddhas.

Patiṭṭhitāti niccalabhāvena aṭṭhiṃ katvā paccayāyattabhāvato avisaṃvādanakā. Ubhayathā paṭipattiṃ āha “attano ca paresañca atthe patiṭṭhitā”ti. Atthe diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādihite patiṭṭhitattā eva dhamme avihiṃsādidhamme patiṭṭhitā. Anuparodhakaranti etena hitapariyāyoyaṃ attha-saddoti dasseti. Dhammikanti dhammato anapetaṃ, atthadhammūpasaṃhitaṃ vā.

Established: meaning, being firm due to unwavering nature, and non-deceptive due to dependence on conditions. It speaks of the practice in both ways: “established in the welfare of oneself and others.” Being established in welfare, that is, being established in benefits such as those visible in this life and those pertaining to the future, indeed established in the Dhamma, that is, in virtues such as non-harming. Non-obstructing: by this it is shown that this word, 'attha', is a synonym for 'hita' (benefit). Righteous: meaning, not deviating from the Dhamma, or connected with both benefit and Dhamma.

Nibbānappattiyāti nibbānappattiyatthaṃ. Dukkhassa antakiriyāya antakaraṇatthaṃ. Yasmā buddho khemāya bhāsati, tasmā khemuppattihetuyā khemā, tasmā sā sabbavācānaṃ uttamāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Mantāvacanavasenāti sabbadosarahitavasena.

For the attainment of Nibbāna: meaning, for the purpose of attaining Nibbāna. For making an end to suffering: meaning, for the purpose of making an end to suffering. Because the Buddha speaks for safety, therefore it is safe, being the cause for the arising of safety; thus, it is the supreme of all speech—this is how the meaning should be understood here. In the way of sagely utterance: meaning, in the way of being free from all faults.

Subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta is completed.

6. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Sāriputta Sutta Commentary

214. Vākkaraṇacāturiyato vacanaguṇahetūnaṃ pūriyā pūre bhavāti porī, tāya poriyā. Tenāha “akkharādiparipuṇṇāyā”ti. Avibaddhāyāti pittādīhi na vibaddhāya anupaddutāya. Tenāha “apalibuddhāyā”tiādi. Niddosāyāti atthato byañjanato vigatadosāya. Akkhalitapadabyañjanāyāti [V 1.0253] agalitapadabyañjanāya, atthassa viññāpaniyāti diṭṭhadhammikādiatthassa bodhane pariyattāya. Bhikkhunanti gāthāsukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vuttaṃ.

214. From skill in speech and the completion of the causes of excellence in speech, one becomes accomplished (porī); by that accomplishment (poriyā). Therefore it is said: “Perfect in letters, etc.” Avibaddhā (unobstructed): meaning, not obstructed by bile, etc., undisturbed. Therefore it is said: “unhindered,” etc. Niddosā (faultless): meaning, free from faults in meaning and wording. Akkhalitapadabyañjanā (with unslurred words and syllables): meaning, with words and syllables that are not slurred, capable of making the meaning known—that is, fit for the enlightenment of the meaning pertaining to visible realities, etc. Bhikkhunaṃ: this is said shortened for the sake of ease in the verse.

“Saṃkhittenapi deseti, vitthārenapi bhāsatī”ti nayidaṃ paṭhamaṃ uddisitvā tassa atthassa kittanavasena pavattitaṃ vacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sā hi vitthāradesanā eva hoti. Yā pana desanā kadāci dhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena [M 1.0289] saṃkhitteneva dassetvā nikkhipati, yā ca kadāci vitthārena, tadubhayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “cattārimānī”tiādi. Sabhāvamadhuro paccayavasena madhurataro hotīti dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vividhākāraṃ katvā dhammaṃ kathetuṃ paṭibhātīti paṭibhānaṃ, desanāpakārañāṇaṃ. Tenāha “samuddato”tiādi. Odahantīti avajānanavasena gamenti.

“One teaches briefly, one speaks in detail”—this is not said referring to a statement that is first put forward and then explained by elaborating on its meaning. For that is indeed a detailed teaching. But that teaching which sometimes, according to the inclinations of those who receive the Dhamma, presents it briefly and puts it aside, and that which is sometimes detailed, is what is referred to by both. Therefore, he said, “These four,” etc. To show that what is naturally sweet becomes even sweeter due to conditions, it is said: “Just as,” etc. Paṭibhāna (inspired understanding): meaning, the ability to speak the Dhamma in various ways, knowledge of modes of teaching. Therefore, he said: “Like the ocean,” etc. Odahanti (they apply): meaning, they cause to go (down) in the sense of disparaging.

Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Sāriputta Sutta Commentary is concluded.

7. Pavāraṇāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary to the Pavāraṇā Sutta

215. Tasmiṃ ahūti tasmiṃ ahanīti āha “tasmiṃ divase”ti. Anasanenāti sabbaso āhārassa abhuñjanena. Sāsanikasīlena bāhirakaanasanena vā upetā hutvāti yojanā. Vā-saddena khīrapānamadhusāyanādīnipi saṅgaṇhāti. Pakārehi diṭṭhādīhi vāreti kāyakammādike sarāpeti gārayhe karoti etāyāti pavāraṇā, paṭipattivisodhanāya attano attano vajjasodhanāya okāsadānaṃ. Yasmā yebhuyyena vassaṃvuṭṭhehi kātabbā esā visuddhidesanā, tasmā vuttaṃ “vassaṃvuṭṭhapavāraṇāya. Visuddhipavāraṇātipi etissāva nāma”nti. Tadā tassa bhikkhusaṅghassa tuṇhībhāvassa anavasesatāyapi vaṇṇaṃ dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “tuṇhībhūta”nti vuttanti āha “yato yato…pe… natthī”ti. Hatthassa kukkuccatā asaṃyamo asampajaññakiriyā hatthakukkuccaṃ. Tathā pādakukkuccaṃ veditabbaṃ, vā-saddo avuttavikappattho, tena tadaññesamabhāvo vibhāvitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

215. Tasmiṃ ahū means tasmiṃ ahani; thus it is said, “on that day.” Anasanena (without eating) means by completely abstaining from food. The construction is: being endowed with fasting according to the Dispensation or with external fasting. The word “or” also includes drinking milk, honey, and so forth. Pavāraṇā means that by which one restrains through modes such as sight, reminds one of bodily actions, and reproaches what is blameworthy—that is, it is the giving of an opportunity for purifying one’s conduct, for cleansing one’s own faults. Because this declaration of purity is mostly to be made by those who have completed the rains retreat, it is called the “Pavāraṇā of the Rains Retreat.” It is also called the “Pavāraṇā of Purification.” To show the quality of the completeness of the silence of that monastic community, the Pāli says, “they were silent.” Hence it is said: “From wherever... there is none.” Hatthakukkucca (hand-restlessness) is the restlessness of the hand, lack of restraint, an action lacking clear comprehension. Similarly, pādakukkucca (foot-restlessness) should be understood. The word “or” has the meaning of an unstated alternative; by this, the absence of other such things should be understood as being clarified.

Pañcapasādehīti pañcavaṇṇehi pasādehi. Vossaggattho yathāruci kiriyāya vossajjanaṃ. Pucchanattheti paṭikkhepamukheneva pucchanatthe nakāro, me kiñci kiriyaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā na garahatha, kiṃ nu garahatha kāyavācāhīti attho. Keci “dvārānevā”ti dvārasīsena dvārappavattacariyaṃ vadanti. Visuddhipavāraṇāya adhippetattā yena pavāritaṃ, teneva visuddhīti ñāyati, yena na pavāritaṃ. Kiṃ nu taṃ avisuddhanti siyā kassaci puthujjanassa āsaṅkā? Tannivāraṇatthamāha [V 1.0254] “no aparisuddhattā”ti. Manodvāraṃ [M 1.0290] parisuddhaṃ asucikārakaupakkilesānaṃ dūrīkatattā. Idāni etarahi buddhakāle. Etthāti manodvāraparisuddhiyaṃ.

Pañcapasādehi means with the five kinds of lucid faith. Vossaggattho (for the purpose of relinquishment) means the relinquishing of action according to one’s wish. Pucchanatthe (in the sense of asking): the particle ‘na’ is in the sense of asking by way of negation, meaning, “Do you not blame me for any bodily or verbal action; what then do you blame regarding body and speech?” Some say “dvārāneva” (only the doors), referring to conduct that occurs at the sense-doors by the heading of 'door'. Since purity is the intended aim of the Pavāraṇā, purity is known by the one who has invited criticism. For one who has not invited criticism, might there be a doubt for some ordinary person that they are impure? To dispel that doubt, it is said, “no aparisuddhattā” (not because of being impure). The mind-door is pure because defilements that cause impurity have been removed. Idāni (now) means at this time, during the Buddha’s time. Ettha (here) means in the purity of the mind-door.

Kāyavacīsamācāraparisuddhiyā paveditāya manosamācāraparisuddhi atthato paveditāva hotīti “kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā”iccevāha. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vāti idaṃ catunnaṃ arakkhiyataṃ sandhāya thero āhā”ti. “Bhikkhave, pavāremi vo”ti bhikkhusaṅghavisayattā pavāraṇāya tattha bhikkhusaṅghena vattabbaṃ paṭivacanaṃ dento dhammasenāpati “bhikkhusaṅghassa bhāraṃ vahanto”ti vutto. Tenāha “na kho mayaṃ, bhante”tiādi. Arakkhiyānīti parānuvādato na bhāyitabbāni suparisuddhabhāvato.

When the purity of bodily and verbal conduct has been declared, the purity of mental conduct is thereby declared in meaning; thus it is said, “bodily or verbal.” As it is stated: “The Elder spoke this, ‘bodily or verbal,’ in reference to the four unguarded things.” “Monks, I invite you”: since the Pavāraṇā pertains to the community of monks, the General of the Dhamma, bearing the burden of the Sangha, is said to respond with the appropriate reply that should be uttered by the Sangha. Therefore, he said, “Indeed, Venerable Sir, we do not,” etc. Arakkhiyāni (not to be guarded): meaning, because of their complete purity, they need not be feared from others’ reproach.

“Anuppannassā”ti idaṃ adhippāyikavacananti tadadhippāyaṃ vivaranto “kassapasammāsambuddhato paṭṭhāyā”tiādimāha. Kassapasammāsambuddhatoti vibhatte nissakkaṃ, tasmā kassapasammāsambuddhato oranti atthoti. Aññenāti ito bhagavato aññena. Anuppāditapubbassāti parasantāne na uppāditapubbassa. Sasantāne pana paccekabuddhānaṃ vasena na uppāditoti na sakkā vattuṃ. Samanuāgatāti sammā anu upagatā. Bhagavato sīlādayo guṇāti buddhabhūtassa guṇā adhippetāti āha “arahattamaggameva nissāya āgatā”ti. Sabbaguṇāti dasabalañāṇādayo sabbe buddhaguṇā. Bhanteti ettha itisaddo ādiattho. Tena “imesaṃ pana…pe… vācasikaṃ vā”ti yāvāyaṃ pāḷipadeso, taṃ sabbaṃ gaṇhāti. Tenāha “idaṃ thero…pe… pavārento āhā”ti.

Anuppannassa (of that which has not arisen): this is an intentional statement; explaining its intent, he says, “starting from Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,” etc. Kassapasammāsambuddhato: this is a departure in case ending; therefore, the meaning is “after Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.” Aññena (by another) means by another than this Blessed One. Anuppāditapubbassa (not previously produced) means not previously produced in the mental continuum of others. However, regarding one’s own mental continuum, it cannot be said that it did not arise in the case of the Paccekabuddhas. Samanuāgatā (endowed) means properly, closely, approached. Bhagavato sīlādayo guṇā (the qualities such as virtue of the Blessed One): the qualities of one who has become a Buddha are intended; thus it is said, “having come relying solely on the path to arahantship.” Sabbaguṇā (all qualities) means all the Buddha’s qualities, such as the ten powers and knowledges. Bhante (Venerable Sir): here the particle ‘iti’ has the meaning of 'and so on'. Therefore, it encompasses the entire Pāli passage from “imesaṃ pana…pe… vācasikaṃ vā.” Hence, it is said, “this the elder…pe… spoke while inviting criticism.”

Yaṃ attano puññānubhāvasiddhaṃ cakkaratanaṃ nippariyāyato tena pavattitaṃ nāma, na itaranti paṭhamanayo vutto. Yasmā pavattitasseva anupavattanaṃ, paṭhamanayo ca taṃsadise tabbohāravasena vuttoti taṃ anādiyitvā dutiyanayo vutto. Dasavidhanti antojanasmiṃ, balakāye rakkhāvaraṇaguttiyā saṃvidhānaṃ, khattiyesu anuyuttesu, brāhmaṇagahapatikesu, negamajānapadesu, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu, migapakkhīsu adhammacārapaṭikkhepo, adhanānaṃ dhanānuppadānaṃ, samaṇabrāhmaṇe upasaṅkamitvā pañhapucchananti evaṃ dasavidhaṃ. Tattha gahapatike pakkhijāte ca visuṃ katvā gahaṇavasena dvādasavidhaṃ. Cakkavattivattanti cakkavattibhāvāvahaṃ vattaṃ. Yasmā yāthāvato [M 1.0291] pavattitaṃ, tadanurūpakaṃ pana ñāyena yuttakena pavattitaṃ nāma hotīti āha “sammā nayena hetunā kāraṇenā”ti. Ubhatobhāgavimuttāti ubhayabhāgehi ubhayabhāgato vimuttāti ayamettha atthoti dasseti “dvīhi bhāgehi vimuttā, arūpā…pe… nāmakāyato”ti iminā. Tevijjādibhāvanti [V 1.0255] tevijjachaḷabhiññacatuppaṭisambhidabhāvaṃ. Paññāvimuttā hi taṃ tividhaṃ appattā kevalaṃ paññāya eva vimuttā.

The wheel-treasure, achieved by the power of one's own merit, is directly set in motion by him, not by another—this is the first method stated. Since the turning is a following-on of what has been set in motion, and the first method is stated by way of that usage in a similar case, disregarding that, the second method is stated. The tenfold duty is as follows: providing protection, guard, and security for the people within, for the army, for the attendant nobles, for brahmins and householders, for the town and country folk, and for ascetics and brahmins; the prohibition of unrighteous conduct towards beasts and birds; the granting of wealth to the destitute; and approaching ascetics and brahmins to ask questions—thus, it is tenfold. Here, by taking householders and the class of birds separately, it becomes twelvefold. Cakkavattivatta (the practice of a wheel-turning monarch) refers to the practice that brings about the state of a wheel-turner. Because it is set in motion in accordance with reality, what is in conformity with that is said to be 'set in motion' by a proper method, reason, and cause; thus it is said: 'rightly, by method, by reason, by cause.' Ubhatobhāgavimutta (liberated in both ways) means liberated from both parts, from both sides—this meaning is shown here by this: 'liberated by two parts, from the formless...from the mental body.' The state of the threefold knowledge and so forth refers to the state of possessing the threefold knowledge, the six higher knowledges, and the four analytical insights. Those liberated by wisdom, not having attained that threefold state, are liberated solely by wisdom.

Visuddhatthāyāti visuddhipavāraṇatthāya. Saṃyojanaṭṭhena saṃyojanasaṅkhāte ceva bandhanaṭṭhena bandhanasaṅkhāte ca. Vijitasaṅgāmanti yathā rāgādayo puna na sīsaṃ ukkhipanti, evaṃ ariyamaggasenāya vasena vijitasaṅgāmaṃ. Tenāha “vijitarāgadosamohasaṅgāma”nti. Mārabalassāti mārasenāya, mārassa vā sāmatthiyassa. Veneyyasatthanti vinetabbajanasamūhaṃ. Sakaṭādisatthasabhāgato vineyyova satthoti taṃ veneyyasatthaṃ. Sīlasārādiabhāvato antotuccho.

Visuddhatthāya means for the purpose of the Pavāraṇā of purity. In the sense of a fetter, that is, termed a fetter, and in the sense of a bond, that is, termed a bond. Vijitasaṅgāma (victor in battle) means that just as lust and the like do not raise their heads again, so the battle is won by means of the army of the Noble Path. Therefore, it is said, 'victor over the battles of lust, hatred, and delusion.' Mārabalassa (of Māra's army) means of Māra's army, or of Māra's power. Veneyyasattha (a group of those to be trained) means a multitude of people to be trained. Just as a caravan of carts and so forth is a group to be guided, so this is a group to be trained; thus, it is a 'group of those to be trained.' Antotuccho (empty inside) means because of the absence of the essence of virtue and so forth.

Pavāraṇāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pavāraṇā Sutta is concluded.

8. Parosahassasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Parosahassa Sutta

216. Sahassato paraṃ aḍḍhateyyabhikkhusataṃ tadā bhagavantaṃ payirupāsatīti āha “parosahassanti atirekasahassa”nti. Nibbāne kutoci bhayaṃ natthīti kutocipi kāraṇato nibbāne bhayaṃ natthi asaṅkhatabhāvena sabbaso khemattā. Tenāha bhagavā – “khemañca vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi khemagāminiñca paṭipada”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 4.379-408). Na kutoci bhayaṃ etasmiṃ adhigateti akutobhayaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Tenāha “nibbānappattassā”tiādi. Vipassito paṭṭhāyāti amhākaṃ bhagavato nāmavasena isīnaṃ sattamabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Te hi tattha tattha sutte bahuso kittitā. Isīnanti vā paccekabuddhasāvakabāhirakaisīnaṃ sattamo uttaro seṭṭhoti attho.

216. It is said: 'Parosahassa (beyond a thousand) means more than a thousand,' because at that time, two and a half hundred bhikkhus beyond a thousand were attending upon the Blessed One. In Nibbāna, there is no fear from any quarter; that is, for any reason whatsoever there is no fear in Nibbāna, because being unconditioned, it is entirely safe. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that is safe and the path that leads to safety,' and so on. Akutobhayaṃ (fearless from any quarter), Nibbāna, is so called because when this is attained, there is no fear from any quarter. Hence, it is said, 'for one who has attained Nibbāna,' and so on. 'Vipassito paṭṭhāya' (starting from Vipassī) was spoken to show the state of being the seventh among the sages, by way of the names in the lineage of our Blessed One. For they are often praised in various suttas. Or, 'among sages' means the seventh, superior, and foremost among Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and external sages.

Aṭṭhuppattivasenāti [M 1.0292] kāraṇasamuṭṭhānavasena. Tadassa aṭṭhuppattiṃ vibhāvetuṃ “saṅghamajjhe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭibhānasampannavācāya aññe īsati abhibhavatīti vaṅgīso. Tenāha “paṭibhānasampatti”ntiādi.

Aṭṭhuppattivasena means by way of the arising of a cause. To explain that arising of a cause, 'in the midst of the Sangha,' and so on, is stated. Vaṅgīsa is so called because he masters and surpasses others with speech endowed with ready wit. Therefore, it is said, 'the accomplishment of ready wit,' and so on.

Kilesummujjanasatānīti rāgādikilesānaṃ rajjanadussanādinayehi savisaye ayoniso uṭṭhānāni. Yadi anekāni satāni, atha kasmā “ummaggapatha”nti? Vuttanti āha “vaṭṭapathattā pana patha”nti. Rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhivasena rāgakhilādīni pañcakhilāni. Vibhajantanti vibhajanavasena kathentaṃ. Vibhajitvāti ñāṇena vivecetvā.

'Kilesummujjanasatāni' means the unskillful arisings of defilements such as lust, in their respective objects, in the manner of attachment, aversion, and so on. If there are many hundreds, then why is it called 'ummaggapatha' (a divergent path)? It is said in reply: 'Because it is a path, it is the path of the round of existence.' The five 'khilas' (barriers), beginning with the barrier of lust, are so called by way of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, and wrong view. 'Vibhajantaṃ' means explaining by way of analysis. 'Vibhajitvā' means having discerned with knowledge.

Amate [V 1.0256] akkhāteti amatāvahe dhamme desite. Dhammassa passitāro saccasampaṭivedhena. Asaṃhīrā diṭṭhivātehi.

'Amate akkhāte' means when the Dhamma leading to the Deathless has been taught. 'Dhammassa passitāro' means those who see the Dhamma by means of the penetration of the truth. 'Asaṃhīrā' means unshaken by the winds of views.

Ativijjhitvāti paṭivijjhitvā. Atikkamabhūtanti atikkamanaṭṭhena bhūtaṃ. Dasaddhānanti dasannaṃ upaḍḍhānaṃ. Tenāha “pañcanna”nti. Jānantenāti dhammassa sudullabhataṃ jānantena.

'Ativijjhitvā' means having thoroughly penetrated. 'Atikkamabhūtaṃ' means become in the sense of transcending. 'Dasaddhānaṃ' means ten halves. Therefore, it is said, 'of five.' 'Jānantena' means by one knowing the extreme rarity of the Dhamma.

Parosahassasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Parosahassa Sutta is concluded.

9. Koṇḍaññasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Koṇḍañña Sutta

217. Evaṃgahitanāmoti “aññāsi vata, bho, koṇḍañño”ti satthu vacanaṃ nissāya bhikkhūhi aññehi koṇḍaññanāmakehi visesanatthaṃ evaṃgahitanāmo. Dvādasannaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ vasena cirassaṃ. Chaddantabhavaneti chaddantanāgarājabhavanaṭṭhāne. Paññavā mahāsāvako rattaññutāya. “Dasasahassacakkavāḷe devamanussānanti dasasahassacakkavāḷe devānaṃ, imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe devamanussānañcāti evaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷe devamanussāna”nti vadanti. Aggantiādito. Tatthāti mandākinitīre.

217. 'Evaṃgahitanāmo' means he was thus named by the bhikkhus to distinguish him from others named Koṇḍañña, based on the Teacher’s words, "Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood, friend." 'Dvādasannaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ vasena cirassaṃ' means after a long time, that is, after twelve years. 'Chaddantabhavaneti' means in the place of the abode of the six-tusked elephant king. 'Paññavā mahāsāvako' means the wise great disciple, due to his seniority. 'Dasasahassacakkavāḷe devamanussānanti'—some say this means 'the devas in the ten-thousandfold world-system and the devas and humans in this world-system'—thus, 'devas and humans in the ten-thousandfold world-system.' 'Aggantiādito' means foremost from the beginning. 'Tatthāti' means there, at the Mandākinī River.

Vassaggenāti vassapaṭipāṭiyā. Tanti aññāsikoṇḍaññattheraṃ. Mahābrahmānaṃ viya lokiyamanussā harāyanti. Pāmokkhabhūto āyasmā [M 1.0293] thero antarantarā tattha tattha janapade vasitvā tadanukkamena mandākinitīraṃ upagato, tasmā vuttaṃ – “icchāmahaṃ, bhante, janapade vasitu”nti.

'Vassaggenāti' means in the sequence of the rains. 'Tanti' refers to the elder Aññāta Koṇḍañña. Worldly people are abashed before him, as before a Mahābrahmā. The venerable elder, being foremost, dwelt here and there in various regions and gradually arrived at the shore of the Mandākinī river. Therefore, it is said: "I wish, venerable sir, to dwell in a region."

Ānubhāvasampannā dibbāyukā te hatthināgāti vuttaṃ “pubbe paccekabuddhānaṃ pāricariyāya kataparicayā”ti. Therassa sañcaraṇaṭṭhāne āvaraṇasākhā haritvā apanetvā. Mukhodakañceva dantakaṭṭhañca ṭhapetīti saḷaladevadārukaṭṭhādīni aññamaññaṃ ghaṃsitvā aggiṃ nibbattetvā jāletvā tattha pāsāṇakhaṇḍāni tāpetvā tāni daṇḍakehi vaṭṭetvā taḷākāsu udakasoṇḍīsu khipitvā udakassa tattabhāvaṃ ñatvā nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ upanento mukhodakañca ṭhapeti. Vattaṃ karotīti antokuṭiyā bahi ca pamukhepi aṅgaṇepi sākhābhaṅgehi sammajjanto vakkhamānanayena āhāraṃ upanento vattaṃ karoti.

It is said of those elephant-nāgas that they possessed power and a divine lifespan because, as stated, 'They had previously cultivated familiarity through service to the Paccekabuddhas.' In the Elder's walking place, they took away and removed obstructing branches. 'Mukhodakañceva dantakaṭṭhañca ṭhapeti' means they provided water for washing the face and a tooth-stick. Rubbing together pieces of wood such as salala and devadāru, they generated fire, kindled it, heated fragments of stone in it, rolled them with sticks, and threw them into ponds or water channels; knowing the water was hot, they presented a nāgalatā tooth-stick and provided water for washing the face. 'Vattaṃ karotīti' means he performs his duties by sweeping inside the hut and outside, in the porch and the courtyard, with broken branches, and by bringing food in the manner to be described.

Patiṭṭhappamāṇeti kaṭippamāṇe, ayameva vā pāṭho tāva mahantamevāti yāva mahantaṃ setapadumavanaṃ[V 1.0257], tāva mahantameva. Eseva nayo rattakumudavanādīsu. Khādantā manussā. Pakkapayoghanikā viyāti supakkapayoghanaṃ viya. Ghanabhāvena pana pakkhittakhuddamadhu viya hoti. Tenāha “etaṃ pokkharamadhu nāmā”ti. Muḷālanti setapadumānaṃ mūlaṃ. Bhisanti tesaṃyeva kandaṃ. Ekasmiṃ pabbeti ekekasmiṃ pabbantare. Pādaghaṭakanti doṇassa catubhāgo saṇṭhānato khuddako, tasmā pādaghaṭakappamāṇanti tumbamattaṃ. Soṇḍiāvāṭeti khuddakasoṇḍiyo ceva khuddakaāvāṭe ca.

'Patiṭṭhappamāṇeti' means the measure of the hip; or this very reading means 'as vast as the white lotus grove, just so vast.' The same method applies to the red water-lily groves, etc. 'Khādantā manussā' means people eating. 'Pakkapayoghanikā viyāti' means like a well-ripened payoghana fruit. In terms of density, it is like honey from small bees that has been put in. Hence, it is said, 'this is called lotus honey.' 'Muḷālanti' means the root of white lotuses. 'Bhisanti' means their tubers. 'Ekasmiṃ pabbeti' means in each joint. 'Pādaghaṭakanti' means a quarter of a doṇa, small in shape; hence, 'pādaghaṭakappamāṇaṃ' means the size of a gourd. 'Soṇḍiāvāṭeti' means small water channels and small pits.

Etaṃ bhojananti yathāvuttaṃ nirudakapāyasabhojanaṃ. Keci sañjānanti ye therā vuḍḍhatarā. Keci na sañjānanti ye navā acirapabbajitā.

'Etaṃ bhojananti' means the food as mentioned, the meal of milk-rice without water. Some recognize it—those elders who are older. Some do not recognize it—those who are new and recently gone forth.

Buddhānubuddhoti buddhassa anubuddho. Bāḷhavīriyoti catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ vasena ciranicitavīriyo. Tiṇṇaṃ vivekānanti kāyacittaupadhivivekānaṃ lābhīti yojanā. Catasso vadati vaṅgīsatthero sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ, na sesābhiññānaṃ abhāvatoti āha “itarā”tiādi. Parisā sannisīdi nissaddabhāvena tuṇhī ahosīti attho. Anujānāpesīti paṭhamaṃ attanā ñātaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ attano parinibbānakālaṃ anu pacchā satthāraṃ jānāpesīti evaṃ ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Buddhānubuddhoti' means one who is enlightened after the Buddha. 'Bāḷhavīriyoti' means one of strong effort, with energy long cultivated on the basis of the four right exertions. 'Tiṇṇaṃ vivekānanti'—the construction is that he is an obtainer of the three kinds of seclusion: seclusion of body, mind, and substrates. 'Catasso vadati' means the elder Vaṅgīsa speaks four stanzas spontaneously; it is not due to the absence of the other higher knowledges that he says 'the others,' etc. 'Parisā sannisīdi' means the assembly sat down and became silent. 'Anujānāpesīti'—here the meaning should be understood thus: first he knew himself that his time to pass away was at hand, and then afterwards informed the Teacher.

Tanti [M 1.0294] āsāḷhipuṇṇamāya isipatane yaṃ dassanaṃ, yaṃ vā dukkaracariyāyaṃ tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ ādito dassanaṃ, taṃ, bhante, paṭhamadassanaṃ. Onatavinatāti heṭṭhā upari ca onatā vinatā. Kampetvāti thokaṃ cāletvā dassanatthaṃ ekaninnādo tesaṃ hatthināgānañceva nāgayakkhakumbhaṇḍānaṃ devatānañca saddena. Brahmāno devānaṃ adaṃsūti sambandho.

'Tanti' means that, venerable sir, was the first sight: the sight at Isipatana on the Āsāḷhi full moon, or the sight of you from the beginning of our attendance on you during the difficult practice. 'Onatavinatāti' means bent down below and bent up above. 'Kampetvāti' means having shaken them a little to show them, with a single sound from those elephant-nāgas, nāga-yakkhās, kumbhaṇḍas, and deities. 'Brahmāno devānaṃ adaṃsūti' is the connection, meaning 'the Brahmās gave to the devas.'

Sajjhāyamakaṃsu pasādanīyesu pasādavasena sannipatitaparisāya pasādajananatthaṃ bhagavati nikkhamitvāti bhagavati gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā. Dharatiyevāti aduṭṭhataṃ patvā tiṭṭhateva.

They recited to generate faith in the assembly that had gathered by way of faith in inspiring things. 'Bhagavati nikkhamitvāti' means having gone out from the Blessed One's perfumed chamber. 'Dharatiyevāti' means he remains, having reached a state of non-corruption.

Koṇḍaññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Koṇḍañña Sutta is concluded.

10. Moggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta

218. Paccavekkhatīti tesaṃ ariyānaṃ cittaṃ attano ñāṇacakkhunā pati avekkhati paccavekkhati. Pabbatassāti isigilipabbatassa. Dukkhapāraṃ gatanti vaṭṭadukkhassa pāraṃ pariyantaṃ gataṃ[V 1.0258]. Sabbaguṇasampannanti sabbehi buddhaguṇehi ca sāvakaguṇehi ca paripuṇṇaṃ. Anekākārasampannanti rūpaghosalūkhadhammappamāṇikānaṃ sattānaṃ tehi tehi ākārehi sabbesañca anekehi anantāparimeyyehi pasīditabbākārehi samannāgataṃ. Te pana ākārā yasmā anaññasādhāraṇā buddhaguṇā eva, tasmā āha “anekehi guṇehi samannāgata”nti.

218. 'Paccavekkhati' means he examines the minds of those noble ones with his own eye of wisdom. 'Pabbatassāti' means of the Isigili mountain. 'Dukkhapāraṃ gataṃ' means gone to the far shore, the limit, of the suffering of the round of existence. 'Sabbaguṇasampannaṃ' means complete with all the qualities of a Buddha and the qualities of a disciple. 'Anekākārasampannaṃ' means endowed with many aspects that inspire faith in beings who are fond of form, sound, coarse practice, and measure, and endowed with countless, immeasurable aspects that inspire faith in all. Since these aspects are indeed the unique qualities of a Buddha, therefore it is said, 'endowed with many virtues.'

Moggallānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta is concluded.

11. Gaggarāsuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Gaggarā Sutta

219. Teti te devamanusse. “Sarīravaṇṇenāti sarīre chavivaṇṇenā”ti vadanti. Sarīravaṇṇenāti vā dhammarūpakāyaguṇena. “Yasasā”tipi pāṭho, so evattho. Vigatamaloti abbhāmahikādīhi vigatūpakkileso[M 1.0295]. Bhāṇu vuccati pabhā, sātisayo bhāṇu etassa atthīti bhāṇumā. Sūriyoti āha “ādicco viyā”ti.

219. 'Teti' means those devas and humans. 'Sarīravaṇṇenāti'—some say this means 'by the color of the skin of the body.' Or 'sarīravaṇṇenā' can mean by the qualities of the Dhamma-form-body. 'Yasasā' is also a reading, and it has the same meaning. 'Vigatamaloti' means free from defilements such as clouds and mist. 'Bhāṇu' is called radiance. One who possesses surpassing radiance is 'bhāṇumā.' 'Sūriyoti'—he said, 'like the sun.'

Gaggarāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Gaggarā Sutta is concluded.

12. Vaṅgīsasuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta.

220. So kira vicaratīti sambandho. “Yathāyaṃ dīpo jambudīpoti jambunā paññāto, evāhampi tena jambunā paññāyissa”nti jambusākhaṃ pariharitvā. Vādaṃ katvāti “imasmiṃ vāde sace te parājayo hoti, tvaṃ me dāso hohi. Sace me parājayo, ahaṃ te bhariyā”ti evaṃ katikaṃ katvā. Vāde jayaparājayānubhāvenāti tathāpavattite vāde paribbājakassa jayānubhāvena ceva attano parājayena ca. Vayaṃ āgammāti sippuggahaṇavayaṃ āgamma. Vijjanti mantaṃ.

220. 'So kira vicaratīti' is the connection. Carrying a branch of the jambu tree, he thought: 'Just as this island is known as Jambudīpa because of the jambu tree, so too shall I be known by that jambu tree.' 'Vādaṃ katvāti' means having made an agreement thus: 'If you are defeated in this debate, you shall be my slave. If I am defeated, I shall be your wife.' 'Vāde jayaparājayānubhāvenāti' means by the power of the wanderer's victory and his own defeat in the debate that proceeded thus. 'Vayaṃ āgammāti' means having come to the age for learning crafts. 'Vijjanti' means a mantra.

Nibbattagativibhāvanavasena chavasīsabhāvaṃ dūseti vināsetīti chavadūsakaṃ sippaṃ, tathāpavattaṃ mantapadaṃ. Attano ānubhāvenāti niraye nibbattasattassa sīsaṃ yattha katthaci ṭhitaṃ buddhānubhāvena ānetvā dassetvā. Khīṇāsavassa sīsanti paramappicchatāya kañcipi ajānāpetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā parinibbutassa khīṇāsavassa chaḍḍitaṃ sīsakaṭāhaṃ. Dassesīti attano ānubhāvena ānetvā dassesi.

'The art of skull destruction' (chavadūsakaṃ sippaṃ) means the art that corrupts and destroys the state of having a skull by way of revealing the state of rebirth; it is a mantra that operates in the same way. 'By one's own power' (attano ānubhāvena) means having brought and shown the head of a being born in hell, wherever it may be, by the power of the Buddha. 'The skull of one whose defilements are destroyed' (khīṇāsavassa sīsaṃ) means the discarded skull-bowl of an arahant who, due to extreme contentment, entered the forest without informing anyone and attained final Nibbāna. 'He showed it' (dassesi) means he brought it by his own power and displayed it.

“Tumhe, bho gotama, jānāthā”ti kāmaṃ vaṅgīso nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya pucchati, bhagavā pana [V 1.0259] anupādisesanibbānaṃ sandhāya “āma, vaṅgīsa…pe… gatiṃ jānāmī”ti āha. Vuttañhetaṃ “nibbānaṃ arahato gatī”ti. Vaṅgīso sayaṃ mantabalena gatipariyāpannassa gatiṃ jānanto bhagavantampi “ayampi tathā”ti maññamāno “mantena jānāsi, bho gotamā”ti āha. Bhagavā attano buddhañāṇameva mantaṃ katvā dīpento “āma, vaṅgīsa, ekena manteneva jānāmī”ti āha. Mudhā eva dātabbanti amūliko. Anantarahitāya bhūmiyā sayanaṃ thaṇḍilaseyyā. Ādi-saddena sāyatatiyaṃ udakorohaṇabhūmiharaṇādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. So taṃ…pe… arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti iminā vaṅgīsatthero pabbajitvā na cirasseva sukhāya paṭipadāya arahattaṃ patto viya dissati, na kho panetaṃ [M 1.0296] evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, āyatiṃ thero pabbajitvā samathavipassanāsu kammaṃ ārabhitvāpi dukkhāya paṭipadāya tādisaṃ kālaṃ vītināmetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tenāha –

'You, Venerable Gotama, know it' (tumhe, bho gotama, jānātha)—though Vaṅgīsa asks referring to the place of rebirth, the Blessed One answers with reference to remainderless Nibbāna: 'Yes, Vaṅgīsa… I know the destination.' For it is said, 'Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant.' Vaṅgīsa, knowing the destination included in the range of his own mantra power, thinking that the Blessed One also knew in that way, says, 'You know it by mantra, Venerable Gotama?' The Blessed One, revealing his own Buddha-knowledge as the mantra, says, 'Yes, Vaṅgīsa, I know it by a single mantra.' 'To be given in vain' (mudhā eva dātabbaṃ) means groundless. 'Lying on the ground without an intervening layer' (anantarahitāya bhūmiyā sayanaṃ) is a hard ground bed (thaṇḍilaseyyā). The word 'etc.' (ādi-saddena) includes descending into water at the three times of day, sweeping the grounds, and so forth. 'He… attained arahantship' (so taṃ…pe… arahattaṃ pāpuṇi)—by this, the elder Vaṅgīsa, having gone forth, seems to have quickly attained arahantship by the pleasant practice. But it should not be seen like that. In the future, after going forth, the elder undertook work on serenity and insight, spent such a time by the painful practice, and then attained arahantship. Therefore it is said:

“Nikkhantaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

Vitakkā upadhāvanti, pagabbhā kaṇhato ime”. (saṃ. ni. 1.209; theragā. 1218);

'Indeed, though calm, I have gone forth from home to homelessness; yet these bold thoughts from the Dark One rush upon me.' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.209; Thag 1218)

Āyasmato vaṅgīsassa anabhirati uppannā hoti, rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃseti, “kāmarāgena ḍayhāmi, cittaṃ me pariḍayhatī”tiādi (theragā. 1232).

Discontent arose in the Venerable Vaṅgīsa; passion assailed his mind: 'I am scorched by sensual passion, my mind is scorched,' and so forth (Thag 1232).

Vimuttisukhanti sabbaso kilesavimuttiyaṃ nibbāne ca uppannaṃ sampatiarahattaphalasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentoti yathāparicchinnaṃ kālaṃ pati sammadeva vedento anubhavanto. Kavinā kataṃ, tato vā āgataṃ, tassa vā idanti kāveyaṃ, tadevettha “kāveyya”nti vuttaṃ. Ye niyāmagataddasāti ye bhikkhū ariyā buddhānaṃ sāvakā phalaṭṭhabhāvena niyāmagatā ceva maggaṭṭhabhāvena niyāmadasā ca. Niyāmoti hi sammattaniyāmo adhippeto. Suāgamananti mama imassa satthuno santike āgamanaṃ upagamanaṃ, imasmiñca dhammavinaye āgamanaṃ pabbajanaṃ upasampadā sundaraṃ āgamanaṃ. Tattha kāraṇamāha “tisso vijjā”tiādi. Avuttampi gāthāya atthato gahitameva therassa chaḷabhiññabhāvato.

'The bliss of liberation' (vimuttisukhaṃ) means experiencing and enjoying rightly for the precisely determined time the present happiness of the fruit of Arahantship that has arisen in complete freedom from defilements and in Nibbāna. 'Kāveyya' means what is made by a poet, or comes from that, or belongs to him; that is what is called 'kāveyya' here. 'Those who have attained and seen the fixed order' (ye niyāmagataddasā) means those monks, noble disciples of the Buddhas, who have attained the fixed order by being established in the fruit and have seen the fixed order by means of the path. For 'the fixed order' (niyāmo) here refers to the right fixed order (sammattaniyāmo). 'A good arrival' (suāgamanaṃ) means my coming to this Teacher, approaching him, and entering this Dhamma-Vinaya, ordination and full admission, is a beautiful arrival. Here, the reason is stated: 'the threefold knowledge' (tisso vijjā) and so forth. Even what is unsaid in the verse is already grasped in meaning by the Elder due to his possessing the sixfold direct knowledges.

Vaṅgīsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta is concluded.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

The Sāratthappakāsinī: The Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Vaṅgīsasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of subtle meanings in the Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta is concluded.

9. Vanasaṃyuttaṃ

9. The Connected Discourses on the Forest

1. Vivekasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Seclusion

221. Saṃvejetukāmāti [V 1.0260][M 1.0297] atthato saṃvegaṃ uppādetukāmā. Tathābhūtā naṃ kilesasaṅgaṇikādito vivecetukāmā nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “vivekaṃ paṭipajjāpetukāmā”ti. Bāhiresūti gocarajjhattato bahibhūtesu. Puthuttārammaṇesūti rūpādinānārammaṇesu. Caratīti pavattati. Tvaṃ janoti tvaṃ attano kilesehi jananato visuṃ jāto tādise eva aññasmiṃ jane imaṃ ayonisomanasikāravasena pavattamānaṃ chandarāgaṃ vinayassu vinodehi. Sataṃ taṃ sārayāmaseti niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññavāsena ca satimantaṃ paṇḍitaṃ taṃ mayampi yathāuppannaṃ vitakkaṃ vinodanāya sārayāma, sataṃ vā sappurisānaṃ kilesavigamanadhammaṃ paṭipajjitvā vasantaṃ taṃ sārayāma vaṭṭadukkhaṃ. Pātālanti mohapātālaṃ kilesarajo, tadeva “pātāla”nti vuttaṃ. Mā avaharīti heṭṭhā duggatisotaṃ mā upanesi. Sitanti sambandhaṃ. Tenāha “sarīralagga”nti. Vivekamāpannoti kilesavivekaṃ samathavipassanābhāvanamāpanno. Uttamavīriyanti ussoḷhilakkhaṇappattaṃ vīriyaṃ, catubbidhaṃ samappadhānavīriyaṃ vā sampattaṃ. Paggayhāti āropetvā. Paramavivekanti paramaṃ samucchedavivekaṃ.

221. "Desiring to arouse urgency" means, in essence, wishing to generate a sense of urgency. Such a one is called "desiring to detach" from the entanglement of defilements and the like, as it is said, "desiring to lead to seclusion." "External" refers to what is external to the internal domain. "With diverse objects" means with various objects such as forms, etc. "Wanders" means occurs. You, person, you who have arisen distinct from the generation by your own defilements, subdue and dispel this lust that arises through unwise attention in such another person. "We will remind him, the mindful one"—having gone forth under the teaching that leads to liberation, receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, and dwelling in the forest—we too will remind that wise and mindful one to dispel arisen thoughts, or we will remind him, who dwells practicing the Dhamma of abandoning defilements of the virtuous ones, of the suffering of the cycle. "The abyss" is the abyss of delusion, the dust of defilements; that itself is called "the abyss." "Do not drag down"—do not lead downward to the stream of bad destinations. "Clinging" means connection. Therefore, it is said, "clinging to the body." "Attained to seclusion" means having attained the seclusion from defilements through the development of serenity and insight. "Supreme energy" means energy that has reached the characteristic of striving, or the fourfold right effort attained. "Having exerted" means having roused. "Ultimate seclusion" means the supreme seclusion of eradication.

Vivekasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Seclusion is concluded.

2. Upaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Upaṭṭhāna Sutta

222. Kāyadaratho hotiyeva niyamena, na cittadaratho tassa maggeneva samugghāṭitattā.

222. Bodily distress certainly exists, but not mental distress, for that has been completely eradicated by the path.

Jarāturoti jarābhibhavanena āturoyeva. Padadvayepi eseva nayo. Upariṭṭhatāya parito dīghaputhulatāya ativiya vijjhatīti sattisallaggahaṇaṃ. Evaṃ hissa taṇhāsallassa sadisatā. Avijjāya pana sammohāpādanena [M 1.0298] dukkhāpādanena ca visasadisatā. Ruppatoti vikāraṃ āpādiyamānassa pīḷiyamānassāti atthoti āha “ghaṭṭiyamānassā”ti.

"Afflicted by old age" means being truly afflicted by being overcome by old age. The same method applies to both terms. The term 'spear-dart' is used because it pierces exceedingly from above, all around, in length and breadth. Thus, there is similarity to the dart of craving. But ignorance has similarity to poison because it produces delusion and suffering. "Tormented" means being altered and oppressed; that is, it means, he said, "being ground down."

Pabbajitanti [V 1.0261] sasantānato pabbajitaṃ vā rāgādimalato pabbajitaṃ vā. Tasmāti yasmā therassevetaṃ vacanaṃ, tasmā ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno ettha gāthāya attho. Devatāya hītiādi vuttasseva atthassa pākaṭakaraṇaṃ. Etthāti sesagāthāsu. Atthassa vuttanayattā “anuttānapadavaṇṇanā”ti āha. Vinayāti hetumhi nissakkavacananti tassa hetumhi karaṇavacanena atthamāha “vinayenā”ti. Tathā “samatikkamā”ti etthāpi. Paramaparisuddhaṃ saṃkilesasamucchindanato. Āraddhavīriyanti sambhāvitavīriyaṃ. Sambhāvanañcassa paggaṇhanaṃ paripūraṇañcāti āha “paggahitavīriyaṃ paripuṇṇavīriya”nti.

"One gone forth" refers either to one gone forth from one's own continuum or to one gone forth from defilements like lust and so on. "Therefore" means: because this is a statement of the Elder, therefore, this is the meaning of the verse now being spoken here. "By the deity" and so on is a making clear of the meaning already stated. "Here" refers to the remaining verses. Since the meaning has been explained, he said, "an explanation of words that are not clear." "Vinaya" is a word indicating cause; thus, its meaning is stated by the instrumental case in the sense of cause, as 'by discipline'. Likewise also for "by transgression." "Utterly pure" because of the complete cutting off of defilements. "With energy aroused" means energy that is esteemed. And the esteeming of it is the undertaking and the fulfilling, hence he said, "energy undertaken and energy fulfilled."

Upaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Upaṭṭhāna Sutta is concluded.

3. Kassapagottasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Kassapagotta Sutta

223. Chetanti migānaṃ jīvitaṃ chetaṃ. Tenāha “migaluddaka”nti. Rohitamiganti lohitavaṇṇaṃ khuddakamigaṃ, “mahārohitamiga”nti keci. Satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā tassa janapadassa sulabhabhikkhatāya tattha gantvā viharatīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya “paṭhamasutte vuttanayenevā”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana thero pañcābhiñño vipassanākammiko. Ṭhatvāti padānubandhanavasena gamanaṃ upacchinditvā therassa āsannaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā. Tassa vacanaṃ sotuṃ āraddho. Aṅguṭṭhakaṃ jālāpesīti adhiṭṭhānabalena daṇḍadīpikaṃ viya attano aṅguṭṭhakaṃ jālāpesi. Akkhīhipi passati aṅguṭṭhakaṃ jālamānaṃ. Kaṇṇehipi suṇāti tena vuccamānaṃ dhammaṃ ekadesena. Cittaṃ panassa dhāvatīti sambandho. Etassapīti luddakassapi.

223. “Hunter” means one who destroys the lives of animals; hence, it is said, “a deer hunter.” “Rohita deer” refers to a small deer of reddish color; some say “great rohita deer.” Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and because alms were easily obtainable in that region, he went there to dwell—this is the meaning implied by “as explained in the first sutta.” This elder, however, possessed the five supernormal knowledges and practiced insight meditation. “Stood” means stopping his journey by tracing the footsteps and standing near the elder. He began to listen to his words. “Made his thumb glow” means, by the power of determination, he caused his own thumb to glow like a torch. With his eyes, he saw his thumb glowing. With his ears, he heard a part of the Dhamma being spoken. But his mind was wandering—this is the connection. “Of this one too” refers also to the hunter.

Appapaññanti ettha appa-saddo “appaharite”tiādīsu viya abhāvatthoti āha “nippañña”nti. Kāraṇajānanasamatthenāti iminā kāraṇena sattānaṃ sukhaṃ, iminā dukkhanti evaṃ samācaramānena kāraṇaṃ jānituṃ [M 1.0299] samatthena kammassakatañāṇasampayuttacittenāti attho. Suṇātīti kevalaṃ savanamattavasena suṇāti, na tadatthavasena. Tenāha “atthamassa na jānātī”ti. Kāraṇarūpānīti sabhāvakāraṇāni. Kiṃ me imināti? “Idaṃ papañca”nti pahāya. Vīriyaṃ paggayhāti catubbidhaṃ sammappadhānaṃ vīriyaṃ paggaṇhitvā.

“Appapañña” (lacking wisdom): here the word “appa” signifies absence, as in “appaharite” (lacking greenery) and similar terms; thus, it is said, “nippañña” (without wisdom). “Kāraṇajānanasamatthena” (capable of understanding causes) means with a mind endowed with the knowledge of ownership of kamma, which is capable of understanding the cause by practicing thus: “Through this cause beings experience happiness; through this, suffering.” “Suṇāti” (hears) means one merely hears, only in terms of the act of hearing, not in terms of its meaning. Hence, it is said, “he does not know its meaning.” “Kāraṇarūpāni” (forms of cause) refers to intrinsic causes. “Kiṃ me iminā?” (What is this to me?) means abandoning it as “this is proliferation.” “Vīriyaṃ paggayha” (exerting energy) means having exerted the fourfold right exertion.

Kassapagottasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kassapagotta Sutta is concluded.

4. Sambahulasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta

224. Sambahulāti [V 1.0262] suttantanayena sambahulā. Suttante sajjhāyiṃsūti suttantikā. Vinayaṃ dhārentīti vinayadharā. Yuñjantīti vāsadhure yogaṃ karonti. Ghaṭentīti tattha vāyāmaṃ karonti. Karontānaṃyeva aruṇo uggacchatīti sambandho.

224. “Sambahulā” means “many” in the sense of the suttas. “Suttantikā” means “those who recite the suttas.” “Vinayadharā” means “those who uphold the Vinaya.” “Yuñjanti” means they apply themselves, making effort in the burden of dwelling. “Ghaṭenti” means they strive therein. The connection is that dawn breaks while they are still doing so.

Kometi kiṃ ime? Tenāha “kahaṃ ime”ti? Vajjibhūmiṃ vajjiraṭṭhaṃ gatāti vajjibhūmiyā. Tenāha “vajjiraṭṭhābhimukhā gatā”ti. Natthi etesaṃ nikebhaṃ nibaddhanivāsaṭṭhānanti aniketā tenāha “agehā”ti. Utu eva sappāyaṃ, utuvasena vā kāyacittānaṃ kallattā sappāyaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi.

“Kome ti kiṃ ime?” means “What of these?” Therefore it is said, “Where are these?” “Vajjibhūmiyā” means “to the Vajji territory,” having gone to the Vajji country. Therefore it is said, “they have gone facing the Vajji country.” “Aniketā” means they have no fixed abode, no permanent dwelling place. Therefore it is said, “homeless.” “Utu eva sappāyaṃ” means the season itself is suitable, or it is suitable because the body and mind are healthy due to the season. This same method applies in the remaining cases.

Sambahulasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta is concluded.

5. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

225. Ativelanti atibahukālaṃ. Bhikkhunā nāma upagatānaṃ upanisinnakathāmattaṃ vatvā ganthadhurehi vāsadhurehi vā yuttapayuttacittena bhavitabbaṃ, nātivelaṃ tesaṃ saññattibahulena. Thero pana tadā kenaci kāraṇena bahuvelaṃ gihisaññattibahulo ahosi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ativela”ntiādi. Idāni tamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “bhagavatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti taṃ tādisaṃ saññāpanaṃ sandhāya etaṃ “ativelaṃ gihisaññattibahulo”ti vacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhikkhusaṅghassa kathaṃ sutvāti saṅghassa [M 1.0300] majjhe nisīditvā therena kathitattā vuttaṃ. Satthusāsananti piṭakattayaṃ vadati.

225. “Ativelaṃ” means for an excessively long time. A monk, when approached, should speak only briefly and then remain with a mind devoted either to the burden of study or to the burden of dwelling, not being much occupied with instructing them for too long. But the elder at that time, for some reason, was much occupied with instructing householders for a long time. With reference to that, “ativela” and so on was said. Now, to clarify that meaning, “bhagavatī” and so on was said. That is to say, with reference to that kind of instruction, this statement “was much occupied with instructing householders for a long time” was made. The phrase “having heard the talk of the Sangha of monks” is stated because the elder spoke while seated in the midst of the Sangha. “Satthusāsana” refers to the three Piṭakas.

Pasakkiyāti upasakkitvā gantvā. Taṃ pana tattha ajjhogāhanaṃ hotīti āha “pavisitvā”ti. Saṅkhāradukkhato nibbinnahadayassa sabbasaṅkhāravinissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ yāthāvato paccavekkhantassa sammadeva samassāsakaraṃ hutvā upaṭṭhahantaṃ taṃ upari adhigamāya ussukkaṃ karonto nibbānaṃ hadaye nikkhipati nāmāti āha – “nibbānaṃ…pe… opeti nāmā”ti. Nibbānaṃ…pe… ārammaṇato opeti nāmāti ānetvā sambandho. Atthavirahitā “biḷibiḷī”ti pavattakiriyā biḷikā, ayaṃ pana gihisaññattikathā therassa attano sāmaññatthaasādhanato devatāya biḷikā viyāti biḷibiḷikāti vuttā.

“Pasakkiyā” means having approached and gone. That indeed is immersion there; thus it is said, “having entered.” For one whose heart is weary of the suffering of formations, Nibbāna—the complete release from all formations—appears as it truly is when one reflects upon it. Having become a source of true comfort, it presents itself.
