Making an effort for higher attainment, one indeed places Nibbāna in the heart—thus it is said, “Nibbāna...as it were, implants.” The connection is drawn by bringing in the words, “implants Nibbāna as an object.” The meaningless activity that proceeds as “biḷibiḷī” is called chattering. But this talk of instructing householders, because it does not accomplish the elder's own goal of recluseship, is like the chattering of a deity; thus it is called “biḷibiḷikā.”

Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is concluded.

6. Anuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta

226. Anantare [V 1.0263] attabhāveti atītānantare devattabhāve. Thero hi tāvatiṃsadevalokā cavitvā idhūpapanno. Aggamahesīti kāci paricārikā devadhītā cittapaṇidhānamattena idānipi devakāye bhavissati upacitakusaladhammattāti maññamānā tasmiṃ vattamānaṃ viya kathentī “sobhasī”ti āha. Evaṃ atītampissa dibbasotaṃ paccuppannaṃ viya maññeyya nāticirakālattāti dassento “pubbepi sobhasī”ti āha. Sugatinirayādiduggatiyā vasena duggatā etarahīti adhippāyo. Paṭipattiduggatiyā kāmesu sammucchitabhāvato.

226. “In the immediately following existence” means in the immediately preceding divine existence. For the Elder, having passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa divine realm, was reborn here. “The chief queen”—some attendant goddess, thinking, “Even now, by the mere power of her aspiration, she will exist in the divine realm, as her wholesome qualities have accumulated,” spoke as if referring to something happening in the present: “You shine.” Thus, showing that his past divine state should be regarded as if it were present, as it was not a very long time ago, she said, “You shone even in the past.” The meaning is that she is now in a wretched state by way of a miserable destination such as hell. She is wretched in practice due to being utterly infatuated with sensual pleasures.

Patiṭṭhahantoti nivisanto. Aṭṭhahi kāraṇehīti cirakālaparibhāvanāya viruḷhamūlehi ayonisomanasikārādipaccayamūlakehi vuccamānehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi. Ratto rāgavasenāti sabhāvato saṅkappato ca yathāsamīhite iṭṭhākāre sakkāye sañjātarāgavasā ratto giddho gadhito. Patiṭṭhātīti oruyha tiṭṭhati. Duṭṭho dosavasenāti [M 1.0301] sabhāvato saṅkappato ca yathāsamīhite aniṭṭhākāre sakkāye sañjātadosavasena duṭṭho rupitacitto. Mūḷho mohavasenāti asamapekkhanena mūḷho muyhanavasena. Vinibaddhoti ahaṃkārena visesato nibandhanato mānavatthusmiṃ bandhito. Mānavasenāti tena tena maññanākārena. Parāmaṭṭhoti dhammasabhāvaṃ niccādivasena parato āmaṭṭho. Diṭṭhivasenāti micchādassanavasena. Thāmagatoti rāgādikilesavasena thāmaṃ thirabhāvaṃ upagato. Anusayavasenāti maggena appahīnatāya anu anu santāne sayanavasena. Appahīnaṭṭho hi tesaṃ anusayaṭṭho. Aniṭṭhaṅgatoti saṃsayito. Vikkhepagatoti vikkhittabhāvaṃ upagato. Uddhaccavasenāti cittassa uddhatabhāvavasena. Tāpīti tāpi devakaññāyo. Evaṃ patiṭṭhitāvāti yathāvuttanayena rattabhāvādinā sakkāyasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā eva. Naradevānanti purisabhūtadevānaṃ.

“Patiṭṭhahanto” means settling down. “By eight causes” refers to the eight causes mentioned, which are deeply rooted due to long-term cultivation and have unwise attention and so on as their root condition. “Infatuated by lust” means, naturally and by intention, one is infatuated, greedy, and attached due to the arising of lust for a pleasing form of selfhood, as desired. “Patiṭṭhāti” means descending and standing firm. “Hostile by hatred” means, naturally and by intention, one is hostile and with a resentful mind due to the arising of hatred for an unpleasing form of selfhood, as desired. “Confused by delusion” means confused due to lack of proper investigation, by way of bewilderment. “Bound” means being especially bound by ego-conceit, tied to the object of pride. “By pride” means by that particular manner of conceiving. “Grasped” means the nature of things wrongly grasped as permanent, etc. “By wrong view” means by way of false seeing. “Obstinate” means having attained firmness due to defilements like lust. “By latent tendencies” means due to their not being abandoned by the path, lying latent in the continuum again and again. For the state of those not abandoned is their latent state. “Uncertain” means doubtful. “Distracted” means having attained a scattered state. “By restlessness” means due to the agitated nature of the mind. “Tāpī” refers to those tormented celestial maidens. “Thus established” means indeed established in selfhood in the manner described—by being infatuated, etc. “Among human and divine beings” means among men who are like gods.

Paṭigantunti apekkhāvasena tato apagantuṃ apekkhaṃ vissajjetuṃ. Dussantanti dasantaṃ, “vattha”nti keci. Sūciṃ yojetvāti sibbanasuttena sūciṃ yojetvā pāse ca pavesetvā. Manāpakāye devanikāye jātā manāpakāyikā. Tesaṃ pabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “manasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samajjanti saṃhitaṃ. Gamanabhāvanti gamanajjhāsayaṃ. Vikkhīṇoti vicchindanavasena khīṇo. Devatānaṃ uttarimanussadhammārocane doso natthīti tāsaṃ puna anāgamanatthaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi.

“Paṭigantuṃ” means to relinquish the expectation of departing from there. “Dussantaṃ” means biting; some say “cloth.” “Sūciṃ yojetvā” means having joined the needle with sewing thread and having inserted it into the loop. Those born in the delightful celestial group are called “manāpakāyikā.” To show their power, “manasā” and so on was said. “Samajjaṃ” means compact. “Gamanabhāvaṃ” means the intention to go. “Vikkhīṇo” means exhausted in the sense of being cut off. There is no fault for devas in declaring supramundane qualities; therefore, he declared his attainment of arahantship so that they might not return.

Anuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta is concluded.

7. Nāgadattasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Nāgadatta Sutta

227. Atikālenāti [V 1.0264] ativiya pubbaṇhakālena, kālassevāti attho. Koṭisammuñjaniyāti sammuñjanikoṭiyā, sammuñjaniyā ekadesenevāti attho. Iminā sammajjane amanāpakāritaṃ dasseti. Majjhanhike vītivatteti gihisaṃsaggavasena kālaṃ vītināmento majjhanhe bahuvītivatte. Aññehi bhikkhūhīti nātikālaṃ paviṭṭhehi. Nissakkavacanañcetaṃ. Bhāyāmi nāgadattanti tassa paṭipattiṃ bhāyitabbaṃ katvā devatā vadantī [M 1.0302] paṭipattiyaṃ niyojeti. Suppagabbhanti kāyapāgabbiyādīhi ativiya samannāgataṃ.

227. "Atikālenāti" means excessively in the morning time, that is, too early. "Koṭisammuñjaniyāti" means with the tip of the broom, that is, with just one part of the broom. This indicates that the sweeping was done in an unpleasant manner. "Majjhanhike vītivatteti" means spending time in association with householders, letting much of the midday pass. "Aññehi bhikkhūhīti" refers to those monks who have not entered at an excessive time. This is an ablative expression. "Bhāyāmi nāgadattanti" means the deity, making his conduct something to be feared, urges him to apply himself to the practice. "Suppagabbhanti" means exceedingly endowed with bodily audacity and other such qualities.

Nāgadattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Nāgadatta Sutta is concluded.

8. Kulagharaṇīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary to the Kulagharaṇī Sutta

228. Ogāhappattoti vissāsavasena anuppavesaṃ patto. Aññataraṃ kulanti tasmiṃ kule jāyampatiṃ sandhāya vadati. “Bahūpakāraṃ me etaṃ kulaṃ ciraṃ sappāyāhāradānādinā; tasmā idhāhaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyo jāto; imesaṃyeva deyyadhammapaṭiggaṇhanena puññaṃ vaḍḍhessāmī”ti cintesi. Tenāha “aññattha gantvā kiṃ karissāmī”tiādi. Sāti devatā. Ubhopeteti taṃ bhikkhuñca gharaṇiñca sandhāya vadati. Paṭigādhappattāti paṭigādhaṃ pattā aññamaññasmiṃ patiṭṭhitavissāsena.

228. "Ogāhappattoti" means having gained entry due to trust. "Aññataraṃ kulanti" refers to a certain family, speaking of the husband and wife in that family. He thought, "This family has long been very helpful to me by providing suitable food and other necessities; therefore, I have become the foremost recipient of their offerings here. By accepting their gifts, I will increase their merit." Thus, he said, "What would I gain by going elsewhere?" and so on. "Sā" is the deity. "Ubhopeteti" refers to both that monk and the housewife. "Paṭigādhappattāti" means having reached a firm footing, with mutual trust established in each other.

Vissamappattivasena santiṭṭhanti etthāti saṇṭhānaṃ, vissamanaṭṭhānaṃ. Samāgantvāti sannipatitvā. Paṭiññūdāharaṇehi mantayatīti mantanaṃ, ñāpakaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Paṭilomasaddāti paṭilomabhāvena patitattā asaccavibhāvanā paṭikūlasaddā. Tena kāraṇenāti tena kāraṇapaṭirūpakena micchāvacanena. Na maṅkuhotabbaṃ akārakabhāvato. Saddena paritassatīti parehi attani payuttamicchāsaddamattena paritassanasīlo. Vataṃ na sampajjatīti yathāsamādinnavataṃ lahucittatāya na pāripūriṃ gacchati. Sampannavatoti paripuṇṇasīlādivataguṇo

"Saṇṭhānaṃ" is where they are established by way of having attained trust; it is a place of rest. "Samāgantvāti" means having assembled. "Mantanaṃ" is deliberation with reasons and examples; an informative cause. "Paṭilomasaddāti" means disagreeable words, manifesting untruth because they have fallen into a contrary state. "Tena kāraṇenāti" means by that semblance of a reason, by that false statement. One should not be confused, as there is no agent. "Saddena paritassatīti" means one is prone to be anxious merely due to false words used by others regarding oneself. "Vataṃ na sampajjatīti" means the vow as undertaken does not reach completion due to a fickle mind. "Sampannavatoti" means one endowed with the perfected qualities of virtue and other vows.

Kulagharaṇīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Kulagharaṇī Sutta is concluded.

9. Vajjiputtasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary to the Vajjiputta Sutta

229. Vajjiraṭṭhe rājaputtoti vajjiraṭṭhe jātasaṃvaddho vajjirājaputto. Sabbaratticāroti chaṇasampattiyā ito cito carantehi anubhavitabbanakkhattamaho. Tenāha “kattikanakkhattaṃ ghosetvā” [V 1.0265] tiādi. Ekābaddhaṃ hotīti yasmā cātumahārājikadevā tasmiṃ divase nakkhattaṃ [M 1.0303] ghosetvā attano puññānubhāvasiddhāya dibbasampattiyā mahantaṃ nakkhattakīḷāsukhaṃ anubhavanti, tasmā taṃ tehi ekābaddhaṃ viya hoti. Bheriāditūriyānanti bherimudiṅgasaṅkhapaṇavavīṇāditūriyānaṃ. Tāḷitānanti āraddhalayānurūpaṃ pahaṭānaṃ. Vīṇādīnanti vīṇāveṇugomukhīādīnaṃ. Vāditānanti yathāraddhamucchanānurūpaṃ saṅghaṭṭitānaṃ. Abhāsīti tena saddena ākaḍḍhiyamānahadayo ayoniso ummujjitvā “mahatī vata me jānī”ti anutthunanto abhāsi. Chaḍḍitadārukaṃ viyāti vane chaḍḍitaniratthakakaḷiṅgaraṃ viya. Lāmakataroti nihīnataro. Devatā paṭhamappitaṃ āṇiṃ paṭāṇiyā nīharantī viya tena bhikkhunā vuttamatthaṃ apanentī “tassa te bahukā pihayantī”ti avocāti vuttanti dassento “thero”tiādimāha. Saggaṃ gacchantānaṃ yathā nerayikā pihayanti, evaṃ sammāpaṭipannassa tuyhaṃ bahū pihayanti, tasmā tvaṃ “pāpiyo”ti attānaṃ mā maññitthāti adhippāyo.

229. "A prince in the land of the Vajjis" means a Vajji prince, born and raised in the Vajji territory. "Sabbaratticāroti" refers to the great festival of the constellation that is to be enjoyed by those roaming here and there on account of the festive occasion. Hence it is said, "Having proclaimed the Kattika constellation," etc. "Ekābaddhaṃ hotīti" means that because the Four Great Kings, on that day, having proclaimed the constellation, enjoy the great pleasure of the constellation festival through the divine fortune accomplished by the power of their own merit, it is as if it were bound up with them. "Bheriāditūriyānanti" refers to kettledrums, tabors, conches, panava drums, lutes, and other musical instruments. "Tāḷitānanti" means struck in accordance with the established rhythm. "Vīṇādīnanti" refers to lutes, flutes, gomukhi horns, and the like. "Vāditānanti" means played in accordance with the established melody. "Abhāsīti" means, his heart being drawn by that sound, he emerged improperly and, lamenting, "Alas, great is my loss!", he spoke. "Chaḍḍitadārukaṃ viyāti" means like a worthless log discarded in the forest. "Lāmakataroti" means more inferior. Just as a deity removes a previously inserted peg with a counter-peg, so the deity, refuting what was said by that bhikkhu, said, "Many envy you." To show this, the commentator said, "the elder," etc. Just as beings in hell envy those going to heaven, so many envy you who are rightly practicing; therefore, do not think of yourself as "more sinful"—this is the meaning.

Vajjiputtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Vajjiputta Sutta is concluded.

10. Sajjhāyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary to the Sajjhāya Sutta

230. Nissaraṇapariyattivasenāti addhā imaṃ pariyattiṃ nissāya vaṭṭadukkhato nissarituṃ labbhāti evaṃ nissaraṇapariyattivasena. Sajjhāyanatoti vimuttāyatanasīse ṭhatvā sajjhāyanato. Idāni tassa nissaraṇapariyattivasena sajjhāyanakaraṇaṃ, paṭipattivasena vattapaṭivattakaraṇaṃ, vipassanābhāvanañca dassetuṃ “so kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Arahattaṃ pattadivase paṭipattikittanāya purimadivasesupi tathā paṭipajji, vipassanaṃ pana ussukkāpetuṃ nāsakkhīti dasseti. Kālaṃ ativattetīti idaṃ “saṅkasāyatī”ti padassa atthavacanaṃ. Therassāti sajjhāyakattherassa.

230. "Nissaraṇapariyattivasenāti" means: "Surely, relying on this scripture, one can escape from the suffering of the round of rebirths"—thus, it is in terms of scripture for release. "Sajjhāyanatoti" means from reciting while established at the head of the bases of liberation. Now, to show his recitation in terms of scripture for release, his performance of duties and counter-duties in terms of practice, and the development of insight, it is said, "he indeed," etc. To declare his practice on the day he attained arahantship, it is shown that he practiced thus even on previous days, but was unable to arouse effort for insight. "Kālaṃ ativattetīti" is an explanation of the meaning of the word "saṅkasāyati." "Therassāti" means of the elder who was the reciter.

Dhammapadānīti sīlādidhammakkhandhadīpakāni padāni. Tenāha “sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ adhippeta”nti. Na gaṇhāsi uddesanti adhippāyo. Pāḷiyaṃ “bhikkhūhi saṃvasanto”ti iminā tesaṃ dhammassavanatthāyapi dhammo pariyāpuṇitabboti dasseti. Virajjati etenāti virāgo, ariyamaggo. Jānitvāti pariññābhisamayavasena diṭṭhasutādiṃ yāthāvato jānitvā paṭivijjhitvā. Vissajjananti [M 1.0304] pahānaṃ. Na buddhavacanassa vissajjanaṃ. Bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattiyāpi anuññātattā pageva nissaraṇatthāya, tattha pana mattā jānitabbāti dassento “ettāvatā”tiādimāha.

"Dhammapadānīti" refers to the verses that illuminate the aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue. Therefore, it is said, "All the words of the Buddha are intended." The meaning is: you do not grasp the instruction. In the Pāli, "living together with the monks" shows that the Dhamma should also be learned for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma from them. "Virajjati etenāti virāgo" means dispassion is that by which one becomes dispassionate; it is the Noble Path. "Jānitvāti" means having truly known and penetrated what is seen, heard, etc., according to reality, through full understanding and realization. "Vissajjananti" means abandoning. It is not the abandoning of the Buddha’s words, since learning like a treasurer is also permitted—all the more so for the purpose of release. But showing that measure should be known there, he said "to this extent," etc.

Sajjhāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Sajjhāya Sutta is concluded.

11. Akusalavitakkasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary to the Akusalavitakka Sutta

231. Akusale [V 1.0266] vitakketi akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena akusale micchāvitakke. Yoni vuccati upāyo, tasmā asubhādike subhādivasena manasikāro ayonisomanasikāroti āha “anupāyamanasikārenā”ti. Pāsādikakammaṭṭhānanti pasādāvahaṃ buddhānussatiādikammaṭṭhānaṃ. Balavapītiñca sukhañcāti nīvaraṇavikkhambhanato balavantaṃ upacārajjhānasahagataṃ pītiñca sukhañca.

231. "Akusale vitakke" means unwholesome, wrong thoughts, because they are born from unskillfulness. "Yoni" is said to be a means; therefore, attending to the unattractive etc. as if it were attractive etc. is improper attention, as it is said, 'through attention that is not the means.' A 'serene meditation subject' means a meditation subject that brings serenity, such as the recollection of the Buddha and so forth. 'Strong joy and happiness' refers to the joy and happiness accompanied by access concentration, which are strong due to the suppression of the hindrances.

Akusalavitakkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Akusalavitakka Sutta is concluded.

12. Majjhanhikasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary to the Majjhanhika Sutta

232. Nandanavaggeti nandanavaggavaṇṇanāyaṃ tattha idhāpi gāthāya visesābhāvato. Yadi evaṃ kasmā tattha saṅgītaṃ idha gahitanti? Devatāpaṭisaṃyuttataṃ upādāya devatāsaṃyutte saṅgahitampi aṭṭhuppattiyā paṭisaṃyuttattā idha gahitaṃ.

232. "In the Nandana Vagga": in the commentary on the Nandana Vagga, what is said there applies here too, because there is no difference in the verse. If so, why was what was compiled there taken here? On account of its connection with deities, although it was compiled in the Devatāsaṃyutta, it is taken here because of its connection with the occasion of its arising.

Majjhanhikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Majjhanhika Sutta is concluded.

13. Pākatindriyasuttavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary to the Pākatindriya Sutta

233. Terasame yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vitthāritamevāti yojanā. Jantudevaputtasutteti jantudevaputtasuttasaṃvaṇṇanāya. “Tattha saṅgītaṃ idhāpī”tiādi anantarasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayameva.

233. The connection is: what should be stated in the thirteenth discourse has already been explained in detail. "Jantudevaputtasutteti" means in the commentary on the Jantudevaputta Sutta. The phrase 'what was compiled there, here too,' and so forth, is just the method stated in the commentary on the immediately preceding discourse.

Pākatindriyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Pākatindriya Sutta is concluded.

14. Gandhatthenasuttavaṇṇanā

14. Commentary to the Gandhatthena Sutta

234. Gandhārammaṇaṃ [M 1.0305] upanijjhāyatīti gandhasaṅkhātaṃ ārammaṇaṃ upecca nijjhāyati, rūpārammaṇena viya viññāṇena rūpaṃ, gandhārammaṇena taṃ upecca nijjhāyati paccakkhato, yāthāvato sabhāvato paṭivijjhatīti attho. Upasiṅghissatīti taṇhāvasena upagantvā siṅghissati.

234. "Gandhārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyati" means one approaches and contemplates an object designated as 'smell.' Just as form is contemplated by consciousness by means of a form-object, so one approaches and contemplates that smell-object directly, penetrating it as it really is, according to its intrinsic nature—this is the meaning. "Upasiṅghissatīti" means one will approach through craving and sniff.

Ekaṅgametaṃ [V 1.0267] theyyānanti ārammaṇavasena theyyavatthūsu vibhajiyamānesu ekamaṅgametaṃ gandhārammaṇanti āha “thenitabbāna”ntiādi. Ojāpekkhāya theyyāya pavattamānāya dhammārammaṇatāpi tassā siyā, sā pana na madhurā theyyakatā cāti “pañcakoṭṭhāsāna”nti vuttaṃ. Kāmañca taṃ gandhārammaṇaṃ kenaci pariggahitaṃ na hotīti ādiyituṃ sakkā, satthārā pana ananuññātattā na yutto tassa paribhogo. Yaṃ pana tena bhikkhunā vuttaṃ “na harāmi na bhañjāmī”ti, tassapi ayameva parihāro. Vaṇṇīyati phalaṃ etenāti vaṇṇaṃ, kāraṇanti vuttaṃ “vaṇṇenāti kāraṇenā”ti.

Regarding 'this is one factor in thefts,' when the objects of theft are distinguished according to their sense-object, this scent-object is one factor; thus he said, 'of things to be stolen,' and so forth. When theft occurs motivated by a desire for sap, it may also involve a mental object, but that is not pleasant, and it is an act of theft; thus it is said, 'of the five parts.' Although that scent-object is not possessed by anyone and so can be taken, its use is not proper because the Teacher has not permitted it. As for what that monk said—'I do not take it away, I do not break it'—the same refutation applies. That by which a fruit is praised is 'praise' (vaṇṇa), meaning 'reason.' Thus it is said, 'by praise, meaning by reason.'

Tasminti tasmiṃ bhikkhusmiṃ. Ākiṇṇakammantoti taṇhādiṭṭhiādivasena akusalakammanto diṭṭhimohataṇhādivasena ādito paṭṭhāya kusalakammānaṃ paṭikkhepanato. Diṭṭhivasena ca kathinakakkhaḷakharigatattā “akhīṇakammanto kakkhaḷakammanto”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'in that,' it means in that monk. Regarding 'one whose actions are defiled,' it means one with unwholesome actions on account of craving, wrong view, and so forth, and because of rejecting wholesome actions from the very beginning on account of wrong view, delusion, craving, and so forth. And because of being unyielding, hard, and rough due to wrong view, it is said, 'one whose actions are not exhausted, one whose actions are harsh.'

Ākiṇṇaluddoti ākiṇṇo hutvā kakkhaḷo. Tenāha “bahupāpo”tiādi. Makkhitoti litto. Tanti devatācodanaṃ. Tasmāti atikkamma ṭhitattā“tvañcārahāmi vattave”ti evamāha.

Regarding 'one who is defiled and cruel,' it means being defiled and harsh. Therefore he said, 'very wicked,' and so forth. Regarding 'stained,' it means smeared. Regarding 'that,' it refers to the deity's urging. Regarding 'therefore,' because he stood having transcended, he thus said, 'You too are worthy to speak.'

Gavesantassa attano santāne uppādanavasena pariyesantassa. Anekayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ gaganatalaṃ byāpetvā uppannavalāhakakūṭappamāṇaṃ viya. Suddhoti sīlena parisuddho ayanti jānāsi. Sugatinti sundaranibbattiṃ. Tena nibbānassapi saṅgaho siddho.

Regarding 'seeking,' it means searching by way of producing it in one's own continuum. Like a mass of clouds that has arisen, spreading across the expanse of the sky that is many leagues in length and breadth. Regarding 'pure,' it means you know him as one purified by virtue. Regarding 'a good destination,' it means a beautiful rebirth. Thus, the inclusion of Nibbāna is also established.

Gandhatthenasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Thief of Scent is concluded.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

The Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Connected Discourses.

Vanasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of Hidden Meanings in the Explanation of the Connected Discourses on Forests is concluded.

10. Yakkhasaṃyuttaṃ

10. The Connected Discourses on Yakkhas

1. Indakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Discourse on Indaka

235. Attano [V 1.0268][M 1.0306] pariṇāyakattena indo nāma mahesakkho, indoti samaññā assāti katvā “indako”tipi vuccati, tassa indakassa. Indakūṭe pabbate nivasatīti indakūṭanivāsī, tassa indakūṭanivāsino. Balikammehi yajitabbato pūjitabbato yakkho, tassa yakkhassa. Indassa nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ kūṭaṃ indakūṭanti yakkhato kūṭena nāmaṃ laddhaṃ. Indakūṭo indo uttarapadalopena yathā “kelāsakūṭo kelāso”ti. Indo yakkhoti kūṭato yakkhena nāmaṃ laddhaṃ. Na cettha itarītaranissayadoso aññamaññūpalakkhaṇabhāvato yathā taṃ “kāyakammaṭṭhāna”nti. Rūpanti sakalaṃ rūpakkhandhamāha, na rūpāyatananti. Imaṃ sarīraṃ pecca ayaṃ kinti paṭilabhatīti codeti.

235. Because he is his own leader, he is a mighty one named 'Inda'; and because he has the designation 'Inda,' he is also called 'Indaka'; hence, 'of Indaka.' Because he dwells on Mount Indakūṭa, he is 'one who dwells on Indakūṭa'; hence, 'of the one dwelling on Indakūṭa.' Because he is to be worshipped with offerings and honored, he is a yakkha; hence, 'of the yakkha.' The peak that is the dwelling place of Inda is Indakūṭa; the peak obtained its name from the yakkha. Indakūṭa is called 'Inda' by the omission of the latter part, just as 'Kelāsakūṭa' is called 'Kelāsa.' Regarding 'Inda the yakkha,' the yakkha obtained his name from the peak. Here, there is no fault of mutual dependence, because they are mutual designations, like 'body meditation subject.' Regarding 'form,' it refers to the entire aggregate of form, not the form-base. He questions: 'Having departed from this body, what does this one obtain?'

Kuto āgacchatīti parādhārarūpe jīve attani mātukucchimokkante rūpassa sambhavoti kuto nāma ṭhānato āgacchati. Tenāha “imāni ca aṭṭhīni imā ca maṃsapesiyo”tiādi. Kathaṃ nvayanti ayaṃ kucchisaṅkhāte gabbhare kathaṃ sajjatīti pucchati. “Sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ, dāṭhīnaṃ girigabbhare”tiādinā (theragā. nidānagāthā) gabbharo ca kucchivācako āgato. Tenāha “gabbharasminti mātukucchismi”nti. Puggalavādīti attavādupādāno. Yathā hi macchamaṃsaṃ bhuttaṃ pheṇaṃ viya hutvā vilīyati, na ca paññāyati sattabhāvena appavattanato, evamevaṃ yadi mātukucchismiṃ gabbhabhāvena uppannaṃ rūpaṃ satto na bhaveyya no vaḍḍheyya, vilīyitvā gaccheyya, paññāyati ca taṃ rūpaṃ, tasmā jīvoti imāya laddhiyā. Evamāhāti “rūpaṃ…pe… gabbharasmi”nti evamavoca. Paṭhamanti etesaṃ pañcannaṃ paṭhamaṃ. Tenāha “paṭhamena paṭisandhiviññāṇena saddhi”nti. “Jātiuṇṇaṃsūhīti jātieḷakāya uṇṇaṃsūhī”ti vadanti. “Gabbhaṃ phāletvā gahitauṇṇā jātiuṇṇā. Tassā aṃsūhi tīhi katasuttagge”ti saṃyuttabhāṇakānaṃ adhippāyo.

Regarding 'from where does it come?': When a being, whose form is dependent on another, has descended into the mother's womb, from what place does the arising of form come? Therefore he said, 'these bones and these masses of flesh,' and so forth. Regarding 'how indeed?': He asks how this being is fastened in the 'gabbhara,' that is, the womb. By 'like the roaring of lions, with tusks in the mountain cave,' and so forth, the word 'gabbhara' has come to mean 'womb.' Therefore he said, 'in the gabbhara,' meaning in the mother's womb. Regarding 'personalist,' it means one who clings to the doctrine of a self. Just as eaten fish meat dissolves like foam and is no longer perceived, because it does not continue as a being, so too, if the form that has arisen as an embryo in the mother's womb were not a being, it would not grow but would dissolve and disappear. Yet that form is perceived; therefore, it is a living being—this is according to that doctrine. Regarding 'thus he said,' he thus said, 'form... in the womb,' and so forth. Regarding 'first,' it means the first of these five. Therefore he said, 'together with the first rebirth-linking consciousness.' They say, 'With the hairs of jātiuṇṇā' means with the hairs of a newborn lamb. The intention of the Saṃyutta reciters is: 'Jātiuṇṇā is wool taken by splitting the womb. At the tip of a thread made with three of its fibers.'

Anāviloti [V 1.0269] accho, suppasannoti attho. Evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāganti vuttappamāṇasaṇṭhānasamparicchinnaṃ. Kalalaṃ sampavuccatīti attabhāvo bhūtupādārūpasaṅkhāto [M 1.0307] santānavasena pavattamāno kalalaṃ nāmāti kathīyati.

Regarding 'unclouded,' it means clear, very pure—this is the meaning. Regarding 'of such color and appearance,' it means determined by the stated measure and shape. Regarding 'kalala is spoken of,' it is said that the individual existence, consisting of the primary elements and derived materiality, proceeding as a continuity, is called 'kalala.'

Kalalāti yathāvuttakalalarūpahetu taṃ nissāya paccayaṃ katvā. Maṃsadhovanaudakavaṇṇanti vaṇṇato maṃsadhovanaudakavaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānato pana vilīnatipusadisaṃ.

Regarding 'from the kalala,' it means because of the aforementioned kalala-form, depending on it and making it a condition. Regarding 'the color of meat-washing water,' in color, it is the color of meat-washing water, but in shape, it is like melted tin.

Paripakkanti paripākakalalabhāvato paripākaṃ gataṃ suparipākaṃ gataṃ. Samūhatanti samūhabhūtaṃ saṅgataṃ. Vivaṭṭamānanti pariṇamantaṃ. Tabbhāvanti karaṇe etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, tabbhāvena pariṇamantanti attho. Nissakke vā upayogavacanaṃ, tabbhāvato kalalabhāvato kalalaṃ vipariṇamantaṃ. Abbudaṃ nāma jāyati, abbudaṃ nāma sampajjatīti attho.

Regarding 'ripened,' it means it has reached ripening, reached full ripening, due to its state of being a ripened kalala. Regarding 'gathered,' it means become a mass, united. Regarding 'transforming,' it means changing. Regarding 'that state,' this is a term used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is that it transforms by that nature. Or it is a term used in the sense of the ablative; meaning that the kalala transforms from that state, from the state of being a kalala. The meaning is that an 'abbuda' arises, an 'abbuda' comes into being.

Vilīnatipusadisā saṇṭhānavasena, vaṇṇavasena pana sitā arattāva hotīti vadanti. Maṇḍanti dārikānaṃ tathā pīḷanato nibbattamaricapakkassa sārabhūtaṃ rasaṃ. Sabbabhāgehi muccatīti so maṇḍo kapāle alaggo hutvā tassa sabbabhāgehi mucchitvā piṇḍito hutvā tiṭṭhati. Evarūpā pesi hotīti sā pesi gabbhāsaye katthaci alaggā yathāvuttamaṇḍo viya piṇḍito hutvā tiṭṭhati. Tenāha “vilīnatipusadisā”ti.

They say that in terms of shape, it is like melted tin, but in terms of color, it is white or reddish. Regarding 'scum,' it means the essential juice of ripe pepper produced from pressing, as is done for girls. Regarding 'it becomes detached from all parts,' it means that the scum, unattached to the pot, having coagulated from all its parts, remains as a lump. Regarding 'such a pesi arises,' it means that the pesi remains in the womb, unattached anywhere, like the aforementioned scum, forming a lump. Therefore he said, 'like melted tin.'

Pesi nibbattatīti ettha pesīti nissakke paccattavacananti āha “tato pesito”ti.

Regarding 'a pesi arises,' here 'pesi' is a word in the nominative case used in the ablative sense; thus he said, 'from that pesi.'

Ghanassa saṇṭhānaṃ. Nibbattaṃ kammapaccayāti taṃsaṇṭhānaṃ rūpadhammanibbattiyā jāyati. “Jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) hi vuttaṃ.

The form of the solid mass. Regarding 'arisen due to kamma as condition,' that form arises by the arising of material phenomena. For it is said, 'Aging and death are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen.'

Pīḷakāti pīḷakasadisā maṃsapiṇḍā jāyanti.

Regarding 'boils,' it means lumps of flesh arise resembling boils.

Sattamādīnīti ādi-saddena aṭṭhamasattāhato paṭṭhāya yāva ekacattālīsā catuttiṃsa sattāhāni saṅgaṇhāti. Pariṇatakālanti gabbhassa pariṇatakālaṃ. Navamāsato bahi paripakko nāma hoti kesalomādinibbattito. Tenāha “dvācattālīse sattāhe etāni jāyantī”ti.

Regarding 'seven weeks and so forth,' by the word 'and so forth,' it includes from the eighth week onwards, up to forty-one or thirty-four weeks. Regarding 'time of maturation,' it means the time of the embryo's maturation. Beyond nine months, it is said to be fully developed, from the arising of head-hair, body-hair, and so forth. Therefore he said, 'these arise in the forty-second week.'

Tassāti [M 1.0308] gabbhaseyyakasattassa. Mātuudarapaṭalena ekābaddho hoti yato mātarā paribhuttaāhāro [V 1.0270] āmāsaye patiṭṭhite gabbhassa nābhināḷānusārena gabbhagatassa sarīraṃ sampatvā āhārakiccaṃ karoti. Āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti gabbhagatassa kāye ojāya paccayo hoti. Sā ca taṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ mātarā paribhuttaāhārapaccayena gabbhagato dasa māse yāpeti attano nābhināḷānusāragateneva tena yāva āhārasamuṭṭhānasattāho, tato paṭṭhāya āharaṇato. Keci pana “mātarā paribhuttaāhāro bāhiravaggo viya tassa kāyaṃ abhisanneti parisanneti, tena so yāpetī”ti vadanti. Kucchigataṃ udarapaṭalena tirohitattā bahi ṭhitanti vattabbataṃ na arahatīti “kucchiyā abbhantaragato”ti āha. Mātukucchigato naroti mātu tirokucchigato. Evaṃ khoti iminā yathāvuttākārena ayaṃ satto…pe… nibbattati, tasmā rūpaṃ na jīvo. Na hi diṭṭhigatassa sattāhakkamena vuḍḍhippatto icchito aniccatāpattito.

‘That being’ refers to the being lying in the womb. It is bound by the membrane of the mother's belly. When the nourishment consumed by the mother is established in her stomach, it reaches the body of the one in the womb by way of the umbilical cord and performs the function of nourishment. It generates nutriment-originated matter, thus becoming a condition for the nutritive essence in the body of the one in the womb. And that essence, having obtained that condition, generates matter with nutriment as the eighth. In this way, the one in the womb is sustained for ten months by the nourishment consumed by the mother, which passes through its own umbilical cord, for as long as the seven days of nutriment-originated matter, and thereafter by assimilation. Some, however, say: ‘The nourishment consumed by the mother, like an external mass, suffuses and permeates its body, and by that it is sustained.’ Because what is in the womb is concealed by the membrane of the belly, it is not fit to be called ‘situated outside’; thus, it is said, ‘gone into the interior of the womb.’ ‘A person gone into the mother’s womb’ means gone inside the mother’s belly. Thus, indeed, in this aforesaid manner, this being… is born. Therefore, form is not the life-principle. Indeed, for one holding such a view, the attainment of growth through a weekly process is not what is desired, because it falls into impermanence.

Indakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Indaka Sutta is concluded.

2. Sakkanāmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta

236. Sakkanāmakoti baliputto viya sakkassa vasena gahitanāmo. “Eso kirā”ti pāṭho. “Eko kirā”tipi likhanti. Mārassa pakkhe gato mārapakkhiko. Yadaññanti ettha yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ, tasmā yaṃ aññassa anusāsanaṃ, taṃ samaṇassa na sādhūti yojanā. Kāraṇenāti kāraṇamattena saṃvāso jāyati. Yena kenaci gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā. Taṃ kāraṇantaraṃ samāgataṃ purisaṃ sappañño sambuddho anukampituṃ nārahati visesādhigamābhāvā, sati pana tasmiṃ savisesaṃ pasādo hotīti. Manasā ce…pe… na tena hoti saṃyutto sinehavasena anukampā anuddayā tassā asaṃkiliṭṭhasabhāvattā.

236. ‘Named Sakka’ means one whose name is taken by way of Sakka, like the son of Bali. The reading is ‘Eso kirā’; some also write ‘Eko kirā.’ ‘Gone to Māra’s faction’ means being on Māra’s side. In ‘Yadaññaṃ,’ ‘yaṃ’ refers to the action; therefore, the construction is: ‘Whatever is another’s instruction, that is not suitable for a contemplative.’ ‘By a reason’ means association arises merely by some reason, with any householder or renunciant. A wise, fully awakened one is not fit to show compassion to a person who has come for some other reason, due to the absence of special attainment; but if there is such attainment, there is special confidence. ‘If with the mind… he is not thereby connected’ means there is no compassion or pity based on affection, due to its undefiled nature.

Sakkanāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta is concluded.

3. Sūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta

237. Gayāya [M 1.0309] avidūre bhavo gāmo “gayā”ti vuttoti āha “gayāya”nti, tenāha “gayāya avidūre niviṭṭhagāmaṃ upanisāyāti attho”ti. Gocaragāmanidassanaṃ hetaṃ. Idaṃ upari idaṃ heṭṭhāti natthi uppaṭipāṭiyo mañcapādānaṃ dvīsu passesu dīghabhāvena. Balikammatthāya kataṃ devatādhiṭṭhānanti adhippāyena devaṭṭhāne ṭhapenti. Aṭṭhapādamañcasadiso kira so heṭṭhupariparivattetabbato. Kathinasibbanasūci kathinasūci. Apaccattharitvāti kiñci saṅghikasenāsanassa [V 1.0271] upari paṭicchadanaṃ apaccattharitvā. Gavacchivijjhitaṃ viyāti tehi sūcilomehi gavacchijālaṃ viya gataṃ sabbaso samohataṃ.

237. Because a village that exists not far from Gayā is called ‘Gayā,’ he said ‘at Gayā.’ Therefore, he said the meaning is ‘near a village established not far from Gayā.’ This is an indication of an alms-resort village. There is no reverse order of ‘this is above, this is below’ for the bed legs, because of their length on both sides. They place it in a deity’s shrine with the intention that it is an abode for a deity, made for the purpose of offerings. It is said to be like an eight-legged bed because it can be turned over, below and above. A needle for sewing the kathina robe is a kathina needle. ‘Without having spread’ means without having spread any covering over a lodging belonging to the Sangha. ‘Like a pierced window’ means that with those needle-like hairs, it was completely covered, like a window lattice.

Idhāpi “kharasarīro”ti vatvā kharasarīraṃ kathinasūcisadisatāya lomassāti tassa tathābhāvassa kāraṇaṃ dassento “so kirā”tiādimāha. Attano hatthehīti saṅghikatelasammakkhitehi attano sarīraṃ makkhesi. Itīti vuttākārena.

Here too, having said ‘with a rough body,’ and showing the reason for its being so—that the roughness of the body is due to the hair’s likeness to a kathina needle—he said, ‘indeed, he…’ and so on. ‘With his own hands’ means with his own hands, smeared with oil belonging to the Sangha, he anointed his own body. ‘Thus’ means in the manner described.

Samāgamaṭṭhānanti yakkhasannipātaṭṭhānaṃ. Soti sūcilomo yakkho. Manti ca tameva vadati.

‘The place of coming together’ means the place of assembly for yakkhas. ‘He’ is the yakkha Sūciloma. And by ‘me’ he refers to that very same one.

Uṭṭhāpetvāti uddhaggā katvā. Apanāmesīti yathā so attano kāyaṃ upanetuṃ na sakkoti, tathā karonto thokaṃ apanāmesi. Amanuññoti pharusatikkhatāya na manuñño. Cittaṃ vā te khipissāmīti mayhaṃ ānubhāvena tava cittavikkhepaṃ vā karissāmi. Yathā pana so cittavikkhepaṃ kareyya, taṃ dassetuṃ “yesañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bheravaṃ vāti vuttākārena aññathā vā bhayānakaṃ dassanamatteneva sattānaṃ bhayaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃsaṃ uppādetuṃ samatthaṃ. “Kathentānaṃyevā”ti vā pāṭho. Taṃ dvīsu pādesu gahetvā pāraṃ gaṅgāya khipissāmīti yojanā.

‘Having raised’ means having made it stand upright. ‘He moved it away’ means he moved it away a little, acting in such a way that he could not bring his own body near. ‘Unpleasant’ means not pleasing due to harshness and bitterness. ‘Or I will agitate your mind’ means ‘I will cause you mental distraction through my power.’ To show how he might cause mental distraction, it is said, ‘for those who…’ and so on. ‘Or terrifying’ means a frightful appearance, in the manner described or otherwise, capable of instilling fear, stupefaction, and hair-raising horror in beings merely by being seen. An alternative reading is ‘even while they are speaking.’ The construction is: ‘Taking him by the two feet, I will throw him to the far shore of the Ganges.’

Kutonidānāti kasmā kāraṇā? Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana samāsapadametaṃ, vibhattialopena niddesoti dassetuṃ “kiṃnidānā kiṃpaccayā”ti? Attho vutto. Cittaṃ ossajantīti kusalacittaṃ pavattituṃ appadānavasena [M 1.0310] purato khipanti. Kuto samuṭṭhāyāti micchāvitakkānaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ pucchati?

‘From what cause?’ means from what reason? In the commentary, however, this is a compound word; to show that it is an explanation with non-elision of the case ending, the meaning is stated as ‘from what cause, from what condition?’ ‘They release the mind’ means they cast forth the wholesome mind, by way of not allowing it to proceed. ‘From what do they arise?’ asks about the origin of wrong thoughts.

Kāmarāgādayo subhanimittādīsu ayonisomanasikārahetū. Kāmo pana ayonisomanasikāro ca niyakajjhattapariyāpannoti āha “ayaṃ attabhāvo nidānaṃ etesanti itonidānā”tiādi. Evamevāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ kīḷāpasutakumārakā viya micchāvitakkā daṭṭhabbā, tesaṃ uppattiṭṭhānabhūto loko viya ayaṃ attabhāvaloko. Tehi ossajiyamānaṃ dhaṅkaṃ viya cittaṃ, tassa pāde baddhadīghasuttakaṃ viya taṃ dūrānubandhaṃ saṃyojananti evaṃ upamāya saṃsandanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Sensual lust and other defilements are caused by unwise attention to the sign of the beautiful and so on. But since desire and unwise attention are included within one’s own person, it is said: ‘This individual existence is the source of these; they originate from this,’ and so on. Similarly, in the commentary, wrong thoughts should be seen as being like playful young boys, and this world of individual existence is like the world that is their birthplace. The mind, being released by them, is like a crow; the fetter that follows it from afar is like a long thread tied to its foot. Thus, the comparison by way of this simile should be understood.

Pāpavitakkānaṃ taṃsampayuttakilesānañca taṇhā visesapaccayo tadabhāvena tesaṃ abhāvatoti [V 1.0272] āha “taṇhāsinehato jātā”ti. Attabhāvapariyāpannattā “attani sambhūtā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena nesaṃ anaññahetukataṃ dasseti, nigrodhasseva khandhajātīti iminā pana puthubhāvañca, visattātiādinā dubbinissaṭatañca. Vatthukāmesu rūpārammaṇādīsu puthūsu. Puthū kilesakāmā kāmarūpataṇhādayo. Tehi kilesakāmehi karaṇabhūtehi. Attabhāvaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Ye vipassanāya yuttapayuttā yāthāvato jānanti.

Craving is a special condition for evil thoughts and the defilements associated with them, because in the absence of craving, they are absent; hence it is said, ‘born from the affection of craving.’ Because they are included in individual existence, it is said, ‘arisen in the self.’ By this, he shows that they have no other cause. And by ‘born from the trunk of a banyan tree,’ he shows their multiplicity, and by ‘entangled’ and so on, the difficulty of their removal. ‘In the manifold objects of sensual pleasure’ means in visible forms and other sense objects. ‘Manifold defilements of desire’ means craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and so on. ‘By those defilements of desire’ means by those which are the instruments. ‘Individual existence’ means the five aggregates. ‘Those who know them as they truly are’ are those who are devoted and engaged in insight.

Yatoti paccatte nissakkavacananti āha “yaṃ nidānamassā”ti. “Vinodentī”ti kattuniddesena yena na vinodenti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ bādhitamevāti āha “maggasaccena vinodentī”ti. Vinodanañcettha santānato nīharaṇaṃ bahikaraṇaṃ sabbaso pahānaṃ, pahīne ca tasmiṃ kilese oghaṃ tarantīti dassento “duttara”ntiādimāha. Etasmiṃ adhigate na puna bhavoti apunabbhavo, nibbānanti āha “apunabbhavasaṅkhātassā”tiādi. Yasmā ettha “ye naṃ pajānanti, yatonidāna”nti padadvayena dukkhasamudayasaccāni, vinodanaggahaṇena maggasaccaṃ, apunabbhavaggahaṇena nirodhasaccaṃ pakāsitaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “cattāri saccāni pakāsento”ti.

Because ‘yato’ (whence) is a word indicating removal in the sense of ‘from oneself,’ he says, ‘what is its source?’ By specifying the agent with ‘they dispel,’ he shows that any reason for not dispelling is refuted; therefore he says, ‘they dispel by the truth of the path.’ And here, dispelling means removing from the mental continuity, expelling, abandoning completely. And showing that when that defilement is abandoned they cross the flood, he says, ‘hard to cross,’ and so on. When this is attained, there is no further becoming; this is non-rebirth, Nibbāna. Therefore he says, ‘of that which is designated as non-rebirth,’ and so on. Because here, by the two phrases, ‘those who understand it’ and ‘from what source,’ the truths of suffering and its origin are revealed; by the mention of ‘dispelling,’ the truth of the path is revealed; and by the mention of ‘non-rebirth,’ the truth of cessation is revealed, therefore it is said, ‘revealing the four truths.’

Tasmiṃyevāti yattha ṭhito “rāgo ca doso cā”tiādinā pañhaṃ pucchi, tasmiṃyeva padese ṭhito. Desanānusārenāti satthu sāmukkaṃsikadhammadesanāya anussaraṇena. Ñāṇaṃ pesetvāti vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā [M 1.0311] nibbānaṃ pati anubodhañāṇaṃ pesetvā pavattetvā. Sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitoti sahassanayapaṭimaṇḍitassa paṭhamamaggassa adhigamena paṭhamaphale patiṭṭhito paṭilabhatīti yojanā. Na kiliṭṭhattabhāve tiṭṭhanti mahānubhāvattā ariyadhammassa. Setakaṇḍupīḷakasūciyoti setabhāvaṃ patvā kaṇḍupīḷakā lomasūciyo sabbā anavasesā patitā paribhaṭṭhā apagatā. Bhummadevatāparihāranti bhummadevattabhāvanti.

In that very place: where he stood, he asked the question beginning with "Is there lust and hatred?"—in that very spot he stood. Following the teaching: by recalling the Teacher’s elevating Dhamma discourse. Having sent forth knowledge: having directed and initiated the knowledge of awakening towards Nibbāna through the sequence of insight. Established in the fruit of stream-entry: the interpretation is that he is established in the first fruit by the attainment of the first path, which is adorned with a thousand aspects. They do not remain in a state of defilement: because of the great power of the noble Dhamma. White needle of itching blisters: having attained a white state, all the itching blisters, which are hair-needles, have completely fallen away, been cast off, and removed without remainder. The attendants of earth-deities: meaning the state of being an earth-deity.

Sūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta is concluded.

4. Maṇibhaddasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Maṇibhadda Sutta

238. Sukhaṃ paṭilabhatīti diṭṭhadhammikādibhedaṃ sukhaṃ adhigacchati. Niccameva seyyo satimato āyatiṃ hitacaraṇato. Maṇibhaddo “satimāpuggalo satokārī sampati veraṃ nappasavatī”ti adhippāyena “verā ca parimuccatī”ti āha. Bhagavā pana satimantatāsiddhiyā veraparimuccanaṃ na accantikaṃ, nāpi ekantikaṃ paṭipakkhena parato ca appahīnattāti taṃ nisedhento “verā ca na parimuccatī”ti vatvā, yaṃ accantikaṃ ekantikañca [V 1.0273] parassa vasena veraparimuccanaṃ, taṃ dassento “yassā”ti gāthamāha. Karuṇāyāti appanāppattāya karuṇāya. Karuṇāpubbabhāgeti karuṇābhāvanāya vasena uppāditapaṭhamajjhānūpacāre. Soti karuṇābhāvanaṃ bhāvento puggalo. Mettaṃsoti mettacittaṃ aṃso eko kusalakoṭṭhāso etassāti mettaṃso. Tassa kenacīti tassa arahato karuṇāya mettābhāvanāya ca sātisayattā tadabhāvena kenaci puggalena saddhiṃ verappasaṅgo nāma natthi. Iminā khīṇāsavepi mettākaruṇābhāvanārahite koci attano cittadosena veraṃ kareyya, na pana tasmiṃ mettākaruṇācetovimuttisamannāgate koci veraṃ kareyya. Evaṃ mahiddhikā brahmavihārabhāvanāti dasseti.

238. He attains happiness: he achieves happiness of various kinds, such as that pertaining to the present life. Always better is the mindful one, because of his conduct that is beneficial for the future. Maṇibhadda, intending to say, "A mindful person, acting with awareness, does not at present incur enmity," said, "and he is freed from enmity." But the Blessed One, denying that liberation from enmity through the accomplishment of mindfulness is either absolute or certain, since opposing factors from another are not abandoned, said, "and he is not freed from enmity," and then, to show the absolute and certain liberation from enmity that comes by way of another, he spoke the verse beginning with "For whom." Out of compassion: through compassion that has reached absorption. The preliminary stage of compassion: in the access concentration to the first jhāna, produced by means of cultivating compassion. He: the person cultivating compassion. Mettaṃso: one who has a share of loving-kindness, meaning one for whom a mind of loving-kindness is a wholesome portion. For him, by anyone: because of the excellence of that arahant’s compassion and cultivation of loving-kindness, there is no occasion for enmity arising with any person. By this it is shown that even towards one whose cankers are destroyed but who is devoid of the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion, someone might bear enmity due to their own mental fault; but no one would bear enmity towards one endowed with the liberation of mind through loving-kindness and compassion. Thus it is shown how powerful is the cultivation of the divine abidings.

Maṇibhaddasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Maṇibhadda Sutta is concluded.

5. Sānusuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sānu Sutta

239. Yakkhena [M 1.0312] gahito hotīti yakkhena anupaviṭṭho hoti. Tassa yakkhagahaṇassa kāraṇaṃ mūlato pabhuti vitthārato dassetuṃ “so”tiādimāha. Tassa antimabhavikattā ādito paṭṭhāya adhisīlasikkhāya sakkaccaṃ pūraṇanti dasseti “so pabbajitakālato”tiādinā. Paccāhāranti paṭikkhepaṃ. Imasmiṃ sarabhaññeti imasmiṃ mama dhammabhaṇane. Pattinti pattidānaṃ. Piyā honti, tenāha bhagavā “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’ti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti (ma. ni. 1.65). Tathā cāha “tasmiṃ sāmaṇere”tiādi.

239. Seized by a yakkha: means he is possessed by a yakkha. To explain in detail from the root the reason for this possession by the yakkha, he said, "so" and so on. To show that, due to his being in his final existence, he diligently fulfilled the higher training in virtue from the beginning, he stated, "from the time of his going forth" and so on. Rejection: means repelling. In this recitation: means in this recitation of my Dhamma. Sharing: means the giving of merit. They become dear; therefore, the Blessed One said, "If, monks, a monk should wish, 'May I be dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by my fellows in the holy life,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues" (MN 6). Similarly, he said, "in that novice" and so on.

Vuḍḍhimanvāyāti yobbanappattiyā aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ parivuḍḍhimāgamma. Kāmasambhogasamatthatāvasena paripakkindriyo. Anuyojetvāvāti vissajjetvāva, gihibhāve vā anuyojetvāva. “Pubbe tuyhaṃ putto sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmoti sambhāvito, idāni tato aññathā jāto”ti ghosanāvasena devatānaṃ antare māheva me lajjaṃ uppādeyya.

Following growth: means upon reaching youth and attaining the full development of his major and minor limbs. Mature in faculties: by way of being capable of sensual enjoyment. Having urged him: meaning having sent him away, or having urged him towards the household life. Do not create shame for me among the devas by announcing: 'Previously, your son was virtuous, of good qualities, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training—so he was esteemed. Now he has become otherwise.'

Pāṭihāriyapakkhañcāti cātuddasīpañcadasīaṭṭhamīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ ādito antato ādiantato ca pavesananikkhamanavasena uposathasīlassa paṭi paṭi abhimukhaṃ paccāvahitabbapakkhañca. Terasiyāpīti paraṃ sattamīnavamīsupīti attho. Pavesabhūtañhi uposathasīlassa sattamīsu samādinnaṃ sīlaṃ paṭipadaṃ, navamīsu nikkhamabhūtanti ācariyā. Porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana paccuggamanānugamanapariyāyena vuttanti āha “manussā”tiādi. Aḍḍhamāsanti sakalakālapakkhaṃ[V 1.0274]. Evañhi vassavāsassa anugamanaṃ gataṃ hoti. Suṭṭhu samāgatanti suparisuddhaṃ sampannaṃ katvā attano santānaṃ āgataṃ. Taṃ pana attano cittena samaṃ pakārehi yuttaṃ hotīti āha “sampayutta”nti. Arahantānaṃ anukaraṇena seṭṭhacariyaṃ. “Na te hi yakkhā kīḷantī”ti attano puttassa kāye adhimuccanaṃ attano kīḷanaṃ viya hotīti katvā āha.

And the special observance period: refers to the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days, and the period to be attended to before, after, and both before and after them respectively, by way of entering and exiting the Uposatha observance. And on the thirteenth: this implies also the seventh and ninth days. For, the virtue undertaken on the seventh day is the approach to the Uposatha observance, and that on the ninth day is the departure—so say the teachers. But in the ancient commentary, it is said to be explained in terms of meeting and accompanying, as stated, "people" and so on. Half-month: the entire period of the fortnight. In this way, the accompanying of the rains-residence is accomplished. Well-gathered: having made his own mental continuity thoroughly pure and accomplished, he has come. And that, it is said, is 'connected' because it is endowed with qualities in accordance with one's own mind. The supreme practice is the imitation of the arahants. "For those yakkhas do not play": he said this considering that possessing his son's body is like his own play.

Upāsikā [M 1.0313] yathāvuttauposathasīlena sīlavatī, sāmaṇero pana attano sāmaṇerasīlena sīlavā. Uppatitvāti ākāse uppatitvā. Mokkho natthi dukkhāvahassa kammassa katūpacitattā.

A laywoman is virtuous with the Uposatha precepts as described, while a novice is virtuous with his own novice precepts. Having risen up: means having risen up into the sky. There is no escape, because the suffering-bringing kamma has been done and accumulated.

Duvidhepi kāmeti vatthukāmakilesakāme. Kilesakāmaṃ pariccajanto eva hi vatthukāme pariccajati nāma. Vibbhamanavasena āgacchati bhikkhāya āhiṇḍanādipabbajitakiccato. Uppabbajitvā vigatasīlassa jīvato ānāpānamattena jīvantopi so matakova. Vuttañhetaṃ “maraṇañhetaṃ, sunakkhatta, ariyassa vinaye, yo sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.45).

Two kinds of sensual pleasures: sensual objects and sensual defilements. For it is only by abandoning sensual defilements that one is said to abandon sensual objects. It comes from the duties of a renunciant, such as wandering for alms, by way of mental wandering. For one who has disrobed and is without virtue, even if he lives, he is as good as dead, living only by way of breathing. For this was said: "This, Sunakkhatta, is death in the Noble One's Discipline: that one renounces the training and returns to the lower life" (MN 105).

Uṇhaṭṭhenāti sapariḷāhaṭṭhena. Abhidhāvathāti abhidhāvatīti imasmiṃ abhidhāvanakicce bhaddaṃ te hotūti vatvā gihibhāvāya abhidhāvatha. Nīharitvāti nikkhāmetvā. Ekādasahi aggīhi ādittattā mahāḍāhasadise. Sallakkhetvāti gihibhāve ādīnavaṃ, pabbajjāya ānisaṃsañca sallakkhetvā. Hirottappaṃ paṭilabhitvā “mama uppabbajitukāmataṃ sabrahmacārino jānissantī”ti. Catunnaṃ parisānaṃ cittasaṅkhobhavasena sakalajambudīpaṃ khobhetvā.

By the meaning of 'hot': by the meaning of being intensely scorched. 'Run forth': having said, 'May it be well with you in this act of running forth,' run forth to the household life. Having expelled: means having driven out. Similar to a great conflagration: because it is ignited by the eleven fires. Having discerned: means having discerned the danger in household life and the benefit in renunciation. Having regained shame and fear of wrongdoing, he thought, "My fellows in the holy life will know of my wish to disrobe." Having agitated the entire Jambudīpa by the force of agitating the minds of the four assemblies.

Sānusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sānu Sutta is concluded.

6. Piyaṅkarasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Piyaṅkara Sutta

240. Paccanteti pariyante. Pāṭiyekkanti saṅgītikāle visuṃ. Yamakavaggādikā brāhmaṇavaggapariyosānā chabbīsati vaggā etissāti chabbīsativaggā, tantīti pāḷi. Uccārapassāvādi evarūpaṃ dubbhojanaṃ, “asucijegucchabhāvena duṭṭhu bhojana”nti katvā, dubbhojanaggahaṇena vā vantagabbhamalādīni atidisati. Chaviādīni chetvāti chaviādīni ativijjha ativiya pavisitvā. Aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi pītisamuṭṭhānauḷāroḷārarūpappavattiyā. Tenāha “hadayaṅgamanīyo hutvā”ti.

240. Border region: the periphery. Separately: means distinctly at the time of the council. The twenty-six sections: this text has twenty-six sections, beginning with the Yamaka Vagga and ending with the Brāhmaṇa Vagga. The canon: means the Pāli text. Such bad food as excrement, urine, and so forth is so called because it is 'food that is bad due to its impure and repulsive nature'; or, the term 'bad food' also indicates such things as vomit and uterine filth. Having cut through the skin, etc.: means having pierced through, having penetrated excessively. Striking the bone marrow, he stood still, owing to the occurrence of an exceedingly expansive physical form arisen from rapture. Therefore, he said, "becoming heart-ravishing."

Dhammatāya [V 1.0275][M 1.0314] samādiṇṇanti kassaci santike aggahetvā sayameva tasmiṃ khaṇe saṃyatā homāti yathāsaṃyatā. Tatiyapadenāti “sikkhema susīlya”nti iminā padena. Sesāti vuttāvasesā. Tisso adinnādānamicchācārasurāpānaviratiyo. Gahitā gobalībaddañāyena. Chātakaṃ dubbhikkhañca etthāti chātakadubbhikkhā, jighacchādubbhikkhābahulāyāti attho. Pisācayakkhayoniyāti pettivisayasadisayakkhayoniyā api nāma muccemāti yojanā.

'Undertaken by nature' means: without receiving it from anyone, at that very moment they resolved, 'Let us be restrained,' thus they are restrained as is proper. 'By the third phrase' means by this phrase, 'Let us train ourselves in good conduct.' 'The rest' means the remaining abstinences to be spoken of. The three abstinences—from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and intoxicants—are included by the 'ox and bull' maxim. 'Famine and scarcity' means a place where there is famine and scarcity; the meaning is 'abounding in hunger and scarcity.' 'In the realm of ghosts and demons' means 'may we be freed even from a yaksha realm similar to the realm of departed spirits'—this is the connection.

Piyaṅkarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Piyaṅkara Sutta is finished.

7. Punabbasusuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Punabbasu Sutta

241. Vasanaṭṭhānaggahaṇena rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Dvādasahatthamattameva gaṇhāti pakatisañcaraṇūpacāramattabyāpanato. Yathāparisanti parisānurūpaṃ, yattha yattha parisā tiṭṭhati, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati parisapariyantikattā. Satthu mukhavikārābhāvato pavesānuññaṃ sallakkhentī “nūna ayaṃ katādhikārā bhavissatī”ti anumānasiddhaṃ upanissayaṃ disvā. Ekībhāvagamanenāti hatthapāsūpagamanena parisāya missībhāvappattiyā. Puttakāti puttaputtiyo. Anukampāyañhi ka-saddo.

241. By 'taking the place of dwelling,' it includes places for the night, places for the day, and so on. It takes only about twelve hands' length, because it covers just the area for normal movement and access. 'According to the assembly' means in conformity with the assembly; wherever the assembly is situated, it goes to that place, because it is bounded by the assembly. Observing the absence of any change in the Teacher's facial expression and thus marking the permission to enter, and having seen by inference the supporting condition, she thought, 'Surely, this one must have performed meritorious deeds.' 'By going into oneness' means by approaching within arm's reach, by attaining a state of mingling with the assembly. 'Puttakā' means sons and daughters. For the particle 'ka' here is in the sense of compassion.

Nibbānārammaṇena ariyamaggena muñciyamānā ganthā “nibbānaṃ āgamma pamuccantī”ti vuttā. Velātikkantāti pamāṇato paricchindituṃ na sakkāti āha “pamāṇātikkantā”ti. Piyāyanāti āsīsanā. Āsīsanaṃ pemavasena pemavatthuno esanā patthanāva hotīti āha “magganā patthanā”ti. Tatoti piyaputtādito. Pāṇīnanti sāmiatthe puthuvacanaṃ dukkhasaddāpekkhaṃ. Ke mocetīti mocanakiriyāya kammaṃ pucchati? Ibharo pana atthavasena vibhattivipariṇāmoti “pāṇineti āharitvā vattabba”nti āha. Abhisambudhanti abhisambudhanto. Tenāha “abhisambuddho”ti. Saddhammassāti upayogatthe sāmivacananti āha “saddhammameva ajānitvā”ti.

The fetters, being released by the noble path which has Nibbāna as its object, are said to be 'released by relying on Nibbāna.' 'Beyond measure' means it cannot be defined by limits; hence it is said, 'transcending measure.' 'Piyāyanā' means wishing. Wishing, on account of affection, is the seeking or longing for a beloved object; hence it is said, 'seeking, longing.' 'From that'—that is, from a beloved son, etc. 'Pāṇīnaṃ' is a plural in the sense of ownership, in relation to the word 'suffering.' 'Whom does he release?'—it asks for the object of the action of releasing. But Ibharo says that for the sake of meaning there is a change of case-ending, and that it should be stated by supplying 'pāṇine.' 'Abhisambudhanti' means 'fully understanding.' Therefore, it is said, 'the fully enlightened one.' 'Of the true Dhamma'—the genitive case is in the sense of 'with respect to'; hence it is said, 'not knowing the true Dhamma itself.'

Puttassa anumodanaṃ karontīti puttassa paṭipattianumodanaṃ karontī. Uggatāti ettha kalale vaṭṭadukkhe nimujjamānā tato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ asakkonti [M 1.0315] ajja buddhānubhāvena paññāsīsaṃ ukkhipitā uggatā. Puna vinipātābhāvato sammadeva uggatattā samuggatā. Tathābhūtā sāsanepi uggatā samuggatā jātā. Catusaccapaṭivedhabhāvanti catusaccapaṭivedhassa atthibhāvaṃ. Kaṇḍukacchuādīti ādi-saddena jegucchaasātādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Dibbasampattiṃ paṭilabhati [V 1.0276] pavattiyaṃ sampattidāyino kammassa katokāsattā. Tuṇhī uttarike hohīti mātu-vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tassa visesādhigamassa avibandhakaraṇasammāpayogena yathāladdhavisesāya mātuyā vasena yasmā dhītā diṭṭhadhammikasampattilābhī, tasmā vuttaṃ “mātu ānubhāvenevā”ti.

'Rejoicing in the son' means rejoicing in the son’s practice. 'Uggatā'—here, sinking in the mire of the suffering of the cycle of existence, unable to lift their heads, now by the Buddha’s power, having lifted the head of wisdom, they are 'risen.' Furthermore, because they have truly risen with no possibility of falling back, they are 'well-risen.' Being such, they have also become risen and well-risen in the Dispensation. 'The state of penetrating the four truths' means the existence of the penetration of the four truths. 'Scabies, itch, etc.'—by the word 'etc.' it includes repugnance, unpleasantness, and so on. She attains divine prosperity because an opportunity has been made for the kamma that gives prosperity in the course of existence. Having accepted her mother's words, 'Be silent, my dear Uttarikā,' the daughter attained prosperity in this very life through the right effort of not obstructing the attainment of further distinction, and by means of her mother who had attained her own distinction. Therefore it is said, 'by the mother’s power alone.'

Punabbasusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Punabbasu Sutta is concluded.

8. Sudattasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta

242. Karaṇīyenāti ettha karaṇīyanti vāṇijjakammaṃ adhippetanti taṃ vivaranto “anāthapiṇḍiko cā”tiādimāha. Vikkīyatīti vikkayaṃ gacchati. Tatheva karotīti yathā rājagahaseṭṭhinā sāvatthiṃ gantvā kataṃ, tatheva rājagahaṃ gantvā karoti. Svāyanti anāthapiṇḍiko.

242. 'By what is to be done': here, 'to be done' is intended to mean the business of trade. Explaining this, the text says, 'And Anāthapiṇḍika…' and so on. 'It is sold' means it goes for sale. 'He does it in the same way' means: just as the merchant of Rājagaha did when he went to Sāvatthi, so too does he, going to Rājagaha. 'He' refers to Anāthapiṇḍika.

Taṃ divasanti yaṃ divasaṃ anāthapiṇḍiko, gahapati, rājagahasamīpaṃ upagato, taṃ divasaṃ. Paṇṇanti sāsanaṃ. Na suṇīti asuṇanto “paṇṇaṃ na suṇī”ti vutto. Dhammagāravena hi so seṭṭhi aññaṃ kiccaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññi. Tenāha “dhammassavanatthāyā”tiādi. Dārakarūpānanti dārakānaṃ. Anatthantarakaro hi rūpa-saddo yathā “gorūpāna”nti. Pañcavaṇṇanti khuddikādibhedaṃ pañcappakāraṃ pītiṃ paṭilabhi. Anukkamena hi tā etassa sambhavanti. “Sīsena uṭṭhāya…pe… gacchatī”ti padaṃ pītisamuṭṭhānarūpavasena lakkhetvā vuttaṃ.

'On that day' means the day on which Anāthapiṇḍika, the householder, approached the vicinity of Rājagaha. 'The letter' means the message. 'He did not listen' means, not listening, he was said 'not to have listened to the letter.' For out of reverence for the Dhamma, that merchant did not consider any other task to be worth even a blade of grass. Therefore it says, 'For the sake of hearing the Dhamma…' and so on. 'Of the form of boys' means 'of the boys.' For the word 'form' makes no difference in meaning, as in 'of the form of cows.' 'Of five colors' means he obtained the five kinds of joy, distinguished as minor, etc. For they arose in him successively. The phrase 'rising with his head... going' was stated, indicating it as the physical manifestation arisen from joy.

Sivathikāya vasatīti sivathikāya samīpe vasati. Susānassāsannaṭṭhāne hi so vihāro. Athassāti athassa anāthapiṇḍikassa “akālo…pe… upasaṅkamissāmī”ti etaṃ ahosi. Buddhagatāya satiyāti [M 1.0316] aññaṃ kiñci acintetvā buddhagatāya eva satiyā sayanavaragato nipajji. Tena vuttaṃ “taṃ divasa”ntiādi.

'He dwells in the charnel ground' means he lives near the charnel ground. For that monastery was in a place near the cemetery. 'Then to him' means then, the following thought arose in Anāthapiṇḍika: 'It is not the time... I will approach.' 'With mindfulness directed to the Buddha' means: not thinking of anything else, with mindfulness directed solely to the Buddha, he lay down on his excellent bed. Hence it is said, 'On that day…' etc.

Balavappasādoti buddhārammaṇā balavatī saddhā. Pītiālokoti purimabuddhesu cirakālaṃ paricayaṃ gatassa balavato pasādassa vasena “buddho”ti nāmaṃ savanamattena uppannāya uḷārāya pītiyā samuṭṭhāpito vipassanobhāsasadiso sātisayo āloko hoti cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhāno. Tenāha “sabbatamaṃ vigacchī”tiādi. “Devatā hi katā”tipi vadanti, purimo evettha yutto.

'Strong faith' means strong faith with the Buddha as its object. 'The light of joy' means: by the power of strong faith developed over a long time with past Buddhas, upon merely hearing the name 'Buddha,' sublime joy arose, producing an excellent radiance like the light of insight, arisen from mind, conditions, and temperature. Therefore, it is said, 'All darkness vanished…' and so on. Some say, 'The devas made it,' but the former explanation is appropriate here.

Amanussāti [V 1.0277] adhigatavisesā devatā. Tā hi seṭṭhissa sampattiṃ paccakkhato passiṃsu. Tenāha “ayaṃ mahāseṭṭhī”tiādi. Allasarīranti tāvadeva chaḍḍitaṃ acchinnaṃ vā kaḷevaraṃ. Aparampīti mataṃ kuthitakuṇapaṃ. Parikiriṃsūti samantato osaritā ahesuṃ. Āloko antaradhāyipītivegassa mandabhāvena taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ dubbalabhāvato.

'Non-humans' means devas who have attained distinction. For they directly saw the merchant's prosperity. Hence it is said, 'This great merchant…' and so on. 'A fresh body' means a corpse just discarded or unclaimed. 'Another' means a dead, putrid corpse. 'They scattered around' means they withdrew on all sides. The light disappeared due to the weakening of the force of joy and, consequently, the feebleness of the physical forms arising from it.

Imināvāti adhikārena sahassapadena eva sambandhitabbāni. Padaṃ vītiharati etthāti padavītihāro, padavītihāraṭṭhānaṃ. Samagamaneti dutavilambitaṃ akatvā samagamane. Tatoti tesu soḷasabhāgesu. Eko koṭṭhāsoti yathāvuttaṃ padavītihārapadesaṃ soḷasadhā bhinnassa eko bhāgo. Pavattacetanāti yathāvuttakalāsaṅkhātassa padesassa laṅghanadhāvanapavattacetanā. Padaṃ vā vītiharati etenāti padavītihāro, tathāpavattā kusalacetanā. “Tassā phalaṃ soḷasadhā katvā”ti vadanti. Patiṭṭhahantassa vasena gahitanti yojanā. Vivaṭṭanissitāya eva ratanattayapūjāya dhammassavanassa sikkhāpadasamādānassa saraṇagamanassa ca atthāya gacchatopi vasena vaṭṭati. Paṭhamaṃ vuttagamanaṃ lokuttaravisesādhigamassa ekantikaṃ, dutiyaṃ anekantikanti “vaṭṭatiyevā”ti sāsaṅkavacanaṃ.

'By this': they should be connected with the thousand-fold phrase in this section. 'A step is taken here,' thus `padavītihāro`, the place of taking a step. 'In coming together' means in gathering together without a second's delay. 'From that' refers to those sixteen parts. 'One portion' means one part of the aforementioned place of taking a step, when it is divided sixteen-fold. 'Occurring volition' refers to the volition occurring while running or leaping over the area designated by the aforementioned fraction. Or, 'a step is taken by this,' thus `padavītihāro`; it is the wholesome volition that so occurs. They say, 'making its fruit sixteen-fold.' The connection is that this is taken in the sense of one who is becoming established. It is also fitting in the sense of one who goes for the sake of venerating the Triple Gem, listening to the Dhamma, undertaking the training rules, and going for refuge, which is solely dependent on the rolling back of the cycle. The first-mentioned going is certain for the attainment of supramundane distinction, while the second is not certain; thus, the statement 'it is fitting indeed' is a qualified one.

Soti anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi. Anuyuttāti anugāmino sahāyā. Teva sandhāya vadati. “Sivako amanusso”ti apare. Na kevalaṃ “anuyuttāpi me atthi, kasmā bhāyāmī”ti evaṃ sūro ahosi? Atha kho buddhagatāya tikkhavisadasabhāvena sabbaṃ parissayaṃ madditvāpi [M 1.0317] agamāsīti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pakkhandanalakkhaṇā hi saddhā, tāya yuttako sappurisopi saddhammaguṇavasena sabbaṃ parissayaṃ madditvā pakkhandatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Soti is the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. Anuyuttā means his followers and companions. This is spoken with reference to them. Some say, “Sivaka is a non-human.” Was he merely bold, thinking, “I have followers too, why should I fear?” But to show that he went forth even after crushing all dangers with the sharp and clear nature of his faith in the Buddha, “apicā” and so on is said. For faith has the characteristic of leaping forward; endowed with it, even a virtuous person, through the qualities of the true Dhamma, crushes all dangers and leaps forward—this should be seen.

Sabbakāmasamiddhatā pariccāgasīlatā uḷārajjhāsayatā paradukkhāpanayakāmatā paresaṃ hitesitā parasampattipamodanāti evamādīnaṃ mahāguṇānaṃ vasena niccakālaṃ anāthānaṃ piṇḍadāyakattā “anāthapiṇḍiko”ti evaṃ uppannaṃ nāmaṃ. Evamāhāti “ehi sudattā”ti evaṃ āha.

Because he always gave alms to the destitute, by virtue of great qualities such as the fulfillment of all desires, the virtue of generosity, lofty intentions, the desire to remove the suffering of others, seeking the welfare of others, and rejoicing in the prosperity of others, the name “Anāthapiṇḍika” arose. “Thus he said” means he spoke thus: “Come, Sudatta.”

Kilesaparinibbānenāti sabbaso rāgādikilesavūpasamena. Kilesavūpasamanti sabbaso sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ vūpasamaṃ aggamaggena patvā. Anupubbikathanti dānādikathaṃ. Sā hi anupubbena kathetabbattā “anupubbikathā”ti vuccati. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Seyyathidaṃ – dānakathaṃ sīlakathaṃ saggakathaṃ kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesī”ti (cūḷava. 305). Matthaketi anupubbikathāya upari parato. Cattāri saccāni pakāsesīti yathā mahāseṭṭhi sahassanayapaṭimaṇḍite sotāpattiphale [V 1.0278] patiṭṭhāti, evaṃ pavattinivattiyo saha hetunā vibhajanto cattāri ariyasaccāni pakāsesīti.

“By the complete cessation of defilements” means by the total pacification of defilements such as lust and so forth. “The pacification of defilements” means having attained the complete pacification of all defilements by means of the highest path. “Gradual discourse” means a talk on generosity and so forth, for it is called “gradual discourse” because it should be spoken in sequence. In reference to that, it was said: “Then the Blessed One gave a gradual discourse, that is, a talk on generosity, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation” (Cūḷavagga 305). “At the culmination” means above, after the gradual discourse. “He revealed the Four Noble Truths” means that by analyzing arising and ceasing together with their cause, he revealed the Four Noble Truths in such a way that the great merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry, which is adorned with a thousand methods.

Sudattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta is concluded.

9. Paṭhamasukkāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the First Sukkā Sutta

243. Rathikanti racchaṃ. Gahetvāti gantvā. Siṅghāṭakanti aññattha tikoṇā racchā vuccati. Idha pana “catukka”nti vuttaṃ. “Madhupīkā”ti ettha madhu-saddena madhuviseso vuccatīti āha “gandhamadhupānaṃ pītā viyā”ti. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese tiṭṭhatīti gandhamadhūti ca ativiya madhuro madaniyo eko madhuviseso. Tenāha “asaññī hutvā sayatevā”ti.

243. “Rathikaṃ” means a road. “Gahetvā” means having gone. “Siṅghāṭakaṃ” elsewhere is called a three-way intersection, but here it is said to mean a four-way junction. Regarding “Madhupīkā”: here, by the word “madhu,” a specific kind of honey is meant; thus it is said, “like one who has drunk fragrant honey.” For a general term indeed stands for a specific instance; thus, “fragrant honey” is an exceedingly sweet and intoxicating kind of honey. Therefore, he said, “Becoming unconscious, she simply lay down.”

Na paṭivānīyaṃ [M 1.0318] na apanetabbanti appaṭivānīyaṃ. Tenāha “bāhirakañhī”tiādi. Yaṃ kiñci santapaṇītabhāvāvahaṃ na secananti asecanakaṃ. Tato eva anāsittakaṃ. Ojavantanti bahusammataojavantasadisatāya ojavantaṃ. Tenāha “yathā hī”tiādi. Dhammatāyāti attano sabhāveneva. Madhuro iṭṭho. Pivantī viyāti sukkāya bhikkhuniyā upanīyamānaṃ saddhammāmatarasaṃ attano sotañjaliṃ pūretvā odahantīva. Valāhakato āgataṃ valāhakaṃ.

That which is not to be warded off, not to be removed, is “appaṭivānīyaṃ.” Hence it is said, “external,” and so forth. That which brings about a state of peace and excellence without needing irrigation is “asecanakaṃ.” For that very reason, it is “anāsittakaṃ,” unmoistened. “Ojavantaṃ” means possessing sap, due to its similarity to that which is highly regarded as possessing sap. Hence it is said, “just as,” and so forth. “Dhammatāya” means by its own inherent nature. Sweet and agreeable. “Pivantī viya” means as if filling her cupped ears with the nectar-flavor of the true Dhamma presented by the bhikkhunī Sukkā, she was placing it within. “Valāhakaṃ” means come from a cloud.

Paṭhamasukkāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Sukkā Sutta is concluded.

10. Dutiyasukkāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Second Sukkā Sutta

244. Bahuṃ vata puññaṃ pasavati sabbaganthavimuttiyā sīlasamannāgatena aggadakkhiṇeyyāya sukkāya theriyā bhojanassa dinnattā.

244. Indeed, much merit is generated by giving food to the elder nun Sukkā, who is endowed with virtue, liberated from all bonds, and the foremost worthy of offerings.

Dutiyasukkāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Sukkā Sutta is concluded.

11. Cīrāsuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Cīrā Sutta

245. Ekādasamaṃ uttānameva dasamena sadisattā. Tattha hi bhojanaṃ upāsakassa ābhataṃ, idha cīvaradānanti ayameva viseso.

245. The eleventh sutta is straightforward, being similar to the tenth. For there, food was brought for a lay follower, whereas here it is the gift of a robe; this is the only difference.

Cīrāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cīrā Sutta is concluded.

12. Āḷavakasuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta

246. Āḷaviyanti [V 1.0279] itthiliṅgavasena taṃ raṭṭhampi nagarampi vuccati. Raṭṭhe adhippetepi na ettha bahuvacanaṃ tathāruḷhiyā abhāvato. Tañca bhavananti tañca āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavanaṃ. Tatthāti āḷavakassa bhavane. “Atha kho āḷavako yakkho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”ti ettha tasmiṃ pāṭhapadese. Ayamanupubbikathāti ayaṃ idāni vuccamānā anupubbato āgatā kathā. Āḷaviyā issaroti āḷavo, āḷavakoti ca [M 1.0319] rājā vutto. Kadāci corapaṭibāhanatthaṃ, kadāci ussāhasattivibhāvanavasena paṭirājanisedhanatthaṃ, kadāci lakkhayogyaviniyogavasena byāyāmakaraṇatthañca. Migānaṃ vananato vasanato vānato vā “migavā”ti laddhasamaññaṃ migavaṃ. Tassevāti rañño eva. Migoti eko eṇimigo. Tiyojananti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Udakaṃ viya pavisitvā ṭhitanti yathā parissamappatto udakaṃ pavisitvā ṭhito nirassāso hoti, evaṃ viya ṭhitaṃ. Mūlanti samīpaṃ. Yakkhaṃ disvāva rañño bhayaṃ chambhitattaṃ ūrutthambhaṃ ahosi, tasmā rājā palāyituṃ nāsakkhi. Tena vuttaṃ “khādituṃ upagato”ti. Atha rājā dvidhā chinnaṃ migaṃ datvā attānaṃ mocetukāmo ahosi. Yakkho “nanu mama hatthagatakālato paṭṭhāya migopi mama santako, tattha kinnāma te kerāṭiyamidaṃ datvā attano mocana”nti rājānaṃ na muñci. Atha rājā tassa tādisaṃ paṭiññātaṃ akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “rājā tena saddhi”ntiādi. Bhavanaṃ anupagatanti idaṃ mama bhavanaṃ anupagataṃ. Ananuññātanti upagatena sāmibhūtena ananuññātañca. Etena upagataṃ taṃ, idāni tādisena anuññātañca khādituṃ labhāmīti dasseti.

246. “Āḷaviyaṃ” refers to both the country and the city, so called due to the feminine gender. Even when the country is intended, the plural is not used here due to the absence of such a convention. “Tañca bhavanaṃ” means that dwelling of the yakkha Āḷavaka. “Tattha” means in the dwelling of Āḷavaka. ‘Here’ refers to that passage of the text: “Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One.” “Ayam anupubbikathā” means this discourse, now being spoken, which has come down in sequence. “Āḷaviyā issaro” is Āḷava, and the king is also called Āḷavaka. Sometimes for the purpose of preventing thieves, sometimes for the purpose of restraining rival kings by displaying power and vigor, and sometimes for the purpose of exertion by assigning suitable tasks through target practice. The hunting ground, “migavaṃ,” gets its name from the roaming, dwelling, or desiring of deer, being designated “migavā.” “Tassa eva” means of the king alone. “Migo” means a single antelope. “Tiyojanaṃ” is a term used in the sense of extreme connection. “Udakaṃ viya pavisitvā ṭhitaṃ” means standing as if breathless, just as one who, after exertion, has entered water and stands there. “Mūlaṃ” means nearby. Upon seeing the yakkha, the king was struck with fear, terror, and stiffness of the thighs; therefore, the king could not flee. Hence it is said, “approached to devour.” Then the king, wishing to free himself, offered the deer cut in two. The yakkha said, “Indeed, from the moment it came into my hands, the deer is also mine. What kind of trickery is this, offering it to free yourself?” and did not release the king. Then the king made such a promise to him. Hence it is said, “the king with him,” and so forth. “Bhavanaṃ anupagataṃ” means “this dwelling of mine has not been entered.” “Ananuññātaṃ” means “and not permitted by the one who has arrived and become the owner.” By this, he shows: “He has entered, and now, being permitted by such a one, I get to devour him.”

Maccupatheti maccugocare. Āsannamaraṇatāya evamāhaṃsu.

“Maccupathe” means in the domain of death. Because death was near, they spoke thus.

Taṃ āḷavakakumāraṃ ādāya pakkamiṃsūti yojanā. Tassa rañño mahesī āḷavakakumārassa mātāti vuttā. Devisahassānaṃ vippalapantīnanti vacanaṃ pariṇāmetabbaṃ.

The construction is: “Taking that Āḷavaka prince, they departed.” The chief queen of that king is said to be the mother of the Āḷavaka prince. The phrase, “of a thousand queens lamenting,” should be construed.

Desanāpariyosāneti yakkhaṃ dametvā paccāgantvā nagaradvārasamīpe rukkhamūle nisinnena bhagavatā sarājikāya mahatiyā parisāya desitadesanāya pariyosāne. Soti bhagavā. Bhavane evāti vimāne eva. Bhagavāpi passati pakaticakkhunāva nigrodhassa upari nibbattattā.

“Desanāpariyosāne” means at the conclusion of the discourse taught by the Blessed One, who, after taming the yakkha and returning, was seated at the foot of a tree near the city gate, to the great assembly together with the king. “So” means the Blessed One. “Bhavane eva” means in the mansion itself. The Blessed One also sees with his normal eye, since he had arisen above the banyan tree.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ “rosetukāmatāyā”ti vacane. Tesanti sātāgirihemavatānaṃ. Kāladīpadesakulajanettiāyuppamāṇavisayaṃ [V 1.0280] pañcamahāvilokitaṃ. “Sītaṃ byapagataṃ hoti, uṇhañca upasammatī”tiādinā (bu. vaṃ. 2.83) āgatāni dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni. Kaṭippadesavatthikosakaṇṇato tidhā. Saddoti āḷavakassa ugghositasaddo.

“Tatra” refers to that in the phrase “desiring to enrage.” “Tesaṃ” refers to Sātāgiri and Hemavata. The five great investigations have as their scope: time, continent, region, family, and the mother's lifespan. The thirty-two premonitory signs are found in the passage beginning, “the cold disappears, and the heat subsides” (Bu.vaṃ. 2.83). Threefold from the hip region, garment, and scrotum. “Saddo” refers to the sound proclaimed by Āḷavaka.

Iminā [M 1.0320] pasaṅgena sakalajambudīpaṃ byāpetvā pavatte aparepi tayo sadde yathā ete, evaṃ āḷavakassa ugghositasaddopīti dassetuṃ “cattāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Osakkanteti parihāyamāne.

By this connection, to show that the sound proclaimed by Āḷavaka was also like these three other sounds that arose pervading the entire Jambudīpa, it is said, “four,” and so forth. “Osakkante” means receding.

Cuṇṇentāti cuṇṇetuṃ samatthataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana cuṇṇanavasena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “mā kassacī”tiādi. Ussāvabindumattampīti ussāvapatanamattampi. Khurappaṃ sallaṃ.

“Capable of crushing” (cuṇṇente) is said with reference to the ability to crush, not with reference to the act of crushing itself. Therefore, he said, “Let no one…” and so forth. “Even the slightest drop” (ussāvabindumattampi) means even the amount of a falling drop. “Khurappaṃ” means a dart.

Seṭṭhānīti ajeyyena appaṭihatabhāvena uttamāni. Dussāvudhanti āvudhakiccakaraṃ uttariyaṃ dussaṃ. Imāni kira sakkādīnaṃ puññānubhāvena nibbattāni appaṭihatappabhāvāni paṭipakkhavidhamanayuttāni avajjhāni āvudhāni. Tenāha “yadi hī”tiādi.

“Supreme” (seṭṭhāni) means excellent due to being unconquerable and unassailable. “Cloth weapon” (dussāvudhaṃ) is an upper garment that serves the function of a weapon.
