These weapons, it is said, were produced by the power of the merit of Sakka and others—unobstructed in their potency, capable of destroying opponents, and invulnerable. Therefore, it is said, “If indeed,” and so forth.

Asanivicakkaṃ viyāti asanimaṇḍalaṃ viya.

“Like a wheel of lightning” (asanivicakkaṃ viya) means like a lightning disc.

Pittanti alagaddapittaṃ. Bhindeyyāti āsiñceyya. Sukhanti sukaraṃ. Mudubhūtacittavavatthānakaraṇatthanti mudubhūtaṃ attano citte vavatthānassa karaṇatthaṃ.

“Bile” (pittaṃ) means the bile of a water-snake. “Bhindeyya” means one should pour it out. “Sukhaṃ” means easy. “For the purpose of making the mind pliable and establishing it” (mudubhūtacittavavatthānakaraṇatthaṃ) means for the purpose of making one’s own mind pliable and establishing it.

Evaṃ vutteti “na khvāha”nti evaṃ vutte. Bhagavato sāsane ṭhite payirupāsitvā uggahitaṃ bhagavantaṃ payirūpāsitvā uggahitameva nāmāti āha “kassapaṃ…pe... uggahesu”nti. Puṭṭhapañhāti sammāsambuddhena puṭṭhapañhā. Yasmā buddhavisaye puṭṭhapañhā, tasmā buddhavisayāva honti.

“When it was thus said” (Evaṃ vutte) refers to when it was said, “Indeed, I do not say so.” Having stood in the Blessed One’s dispensation, having attended upon the Blessed One and learned, it is indeed called “learned” when one has attended upon the Blessed One and learned from him; thus he said, “Kassapa…learned.” “The questions asked” (Puṭṭhapañhā) are questions asked by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Since the questions asked are in the Buddha’s domain, they are therefore indeed in the Buddha’s domain.

Paṭisedhetvāti vācāya asakkuṇeyyabhāveneva paṭisedhetvā. “Yadākaṅkhasī”ti padasandhivasena niddesoti āha “yadi ākaṅkhasī”ti. Tena tuyhaṃ pucchaṃ tāva sutvā vissajjessanti dasseti. Tenāha “na me”tiādi. Dutiyavikappe da-kāro padasandhikaroti āha “yaṃ ākaṅkhasī”ti. “Puccha, āvuso, sutvā jānissāmī”ti avatvā sabbaññubuddhassa aniyametvā vacanaṃ sabbavisayaṃ hotīti āha “sabbaṃ te”tiādi.

“Having rejected” (paṭisedhetvā) means having rejected merely through the inability to speak. “When you wish” (yadākaṅkhasi): the designation is by way of word combination, therefore he said, “If you wish.” By that, he shows that they will answer after first hearing your question. Therefore he said, “Not for me,” and so forth. In the second alternative, the letter ‘da’ forms a word connection, therefore he said, “Whatever you wish.” Without saying, “Ask, friend, having heard I will know,” because the speech of the All-Knowing Buddha is not restricted, it encompasses every sphere; therefore he said, “All to you,” and so forth.

Kiṃ [V 1.0281] sūti ettha kinti pucchāyaṃ, sūti saṃsaye, kiṃ nūti attho? Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Tasmā vittanti yasmā vittikaraṇato vittaṃ. Sukatanti suṭṭhu sakkaccaṃ kataṃ. Sukhanti iṭṭhaphalaṃ. Tattha yaṃ padhānaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “kāyikacetasikaṃ sāta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Nissandaphalañhi taggahaṇena gahitameva [M 1.0321] hoti. Appetīti pāpeti. Atisayatthajotano tara-saddoti āha “atisayena sādū”ti. Rasasaññitāya iṭṭhānaṃ rāgādidhammānaṃ. Kena pakārenāti kathaṃ-saddassa atthamāha. Kathaṃjīvinti yadi samāsapadametaṃ, “katha”nti sānunāsikā katāti āha “gāthābandhasukhattha”ntiādi.

Here, in 'kiṃ sū', 'kiṃ' is a question and 'sū' implies doubt; the meaning is 'what then?' 'Idha' means 'in this world.' 'Vitta' (wealth) is so called because it is a means of providing (vittikaraṇato). 'Sukata' means 'well-done' or 'carefully done.' 'Sukha' means 'the desired fruit.' There, to show what is principal, it is said, 'bodily and mental satisfaction,' and so on. For the resultant fruit is indeed included by that expression. 'Appeti' means 'causes to reach.' It is said that the suffix '-tara' indicates excess, meaning 'exceedingly savory.' Due to the designation of 'flavor,' it refers to desirable qualities such as lust, and so on. 'Kena pakārena' explains the meaning of the word 'kathaṃ.' Regarding 'kathaṃjīvin', if this is a compound word, it is said that 'kathaṃ' is made nasal for the sake of metrical ease, and so on.

Saddhīdha vittanti ekadesena samudāyadassanaṃ samuddapabbatanidassanaṃ viya. Iti-saddo ādiattho daṭṭhabbo. “Vittikaraṇato vitta”nti vuttamatthaṃ sandhāya hetūpamāhi yojetvā dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena sukhāvahanato, dukkhapaṭibāhanato, dāliddiyūpasamanato, ratanapaṭilābhahetuto, lokasantatiāvahanato ca saddhā vittaṃ yathā taṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādīni. Tenāha “eva”ntiādi. Nanu cetanā sammādiṭṭhiādayo ca sātisayaṃ vipākasukhaṃ āvahanti, taṃ kathaṃ saddhā āvahatīti? Saddhādhurabhāvasabhāvato. Tenāha “saddhādhurena paṭipannāna”nti. Tassa ca sesapadesupi yojetabbaṃ.

'Saddhīdha vittaṃ' (Here, faith is wealth)—this is a partial way of seeing the collective, like the illustration of the ocean or a mountain. The word 'iti' should be understood as having the meaning of 'and so on.' Referring to the stated meaning, 'Vitta is so called because it is a means of providing (vittikaraṇato),' and to illustrate it by connecting it with causal similes, the passage beginning with 'just as' is stated. Therefore, because faith brings happiness, wards off suffering, alleviates poverty, is a cause for obtaining treasures, and brings about the continuity of the world—just like gold, silver, and other valuables—it is wealth. Thus it is said, 'even so,' and so on. But one might ask: 'Do not volition, right view, and the like also bring about an abundance of happiness as a result? How then does faith bring it about?' It is due to the nature of faith's leading role. Hence it is said, 'for those who have undertaken with the yoke of faith.' And this should be applied to the remaining terms as well.

Idāni yaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādi saddhāvittassa opammaṃ, taṃ hīnaṃ, saddhāvittameva uttamanti pāḷiyaṃ seṭṭhaggahaṇaṃ katanti dassetuṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paralokaṃ gataṃ anugacchatīti anugāmikaṃ. Aññehi na sādhāraṇanti anaññasādhāraṇaṃ. Sabbasampattihetūti sabbāsaṃ sīlasampadādīnaṃ lokiyalokuttarānaṃ sampattīnaṃ hetu. Anatthāya hoti anupāyapaṭipattito. Tasmā anugāmikattā. Anaññasādhāraṇattā sabbasampattihetubhāvato hiraññādivittanidānattā ca saddhāvittameva seṭṭhaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedadesanā yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti.

Now, to show that the comparison of gold, silver, and other wealth to the wealth of faith is inferior, and that the wealth of faith alone is supreme, the Pāli text uses the term 'best' (seṭṭha); thus the passage beginning with 'But because...' is stated. That which follows one to the next world is called 'anugāmika' (accompanying). Not shared with others is called 'anaññasādhāraṇa' (exclusive). 'Sabbasampattihetu' (the cause of all attainments) means it is the cause of all worldly and supramundane accomplishments, such as the accomplishment of virtue, and so on. It leads to harm due to improper practice. Therefore, because it is accompanying, because it is exclusive, because it is the cause of all attainments, and because it is the source of wealth such as gold and so on, the wealth of faith alone is supreme. The statement of its superior distinction is like: 'The Teacher of gods and humans'.

“Dasakusaladhammo”ti iminā ekaccānaṃyeva dānādidhammānaṃ saṅgaho, na sabbesanti asaṅgahitasaṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “dānasīlabhāvanādhammo vā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sukha”nti tividhassapi sukhassa sādhāraṇaggahaṇametanti taṃ savisesaladdhaṃ puggalavasena dassento “soṇaseṭṭhi…pe… āvahatī”ti āha. Yo so padumavatiyā deviyā putto mahāpadumo nāma rājā dibbasukhasadisaṃ rajjasukhamanubhavitvā pacchā paccekabuddho hutvā nibbānasukhamanubhavi, taṃ nidassanabhāvena gahetvā āha “mahāpadumādīnaṃ viya nibbānasukhañca āvahatī”ti.

'Dasakusaladhammo' (the ten wholesome qualities)—by this, only some qualities such as giving are included, not all; to include what was not included, it is said, 'or the qualities of giving, virtue, and mental development.' 'Sukha' (happiness) is a general term encompassing all three kinds of happiness. To show how it is attained with specific distinctions according to the individual, it is said, 'the merchant Soṇa... brings.' King Mahāpaduma, the son of Queen Padumavatī, experienced royal happiness comparable to divine happiness and later, becoming a Paccekabuddha, experienced the bliss of Nibbāna; taking him as an illustration, it is said, 'like Mahāpaduma and others, it brings the bliss of Nibbāna'.

Atthuddhāranayena [V 1.0282][M 1.0322] saccasaddaṃ saṃvaṇṇento “anekesu atthesu dissatī”ti āha. Vācāsacce dissati saccasaddo “bhaṇe”ti vuttattāti adhippāyo. Viratisacce dissati. Veramaṇīsu hi patiṭṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā “sacce ṭhitā”ti vuccanti. Attākārampi vatthuṃ idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti pavattiyākāraṃ upādāya diṭṭhi eva saccanti diṭṭhisaccaṃ, tasmiṃ diṭṭhisacce dissatīti yojanā. Brāhmaṇasaccānīti paramatthabrahmānaṃ saccāni, yāni “sabbe pāṇā avajjhā, sabbe kāmā aniccā, sabbe bhavā aniccā, nāhaṃ kvacani kassaci kiñcanatasmi”ntiādinā (a. ni. 4.185) catukkanipāte āgatāni. Paramatthabhūtaṃ saccaṃ nibbānaṃ. Abbhantaraṃ katvāti antogadhameva katvā, tehi saddhinti attho paramatthasaccānampi sādutarattā. Yassānubhāvenāti yassa vācāsaccassa ānubhāvena.

Explaining the word 'sacca' (truth) by the method of extracting meanings, he said, 'It is seen in many senses.' The word 'sacca' is seen in 'vācāsacca' (truth in speech), because it is said, 'speak' (bhaṇe)—this is the intended meaning. It is seen in 'viratisacca' (truth in abstinence). For ascetics and brahmins established in abstinences are called 'established in truth.' Taking the mode of occurrence that 'this very thing is true and something else is false' regarding even a self-form or an object, that view itself is truth—this is 'diṭṭhisacca' (truth of view). The connection is that it is seen in that truth of view. 'Brāhmaṇasaccāni' (truths of the brahmins) are the truths of the brahmins in the ultimate sense, which are stated in the Catukkanipāta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.185) as: 'All beings are not to be harmed, all sensual pleasures are impermanent, all states of existence are impermanent, I am not anything to anyone anywhere,' and so on. The ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) is Nibbāna. 'Abbhantaraṃ katvā' (having made internal) means having fully absorbed within—the meaning is that they are even more pleasing than the ultimate truths. 'Yassānubhāvena' (by whose power) means by the power of that truth in speech (vācāsacca).

Udakamhi dhāvatīti udakapiṭṭhiyaṃ abhijjamānāyaṃ pathaviyā viya dhāvati gacchati mahākappinarājā viya. Visampi saccena hananti paṇḍitāti kaṇhadīpāyanādayo viya. Saccenāti macchajātake bodhisattassa viya saccena devo thanayaṃ pavassati. Sacce ṭhitāti viratisacce vācāsacce ca ṭhitā tayopi bodhisattā. Nibbutinti nibbānaṃ patthayanti. Sādutaranti sātataraṃ iṭṭhataravipākadānato.

'Udakamhi dhāvati' (runs on water) means one runs and goes on the surface of the water as if on the earth without it breaking, like King Mahākappina. 'Visampi saccena hananti paṇḍitā' (the wise destroy even poison with truth)—like Kaṇhadīpāyana and others. 'Saccena' (by truth)—as in the Fish Jātaka, where by the Bodhisatta's truth the deva rained, thundering. 'Sacce ṭhitā' (established in truth) refers to all three Bodhisattas who were established in the truth of abstinence and the truth of speech. 'Nibbuti' (quenching) means they aspire to Nibbāna. 'Sādutara' (more delightful) means because it yields a more pleasing result.

Rasānanti niddhāraṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Niddhāraṇañca koci kutoci kenaci imanti kassaci vacanaṃ na sādhetīti dassento “ye ime”tiādimāha. Tena hi nibbānaṃ rasasamudāyato sādutaratāvisesena niddhārīyati. Tattha ye ime vuccantīti yojanā. Sāyanīyadhammāti jivhāya sāyitabbā dhammā. Rasāyatanaṃ rasoti āha “mūlaraso khandharaso”tiādi. Phalarasanti phalassa rasaṃ, phalaṃ pīḷetvā tāpetvā gahetabbarasanti attho. Arasarūpoti ācārarahitasabhāvo. Rūpassa assādanavasena uppajjanakasukhadhammā rūparasā. Esa nayo saddarasādīsu. Saddarasoti byañjanasambhūto raso. Vimuttirasoti vimuttisampattiko raso. Attharasoti atthassa paṭivijjhanavasena uppajjanakasukhaṃ attharaso, tathā dhammaraso veditabbo. Rūpācārātiādīsu rasaggahaṇena phalarasaṃ vadati. So hi phalassa rūpo ca, rasitabbato āsādetabbato raso cāti “rūparaso”ti vuccati. Ācāro [M 1.0323] pana sāmaggīrasahetutāya “raso”ti vutto. Saccaṃ haveti ettha haveti ekaṃsatthe nipāto, ekaṃsattho ca avadhāraṇamevāti āha “saccameva sādutara”ntiādi. Sarīramupabrūhenti, na cittaṃ. Nanu ca sukhuppattipayojanattā cittampi upabrūhentīti? Na, sukhassa sarīrabrūhanaṃ paṭicca uppannattā. Viratisaccavācāti saccavisesena sampajjanaṃ vadati. Cittamupabrūheti padālikāya virativācāya saccarase sati samathavipassanādīhi [V 1.0283] cittaparibrūhanassa sambhavato maggaphalānisaṃsaṃ gaṇhāti. Asaṃkilesikañca sukhamāvahati vivaṭṭasannissitattā. Vimuttirasoti phalasukhaṃ vadati nibbānasukhampi vā. Paramatthasaccaraso nāma nibbānaraso. Tathā hi taṃ “accutirasaṃ assāsakaraṇarasa”ntipi vuccati. Tena paribhāvitattāti vimuttirasassa sādutarabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Evaṃ santepi “vimuttirasaparibhāvitattā”ti etena kāmaṃ vimuttiraso vā paramatthasaccaraso vā sādutararasāti dasseti. Tadadhigamūpāyabhūtanti tassa paramatthasaccassa adhigamūpāyabhūtaṃ. Atthañca dhammañcāti phalañca kāraṇañca nissāya pavattito attharasā dhammarasā ca sādū, tatopi paramatthasaccameva sādurasanti adhippāyo.

'Rasānaṃ' (of flavors) is a genitive case used in the sense of determination. To show that determination means that no statement can establish anything as 'this' or 'that' from any source, by any means, or for anyone, he said, 'those who...' and so on. Therefore, Nibbāna is determined by its special superior sweetness arising from the aggregate of flavors. Here, the construction is 'those who are called these.' 'Sāyanīyadhammā' (things to be tasted) refers to phenomena that can be experienced by the tongue. The sphere of taste, or 'rasa,' is described as 'the flavor of roots, the flavor of stalks,' and so on. 'Phalarasa' (the flavor of fruit) means the flavor of the fruit, the meaning being the juice obtained by crushing or heating the fruit. 'Arasarūpa' (devoid of taste) refers to a nature lacking proper conduct. 'Rūparasā' (flavors of form) are pleasant phenomena arising based on the enjoyment of form. The same applies to the flavors of sound, etc. 'Saddarasa' (the flavor of sound) refers to the flavor produced by syllables. 'Vimuttirasa' (the flavor of liberation) is the taste associated with the attainment of liberation. 'Attharasa' (the flavor of meaning) is the pleasant experience arising from penetrating the meaning; similarly, the 'dhammarasa' (flavor of Dhamma) should be understood. In expressions like 'rūpācāra' (conduct of form) and so on, the term 'rasa' refers to the taste of fruit. For it is both the form of the fruit and, being enjoyable and delightful, is called 'rūparasa' (the flavor of form). Conduct, however, is called 'rasa' because it is the cause of harmoniousness. 'Saccaṃ haveti' (truth indeed)—here, 'haveti' is a particle indicating certainty, and certainty means affirmation—hence it is said, 'truth alone is sweeter,' and so on. They nurture the body, not the mind. But since happiness arises for the sake of well-being, doesn’t the mind also get nurtured? No, because happiness arises dependent on the nurturing of the body. 'Viratisaccavācā' (truthful speech of abstinence) refers to the accomplishment of a special truthfulness. The mind is nurtured—in the verse, when there is the flavor of truth in the speech of restraint, the development of the mind through serenity and insight, and so on, is possible, thus one obtains the benefits of the path and its fruits. It also brings about undefiled happiness due to its reliance on detachment. 'Vimuttirasa' (the flavor of liberation) refers either to the happiness of the fruit or the happiness of Nibbāna. 'Paramatthasaccaraso' (the flavor of ultimate truth) is specifically the flavor of Nibbāna. For it is also called 'the deathless flavor, the flavor of reassurance.' 'Tena paribhāvitattā' (because it is cultivated by that)—this is said to show the superior sweetness of the flavor of liberation. Even so, by 'vimuttirasaparibhāvitattā' (because it is cultivated by the flavor of liberation), it is shown that either the flavor of liberation or the flavor of ultimate truth is the sweetest flavor. 'Tadadhigamūpāyabhūtaṃ' (being the means to attain that) means it is the means to attain that ultimate truth. 'Atthañca dhammañca' (meaning and Dhamma)—the fruit and the cause—are sweet because the flavor of meaning and the flavor of Dhamma depend on it, but the ultimate truth itself is the sweetest flavor—this is the intended meaning.

Lokuttaraṃ lokiyañca atthaṃ ajānanto andho, lokiyatthameva jānanto ekacakkhu, ubhayaṃ jānanto dvicakkhu. Parahitaṃ attahitañca ajānanto andho, attahitameva jānanto ekacakkhu, ubhayatthaṃ jānanto dvicakkhu. So dvicakkhupuggalo paññājīvī. Taṃ pana gahaṭṭhapabbajitavasena vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “gahaṭṭho vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gahaṭṭhapaṭipadaṃ ārādhetvā cāti yojanā. Ārādhetvāti ca sādhetvāti attho.

One who does not know the supramundane and the mundane benefit is blind; one who knows only the mundane benefit is one-eyed; one who knows both is two-eyed. One who does not know the welfare of others and one's own welfare is blind; one who knows only one's own welfare is one-eyed; one who knows the welfare of both is two-eyed. Such a two-eyed person lives by wisdom. Now, to explain this by distinguishing between householders and renunciants, it is said, 'whether a householder or...' and so on. The meaning is to be understood by connecting it with 'having cultivated the householder's practice.' 'Ārādhetvā' (having cultivated) means 'having accomplished'; that is the meaning.

Purimanayenevāti kassapasammāsambuddhavissajjitanayeneva. Kiñcāpīti anujānanasandassanatthe nipāto. Kiṃ anujānātīti? Gāthāya catūhi padehi vuttesu atthesu ekassa atthassa siddhiyaṃ itaresampi siddhiṃ anujānāti. Tenāha “yo catubbidhamoghaṃ…pe… parisujjhatī”ti. Kiṃ sandassetīti? Yesaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ balavabhāvena oghataraṇādi na sijjhati, tesaṃ paṭipakkhānaṃ nissandehavasena sandassanaṃ. Tenāha “evaṃ santepī”tiādi. Oghataraṇanti oghataraṇapaṭipattiṃ. Asaddahantoti evaṃ paṭipajjanto [M 1.0324] imāya paṭipattiyā oghaṃ taratīti na saddahanto. Na pakkhandatīti pakkhandanalakkhaṇāya saddhāya na ugghāṭīyatīti na otarati. Cittavossaggenāti yathākāmācāravasena cittassa vossajjanena. Pamatto pamādaṃ āpanno. Tatthevāti kāmesu eva. Visattattā laggattā. Vokiṇṇoti visevito. Tasmāti vuttassa catubbidhassapi atthassa hetubhāvena paccāmasanaṃ. Tappaṭipakkhanti assaddhiyādīnaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ saddhādīnaṃ okāsattā.

“Purimanayenevāti”: in the same way as it was expounded by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Kassapa. “Kiñcāpi”: a particle used in the sense of permission and demonstration. What does it permit? It permits the fulfillment of the other meanings through the fulfillment of one meaning stated in the four lines of a verse. Hence it is said: “One who purifies the fourfold flood… becomes purified.” What does it demonstrate? For those whose strong unwholesome qualities prevent them from crossing the flood, etc., it demonstrates the certainty of their counteracting factors. Hence it is said: “Even so,” etc. “Oghataraṇa”: the practice for crossing the flood. “Asaddahanto”: not believing that by practicing thus, one crosses the flood by means of this practice. “Na pakkhandati”: does not plunge in, meaning it is not opened by faith, which has the characteristic of enthusiasm. “Cittavossaggena”: by the abandonment of the mind through unrestrained conduct. “Pamatto”: one who has fallen into heedlessness. “Tattheva”: right there in sensual pleasures. “Visattattā”: due to clinging, due to attachment. “Vokiṇṇo”: indulged in. “Tasmā”: a review due to the aforementioned fourfold meaning being the cause. “Tappaṭipakkhaṃ”: the counteracting factors—faith and so on—because they are the opportunity for faith and the like, which are the antidotes to disbelief and the like.

Etāyāti gāthāyaṃ iminā padenāti sambandho. Sappurisasaṃsevo saddhammassavanaṃ yonisomanasikāro dhammānudhammapaṭipattīti imesaṃ sotāpattimaggādhigamassa aṅgānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ saddhindriyanti āha “sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānaṃ saddhindriya”nti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “saddhājāto upasaṅkamati[V 1.0284], upasaṅkamanto payirupāsati, payirupāsanto sotaṃ odahati, ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇātī”tiādi (ma. ni. 2.183, 432). Diṭṭhoghaṃ tarati etenāti diṭṭhoghataraṇaṃ, diṭṭhoghassa taraṇaṃ. Kāmañcettha “tarati ogha”nti vuttaṃ, vattamānasamīpepi pana vattamānaṃ viya voharaṇaṃ yuttaṃ diṭṭhoghassa tiṇṇabhāvassa ekantikattāti “sotāpannañca pakāsetī”ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Diṭṭhivicikicchādipaṭipattantarāyakarānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ samucchinnattā sotāpanno…pe… appamādena samannāgato. “Sotāpatti…pe… taratī”ti ettake vutte sakideva imassa lokassa āgamanampi gahitaṃ siyāti tannivattanatthaṃ “ārādhetvā…pe… avasesa”nti vuttaṃ. Nanu “avasesa”nti vuttattā sotāpattimaggena atiṇṇaṃ anavasesaṃ bhavoghavatthu gahitameva siyāti? Na, upari dvīhi maggehi taritabbānaṃ tesaṃ parato dvinnaṃ pahānavasena vuccamānattā. Apavādavisayampi pariharati – “evaṃ esā codanā attano visaye na patiṭṭhātī”ti. Anādikālabhāvattā kāmasaññāya kāmoghataraṇaṃ mahatā eva vīriyena sādhetabbanti āha “vīriyenā”ti. Tatiyaṃ maggaṃ ārādhetvā. Kāmoghassa vatthu kāmoghavatthu, kāmaguṇehi saddhiṃ sabbo kāmabhavo. Kāmoghasaññitanti kāmoghasaṅkhātaṃ. Kāmanaṭṭhena kāmo ca so dukkho cāti kāmadukkhaṃ. Assādanaṭṭhena kāmo eva saññāti kāmasaññā, sabbaso samucchinnattā vigatā kāmasaññā etissāti vigatakāmasaññā[M 1.0325]. Sabbesaṃ rāgādimalānaṃ mūlabhūtattā sattasantānassa visesato malīnasabhāvāpādanato paramaṃ ukkaṃsagataṃ malanti paramamalaṃ, avijjā. Tenāha bhagavā – “avijjāparamaṃ mala”nti (dha. pa. 243).

“Etāya”: the connection is made with this phrase in the verse. He says that the faculty of faith is the proximate cause of these factors for the attainment of the stream-entry path: associating with good people, listening to the true Dhamma, wise reflection, and practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Hence it is said: “The faculty of faith is the foundation for the factors of stream-entry.” For it is said: “One who has faith approaches; having approached, they associate closely; having associated closely, they lend an ear; having lent an ear, they hear the Dhamma,” and so on (MN 2.183, 432). “Diṭṭhoghaṃ tarati etenāti”: by this one crosses the flood of views. Thus, it is the means for crossing the flood of views, or the crossing of the flood of views. Although it is said here, “one crosses the flood,” the use of the present tense is appropriate for what is near the present, because the state of having crossed the flood of views is definitive. Thus, it is said, “and reveals the stream-enterer.” The same applies to the rest. Because the stream-enterer has cut off the unwholesome qualities that create obstacles to practice, such as wrong view and doubt, they are endowed with heedfulness. When it is said, “the stream-enterer… crosses,” it could imply coming to this world just once. To negate that, it is said, “having attained… the remainder.” But doesn’t the term “the remainder” imply that the flood of becoming, not yet crossed by the stream-entry path, is entirely included? No, because those remaining floods are to be crossed by the higher two paths, and their abandonment is mentioned subsequently. It also avoids the scope of criticism: “Thus, this reproach does not stand in its own sphere.” Because sensual perception has existed since beginningless time, the crossing of the flood of sensuality must be accomplished with great effort. Thus, it is said, “by energy.” Having attained the third path. “Kāmoghassa vatthu”: the basis of the flood of sensuality, meaning the entire realm of sensual existence along with the strands of sensual pleasure. “Kāmoghasaññitaṃ”: that which is called the flood of sensuality. “Kāmadukkhaṃ”: suffering of sensuality, in the sense of desire, and that very suffering. “Kāmasaññā”: sensual perception, in the sense of savoring, sensuality itself is perception. “Vigatakāmasaññā”: free from sensual perception, because sensual perception is utterly destroyed for this one. “Paramamalaṃ”: the supreme defilement, which is ignorance, because it is the root of all defilements like lust, and it especially makes the beings’ continuum impure, thus reaching the highest degree of defilement. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Ignorance is the supreme defilement” (Dhp 243).

Paññāpadaṃ gahetvāti yathāvuttaṃ paññāpadaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā. Tappasaṅgena attano paṭibhānena sabbehi viya uggahitaniyāmena. Sabbatthevāti pañcasupi ṭhānesu. Atthayuttipucchāti paññādiatthasamadhigamassa yuttiyā kāraṇassa pucchā. Tenāha “ayaṃ hī”tiādi. Paññādiatthaṃ ñatvāti paññādhana-kitti-mitta-abhisamparāyasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sarūpato saccapaṭivedhanipphādanena ñāṇena jānitvā. Nanu esa lokuttaraṃ sotāpattimaggaphalapaññaṃ tadadhigamūpāyaṃ lokiyapaññañca abhibhavitvā ṭhito, so kasmā tattha atthayuttiṃ pucchatīti? Saccametaṃ, upari pana samādhissa yuttiṃ pucchitukāmo paññāya seṭṭhabhāvato, tassa ca ekadeseneva adhigatattā tameva ādiṃ katvā pucchati. “Kāya yuttiyā”tiādi atthavaṇṇanaṃ atidissati “esa nayo dhanādīsū”ti. Tatthāpi atthayuttipucchābhāvo pana “sabbatthevā”ti iminā vibhāvitoti.

“Paññāpadaṃ gahetvā” (Having taken up the theme of wisdom): this means establishing the aforementioned theme of wisdom in the heart. Through its connection, by one’s own intuition, as if by a principle grasped by all. “Sabbattheva” (in all respects): in all five instances. “Atthayuttipucchā” (a question about the reason for the meaning): the inquiry into the reason or method for realizing the meaning related to wisdom, etc. Hence, it is said: “This is because,” etc. “Paññādiatthaṃ ñatvā” (having known the meaning related to wisdom, etc.): having understood the meaning designated as the wealth of wisdom, fame, friends, and the hereafter, by means of the knowledge that accomplishes the penetration of the truths in their own nature. Is it not so that this one, having overcome worldly wisdom and the means to attain it, stands established in the supramundane wisdom of the path and fruit of stream-entry? Why then does he ask about the reason for the meaning in this case? This is true. However, wishing to inquire later about the reason for concentration, and because of wisdom’s superiority, and because he has attained it only in part, he begins by asking about that very thing. The explanation of the meaning, “By what reason?” etc., is indicated by the phrase, “this is the method regarding wealth, etc.” There, however, the absence of a question about the reason for the meaning is clarified by the phrase, “in all respects indeed.”

Saddhāsussūsāappamādauṭṭhānasaṅkhātehi catūhi kāraṇehi. Kāyasucaritādibhedena ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlabhūtena. Samathavipassanābhūtena nippariyāyena bodhipakkhiye eva gaṇhanto “aparabhāge”ti [V 1.0285] āha. Pariyāyabodhipakkhiyā pana visesato vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanākālepi labbhanti. Pubbabhāgeti vā taruṇavipassanākālaṃ. Tato pubbasādhanañca sandhāya “aparabhāge”ti punāha, tato paranti attho. Dhammanti paṭipattidhammaṃ. Na saddhāmattakeneva paññaṃ labhatīti yojanā. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “saddahāno”ti vuttanti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hotītiādinā vuttameva atthaṃ vivarati. Na kevalaṃ sussūsāmattena paññāpaṭilābho, atha kho appamādena paññaṃ labhatīti dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “appamatto vicakkhaṇo”ti vuttanti tadatthaṃ dassento “eva”ntiādimāha.

By the four causes designated as faith, the desire to hear, heedfulness, and exertion. By means of good bodily conduct, etc., which constitutes the virtue with right livelihood as the eighth factor. Taking up the factors of enlightenment directly, in the form of serenity and insight, he says, “in the latter stage.” But the factors of enlightenment through indirect means are especially obtained even at the time of insight leading to emergence. “Pubbabhāga” (preliminary stage): or the time of initial insight. Then, referring to the preliminary practice, he again says, “in the latter stage,” meaning what comes after that. “Dhamma”: the Dhamma of practice. The construction is that wisdom is not obtained by mere faith. If so, why is it said, “having faith”? He explains, “but because,” etc. By “Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti” (What is meant?), etc., he elaborates on the meaning already stated. To show that the acquisition of wisdom is not by the mere desire to hear, but that one obtains wisdom through heedfulness, it is said in the Pāli, “the heedful one is discerning.” Explaining the meaning of that, he says, “thus,” etc.

Idāni saddhādīnaṃ paññāpaṭilābhassa taṃtaṃvisesapaccayāni nīharitvā dassetuṃ “eva”nti vuttaṃ. Sussūsāyāti sotukāmatāya. Sā atthato [M 1.0326] upasaṅkamanādi. Paññādhigamūpāyanti pariyattidhammamāha. Tenāha “suṇātī”ti. Gahitaṃ na pamussati, satiavippavāsalakkhaṇo hi appamādoti. Na kevalaṃ yāthāvato gahaṇakosallameva vicakkhaṇatā, atha kho yāthāvato paññāsampavedhanañcāti āha “vitthārikaṃ karotī”ti. Idāni paññāpaṭilābhahetuṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassetuṃ “sussūsāya vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atthamupaparikkhatīti sutakatānaṃ dhammānaṃ pāḷiatthūpaparikkhāpubbakaṃ rūpārūpavibhāgaṃ paramatthaṃ salakkhaṇato sāmaññalakkhaṇato ca upaparikkhati vīmaṃsati. Anupubbenāti evaṃ ñātapariññaṃ patvā tīraṇapariññāya tato anukkamena tīraṇapariññaṃ pahānapariññañca matthakaṃ pāpento maggappaṭipāṭiyā paramatthasaccabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti.

Now, to extract and show the specific conditions for the acquisition of wisdom from faith and so on, it is said, “Thus.” “Sussūsāya” (by the desire to hear): by the wish to listen. In essence, this refers to approaching, etc. “Paññādhigamūpāyaṃ” (the means to attain wisdom): he refers to the Dhamma of learning. Hence it is said: “He listens.” What is grasped is not forgotten, for heedfulness is characterized by the non-absence of mindfulness. Discernment is not only skill in grasping accurately, but also in thoroughly clarifying wisdom; therefore, it is said, “He elaborates in detail.” Now, to show the cause for acquiring wisdom, bringing it to its culmination, it is said, “Through the desire to hear,” etc. “Atthamupaparikkhati” (he examines the meaning): preceded by the examination of the Pāli text and the meaning of the teachings one has heard, he examines and investigates the ultimate reality—the analysis of form and formlessness—both by its specific and general characteristics. “Anupubbena” (gradually): having thus attained the full understanding of what is known, then by means of the full understanding by discernment, proceeding in sequence, bringing the full understanding by discernment and the full understanding by abandonment to their culmination through the order of the path, he realizes Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth.

Imāni saddhādīni cattāri kāraṇāni matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassento āha “desakālādīni ahāpetvā”ti. Yasmiṃ dese yasmiṃ kāle ye ca sahāyake nissāya yaṃ kiccaṃ tiretabbaṃ, tāni desakālādīni anatikkamitvā attano abhivuḍḍhiṃ icchantena “ayaṃ nāma deso, yatthāhaṃ etarahi vasāmi, ayaṃ kālo, ime mittā, ime amittā, ime āyavayā, ahañca ediso jāti-kula-padesa-balabhoga-parivārādīhi, taṃ kiccaṃ idāni āraddhabbaṃ, idāni nāraddhabba”nti sabbaṃ upaparikkhitvā paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipajjanto hi lokiyassa dhanassa paṭirūpādhigamūpāyaṃ karoti nāma. Lokuttarassa pana sīlavisodhanādivasena veditabbaṃ. Vahitabbabhāvena dhuro viyāti dhuro, bhāro. Idha pana dhurasampaggaho uttarapadalopena dhuro, vīriyaṃ. So sātisayo etassa atthīti dhuravā. “Uṭṭhātā”ti padena kāyikavīriyassa vakkhamānattā “cetasikavīriyavasenā”ti visesitaṃ. Anikkhittadhuro dhorayhabhāvato. Tiṇā bhiyyo [V 1.0286] na maññatīti tiṇaṃ viya paribhavanto atibhuyya vattatīti attho. Ādinā nayenāti ettha ādi-saddena –

Showing these four factors—faith and so on—brought to their culmination, he says, “without abandoning place, time, etc.” In whatever place, at whatever time, and relying on whatever companions a task needs to be accomplished, one who desires their own growth should, without neglecting those factors of place, time, etc., reflect thus: “This is the place where I now dwell; this is the time; these are friends; these are foes; these are gains and losses; and I am of such birth, family, region, strength, wealth, and retinue. This task should be undertaken now; this should not be undertaken now.” Having considered everything, one should proceed accordingly. For one who proceeds thus truly employs a suitable means for attaining worldly wealth. As for the supramundane, it should be understood in terms of the purification of virtue, etc. A `dhura` is a burden (bhāro), because it is to be borne (vahitabba). Here, however, `dhurasampaggaha` (undertaking the burden) becomes `dhura` by the elision of the final member, meaning effort. One who has this in abundance is called `dhuravā` (one who bears the burden). Since bodily effort will be described by the word `uṭṭhātā` (energetic), `dhuravā` is specified as being “by way of mental effort.” “Anikkhittadhuro” (one who has not laid down the burden): this is due to having the nature of a beast of burden. “Tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati” (he does not think more of it than of grass): this means he proceeds by completely overcoming it, treating it with contempt as if it were grass. “Ādinā nayena” (by the method beginning with): here, the word ‘beginning’ includes—

“Karaṃ purisakiccāni, so sukhā na vihāyati; (Dī. ni. 3.253);

“Na divā soppasīlena, rattimuṭṭhānadessinā;

Niccaṃ mattena soṇḍena, sakkā āvasituṃ ghara”nti ca. (dī. ni. 3.253); –

“One who performs a man’s duties does not fall away from happiness. A house cannot be managed by one given to sleeping by day, who is averse to rising at night, who is constantly intoxicated and dissolute.”

Evamādīnaṃ [M 1.0327] saṅgaho. Asithilaparakkamo analasabhāvato. Ekamūsikāyāti ekāya matamūsikāya. Nacirassevāti catumāsabbhantareyeva. Catusatasahassasaṅkhaṃ cūḷantevāsī viyāti kākaṇikaḍḍhakahāpaṇa-soḷasa-kahāpaṇa-catuvīsati-kahāpaṇa-sataharaṇakkamena dve satasahassāni, cūḷakamahāseṭṭhino dhītulābhavasena dve satasahassānīti evaṃ catusatasahassasaṅkhaṃ dhanaṃ ekamūlena yathā cūḷantevāsī vindi, evaṃ aññopi patirūpakārī dhuravā uṭṭhātā vindate dhanaṃ. Ayañca attho cūḷakaseṭṭhijātakena dīpetabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

This is a collection of such verses. He was of unremitting effort, by nature not slothful. “By a single mouse” means by a single dead mouse. “Not long after” means within just four months. “The wealth amounting to four hundred thousand”: just as the young apprentice, with a single mouse as his capital, obtained wealth amounting to four hundred thousand—that is, two hundred thousand through the sequence of a small coin, a half kahāpaṇa, sixteen kahāpaṇas, twenty-four kahāpaṇas, and a hundred transactions, and two hundred thousand by way of obtaining the daughter of the merchant Cūḷaka—so too, any other suitable person who bears the burden and is energetic obtains wealth. And this meaning should be illustrated by the Cūḷakaseṭṭhi Jātaka. For it was said:

“Appakenapi medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo;

Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti. (jā. 1.1.4);

“Even with little capital, a wise and discerning person can raise himself up, just like one fanning a small fire.”

Vattaṃ katvāti adhiṭṭhānavattaṃ katvā. “Saccavādī bhūtavādī”ti kittiṃ pappotīti yojanā. Icchitapatthitanti yehi mittaṃ icchati, tehi itaraṃ patthitaṃ. Mittāni ganthatīti mittabhāvaṃ ghaṭeti. Dānassa piyabhāvakaraṇato “dadaṃ piyo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ dānaṃ ekantato mittabhāvāvahaṃ, taṃ dassento “duddadaṃ vā dadaṃ taṃ ganthatī”ti āha. Dadanti ca lakkhaṇavacanametanti āha “dānamukhena vā”tiādi.

“Having made a practice” means having undertaken a practice of resolution. The construction is: “One who speaks truth, one who speaks fact, attains fame.” “Desired and wished for” means: by those by whom he is desired as a friend, by them he is also wished for in other respects. “He binds friends” means he forges a state of friendship. Because giving brings about a state of being dear, it is said, “The giver becomes dear.” Showing that giving which certainly brings about a state of friendship, he says, “Giving even what is hard to give, he binds them as friends.” And that this is a statement of a characteristic, he says, “by way of giving,” etc.

Āḷavakassa ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ gahaṭṭhavasena vissajjento. Saddhā etassa atthīti saddho, tassa saddhassa. Gharamesinoti gharāvāsasaṅkhātaṃ gharaṃ esantassa. Gharāvāsasannissitattā “ghara”nti kāmaguṇā vuccantīti āha “pañca kāmaguṇe”ti. “Ete caturo dhammā”tiādinā gahitā anantaragāthāya vuttadhammā evāti dassento “vuttappakāraṃ sacca”ntiādimāha. Tattha “ime kusalā, ime akusalā”tiādinā te atthe yāthāvato dhāraṇato upadhāraṇato dhammo. Saññā cittacetasikānaṃ [V 1.0287] dhāraṇaṃ, avicchedato sandhāraṇato kusalasantānaṃ dhāretīti dhiti, vīriyaṃ. Cajati etenāti cāgo, dānaṃ. Paccayavekallato phaluppādanasamatthatāvasena santi.

Responding in accordance with Āḷavaka's disposition, in the manner of a householder. 'He has faith, thus he is faithful'; of such a faithful one. 'Seeking a home' means of one who seeks a home designated as the household life. Because of its connection to the household life, 'home' refers to the strands of sensual pleasure; thus it is said, 'the five strands of sensual pleasure.' To show that the qualities mentioned in the immediately following verse, introduced by 'these four things,' are just those, he said, 'the truth as explained,' and so on. Therein, Dhamma is the holding and discerning of those meanings as they are, such as 'these are wholesome, these are unwholesome.' Perception is the holding of mind and mental factors; because it sustains without interruption, it maintains the continuity of wholesomeness—this is steadfastness, energy. 'One relinquishes by this,' thus it is relinquishment, generosity. Due to the absence of deficiencies in conditions, they are capable of producing a result; thus they exist.

Aññepīti ito yathāvuttadhammasamudāyato aññepi dhammā yadi santi, te dhamme pucchassūti. Kilese, kāyavācādike vā dametīti damo[M 1.0328], paññā. Uṭṭhahati ussahati etenāti uṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyaṃ. Etthāti etissā pucchāya. Saddhinti saṅkhepato bhāvatthapadānaṃ bandhanena saha. Ekamekaṃ padanti paññādikamekekaṃ padaṃ. “Paññā imasmiṃ ṭhāne paññāti dhammoti ca āgatā”tiādinā paññādiatthassa uddharaṇaṃ atthuddhāro. Tassa tassa atthassa “paññā pajānanā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 16) vevacanapadānaṃ uddharaṇaṃ paduddhāro. Pajānātīti paññā, dhāretīti dhammo, dametīti damoti evaṃ padassa kathanaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

'Others too' means: if there are other phenomena apart from this aforementioned collection of phenomena, you should ask about those phenomena. 'Taming' (damo) is that which tames defilements or bodily and verbal actions, etc.; it is wisdom. 'One rises up and strives with this,' thus it is 'rising up' (uṭṭhānaṃ), which is energy. 'Here' means in this question. 'With' (saddhiṃ) means: in brief, along with the connection of the terms expressing the meaning. 'Each term' means each single term such as wisdom, etc. The extraction of meaning (atthuddhāro) is the drawing out of the meaning of wisdom, etc., as in: 'Wisdom in this context is called wisdom and also Dhamma.' The extraction of terms (paduddhāro) is the drawing out of synonymous words for each meaning, as in: 'Wisdom is understanding,' etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 16). The explanation of the term (padavaṇṇanā) is the stating of the word's derivation, such as: 'One understands (pajānāti), thus it is wisdom (paññā); one upholds (dhāreti), thus it is the Dhamma; one tames (dameti), thus it is taming (damo).'

Ajjāti vā etarahi. Yathāvuttena pakārenāti “saddahāno arahata”ntiādinā vuttappakārena. Saccasampaṭivedhāvagahaṇaṃ vā yathāvuttena pakārena diṭṭhasaccatāya idhalokaparalokatthaṃ yāthāvato jānanto. Evañca yakkho satthu desanānubhāvasiddhaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanena attano paṭilābhasampattiṃ vibhāvento “kathaṃsu labhate pañña”ntiādimāhāti ācariyā. Samparāyikoti ettha ca-saddo luttaniddiṭṭho, tena “diṭṭhadhammiko cā”ti ayamattho vutto evāti dassento “yo attho…pe… dassetī”ti āha. Arīyati phalaṃ etasmāti attho, kāraṇaṃ. Vicakkhaṇe sapayojanatāya.

'Today' or 'now.' 'In the manner stated' means in the manner described beginning with 'having faith in the arahants.' Or, knowing the benefit of this world and the next as it actually is, through having seen the truth, by means of the penetration and grasp of the truth in the manner stated. And thus the teachers say that the yakkha, explaining his own attainment of success by asking a question that was accomplished through the power of the Teacher’s teaching, said, 'How does one gain wisdom?' and so on. 'Pertaining to the hereafter': here the particle 'ca' is indicated as elided, thereby showing that this meaning, 'and pertaining to the present life,' is indeed stated, he says, 'the meaning... shows.' The fruit is obtained from this, thus it is a benefit (attho); it is a cause. In the discerning one, because there is a purpose.

Tassa ñāṇassāti tassa atthassa āvibhāvanassa ñāṇassa. Guṇavisesehi ca sadisassapi aññassa abhāvato aggadakkhiṇeyyo buddho bhagavā. Tenāha –

'Of that knowledge' means of the knowledge that makes that meaning manifest. And because there is no other who is even similar in terms of special qualities, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is the foremost recipient of offerings. Therefore, it is said:

“Nayimasmiṃ loke parasmiṃ vā pana,

Buddhena seṭṭhova samova vijjati;

Āhuneyyānaṃ paramāhutiṃ gato,

Puññatthikānaṃ vipulaphalesina”nti. (vi. va. 1047);

Neither in this world nor in the next is there found one better than or equal to the Buddha; he has become the supreme object of offering for those worthy of offerings, for those desiring merit and seeking abundant fruit.

Sahitapaṭipattinti paññāsaṅgāhikaṃ attano paṭipattiṃ. Sundarā bodhi subodhi, buddhassa subodhi buddhasubodhi, sā eva buddhasubodhitā. Dhammassavanatthaṃ sannipatitadevatāhi saṅghuṭṭhasādhukārasadduṭṭhānañca.

'Beneficial practice' means one's own practice that comprises wisdom. Excellent enlightenment is 'good enlightenment' (subodhi); the Buddha's good enlightenment is 'Buddha's good enlightenment' (buddhasubodhi); that itself is the state of the Buddha's good enlightenment (buddhasubodhitā). And the arising of the sound of acclamation proclaimed by the deities assembled to hear the Dhamma.

Satapuññalakkhaṇanti [V 1.0288] satasahassakappe puññasambhārassa katattā tesaṃ puññānaṃ vasena satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ anekapuññanibbattalakkhaṇaṃ. Abhinandiyatāya sabbehi aṅgehi samupetaṃ samannāgataṃ. Katapuññabhāvaṃ byañjentīti byañjanāni[M 1.0329], aṅgapaccaṅgāni. Tesaṃ paripuṇṇattā paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ. Taṃ yakkho…pe… pūresīti gāthāpūraṇatthameva hi bhagavā tathārūpāni akāsi. Abyādhitāti arogā. “Abyathitā”ti keci paṭhanti, sayasantāsarahitāti attho.

'The mark of a hundred merits': because the store of merit was accumulated over a hundred thousand eons, by the power of those merits it is the mark of a hundred merits, a mark produced by numerous merits. On account of its delightfulness, it is endowed and possessed with all limbs. They make manifest the state of having made merit, thus they are 'marks' (byañjanāni); they are the major and minor limbs. Because of their completeness, it is 'complete in marks' (paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ). That the yakkha... filled it: indeed, the Blessed One did such things merely for the sake of completing the verse. 'Unafflicted' (abyādhitā) means free from disease. Some read 'unperturbed' (abyathitā), which means free from inner fear and trembling.

“Hatthayo”ti vattabbe “hatthako”ti vuttaṃ. Āḷavinagaranti āḷavinagaravāsino vadati. Bhavati hi tatraṭṭhatāya taṃ-saddo yathā “gāmo āgato, mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Ekakolāhalena vattamānena.

When 'Hatthayo' should be said, 'Hatthako' was said. 'The city of Āḷavi' refers to the residents of the city of Āḷavi. For the word for that place is used for those who reside there, as in 'the village has come,' or 'the beds are making a noise.' With a single uproar occurring.

Sampiṇḍitvāti sannipatitvā. Kāmaṃ sambhāro tena katoti natthi, yuddhatthaṃ pana bahuso ussāhassa katattā “yuddhamādiṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ. Tameva āḷavakasuttaṃ kathesi tassā eva desanāya sannipatitaparisāya sappāyattā. Tenāha “kathāpari…pe… ahosī”ti. Catūhi vatthūhīti catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi. Parisanti attano parisaṃ. “Itarañcā”tipi vadanti.

'Having amassed' means having gathered together. Although the preparation was not made by him, because much effort was made for the sake of battle, it is said, 'having initiated the battle.' He taught that very Āḷavaka Sutta because that teaching was suitable for the assembly that had gathered. Therefore it is said, 'at the end of the talk... there was.' 'With four things' means with the four bases of sympathy. 'The assembly' means his own assembly. Some also say, 'and the other.'

Āḷavakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta is finished.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Yakkhasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Yakkha Saṃyutta is complete.

11. Sakkasaṃyuttaṃ

11. The Connected Discourses with Sakka

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Suvīrasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Suvīra Sutta

247. Abhiyaṃsūti [V 1.0289][M 1.0330] yuddhasajjābhimukhā hutvā gacchiṃsu. Tatrāti tasmiṃ asurānaṃ abhiyāne ayaṃ dāni vuccamānā anupubbato kathā. Tettiṃsa purise gahetvāti tettiṃsa purise puññakiriyāya sahāyabhūte gahetvā. “Yāvajīvaṃ mātāpitubharo assa”ntiādinā samādinnāni satta vatapadāni pūretvā. Adhigaṇhantaṃ abhibhavantaṃ. Puttahatāyāti hataputtāya. Sā surā na hoti, na suraṃ pivimhāti adhippāyo. Tato paṭṭhāyāti “na surā”ti vuttakālato paṭṭhāya. “Na suranti na dibbantīti asurā”ti keci. Heṭṭhimatale antobhūmiyaṃ āyāmato dasayojanasahassaṃ.

247. 'They advanced' means they went forth, having become ready and facing battle. 'Therein' means, during that advance of the asuras, this is the story now being told in sequence. 'Having taken thirty-three men' means taking thirty-three men as companions for meritorious deeds. Having fulfilled the seven vows undertaken, beginning with, 'For as long as I live, I shall support my parents.' 'Overcoming' means overpowering, subduing. 'For one whose son was slain' means for one whose son was slain. 'That is not liquor; we did not drink liquor'—this is the intended meaning. 'From then on' means from the time 'not liquor' was stated. Some say, 'They are not gods (suras), they do not shine—thus, asuras.' The lowest level, the inner ground, extends ten thousand yojanas in length.

Uragādisahacaritāni ṭhānāni uragādīnīti āha “uragādīsu pañcasu ṭhānesū”ti. Paṭhamālindeti paṭhame paribhaṇḍe. Pañcayojanasahassavitthāraputhubahalāhi sinerussa catūsupi passesu cattāro paribhaṇḍā. Sinerussa hi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ passe yugandharādīsu pañcasataparittadīpaparivāre mahādīpe ca labhitabbassa mahato atthassa vasena mahatthā. Kupitāvilacittāti kupitena kopena ākulacittā. Yuddhesīti yuddhesino. Sesesūti sesesu paribhaṇḍesu. Sesāti supaṇṇādayo.

Places associated with serpents, etc., are 'of the serpents, etc.'; thus he says, 'among the five locations of the serpents, etc.' 'On the first terrace' means on the first surrounding ledge. On all four sides of Mount Sineru are four surrounding ledges, which are five thousand yojanas wide, broad and thick. Indeed, on each respective side of Sineru, in places like Yugandhara and so forth, and on the great continent surrounded by five hundred small islands, they are of great value on account of the great benefit to be obtained. 'With minds agitated by anger' means with a mind disturbed by aroused anger. 'Seeking battle' means those who seek battle. 'In the remaining' means in the remaining surrounding ledges. 'The remaining' means the supaṇṇas and others.

Vammikamakkhikāti sapakkhikaupacikā. Osakkitvāti piṭṭhibhāgena nivattitvā.

'Ant-hill flies' means winged termites. 'Having retreated' means having turned back with the rear part of the body.

Pamādaṃ āpādesīti sakkassa āṇāya pamādaṃ āpajji. Saṭṭhiyojanaṃ vitthārena. Suvaṇṇamahāvīthinti suvaṇṇamayabhūmijagativīthiṃ.

'He became negligent' means he fell into negligence by Sakka’s command. Sixty yojanas in width. 'The great golden street' means a street with a golden surface and parapet.

Anuṭṭhahantoti [V 1.0290] uṭṭhānaṃ kāyikavīriyaṃ akaronto. Avāyamantoti vāyāmaṃ cetasikavīriyaṃ akaronto. Kiñci kiccanti kasivāṇijjādibhedaṃ aññataraṃ kiccaṃ kattabbakammaṃ. Varanti pavaraṃ. Tenāha “uttama”nti. Tañca kho kasitabbaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0331] adhippetanti āha “okāsa”nti. Kammaṃ akatvāti kiñcipi jīvitahetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ akatvā. Jīvitaṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti tassa jīvitassa hetu nāma. Nibbānassa maggoti nibbānassa adhigamupāyabhūto maggo.

'Not striving' means not making an effort, which is bodily energy. 'Not exerting' means not making an exertion, which is mental energy. 'Any duty' means some duty, some work to be done, of the kind such as farming, trade, etc. 'Excellent' means superior. Therefore he says 'supreme.' And that, indeed, is intended as the place to be cultivated; thus he says 'opportunity.' 'Without doing work' means without doing any work that is a cause for livelihood. 'A basis for living' means the cause of that life. 'The path to Nibbāna' means the path that is the means for attaining Nibbāna.

Suvīrasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Suvīra Sutta is concluded.

2. Susīmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Susīma Sutta

248. Antareti abbhantare. Evaṃnāmakanti “susīmo”ti evaṃnāmakaṃ. Ekaṃ puttameva aññataraṃ attano puttameva.

248. ‘Antare’ means within. ‘Evaṃnāmakaṃ’ means named thus: ‘Susīma’. ‘Ekaṃ puttameva’ means a certain son, his very own son.

Susīmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Susīma Sutta is concluded.

3. Dhajaggasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Dhajagga Sutta

249. Samupabyūḷhoti ubhinnaṃ saha eva samāgamo, bhusaṃ vā byūḷhoti attho. Bhusā panassa byūḷhatā dvinnaṃ senānaṃ samāgantvā sampiṇḍitabhāvenāti āha “sampiṇḍito rāsibhūto”ti. Pacchimantoti rathapañjarassa paranto pacchimanto pacchimakoṭṭhāso. Rathasandhitoti rathapañjarassa kubbarena saddhiṃ sambandhanaṭṭhānato. Tadeva pamāṇanti tadeva “diyaḍḍhayojanasatāyāmo”ti vuttappamāṇameva. Diguṇaṃ katvāti “pacchimanto satayojano”tiādinā diguṇaṃ katvā. Candamaṇḍalasūriyamaṇḍalakiṅkiṇikajālādibhedassa sesālaṅkārassa. Passantānaṃ devānaṃ. Rājā noti amhākaṃ rājā devaseṭṭho. Dutiyaṃ āsanaṃ labhatīti sakke nisinne tassa anantaraṃ dutiyaṃ āsanaṃ labhati. Tasmā devaseṭṭhatāya sakko viya gāravaṭṭhāniyo, yato sakko “tassa dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyāthā”ti āha. Esa nayo sesesupi. Asurehi parājitoti asurehi parājayaṃ āpādito. Rajadhajaṃ disvāti parasenāya upagacchantiyā uṭṭhitarajamattampi disvā ṭhitopi taṃ rajadhajaṃ disvā bhīrubhāvena palāyanadhammo.

249. ‘Samupabyūḷho’ means the coming together of both sides, or it means a great conflict. Its great conflict is due to the two armies meeting and merging into one mass, hence it is said, ‘crowded together, formed into a mass’. ‘Pacchimanto’ refers to the rear end, the back section of the chariot frame. ‘Rathasandhito’ means from the connecting point of the chariot frame with the pole. ‘Tadeva pamāṇaṃ’ refers to the very measure stated as ‘one hundred and fifty yojanas in length’. ‘Diguṇaṃ katvā’ means making it twice as much, as in ‘the rear end is one hundred yojanas’, etc. This refers to the remaining ornaments, such as the moon disc, sun disc, nets of tinkling bells, and so forth. For the devas who see. ‘Rājā no’ means our king, the foremost of devas. ‘Dutiyaṃ āsanaṃ labhati’ means that when Sakka is seated, he obtains the second seat immediately after him. Therefore, due to being the foremost of devas, he is worthy of respect like Sakka, for which reason Sakka said, ‘You should look up at his banner-top.’ This principle applies to the rest as well. ‘Asurehi parājito’ means brought to defeat by the asuras. ‘Rajadhajaṃ disvā’ means that having seen even just the cloud of dust raised by the approaching enemy army, one who sees that dust-banner, even while standing firm, becomes fearful and prone to fleeing.

Yassa [M 1.0332] dhajaggaparittassa. Ānubhāvo vattati asammukhībhūtāhipi devatāhi sirasā sampaṭicchitabbato. Corabhayādīhīti ādi-saddena rogabhayādīnañceva vaṭṭadukkhassa ca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo vidhinā bhāvite parittassa atthe upacārajjhānādīnampi ijjhanato.

The power of the Dhajagga Paritta prevails because it is to be accepted with bowed heads even by unseen deities. ‘Corabhayādīhi’ means that by the word ‘etc.’, the dangers of disease and so forth, as well as the suffering of the round of existence, should be understood to be included, since success is achieved even in access concentration and so forth when the meaning of the Paritta is cultivated according to the method.

Dīghavāpīnāmake [V 1.0291] gāme cetiyaṃ dīghavāpicetiyaṃ. Muddhavedikā nāma hammiyaṃ parikkhipitvā katavedikā. Buddhagataṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā parittarakkhaguttiṃ āha. Parittassa ānubhāvena dve iṭṭhakā…pe… aṭṭhaṃsu. Tathā hi tasmiṃ nisseṇiyaṃ ṭhite…pe… aṭṭhaṃsūti.

The shrine in the village named Dīghavāpī is the Dīghavāpicetiya. ‘Muddhavedikā’ is the name of a railing constructed to surround a storied building. Having established mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, he spoke of the protective safeguard of the Paritta. By the power of the Paritta, two bricks… remained. Thus, indeed, while he was standing on that ladder… they remained.

Dhajaggasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhajagga Sutta is concluded.

4. Vepacittisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vepacitti Sutta

250. “Mahānubhāvatāya asurānaṃ cittavepanena vepacittī”ti vadanti. Isīhi pana abhayaṃ yācite “bhayameva dadāmī”ti vatvā tehi “akkhayaṃ hotu te bhaya”nti abhisapavasena vuttakālato paṭṭhāya vepanacittatāya “vepacittī”ti vuccati, yaṃ lokiyā “pulomo”ti ca vadanti. Nipātapadānipi kānici atthavisesajotakāni hontīti āha “nipātamatta”nti hetuatthādīnamettha asambhavato. Tanti sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ. Kaṇṭhe pañcamehīti kaṇṭhabandhanapañcamehi, vibhattialopena niddeso. Cittenevāti “imaṃ bandhāmi, ayaṃ bajjhatū”ti uppannacitteneva. Bajjhati baddho hoti, ayaṃ devānubhāvo. Muccatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Dasahīti “corosī”tiādinā idha vuttehi dasahi. Tenāha “imehī”ti. Nibbattitvā cirakālataṃ upādāya khuṃsanavasena vadati “jarasakkā”ti. Na taṃ akkosaṃ manasi karoti dīgharattaṃ khantisoraccesu niruḷhaajjhāsayattā. Mahāpaṭiggahaṇanti mahantaṃ upasamabyañjanaṃ. Assāti vepacittassa.

250. They say: ‘He is called Vepacitti because, due to his great power, he causes the minds of the asuras to tremble.’ However, when the seers requested fearlessness, he said, ‘I give only fear,’ and they, by way of a curse, said, ‘May your fear be unending.’ From that time onward, because of his trembling mind, he is called ‘Vepacitti,’ whom worldly people also call ‘Puloma.’ He says, ‘merely a particle,’ because some particles also illuminate special meanings, since causal meanings and so on are impossible here. ‘Taṃ’ refers to Sakka, the lord of the devas. ‘Kaṇṭhe pañcamehi’ means with the five neck-bindings; this is a designation by the elision of the case ending. ‘Citteneva’ means with the very thought that has arisen, ‘I will bind this one; let this one be bound.’ ‘Bajjhati’ means he becomes bound; such is the power of the devas. The same principle applies to ‘muccati’. ‘Dasahi’ refers to the ten things mentioned here, beginning with ‘You are a thief.’ Therefore, he said, ‘by these.’ Having been reborn and existing for a long time, he speaks in a reviling manner, saying ‘Old Sakka!’ He does not take that insult to heart, because his disposition has long been established in patience and gentleness. ‘Mahāpaṭiggahaṇaṃ’ means a great manifestation of peacefulness. ‘Assa’ refers to Vepacitti.

Paṭisaṃyujeti paṭisattu hutvā saṃyuddhaṃ kareyya. Tenāha “paṭipphareyyā”ti. Upasamaṃ…pe… maññe upasameneva paccatthikassa nāyakabhūtassa kodhassa [M 1.0333] paṭisedhanato. Tādise hi kodho paṭikiriyaṃ alabhanto anupādāno viya jātavedo vūpasammati. Yadā-saddo hetuattho, na kālatthoti āha “yasmā taṃ maññatī”ti. Tāvadeva dve gāvo yujjhanteti tasmiṃyeva khaṇe dvīsu goṇesu yujjhantesu.

‘Paṭisaṃyujeti’ means having become an opponent, one would engage in battle. Therefore, he said, ‘one would strike back.’ ‘Upasamaṃ…pe… maññe’: I think that by pacification itself the anger that is the leader of the adversary is prevented. For in such a case, anger, not receiving a reaction, subsides like a fire without fuel. The word ‘yadā’ has the meaning of cause, not the meaning of time; therefore, he said, ‘because he thinks that.’ ‘Tāvadeva dve gāvo yujjhanti’ means at that very moment, while two bulls are fighting.

Khantito uttaritaro añño attho na vijjati anantareva assa virodhaṃ anatthaṃ paṭibāhitvā diṭṭhadhammikassa ceva samparāyikassa ca saṃvidhānato. Taṃ khantiṃ paramaṃ āhu seṭṭhabalaṃ virodhapaccayaṃ abhibhuyya pavattanato. Bālayogato bālo, tassa balaṃ bālabalaṃ, aññāṇanti āha “bālabalaṃ nāma aññāṇabala”nti. Taṃ yassa balanti taṃ aññāṇabalaṃ yassa puggalassa balaṃ, abalameva taṃ paññābalena viddhaṃsetabbato. Paṭivattā na vijjatīti dhammaṭṭhaṃ [V 1.0292] paṭippharitvā abhibhavitvā pavattā natthi. Paṭivacanamattaṃ pana koci vadeyyāpi, taṃ akāraṇanti dassento “paṭippharitvā vā”tiādimāha. Bālabalanti “paṭippharitvā”ti vacanassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tasseva puggalassa paṭikujjhanakassa. Nānattāvitakkanato ubhinnaṃ atthaṃ. Tikicchantanti anatthapaṭibāhanamukhena paṇḍitakiccakaraṇena paṭisedhentaṃ. “Bālo aya”nti evaṃ paññapetuṃ hetuphalānaṃ anavabodhato catusaccadhamme achekāti.

No benefit higher than patience is found, for by immediately warding off opposition and harm, it provides for well-being both in this present life and in the future. They call that patience the supreme, the best strength, because it proceeds having overcome the cause of opposition. A fool is so from connection with folly; his strength is a fool's strength, which is ignorance. Therefore, he says, ‘A fool's strength is the strength of ignorance.’ That which is the strength of a fool, that strength of ignorance which is the strength of a certain person, is indeed no strength, because it is to be destroyed by the strength of wisdom. ‘Paṭivattā na vijjati’ means there is no one who proceeds having struck back at and overcome one who stands in Dhamma. But someone might speak a mere reply; showing that this is without reason, he said ‘or having struck back,’ and so on. ‘Bālabalaṃ’ is the causal statement for the saying ‘having struck back.’ It refers to that very person who gets angry in return. Because of the diversity of thoughts, the benefit of both. ‘Tikicchanti’ means they prevent him by performing the task of the wise by way of warding off harm. To declare, ‘This is a fool,’ is because of not understanding cause and effect, being unskilled in the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

Vepacittisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vepacitti Sutta is concluded.

5. Subhāsitajayasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Subhāsitajaya Sutta

251. “Chekatāyā”ti vatvā tassa vattuṃ chekabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ kirassā”tiādimāha. Gāhanti laddhiṃ. Mocetvāti yassa puna “coro”ti uttari vattuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ vimocetvāti paṭhamaṃ vattuṃ na sakkā. Garūti bhāriyaṃ, dukkaranti attho. Pacchāti “parassā”ti vutto so kiñci paṭhamaṃ vadanto attano adhippāyaṃ pavedeti nāma, taṃ yathāsatti viditamano tassa uttari vattuṃ sakkoti. Tenāha “parassa vacanaṃ anugantvā pana pacchā sukhaṃ vattu”nti. Api ca asurindena “hotu, devānaminda, subhāsitena jayo”ti paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ, viseso ca pubbaṃ upanentaṃ anuvattati. Vacasi kusalo sakko devarājā taṃ visesaṃ teneva pubbaṃ upanayāpento upalāpanavasena “tumhe [M 1.0334] khvetthā”tiādimāha. Pubbadevāti sakkapamukhāya devaparisāya loke pubbeva uppannattā “pubbadevā”ti pasaṃsavacanaṃ. Vepacittiṃ sandhāya “tumhe”ti “pubbadevā”ti ca vuttattā “tumhākaṃ tāva paveṇiāgataṃ bhaṇathā”ti vuttaṃ. Gāravaṭṭhāniyattā vepacittino bahuvacanapayogo. Daṇḍena avacāro avacaraṇaṃ daṇḍāvacaro, natthi ettha vutto daṇḍāvacaroti adaṇḍāvacarā, sakkena vuttā gāthāyo.

251. Having said ‘by cleverness,’ to show his cleverness in speaking, he began with ‘Evaṃ kirassā,’ and so on. ‘Gāhanti’ means they grasp a doctrine. ‘Mocetvā’ means that when one is unable to say anything further to someone, such as ‘thief,’ having thus released them, it is not possible to speak first. ‘Garū’ means heavy; the meaning is difficult. ‘Pacchā’ refers to what was said as ‘parassa’; when someone speaks first, they make known their own intention, and one who has understood this according to their ability can then speak further. Therefore, it is said, ‘But having followed another’s speech, one can speak with ease afterward.’ Moreover, the lord of the asuras first said, ‘So be it, O lord of devas, let victory be through what is well-spoken.’ And the advantage follows the one who brings the matter up first. Sakka, the king of devas, skilled in speech, making Vepacitti bring up that point first, said by way of persuasion, ‘You, indeed, are here,’ and so on. ‘Pubbadevā’ is a word of praise because the assembly of devas led by Sakka arose in the world before; hence they are ‘former devas.’ Referring to Vepacitti, because ‘you’ and ‘former devas’ were said, it is stated, ‘First, you speak what has come to you by tradition.’ Because Vepacitti is worthy of respect, the plural form is used. Transgression by the rod is `daṇḍāvacaro`; here there is no transgression by the rod spoken of. Therefore, the verses spoken by Sakka are `adaṇḍāvacarā`, that is, without transgression by the rod.

Subhāsitajayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Subhāsitajaya Sutta is concluded.

6. Kulāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Kulāvaka Sutta

252. Rathasaddoti rathālaṅkārabhūtānaṃ kiṅkiṇikajālādīnaṃ saddo. Tathā dhajasaddo. Ājānīyasaddoti ājānīyānaṃ hasitasaddo ca. Karuṇāsamāvajjitahadayoti pāṇānaṃ anuparodhena paṇāmitacitto. Īsāmukhenāti rathakapparamukhena. Puññapaccayanibbattoti uḷāraṃ suvipulaṃ puññaṃ paccayaṃ katvā nibbatto. Na sajjati katthaci appaṭighaṭṭanena gacchanto. Simbalivanenāti simbalivanamajjhena[V 1.0293]. Vibhaggaṃ nimmathitanti ito cito vibhaggañceva niravasesato mathitañca hoti.

252. "The sound of chariots" refers to the sound of ornaments such as nets of small bells that adorn chariots. Similarly, "the sound of banners." "The sound of thoroughbreds" refers to the neighing of thoroughbreds. "With a heart inclined to compassion" means a mind bent on compassion, without harming living beings. "With the tip of a chariot-pole" refers to the front of the chariot's shaft. "Born from the cause of merit" means produced by making abundant and very extensive merit the cause. "He does not cling anywhere" means moving without encountering any obstruction. "Through the Simbali grove" means through the middle of the Simbali forest. "Completely crushed and destroyed" means broken to pieces here and there and utterly churned up.

Kulāvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kulāvaka Sutta is concluded.

7. Nadubbhiyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Nadubbhiya Sutta

253. Supaccatthikoti suṭṭhu ativiya paccatthiko paṭisattu. Gahitosīti devapāsena bandhitvā gahito asi. Baddhova ahosi sakkassa puññānubhāvena. Cetiyarājā kira imasmiṃ kappe tato pubbe kenaci avuttapubbaṃ kharamusāvādaṃ abhāsi, tāvadeva virajjhitvā mahāpathaviyā vivare dine nipatitvā avīciaggijālānamindanamahosi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “cetiyarañño pāpaṃ sandhāyā”ti. Mahāpāpānīti mahantāni garutarāni pāpāni. Tathā hi vepacittino sapathakaraṇe nidassanabhāvena etāni aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatānīti.

253. "A fierce enemy" means a very hostile adversary. "You were seized" refers to being bound and seized by the divine noose. He was bound by the power of Sakka's merit. It is said that the Cetiya king, in this aeon, spoke harsh lies, never uttered before by anyone prior to that, and immediately upon doing so, having erred, he fell into a chasm in the great earth, becoming fuel for the flames of Avīci. This is said referring to "the evil of King Cetiya." "Great evils" means great and weighty evil deeds. Indeed, these are given in the commentary as examples in the case of Vepacitti's oath-making.

Nadubbhiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nadubbhiya Sutta is concluded.

8. Verocanaasurindasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Verocana Asurinda Sutta

254. Dvārapālarūpakāni [M 1.0335] viyāti dvārapālākārena katapaṭimāyo viya. Vāyametheva, na antarā saṃkocaṃ āpajjeyyāti adhippāyo. Nipphannasobhanesūti nipphannabhāvena sundaresu. Sabbe hi anipphannā atthā na sobhanti. Kiccajātāti vippakatabhāvena sañjātakiccā. Akiccajātoti asañjātakicco kiccarahito nāma natthi gamanaṭṭhitasayananisajjādivasena uppajjanakadukkhavinodanabhāvato. Saṃyogaparamātveva sambhogāti imesaṃ sattānaṃ saṃbhuñjitabbavatthūni nāma pakatiyā virodhasīlānipi asaṃyogena vā asundarānipi, tāni abhisaṅkharaṇapacanasaṃyojanaparamāni veditabbāni tathā sati sambhogārahabhāvūpagamanato. Tenāha “pārivāsikaodanādīnī”tiādi. Uṇhāpetvā paribhuñjitabbayutte paribhajjitvāti adhippāyo.

254. "Like gatekeepers" means like images made in the form of gatekeepers. The intention is: "One should strive, not undergoing contraction in between." "In their perfected beauty" means beautiful by way of being perfected. For all unperfected things do not shine. "Engaged in their duties" means having duties that have arisen through various activities. "Not engaged in duties" means there is truly no one without activity, devoid of duties, because suffering that arises is removed by means of walking, standing, lying down, sitting, and so on. "Their enjoyments are utterly bound by combination" means those things of these beings to be enjoyed are, even those naturally of conflicting nature or unattractive from non-combination, to be understood as utterly bound by adornment, cooking, and combination, since they approach a state of being worthy of enjoyment when that is so. Hence he said, "like rice for the Pārivāsika," etc. The meaning is: having heated up and fried what is suitable to be consumed.

Verocanaasurindasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verocana Asurinda Sutta is concluded.

9. Araññāyatanaisisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Araññāyatanaisi Sutta

255. Jāmātikā vuccati dhītupati, sasuro bhariyāya pitā, tasmā ime antaravattino [V 1.0294] dve janā sakkavepacittino sujāya vasena jāmātikasasurā. “Ciradikkhitāna”nti dikkhitvā pabbajitvā cirakālānaṃ vatasamādānavasena ito bāhirakānaṃ pabbajitānanti āha “cirasamādinnavatāna”nti. Ito paṭikkamāti ito yathāṭhitaṭṭhānato apehi apakkama. Na paṭikkūlasaññino guṇe gāravayogato. Devā hi yebhuyyena “mayaṃ pubbe guṇavante payirupāsitvā tesaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā puññāni upacinitvā idhūpapannā”ti guṇavantesu ādarabhāvaṃ upaṭṭhapenti.

255. "Jāmātika" is said to be the husband of a daughter, and "sasuro" is the father of a wife. Therefore, these two people, Sakka and Vepacitti, being connected through Sujā, are son-in-law and father-in-law. "Of those long initiated" means of those external ascetics who, having been initiated and having gone forth, have undertaken vows for a long time; hence it is said, "of those who have long undertaken vows." "Depart from here" means go away, depart from this place where you stand. They do not perceive their qualities as repulsive, due to their respect for virtue. For devas, for the most part, establish a feeling of reverence towards the virtuous, thinking, "Having previously attended upon virtuous ones, abided by their advice, and accumulated merit, we have been reborn here."

Araññāyatanaisisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Araññāyatanaisi Sutta is concluded.

10. Samuddakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Samuddaka Sutta

256. Cakkavāḷamahāsamuddapiṭṭhiyanti [M 1.0336] cakkavāḷapabbatapādasamantā mahāsamuddatīrapiṭṭhiyaṃ. Yatheva sinerusamīpe mahāsamuddo anupubbaninno anupubbapoṇo anupubbapabbhāro, evaṃ yebhuyyena cakkavāḷapādasamīpepi. Tenāha “rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇe vālukapuline”ti. Vuttappakārāsūti anantarasutte vuttappakārāsu. Assamapadenāti assamapadavemajjhena. Evaṃ cintayiṃsūti “yaṃ nūna maya”ntiādinā yathā pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ, evaṃ mantayiṃsu.

256. "On the shore of the great ocean of the Cakkavāḷa" means on the surface of the shore of the great ocean all around the base of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. Just as near Mount Sineru, the great ocean gradually slopes downwards, gradually deepens, and gradually descends, so it is for the most part near the base of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. Therefore, it is said, "on a sandy shore the color of a silver plate." "In the manner described" refers to the manner described in the immediately preceding sutta. "In the hermitage grounds" means in the middle of the hermitage. "They thought thus" means they conferred thus, as it comes in the Pāli, beginning with "What if we...?"

Icchitakaroti yadicchitakaraṇaṃ. Duṭṭhānanti durāsayānaṃ. Te pana duṭṭhajjhāsayā viruddhā hontīti āha “duṭṭhānaṃ viruddhāna”nti. Pavuttanti bījaṃ sandhāya vapitaṃ. Tenāha “khette patiṭṭhāpita”nti.

"Doing as one wishes" means doing what one wishes. "Of the wicked" refers to those with evil intentions. Furthermore, they are hostile due to their wicked inclinations; hence it is said, "of the wicked, of the hostile." "Sown" refers to something sown, referring to seeds. Therefore, it is said, "established in the field."

Sāyamāsabhattanti sāyaṃ asitabbabhojanaṃ. Yathāvāraṃ bhakkhitametaṃ devānaṃ viya sukhumaṃ guruvāsañca na hotīti “bhatta”nti vuttaṃ. Gelaññajātanti sañjātagelaññaṃ. Vepatīti kampati pavedhati.

"The evening meal" means food to be eaten in the evening. This, eaten according to turn, is subtle like the food of the devas and is not a heavy meal; hence, it is called "bhatta." "Illness having arisen" means illness has arisen. "He trembles" means he shakes, he quivers.

Samuddakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samuddaka Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Vatapadasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Vatapada Sutta

257. Samādātabbato [V 1.0295] vatāni, aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarasabhāvena pabbajitabbato padāni, tato eva asaṃkiṇṇabhāgāti katvā “vatakoṭṭhāsānī”ti vuttaṃ. Samattānīti puññavisesatāya pujjabhavaphalanibbattanena kittisaññānena ca samaṃ attāni samattāni. Paripuṇṇānīti akhaṇḍādibhāvena sabbaso puṇṇāni. Samādinnānīti tattha sakkaccakāritāya sammā ādinnāni. Mātulānīti pitubhaginī, na yā kāci mātulassa bhariyā kulajeṭṭhakānaṃ adhippetattā, bhariyāpi vā mātulasambandhato gahetabbā, tathā sati mahāpitubhariyādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

257. "Vows" (vatāni) are so called because they are to be undertaken, and "steps" (padāni) because they are to be practiced with a nature of non-intermixture with one another; hence, because they are unmixed portions, they are called “divisions of vows.” "Fully perfected" means that they are perfected together with oneself by the distinction of merit, by producing the result of an honorable existence, and by renown. "Complete" means entirely full due to being unbroken and so on. "Rightly undertaken" means properly adopted through careful performance. "Aunts" refers to the father’s sister, not just any wife of a maternal uncle, since the elders in the family are intended; or even the wife can be included due to her connection with the maternal uncle; in that case, the inclusion of the wives of the grandfather and so on should be seen.

Ādi-saddena [M 1.0337] jeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ saṅgaho. Apacitikārakoti tesaṃ paccuṭṭhānakaro. Yo koci dadantopi sāpekkho deti, so muttacāgo na hoti, ayaṃ pana na evanti “muttacāgo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Vissaṭṭhacāgoti nirapekkhapariccāgoti attho. Yathā pāṇātipātabahulo “lohitapāṇī”ti vuccati, tathā dānabahulo “payatapāṇī”ti vuttoti āha “deyyadhammadānatthāya sadā dhotahattho”ti. Vossaggaratoti deyyadhammassa pariccajane abhirato. Parehi yācitabbārahoti parehi yācituṃ yutto icchitassa atthassa tāvadeva vissajjanato. Dāneneva yuttoti sabbakālaṃ dāneneva yutto abhiṇhaṃ pavattamahādānattā. Dāne ca saṃvibhāge cāti parassa sampuṇṇaṃ katvā pariccajanasaṅkhāte dāne ca attanā paribhuñjitabbato saṃvibhajanasaṅkhāte saṃvibhāge ca rato abhirato.

By the word “etc.,” the inclusion of elder sisters is meant. "One who shows respect" means one who rises to greet them. Whoever gives with expectation is not a liberal giver. But this one is not like that, so it is said that he is a “liberal giver.” "One who gives freely" means one who gives without expectation. Just as one who frequently kills living beings is called “bloody-handed,” so too one who frequently gives is called “pure-handed.” Thus it is said, “always with clean hands for giving gifts.” "Delighting in relinquishing" means he delights in relinquishing gifts. "Fit to be asked by others" means he is fit to be asked by others because he immediately gives away what is desired. "Devoted to giving" means he is always devoted to giving because he constantly engages in great generosity. "In charity and in sharing" means he delights in both charity, which is defined as completely giving away possessions to others, and in sharing, which is defined as distributing what is to be enjoyed by oneself.

Vatapadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vatapada Sutta is concluded.

2. Sakkanāmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta

258. Manussabhūtoti manussesu bhūto, manussattaṃ vā patto. Āvasathanti nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ kāretvā adāsi, tasmā vāsaṃ adāsīti vāsavo. Attha-saddo idha kāraṇapariyāyoti āha “sahassampi kāraṇāna”nti. Svāyamattho heṭṭhā vibhāvitova. Vinicchinati, tasmā sahassaṃ paññāakkhīni etassāti sahassakkho. Maghaṃ vuccati dhanaṃ, taṃ pana saddhāsaṅkhātaṃ maghaṃ assa atthīti [V 1.0296] maghavā. Pure dānaṃ dadātīti purindado anunāsikalopaṃ akatvā. Puññāni kātuṃ sakkotīti sakko.

258. "Having become human" means having been born among humans, or having attained human existence. "A public rest house" means he had a dwelling place made and gave it; because he gave a dwelling (vāsaṃ adāsi), he is called "Vāsava." Here, the word "attha" is a synonym for reason, as it is said, "even a thousand reasons." This meaning has already been explained below. He discerns; therefore he has a thousand eyes of wisdom, hence he is called "Sahassakkha." "Magha" is called wealth; he possesses the wealth known as faith, thus he is "Maghavā." He gives gifts in the past (pure), hence "Purindada" (without the elision of the nasal). He is capable (sakkoti) of performing meritorious deeds, hence "Sakko."

Sakkanāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta is concluded.

3. Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta

259. Soti sakko devarājā. Bahuvacane vattabbe ekavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Vuccatīti vacanaṃ, attho. Tasmā bahuvacaneti bahumhi attheti attho[M 1.0338]. Yathā paṭipajjanto anukkamena te dhamme samādiyitvā sakko sakkattaṃ ajjhagā, taṃ paṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ “sakko kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Anantareti sakkabhāvassa atītānantare attabhāve. Taṃ sabbanti sakkassa maghamāṇavakāle sammāpaṭipattiṃ, tāya sakkabhāvūpagamanañcāti taṃ sabbaṃ. Vutto, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabboti adhippāyo.

259. So means Sakka, king of the devas. When it should be spoken in the plural, the singular is spoken. 'Vuccati' means the expression, the meaning. Therefore, 'in the plural' means 'in the sense of many.' To show the practice by which, having gradually undertaken those qualities, Sakka attained the state of Sakka, it is said, "Sakka, indeed," and so on. 'Immediately after' means in the existence immediately preceding the state of Sakka. 'All that' means the right practice of Sakka in the time of the young man Magha, and by that, the attainment of the state of Sakka—all that. It has been said; therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained there—this is the intention.

Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta is concluded.

4. Daliddasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Dalidda Sutta

260. Manussadaliddoti manussesu duggato. Manussakāruññatanti manussesu paramanihīnataṃ. Manussakapaṇoti manussesu vā paramanihīno. Tasmiṃ ṭhāneti tassa devaputtassa tasmiṃ uppajjanaṭṭhāne. Lāmakato cintentīti tassa purimavatthuṃ nissāya hīnato cintenti. Kathentīti tameva paresaṃ kathenti. Vitthārentīti vuttamatthaṃ vitthārikaṃ karonti. Sabbadā paricchijja parivārasampanno hutvā aḍḍhaṭṭharatane hatthikkhandhe mahaccarājānubhāvena nisinnattā janakāyena samullokiyamāno. Avalambantīti olambanti. Vandanamattaṃ vā nāhosi, aññadatthu paccekabuddhato attano samānādarakiriyaṃ paccāsīsati. Tena vuttaṃ “so”tiādi. Kvāyanti ko ayanti byāpannavasena vadati. Kāḷarattehi suttehi sibbitattā vaṇṇavikāraṃ disvā “kuṭṭhicīvarāni pāruto”ti āha. Mahāniraye nibbattitvā mahādukkhaṃ paccanubhoti. Tadanurūpapāpakammassa vipākāvasesena laddhokāsena rājagahe…pe… paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Kāmañca ettha paṭisandhiggahaṇaṃ kusalakammeneva, tassa pana akusalakammassa vipākino balavabhāvato vuttaṃ “vipākāvasesenā”ti. Tenāha “gahitakālato…pe… nikkhanto”ti. Bhikkhāya carituṃ samatthakālato paṭṭhāya rogassa balavatāya maṃsāni…pe… patanti. Ñāṇaṃ pesetvāti vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā bhāvanāñāṇaṃ nibbānaṃ paṭipesetvā pavattetvā. Indriyānaṃ paripakkattā [V 1.0297] satthu desanāvilāsena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito. Cumbaṭanti pādacumbaṭaṃ. Kuṭṭhino hi sakalapādatalaṃ mā rujīti cumbaṭaṃ [M 1.0339] katvā taṃ pādatale bandhitvā gacchanti, mattikapātiṃ bhinditvā viya tathā nihīnamanussattabhāvato cavitvā suvaṇṇapātiṃ paṭilabhanto viya devattabhāvaṃ gaṇhanto cuticittato dutiyacittavāre ādānacittakkhaṇe devaloke nibbatto.

260. "Manussadaliddo" means a destitute person among humans. "Manussakāruññata" means the state of utter wretchedness among humans. "Manussakapaṇo" means exceedingly wretched among humans. "Tasmiṃ ṭhāne" refers to that devaputta’s place of birth. "Lāmakato cintenti" means they think of him as lowly, based on his former condition. "Kathenti" means they relate that to others. "Vitthārenti" means they expand upon what was stated. Being always distinguished by a complete retinue, seated on the neck of an elephant of seven and a half cubits with the great power of a king, he was looked up at by the assembly of people. "Avalambanti" means they hang down. There was not even a mere salutation; on the contrary, he expected from the Paccekabuddha an action of equal respect to himself. Therefore, it is said, "so," and so on. "Kvāyanti" means he speaks with ill will, saying, "Who is this?" Seeing the discoloration from being stitched with black and red threads, he said, "Clothed in a leper's rags." Having been reborn in the great hell, he experienced great suffering. Through an opportunity afforded by the remaining result of that evil kamma, he took rebirth in Rājagaha... And although here the taking of rebirth-linking was by wholesome kamma, because of the powerful nature of that ripening unwholesome kamma, it is said "by the remaining result." Therefore, he said, "from the time he was taken... he departed." From the time he was able to go for alms, due to the severity of the disease, his flesh... fell off. "Ñāṇaṃ pesetvā" means having directed his knowledge, that is, having sent forth and caused to proceed the knowledge of development in the sequence of insight towards Nibbāna. Due to the maturity of his faculties, through the grace of the Teacher's teaching, he was established in the fruition of stream-entry. "Cumbaṭa" means a foot-pad. For lepers, lest the entire sole of their foot should hurt, make a pad, bind it to the sole of the foot, and go. Just as one might break an earthen bowl and obtain a golden one, so too, having passed away from that lowly human existence and taking up a divine existence, he was reborn in the deva world at the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness, which is the second thought-moment after the death-consciousness.

Maggenāgatāti maggādhigamanena āgatā uppannā. Ariyakantasīlanti ariyānaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ manoramaṃ sīladhammaṃ.
